## Preface to the First Edition (1781)

In one domain of its knowledge, human reason faces questions it cannot dismiss, because they arise from its own nature, and yet cannot answer, because they exceed every power of the mind.

Reason falls into this predicament through no fault of its own. It begins with principles it cannot do without in the field of experience, principles whose truth and adequacy experience itself confirms. Guided by them, and obeying the laws of its own nature, it climbs toward ever higher and more remote conditions. It soon discovers, however, that along this path its work must always remain unfinished, because new questions never stop arising. It is therefore driven to adopt principles that reach beyond the realm of experience altogether, even though ordinary common sense accepts them without suspicion. At that point reason falls into confusion and contradiction. It suspects that hidden errors lie somewhere beneath its reasoning, but it cannot locate them, because the principles it now relies on have passed beyond the limits of experience and can no longer be tested against it. The battlefield of these endless disputes is called metaphysics.

There was a time when metaphysics was hailed as the queen of all the sciences, and if we judge by aspiration rather than achievement, the supreme importance of her subject certainly entitles her to that honor. Today, however, the fashion is to heap contempt and scorn upon her, and the aged matron mourns, abandoned and forsaken, like Hecuba, the queen of Troy whose lament after the fall of her city Ovid records in the *Metamorphoses*: *Modo maxima rerum, tot generis natisque potens... nunc trahor exul, inops*. "Lately the greatest of all, powerful in so many sons-in-law and children... now I am dragged away, an exile and destitute."

At first her rule, under the administration of the dogmatists, was an absolute despotism. But because her laws still bore the marks of an ancient barbarism, her empire gradually disintegrated, and civil wars brought on a reign of anarchy. Meanwhile the skeptics, like nomadic tribes who despise any permanent dwelling or settled way of life, attacked from time to time those who had organized themselves into civil communities. Fortunately their numbers were small, so they could not entirely halt the labors of those who persisted in raising new structures, though on no settled or uniform plan. In more recent times it seemed for a moment that these disputes might at last be ended, and the legitimacy of her claims finally decided, by a kind of physiology of the human understanding, the one offered by the celebrated Locke. According to this account, the so-called queen could trace her descent to nothing higher than common experience, a lineage that ought to have cast suspicion on her pretensions. But because this genealogy turned out to be false, she went on asserting her claims to sovereignty. Metaphysics therefore slid back into the antiquated and decaying constitution of dogmatism, and once again exposed itself to the very contempt from which these efforts had tried to rescue it. Now that every method, so the general opinion holds, has been tried in vain, nothing reigns but weariness and complete indifference. This indifference is the mother of chaos and night in the world of learning, yet it is also the source, or at least the prelude, of the renewal and restoration of a science that misguided effort has left confused, obscure, and neglected.

It is futile, after all, to profess indifference toward inquiries whose object can never be a matter of indifference to humanity. Moreover, these self-declared indifferentists, however much they try to disguise themselves by adopting a popular style or by reworking the vocabulary of the schools, inevitably lapse into the very metaphysical assertions and propositions they claim to despise. Still, this indifference, which has spread through the world of learning and attaches to precisely the kind of knowledge we would wish to see perish last of all, is a phenomenon that deserves our attention and reflection. It is plainly the product not of frivolity but of the matured judgment of the age. We often hear complaints about the shallowness of our times and the decline of profound learning. Yet I do not believe that the sciences resting on secure foundations, such as mathematics and natural science, deserve this reproach in the slightest. On the contrary, they maintain their ancient reputation, and natural science in fact far surpasses it. The same would be true of the other branches of knowledge if only their principles were firmly established. Until they are, indifference, doubt, and finally severe criticism are signs not of shallowness but of a deep habit of thought. Ours is the age of criticism, and everything must submit to it. Many regard the sanctity of religion and the majesty of law as grounds for exemption from this tribunal. But if they claim exemption, they rightly arouse suspicion, and they forfeit the sincere respect that reason grants only to what has withstood free and public examination. This matured judgment of the age refuses to be entertained any longer with illusory knowledge. It amounts to a summons to reason to take up once more the most demanding of all its tasks, that of knowing itself, and to establish a tribunal that will uphold its legitimate claims while dismissing every groundless assumption and pretension, not by arbitrary decree but according to reason's own eternal and unchangeable laws. This tribunal is nothing other than the critique of pure reason itself.

By this I do not mean a critique of books and systems, but a critique of the faculty of reason in general, with respect to all the knowledge it strives to reach independently of experience. The task is therefore to decide whether metaphysics is possible or impossible at all, and to determine its sources as well as its extent and limits, all on the basis of principles.

I have set out on this path, the only one that remains, and I flatter myself that by following it I have discovered the cause of all the errors that have so far set reason at odds with itself whenever it operates beyond experience, and with that cause, the means of removing them. I have not evaded reason's questions by pleading the weakness and limitations of the human mind. On the contrary, I have examined them fully according to principles, and after discovering the source of the doubts and contradictions into which reason had fallen, I have resolved them to its complete satisfaction. These questions have not, admittedly, been answered in the way dogmatism, with its idle fancies and cravings, had hoped, for dogmatism could be satisfied only by feats of magic, and of magic I know nothing. But such feats lie beyond the reach of our mental powers in any case, and it was the duty of philosophy to dispel the illusions that sprang from misunderstanding, however many cherished hopes and prized expectations its explanations might destroy. My chief aim in this work has been thoroughness, and I venture to say that there is not a single metaphysical problem that does not find its solution here, or at least the key to its solution. Pure reason is a perfect unity. If its principle proved inadequate to resolve even one of the questions that reason's own nature poses, we would have to reject it, since we could then no longer be fully confident of its adequacy for any of the others.

As I say this, I fancy I can see on the reader's face a look of displeasure mixed with contempt at claims that sound so boastful and extravagant. Yet they are incomparably more modest than those made by the most ordinary author of the most ordinary philosophical program, in which the dogmatist undertakes to prove the simple nature of the soul or the necessity of a first being. Such a dogmatist promises to extend human knowledge beyond the limits of all possible experience, whereas I freely confess that this lies entirely beyond my power. Instead of any such undertaking, I confine myself to examining reason alone and its pure thinking, and I need not search far to find the whole of its knowledge, because that knowledge resides within my own mind. Ordinary logic, moreover, already provides a complete and systematic catalog of all of reason's simple operations. My task is to determine how far reason can proceed when it is deprived of all the material and assistance that experience supplies.

So much for the completeness and thoroughness required to carry out the present task. The goals set before us are not chosen arbitrarily. They are imposed on us by the nature of knowledge itself.

These remarks concern the substance of our critical inquiry. As for its form, anyone who undertakes so difficult a task as a critique of pure reason must satisfy two indispensable conditions: certainty and clarity.

With respect to certainty, I am fully convinced that in this sphere of thought mere opinion is entirely inadmissible, and that anything bearing even the faintest resemblance to a hypothesis must be ruled out as worthless. Every piece of knowledge that is to be established a priori, independently of experience, must by its very nature be held as absolutely necessary. This holds all the more for an attempt to determine the whole of pure a priori knowledge, an attempt meant to supply the standard, and therefore the model, of all apodictic certainty, the strictly necessary certainty proper to philosophy.

Whether I have achieved what I set out to do is for the reader to decide. An author's business is only to present grounds and reasons, not to dictate what effect they should have on the minds of those who judge him. Still, so that nothing he has said may become the innocent cause of doubt in their minds, or weaken the force his arguments might otherwise carry, he may be permitted to point out those passages that could give rise to mistrust or difficulty, even though they do not touch the main purpose of the work. He does so only to clear away any doubts that might affect the reader's judgment of the work as a whole and of its ultimate aim.

I know of no investigations more necessary for a full understanding of the faculty we call the understanding, and at the same time for fixing the rules and limits of its use, than those I have undertaken in the second chapter of the Transcendental Analytic, under the title "Deduction of the Pure Concepts of the Understanding." They have also cost me by far the greatest effort, effort that I hope will not go unrewarded. This inquiry, which reaches fairly deep, has two sides. The first concerns the objects of the pure understanding. Its purpose is to demonstrate and make intelligible the objective validity of the understanding's a priori concepts, and for that reason it is an essential part of the Critique. The second side examines the pure understanding itself, its possibility and the cognitive powers on which it rests, and so considers it from a subjective point of view. Although this second exposition is of great importance, it does not belong essentially to the main purpose of the work, because the central question is what, and how much, understanding and reason can know apart from all experience, not how the faculty of thought is itself possible. Because this latter question amounts to a search for the cause of a given effect, it carries some appearance of a hypothesis, although, as I shall show elsewhere, this is not actually the case. It might therefore seem that here I have permitted myself to put forward a mere opinion, and that the reader is free to hold a different one. I would remind him, however, that even if my subjective deduction fails to produce in him the full conviction I intended, the objective deduction, which is the real concern of this work, retains its full force.

With respect to clarity, the reader is entitled to demand two kinds. The first is discursive or logical clarity, which rests on concepts. The second is intuitive or aesthetic clarity, which rests on intuitions, that is, on examples and other concrete illustrations. I have done what I could to achieve the first kind. It was essential to my purpose, and for that very reason it became the incidental cause of my failure to satisfy the second requirement fully. Throughout the writing of this work I was almost constantly undecided about how to handle this question. Examples and illustrations always struck me as necessary, and in my first draft of the Critique they fell naturally into place. But I soon grasped the scale of my task and the sheer number of problems I would have to address, and since I could see that this critical investigation would be far from short even if presented in the driest scholastic manner, I judged it unwise to swell it further with examples and explanations that are needed only for a popular audience. I was confirmed in this decision by several further considerations: this work is not intended for popular use; those devoted to learning do not need such aids, welcome as they always are; and the aids themselves would have seriously obstructed my present purpose. The Abbé Terrasson observes, quite rightly, that if we measure the length of a book not by its number of pages but by the time it takes us to master it, we can say of many a book that it would be much shorter if it were not so short. By the same token, when it comes to the intelligibility of a system of speculative knowledge united under a single principle, we may say with equal justice that many a book would have been much clearer if it had not tried so hard to be clear. Explanations, examples, and other aids to understanding help us grasp the parts, but they scatter the reader's attention, divide his mental energy, and prevent him from forming a clear conception of the whole. He cannot reach a survey of the system quickly enough, and the coloring and ornament laid over it keep him from seeing its structure and organization, which matter most to him when he comes to judge its unity and soundness.

The reader should have no small incentive to collaborate with the present author, if he means to build a complete and durable edifice of metaphysics according to the plan now laid before him. Metaphysics, as presented here, is the only science that can be brought to completion, and with modest effort, provided that effort is united, it can be completed in a short time, leaving future generations nothing to do but present it for teaching and apply it. For this science is nothing more than an inventory, systematically arranged, of everything we possess through pure reason. Nothing can escape our notice, because whatever reason produces entirely out of itself cannot remain hidden, but must be brought to light by reason itself as soon as we have discovered the common principle underlying it. The perfect unity of this kind of knowledge, which derives from pure concepts alone and is untouched by anything empirical or by any particular intuition that would lead to a determinate experience, makes such completeness not only possible but necessary. The words of the Roman satirist Persius apply here: *Tecum habita, et noris quam sit tibi curta supellex*. "Live within your own house, and you will learn how meager your furnishings are."

I hope to publish such a system of pure speculative reason under the title *Metaphysics of Nature*, as distinct from a metaphysics of morals. It would be less than half as long as the present Critique but far richer in content. The Critique has a different task: to uncover the sources of this knowledge and the conditions of its possibility, and to clear and level ground fit for the structure of science. In the present work I ask of the reader the patience and impartiality of a judge; in the other, the goodwill and assistance of a fellow worker. However complete the Critique's list of principles for that system may be, the system itself, to be correct, must leave out none of the derived concepts. These cannot be laid out a priori in advance but must be discovered one by one. And while the Critique exhausts the synthesis of concepts, the proposed work must do the same for their analysis. But that will be more a pleasure than a labor.

## Preface to the Second Edition (1787)

Whether our treatment of the knowledge that falls within the province of pure reason is advancing with the steady certainty that marks the progress of a science is a question we can settle without difficulty. If we find that those engaged in metaphysical inquiry cannot agree on the method they ought to follow; if we find that, after the most elaborate preparations, they are invariably brought to a halt before reaching their goal and forced to retrace their steps and strike out along new paths, then we may be quite sure that they are far from having attained the certainty of scientific progress. They might more accurately be described as groping in the dark. Under such conditions we will render reason an important service if we can simply point out the path it must travel to arrive at any results at all, even if this means abandoning many of the aims that were set for it without due reflection.

That logic has followed this sure course from the earliest times is evident from the fact that, since Aristotle, it has been unable to advance a single step, and so, to all appearances, has reached completion. Some modern writers have thought to enlarge its domain by introducing psychological discussions of the mental faculties, such as imagination and wit; metaphysical discussions of the origin of knowledge and of the different kinds of certainty that correspond to different kinds of objects, as in idealism, skepticism, and the like; or anthropological discussions of prejudices, their causes, and their remedies. These attempts only reveal their authors' ignorance of the peculiar nature of logic. We do not enlarge the sciences but disfigure them when we lose sight of their respective boundaries and allow them to run into one another. Logic, by contrast, is enclosed within limits that can be defined with perfect clarity. It is a science whose sole object is to set out and prove the formal laws of all thought, whether that thought is *a priori* or empirical, whatever its origin or its object, and whatever obstacles, natural or accidental, it meets in the human mind.

The early success of logic must be credited entirely to the narrowness of its field. Here one may, and indeed must, set aside all the objects of knowledge together with their distinguishing features, so that the understanding has nothing to deal with but itself and its own forms. It is obviously a far harder task for reason to enter upon the sure path of science when it must deal not only with itself but with objects outside itself. Logic, therefore, is properly only a propaedeutic, a preparatory discipline that forms, as it were, the vestibule of the sciences. It is necessary if we are to judge correctly about the various branches of knowledge, but real, substantive knowledge must be sought only in the sciences properly so called, that is, in the objective sciences.

If these sciences can be called rational at all, they must contain elements of *a priori* knowledge, and such knowledge can stand in a twofold relation to its object. It may have to determine the concept of the object, which must be supplied from elsewhere, or it may have to make the object real. The first is theoretical rational knowledge; the second is practical. In both, the pure or *a priori* element must be treated first and carefully distinguished from whatever is supplied from other sources. Any other method can lead only to hopeless confusion.

Mathematics and physics are the two theoretical sciences that must determine their objects *a priori*. Mathematics does so purely; physics does so only in part, and depends as well on other sources of knowledge.

As far back as history allows us to see, mathematics had already entered upon the sure course of science among that remarkable people, the Greeks. Yet we should not suppose that it was as easy for this science to find, or rather to build for itself, that royal road as it was for logic, in which reason has only itself to deal with. On the contrary, I believe that mathematics must long have remained, chiefly among the Egyptians, at the stage of blindly groping after its true aims and purpose, and that it was transformed by the happy inspiration of a single man, who marked out and fixed for all time the path the science must follow, a path that permits indefinite advance. The history of this intellectual revolution, far more important in its consequences than the discovery of the sea route around the celebrated Cape of Good Hope, has not come down to us, and neither has the name of its author. Diogenes Laertius, however, names the supposed discoverer of some of the simplest elements of geometrical demonstration, elements that common opinion holds do not even need proof. In doing so he shows that the change brought about by the first glimpse of this new path must have struck the mathematicians of that age as supremely important, which is why it was preserved from oblivion. A new light must have dawned on the first man, Thales or whatever his name may have been, who demonstrated the properties of the isosceles triangle. He discovered that it was not enough to contemplate the figure as it lay before his eyes, or the concept of it as it existed in his mind, and to try in that way to learn its properties. He had instead to bring those properties forth, so to speak, through a deliberate construction carried out *a priori*. And he saw that if he was to arrive at *a priori* knowledge with certainty, he must attribute to the object no properties other than those that followed necessarily from what he himself had placed in it in accordance with his concept.

A much longer time passed before physics found the highway of science. It is only about a century and a half since the wise Bacon gave a new direction to the study of nature, or rather, since others were already on the right track, gave fresh vigor to the pursuit of that new direction. Here too, as with mathematics, we find evidence of a swift intellectual revolution. In the remarks that follow I shall confine myself to the empirical side of natural science. Nor do I mean to trace the history of the experimental method with precision; its first steps are, in any case, somewhat obscure.

When Galileo rolled balls of a known weight down an inclined plane; when Torricelli made the air support a weight that he had calculated in advance to equal that of a given column of water; or when Stahl, at a later date, turned metals into calx, the earthy powder left behind when a metal is roasted, and turned the calx back into metal by adding and removing certain elements, a light broke upon every student of nature. They learned that reason perceives only what it produces according to its own design. It must not be content to be led by nature as a child is led by the leading-strings, the cords by which children were once steadied as they learned to walk. It must go forward with principles of judgment based on fixed laws and compel nature to answer its questions. Chance observations, made according to no plan laid down in advance, can never be united under a necessary law, and a necessary law is exactly what reason seeks and requires. Only the principles of reason can give agreeing phenomena the standing of laws, and only when experiment is guided by those principles does it have any real use. Reason must approach nature in order to learn from it, but not in the manner of a pupil who listens to whatever his teacher chooses to say. It must come as a judge who compels the witnesses to answer the questions he himself sees fit to put to them. To this single idea we must credit the revolution by which natural science, after groping in the dark for so many centuries, was at last set on the path of sure progress.

We come now to metaphysics, a purely speculative science that stands entirely apart and is wholly independent of the lessons of experience. It deals with concepts alone, not, as mathematics does, with concepts applied to intuition, and in it reason is taught by no one but itself. It is the oldest of the sciences, and it would survive even if all the others were swallowed up in the abyss of a barbarism that destroyed everything. Yet it has not had the good fortune to find the sure method of science. This becomes plain when we apply the tests proposed at the outset. We find that reason constantly comes to a halt when it tries to grasp *a priori* even those laws that the most ordinary experience confirms. We find it forced, in countless cases, to retrace its steps and abandon a path because the path does not lead where it wanted to go. And we find that those engaged in metaphysics are far from agreeing among themselves. On the contrary, the science seems to offer an arena built expressly for displays of skill and trials of strength in mock combat, a field on which no contestant has ever gained an inch of ground, or at least on which no victory has ever been secured by lasting possession.

This leads us to ask why the sure path of science has not yet been found in metaphysics. Are we to suppose that it cannot be found? Why, then, should nature have afflicted our reason with a restless longing for it, as though it were among our weightiest concerns? Worse still, how little reason we would have to trust our reason if it deserted us on the very question about which we most want to know the truth, and, more than that, lured us on in pursuit of empty phantoms only to betray us in the end. Or, if the path has merely been missed until now, what signs do we have to guide a fresh inquiry and give us hope of greater success than our predecessors enjoyed?

The examples of mathematics and natural science, which, as we have seen, reached their present state through a sudden revolution, seem to me remarkable enough to direct our attention to the essential features of the change that served them so well, and to encourage us to try imitating them, so far as the analogy between them and metaphysics, as fellow rational sciences, allows. Until now it has been assumed that all our knowledge must conform to objects. But every attempt to establish something about those objects *a priori*, through concepts, and so to extend our knowledge, has come to nothing under this assumption. Let us therefore try the experiment of seeing whether we fare better in metaphysics if we assume that objects must conform to our knowledge. This assumption at least agrees better with the possibility of what we are seeking, namely a knowledge of objects *a priori*, a knowledge that determines something about objects before they are given to us. We propose to do exactly what Copernicus did in trying to explain the movements of the heavens. Finding that he could make no headway on the assumption that all the heavenly bodies revolved around the observer, he reversed the procedure and tried the experiment of supposing that the observer revolved while the stars stood still. We can try the same experiment with the intuition of objects. If intuition must conform to the nature of objects, I do not see how we could know anything about them *a priori*. If, on the other hand, the object conforms to the nature of our faculty of intuition, I can readily conceive how such *a priori* knowledge is possible. But I cannot stop at mere intuitions. If they are to become knowledge, I must refer them, as representations, to something as their object, and determine that object by means of them. Here again two courses lie open. I may assume, first, that the concepts by which I carry out this determination conform to the object, and in that case I am left in the same perplexity as before. Or I may assume, second, that the objects, or what amounts to the same thing, experience, in which alone they are known as given objects, conform to my concepts, and then I see at once how to proceed. For experience is itself a kind of knowledge that requires understanding, and before any objects are given to me, that is, *a priori*, I must presuppose within myself rules of the understanding expressed in *a priori* concepts. All objects of experience must necessarily conform to these concepts. There are, however, objects that reason thinks, and thinks necessarily, but that cannot be given in experience, or at least cannot be given in the way reason thinks them. The attempt to think such objects will later provide an excellent test of the new method of thought we have adopted, a method founded on the principle that we know *a priori* in things only what we ourselves put into them.

This method, which we have borrowed from the student of nature, consists in looking for the elements of pure reason in what can be confirmed or refuted by experiment. But the propositions of pure reason, especially those that venture beyond the limits of possible experience, do not allow us to experiment with their objects as natural science does. With regard to the concepts and principles we assume *a priori*, then, our only course is to arrange matters so that the same objects can be viewed from two different sides. We must consider one and the same concept, on the one hand, in relation to experience, as an object of the senses and the understanding, and on the other hand in relation to reason alone, cut off from experience and passing beyond its limits, as an object of mere thought. If we then find that viewing things from this double standpoint brings the result into agreement with the principle of pure reason, while viewing them from a single standpoint entangles reason in contradiction with itself, the experiment will have shown that the distinction is correct.

The experiment succeeds as well as we could wish, and it promises metaphysics the sure course of science in its first part, the part concerned with *a priori* concepts whose corresponding objects can be given in experience. By this new method we can fully explain how *a priori* knowledge is possible, and, what is more, give satisfactory proofs of the laws that lie *a priori* at the foundation of nature, understood as the sum of all objects of experience. Under the procedure followed until now, neither was possible. But this deduction of our capacity for *a priori* knowledge, in the first part of metaphysics, yields a surprising result, one that appears to run directly counter to the great aim of metaphysics as pursued in its second part. We conclude that our faculty of knowledge can never pass beyond the limits of possible experience, and yet doing so is precisely the most essential concern of this science. Our assessment of rational *a priori* knowledge is that it reaches only appearances, and that things in themselves, though they are indeed real, lie beyond its reach. Here we have a way of testing whether this assessment is correct. What necessarily drives us beyond the limits of experience and of all appearances is the unconditioned, which reason demands in things as they are in themselves in order to complete the series of conditions. Suppose it turns out that if we assume our knowledge conforms to its objects as things in themselves, the unconditioned cannot be thought without contradiction; and that if we assume instead that our representation of things as they are given to us does not conform to them as they are in themselves, but that these objects, as appearances, conform to our way of representing, the contradiction disappears. We will then be convinced of the truth of what we first assumed only as an experiment, and may regard it as established that the unconditioned is not to be found in things as we know them, as they are given to us, but in things as they are in themselves, beyond the range of our knowledge.

This experiment of pure reason closely resembles the one chemists call the experiment of reduction, or more commonly the synthetic process. The metaphysician's analysis separates pure *a priori* knowledge into two dissimilar elements: the knowledge of things as appearances and the knowledge of things in themselves. Dialectic then recombines them, bringing them into harmony with the necessary rational idea of the unconditioned, and finds that this harmony can never be achieved except by way of that distinction, which must therefore be the correct one.

Having denied speculative reason any power to advance in the realm of the supersensible, we must still consider whether practical knowledge may not supply data by which we could determine the transcendent rational concept of the unconditioned, and so pass beyond the limits of all possible experience, from a practical standpoint, in the way metaphysics has always wished. Speculative reason has at least made room for such an extension of our knowledge. Though it must leave that space empty, it does not deprive us of the freedom to fill it, if we can, with practical data. Indeed, it even invites us to try.

In the same way, the central laws governing the motions of the heavenly bodies established as certain what Copernicus had at first assumed only as a hypothesis, and at the same time brought to light the invisible force, Newtonian attraction, which holds the universe together. That force would have remained undiscovered forever had Copernicus not ventured on an experiment that contradicted the evidence of the senses yet was correct: he looked for the observed motions not in the heavenly bodies but in the spectator. In this Preface I present the new method of metaphysics as a hypothesis, only to make visible the first attempts at such a change of method, which are always hypothetical. In the Critique itself, however, the change will be demonstrated not hypothetically but apodictically, as a matter of strict necessity, from the nature of our representations of space and time and from the elementary concepts of the understanding.

The purpose of the Critique of Pure Speculative Reason is to carry out a complete revolution in the procedure of metaphysics, following the example of the geometers and the natural scientists. It is a treatise on method, not a system of the science itself. At the same time, it marks out both the outer boundaries of that science and its entire inner structure. Pure speculative reason has this peculiarity: by distinguishing the different ways in which it selects its objects of thought, it can measure the extent of its own capacities, and it can even list completely every possible way of setting problems for itself. In doing so it sketches the whole system of metaphysics. This is possible for two reasons. First, in a priori cognition nothing may be attributed to objects except what the thinking subject draws from itself. Second, with respect to its principles of cognition, pure reason is a wholly distinct and self-sufficient unity. In this unity, as in an organized body, every member exists for the sake of all the others and all for the sake of each, so that no principle can safely be taken in any one relation unless it is also examined in its relation to the entire use of pure reason. Metaphysics therefore enjoys an advantage that falls to no other science dealing with objects. Once this critique has set it on the secure path of a science, it can take in the whole field of its cognitions, complete its work, and leave that work to posterity as a capital to which nothing can ever be added. Metaphysics deals only with principles and with the limits of their use, limits those principles themselves determine. As the fundamental science, it is therefore obliged to reach this completeness, and the old maxim may justly be applied to it: *Nil actum reputans, si quid superesset agendum*, "count nothing done while anything remains to be done."

It will be asked what kind of treasure we mean to leave to posterity. What is the real value of this system of metaphysics, purified by criticism and thereby brought to a permanent condition? A quick look at the present work may suggest that its use is merely *negative*: it only warns us never to venture with speculative reason beyond the limits of experience. That is in fact its first use. But this use becomes *positive* once we see that the principles by which speculative reason tries to exceed its limits do not in fact extend the use of reason. They *narrow* it, because they threaten to stretch the limits of sensibility, which is the proper domain of those principles, over the entire realm of thought, and so to crowd out the pure, practical use of reason. Insofar as this critique confines speculative reason within its proper bounds, its work is only negative. Insofar as it thereby removes an obstacle that hinders the practical use of reason, and even threatens to destroy it, its value is positive and very great. To grant this, we need only be persuaded that there is an absolutely necessary use of pure reason, the moral use. In that use reason unavoidably goes beyond the limits of sensibility without any help from speculation, and it needs only to be protected against a speculation that would set it in contradiction with itself. Denying that this critique does us positive service would be as absurd as claiming that the police, the whole system of public order within a state, confer no positive benefit, merely because their chief business is to prevent the violence that citizens have reason to fear from one another, so that each may pursue his calling in peace and security.

The analytical part of the Critique proves the following. Space and time are only forms of sensible intuition and are therefore only conditions of the existence of things as appearances. We have no concepts of the understanding, and therefore no elements for the cognition of things, except insofar as an intuition corresponding to those concepts can be given. Consequently we can have no cognition of any object as a thing in itself, but only as an object of sensible intuition, that is, as an appearance. From this it follows necessarily that all possible speculative cognition is limited to objects of experience alone. Even so, we must keep firmly in mind that although we give up the power to *cognize* objects as things in themselves, we keep the power to *think* them as such. Otherwise we would have to say that there is an appearance without anything that appears, which is absurd.

Now suppose for a moment that we had not undertaken this critique and so had not drawn the necessary distinction between things as objects of experience and the same things as they are in themselves. The principle of causality, and with it the mechanism of nature that causality determines, would then hold without exception for all things as efficient causes. In that case I could not say of one and the same being, the human soul for instance, that its will is free and yet also subject to natural necessity, that is, *not* free, without falling into open contradiction. In both statements I would be taking the soul *in one and the same sense*, as a thing in general, a thing in itself, and without a prior critique I could not have taken it in any other way. Now suppose instead that we *have* undertaken this critique and have learned that an object can be taken *in two senses*: first as an appearance, and second as a thing in itself. Suppose too that the deduction of the concepts of the understanding has shown that the principle of causality applies only to things in the first sense. Then there is no contradiction in saying that the will, in the domain of appearances, that is, in visible action, necessarily obeys the law of nature and in that respect is *not free*, while the same will, as belonging to a thing in itself, is not subject to that law and is therefore *free*.

I admit that I cannot *cognize* my soul as a thing in itself, whether through speculative reason or, still less, through empirical observation. So I cannot cognize freedom as a property of a being to which I ascribe effects in the world of the senses. To do so I would have to cognize that being as existing and yet not existing in time, and since I can support that concept with no intuition at all, such cognition is impossible. But although I cannot cognize freedom, I can quite well *think* it. My representation of freedom at least contains no contradiction, provided we keep in mind the critical distinction between the two modes of representation, the sensible and the intellectual, together with the resulting limitation on the pure concepts of the understanding and on the principles derived from them.

Now suppose that morality necessarily presupposed freedom, in the strictest sense, as a property of our will. Suppose that reason contained certain original practical principles, given a priori, that would be utterly impossible without this presupposition. And suppose that speculative reason had proved that freedom cannot be thought at all. Then the moral presupposition would have to give way to the speculative claim, whose opposite contains an evident contradiction, and freedom, and morality with it, would have to yield to the *mechanism of nature*. Denying morality involves no contradiction unless freedom is presupposed. But morality does not need a speculative cognition of freedom. It is enough that I can think freedom, that its concept contains no contradiction, and that it does not interfere with the mechanism of nature. Even this modest requirement we could not meet had we not learned the twofold sense in which things can be taken, and only in this way are the doctrine of morality and the doctrine of nature each kept within their proper limits. We owe this result to a critique that warns us of our unavoidable ignorance of things in themselves and limits all that we can *theoretically cognize* to mere appearances.

To cognize an object, I must be able to prove that it is possible, either from its actuality as experience attests it, or a priori, through reason. But I can think whatever I please, provided only that I do not contradict myself, that is, provided my concept is a possible thought, even if I cannot vouch that any corresponding object exists within the sum of all possibilities. Something more is needed before I can ascribe objective validity to such a concept, meaning real possibility, as distinct from the merely logical kind. That additional requirement, however, need not be met from theoretical sources of cognition alone. It may be met from practical ones.

The positive value of the critical principles of pure reason could be shown in the same way with respect to the concept of *God* and of the *simple nature of the soul*, but I will not dwell on this. I cannot even *assume* God, freedom, and immortality, as the practical interests of morality require me to, unless I first take away speculative reason's claim to transcendent insight. To reach such insight, speculative reason must use principles that in fact extend only to objects of possible experience. When these principles are nevertheless applied to what lies beyond experience, they always turn it into an appearance, and so they make any practical extension of pure reason impossible. I therefore had to *deny knowledge* in order to make room for *faith*. The dogmatism of metaphysics, the assumption that one can make progress in metaphysics without first criticizing reason, is the true source of all the unbelief that opposes morality, and that unbelief is always dogmatic itself.

It may be no very hard task to leave posterity a system of metaphysics built according to the Critique of Pure Reason, but the value of such a legacy should not be underrated. It will do reason a great service by replacing the aimless groping after results, without guiding principles, that has so far marked metaphysical study with the certainty of scientific method. It will do a great service to the inquiring minds of the young, by leading students to spend their powers on genuine science instead of wasting them, as they do now, on speculations that can never lead anywhere or on idle efforts to invent new ideas and opinions. Above all, it will be of immeasurable benefit to morality and religion, because it will show that every objection raised against them can be silenced for good by the *Socratic method*, that is, by proving the ignorance of the objector. The world has never been without some system of metaphysics, and it surely never will be. The highest and most serious task of philosophy is therefore to make metaphysics harmless by closing off the sources of its errors.

This important change in the field of the sciences means that speculative reason must give up possessions it only imagined it had. Yet the change does no harm at all to the general interests of humanity, and the advantages the world has drawn from the teachings of pure reason remain intact. The loss falls entirely on the *monopoly of the schools*. It does not touch the *interests of humanity* in the slightest. I appeal to the most stubborn dogmatist. Consider the proof that the soul continues to exist after death because its substance is simple. Consider the proof that the will is free in spite of the general mechanism of nature, drawn from the subtle but powerless distinction between subjective and objective practical necessity. Consider the proofs of God's existence, deduced from the concept of an *ens realissimum*, a "most real being," from the contingency of changeable things, and from the necessity of a first mover. Has any of these proofs ever made its way beyond the schools into the public mind, or had the slightest influence on what ordinary people believe? It must be admitted that none has, and because common understanding is not suited to such fine-spun speculation, none ever can be expected to.

On the contrary, it is plain where these convictions come from. The hope of a future life arises from the feeling, present in every human heart, that nothing temporal can meet and satisfy the demands of our nature. In the same way, there can be no doubt that the clear presentation of our duties, set against all the claims of inclination, gives rise to the consciousness of freedom. And the splendid order, beauty, and providential care displayed everywhere in nature give rise to faith in a wise and great Author of the universe. These are the origins of the general convictions of humanity, insofar as they rest on rational grounds. This common property not only remains undisturbed but gains in standing, through the teaching that the schools have no right to claim a deeper insight into a matter of universal human concern than the great mass of people, whom we must always hold in the highest regard, can reach without difficulty. The schools should therefore confine themselves to developing these proofs, which everyone can grasp and which are, from a moral point of view, entirely sufficient. The change thus affects only the arrogant pretensions of the schools, which would gladly keep for themselves alone the key to the truths they hand on to the public. Horace has the line for such men: *Quod mecum nescit, solus vult scire videri*, "what he does not know any more than I do, he wants to be thought the only one who knows."

Even so, the change does not strip the speculative philosopher of his rightful claim to be the sole custodian of a science that benefits the public without the public knowing it: I mean the critique of pure reason. That science can never become popular, and it has no need to. Fine-spun arguments in favor of useful truths make as little impression on the public mind as the equally subtle objections raised against those truths. Both, however, inevitably press upon anyone who rises to the level of speculation. So the schools have a clear duty to undertake a thorough inquiry into the rights of speculative reason, and in this way to prevent the scandal that metaphysical disputes are bound, sooner or later, to cause even among ordinary people. Only critique can save metaphysicians, and theologians in their capacity as metaphysicians, from these disputes and from the distortion of their doctrines that follows. Critique alone can cut off at the root materialism, fatalism, atheism, freethinking unbelief, fanaticism, and superstition, which can do harm to everyone. It can also cut off idealism and skepticism, which are dangerous mainly to the schools and can hardly spread to the public. If governments see fit to concern themselves with the affairs of scholars, a wise regard for both science and society would lead them to favor a critique of this kind, which alone can place the labors of reason on a firm footing. That would be far better than supporting the ridiculous despotism of the schools, which raise a loud alarm about danger to the public whenever their cobwebs are torn down, cobwebs the public has never noticed and whose loss it can therefore never feel.

This critique is not opposed to the *dogmatic procedure* of reason in pure cognition, for pure cognition must always be dogmatic, that is, it must rest on strict demonstration from secure a priori principles. What the critique opposes is *dogmatism*: the assumption that one can make progress with pure cognition from philosophical concepts alone, using principles that reason has long been accustomed to employ, without first asking how reason came to possess those principles and by what right. Dogmatism, then, is the dogmatic procedure of pure reason *without a prior critique of its own capacity*. In opposing it, we should not be taken to support the garrulous shallowness that likes to call itself popular philosophy, nor skepticism, which makes short work of the whole of metaphysics. On the contrary, our critique is the necessary preparation for a thoroughly scientific metaphysics, which must carry out its task wholly a priori, to the complete satisfaction of speculative reason, and must therefore be treated not in a popular manner but with the rigor of the schools. In carrying out the plan the critique lays down, that is, in the future system of metaphysics, we will have to follow the strict method of the celebrated Christian Wolff, the greatest of all dogmatic philosophers. Wolff was the first to show the need to establish principles according to rule, to define our concepts clearly, and to subject our demonstrations to the strictest scrutiny instead of leaping rashly to conclusions. His example awakened the spirit of deep and thorough inquiry that is still alive in Germany. He would have been especially well qualified to give metaphysics the character of a true science, if it had occurred to him to prepare the ground first by a critique of the organon, the instrument of knowledge, which is to say a critique of pure reason itself. That he failed to see the need for such a procedure must be blamed on the dogmatic way of thinking that characterized his age, and on this point the philosophers of his own time, like those of every earlier time, have no grounds to reproach one another. Those who reject both Wolff's method and the method of the *Critique of Pure Reason* can have no other aim than to throw off the constraints of science altogether: to turn labor into play, certainty into opinion, and philosophy, the love of wisdom, into philodoxy, the mere love of opinion.

In this second edition I have tried, as far as possible, to remove the difficulties and obscurities that have given rise to many misunderstandings, even among sharp-minded thinkers, though perhaps through no fault of mine. In the propositions themselves and in the proofs that support them, as well as in the form and overall plan of the work, I have found nothing to change. This is owing partly to the long scrutiny to which I subjected the whole before presenting it to the public, and partly to the nature of the subject. Pure speculative reason is an organic structure in which nothing stands isolated or independent. Every single part is essential to all the others, so that even the slightest flaw, whether an omission or an outright error, would inevitably reveal itself in use. I venture to hope, moreover, that this system will keep the same unchanging character in the future. What leads me to this confidence is not vanity but the evidence of the results themselves, which agree whether we proceed from the simplest elements up to the complete whole of pure reason or work back again from the whole to each part. Any attempt to alter even the smallest part leads inevitably to contradictions, not merely within this system but within human reason itself. Still, there remains much room for improvement in the way the work's doctrines are presented. In this edition I have tried to correct misunderstandings of the Aesthetic, the part dealing with sensibility, especially regarding the concept of time. I have also tried to clear away the obscurity found in the deduction of the concepts of the understanding, to supply what some felt was insufficient evidence in the proof of the principles of the pure understanding, and finally, to forestall the misreading of the paralogisms that immediately precede rational psychology. Beyond this point, which marks the end of the second main division of the "Transcendental Dialectic," I have made no changes. This is partly for lack of time and partly because I am not aware that any of the remainder has caused misunderstanding among intelligent and impartial critics. I do not name these critics here with the praise they deserve, but they will find that their suggestions have been heeded in the work itself.

The only genuine addition I have made in this edition, and even that concerns only the method of proof, is a new refutation of psychological idealism. It includes a rigorous demonstration, the only one possible, I believe, of the objective reality of outer intuition. However harmless idealism may be thought to be with respect to the essential aims of metaphysics (though in truth it is not harmless), it remains a scandal to philosophy and to human reason in general that we should have to accept the existence of things outside us as a mere article of faith. These are the very things from which we derive the entire material of knowledge, even for our inner sense, and yet we cannot answer anyone who chooses to doubt their existence with a satisfactory proof. Because the proof as it stands in the text is somewhat obscurely worded, I propose to revise the passage as follows: "But this permanent element cannot be an intuition in me. For all the grounds that determine my existence which can be found in me are representations, and as such they themselves require something permanent, distinct from them, by reference to which my existence can be determined in relation to their changes. That is, they require something by which my existence in time, in which they change, can be determined."

Someone may well object to this proof that, after all, I am immediately conscious only of what is in me, namely my representation of external things, and that it must therefore always remain uncertain whether anything corresponding to this representation actually exists outside me. But through inner experience I am conscious of my existence in time (and therefore also of its determinability in time), and that is more than the bare consciousness of my representation. It is, in fact, the same thing as the empirical consciousness of my existence, which can be determined only in relation to something that is connected with my existence yet lies outside me. This consciousness of my existence in time is therefore identical with the consciousness of a relation to something outside me. It is experience, then, and not fiction, sense and not imagination, that inseparably binds the external to my inner sense. Outer sense is in itself the relation of intuition to something real outside me, and the reality of this something, as opposed to a mere imagining of it, rests solely on its inseparable connection with inner experience as the condition that makes inner experience possible.

The intellectual consciousness of my existence is contained in the representation "I am," which accompanies all my judgments and every operation of my understanding. If, along with that consciousness, I could at the same time determine my existence through intellectual intuition, then the consciousness of a relation to something outside me would not be necessary. But the inner intuition in which alone my existence can be determined, although it is preceded by that purely intellectual consciousness, is itself sensible and bound to the condition of time. This determination of my existence, and with it my inner experience itself, must therefore depend on something permanent that is not in me. It can only be something outside me, to which I must regard myself as related. Thus the reality of outer sense is necessarily bound up with that of inner sense if experience in general is to be possible at all. I am just as certainly conscious that there are things outside me, related to my senses, as I am conscious that I myself exist as determined in time.

But to establish which given intuitions actually correspond to objects outside me, and so which intuitions belong to outer sense rather than to imagination, I must turn in each particular case to the rules by which experience in general, even inner experience, is distinguished from imagination. These rules always rest on the proposition that there really is outer experience. We may add that the representation of something permanent in existence is not the same as a permanent representation. A representation may be highly variable and changeable, as all our representations are, even that of matter, and yet refer to something permanent. That permanent thing must therefore be distinct from all my representations and external to me. Its existence is necessarily included in the determination of my own existence, and together with my existence it makes up a single experience. That experience could not take place even internally unless it were also, at the same time, partly external. We can no more answer the question of how this is so than we can explain how, in general, we come to think what abides in time, whose coexistence with what varies gives rise to the concept of change.

In trying to make my views as intelligible as possible, I have had to omit or shorten various passages that were not essential to the completeness of the work but that many readers might find useful in other respects and be reluctant to lose. This small loss could not have been avoided without swelling the book beyond reasonable length. The reader may make it good, if he wishes, by comparing this edition with the first, and I hope it will be more than offset by the greater clarity of the presentation as it now stands.

I have noticed with pleasure and gratitude, in various reviews and treatises, that the spirit of deep and thorough inquiry is not dead in Germany. It may have been drowned out and silenced for a while by a fashionable license in thinking that gives itself the airs of genius. Even so, the difficulties that beset the paths of criticism have not prevented vigorous and acute thinkers from mastering the science of pure reason to which those paths lead. This science is not popular but scholastic in character, and it is the only kind that can hope to last or to hold enduring value. To these worthy men, who so happily combine depth of insight with a gift for clear exposition, a gift I am not aware of possessing myself, I leave the task of removing whatever obscurity may still cling to the statement of my doctrines. In this case the danger is not of being refuted but of being misunderstood. For my own part, I must from now on refrain from controversy, though I will attend carefully to every suggestion, from friends and opponents alike, that may help in the further development of the system of this Propaedeutic, this preparatory study.

During these labors I have grown fairly advanced in years; this month I enter my sixty-fourth year. I must therefore be sparing with my time if I am to carry out my plan of working out the metaphysics of nature as well as the metaphysics of morals, as confirmation of the correctness of the principles of reason, both speculative and practical, established in this *Critique of Pure Reason*. I must leave to those worthy men who have made my system their own the task of clearing up the obscurities of the present work, which were perhaps unavoidable at the start, as well as the defense of the whole. A philosophical system cannot come forward armed at every point like a mathematical treatise. It is quite possible, then, to find fault with particular passages while the organic structure of the system, taken as a unity, faces no danger at all. Yet few have the ability, and fewer still the inclination, to take in a new system as a whole. By narrowing one's view to particular passages, lifting them out of context and setting them against one another, it is easy to find apparent contradictions, especially in a work written with any freedom of style. In the eyes of those who rely on others' judgment, such contradictions cast the work in an unfavorable light, but those who have grasped the idea of the whole can easily reconcile them. If a theory is inherently stable, the action and reaction that at first seemed to threaten its existence will, over time, only wear away its superficial roughness and unevenness. And if men of insight, impartiality, and a genuine gift for popular expression turn their attention to it, they will soon give it the elegance it requires as well.

KÖNIGSBERG, April 1787.

## Introduction

### I. On the Difference Between Pure and Empirical Knowledge

There can be no doubt that all our knowledge begins with experience. How else could our faculty of knowing be awakened into action, if not by objects that affect our senses? These objects partly produce representations on their own, and partly rouse our understanding into activity: to compare these representations, to connect or separate them, and so to work the raw material of sense impressions into a knowledge of objects, which we call experience. In the order of time, then, no knowledge of ours comes before experience; all of it begins there.

But although all our knowledge begins with experience, it does not follow that all of it arises from experience. It is quite possible that even our empirical knowledge is a compound, partly made of what we receive through impressions and partly supplied by our faculty of knowledge out of its own resources, with sense impressions providing merely the occasion. We may be unable to tell this addition apart from the original material of sense until long practice has made us alert to it and skilled at separating the two. Whether there exists any knowledge entirely independent of experience, and even of all sense impressions, is therefore a question that demands close investigation and cannot be answered at first glance. Knowledge of this kind is called *a priori*, in contrast to empirical knowledge, which has its sources *a posteriori*, that is, in experience.

The expression "a priori," however, is not yet precise enough to capture the full meaning of the question just raised. Even of knowledge that has its sources in experience, we commonly say that this or that can be known a priori, because we do not derive it directly from experience but from a general rule, a rule that we nonetheless borrowed from experience in the first place. Thus, of a man who dug away the foundations of his house, we say that he could have known a priori that it would collapse; he did not need to wait for the experience of its actually falling. Yet he could not have known even this entirely a priori. That bodies are heavy, and therefore fall when their supports are removed, is something he must first have learned through experience.

In what follows, therefore, we shall understand by "a priori knowledge" not knowledge that is independent of this or that particular experience, but knowledge that is absolutely independent of all experience. Opposed to it is empirical knowledge, which is possible only a posteriori, that is, through experience. A priori knowledge may be either pure or impure. Pure a priori knowledge is knowledge with which nothing empirical is mixed. The proposition "Every change has a cause," for example, is a priori but impure, because change is a concept that can only be drawn from experience.

### II. The Human Intellect, Even in an Unphilosophical State, Possesses Certain A Priori Cognitions

The question now is what criterion allows us to distinguish reliably between pure and empirical knowledge. Experience certainly teaches us that an object is constituted in such and such a way, but not that it could not possibly be otherwise. First, then, if we find a proposition whose very concept includes the idea of necessity, it is a priori; and if, in addition, it is derived from no other proposition except one that likewise involves necessity, it is absolutely a priori. Second, an empirical judgment never possesses strict and absolute universality, only an assumed and comparative universality arrived at by induction. The most such a judgment can claim is that, so far as we have observed, there is no exception to this or that rule. If, on the other hand, a judgment carries strict and absolute universality with it, so that it admits no possible exception, then it is not derived from experience but is valid absolutely a priori.

Empirical universality, then, is only an arbitrary extension of validity: we take what holds in most cases and assert that it holds in all, as in the statement "All bodies are heavy." When strict universality belongs essentially to a judgment, by contrast, it points to a distinct and special source of knowledge, namely a faculty of a priori cognition. Necessity and strict universality are therefore infallible tests for distinguishing pure from empirical knowledge, and the two are inseparably bound together. Yet in applying these criteria, it is sometimes easier to detect the empirical limitation of a judgment than its contingency, and the unlimited universality we ascribe to a judgment is often more convincing than its necessity. It is therefore advisable to use the two criteria separately, since each one by itself is infallible.

It is easy to show that human knowledge actually contains judgments that are necessary and universal in the strictest sense, and therefore pure a priori. For an example from the sciences, we need only take any proposition of mathematics. For an example from the most ordinary operations of the understanding, the proposition "Every change must have a cause" will do perfectly well. In this latter case, the concept of a cause so plainly contains the concept of a necessary connection with an effect, and of the strict universality of the law, that the concept of cause would disappear entirely if we tried, as Hume did, to derive it from the frequent association of what happens with what precedes it, and from the habit of connecting representations that such association produces. On that account, the necessity in the judgment would be merely subjective. Moreover, without searching for examples of this kind, we could show that such a priori principles are the indispensable basis of the very possibility of experience, and so prove their a priori existence. For where could experience itself acquire its certainty, if all the rules on which it depends were themselves empirical, and therefore merely contingent? No one could accept rules of that kind as first principles. For the present, however, it is enough to have established, first, that we do possess and exercise a faculty of pure a priori knowledge, and second, to have identified its proper marks: universality and necessity.

An a priori origin shows itself not only in judgments but even in concepts. Take the concept of a body, and strip away from it, one by one, everything that belongs to mere sense experience: its color, its hardness or softness, its weight, even its impenetrability. The body itself vanishes, but the space it occupied remains, and that space we cannot possibly annihilate in thought. Similarly, if we remove from our empirical concept of any object, physical or nonphysical, every property that experience alone has taught us to associate with it, we still cannot think away the property by which we conceive of it as a substance, or as inhering in a substance, even though the concept of substance is more determinate than the concept of an object in general. Compelled, then, by the necessity with which this concept forces itself upon us, we must admit that it has its seat in our faculty of a priori knowledge.

### III. Philosophy Needs a Science That Determines the Possibility, Principles, and Extent of Human Knowledge A Priori

Far more important than anything said so far is the fact that certain of our cognitions rise completely above the field of all possible experience and, by means of concepts to which no object anywhere in experience corresponds, appear to extend our judgments beyond its limits. It is precisely in this transcendental or supersensible realm, where experience offers neither instruction nor guidance, that reason carries out its inquiries. We regard these inquiries as far more important, and their aim as far loftier, than anything the understanding can accomplish within the field of sensory appearances. We value them so highly that we pursue them even at the risk of error, and allow neither doubt, nor disdain, nor indifference to hold us back. The unavoidable problems of pure reason itself are God, freedom of the will, and immortality. The science whose particular object, together with all its preparatory work, is the solution of these problems is called metaphysics. From the very outset it is dogmatic: it confidently undertakes this task without first examining whether reason is capable or incapable of so great an undertaking.

Once we have abandoned the safe ground of experience, it would seem natural to hesitate before raising a building out of knowledge whose origins we do not know, on the strength of principles whose source has never been discovered. Instead of trying to build without a foundation, one would expect us long ago to have asked how the understanding arrives at these a priori cognitions, and what extent, validity, and value they may possess. And this is indeed natural, if by "natural" we mean what accords with a just and reasonable way of thinking. But if we mean what usually happens, then nothing could be more natural or more understandable than that this inquiry should have been left unattempted for so long. One branch of our pure knowledge, mathematics, has long been firmly established, and its success leads us to form flattering expectations about other branches, though these may be of an entirely different nature. Besides, once we pass beyond the limits of experience, we are naturally safe from being contradicted by it; and the allure of enlarging our knowledge is so strong that, unless some evident contradiction brings us to a halt, we press on without a doubt. Even contradiction can be avoided, if we are careful enough in constructing our fictions, which are no less fictions for that.

Mathematics offers a splendid example of how far we can carry our a priori knowledge independently of all experience. It is true that the mathematician deals with objects and cognitions only insofar as they can be represented in intuition. But this fact is easily overlooked, because the intuition in question can itself be given a priori, and is therefore hardly distinguishable from a mere pure concept. Misled by this proof of reason's power, we can see no limit to the expansion of our knowledge. The light dove, cutting through the air in free flight and feeling its resistance, might imagine that she would fly far more freely and swiftly in airless space. In just the same way, Plato abandoned the world of the senses because it confines the understanding within such narrow limits, and ventured beyond it on the wings of ideas into the empty space of pure intellect. He did not notice that all his efforts gained him no ground, because he met no resistance: nothing to give him a foothold, as it were, on which to rest and against which to exert his powers, so that the intellect might gain momentum for its advance. It is, in fact, the common fate of human reason in speculation to finish its imposing structure of thought as quickly as possible, and only afterward to begin asking whether the foundation is sound. At that point, all sorts of excuses are sought to console us for its lack of stability, or rather to spare us altogether from so belated and dangerous an inquiry. What frees us from all apprehension and suspicion while we are building, and flatters us into believing in the solidity of our work, is this. A large part, perhaps the largest part, of reason's business consists in analyzing the concepts we already possess of objects. This gives us a great many cognitions which, although they are really nothing more than clarifications or explanations of what was already thought in our concepts, if only in a confused way, are nonetheless prized as new insights, at least as far as their form is concerned. As far as their matter or content is concerned, we have added nothing to our concepts; we have only unfolded them. But since this procedure does yield genuine a priori knowledge, which advances securely and produces useful results, reason is deceived by it. Without being aware of it, reason slips in assertions of an entirely different kind, in which it attaches to given concepts other concepts that are a priori, to be sure, but wholly foreign to them, without our knowing how it arrives at them, and indeed without the question ever occurring to us. I shall therefore proceed at once to examine the difference between these two kinds of knowledge.

### IV. On the Difference Between Analytic and Synthetic Judgments

In every judgment in which the relation of a subject to a predicate is thought (I consider only affirmative judgments here; the application to negative judgments will be easy), this relation is possible in two different ways. Either the predicate B belongs to the subject A as something contained, however covertly, in the concept A; or B lies entirely outside the concept A, although it stands in some connection with it. In the first case I call the judgment analytic; in the second, synthetic. Affirmative analytic judgments, then, are those in which the connection of predicate and subject is thought through identity; those in which the connection is thought without identity are called synthetic. The former may also be called explicative judgments, and the latter augmentative. The former add nothing to the concept of the subject through the predicate, but merely break it down into its constituent concepts, which were already thought in it, though confusedly; the latter add to the concept of the subject a predicate that was not contained in it, and that no analysis could ever have discovered there. When I say, "All bodies are extended," for example, the judgment is analytic. I need not go beyond the concept of body to find extension connected with it; I need only analyze the concept, that is, become conscious of the various properties I think in it, in order to find this predicate there. It is therefore an analytic judgment. But when I say, "All bodies are heavy," the predicate is something quite different from anything I think in the mere concept of a body. Adding such a predicate therefore produces a synthetic judgment.

Judgments of experience, as such, are always synthetic. It would be absurd to base an analytic judgment on experience, since in forming such a judgment I need not step outside the sphere of my concepts at all, and so have no need for the testimony of experience. That bodies are extended is not an empirical judgment but a proposition that stands firm a priori. Before I turn to experience at all, I already have in my concept every condition the judgment requires. I need only draw out the predicate in accordance with the principle of contradiction, and in doing so I become aware, at the same time, of the judgment's necessity, a necessity that experience could never teach me. By contrast, although I do not at first include the predicate of weight in my concept of body in general, that concept still designates an object of experience, a part of the totality of experience, to which I can add further parts; and this is exactly what I do when I recognize through observation that bodies are heavy. I can know the concept of body in advance, by analysis, through the characteristics of extension, impenetrability, shape, and so on, all of which are thought in this concept. But now I extend my knowledge. Looking back to the experience from which I drew this concept of body, I find weight always connected with those characteristics, and so I add it synthetically to my concept as a predicate and say, "All bodies are heavy." It is experience, then, that makes possible the synthesis of the predicate of weight with the concept of body. The two concepts, though neither is contained in the other, still belong to each other, if only contingently, as parts of a whole: namely, experience, which is itself a synthesis of intuitions.

For synthetic a priori judgments, however, this help is entirely lacking. If I am to go beyond the concept A in order to recognize another concept B as connected with it, what can I rely on to make the synthesis possible? Here I no longer have the advantage of searching the field of experience for what I need. Take the proposition "Everything that happens has a cause." In the concept of something that happens, I do think of an existence preceded by a certain stretch of time, and from this I can derive analytic judgments. But the concept of a cause lies entirely outside that concept. It signifies something altogether different from "that which happens," and so is not contained in it. How, then, can I assert of the general concept "that which happens" something entirely different from it, and recognize the concept of cause as belonging to it, and even necessarily, though it is not contained in it? What is the unknown X on which the understanding relies when it believes it has found, outside the concept A, a foreign predicate B that it nonetheless considers connected with A? It cannot be experience, because the principle in question attaches the representations of cause and effect to the representation of existence not only with a universality that experience cannot supply, but also with the stamp of necessity, and therefore entirely a priori and from pure concepts. The whole aim of our speculative a priori knowledge depends on synthetic, or augmentative, propositions of this kind. Analytic judgments are indeed highly important and necessary, but only for achieving the clarity of concepts required for a secure and extended synthesis, and that synthesis alone is a genuine gain.

### V. All Theoretical Sciences of Reason Contain Synthetic A Priori Judgments as Principles

1. Mathematical judgments are always synthetic. This fact, though undeniably true and of great consequence, seems until now to have escaped those who have analyzed the human mind, and even to stand in direct opposition to all their conjectures.
