Because it was found that mathematical inferences all proceed according to the principle of contradiction, as the nature of all apodictic certainty, the certainty of what is demonstrably necessary, requires, people became convinced that the fundamental principles of the science were likewise known and accepted on that basis. But this notion is mistaken. A synthetic proposition can indeed be grasped by means of the principle of contradiction, but only if another synthetic proposition comes first, from which it can be deduced, and never on its own.

It must be noted, first of all, that genuinely mathematical propositions are always a priori judgments and never empirical ones, because they carry with them the concept of necessity, which experience cannot supply. If anyone objects to this, it makes no difference; I will then confine my claim to pure mathematics, whose very concept implies that it consists of knowledge that is entirely non-empirical and a priori.

At first one might suppose that the proposition 7 + 5 = 12 is merely analytic, following by the principle of contradiction from the concept of a sum of seven and five. But on closer inspection, we find that our concept of the sum of seven and five contains nothing more than the joining of both numbers into one, and that this concept tells us nothing at all about what that single number is which includes them both. The concept of twelve is by no means already thought simply because I think of the union of seven and five; I may analyze my concept of such a possible sum for as long as I like, and I will never find the number twelve in it. We must go beyond these concepts and call on the help of an intuition corresponding to one of them: our five fingers, for instance, or, as the mathematician Segner does in his *Arithmetic*, five points. Then, step by step, we add the units of the five given in intuition to the concept of seven. I first take the number 7. Then, calling on the fingers of my hand as an intuition for the concept of 5, I add to 7, one at a time and with the help of that concrete image, the units I had previously grouped together to make up 5; and in this way I see the number 12 emerge. That 7 was to be added to 5, I had indeed already thought in my concept of a sum 7 + 5, but not that this sum equals 12. Arithmetical propositions are therefore always synthetic, and we can convince ourselves of this more clearly by trying larger numbers. It then becomes quite evident that, however we turn and twist our concepts, we could never arrive at the sum or product by mere analysis of them, without the help of intuition. Nor is any principle of pure geometry analytic. "A straight line is the shortest line between two points" is a synthetic proposition. My concept of straightness contains nothing about quantity; it is purely a concept of quality. The concept of "shortest" is therefore entirely an addition, and no analysis of the concept of a straight line could extract it. Intuition must come to our aid here, and only by its means is the synthesis possible.

A few principles that geometers presuppose are indeed analytic and rest on the principle of contradiction. Like identical propositions, however, they function as links in the chain of method, not as principles. Examples include a = a, the principle that the whole is equal to itself, and (a + b) > a, the principle that the whole is greater than its part. Yet even these principles, though they derive their validity from pure concepts, are admitted into mathematics only because they can be presented in intuition. We commonly believe that the predicate of such apodictic, or necessarily certain, judgments is already contained in our concept, and that the judgment is therefore analytic. That belief arises merely from an ambiguity in how we express ourselves. We are obliged to join a certain predicate in thought to a given concept, and this necessity is already attached to the concept. But the question is not what we must join in thought to the given concept. The question is what we actually think in it, even if only obscurely. Once we ask this, it becomes clear that the predicate does belong to these concepts necessarily, but not as something thought in the concept itself. It belongs to them by virtue of an intuition that must be added to the concept.

2. Natural philosophy, or physics, contains synthetic a priori judgments as its principles. I will cite two such propositions: "In all changes in the material world, the quantity of matter remains unchanged," and "In all communication of motion, action and reaction must always be equal." In both cases it is clear not only that they are necessary, and therefore a priori in origin, but also that they are synthetic. For in the concept of matter I do not think its permanence. I think only its presence in space, which it fills. I therefore genuinely go outside and beyond the concept of matter in order to attach to it, a priori, something I did not think in it. The proposition is therefore not analytic but synthetic, and yet it is conceived a priori. The same holds for the other propositions belonging to the pure part of natural philosophy.

3. Metaphysics must also contain synthetic a priori propositions, even if we regard it merely as an attempted science, though the nature of human reason makes it an indispensable one. Its task is not merely to dissect the concepts we form a priori of things, and so to clarify them analytically. We also seek to extend the range of our a priori knowledge. To do so, we must make use of principles that add to the original concept something neither identical with it nor contained in it. Through synthetic a priori judgments we must leave the limits of experience far behind, as in the proposition "The world must have a beginning," and others like it. Thus metaphysics, according to the proper aim of the science, consists entirely of synthetic a priori propositions.

### VI. The Universal Problem of Pure Reason.

It is a great advantage to be able to bring a number of investigations under the formula of a single problem. In this way we not only lighten our own work, since we define it clearly for ourselves, but also make it easier for others to judge whether we have done justice to our undertaking. The proper problem of pure reason, then, is contained in the question: How are synthetic a priori judgments possible?

Metaphysics has until now remained in a wavering state of uncertainty and contradiction. The sole cause is that this great problem did not occur to philosophers sooner, and perhaps the distinction between analytic and synthetic judgments did not occur to them either. The survival or collapse of metaphysics as a science depends on solving this problem, or else on adequately proving that synthetic a priori knowledge is impossible. Of all philosophers, David Hume came closest to this problem. Yet it never took on sufficient precision in his mind, nor did he consider the question in its full generality. He stopped instead at one synthetic proposition, the connection of an effect with its cause (*principium causalitatis*, the principle of causality), and insisted that such a proposition could not be known a priori. By his reasoning, everything we call metaphysics is a mere illusion. On this view, reason imagines that it has insight into something that has in fact been borrowed from experience, and to which habit has merely given the appearance of necessity. This assertion is destructive of all pure philosophy, and Hume would have been protected against it had he kept our problem before him in its full generality. For he would then have seen that, by his own argument, there could be no pure mathematics either, since mathematics certainly cannot exist without synthetic a priori propositions. His good sense would surely have saved him from that absurdity.

The solution of this problem also settles whether pure reason can be used to found and construct all the sciences that contain theoretical a priori knowledge of objects. It answers, that is, the following questions:

How is pure mathematics possible?

How is pure natural science possible?

Since these sciences certainly exist, it is entirely proper to ask how they are possible, for the fact that they actually exist proves that they must be possible. Some may still doubt that a pure natural science, or pure physics, exists. But one need only look at the various propositions commonly treated at the beginning of physics proper, which is empirical. These include the permanence of the same quantity of matter, inertia (*vis inertiae*), and the equality of action and reaction. A reader who considers them will soon be convinced that they form a pure physics (*physica pura*, or *rationalis*). This pure physics fully deserves to be set out separately as a science of its own, in its whole extent, whether that extent proves large or narrow. Metaphysics stands differently. It has made wretched progress so far, and not one of the systems yet put forward can be said, with respect to its true aim, to have made this science actually exist. Anyone is therefore free to doubt, with good reason, whether it is possible at all.

Yet in a certain sense even this kind of knowledge must be regarded as given. Metaphysics must be considered to exist in reality, if not as a science, then as a natural disposition of the human mind (*metaphysica naturalis*). Human reason does not need the vanity of wanting to know a great deal to drive it forward. It presses on unceasingly, urged by its own need, toward questions that no empirical use of reason, and no principles drawn from such use, can answer. So every human being has always had some system of metaphysics, and one will always be present as soon as reason awakens to the exercise of its power of speculation. And so the question arises: How is metaphysics possible as a natural disposition? How, that is, do the questions that pure reason puts to itself arise from the nature of universal human reason, and why does reason feel compelled by its own need to answer them as best it can?

But every attempt so far to answer the questions that reason is prompted by its very nature to ask itself has met with unavoidable contradictions. Whether the world had a beginning or has existed from eternity is one such question. We therefore cannot rest content with the mere natural disposition toward metaphysics, that is, with the existence of the faculty of pure reason, from which some metaphysical system or other always arises. It must be possible to reach certainty about whether we know or do not know the things metaphysics deals with. We must be able to reach a decision either about the objects of its questions or about whether reason is able to judge them at all. Then we can either extend the bounds of pure reason with confidence or set strictly defined and secure limits to its activity. This last question follows from the universal problem stated above, and would properly be put this way: How is metaphysics possible as a science?

Thus the critique of reason leads in the end, naturally and necessarily, to science. The dogmatic use of reason without critique, on the other hand, leads to groundless assertions, against which equally plausible counter-assertions can always be set, and so it ends inevitably in skepticism.

Moreover, this science need not be of great or daunting length, because it does not deal with the objects of reason, whose variety is inexhaustible. It deals only with reason itself and its own problems. These problems arise from within reason, and they are posed to it by its own nature, not by the nature of external things. Once reason has come to understand fully its own power with respect to the objects it encounters in experience, it will be easy to determine with certainty the extent and limits of its attempts to apply itself to objects beyond the bounds of experience.

We may, and indeed must, therefore treat all previous attempts to establish metaphysics dogmatically as if they had never been made. Whatever analysis one or another of them contains, that is, whatever mere dissection of concepts, is not the aim of metaphysics proper but only a preparation for it. Metaphysics proper has as its object the extension of our a priori knowledge through synthesis. For that purpose mere analysis is useless, since it shows only what is contained in these concepts, not how we arrive at them a priori. Showing this is precisely the task of metaphysics, so that it can afterward determine the valid use of these concepts with respect to all objects of experience and to knowledge in general.

Little self-denial is needed to give up these pretensions. The dogmatic method makes contradictions of reason with itself inevitable, and these undeniable contradictions have long since ruined the reputation of every metaphysical system that has appeared so far. More firmness will be needed for the next task. We must not be deterred by difficulties from within or by opposition from without. We must persist, by a method entirely opposed to all those followed until now, in promoting the growth and fruitfulness of a science indispensable to human reason. Every branch this science has borne may be cut away, but its roots cannot be destroyed.

### VII. Idea and Division of a Particular Science, under the Name of a Critique of Pure Reason.

From everything said so far there emerges the idea of a particular science, which may be called the Critique of Pure Reason. Reason is the faculty that supplies us with the principles of a priori knowledge. Pure reason, accordingly, is the faculty that contains the principles by which we know anything absolutely a priori. An organon of pure reason, meaning an instrument or body of rules for acquiring knowledge, would be the complete collection of those principles according to which alone all pure a priori knowledge can be obtained. The fully extended application of such an organon would give us a system of pure reason. But that is asking a great deal, and it remains doubtful whether any extension of our knowledge is possible here at all, and if so, in which cases. We may therefore regard a science that merely examines pure reason, its sources, and its limits as the propaedeutic, or preparatory study, for a system of pure reason. Such a science should not be called a doctrine but only a critique of pure reason. Its use in speculation would be purely negative. Its purpose would be not to enlarge our reason but to purify it and guard it against error, which in itself is no small gain. I call *transcendental* all knowledge that is occupied not so much with objects as with our way of knowing objects, insofar as this way of knowing is possible a priori. A system of such concepts would be called transcendental philosophy. But this, too, lies beyond the scope of the present work. Such a science would have to contain a complete account of our analytic a priori knowledge as well as our synthetic a priori knowledge. It is therefore too broad for our present purpose. We need to carry our analysis only as far as is necessary to understand, in their full extent, the principles of a priori synthesis, which are our sole concern. This investigation is the sole object of the present work. We cannot properly call it a doctrine, only a transcendental critique, because it aims to correct and guide our knowledge rather than to enlarge it. It is meant to act as a touchstone for testing the worth or worthlessness of all a priori knowledge. Such a critique is therefore, so far as possible, a preparation for an organon. Should that organon prove unattainable, the critique is at least a preparation for a canon of pure reason, a set of rules for its correct use. According to that canon, the complete system of the philosophy of pure reason might one day be presented both analytically and synthetically, whether that system extends the bounds of reason or limits them. Such a system is evidently possible, and it is evidently not so vast as to rule out the hope of ever completing it. For we are dealing here not with the nature of external objects, which is infinite, but solely with the mind that judges the nature of objects. Further, we deal with the mind only with respect to its a priori knowledge. Since the object of our inquiry is to be sought not outside us but entirely within ourselves, it cannot remain hidden. In all likelihood it is limited enough to be surveyed completely and assessed fairly as to its worth or worthlessness. Still less should the reader expect here a critique of books and systems of pure reason. Our object is exclusively a critique of the faculty of pure reason itself. Only when we take this critique as our foundation do we have a sure touchstone for assessing the philosophical value of ancient and modern writings on the subject. Without that standard, the unqualified historian or critic judges and corrects the groundless assertions of others with assertions of his own, which have just as little foundation.

Transcendental philosophy is the idea of a science for which the Critique of Pure Reason must draw up the complete plan architectonically. That is, the Critique must lay out the plan from principles, with a full guarantee of the validity and stability of all the parts that make up the building. Transcendental philosophy is the system of all the principles of pure reason. The Critique does not itself claim the title of transcendental philosophy only because a complete system would have to include a full analysis of all human a priori knowledge. Our critique must certainly set before us a complete enumeration of all the fundamental concepts that make up such pure knowledge. But it rightly refrains from a complete analysis of these concepts themselves, and from a complete examination of the concepts derived from them. It has two reasons for this restraint. First, such analysis would stray from its purpose, since this process involves none of the difficulty and uncertainty found in synthesis, to which our critique is wholly devoted. Second, it would be inconsistent with the unity of our plan to burden this work with defending the completeness of such an analysis and derivation, which in any case is not our present concern. This completeness can easily be achieved later, both in the analysis of these fundamental concepts and in the derivation of further concepts from the a priori concepts the analysis yields. The only requirement is that we possess all the fundamental concepts that are to act as principles of synthesis, and that nothing is lacking with respect to this main purpose.

Everything that constitutes transcendental philosophy therefore belongs to the Critique of Pure Reason. The Critique is the complete idea of transcendental philosophy, but it is not yet the science itself, because it carries its analysis only as far as is needed to judge fully our synthetic a priori knowledge.

In dividing the parts of a science of this kind, the chief thing to observe is that no concepts containing anything empirical may enter into it. The a priori knowledge must be entirely pure. Thus the highest principles and fundamental concepts of morality are certainly a priori knowledge, but they do not belong to transcendental philosophy. It is true that morality does not place the concepts of pain, pleasure, desire, inclination, and the like at the foundation of its precepts, and all of these concepts are empirical in origin. Yet in constructing a system of pure morality, these empirical concepts must necessarily enter into the concept of duty. They enter either as an obstacle to be overcome or as an incentive that ought not to be made into a motive. Transcendental philosophy is therefore a philosophy of pure and merely speculative reason. For everything practical, insofar as it involves motives, relates to feelings, and feelings belong to the empirical sources of knowledge.

If we wish to divide this science from the general standpoint of any science, it should comprise, first, a Doctrine of the Elements and, second, a Doctrine of the Method of pure reason. Each of these main divisions will have its subdivisions, though the separate grounds for them cannot be set out here. By way of introduction and advance notice, only one point seems necessary. There are two sources of human knowledge, sensibility and understanding, and they perhaps spring from a common root unknown to us. Through sensibility objects are given to us, and through understanding they are thought. Sensibility may contain a priori representations that form the conditions under which objects are given to us, and to that extent it belongs to transcendental philosophy. The transcendental doctrine of sensibility must form the first part of our science of elements, because the conditions under which alone the objects of human knowledge are given must come before those under which they are thought.

## The Transcendental Aesthetic

*Transcendental Doctrine of Elements, Part One*

### § 1. Introductory

Whatever the way, and whatever the means, by which our knowledge relates to objects, one thing at least is clear: the only way it relates to them *immediately* is through intuition. Intuition is the indispensable groundwork toward which all thought is directed. But an intuition can occur only if the object is given to us, and this in turn is possible, for human beings at least, only if the object affects the mind in a certain way. Our capacity to receive representations through the way in which objects affect us is a capacity of receptivity, and it is called sensibility. Through sensibility, then, objects are given to us, and sensibility alone supplies us with intuitions. Through the understanding, objects are thought, and from the understanding arise concepts. Yet all thought must ultimately relate to intuitions, whether directly or indirectly by means of certain signs. In our case, therefore, all thought must relate to sensibility, because there is no other way in which an object can be given to us.

The effect of an object on our faculty of representation, insofar as we are affected by it, is sensation. An intuition that relates to its object through sensation is called an empirical intuition. The undetermined object of an empirical intuition is called a phenomenon, or appearance. Whatever in the phenomenon corresponds to sensation I call its *matter*. Whatever allows the content of the phenomenon to be arranged in certain relations I call its *form*. Now, that within which our sensations are arranged, and through which they are able to take on a certain form, cannot itself be sensation. The matter of all phenomena is given to us only à posteriori, through experience, but their form must lie ready in the mind à priori, prior to experience, and can therefore be considered apart from all sensation.

I call a representation *pure*, in the transcendental sense of the word, when it contains nothing that belongs to sensation. Accordingly, we find in the mind, à priori, the pure form of sensuous intuitions in general: the form in which all the manifold content of the phenomenal world is arranged and viewed in certain relations. This pure form of sensibility I shall call pure intuition. Suppose I take my representation of a body and remove from it everything the understanding thinks as belonging to it, such as substance, force, and divisibility. Suppose I also remove everything that belongs to sensation, such as impenetrability, hardness, and colour. Something of this empirical intuition still remains, namely extension and shape. These belong to pure intuition, which exists à priori in the mind as a mere form of sensibility, without any actual object of the senses and without any sensation.

The science of all the à priori principles of sensibility I call the transcendental aesthetic. There must be such a science, and it forms the first part of the transcendental doctrine of elements. It stands apart from the second part, which contains the principles of pure thought and is called transcendental logic.

At present the Germans are the only people who use the word "aesthetic" to mean what others call the critique of taste. Behind this usage lies a disappointed hope held by the eminent analytical thinker Baumgarten. He hoped to bring the criticism of the beautiful under rational principles and so to raise its rules to the rank of a science. His efforts were in vain. In their chief sources, the rules or criteria of taste are merely empirical, so they can never function as determinate à priori laws that direct our judgement in matters of taste. On the contrary, it is our judgement that provides the real test of whether such principles are correct. There are two sensible courses. The first is to give up the word as a name for the critique of taste and reserve it for the doctrine that is a true science, the science of the laws of sensibility. That would bring us closer to the language and meaning of the ancients, with their well-known division of the objects of knowledge into *aistheta kai noeta*, things perceived by the senses and things grasped by thought. The second is to share the term with speculative philosophy, using it partly in a transcendental sense and partly in a psychological one.

In the transcendental aesthetic, then, we shall first isolate sensibility by separating from it everything that the concepts of the understanding attach to its perceptions, so that nothing remains but empirical intuition. Next we shall remove from this intuition everything that belongs to sensation, so that nothing remains but pure intuition and the mere form of phenomena, which is all that sensibility can supply à priori. This investigation will show that there are two pure forms of sensuous intuition, which are principles of à priori knowledge: space and time. We now turn to these.

### Section I. Of Space

### § 2. Metaphysical Exposition of This Concept

Through outer sense, which is a property of the mind, we represent objects to ourselves as outside us, and all of them as in space. In space alone are their shape, size, and relations to one another determined or determinable. Inner sense, through which the mind contemplates itself or its own internal state, gives us no intuition of the soul as an object. There is nevertheless a definite form under which alone the contemplation of our internal state is possible, so that everything belonging to the mind's inner determinations is represented in relations of time. We can no more have an outer intuition of time than an inner intuition of space. What, then, are space and time? Are they real existences? Are they merely relations or determinations of things, yet of a kind that would belong to these things in themselves even if those things were never intuited? Or do they belong only to the form of intuition, and therefore to the subjective constitution of the mind, without which the predicates of space and time could not be attached to any object at all?

To settle these questions, we shall begin with an exposition of the concept of space. By *exposition* I mean a clear, though not exhaustive, representation of what belongs to a concept. An exposition is *metaphysical* when it presents the concept as given à priori.

1. Space is not a concept derived from outer experiences. Suppose certain sensations are to be related to something outside me, that is, to something in a different part of space from the one I occupy. Suppose, likewise, that I am to represent them not merely as outside and beside one another but as in different places. In both cases the representation of space must already be present as their foundation. The representation of space therefore cannot be borrowed through experience from the relations of outer phenomena. On the contrary, outer experience is itself possible only through this prior representation.

2. Space, then, is a necessary à priori representation that underlies all outer intuitions. We can never imagine or represent to ourselves that there is no space, although we can easily think of space as empty of objects. Space must therefore be regarded as the condition of the possibility of phenomena, and not at all as a determination that depends on them. It is an à priori representation that necessarily provides the basis for outer phenomena.

3. Space is not a discursive or, as we say, general concept of the relations of things, but a pure intuition. In the first place, we can represent to ourselves only one space. When we speak of many spaces, we mean only parts of one and the same space. Moreover, these parts cannot precede the one all-embracing space as components out of which it could be assembled; they can be thought only as existing within it. Space is essentially one, and the multiplicity within it, including the general notion of spaces, of this space or that, rests entirely on limitations of it. It follows that an à priori, non-empirical intuition lies at the root of all our concepts of space. In the same way, the principles of geometry are never deduced from general concepts of line and triangle. The principle that "in a triangle, any two sides together are greater than the third" is derived from intuition, and from à priori intuition at that, with apodeictic certainty, the certainty of what must necessarily be so.

4. Space is represented as an infinite given magnitude. Every concept must be thought of as a representation contained in an infinite multitude of different possible representations, which it therefore holds under itself. But no concept, as such, can be thought of as containing an infinite multitude of representations *within* itself. Yet this is exactly how space is thought, since every part of space can be extended to infinity. The original representation of space is therefore an à priori intuition, not a concept.

### § 3. Transcendental Exposition of the Concept of Space

By a *transcendental* exposition I mean the explanation of a concept as a principle from which the possibility of other synthetic à priori knowledge can be understood. Two things are required for this. First, such knowledge must really follow from the given concept. Second, this knowledge must be possible only on the assumption of a particular way of explaining that concept.

Geometry is a science that determines the properties of space synthetically, and yet à priori. What, then, must our representation of space be for such knowledge of it to be possible? It must originally be an intuition, because no proposition that goes beyond a concept can be derived from that concept alone, and yet this is exactly what happens in geometry, as the Introduction has shown. This intuition must also be found in the mind à priori, prior to any perception of objects, and must therefore be pure rather than empirical intuition. Geometrical propositions are always apodeictic: they carry with them the consciousness of their own necessity, as in the proposition "Space has only three dimensions." As the Introduction also showed, propositions of this kind cannot be empirical judgements, nor conclusions drawn from such judgements. How, then, can there exist in the human mind an outer intuition that precedes the objects themselves, and in which our concept of those objects can be determined à priori? Plainly, this is possible only if the intuition has its seat in the subject alone, as the subject's formal capacity to be affected by objects and so to obtain immediate representation, that is, intuition. It is possible, in short, only as the form of outer sense in general.

Our explanation is therefore the only one that makes the possibility of geometry, as a synthetic à priori science, intelligible. Any explanation that fails to show this possibility, however much it may resemble ours, can be distinguished from it with complete certainty by this test.

### § 4. Conclusions from the Foregoing Concepts

(a) Space does not represent any property of things in themselves, nor does it represent them in their relations to one another. Space does not represent to us any determination that belongs to objects themselves and would remain even if all the subjective conditions of intuition were taken away. No determinations of things, whether absolute or relative, can be intuited before the existence of the things to which they belong, and so none can be intuited à priori.

(b) Space is nothing other than the form of all phenomena of outer sense: the subjective condition of sensibility under which alone outer intuition is possible. The subject's receptivity, its capacity to be affected by objects, necessarily precedes all intuitions of those objects. It is therefore easy to understand how the form of all phenomena can be given in the mind before any actual perception, and therefore à priori. It is equally easy to understand how this form, as a pure intuition in which all objects must be determined, can contain principles governing the relations of those objects prior to all experience.

It is therefore only from the human standpoint that we can speak of space, of extended things, and so on. If we abandon the subjective condition under which alone we can receive outer intuition, the condition under which objects affect us, then the representation of space means nothing whatever. This predicate applies to things only insofar as they appear to us, only insofar as they are objects of sensibility. The constant form of this receptivity, which we call sensibility, is a necessary condition of all the relations in which objects can be intuited as existing outside us. When we abstract from these objects, what remains is a pure intuition, to which we give the name of space. Clearly, we cannot make the special conditions of sensibility into conditions of the possibility of things as such, but only of the possibility of their existence as phenomena. We may therefore rightly say that space contains everything that can appear to us externally, but not all things considered as things in themselves, whether or not they are intuited, and by whatever subject. As for the intuitions of other thinking beings, we cannot judge whether they are bound by the same conditions that limit our own intuition and that hold universally for us.

If we attach the limitation of a judgement to the concept of its subject, the judgement then holds unconditionally. The proposition "All objects are beside one another in space," for example, is valid only on the condition that these things are taken as objects of our sensuous intuition. But if I build the condition into the concept and say, "All things, as outer phenomena, are beside one another in space," the rule holds universally and without any limitation. Our exposition therefore establishes the reality, that is, the objective validity, of space with regard to everything that can be presented to us externally as an object. At the same time it establishes the ideality of space with regard to things when reason considers them as they are in themselves, without reference to the constitution of our sensibility. We affirm, then, the empirical reality of space with respect to all possible outer experience, while acknowledging its transcendental ideality. Space is nothing at all once we set aside the condition on which the possibility of all experience depends and treat space as something belonging to things in themselves.

Apart from space, however, there is no representation that is subjective and refers to something outside us that could be called objective à priori. There are no other subjective representations from which we can derive synthetic à priori propositions, as we can from the intuition of space. Strictly speaking, therefore, no ideality belongs to these other representations. They do resemble the representation of space in belonging merely to the subjective character of our mode of sensuous perception: sight, hearing, and touch, for instance, which work through the sensations of colour, sound, and heat. But because these are only sensations and not intuitions, they do not by themselves give us knowledge of any object, least of all à priori knowledge.

My purpose in this remark is simply to warn anyone against illustrating the ideality of space with examples as inadequate as colour or taste. These are rightly regarded not as properties of things but only as changes in the subject, changes that may differ from one person to another. In such cases, what is originally a mere phenomenon, such as a rose, is taken by the empirical understanding for a thing in itself, even though its colour may appear differently to every eye. The transcendental concept of phenomena in space, by contrast, is a critical reminder that nothing intuited in space is a thing in itself, and that space is not a form belonging to things as a property. Objects in themselves are entirely unknown to us, and what we call outer objects are nothing but representations of our sensibility. The form of these representations is space. Their real correlate, the thing in itself, is not known through them and never can be, and in experience no one ever asks about it.

### Section II. Of Time

### § 5. Metaphysical Exposition of This Concept

1. Time is not an empirical concept. Neither coexistence nor succession would be perceived by us at all if the representation of time did not underlie them à priori. Without this presupposition we could not represent to ourselves that things exist together at one and the same time, or at different times, simultaneously or in succession.

2. Time is a necessary representation that underlies all our intuitions. With regard to phenomena in general, we cannot take time away from them and represent them as outside of and unconnected with time, but we can quite well represent time as empty of phenomena. Time is therefore given à priori. In time alone is any reality of phenomena possible. The phenomena may all be annihilated in thought, but time itself, as the universal condition of their possibility, cannot be done away with.

3. This à priori necessity is also the basis for apodeictic principles concerning the relations of time, the axioms of time in general. Examples are "Time has only one dimension" and "Different times are not simultaneous but successive," just as different spaces are not successive but simultaneous. These principles cannot be derived from experience, because experience would give them neither strict universality nor apodeictic certainty. We could only say, "Common experience teaches us so," never "It must be so." They hold as rules that make experience possible in the first place. They instruct us *about* experience, not *through* it.

4. Time is not a discursive or, as it is called, general concept, but a pure form of sensuous intuition. Different times are merely parts of one and the same time, and a representation that can be given only through a single object is an intuition. Moreover, the proposition that different times cannot be simultaneous could not be derived from a general concept. That proposition is synthetic, and so cannot arise from concepts alone. It is therefore contained immediately in the intuition and representation of time.

5. The infinity of time means nothing more than that every determinate quantity of time is possible only through limitations of a single underlying time. The original representation of time must therefore be given as unlimited. The determinate representation of the parts of time, and of every quantity of an object, can be obtained only through limitation. For that reason, the complete representation of time cannot be supplied by concepts, which contain only partial representations. On the contrary, concepts must themselves rest on immediate intuition.

### § 6. Transcendental Exposition of the Concept of Time

Here I may refer to the third point of the metaphysical exposition above, where for the sake of brevity I placed under that heading what is properly transcendental. I will add only this. The concept of change, and with it the concept of motion as change of place, is possible only through and within the representation of time. Change is a combination of contradictory predicates in one and the same object, such as the presence of a thing in a certain place and the absence of that same thing from the same place. If the representation of time were not an inner à priori intuition, no concept of any kind could make the possibility of change intelligible. Only in time can two contradictory determinations be found in one thing, namely one after the other. Our concept of time thus explains the possibility of the large body of synthetic à priori knowledge set out in the general theory of motion, which is far from unfruitful.

### § 7. Conclusions from the Above Concepts

(a) Time is not something that exists on its own. Nor does it inhere in things as an objective determination, which would remain if we abstracted from all the subjective conditions of our intuition of them. In the first case, it would be something real that nonetheless presented no real object to any power of perception. In the second case, as an order or determination inherent in things themselves, it could not precede those things as their condition, nor could it be known or intuited through synthetic à priori propositions. All of this becomes entirely possible once we regard time as merely the subjective condition under which all our intuitions take place. Then this form of inner intuition can be represented prior to its objects, and therefore à priori.

(b) Time is nothing other than the form of inner sense, that is, of our intuition of ourselves and of our inner state. Time cannot be a determination of outer phenomena. It has nothing to do with shape or position, but determines instead the relation of representations within our inner state. Precisely because this inner intuition gives us no shape, we try to make up for the lack by analogies. We represent the course of time as a line extending to infinity, whose parts make up a series of only one dimension. From the properties of this line we infer all the properties of time, with one exception: the parts of the line exist together, whereas the parts of time follow one another. This also makes clear that the representation of time is itself an intuition, since all its relations can be expressed in an outer intuition.

(c) Time is the formal à priori condition of all phenomena whatsoever. Space, as the pure form of outer intuition, is limited as an à priori condition to outer phenomena alone. All representations, by contrast, whether or not they have outer things as their objects, belong in themselves, as determinations of the mind, to our inner state. This inner state is subject to the formal condition of inner intuition, which is time. Time is therefore an à priori condition of all phenomena whatsoever: the immediate condition of all inner phenomena, and thereby the mediate condition of all outer ones. I can say à priori, "All outer phenomena are in space and are determined à priori according to the relations of space." In the same way, from the principle of inner sense I can assert universally, "All phenomena in general, all objects of the senses, are in time and stand necessarily in relations of time."

If we abstract from our inner intuition of ourselves, and from all the outer intuitions that are possible only by virtue of that inner intuition and are presented to us by our faculty of representation, and so take objects as they are in themselves, then time is nothing. It has objective validity only with regard to phenomena, because phenomena are the things we take as objects of our senses. It ceases to be objective the moment we set aside the sensory character of our intuition, the mode of representation peculiar to us, and speak instead of things in general. Time is therefore merely a subjective condition of our human intuition, which is always sensory and arises only insofar as objects affect us. In itself, apart from the mind or subject, time is nothing. Yet with respect to all phenomena, and therefore to everything that can enter our experience, it is necessarily objective. We cannot say, "All things are in time," because the concept of things in general abstracts from every kind of intuition of them, and intuition is precisely the condition under which time belongs to our representation of objects. If we add this condition to the concept and say, "All things as phenomena, that is, as objects of sensory intuition, are in time," then the proposition has full objective validity and a priori universality.

What we have established, then, is the empirical reality of time: its objective validity for every object that can ever be presented to our senses. And since our intuition is always sensory, no object can ever be given to us in experience that does not fall under the conditions of time. At the same time, we deny that time has any claim to absolute reality. We deny, that is, that it belongs to things absolutely, as a condition or property, independent of the form of our sensory intuition. Properties that belong to objects as things in themselves can never be given to us through the senses. This is what constitutes the transcendental ideality of time: if we abstract from the subjective conditions of sensory intuition, time is nothing, and it cannot be counted as subsisting in, or belonging to, objects as things in themselves, apart from their relation to our intuition. This ideality, like that of space, must not be argued for or illustrated by misleading analogies with sensations. Any such argument presupposes that the phenomenon to which these sensory qualities belong has objective reality, whereas here the only objective reality we can find is itself empirical, and regards the object merely as a phenomenon. On this point, the reader may recall the remark made earlier in the discussion of space.

### § 8. Elucidation

Against this theory, which grants time empirical reality but denies it absolute and transcendental reality, intelligent men have raised one objection so consistently that I take it to arise naturally in the mind of every reader for whom these reflections are new. The objection runs as follows. Changes are real, and the continual change in our own representations proves as much, even if one denies the existence of all external phenomena and their changes. But change is possible only in time. Therefore time must be something real. The answer presents no difficulty, and I concede the whole argument. Time is indeed something real: it is the real form of our inner intuition. It therefore has subjective reality with respect to our inner experience. I really do have the representation of time and of my own states as determined within it. Time, then, is to be regarded not as an object but as the way I represent myself as an object. If I could intuit myself, or be intuited by some other being, without this condition of sensibility, then the very determinations that we now represent to ourselves as changes would yield a knowledge in which the representation of time, and with it the representation of change, would not occur at all. The empirical reality of time thus stands, as the condition of all our experience, but absolute reality, for the reasons already given, cannot be granted to it. Time is nothing but the form of our inner intuition. I can certainly say that my representations follow one another, that they are successive; but this means only that I am conscious of them as a succession, in accordance with the form of inner sense. Time is therefore neither a thing in itself nor any objective determination inherent in things. Remove from it the particular condition of our sensibility, and the concept of time vanishes as well. It inheres not in objects themselves but solely in the subject, the mind, that intuits them.

Why is this objection raised so unanimously against our doctrine of time, and by people who can produce no intelligible argument against the ideality of space? The reason is this. They have no hope of proving with strict necessity the absolute reality of space, because idealism stands in their way, and according to idealism the reality of external objects admits of no rigorous proof. By contrast, the reality of the object of our inner sense, myself and my inner state, is evident immediately through consciousness. External objects in space might be mere illusion, but the object of my inner perception is undeniably real. What these critics fail to consider is that both kinds of object, whose reality as representations is not in question, belong alike to the class of phenomena. And every phenomenon has two aspects. The first is the object considered as a thing in itself, apart from the way it is intuited, whose nature for that very reason remains problematic. The second is the form of our intuition of the object, which must be sought not in the object as a thing in itself but in the subject to whom it appears, and which nevertheless belongs really and necessarily to the object as phenomenon.

Time and space are thus two sources of knowledge from which various synthetic cognitions can be drawn a priori. Pure mathematics, built as it is on our knowledge of space and its relations, offers a striking example. Space and time are the two pure forms of all intuition, and for that reason they make synthetic a priori propositions possible. But because these sources of knowledge are merely conditions of our sensibility, they fix their own limits precisely. They do not and cannot present objects as things in themselves, and they apply to objects only insofar as these are considered as sensory phenomena. The realm of phenomena is the only realm in which they are valid, and if we venture beyond it, no further objective use can be made of them. In every other respect, this formal reality of space and time leaves the validity of our empirical knowledge untouched, for our certainty there is equally firm whether these forms necessarily inhere in things themselves or only in our intuition of things.

Those, on the other hand, who assert the absolute reality of space and time, whether as self-subsisting or as properties inhering in things, must find themselves wholly at odds with the principles of experience itself. If they choose the first view and make space and time into substances, as the mathematical natural philosophers do, they must admit two self-subsisting nonentities, infinite and eternal, which exist (though nothing real exists in them) solely in order to contain everything that is real. If they adopt the second view, that of inherence, which certain metaphysical natural philosophers prefer, and regard space and time as relations among things, adjacency in space or succession in time, abstracted from experience and represented confusedly once separated from it, then they are compelled to deny that the a priori doctrines of mathematics hold for real things, such as things in space, or at the very least to deny those doctrines their apodictic, that is, strictly necessary, certainty. Such certainty can never belong to an a posteriori proposition. On this view, moreover, the a priori concepts of space and time are mere creations of the imagination whose true source lies in experience: out of relations abstracted from experience, the imagination has fashioned something that does contain the general features of those relations, yet which cannot be applied without the restrictions that nature has attached to them. The first party gains one advantage, in that it keeps the realm of phenomena open to mathematics. Yet these very conditions, space and time, cause it great embarrassment when the understanding tries to pass beyond that realm. The second party has the advantage that the representations of space and time do not obstruct it when it wishes to judge objects not as phenomena but merely in their relation to the understanding. Lacking, however, any genuine and objectively valid a priori intuition, it can neither explain how a priori mathematical knowledge is possible nor bring the propositions of experience into necessary agreement with those of mathematics. Our theory of the true nature of these two original forms of sensibility overcomes both difficulties.

Finally, it is plain enough that the transcendental aesthetic can contain no more than these two elements, space and time, since every other concept belonging to sensibility, even that of motion, which unites both, presupposes something empirical. Motion presupposes the perception of something movable. But space considered in itself contains nothing movable, so motion must be something found in space only through experience: an empirical datum. Likewise, the transcendental aesthetic cannot count the concept of change among its a priori data, for time itself does not change; only something in time changes. To acquire the concept of change, then, we need the perception of some existing thing and of the succession of its states. We need, in a word, experience.

### § 9. General Remarks on the Transcendental Aesthetic

I. To prevent any misunderstanding, I should first restate as clearly as possible our view of the basic nature of sensory knowledge in general. What we have meant to say is this: all our intuition is nothing but the representation of phenomena. The things we intuit are not in themselves what we represent them as being in intuition, nor are their relations in themselves constituted as they appear to us. If we were to remove the subject, or even only the subjective constitution of our senses in general, then not only the nature and relations of objects in space and time but space and time themselves would disappear, for as phenomena they cannot exist in themselves, but only in us. What objects may be in themselves, apart from the receptivity of our sensibility, remains entirely unknown to us. We know nothing but our own way of perceiving them, a way peculiar to us, which need not belong to every living being, though it belongs to every human being. With this alone are we concerned. Space and time are its pure forms, and sensation is its matter. The forms alone can we know a priori, that is, prior to any actual perception, and such knowledge is therefore called pure intuition. The matter is what in our knowledge is called a posteriori, that is, empirical intuition. The forms belong absolutely and necessarily to our sensibility, whatever kind our sensations may be, while the sensations themselves may vary enormously. Even if we could bring our empirical intuition to the highest possible degree of clarity, we would come not one step closer to knowing the constitution of objects as things in themselves. At best we would arrive at a complete knowledge of our own mode of intuition, our sensibility, and always under the conditions originally attached to the subject, namely space and time. The question "What are objects considered as things in themselves?" would remain unanswerable even after the most thorough examination of the world of phenomena.

It follows that to describe all our sensibility as nothing but a confused representation of things, one that contains only what belongs to them as things in themselves but buries it under a mass of features and partial representations that we cannot consciously tell apart, is to falsify the concept of sensibility and of appearance, and to render our whole doctrine of them empty and useless. The difference between a confused and a clear representation is merely logical and has nothing to do with content. The concept of right, as a sound understanding employs it, doubtless contains everything that the subtlest analysis could draw out of it, even though in ordinary practical use we are not conscious of the many representations it comprises. But we cannot conclude from this that the ordinary concept is a sensory one, containing a mere phenomenon. Right cannot appear as a phenomenon at all; its concept lies in the understanding and represents a property of actions, their moral quality, that belongs to them in themselves. The representation of a body in intuition, by contrast, contains nothing that could belong to an object as a thing in itself. It contains only the appearance of something and the way that appearance affects us. This receptivity of our cognitive faculty is called sensibility, and it remains worlds apart from knowledge of an object in itself, even if we were to examine the content of the phenomenon to its very depths.

It must be acknowledged, then, that the philosophy of Leibniz and Wolff has set every inquiry into the nature and origin of our knowledge on an entirely mistaken footing. It treats the distinction between the sensory and the intellectual as merely logical, when it is plainly transcendental, concerning not only the clarity or obscurity of the two but their content and origin. Sensibility does not give us an indistinct and confused knowledge of objects as things in themselves; it gives us no knowledge of them whatever. On the contrary, as soon as we set aside in thought our own subjective nature, the represented object, together with the properties that sensory intuition ascribed to it, disappears entirely, since it was only this subjective nature that determined the form of the object as a phenomenon.

Among phenomena, we do commonly distinguish what belongs essentially to our intuition of them and holds for the senses of every human being from what belongs to that intuition only accidentally, holding not for sensibility in general but for a particular condition or organization of this or that sense. We are accustomed to say that the first kind of knowledge represents the object itself, while the second presents only a particular appearance of it. This distinction, however, is merely empirical. If we stop there, as people usually do, and fail to regard the empirical intuition itself as a mere phenomenon, as we ought, a phenomenon in which nothing belonging to a thing in itself can be found, then our transcendental distinction is lost. We come to believe that we know things in themselves, although throughout the whole sensory world, however deeply we investigate its objects, we deal with nothing but phenomena. Thus we call the rainbow in a sunlit shower a mere appearance, and the rain the reality, the thing in itself. This is correct enough if we take the latter concept in a merely physical sense: as what, in universal experience and under all varying conditions of sense perception, is known in intuition to be determined in one particular way and no other. But suppose we take this empirical datum generally and ask, without regard to whether it agrees with all our senses, whether anything in it represents an object as a thing in itself. (The raindrops certainly do not, for as phenomena they are empirical objects.) Then the question of how the representation relates to the object is a transcendental one. And the answer is that not only are the raindrops mere phenomena, but their round shape, and even the space through which they fall, are nothing in themselves. All of these are mere modifications or basic forms of our sensory intuition, while the transcendental object remains wholly unknown to us.

The second important concern of our aesthetic is that it should win acceptance not merely as a plausible hypothesis, but should possess as certain a character as can be demanded of any theory meant to function as an organon, an instrument for acquiring knowledge. To convince the reader fully of this certainty, we shall choose a case that makes its validity evident and also clarifies what was said earlier in the transcendental exposition of space.

Suppose, then, that space and time were objective in themselves and were conditions of the possibility of objects as things in themselves. In the first place, it is clear that both furnish a great many apodictic synthetic propositions a priori, and space above all, which is why we shall take it as our example here. Since the propositions of geometry are known synthetically a priori and with apodictic certainty, I ask: Where do you get such propositions, and on what does the understanding rely in arriving at truths so absolutely necessary and universally valid?

There is no other path than through concepts or intuitions, and these are given either a priori or a posteriori. The a posteriori kind, empirical concepts together with the empirical intuition on which they rest, can yield no synthetic proposition that is not itself empirical, a proposition of experience. But an empirical proposition can never possess necessity and absolute universality, and these are the marks of every geometrical proposition. As for the first and only remaining means of reaching such knowledge, namely through mere concepts or through intuitions a priori, it is clear that mere concepts can yield only analytic knowledge, never synthetic. Take the proposition "Two straight lines cannot enclose a space, and with two alone no figure is possible," and try to derive it from the concept of a straight line and the number two. Or take the proposition "A figure can be constructed from three straight lines," and try in the same way to derive it from the mere concept of a straight line and the number three. Every effort is futile, and you find yourself compelled to resort to intuition, as geometry in fact always does. You therefore give yourself an object in intuition. But what kind of intuition is it? Is it pure and a priori, or is it empirical? If empirical, no universally valid proposition can arise from it, let alone an apodictic one, for experience can never supply such a proposition. You must therefore give yourself an object a priori in intuition and base your synthetic proposition on that.

Now suppose there were no faculty of a priori intuition within you. Suppose this subjective condition were not also, as regards its form, the universal a priori condition under which alone the object of this outer intuition is itself possible. Suppose the object, the triangle, were something in itself, with no relation to you as subject. How then could you claim that what lies necessarily in your subjective conditions for constructing a triangle must also necessarily belong to the triangle in itself? You could not add anything new, the figure, to your concepts of three lines as something that must necessarily be found in the object, since on this assumption the object is given prior to your knowledge, not by means of it. If, therefore, space (and time as well) were not a mere form of your intuition, containing the a priori conditions under which alone things can become outer objects for you, conditions without which the objects are nothing in themselves, then you could make no synthetic judgment whatever about outer objects. It is therefore not merely possible or probable but beyond doubt that space and time, as the necessary conditions of all our outer and inner experience, are merely subjective conditions of all our intuition. In relation to these conditions, all objects are mere phenomena, not things in themselves given to us in this particular way. And for this reason a great deal can be said a priori about the form of phenomena, while nothing whatever can be said about the thing in itself that may underlie them.

II. In confirmation of this theory of the ideality of both outer and inner sense, and therefore of all objects of sense as mere phenomena, it is especially worth noting that everything in our knowledge that belongs to intuition contains nothing but relations. (Feelings of pleasure and pain, and the will, which are not forms of knowledge, are excepted.) These are relations of location within an intuition, which is extension; of change of location, which is motion; and of the laws by which such change is determined, which are moving forces. What is present at this or that location, however, or what activity or effect takes place within the things themselves apart from change of location, is not given to us through intuition. Now a thing cannot be known in itself through mere relations. We may therefore fairly conclude that, since outer sense gives us nothing but representations of relations, it can contain in its representation only the relation of the object to the subject, and not the inner nature of the object as it is in itself.

The same holds for inner intuition. This is so not only because the representations of the outer senses make up the material with which the mind is occupied, but also because of time. Time, in which we place these representations, precedes our consciousness of them in experience and underlies them as the formal condition of the way they are placed in the mind; and time contains relations of succession, of simultaneity, and of that which must always be simultaneous with succession, namely the permanent. Now what can precede, as representation, every act of thinking an object is intuition; and when it contains nothing but relations, it is the form of intuition. Since this form presents nothing except insofar as something is placed in the mind, it can be nothing other than the way in which the mind is affected by its own activity: its act of placing representations before itself, and therefore the way in which the mind is affected by itself. In respect of its form, then, it can be nothing other than an inner sense. Everything represented through a sense is, to that extent, phenomenal. We must therefore either refuse to admit any inner sense at all, or else accept that the subject who is the object of that sense can be represented by it only as a phenomenon, and not as the subject would judge itself if its intuition were pure spontaneous activity, that is, if it were intellectual. The whole difficulty comes down to a single question: how can the subject have an inner intuition of itself? Yet this difficulty is shared by every theory. Self-consciousness, or apperception, is the simple representation of the "I." If all the manifold representations in the subject were spontaneously given through that representation alone, our inner intuition would be intellectual. In human beings, however, this consciousness requires an inner perception of the manifold representations already given in the subject. The manner in which those representations are given to the mind without spontaneity must, because of this very difference, the absence of spontaneity, be called sensibility. If the faculty of self-consciousness is to apprehend what lies in the mind, it must affect the mind, and only in this way can it produce an intuition of the self. But the form of this intuition, which lies in the original constitution of the mind, determines, in the representation of time, how the manifold representations are to be combined in the mind. For the subject intuits itself not as it would represent itself immediately and spontaneously, but according to the way the mind is inwardly affected. It therefore intuits itself as it appears, and not as it is.

III. We say that our intuition of external objects, and likewise the subject's intuition of itself, represent both objects and subject in space and time as they affect our senses, that is, as they appear. This is by no means the same as asserting that these objects are mere illusions. When we speak of things as phenomena, the objects themselves, and even the properties we ascribe to them, are regarded as really given. The point is only that, insofar as this or that property depends on the subject's mode of intuition in the relation between the given object and the subject, the object as phenomenon must be distinguished from the object as a thing in itself. So I do not say that bodies merely *seem* to be outside me, or that my soul merely *seems* to be given in my self-consciousness. I do maintain that the properties of space and time, which I treat as the conditions of the existence of both, reside in my mode of intuition and not in the objects in themselves. But it would be my own fault if I turned what I ought to count as phenomenon into mere illusion.

The predicates of a phenomenon can be attached to the object itself in relation to our faculty of sense: the red color or the scent of a rose, for example. Illusion, by contrast, can never be attributed to an object as a predicate, precisely because illusion ascribes to the object in itself what belongs to it only in relation to our faculty of sense, or to the subject in general. A case in point is the pair of "handles" that early telescopic observers once attributed to Saturn, when their instruments could not yet resolve its rings and showed only two odd projections on either side of the planet. Whatever is never found in the object itself, but always in the object's relation to the subject, and which is moreover inseparable from our representation of the object, we call phenomenon. The predicates of space and time are therefore rightly attributed to objects of the senses as such, and there is no illusion in this. If, on the other hand, I ascribe redness to the rose as a thing in itself, or handles to Saturn, or extension to all external objects considered as things in themselves, without regard to the determinate relation of these objects to the subject and without restricting my judgment to that relation, then, and only then, does illusion arise.

My principle of the ideality of all sensuous intuitions prevents this confusion. The opposite course leads straight into it: if we ascribe objective reality to these forms of representation, we cannot avoid turning everything into mere illusion. Suppose we regard space and time as properties that must belong to objects as things in themselves, as the indispensable conditions of those objects' very possibility. Then consider the absurdities this entangles us in. We are forced to admit the existence of two infinite things that are neither substances nor anything genuinely inhering in substances, and yet are the necessary conditions of the existence of all things, and would go on existing even if everything that exists were annihilated. Faced with this, we can hardly blame the good Berkeley for reducing bodies to mere illusion. Indeed, even our own existence, which would then depend on the self-subsisting reality of a mere nonentity such as time, would necessarily be turned into mere illusion along with it, an absurdity no one has yet been guilty of maintaining.

IV. In natural theology we think of an object, God, who can never be an object of intuition for us, and who can never be an object of sensuous intuition even to himself. There we are careful not to attribute the conditions of space and time to his intuition; and all his cognition must be intuition, not thought, since thought always involves limitation. But by what right can we do this if we have made space and time forms of objects as things in themselves, forms that would persist as a priori conditions of the existence of things even if the things themselves were annihilated? As conditions of all existence whatever, space and time would then have to be conditions of the existence of the Supreme Being as well. If we refuse to make them objective forms of all things, the only alternative is to make them subjective forms of our mode of intuition, both external and internal. This mode of intuition is called sensuous because it is not original. It does not itself give the existence of its object, as an intuition that, so far as we can judge, could belong only to the Creator would do. It depends instead on the existence of the object, and is therefore possible only on condition that the subject's representative faculty is affected by that object.

Nor is it necessary to confine intuition in space and time to the sensuous faculty of human beings. It may well be that all finite thinking beings must necessarily agree with us in this respect, although we cannot decide the matter. But even such universality would not make sensibility cease to be sensibility, because it remains a derived intuition (*intuitus derivativus*) rather than an original one (*intuitus originarius*), and so is not an intellectual intuition. Intellectual intuition, for the reasons given above, appears to belong to the Supreme Being alone, and never to a being that is dependent in its existence as well as in its intuition, an intuition that its existence determines and limits in relation to given objects. This last remark, however, should be taken only as an illustration, not as a proof of the truth of our theory of sensibility.

### § 10. Conclusion of the Transcendental Aesthetic

We now have fully before us one part of the solution to the great general problem of transcendental philosophy: how are synthetic propositions a priori possible? We have shown that we possess pure a priori intuitions, namely space and time. When, in an a priori judgment, we go beyond the given concept, we find in these intuitions something that cannot be discovered in the concept itself but is found a priori in the intuition corresponding to it, and that can be synthetically united with it. Yet the judgments these pure intuitions make possible never reach beyond objects of the senses, and they hold only for objects of possible experience.

## Transcendental Logic: Introduction

*Transcendental Doctrine of Elements, Part Two*

### The Idea of a Transcendental Logic

### I. Of Logic in General

Our knowledge arises from two fundamental sources in the mind. The first is the capacity to receive representations, our receptivity to impressions. The second is the power of knowing an object by means of these representations, the spontaneity that produces concepts. Through the first, an object is given to us; through the second, it is thought in relation to that representation, which is merely a determination of the mind. Intuitions and concepts are therefore the elements of all our knowledge, so that neither concepts without some corresponding intuition, nor intuitions without concepts, can yield knowledge. Both can be either pure or empirical. They are empirical when they contain sensation, which presupposes the actual presence of the object, and pure when no sensation is mixed into the representation. Sensation may be called the matter of sensuous knowledge. Pure intuition, accordingly, contains only the form under which something is intuited, and a pure concept contains only the form of thinking an object in general. Only pure intuitions and pure concepts are possible a priori; empirical ones are possible only a posteriori.

We give the name sensibility to the mind's receptivity to impressions, insofar as it is affected in some way. The faculty of producing representations spontaneously, the spontaneity of knowledge, we call understanding. Our nature is so constituted that our intuition can never be anything but sensuous: it contains only the way in which objects affect us. The faculty of thinking the object of sensuous intuition, on the other hand, is the understanding. Neither faculty takes precedence over the other. Without sensibility no object would be given to us, and without understanding no object would be thought. Thoughts without content are empty; intuitions without concepts are blind. It is therefore just as necessary for the mind to make its concepts sensuous, by supplying them with an object in intuition, as to make its intuitions intelligible, by bringing them under concepts. Nor can these faculties exchange their functions. The understanding cannot intuit, and the senses cannot think. Knowledge can arise only from their joint operation. This is no reason, however, to blur the difference between what each contributes; on the contrary, we have every reason to separate and distinguish them with care. We therefore distinguish the science of the rules of sensibility in general, aesthetic, from the science of the rules of the understanding in general, logic.

Logic, in turn, can be considered in two ways: as the logic of the general use of the understanding, or as the logic of its particular use. The first contains the absolutely necessary rules of thought, without which no use of the understanding whatever is possible, and it legislates for the understanding without regard to the differences among the objects to which it may be applied. The logic of the particular use of the understanding contains the rules for thinking correctly about a particular class of objects. The first may be called elementary logic; the second, the organon, or instrument, of this or that particular science. The second is usually taught in the schools as a preparation for the sciences, even though, in the actual course of human reason, it is the last thing we arrive at. It comes only when a science is already mature and needs nothing more than final touches to correct and complete it, since we must already know the objects of a science fairly extensively and thoroughly before we can specify the rules by which a science of them may be established.

General logic is, again, either pure or applied. In pure logic we set aside all the empirical conditions under which the understanding operates: the influence of the senses, the play of fancy or imagination, the laws of memory, the force of habit and inclination, and consequently the sources of prejudice as well. In short, we set aside every cause from which particular cognitions arise, because these causes concern the understanding only under certain circumstances of its application, and knowing them requires experience. Pure general logic therefore deals solely with principles a priori. It is a canon, a set of binding standards, for understanding and reason, but only with respect to the formal side of their use, whatever the content may be, empirical or transcendental. General logic is called applied when it addresses the rules governing the use of the understanding under the subjective empirical conditions that psychology describes. It therefore has empirical principles, although it remains general to the extent that it concerns the use of the understanding without regard to differences among objects. For this reason it is neither a canon of the understanding in general nor an organon of any particular science, but merely a cathartic, a purgative remedy, for the human understanding.

In general logic, then, the part that constitutes pure logic must be carefully separated from the part that constitutes applied logic, which is nonetheless still general. Only the former is properly a science, brief and dry, as the methodical presentation of an elementary doctrine of the understanding ought to be. Logicians must therefore always keep two rules in mind:

1. As general logic, it abstracts from all content of the understanding's cognitions and from all differences among objects, and deals with nothing but the mere form of thought.

2. As pure logic, it has no empirical principles. It therefore borrows nothing from psychology, contrary to what is commonly believed, and psychology has no influence on the canon of the understanding. Pure logic is a demonstrated doctrine, and everything in it must be certain entirely a priori.

What I call applied logic departs from the usual sense of the term, according to which it would consist of exercises for the student based on the rules that pure logic supplies. In my sense, it is a representation of the understanding and of the rules for its necessary use *in concreto*, that is, under the contingent conditions of the subject, which may hinder or assist that use and which are all given only empirically.
