Applied logic therefore treats of attention, its obstacles and consequences, the origin of error, and the states of doubt, hesitation, conviction, and so on. Pure general logic stands to it as pure morality, which contains only the necessary moral laws of a free will, stands to practical ethics in the narrower sense. Practical ethics considers those laws under all the obstacles of feelings, inclinations, and passions to which human beings are more or less subject, and it can never yield a true and demonstrated science, because, like applied logic, it requires empirical and psychological principles.

### II. Of Transcendental Logic

General logic, as we have seen, abstracts from all content of cognition, that is, from every relation of cognition to its object, and considers only the logical form in the relations of cognitions to one another: the form of thought in general. But since there are pure as well as empirical intuitions, as the Transcendental Aesthetic has shown, a similar distinction might be drawn between pure and empirical thinking of objects. There would then be a kind of logic that does not abstract from all content of cognition, for a logic containing only the rules of the pure thinking of an object would exclude every cognition of empirical content. Such a logic would also investigate the origin of our cognitions of objects, insofar as that origin cannot be attributed to the objects themselves. General logic, by contrast, has nothing to do with the origin of our cognitions. It considers our representations, whether they are originally given a priori within us or are merely empirical in origin, solely according to the laws the understanding follows when it uses them in relation to one another in thinking. General logic therefore treats only of the form of the understanding, which can be applied to representations whatever their source.

Here I must make a remark that the reader should keep firmly in mind through everything that follows. Not every a priori cognition is to be called transcendental, but only that by which we know *that* and *how* certain representations, whether intuitions or concepts, are applied or are possible purely a priori. In other terms, only the a priori possibility of cognition and its a priori use are transcendental. Thus neither space nor any a priori geometrical determination of space is a transcendental representation. Only the knowledge that such representations are not empirical in origin, together with the knowledge of how they can nevertheless relate a priori to objects of experience, can be called transcendental. Likewise, the application of space to objects in general would be transcendental; restricted to objects of the senses, it is empirical. The distinction between the transcendental and the empirical therefore belongs only to the critique of cognitions and does not concern the relation of those cognitions to their objects.

It may be that there are concepts which relate a priori to objects, not as pure or sensuous intuitions, but solely as acts of pure thought. They would be concepts, then, but of neither empirical nor aesthetic origin. In that expectation we form in advance the idea of a science of pure understanding and of rational knowledge, by which we think objects entirely a priori. A science of this kind, which would determine the origin, scope, and objective validity of such cognitions, must be called transcendental logic. Unlike general logic, it does not deal with the laws of understanding and reason in relation to both empirical and pure rational cognitions indiscriminately, but only insofar as these laws relate a priori to objects.

### III. Of the Division of General Logic into Analytic and Dialectic

There is an old question with which people have tried to drive logicians into a corner, forcing them either to fall back on wretched sophistries or to confess their ignorance and, with it, the emptiness of their entire art. The question is: "What is truth?" The nominal definition of truth, that it is the agreement of a cognition with its object, is taken for granted in asking it. What is wanted in the answer is a universal and reliable criterion of the truth of any cognition whatever.

Knowing which questions one may reasonably ask is already a considerable proof of good sense and insight. If a question is absurd in itself and admits of no rational answer, then besides embarrassing the person who poses it, it runs the risk of luring an unwary listener into absurd replies. The result is the ridiculous spectacle the ancients described: one person milking a he-goat while another holds a sieve beneath it, the first attempting the impossible and the second trying to catch its nonexistent yield in a vessel that could hold nothing anyway.

If truth consists in the agreement of a cognition with its object, then that object must thereby be distinguished from all others, for a cognition is false if it does not agree with the object to which it refers, even if it contains something that might hold true of other objects. A universal criterion of truth, however, would be one valid for all cognitions regardless of their objects. In such a criterion we abstract from all the content of a cognition, from every relation to its object, and yet truth concerns precisely this content. It is therefore plainly absurd to ask for a mark of the truth of this content, and a criterion of truth that is both sufficient and universal cannot possibly be found. Since we have already called the content of a cognition its matter, we may put it this way: no universal criterion of the truth of cognition with respect to its matter can be demanded, because the demand contradicts itself.

With regard to cognition considered merely in its form, setting aside all content, it is equally clear that logic, insofar as it sets out the universal and necessary rules of the understanding, must supply criteria of truth in those very rules. Whatever contradicts them is false, because the understanding would then be contradicting its own universal rules of thought, and so contradicting itself. These criteria, however, concern only the form of truth, that is, of thought in general. To that extent they are entirely correct, but they are not sufficient. A cognition may conform perfectly to logical form, may contain no contradiction, and still fail to agree with its object. The merely logical criterion of truth, namely the agreement of a cognition with the universal and formal laws of understanding and reason, is therefore only the *conditio sine qua non*, the negative condition of all truth. Logic can go no further than this. It has no test for detecting error that lies not in the form but in the content of a cognition.

General logic, then, breaks down the entire formal business of understanding and reason into its elements and presents them as the principles of every logical assessment of our cognitions. This part of logic may therefore be called analytic, and it is at least the negative touchstone of truth, since all cognitions must first be examined and judged by these rules before we go on to investigate their content and ask whether they contain positive truth about their object. But because the mere form of a cognition, however well it agrees with logical laws, is not enough to establish material, or objective, truth, no one can presume to judge or assert anything about objects by means of logic alone. One must first acquire well-founded information about them independently of logic, and only then examine, according to logical laws, how that information is used and connected into a coherent whole, or, better still, simply test it against those laws. Nevertheless, there is something so seductive about possessing so plausible an art, one that gives all our cognitions the form of the understanding even when we are sorely lacking in their content, that general logic, which is merely a canon for judging, has been used as an organon for actually producing objective assertions, or rather for producing the semblance of them. In this way it has been grossly misused. General logic, when it is taken for an organon, is called dialectic.

However varied the meanings the ancients gave to this term for a science or an art, we can safely infer from the way they actually used it that for them it was nothing but a logic of illusion: a sophistical art for lending ignorance, and even deliberate sophistry, the appearance of truth. Its practitioners imitated the thoroughness of method that logic demands and used their "topics," the stock catalog of commonplaces from which arguments were drawn, to disguise empty pretensions. It may therefore be taken as a sound and useful warning that general logic, when treated as an organon, must always be a logic of illusion; that is, it must be dialectical. General logic teaches us nothing whatever about the content of our knowledge. It gives us only the formal conditions under which our thoughts agree with the understanding, and these conditions have no bearing on objects and are entirely indifferent to them. Any attempt to use it as an instrument, an organon, for extending and enlarging the range of our knowledge must therefore end in empty chatter, in which anyone can defend or attack any assertion whatever with some semblance of truth.

Such instruction is wholly beneath the dignity of philosophy. For these reasons we have chosen to call this part of logic "dialectic" in the sense of a critique of dialectical illusion, and we ask that the term be understood that way here.

### IV. On the Division of Transcendental Logic into Transcendental Analytic and Dialectic

In transcendental logic we isolate the understanding, just as in the transcendental aesthetic we isolated sensibility, and we select from our knowledge only that part of thought which originates in the understanding alone. The exercise of this pure knowledge, however, depends on one condition: objects to which it can be applied must be given to us in intuition. Without intuition, all our knowledge lacks objects and is therefore entirely empty. That part of transcendental logic which deals with the elements of the understanding's pure knowledge, and with the principles without which no object whatever can be thought, is transcendental analytic. It is at the same time a logic of truth, because no piece of knowledge can contradict it without also losing all content, that is, all reference to an object, and therefore all truth. Yet we are very easily tempted to use these pure concepts and principles of the understanding on their own, and even beyond the boundaries of experience, although experience is the only source from which we can obtain the material, the objects, to which those pure concepts can be applied. The understanding thus runs the risk of using empty sophistries to make a material and objective use of what are merely the formal principles of pure understanding, and of passing judgment indiscriminately on objects that are not given to us and perhaps cannot be given to us in any way at all. This kind of logic ought properly to be only a canon, a standard for judging the empirical use of the understanding. It is misused when we try to employ it as an organon for the universal and unlimited exercise of the understanding, and when we attempt, with pure understanding alone, to judge synthetically about objects in general, to make affirmations about them, and to determine their nature. In that case the exercise of pure understanding becomes dialectical. The second part of our transcendental logic must therefore be a critique of dialectical illusion, and we shall call this critique transcendental dialectic. We do not mean by this an art of producing such illusion dogmatically, an art unfortunately all too common among the practitioners of metaphysical conjuring tricks. We mean a critique of understanding and reason with respect to their hyperphysical use, their use beyond the physical world of experience. This critique will expose the groundlessness of the pretensions of these two faculties, invalidate their claim to discover and extend our knowledge by transcendental principles alone, and show that their proper employment is to test the judgments of pure understanding and to guard it against sophistical delusion.

## Transcendental Analytic, Book I: The Analytic of Concepts

### The Transcendental Analytic (§ 1)

Transcendental analytic is the dissection of our entire a priori knowledge into the elements of the understanding's pure cognition. To accomplish this, four conditions must be met. First, the concepts must be pure and not empirical. Second, they must belong not to intuition and sensibility but to thought and understanding. Third, they must be elementary concepts, and as such entirely different from derived or compound ones. Fourth, our table of these elementary concepts must be complete, filling the whole domain of pure understanding. Such completeness in a science cannot be accepted with confidence on the strength of a mere rough estimate, as though the science were an aggregate assembled through repeated experiments and attempts. The completeness we require is possible only through an idea of the totality of the understanding's a priori knowledge, and through the division of concepts that this idea determines. It is possible, that is, only through their connection in a system. Pure understanding distinguishes itself not only from everything empirical but completely from all sensibility. It is a unity that is self-subsistent, self-sufficient, and incapable of being enlarged by any additions from outside. The sum of its knowledge therefore constitutes a system that must be determined by and contained under an idea, and the completeness and articulation of this system can at the same time provide a test of the correctness and genuineness of every component of knowledge that belongs to it. This entire part of transcendental logic consists of two books: one contains the concepts of pure understanding, the other its principles.

### The Analytic of Concepts (§ 2)

By "analytic of concepts" I do not mean the analysis of concepts, the usual procedure in philosophical inquiry of taking whatever concepts present themselves, dissecting their content, and so making them clear. I mean the dissection, rarely attempted until now, of the faculty of understanding itself. Its purpose is to investigate the possibility of a priori concepts by seeking them in the understanding alone, as their birthplace, and by analyzing the pure use of this faculty. This is the proper task of a transcendental philosophy; everything else belongs to the logical treatment of concepts in philosophy generally. We shall therefore trace the pure concepts back to their seeds and first beginnings in the human understanding. There they lie ready until experience gives them occasion to develop, and there the same understanding, freeing them from the empirical conditions attached to them, presents them in their unmixed purity.

### Chapter I. On the Transcendental Clue to the Discovery of All Pure Concepts of the Understanding

#### Introduction. § 3

When we set a faculty of knowledge to work, various concepts come to light according to varying circumstances. They make this faculty known and gather into a collection that is more or less extensive, depending on how much time or insight has been devoted to considering them. Where this process, conducted mechanically, so to speak, will end cannot be determined with certainty. Moreover, concepts discovered in this haphazard way by no means present themselves in order or in systematic unity. In the end they are simply paired according to their resemblances and arranged in series by the amount of their content, from the simpler to the more complex. These series are anything but systematic, though they are not entirely without a certain kind of method in their construction.

Transcendental philosophy has the advantage, and also the duty, of searching for its concepts according to a principle. These concepts spring pure and unmixed from the understanding as an absolute unity, and so they must be connected with one another according to a single concept or idea. Such a connection, moreover, supplies a ready-made rule by which every pure concept of the understanding can be assigned its proper place, and by which the completeness of the whole system can be determined a priori. Without it, both would depend on mere choice or chance.

#### Section I. On the Logical Use of the Understanding in General. § 4

The understanding was defined above only negatively, as a nonsensory faculty of knowledge. Independently of sensibility, however, we cannot have any intuition at all, so the understanding is not a faculty of intuition. Apart from intuition, the only other mode of knowledge is through concepts. The knowledge of every understanding, or at least of every human understanding, is therefore knowledge through concepts: not intuitive but discursive. All intuitions, being sensory, rest on affections, on the ways the senses are acted upon; concepts, by contrast, rest on functions. By "function" I mean the unity of the act of arranging various representations under one common representation. Concepts, then, are grounded in the spontaneity of thought, just as sensory intuitions are grounded in the receptivity of impressions. The understanding can make no other use of these concepts than to judge by means of them. Since no representation except an intuition relates immediately to its object, a concept never relates immediately to an object but only to some other representation of it, whether that be an intuition or itself a concept. A judgment, therefore, is the mediate knowledge of an object: the representation of a representation of it. In every judgment there is a concept that holds for many other concepts and that, among these, also comprehends a given representation, which in turn is related immediately to an object. In the judgment "All bodies are divisible," for example, the concept of the divisible applies to various other concepts. Here, however, it is applied specifically to the concept of body, and the concept of body relates to certain appearances that present themselves to us. These objects are thus represented mediately through the concept of divisibility. All judgments, accordingly, are functions of unity among our representations. Instead of an immediate representation, a higher one that comprises it along with various others is used for knowing the object, and many possible cognitions are thereby gathered into one. We can, moreover, reduce all acts of the understanding to judgments, so that the understanding may be represented as the faculty of judging. For, as was said above, it is a faculty of thought, and thought is knowledge by means of concepts. But concepts, as predicates of possible judgments, relate to some representation of an object not yet determined. The concept of body, for instance, signifies something, such as metal, that can be known through that concept. It is a concept only because other representations are contained under it, through which it can relate to objects. It is therefore the predicate of a possible judgment, such as "Every metal is a body." All the functions of the understanding can therefore be discovered if we can exhibit completely the functions of unity in judgments. The following section will show that this can be done quite easily.

#### Section II. On the Logical Function of the Understanding in Judgments. § 5

If we abstract from all the content of a judgment and consider only its intellectual form, we find that the function of thought in judgment falls under four headings, each containing three moments. They can be conveniently set out in the following table:

1. **Quantity of judgments:** Universal, Particular, Singular
2. **Quality:** Affirmative, Negative, Infinite
3. **Relation:** Categorical, Hypothetical, Disjunctive
4. **Modality:** Problematic, Assertoric, Apodictic

Since this division appears to differ from the usual practice of logicians in some respects, though not essential ones, the following observations may help prevent misunderstandings that might otherwise arise.

1. Logicians rightly say that when judgments are used in syllogisms, singular judgments may be treated like universal ones. Precisely because a singular judgment has no extension at all, its predicate cannot apply to one part of what is contained in the subject concept while being excluded from the rest. The predicate holds for the whole concept, just as if that concept were general and had an extension to the whole of which the predicate applied. But compare a singular judgment with a general one merely as a piece of knowledge, with respect to quantity. The singular judgment stands to the general one as unity stands to infinity, and is therefore essentially different in itself. If, then, we assess a singular judgment (*judicium singulare*) not merely by its internal validity as a judgment but also as knowledge in general, by its quantity compared with that of other cognitions, it is entirely different from a general judgment (*judicium commune*). It therefore deserves a separate place in a complete table of the moments of thought, although this would not be necessary in a logic confined to the use of judgments in relation to one another.

2. In the same way, transcendental logic must distinguish infinite judgments from affirmative ones, even though general logic rightly classes them together as affirmative. General logic abstracts from all content of the predicate, even when that predicate is negative, and considers only whether it is affirmed or denied of the subject. Transcendental logic, however, also considers the worth or content of this logical affirmation, an affirmation made by means of a merely negative predicate, and asks how much the sum of our knowledge gains from it. Suppose I say of the soul, "It is not mortal." By this negative judgment I would at least ward off an error. But in the proposition "The soul is not-mortal," I have, as far as logical form is concerned, actually affirmed something, since I thereby place the soul in the unlimited domain of beings that are not mortal. The mortal occupies one part of the whole domain of possible beings and the not-mortal occupies the other, so the proposition affirms neither more nor less than that the soul is one of the infinite multitude of things that remain once I have removed everything mortal. All this procedure achieves is to limit the infinite domain of all possible beings to the extent that the mortal is excluded from it, while the soul is placed in what remains. Yet even after this exclusion, the remaining part is still infinite, and further parts could be removed from the whole domain again and again without in the least enlarging or positively determining our concept of the soul. These judgments, infinite with respect to their logical extension, are therefore merely limitative with respect to the content of their knowledge. They deserve a place in our transcendental table of all the moments of thought in judgment, because the function of the understanding they exercise may prove important in the field of its pure a priori knowledge.

3. All relations of thought in judgments are those (a) of the predicate to the subject, (b) of a ground to its consequence, and (c) of a divided cognition and all the members of the division to one another. In the first class we consider only two concepts; in the second, two judgments; in the third, several judgments in relation to one another. The hypothetical proposition "If perfect justice exists, the obstinately wicked are punished" really contains the relation between two propositions: "Perfect justice exists" and "The obstinately wicked are punished." Whether these propositions are true in themselves is not decided here. The judgment thinks nothing but a certain consequence. Finally, the disjunctive judgment contains a relation among two or more propositions. This is a relation not of consequence but of logical opposition, insofar as the domain of one excludes that of the other. At the same time, however, it contains a relation of community, insofar as all the propositions taken together fill the domain of the cognition in question. The disjunctive judgment therefore expresses the relation of the parts of the whole domain of a cognition, since the domain of each part complements that of the others, and each contributes to the sum total of the divided cognition. Take the proposition "The world exists either through blind chance, or through inner necessity, or through an external cause." Each of these alternatives covers one part of the domain of our possible knowledge concerning the existence of a world; all of them together cover the whole. To remove the cognition from one of these domains is to place it in one of the others, and to place it in one is to remove it from the rest. A disjunctive judgment therefore involves a certain community of cognitions: they exclude one another, yet in doing so they jointly determine the true cognition, since taken together they make up the complete content of a particular given cognition. This is all I find it necessary to remark here for the sake of what follows.

4. The modality of judgments is a quite distinctive function. Its defining characteristic is that it contributes nothing to the content of a judgment, since apart from quantity, quality, and relation nothing else constitutes that content. It concerns only the value of the copula, the linking word "is," in relation to thought in general. Problematic judgments are those in which affirmation or denial is taken as merely possible, entertained at will (*ad libitum*). In assertoric judgments we regard the proposition as actual, that is, true; in apodictic judgments we regard it as necessary. It is as if thought were, in the first case, a function of the understanding; in the second, of judgment; and in the third, of reason, a remark that will be explained later. Thus the two judgments whose relation constitutes a hypothetical judgment, the antecedent and the consequent (*antecedens et consequens*), are merely problematic, and so are the members of the division whose reciprocity constitutes a disjunctive judgment. In the example given above, the proposition "There exists perfect justice" is not stated assertorically but as a judgment entertained at will, one that someone may choose to adopt; only the consequence is assertoric. Hence such judgments may be plainly false and yet, taken problematically, be conditions of our knowledge of the truth. The proposition "The world exists by blind chance," for instance, has only problematic significance within the disjunctive judgment. One may accept it for the moment, and it helps us find the true proposition, much as identifying the wrong road among all the roads one might take helps a traveler find the right one. The problematic proposition, then, expresses only logical possibility, which is not objective possibility. It expresses a free choice to allow such a proposition to count as valid, a merely arbitrary admission of it into the understanding. The assertoric proposition speaks of logical actuality or truth. In a hypothetical syllogism, for example, the antecedent appears in problematic form in the major premise and in assertoric form in the minor premise, and this shows that the proposition is already bound up with the understanding according to its laws. The apodictic proposition thinks the assertoric one as determined by these very laws of the understanding, and therefore as affirming a priori; in this way it expresses logical necessity. Everything here is incorporated into the understanding by degrees: first we judge something problematically, then we accept it assertorically as true, and finally we affirm it as inseparably united with the understanding, that is, as necessary and apodictic. We may therefore safely regard these three functions of modality as so many moments of thought.

#### Section III. On the Pure Concepts of the Understanding, or Categories. § 6

As has been said repeatedly, general logic abstracts from all content of knowledge and expects representations to be supplied from some other source, so that it can convert them into concepts by analysis. Transcendental logic, by contrast, has before it the manifold content of a priori sensibility, which the transcendental aesthetic presents to it in order to give material to the pure concepts of the understanding. Without this material, transcendental logic would have no content and would be completely empty. Space and time contain an infinite variety of determinations of pure a priori intuition. Yet they are also conditions of the mind's receptivity, the only conditions under which it can receive representations of objects, and they must therefore always affect the concept of those objects. But the spontaneity of thought requires that this variety first be gone through in a certain way, taken up, and connected, so that knowledge can afterward be formed from it. This process I call synthesis.

By synthesis in its most general sense I mean the act of joining different representations together and grasping their variety in one cognition. Such synthesis is pure when the variety is given not empirically but a priori, as is the variety in space and time. Our representations must be given before any analysis of them can take place, and no concept can arise analytically as far as its content is concerned. The synthesis of a manifold, however, whether given a priori or empirically, is the first requirement for producing knowledge. Such knowledge may at first be crude and confused, and therefore in need of analysis. Still, synthesis is what first gathers the elements of our knowledge and unites them into a certain content, and it is therefore the first thing we must attend to if we wish to investigate the origin of our knowledge.

Synthesis in general, as we shall see later, is the mere work of the imagination: a blind but indispensable function of the soul, without which we would have no knowledge at all, but of whose operation we are seldom even conscious. To bring this synthesis to concepts, however, is a function of the understanding, and it is through this function that we first obtain knowledge in the proper sense of the term.

Pure synthesis, represented in general, yields the pure concept of the understanding. By pure synthesis I mean a synthesis that rests on a ground of a priori synthetic unity. Our counting, for example, is a synthesis according to concepts, and this is more noticeable with large numbers, because it proceeds according to a common ground of unity, such as the decade, the grouping of units by tens. Through this concept, the unity in the synthesis of the manifold becomes necessary.

Through analysis, different representations are brought under one concept, an operation dealt with by general logic. Transcendental logic, on the other hand, has the task of bringing to concepts not representations but the pure synthesis of representations. The first thing which must be given to us for the a priori cognition of all objects is the manifold of pure intuition. The second is the synthesis of this manifold by the imagination, although this synthesis still yields no cognition. The concepts that give unity to this pure synthesis, and that consist solely in the representation of this necessary synthetic unity, supply the third requirement for the cognition of an object. These concepts are given by the understanding.

The same function that gives unity to the various representations in a judgment also gives unity to the bare synthesis of various representations in an intuition, and we call this unity the pure concept of the understanding. The understanding, through the very operations by which it produced the logical form of a judgment in concepts by means of analytic unity, also introduces a transcendental content into its representations by means of the synthetic unity of the manifold in intuition. That is why these representations are called pure concepts of the understanding, and why they apply a priori to objects, which general logic cannot accomplish.

In this way there arise exactly as many pure concepts of the understanding, applying a priori to objects of intuition in general, as there are logical functions in all possible judgments. The understanding contains no function or faculty other than those enumerated in that table. Following Aristotle, we shall call these concepts *categories*, since our purpose was originally the same as his, however greatly our execution of it differs.

**Table of the Categories**

1. *Of Quantity*
   - Unity
   - Plurality
   - Totality
2. *Of Quality*
   - Reality
   - Negation
   - Limitation
3. *Of Relation*
   - Of Inherence and Subsistence (*substantia et accidens*, substance and accident)
   - Of Causality and Dependence (cause and effect)
   - Of Community (reciprocity between agent and patient)
4. *Of Modality*
   - Possibility and Impossibility
   - Existence and Non-existence
   - Necessity and Contingency

This, then, is a list of all the original pure concepts of synthesis that the understanding contains a priori. These concepts alone entitle it to be called a pure understanding, because only through them can it make the manifold of intuition intelligible and so think an object of intuition. The division has been made systematically, from a common principle: the faculty of judgment, which is the same thing as the faculty of thinking. It did not arise rhapsodically, from a haphazard hunt for pure concepts. A search of that kind proceeds by induction alone, so we could never be certain of the full number of such concepts, and we could never understand why precisely these concepts, and no others, reside in the pure understanding. To search out these fundamental concepts was a project worthy of so acute a thinker as Aristotle. Lacking any guiding principle, however, he collected them as they happened to occur to him. He first gathered ten, which he called categories, or predicaments. Later he believed he had found five more, which were added under the name of post-predicaments. Even so, his list remained defective. It also includes several modes of pure sensibility: *quando* ("when"), *ubi* ("where"), *situs* ("position"), as well as *prius* ("before") and *simul* ("at the same time"). It further includes an empirical concept, *motus* ("motion"). None of these can belong to this genealogical register of the pure understanding. Moreover, the list counts among the original concepts some that are derivative, *actio* ("action") and *passio* ("passion," or being acted upon), while some of the original concepts are missing altogether.

The categories, as the true primitive concepts of the pure understanding, also have their own pure derivative concepts. In a complete system of transcendental philosophy these could by no means be passed over, but in a merely critical essay we must be content simply to mention the fact.

I ask permission to call these pure but derivative concepts of the understanding the *predicables* of the pure understanding, as distinguished from the *predicaments*. Once we possess the original and primitive concepts, the derivative and subsidiary ones are easily added, and the family tree of the understanding can be drawn in full. Since my present aim is to set out the principles of a system and not a complete system, I reserve this task for another occasion. Anyone can easily carry it out by consulting the textbooks of ontology. Under the category of causality, for example, he would place the predicables of force, action, and passion; under that of community, those of presence and resistance; under the categories of modality, those of coming into being, passing away, and change; and so on with the rest. When the categories are combined with the modes of pure sensibility, or with one another, they yield a great number of derivative a priori concepts. A complete enumeration of these would be a useful and not unpleasant occupation, but here it is entirely dispensable.

I deliberately omit definitions of the categories in this treatise. I shall analyze these concepts only so far as the doctrine of method, which is to form part of this critique, requires. In a system of pure reason I could rightly be asked for their definitions. Supplying them here, however, would only hide the main aim of our investigation from view, and it would raise doubts and objections that can quite properly be postponed to another occasion without harm to our principal purpose. Even from the little we have said, it should be clear that compiling a complete vocabulary of pure concepts, with all the necessary explanations, is not only possible but easy. The compartments already exist and need only be filled. A systematic *topic* such as this one, meaning an ordered scheme of headings under which each concept has its proper place, indicates with perfect precision where each concept belongs and readily reveals any compartment that remains empty.

§ 7

Our table of categories prompts some considerations of real importance, and these may have significant consequences for the scientific form of all rational cognition. The table is useful in the theoretical part of philosophy. Indeed, it is indispensable for sketching the complete plan of any science that rests on a priori concepts, and for dividing such a science mathematically according to fixed principles. This is evident from the fact that it contains all the elementary concepts of the understanding, and even the form of a system of these concepts within the understanding itself. It therefore indicates all the component moments of a projected speculative science, and also its internal arrangement, as I have shown elsewhere, in the *Metaphysical Principles of Natural Science*. Some of these observations follow.

I. This table contains four classes of concepts of the understanding, and it can first be divided into two groups. The first group relates to objects of intuition, both pure and empirical. The second relates to the existence of these objects, either in their relation to one another or in their relation to the understanding.

I would call the first group the *mathematical* categories and the second the *dynamical* categories. As we can see, the first group contains no correlates; these are found only in the second. This difference must have some ground in the nature of the human understanding.

II. Each class always contains the same number of categories, namely three. This fact also calls for reflection, because every other a priori division by means of concepts must be a dichotomy. In addition, the third category in each triad always arises from combining the second with the first.

Thus totality is simply plurality regarded as unity. Limitation is reality combined with negation. Community is the causality of a substance that reciprocally determines other substances and is determined by them. Finally, necessity is existence given through possibility itself. It should not be supposed, however, that the third category is merely a derivative concept and not a primitive concept of the pure understanding. Combining the first and second to produce the third requires a distinct act of the understanding, one by no means identical with the acts exercised in the first and second. The concept of a number, which belongs to the category of totality, is not always possible where the concepts of multitude and unity are present, as in the representation of the infinite. Likewise, if I combine the concept of a cause with that of a substance, it does not follow that I will understand the concept of *influence*, meaning how one substance can be the cause of something in another substance. A distinct act of the understanding is clearly required here, and the same holds in the other cases.

III. In one category, community, which belongs to the third class, it is harder than in the others to see how it corresponds to the disjunctive judgment that stands opposite it in the table of logical functions.

To assure ourselves of this correspondence, we must observe that in every disjunctive judgment the sphere of the judgment, meaning everything contained in it, is represented as a whole divided into parts. No part can be contained in another, so the parts are thought of as coordinate with one another and not subordinate. They therefore determine one another reciprocally, as in an aggregate, and not in one direction only, as in a linear series. If one member of the division is posited, all the others are excluded, and conversely.

A similar connection is thought in a whole made up of things. In such a whole, one thing is not subordinated, as effect, to another as the cause of its existence. Each is coordinated with the others simultaneously and reciprocally, as a cause with respect to their determination, as in a body whose parts mutually attract and repel one another. This kind of connection is entirely different from the one found in the mere relation of cause to effect, or of ground to consequence. In that relation the consequence does not in turn determine the ground, and therefore does not form a whole together with it, just as the Creator does not form a whole together with the world. The understanding represents to itself the sphere of a divided concept, and it uses the same procedure when it thinks of a thing as divisible. In the first case, the members of the division exclude one another and yet are connected within one sphere. In the same way, the understanding represents the parts of a divisible thing as each having an existence of its own, as substances independent of one another, and yet as united in one whole.

§ 8

The transcendental philosophy of the ancients contains one further principal heading of pure concepts of the understanding. The ancients did not count these concepts among the categories, yet they held that, as a priori concepts, these ought to be valid of objects. In that case, however, they would increase the number of the categories, which is impossible. They are expressed in the proposition so famous among the scholastics: *Quodlibet ens est unum, verum, bonum*, "Every being is one, true, and good." The inferences drawn from this principle proved to be mere tautologies, and it keeps a place in modern metaphysics only as a courtesy. Still, a thought that has persisted for so long, however empty it may seem, deserves an inquiry into its origin. Its persistence justifies the suspicion that it rests on some law of the understanding which, as often happens, has simply been misinterpreted. These supposed transcendental predicates are in fact nothing but logical requirements and criteria of all cognition of objects, and they take as the basis of that cognition the categories of quantity: unity, plurality, and totality. These categories ought to be taken as material conditions, belonging to the possibility of things themselves. The scholastics, however, used them in a merely formal sense, as logical requirements of all cognition, and then, quite carelessly, turned these criteria of thought into properties of objects as things in themselves.

Every cognition of an object contains, first, unity of concept. This may be called *qualitative unity*, provided we understand by it only the unity in our connection of the manifold, such as the unity of theme in a play, a speech, or a story. Second, there is truth with respect to the consequences drawn from the concept. The more true consequences follow from a given concept, the more criteria there are of its objective reality. This might be called the *qualitative plurality* of characteristic marks that belong to a concept as their common ground but are not thought in it as a quantity. Third, there is *perfection*, which consists in the plurality leading back to the unity of the concept and agreeing completely with that concept and with no other. This may be called *qualitative completeness*. These logical criteria of the possibility of cognition, then, are simply the three categories of quantity, altered to suit an unauthorized way of applying them. In the three categories proper, the unity in the production of a quantum must be homogeneous throughout. Here they have been transformed solely to connect heterogeneous elements of cognition in a single act of consciousness, by means of the quality of the cognition, which is the principle of that connection.

Thus the criterion of the possibility of a concept, as distinct from the possibility of its object, is its definition. In a definition, the unity of the concept, the truth of everything that can be immediately deduced from it, and the completeness of what has been deduced together make up the requirements for reconstructing the whole concept. The criterion or test of a hypothesis works the same way. The first requirement is the intelligibility of the principle of explanation adopted, or its unity, without the help of any subsidiary hypothesis. The second is the truth of the consequences derived from it, meaning their consistency with one another and with experience. The last is the completeness of the principle in explaining these consequences, which must point back to neither more nor less than what was assumed in the hypothesis, restoring analytically and a posteriori what was thought synthetically and a priori. The concepts of unity, truth, and perfection, therefore, add nothing to the transcendental table of categories, which is complete without them. We have only taken the three categories of quantity, set aside their application to objects of experience, and used them as general logical laws of the agreement of cognition with itself.

### Chapter II. Of the Deduction of the Pure Concepts of the Understanding

#### Section I. Of the Principles of a Transcendental Deduction in General

§ 9

Teachers of law, when they discuss rights and claims, distinguish in any legal case between the question of right (*quid juris*) and the question of fact (*quid facti*). They demand proof of both, and they call the proof of the first, which establishes the right or legal claim, the *deduction*. We use a great many empirical concepts without objection from anyone. Even without attempting any deduction, we consider ourselves justified in assigning them a meaning and an attributed significance, because experience is always at hand to demonstrate their objective reality. There are also, however, usurped concepts, such as *fortune* and *fate*. These circulate with almost universal indulgence, yet they are occasionally challenged with the question "*quid juris?*", or "by what right?" In such cases we have great difficulty finding any deduction for them, since we can produce no clear title, either from experience or from reason, on which a claim to use them could rest.

Human cognition is a highly varied web of many concepts, and some of these are destined for pure a priori use, independent of all experience. Their title to such use always requires a deduction, because proofs from experience cannot justify it. We must know how these concepts can relate to objects without being derived from experience. I therefore call an inquiry into the way concepts can relate a priori to objects their *transcendental deduction*. I distinguish it from their *empirical deduction*, which shows how a concept is acquired through experience and through reflection on experience. Empirical deduction therefore concerns not the legitimacy of our concepts but only the fact of our having acquired them in a particular way. We have already seen that we possess two entirely different kinds of concepts that nonetheless agree in this: both relate to objects completely a priori. These are the concepts of space and time, as forms of sensibility, and the categories, as pure concepts of the understanding. An empirical deduction of either kind would be wasted effort, because what distinguishes their nature is precisely that they relate to their objects without borrowing anything from experience for the representation of those objects. If a deduction of these concepts is needed, it must therefore always be transcendental.

Even so, with these concepts, as with all our cognition, we can find in experience the occasioning causes of their production, though not the principle of their possibility. The impressions of the senses provide the first occasion for setting the whole faculty of cognition in motion and for producing experience. Experience contains two very different elements. One is a matter for cognition, supplied by the senses. The other is a certain form for ordering this matter, which springs from the inner source of pure intuition and thought. These are called into activity on the occasion of sense impressions, and they produce concepts. An investigation into the first efforts of our cognitive faculty to rise from particular perceptions to general concepts is undoubtedly of great value, and we owe thanks to the celebrated Locke for first opening the way to it. A deduction of pure a priori concepts, however, can never be achieved by this route. Their future use must be entirely independent of experience, so they must be able to show a very different birth certificate from one that traces their descent from experience. Such a derivation is *physiological*, a natural history of how the mind comes by its concepts, and it cannot properly be called a deduction, because it concerns only a *quaestio facti*, a question of fact. I shall call it an explanation of how we come to *possess* a pure cognition. Only a transcendental deduction of these concepts is possible, never an empirical one. All attempts at an empirical deduction of pure a priori concepts are futile, and only someone who does not understand the entirely peculiar nature of these cognitions would undertake one.

It may be granted that the only possible deduction of pure a priori cognition is a transcendental one. It does not follow that such a deduction is absolutely necessary. We have already traced the concepts of space and time to their sources by means of a transcendental deduction, and we have explained and determined their objective validity a priori. Geometry nevertheless advances steadily and securely through the domain of pure a priori cognition without needing to ask philosophy for any certificate of the pure and legitimate origin of its fundamental concept of space. In geometry, however, the use of this concept extends only to the external world of the senses, whose pure form of intuition is space. In that world, all geometrical cognition, because it rests on a priori intuition, possesses immediate evidence, and its objects are given a priori in intuition, as regards their form, by and through the cognition itself. With the pure concepts of the understanding, by contrast, there arises an absolute need to seek a transcendental deduction, not only of these concepts but also of space. These concepts make assertions about objects through the predicates of pure a priori thought and not through those of intuition and sensibility, and so they relate to objects without any of the conditions of sensibility. Nor, since they are not grounded in experience, do they have any object in a priori intuition on which they might base their synthesis prior to all experience. The result is doubt about the objective validity and proper limits of their use. Even our concept of space becomes ambiguous, because with the help of the categories we are all too ready to carry that concept beyond the conditions of sensuous intuition, and for this reason we have already found a transcendental deduction of space to be necessary. The reader must therefore be fully convinced of the absolute necessity of a transcendental deduction before taking a single step into the field of pure reason. Otherwise he works blindly, and after wandering in every direction he returns to the utter ignorance from which he set out. He should also recognize clearly from the outset the unavoidable difficulties of the undertaking. He will then not complain later of the obscurity in which the subject itself is deeply wrapped, or lose patience too soon with the obstacles in his path. We have only two choices: to give up at once all claim to knowledge beyond the limits of possible experience, or to carry this critical investigation through to completion.

With very little trouble, we were able to show how the concepts of space and time, although they are a priori cognitions, must necessarily relate to external objects and make possible a synthetic cognition of them independently of all experience. An object can appear to us, and so become an object of empirical intuition, only through such pure forms of sensibility. Space and time are therefore pure intuitions that contain a priori the condition of the possibility of objects as phenomena, and an a priori synthesis in these intuitions has objective validity.

The categories of the understanding, on the other hand, do not represent the conditions under which objects are given to us in intuition. Objects can therefore appear to us without necessarily being connected with the categories, and the understanding is therefore under no necessity to contain the a priori conditions of these objects. We thus face a difficulty that did not arise in the sphere of sensibility, that is to say, we cannot see how subjective conditions of thought could have objective validity, how they could become conditions of the possibility of all knowledge of objects, since phenomena can certainly be given to us in intuition without any help from the functions of the understanding. Take the concept of cause, which signifies a particular kind of synthesis: something, A, is connected according to a law with something entirely different, B. It is not evident a priori why phenomena should contain anything of the kind. We cannot, of course, appeal to experience for proof, because the objective validity of this concept must be demonstrated a priori. It therefore remains doubtful, a priori, whether such a concept might be entirely empty, with no corresponding object anywhere among phenomena. That objects of sensuous intuition must conform to the formal conditions of sensibility lying a priori in the mind is obvious, for without those conditions they could not be objects for us at all. But that they must also conform to the conditions the understanding requires for the synthetic unity of thought is a claim whose grounds are far harder to find. Phenomena might be so constituted that they fail to meet the conditions of the unity of thought. Everything might lie in such confusion that nothing among phenomena suggested a rule of synthesis, nothing that answered, for example, to the concept of cause and effect, so that this concept would be wholly empty, null, and meaningless. Phenomena would nevertheless go on presenting objects to our intuition, since bare intuition has no need whatever of the functions of thought.

We might hope to spare ourselves the labor of these investigations by saying: "Experience constantly offers us examples of cause and effect among phenomena, giving us ample opportunity to abstract the concept of cause and, at the same time, to confirm its objective validity." But this would overlook the fact that the concept of cause cannot arise in this way at all. It must either have an a priori basis in the understanding or be rejected as a mere figment of the imagination. For this concept demands that something, A, be such that something else, B, follows from it necessarily and according to an absolutely universal rule. From phenomena we can indeed gather a rule according to which this or that usually happens, but such a rule never contains necessity. The synthesis of cause and effect therefore carries a dignity, a kind of authority, entirely lacking in any empirical synthesis. It is not a mechanical synthesis, a mere adding of one thing to another, but a dynamical one: the effect is not thought of as simply attached to the cause, but as posited by and through the cause, as following from it. Empirical laws can never possess this strict universality; through induction they acquire only a comparative universality, which amounts to a wide range of practical application. And the pure concepts of the understanding would lose their distinctive character entirely if we treated them as mere products of experience.

#### Transition to the Transcendental Deduction of the Categories § 10

There are only two ways in which a synthetic representation and its objects can coincide, relate to each other necessarily, and, so to speak, meet. Either the object alone makes the representation possible, or the representation alone makes the object possible. In the first case, the relation between them is merely empirical, and an a priori representation is impossible; this holds for whatever in phenomena belongs to mere sensation. In the second case, representation does not by itself bring the object into existence (we are not speaking here of the causality that representation can exercise through the will), but it must nonetheless determine the object a priori, provided that only through the representation can we know anything as an object. Now there are only two conditions under which knowledge of an object is possible: first, intuition, through which the object is given, though only as a phenomenon; second, concept, through which an object corresponding to this intuition is thought. From what was said in the Aesthetic, it is clear that the first condition, under which alone objects can be intuited, does in fact lie a priori in the mind as their formal basis. All phenomena therefore necessarily conform to this formal condition of sensibility, because only through it can they be phenomena at all, that is, be empirically intuited and given. The question now is whether concepts of the understanding also lie a priori in the mind, as conditions under which alone something can be thought as an object, even if it is not intuited. If the answer is yes, then all empirical knowledge of objects necessarily conforms to these concepts, since without presupposing them nothing could be an object of experience. Now, besides the sensory intuition through which an object is given, all experience also contains a concept of an object that is given in intuition. Concepts of objects in general must therefore lie at the foundation of all empirical knowledge as a priori conditions. Consequently, the objective validity of the categories, as a priori concepts, will rest on this: that experience, so far as its form of thought is concerned, is possible only through them. In that case they apply necessarily and a priori to objects of experience, because only through them can any object of experience be thought.

The whole aim of the transcendental deduction of all a priori concepts is to show that they are a priori conditions of the possibility of all experience. Concepts that supply the objective ground of the possibility of experience are necessary for that very reason. Yet an analysis of the experiences in which they turn up is not a deduction but only an illustration, since experience could never confer on them the attribute of necessity. If the categories did not apply originally to all possible experience, the domain in which every object of knowledge presents itself, their relation to objects of any kind would be wholly incomprehensible.

The celebrated Locke, failing to reflect adequately on these points, and finding pure concepts of the understanding in experience, tried to derive them from experience as well. Yet he was inconsistent enough to use them in attempting to reach knowledge that lies far beyond the limits of all experience. David Hume saw that, for this to be possible, the concepts would need an a priori origin. But he could not explain how concepts that are not connected with one another in the understanding should nevertheless be thought as necessarily connected in the object, and it never occurred to him that the understanding itself, through these very concepts, might be the author of the experience in which its objects are presented to it. He was therefore driven to derive them from experience: from a subjective necessity produced by the repeated association of experiences and mistakenly taken to be objective. In a word, he derived them from habit. From there, however, he proceeded with perfect consistency, declaring it impossible to pass beyond the limits of experience with such concepts and the principles that arise from them. Yet the empirical derivation that both philosophers ascribed to these concepts cannot be reconciled with the fact that we do possess scientific a priori knowledge, namely pure mathematics and general physics.

The first of these two celebrated men threw the door wide open to extravagant speculation, for once reason has undoubted right on its side, it will not let itself be held within fixed limits by vague recommendations of moderation. The second surrendered entirely to skepticism, the natural consequence of believing he had discovered that our faculty of knowledge cannot be trusted. We now mean to try whether reason can be steered safely between these two rocks, like a ship between two hazards, given definite limits, and yet left free to range over the whole sphere of its legitimate activity.

First, I shall simply explain what the categories are. They are concepts of an object in general, through which the intuition of that object is regarded as determined with respect to one of the logical functions of judgment. An example will make this clear. The function of the categorical judgment is the relation of subject to predicate, as in the proposition "All bodies are divisible." But as far as the merely logical use of the understanding is concerned, it remains undetermined which of the two concepts takes the role of subject and which the role of predicate, for we could equally say, "Something divisible is a body." When the concept of body is brought under the category of substance, however, the matter is settled: the empirical intuition of a body in experience must always be regarded as subject, never as mere predicate. The same holds for all the other categories.

#### Section II: Transcendental Deduction of the Pure Concepts of the Understanding

#### On the Possibility of Combining the Manifold Representations Given by Sense § 11

The manifold in our representations can be given in an intuition that is merely sensuous, nothing but receptivity, and the form of this intuition can lie a priori in our faculty of representation without being anything other than the way the subject is affected. But the combination (*conjunctio*) of a manifold in intuition can never come to us through the senses, and so it cannot be contained in the pure form of sensuous intuition either; it is a spontaneous act of the faculty of representation. Since we must call this faculty understanding, to distinguish it from sensibility, all combination is an act of the understanding, whether we are conscious of it or not, and whether it is a combination of the manifold of intuition, sensuous or non-sensuous, or of several concepts. To this act we give the general name *synthesis*, to signal at the same time that we cannot represent anything as combined in the object without first having combined it ourselves. Of all our representations, combination is the only one that cannot be given through objects; it can be produced only by the subject itself, because it is an act of the subject's pure spontaneity. The reader will readily see that the possibility of combination must be grounded in the nature of this act itself, that the act must hold equally for every kind of combination, and that analysis, which seems to be its opposite, always presupposes it. Where the understanding has not first combined, it has nothing to take apart, since whatever is to be analyzed can have been given to our faculty of representation only as something the understanding has already combined.

The concept of combination, however, includes not only the concepts of the manifold and of its synthesis but also that of the manifold's unity. Combination is the representation of the synthetic unity of the manifold. The idea of this unity therefore cannot arise from that of combination. Rather, by joining itself to the representation of the manifold, the idea of unity makes the concept of combination possible in the first place. This unity, which precedes all concepts of combination a priori, is not the category of unity, for all the categories rest on logical functions of judgment, and those functions already involve combination, and hence the unity of given concepts. The category of unity plainly presupposes combination. We must therefore look higher still for this unity, unity in the qualitative sense discussed earlier. We must look for it in that which contains the ground of the unity of different concepts in judgments, and hence the ground of the possibility of the understanding itself, even in its logical use.

Whether the representations combined in this way are in themselves identical, so that one could be thought analytically through the other, is a question we need not consider here. When we speak of a manifold, our consciousness of the one representation is always distinguishable from our consciousness of the other, and only the synthesis of this possible consciousness concerns us here.

#### On the Original Synthetic Unity of Apperception § 12

The "I think" must accompany all my representations. Otherwise something would be represented in me that could not be thought at all, and the representation would then be either impossible or, at least for me, nothing. A representation that can be given before all thought is called intuition. All the manifold of intuition therefore has a necessary relation to the "I think" in the same subject in whom that manifold is found. But this representation, "I think," is an act of spontaneity; it cannot be regarded as belonging to mere sensibility. I call it *pure* apperception, to distinguish it from empirical apperception, or *original* apperception, because it is the self-consciousness that produces the representation "I think," which must be capable of accompanying all our representations. In every act of consciousness it is one and the same, and without it no representation can exist for me. I call the unity of this apperception the *transcendental* unity of self-consciousness, to indicate that a priori knowledge can arise from it. For the manifold representations given in an intuition would not all be *my* representations unless they all belonged to one self-consciousness. As my representations, even if I am not conscious of them as such, they must conform to the condition under which alone they can stand together in a common self-consciousness, since otherwise they would not, without exception, belong to me. Many important consequences follow from this original combination.

This thoroughgoing identity of the apperception of the manifold given in intuition, for example, contains a synthesis of representations and is possible only through consciousness of that synthesis. The empirical consciousness that accompanies different representations is in itself scattered and fragmentary, with no relation to the identity of the subject. That relation arises, then, not from my merely accompanying each representation with consciousness, but from my adding one representation to another and being conscious of their synthesis. Only because I can combine a manifold of given representations in one consciousness can I represent to myself the identity of consciousness throughout those representations. The analytic unity of apperception is possible only on the presupposition of a synthetic unity. The thought "These representations given in intuition all belong to me" therefore means the same as "I unite them in one self-consciousness, or at least can unite them." Although this thought is not itself the consciousness of the synthesis of representations, it presupposes the possibility of that synthesis. Only because I can grasp the manifold of my representations in one consciousness do I call them all *my* representations; otherwise I would have a self as many-colored and varied as the representations of which I am conscious. The synthetic unity of the manifold of intuitions, as given a priori, is therefore the ground of the identity of apperception itself, which precedes all determinate thought a priori. Yet combination does not lie in objects, nor can it be borrowed from them, so to speak, and taken up into the understanding through perception. It is, on the contrary, an operation of the understanding itself, which is nothing but the faculty of combining a priori and of bringing the manifold of given representations under the unity of apperception. This principle is the highest in all human knowledge.

All general concepts, as such, depend for their existence on the analytic unity of consciousness. When I think of red in general, for instance, I think of a property that, as a distinguishing mark, can be found somewhere or can be combined with other representations. Only by means of a synthetic unity, conceived in advance as possible, can I think the analytic unity. A representation thought of as common to different representations is regarded as belonging to representations that contain something else besides it. It must therefore first be thought in synthetic unity with other representations, even if only possible ones, before I can think in it the analytic unity of consciousness that makes it a *conceptus communis*, a common concept. The synthetic unity of apperception is thus the highest point, to which we must attach every use of the understanding, the whole of logic itself, and, following logic, transcendental philosophy. Indeed, this faculty is the understanding itself.

This fundamental principle of the necessary unity of apperception is itself an identical, and therefore analytic, proposition. Yet it reveals the necessity of a synthesis of the manifold given in an intuition, without which the identity of self-consciousness could not be thought. The "I," as a simple representation, contains no manifold. A manifold can be given only in intuition, which is entirely distinct from the representation "I," and it is through combination that this manifold is thought in one self-consciousness. An understanding in which all the manifold was given through self-consciousness itself would be intuitive; ours can only think, and must look to the senses for its intuitions. I am therefore conscious of my identical self with respect to all the manifold of representations given to me in an intuition, because I call them all my representations. I am conscious, that is, of a necessary a priori synthesis of them, which is called the original synthetic unity of apperception. All the representations given to me fall under it, but they must be brought under it by means of a synthesis.

#### The Principle of the Synthetic Unity of Apperception Is the Supreme Principle of All Use of the Understanding § 13

According to the Transcendental Aesthetic, the supreme principle of the possibility of all intuition in relation to sensibility was that all the manifold of intuition be subject to the formal conditions of space and time. The supreme principle of the same possibility in relation to the understanding is that all the manifold of intuition be subject to the conditions of the original synthetic unity of apperception. All the various representations of intuition fall under the first principle insofar as they are given to us, and under the second insofar as they must be capable of being combined in one consciousness. Without this, nothing could be thought or known, because the given representations would not share the act of apperception "I think" and so could not be gathered together in one self-consciousness.

Space and time, and every part of them, are intuitions. As the Transcendental Aesthetic showed, they are therefore single representations containing a manifold. They are not pure concepts, through which one and the same consciousness is found in many representations; on the contrary, they are many representations contained in one, and the consciousness of them is, so to speak, compound. The unity of this consciousness is nevertheless synthetic and therefore original. Many important consequences follow from this peculiar character of consciousness.

Understanding, generally speaking, is the faculty of knowledge. Knowledge consists in the determinate relation of given representations to an object, and an object is that in whose concept the manifold of a given intuition is united. But all unification of representations requires unity of consciousness in their synthesis. It is therefore the unity of consciousness alone that makes possible the relation of representations to an object, and with it their objective validity and their becoming knowledge, and so, ultimately, the possibility of the understanding itself.

The first pure knowledge of the understanding, then, on which all its other uses are founded, and which is entirely independent of all conditions of sensuous intuition, is the principle of the original synthetic unity of apperception. The mere form of outer sensuous intuition, space, yields no knowledge by itself; it only supplies the manifold of a priori intuition for possible knowledge. To know something in space, such as a line, I must draw it, and so synthetically produce a determinate combination of the given manifold, such that the unity of this act is at the same time the unity of consciousness in the concept of a line. Only in this way is an object, a determinate space, known. The synthetic unity of consciousness is therefore an objective condition of all knowledge. I do not merely need it in order to know an object; every intuition must stand under it in order to become an object for me, since in no other way, and without this synthesis, could the manifold in intuition be united in one consciousness.

This proposition, as already noted, is itself analytic, although it makes synthetic unity the condition of all thought. It says no more than that all my representations in any given intuition must be subject to the condition under which alone I can relate them, as my representations, to the identical self, and so combine them synthetically in one apperception through the general expression "I think."

Yet this principle is not to be regarded as a principle for every possible understanding, but only for one whose pure apperception, in the representation "I am," supplies no manifold whatever. An understanding that contained the manifold of intuition in and through the very act of its own self-consciousness, an understanding through whose representation the objects of that representation would at the same time exist, would need no special act of synthesis of the manifold to secure the unity of its consciousness. The human understanding, which only thinks and cannot intuit, has absolute need of such an act. But this principle is the first principle of all the operations of our understanding, so that we cannot form the slightest concept of any other possible understanding, whether one that would itself be intuition, or one that would possess a sensuous intuition but with forms different from those of space and time.

**What the Objective Unity of Self-Consciousness Is (§ 14)**

It is through the transcendental unity of apperception that all the manifold given in an intuition is united into a concept of the object. For this reason it is called objective. It must be distinguished from the subjective unity of consciousness, which is a determination of inner sense through which that same manifold of intuition is given empirically for such combination. Whether I can be empirically conscious of the manifold as simultaneous or as successive depends on circumstances, that is, on empirical conditions. The empirical unity of consciousness, which arises through the association of representations, therefore itself concerns appearances and is wholly contingent. By contrast, the pure form of intuition in time, taken merely as an intuition containing a given manifold, is subject to the original unity of consciousness. It is subject to that unity solely through the necessary relation of the manifold of intuition to the "I think," and therefore through the pure synthesis of the understanding, which lies a priori at the foundation of all empirical synthesis. Only the transcendental unity of apperception is objectively valid. The empirical unity, which we do not consider in this work and which is merely derived from the transcendental unity under given conditions *in concreto*, has only subjective validity. One person connects the idea conveyed by a word with one thing, another person with something else. The unity of consciousness in what is empirical is therefore not necessarily and universally valid with respect to what experience gives.

**The Logical Form of All Judgments Consists in the Objective Unity of Apperception of the Concepts They Contain (§ 15)**

I have never been able to satisfy myself with the definition of judgment that logicians give. A judgment, they say, is the representation of a relation between two concepts. I shall not dwell here on one defect of this definition: it fits only categorical judgments and not hypothetical or disjunctive ones, since these latter contain a relation not between concepts but between judgments themselves. That error has had many harmful consequences. More important for our present purpose is that the definition does not determine what this relation consists in.

The tedious doctrine of the four syllogistic figures concerns only categorical syllogisms. It is nothing more than a device for slipping immediate inferences (*consequentiae immediatae*) in among the premises of a pure syllogism, so as to create the appearance that there are more ways of drawing a conclusion than the one in the first figure. Even so, the device would not have had much success had its authors not managed to give categorical judgments an exclusive standing, as the form to which all other judgments must be reduced. As was shown earlier, that doctrine is entirely false.

But suppose I examine more closely how given cognitions are related in every judgment, and distinguish this relation, as belonging to the understanding, from the relation produced according to the laws of the reproductive imagination, which has only subjective validity. I then find that a judgment is nothing other than the way of bringing given cognitions to the objective unity of apperception. This is evident from the copula "is" in judgments, which we use to distinguish the objective unity of given representations from their subjective unity. For this word indicates the relation of those representations to original apperception and their necessary unity, even when the judgment is itself empirical and therefore contingent, as in "All bodies are heavy." I do not mean that these representations necessarily belong to one another in empirical intuition.
