I mean that they belong to one another in the synthesis of intuitions by virtue of the necessary unity of apperception, that is, according to principles of the objective determination of all our representations insofar as cognition can arise from them, and these principles are all derived from the fundamental principle of the transcendental unity of apperception. Only in this way can this relation yield a judgment. A judgment is a relation that is objectively valid, and it is entirely distinct from the relation between those very same representations that has only subjective validity, namely the relation produced according to the laws of association. Under those laws I could say only, "When I hold or carry a body, I feel a sensation of weight." I could not say, "It, the body, is heavy." To say this is to say that the two representations are combined in the object, regardless of the condition of the subject, and do not merely occur together in my perception, however often that perception may be repeated.

**All Sensuous Intuitions Are Subject to the Categories, as the Conditions under Which Alone Their Manifold Content Can Be United in One Consciousness (§ 16)**

The manifold content given in a sensuous intuition necessarily falls under the original synthetic unity of apperception, because only through that unity is the unity of intuition possible, as we have already shown. But the act of the understanding by which the manifold of given representations, whether intuitions or concepts, is brought under one apperception is the logical function of judgment, as the preceding section established. All the manifold, therefore, insofar as it is given in one empirical intuition, is determined with respect to one of the logical functions of judgment, and through this function it is brought together in one consciousness. Now the categories are nothing other than these very functions of judgment, insofar as the manifold of a given intuition is determined with respect to them, as was shown earlier. Consequently, the manifold in a given intuition is necessarily subject to the categories of the understanding.

**Observation (§ 17)**

The manifold contained in an intuition that I call mine is represented, through the synthesis of the understanding, as belonging to the necessary unity of self-consciousness, and this happens by means of the category. The category therefore shows that the empirical consciousness of a given manifold in an intuition is subject to a pure a priori self-consciousness, in the same way that an empirical intuition is subject to a pure sensuous intuition, which is likewise a priori. This proposition contains the beginning of a deduction of the pure concepts of the understanding. The categories originate in the understanding alone, independently of sensibility. In this deduction, then, I must set aside the way in which the manifold of an empirical intuition is given, so as to fix my attention exclusively on the unity that the understanding introduces into intuition by means of the category. Later it will be shown, from the way empirical intuition is given in sensibility, that its unity is none other than the one the category, as just demonstrated, imposes on the manifold of a given intuition. Once the a priori validity of the categories for all objects of the senses has thus been established, the aim of our deduction will be fully achieved.

The proof of this rests on the represented unity of intuition through which an object is given. That unity always includes a synthesis of the manifold to be intuited, together with the relation of this manifold to the unity of apperception.

There is one thing, however, that I could not set aside in the demonstration above: the manifold to be intuited must be given prior to the synthesis of the understanding and independently of it. How this happens remains undetermined here. Suppose I were to think of an understanding that was itself intuitive, such as a divine understanding that would not represent objects already given, but through whose representation the objects themselves would be given or produced. The categories would have no meaning whatever for such a faculty of cognition. They are merely rules for an understanding whose entire power consists in thinking. Thinking is the act of bringing the synthesis of a manifold, which is presented to the understanding in intuition from an altogether different source, to the unity of apperception. Such a faculty therefore knows nothing by itself. It only combines and orders the material of cognition, namely the intuition, which the object must supply to it. But no reason can be given for this peculiar character of our understanding, which achieves the unity of apperception a priori only by means of categories, and only by categories of precisely this kind and number. Such an explanation is as impossible as explaining why we possess just these functions of judgment and no others, or why space and time are the only forms of our intuition.

**In Cognition, the Only Legitimate Use of the Categories Is Their Application to Objects of Experience (§ 18)**

To think an object and to know an object are by no means the same thing. Cognition involves two elements. The first is the concept through which an object is thought at all (the category). The second is the intuition through which the object is given. If no corresponding intuition could be given for the concept, it would still be a thought as far as its form is concerned, but it would have no object. No cognition of anything would be possible through it, since, as far as I could know, nothing would exist, or could exist, to which my thought might apply. Now, every intuition possible for us is sensuous. Consequently, when we think an object by means of a pure concept of the understanding, that thought can become cognition for us only insofar as the concept is applied to objects of the senses. Sensuous intuition is either pure intuition (space and time) or empirical intuition, which is intuition of what is represented, through sensation, as immediately real in space and time. By determining pure intuition we obtain a priori cognitions of objects, as in mathematics, but only with respect to their form as appearances. Whether there can be things that must be intuited in this form is not thereby established. Mathematical concepts, therefore, are not cognitions in themselves, except insofar as we presuppose that there are things that can be represented only in accordance with the form of our pure sensuous intuition. But things in space and time are given only insofar as they are perceptions, which are representations accompanied by sensation, and therefore only through empirical representation. It follows that the pure concepts of the understanding, even when applied to a priori intuitions as in mathematics, yield cognition only insofar as those intuitions, and through them the concepts of the understanding, can be applied to empirical intuitions. The categories, then, do not provide us with any cognition of things even by way of pure intuition. They can do so only insofar as they can be applied to empirical intuition. The categories, accordingly, have no other function than to make empirical cognition possible, and empirical cognition is what we call experience. Therefore, in cognition, the only legitimate use of the categories is their application to objects of experience.

**§ 19**

The foregoing proposition is of the greatest importance. It fixes the limits within which the pure concepts of the understanding may be used with respect to objects, just as the Transcendental Aesthetic fixed the limits within which the pure form of our sensuous intuition may be used. Space and time, as conditions of the possibility of objects being presented to us, hold only for objects of the senses, and therefore only for experience. Beyond these limits they represent nothing to us, for they exist only in the senses and have no reality apart from them. The pure concepts of the understanding are free of this restriction. They extend to objects of intuition in general, whether that intuition resembles ours or not, provided only that it is sensuous and not intellectual. But this extension of concepts beyond the reach of our intuition gains us nothing. Concepts extended in this way are merely empty concepts of objects, and they give us no means of determining whether such objects are even possible. They are mere forms of thought without objective reality. The categories contain nothing but the synthetic unity of apperception, and we have no intuition to which that unity could be applied in order to determine an object. Only our sensuous and empirical intuition can give the categories sense and meaning.

Suppose, then, that an object of non-sensuous intuition were given. We could represent it through all the predicates implied by the assumption that nothing belonging to sensuous intuition pertains to it: that it is not extended or in space, that its duration is not time, that no change (which is the result of determinations in time) is to be found in it, and so forth. But merely indicating what the intuition of an object is not, without being able to say what it does contain, is not genuine knowledge. I have not shown that an object to which my pure concept of the understanding could apply is even possible, because I have been unable to supply any intuition corresponding to it. I can say only that our intuition does not hold for it. The most important point, however, is this: not a single category can be found that applies to such a thing. Take, for example, the concept of substance, which is the concept of something that can exist as a subject but never as a mere predicate. If empirical intuition did not give me occasion to apply this concept, I would have no idea whether anything could actually correspond to such a determination of thought. But more on this later.

**On the Application of the Categories to Objects of the Senses in General (§ 20)**

The pure concepts of the understanding apply, through the understanding alone, to objects of intuition in general, whether that intuition is ours or some other kind, provided only that it is sensuous. Precisely for this reason, however, they are mere forms of thought, and through them alone no determinate object can be known. The synthesis or combination of the manifold in these concepts relates, as we have said, only to the unity of apperception. For that reason it is the ground of the possibility of a priori cognition, insofar as such cognition depends on the understanding. This synthesis is therefore not only transcendental but also purely intellectual. But a certain form of sensuous intuition lies a priori in the mind, and it rests on the receptivity of our capacity for representation, that is, on sensibility. Because of this, the understanding, as a spontaneous power, is able to determine inner sense through the manifold of given representations in accordance with the synthetic unity of apperception. It can thus think a priori the synthetic unity of apperception of the manifold of sensuous intuition as the condition to which all objects of human intuition must necessarily be subject. In this way the categories, which are in themselves mere forms of thought, acquire objective reality, meaning that they apply to objects given to us in intuition. They apply to these objects only as appearances, however, since appearances are the only things of which we are capable of a priori intuition.

This synthesis of the manifold of sensuous intuition, which is both possible and necessary a priori, may be called figurative synthesis (*synthesis speciosa*). It stands in contrast to the synthesis thought in the mere category with respect to the manifold of an intuition in general, which is called the combination of the understanding (*synthesis intellectualis*). Both are transcendental, not only because they themselves precede all experience a priori, but also because they ground the possibility of other a priori cognition.

When the figurative synthesis relates solely to the original synthetic unity of apperception, that is, to the transcendental unity thought in the categories, it must be called the transcendental synthesis of the imagination, to distinguish it from purely intellectual combination. Imagination is the faculty of representing an object even when it is not present in intuition. Now, since all our intuition is sensuous, imagination belongs to sensibility, because of the subjective condition under which alone it can supply an intuition corresponding to the concepts of the understanding. Yet the synthesis of imagination is an act of spontaneity. It determines, rather than being, like sense, merely determinable, and it is therefore able to determine sense a priori with respect to its form, in accordance with the unity of apperception. To that extent the imagination is a faculty of determining sensibility a priori, and its synthesis of intuitions according to the categories must be the transcendental synthesis of the imagination. This synthesis is an action of the understanding upon sensibility. It is the understanding's first application to objects of possible intuition, and at the same time the basis for the exercise of all its other functions. As figurative, it is distinguished from the merely intellectual synthesis, which the understanding carries out alone, without the help of imagination. Insofar as imagination is spontaneity, I sometimes also call it the productive imagination. I distinguish it from the reproductive imagination, whose synthesis is governed entirely by empirical laws, namely the laws of association. The reproductive imagination therefore contributes nothing to explaining how a priori cognition is possible, and for that reason it belongs not to transcendental philosophy but to psychology.

We have now reached the proper place to explain the paradox that must have struck every reader of our earlier account of inner sense. Inner sense presents us to our own consciousness only as we appear to ourselves, not as we are in ourselves, because we intuit ourselves only as we are inwardly affected. This seems contradictory, since it means that we stand in a passive relation to ourselves. For this reason, systems of psychology commonly treat inner sense as identical with the faculty of apperception, whereas we carefully distinguish the two.

What determines inner sense is the understanding, with its original power of combining the manifold of intuition, that is, of bringing it under one apperception. The very possibility of the understanding rests on this power. Now, the human understanding is not itself a faculty of intuition, and it cannot exercise any such power so as to combine, as it were, a manifold of its own intuition. Considered in itself, therefore, its synthesis is nothing but the unity of an act of which it is conscious as such, even apart from sensibility. Through this act, moreover, it is able to determine our inner sense with respect to whatever manifold may be presented to it according to the form of sensuous intuition. Thus, under the name of a transcendental synthesis of the imagination, the understanding exercises an activity upon the passive subject whose faculty it is, and we are right to say that inner sense is affected by it. Apperception and its synthetic unity are by no means the same thing as inner sense. Apperception, as the source of all our synthetic combination, applies under the name of the categories to the manifold of intuition in general, prior to any sensuous intuition of objects. Inner sense, on the other hand, contains merely the form of intuition, without any synthetic combination of the manifold within it, and therefore contains no determinate intuition at all. A determinate intuition becomes possible only through consciousness of the determination of the manifold by the transcendental act of the imagination, which is the synthetic influence of the understanding on inner sense. I have called this act figurative synthesis.

We can always observe this in ourselves. We cannot think a geometrical line without drawing it in thought, nor a circle without tracing it, nor represent the three dimensions of space without drawing three lines perpendicular to one another from a single point. We cannot even think time unless we draw a straight line as an outer, figurative representation of time and attend to the act of synthesizing the manifold. Through that act we successively determine inner sense, and we thereby attend also to the succession of this determination. Motion as an act of the subject, and not as a determination of an object, is what first produces the concept of succession. By this I mean the synthesis of the manifold in space, once we abstract from space itself and attend only to the act by which we determine inner sense according to its form. The understanding, therefore, does not find any such combination of the manifold already present in inner sense. It produces that combination by affecting inner sense. At the same time, there is the question of how the "I" that thinks can be distinct from the "I" that intuits itself (since other modes of intuition are at least conceivable as possible), and yet be one and the same with it as the same subject. How, then, can I say, "I, as an intelligence and thinking subject, know myself as an object that is thought, insofar as I am also given to myself in intuition, but only, like other appearances, as I appear to myself, and not as I am in myself and as the understanding would consider me"? This question involves neither more nor less difficulty than the questions "How can I be an object to myself?" and "How can I be an object of my own intuition and inner perceptions?" But that this must indeed be so, once we grant that space is merely a pure form of the appearances of outer sense, can be clearly proved. We cannot represent time, which is not an object of outer intuition, except under the image of a line that we draw in thought, and without this mode of representation we could not recognize that time has only a single dimension. Moreover, for all our inner perceptions, we must take our determination of lengths of time, or of points in time, from the changes we perceive in outer things. It follows that we must order the determinations of inner sense, as appearances in time, in exactly the same way that we order those of the outer senses in space. Consequently, if we admit of the outer senses that through them we know objects only insofar as we are affected from outside, we must also concede of inner sense that through it we intuit ourselves only as we are inwardly affected by ourselves. As far as inner intuition is concerned, then, we know our own subject only as appearance, not as it is in itself.

Motion of an object in space does not belong to a pure science, and therefore not to geometry, because we cannot know a priori that a thing is movable; we can know it only from experience. But motion, considered as the describing of a space, is a pure act of successive synthesis of the manifold in outer intuition, carried out by the productive imagination, and it belongs not only to geometry but even to transcendental philosophy.

I do not see why people find it so hard to admit that our inner sense is affected by ourselves. Every act of attention is an instance of it. In attending, the understanding determines inner sense through the synthetic combination that it thinks, in accordance with the inner intuition that corresponds to the manifold in the understanding's synthesis. Anyone can observe in himself how much the mind is commonly affected in this way.

#### § 21

By contrast, in the transcendental synthesis of the manifold of representations in general, and therefore in the synthetic unity of apperception, I am conscious of myself neither as I appear to myself nor as I am in myself, but only conscious *that I am*. This representation is a thought, not an intuition.

To know ourselves, however, we need more than the act of thinking that brings the manifold of every possible intuition under the unity of apperception. We also need a determinate kind of intuition through which this manifold is given. Accordingly, although my own existence is certainly not mere appearance, still less mere illusion, the determination of my existence can take place only in conformity with the form of inner sense, according to the particular way in which the manifold that I combine is given in inner intuition. I therefore have no knowledge of myself as I am, but only as I appear to myself. Consciousness of self is thus very far from knowledge of self, despite all the categories, which make up the thought of an object in general by combining the manifold in one apperception. Knowing an object distinct from myself requires not only the thought of an object in general, which the category supplies, but also an intuition through which to determine that general concept. In the same way, knowing myself requires not only consciousness of myself, the thought that I think myself, but also an intuition of the manifold within me through which to determine this thought. I do indeed exist as an intelligence that is conscious only of its power of combination, or synthesis. Yet with respect to the manifold it has to combine, this intelligence is subject to a limiting condition, which is called inner sense. My intelligence, which is to say I myself, can make that combination perceptible only according to relations of time, and these lie entirely outside the proper sphere of the concepts of the understanding. It can therefore know itself, with respect to an intuition that cannot be intellectual and cannot be supplied by the understanding, only as it appears to itself, and not as it would know itself if its intuition were intellectual.

The "I think" expresses the act of determining my own existence. My existence is therefore already given by this act of consciousness. What is not given by it is the way in which I must determine that existence, that is, the way in which I must arrange the manifold that belongs to it. For that, an intuition of myself is required, and this intuition has a form given a priori, namely time, which is sensible and belongs to our receptivity, our capacity to receive what is determinable. Now, I have no second intuition of myself that would give me the determining element in me, the element of whose spontaneity I am conscious, prior to the act of determination, in the way that time gives me what is determinable. It is clear, then, that I cannot determine my existence as that of a spontaneous being. I can only represent to myself the spontaneity of my thought, that is, of my act of determining, while my existence always remains determinable only sensibly, which is to say like the existence of an appearance. Yet it is because of this spontaneity that I call myself an intelligence.

#### Transcendental Deduction of the Universally Possible Use in Experience of the Pure Concepts of the Understanding: § 22

In the metaphysical deduction, the a priori origin of the categories was proved by their complete agreement with the general logical functions of thought. In the transcendental deduction, the possibility of the categories was set out as a priori cognitions of objects of an intuition in general. We now have to explain how it is possible to know a priori, by means of the categories, all objects that can ever be presented to our senses. We will know them not according to the form of their intuition, but according to the laws of their combination, and we will thus, so to speak, prescribe laws to nature and even make nature possible. If the categories were not adequate to this task, we could not see why everything presented to our senses must be subject to laws that originate a priori in the understanding alone.

I should state first that by the *synthesis of apprehension* I mean the combination of the manifold in an empirical intuition through which perception becomes possible, that is, empirical consciousness of the intuition as appearance.

In the representations of space and time we possess a priori forms of outer and inner sensible intuition, and the synthesis of apprehension of the manifold in an appearance must always conform to them, because that synthesis can take place only according to these forms. But space and time are not merely forms of sensible intuition. They are themselves intuitions, which contain a manifold, and they therefore contain within themselves, a priori, the determination of the unity of that manifold, as the Transcendental Aesthetic showed.

Accordingly, the unity of the synthesis of the manifold, whether outside us or within us, is given a priori along with these intuitions, though not in them, as the condition of the synthesis of all apprehension of them. So, too, is a combination to which everything represented as determined in space or time must conform. This synthetic unity, however, can be nothing other than the unity of the combination of the manifold of a given intuition in general in an original act of consciousness, in accordance with the categories, but applied to our sensible intuition. Consequently, all synthesis, which is what makes even perception possible, is subject to the categories. And since experience is cognition through connected perceptions, the categories are conditions of the possibility of experience and are therefore valid a priori for all objects of experience.

Space represented as an object, as geometry in fact requires, contains more than the mere form of intuition. It contains a combination of the manifold, given according to the form of sensibility, into a representation that can be intuited. The form of intuition, then, supplies only the manifold, while formal intuition supplies the unity of the representation. In the Aesthetic I treated this unity as belonging wholly to sensibility, in order to indicate that it precedes every concept. It does, however, presuppose a synthesis that does not belong to the senses, although it is only through this synthesis that any of our concepts of space and time are possible. Since it is through this unity alone, with the understanding determining sensibility, that space and time are given as intuitions at all, the unity of this a priori intuition belongs to space and time, and not to the concept of the understanding.

Suppose, for example, that I turn the empirical intuition of a house into a perception by apprehending its manifold. The necessary unity of space and of my outer sensible intuition underlies this act, and I trace, as it were, the shape of the house in conformity with this synthetic unity of the manifold in space. But this same synthetic unity remains even when I abstract from the form of space. It has its seat in the understanding, and it is in fact the category of the synthesis of the homogeneous in an intuition, namely the category of quantity. The synthesis of apprehension, which is to say the perception itself, must conform completely to this category.

This proves that the synthesis of apprehension, which is empirical, must necessarily conform to the synthesis of apperception, which is intellectual and contained a priori in the category. It is one and the same spontaneity that brings combination into the manifold of intuition, called imagination in the one case and understanding in the other.

To take another example, when I perceive water freezing, I apprehend two states, fluidity and solidity, which stand to each other in a relation of time. But in time, which I lay down as an inner intuition at the basis of this appearance, I represent to myself a synthetic unity of the manifold, without which that relation could not be given in an intuition as determined with respect to temporal succession. Now this synthetic unity, as the a priori condition under which I combine the manifold of an intuition, is the category of cause, once I abstract from the constant form of my inner intuition, which is time. Through this category, when I apply it to my sensibility, I determine everything that happens according to its relations in time. The apprehension of such an event, and therefore the event itself so far as the possibility of perceiving it is concerned, stands under the concept of the relation of cause and effect. The same holds in every other case.

The categories are concepts that prescribe laws a priori to appearances, and therefore to nature regarded as the sum of all appearances, nature considered materially, or *natura materialiter spectata*. The question then arises how we can conceive that nature must conform to the categories, given that the categories are not derived from nature and do not take her as their model, since in that case they would be merely empirical. The question is how the categories can determine a priori the combination of nature's manifold without deriving their origin from her. The solution to this puzzle is as follows.

It is no harder to see how the laws of nature's appearances must agree with the understanding and its a priori form, its power of combining the manifold, than to see how appearances themselves must agree with the a priori form of our sensible intuition. Laws exist in appearances no more than appearances exist as things in themselves. Laws exist only relative to the subject in which the appearances inhere, insofar as that subject has understanding, just as appearances exist only relative to that same subject insofar as it has senses. Things in themselves would necessarily have their conformity to law independently of any understanding that knows them. But appearances are only representations of things that remain wholly unknown as to what they are in themselves. As mere representations, they stand under no law of combination except the one prescribed by the faculty that combines them. What combines the manifold of sensible intuition is the imagination, a mental act to which the understanding contributes the unity of its intellectual synthesis and sensibility contributes the manifoldness of apprehension. All possible perception depends on the synthesis of apprehension, and this empirical synthesis depends in turn on the transcendental synthesis, and therefore on the categories. It follows that all possible perceptions, and so everything that can ever reach empirical consciousness, which is to say all the appearances of nature, must be subject to the categories as regards their combination. Nature, considered simply as nature in general, depends on the categories as the original ground of her necessary conformity to law, nature considered formally, or *natura formaliter spectata*. But the pure faculty of the understanding, which prescribes laws a priori to appearances through the categories alone, cannot prescribe any laws other than, or beyond, those on which a nature in general depends, understood as the lawfulness of appearances in space and time. Particular laws concern empirically determined appearances, and so they cannot be derived completely from the pure laws, although all of them stand under those pure laws. Experience must be added before we can know these particular laws. But with regard to experience in general, and to everything that can be known as an object of experience, these a priori laws are our only rule and guide.

#### Result of This Deduction of the Concepts of the Understanding: § 23

We cannot think any object except through the categories, and we cannot know any object so thought except through intuitions that correspond to those concepts. All our intuitions are sensible, and our cognition, insofar as its object is given, is empirical. But empirical cognition is experience. Consequently, no a priori cognition is possible for us except of objects of possible experience.

Readers may stumble over this claim, or draw hasty conclusions from it, and so I should remind them that the categories, in the act of thinking, are in no way restricted by the conditions of our sensible intuition. Their field is unlimited. Only the knowledge of what we think, the determining of the object, requires intuition. Even without intuition, our thought of an object can still have true and useful consequences for the subject's use of reason. But this use of reason is not always directed toward determining an object, that is, toward knowing it. It is also directed toward determining the subject and its will, and so I shall not discuss it here.

Yet this cognition, though limited to objects of experience, is not for that reason derived entirely from experience. With respect both to the pure intuitions and to the pure concepts of the understanding, there are unquestionably elements of cognition that lie in the mind a priori. There are only two ways in which we can conceive a necessary agreement between experience and the concepts of its objects. Either experience makes the concepts possible, or the concepts make experience possible. The first does not hold for the categories, nor for pure sensible intuition, since they are a priori concepts and therefore independent of experience. To assign them an empirical origin would be to attribute to them a kind of *generatio aequivoca*, like the old doctrine that living things can spring spontaneously from lifeless matter. Nothing remains, then, but the second alternative, which gives us what might be called a system of the *epigenesis* of pure reason. The term is borrowed from the biologists, for whom epigenesis means that an organism builds up its own form in the course of development, rather than unfolding a form already present in the germ. According to this alternative, the categories, on the side of the understanding, contain the grounds of the possibility of all experience. But how they make experience possible, and what principles of its possibility they yield when applied to appearances, will be explained in the following section, on the transcendental use of the faculty of judgment.

Someone might propose a middle path between these two, a kind of *preformation-system* of pure reason, using another term from the biology of generation, where preformation means that the organism already exists complete in the germ. On this view, the categories would be neither original a priori principles of cognition nor derived from experience. They would be merely subjective dispositions for thinking, implanted in us along with our existence and so arranged by our Creator that their use agrees perfectly with the laws of nature that govern experience. Quite apart from the fact that such a hypothesis gives us no way of saying where we should stop in assuming predetermined dispositions, there is a decisive objection to it: the categories would lose the necessity that belongs essentially to their very concept. The concept of cause, for instance, expresses the necessity of an effect under a presupposed condition. It would be false if it rested only on an arbitrary, subjective necessity of connecting certain empirical representations according to such a rule of relation. I could not then say, "The effect is connected with its cause in the object, that is, necessarily," but only, "I am so constituted that I can think this representation as connected in this way and in no other." And this is exactly what the skeptic wants. For then all our knowledge, which depends on the supposed objective validity of our judgments, would be nothing but illusion. Nor would there be any shortage of people who would deny that they have this subjective necessity in themselves, though they must feel it. At any rate, we could not argue with anyone about something that depends merely on the way his own subject is organized.

#### Brief Summary of the Foregoing Deduction

This deduction has presented the pure concepts of the understanding, and with them all theoretical a priori cognition, as principles of the possibility of experience. It has understood experience as the determination of all appearances in space and time in general. And it has derived that experience, finally, from the principle of the original synthetic unity of apperception, as the form of the understanding in relation to space and time, the original forms of sensibility.

I have thought it necessary to divide the text into numbered sections only up to this point, because we were dealing with the elementary concepts. Now that we turn to the way these concepts are used, I shall no longer mark the chapters in this manner.

## Transcendental Analytic, Book II: The Analytic of Principles

General logic is built on a plan that corresponds exactly to the division of the higher cognitive faculties: understanding, judgment, and reason. Accordingly, in its analytic this science treats concepts, judgments, and inferences in exact correspondence with the functions and order of those mental powers that we include under the broad name of understanding.

Because this merely formal logic abstracts from all content of cognition, whether pure or empirical, and concerns itself only with the bare form of thought, that is, with discursive cognition, its analytic must also contain a canon for reason. For the form of reason has its own law. That law can be discovered a priori, without regard to the particular kind of cognition to which reason is applied, simply by analyzing the action of reason into its component moments.

Transcendental logic is restricted to a determinate content, namely that of pure a priori cognitions, and so it cannot follow general logic in this division. The transcendental use of reason is plainly not objectively valid. It therefore does not belong to the logic of truth, which is the analytic. As a logic of illusion, it occupies a separate part of the scholastic system under the name of transcendental dialectic.

In transcendental logic, then, understanding and judgment have a canon of objectively valid, and therefore true, use, and so they belong to its analytic. Reason, however, in its attempts to arrive a priori at some truth about objects and to extend cognition beyond the limits of possible experience, is entirely dialectical, and its illusory assertions cannot be built into the kind of canon that an analytic ought to contain.

The analytic of principles will therefore be solely a canon for the faculty of judgment. It will instruct that faculty in applying to appearances the pure concepts of the understanding, which contain the necessary condition for a priori laws. For this reason, although the subject of the following chapters is the principles of the understanding proper, I shall use the title *Doctrine of the Faculty of Judgment*, so as to indicate my present purpose more precisely.

### Introduction: Of the Transcendental Faculty of Judgment in General

If understanding in general is defined as the faculty of rules, judgment is the faculty of subsuming under rules. It decides whether something does or does not stand under a given rule, whether it is a *casus datae legis*, a case of the given law. General logic contains no precepts for judgment, and it cannot contain any. Because it abstracts from all content of cognition, the only task left to it is to set out analytically the mere form of cognition in concepts, judgments, and inferences, and in this way to establish formal rules for every use of the understanding. Suppose general logic tried to give general instructions for subsuming under these rules, for deciding whether something does or does not fall under them. It could do so only through another rule. But that rule, precisely because it is a rule, would itself require guidance from judgment. Clearly, then, the understanding can be instructed and furnished with rules, but judgment is a special talent that cannot be taught, only practiced. It is therefore the distinctive quality of what is called mother wit, and no schooling can make up for its absence.

Education can supply a limited understanding with plenty of rules borrowed from other minds, and can, so to speak, graft them onto it. But the power to use those rules correctly must belong to the learner himself, and where this natural gift is absent or deficient, no rule we might give him for the purpose is safe from misuse. Hence a physician, a judge, or a statesman may carry in his head many excellent rules of pathology, law, or politics, enough to make him a learned teacher of his subject, and yet he may easily blunder in applying them. He may lack natural judgment, though not understanding, so that while he grasps the general in the abstract, he cannot tell whether a concrete case falls under it. Or his judgment may simply not have been trained enough through examples and actual practice. Indeed, the great and only use of examples is to sharpen judgment. As for the correctness and precision of the understanding's insight, examples generally do more harm than good, because as instances stated in particular terms, *casus in terminis*, they seldom satisfy the conditions of the rule adequately. Besides, they often weaken the understanding's power to grasp rules in their universality, independently of the particular circumstances of experience, and so they accustom us to use rules more as formulas than as principles. Examples are thus the go-cart of judgment, like the wheeled frame in which a child learns to walk, and those who are naturally deficient in this faculty can never do without them.

A deficiency of judgment is what is properly called stupidity, and for that failing we know no remedy. A dull or narrow-minded person who lacks nothing but an adequate degree of understanding can be improved by instruction, even to the point of deserving to be called learned. But because such people often suffer from a deficiency of judgment as well, it is not uncommon to find extremely learned men who, in the application of their science, betray this incurable deficiency to a lamentable degree.

Although general logic cannot give instructions to the faculty of judgment, transcendental logic is in a very different position. Indeed, its special task appears to be to secure and direct judgment, by means of determinate rules, in the use of the pure understanding. As a doctrine, that is, as an attempt to enlarge the reach of the understanding in the field of pure a priori knowledge, philosophy is worse than useless, since all the attempts made so far have gained little or no ground. As a critique, however, philosophy has a different calling. Its task here is to guard against errors of judgment, what the Latin calls *lapsus judicii*, in the use of the few pure concepts of the understanding that we possess. Although this use is purely negative, philosophy must bring all its acuteness and penetration to bear on it.

Transcendental philosophy has a further peculiarity. It indicates the rule, or more precisely the general condition for rules, which is given in the pure concept of the understanding. At the same time, it can also indicate a priori the case to which the rule must be applied. Among all the sciences, only mathematics shares this advantage with it, and the reason lies in the following. Transcendental philosophy deals with concepts that must relate a priori to their objects, so their objective validity cannot be demonstrated a posteriori, from experience. For this reason it is obliged to present, in general but sufficient terms, the conditions under which objects can be given that accord with those concepts. Without such conditions, these concepts would be mere logical forms without content, and not pure concepts of the understanding at all.

Our transcendental doctrine of the faculty of judgment will therefore contain two chapters. The first will treat the sensory condition under which alone the pure concepts of the understanding can be used, which is to say the schematism of the pure understanding. The second will treat the synthetic judgments that are derived a priori from pure concepts of the understanding under those conditions, and that lie a priori at the foundation of all other knowledge. It will, in short, treat the principles of the pure understanding.

### Transcendental Doctrine of the Faculty of Judgment

### Chapter I. Of the Schematism of the Pure Concepts of the Understanding

Whenever an object is subsumed under a concept, the representation of the object must be homogeneous with the concept. The concept must contain what is represented in the object that is to be subsumed under it, and this is exactly what we mean when we say that "an object is contained under a concept." The empirical concept of a plate, for instance, is homogeneous with the pure geometrical concept of a circle, because the roundness that is thought in the first is intuited in the second.

The pure concepts of the understanding are another matter. Compared with empirical intuitions, or indeed with sensory intuitions of any kind, they are entirely heterogeneous, and they can never be encountered in any intuition. How, then, can intuitions be subsumed under these concepts, and how can the categories be applied to phenomena at all? No one can say, for example, that "causality can be intuited through the senses and is contained in the phenomenon." This natural and important question is the real reason a transcendental doctrine of judgment is needed: its purpose is to show how pure concepts of the understanding can be applied to phenomena. In every other science, the concepts through which an object is thought in general are not so different from, and heterogeneous with, the concepts that represent the object concretely, as it is actually given. In those sciences, no special inquiry into how the general concepts apply to the concrete ones is required.

There must clearly be some third thing that is homogeneous with the category on one side and with the phenomenon on the other, and that thereby makes it possible to apply the one to the other. This mediating representation must be pure, free of all empirical content, and yet it must be intellectual on the one side and sensory on the other. Such a representation is the transcendental schema.

A concept of the understanding contains the pure synthetic unity of a manifold in general. Time, as the formal condition of the manifold of inner sense, and therefore of the combination of all representations, contains a priori a manifold within pure intuition. A transcendental determination of time is homogeneous with the category, which constitutes its unity, insofar as it is universal and rests on an a priori rule. It is also homogeneous with the phenomenon, insofar as time is contained in every empirical representation of the manifold. The category can therefore be applied to phenomena by means of the transcendental determination of time, which, as the schema of the concepts of the understanding, mediates the subsumption of phenomena under the categories.

After what was proved in our deduction of the categories, it is to be hoped that no one will hesitate over how to decide the following question: should the use of these pure concepts of the understanding be merely empirical, or may it also be transcendental? Put differently, do the categories, as conditions of a possible experience, relate a priori only to phenomena, or can they, as conditions of the possibility of things in general, be extended to objects as things in themselves? We saw in the deduction that concepts are entirely impossible, and have no meaning whatsoever, unless an object is given either to them or at least to the elements of which they are composed. We saw, consequently, that they cannot possibly apply to objects as things in themselves without regard to whether, and how, such objects might be given to us. We saw further that the only way objects can be given to us is through some modification of our sensibility. And we saw, finally, that pure a priori concepts, in addition to the function of the understanding contained in the category, must also contain a priori formal conditions of sensibility, specifically of inner sense, which in turn contain the general condition under which alone the category can be applied to any object. This formal and pure condition of sensibility, to which the concept of the understanding is restricted in its use, we shall call the schema of that concept. The procedure by which the understanding works with these schemata we shall call the schematism of the pure understanding.

The schema is in itself always merely a product of the imagination. Yet because the synthesis of the imagination aims not at any single intuition but only at unity in the determination of sensibility, the schema must be clearly distinguished from the image. If I set down five dots in a row, `.....`, that is an image of the number five. If, on the other hand, I merely think a number in general, which might be five or a hundred, this thought is less an image than the representation of a method: a way of representing a quantity, say a thousand, in an image that conforms to a concept. An image of a thousand would be one I could survey and compare with the concept only with some difficulty. This representation of a general procedure by which the imagination supplies a concept with its image is what I call the schema of that concept.

In fact, our pure sensory concepts rest not on images of objects but on schemata. No image could ever be adequate to our concept of a triangle in general. It could never reach the generality of the concept, which covers all triangles, whether right-angled, acute-angled, or any other kind, while an image is always confined to a single part of that range. The schema of the triangle can exist nowhere but in thought, and it signifies a rule for the synthesis of the imagination with respect to pure figures in space. Still less is an object of experience, or an image of such an object, ever adequate to the empirical concept. The concept instead always relates directly to the schema of the imagination, which serves as a rule for determining our intuition in accordance with a certain general concept. The concept of a dog signifies a rule by which my imagination can trace the shape of a four-footed animal in general, without being confined to any particular shape that experience offers me, or indeed to any possible image I can picture concretely. This schematism of our understanding, with respect to phenomena and their mere form, is an art hidden in the depths of the human soul, whose true workings we will only with difficulty discover and lay bare. This much alone can be said. The image is a product of the empirical faculty of the productive imagination. The schema of sensory concepts, such as figures in space, is a product of the pure a priori imagination, a kind of monogram through which, and according to which, images first become possible. These images, however, can be connected with the concept only indirectly, through the schema they signify, and in themselves they are never fully adequate to it. The schema of a pure concept of the understanding, by contrast, cannot be brought into any image at all. It is nothing but the pure synthesis expressed by the category, in conformity with a rule of unity according to concepts. It is a transcendental product of the imagination, one that concerns the determination of inner sense in general, according to the conditions of its form, which is time, with respect to all representations, insofar as these must be combined a priori in one concept in accordance with the unity of apperception.

Rather than embark on a dry and tedious analysis of everything that transcendental schemata of the pure concepts of the understanding require, we shall proceed directly to explain them in the order of the categories and in connection with them.

The pure image of all quantities, of all things that have magnitude, is space, insofar as they are objects of outer sense. The pure image of all objects of the senses in general is time. The pure schema of quantity itself, taken as a concept of the understanding, is number: a representation that comprises the successive addition of one unit to another of the same kind. Number is therefore nothing other than the unity of the synthesis of the manifold in a homogeneous intuition in general, achieved because I generate time itself in apprehending the intuition.

Reality, in the pure concept of the understanding, is what corresponds to a sensation in general. It is therefore that whose concept indicates a being, an existence in time. Negation is that whose concept represents a not-being in time. The opposition between the two thus consists in the difference within one and the same time between time that is filled and time that is empty. Since time is only the form of intuition, and therefore of objects as phenomena, what corresponds to sensation in objects is the transcendental matter of all objects as things in themselves, what German calls *Sachheit*, their thinghood or reality. Every sensation has a degree, or magnitude, by which it can fill the same time, that is, fill inner sense with respect to the representation of an object, to a greater or lesser extent, until it dwindles to nothing, to zero, to negation. There is therefore a relation and connection between reality and negation, or more exactly a transition from the one to the other, that makes every reality representable to us as a quantity. The schema of a reality, as the quantity of something insofar as it fills time, is precisely this continuous and uniform production of that reality in time: we descend in time from a sensation of a given degree down to its vanishing, or we rise step by step from negation to the sensation's full magnitude.

The schema of substance is the permanence of the real in time. It is the representation of the real as a substratum of the empirical determination of time in general, a substratum that remains while everything else changes. Time itself does not pass; what passes in time is the existence of what changes. To time, which is itself unchangeable and permanent, there corresponds in the phenomenon what is unchangeable in existence, namely substance, and only through substance can the succession and coexistence of phenomena be determined with respect to time.

The schema of cause, and of the causality of a thing in general, is the real which, once posited, is always followed by something else. It therefore consists in the succession of the manifold, insofar as that succession is subject to a rule.

The schema of community, that is, of reciprocal action and reaction, or the reciprocal causality of substances with respect to their accidents, is the coexistence of the determinations of the one substance with those of the other according to a universal rule.

The schema of possibility is the agreement of the synthesis of various representations with the conditions of time in general. Opposites, for example, cannot exist in the same thing at the same time, but only one after the other. This schema is therefore the determination of the representation of a thing at some time or other.

The schema of actuality is existence at a determinate time.

The schema of necessity is the existence of an object at all times.

All of this makes clear what each schema contains and represents. The schema of quantity contains the generation, or synthesis, of time itself in the successive apprehension of an object. The schema of quality contains the synthesis of sensation with the representation of time, that is, the filling of time. The schema of relation contains the relation of perceptions to one another at all times, which is to say according to a rule for determining time. Finally, the schema of modality and its categories contains time itself as the correlate of the determination of an object: whether, and how, the object belongs to time. The schemata are therefore nothing but a priori determinations of time according to rules. Following the order of the categories and applied to all possible objects, these rules concern the series of time, the content of time, the order of time, and finally the scope or totality of time.

It follows that the schematism of the understanding, working through the transcendental synthesis of the imagination, comes down to nothing other than the unity of the manifold of intuition in inner sense, and thus, indirectly, to the unity of apperception as a function corresponding to inner sense, which is a receptivity. The schemata of the pure concepts of the understanding are therefore the true and only conditions that give these concepts a relation to objects, and with it significance. In the end, then, the categories admit of no use other than an empirical one. They serve only to subject phenomena to universal rules of synthesis through an a priori necessary unity, a unity that arises from the necessary union of all consciousness in one original apperception, and so to make phenomena fit for thoroughgoing connection in one experience. Yet all our knowledge lies within this whole of possible experience, and transcendental truth, which precedes all empirical truth and makes it possible, consists in the general relation to that experience.

It is evident at first glance, however, that although the schemata of sensibility are the only means of realizing the categories, they also restrict them. They limit the categories by conditions that lie outside the understanding, namely in sensibility. The schema is therefore, strictly speaking, only the phenomenon, or the sensory concept, of an object in agreement with the category. As the Latin formulas put it: number is quantity as phenomenon; sensation is reality as phenomenon; the constant and enduring in things is substance as phenomenon; eternity and necessity are phenomena; and so on. Now, it seems that if we remove a restricting condition, we enlarge the concept that was previously restricted. On this reasoning, the categories in their pure meaning, free of every condition of sensibility, ought to hold of things in general as they are, and not merely, as the schemata present them, as they appear. The categories would then have a meaning far wider than the schemata and entirely independent of them. It is true that, once every sensory condition has been stripped away, the pure concepts of the understanding still retain a meaning, but it is a merely logical one, the bare unity of representations. No object is then given to them, and so they lack any meaning that could yield a concept of an object. The concept of substance, for example, if we leave out the sensory determination of permanence, would mean nothing more than a something that can be thought as a subject without ever being a predicate of anything else. I can make nothing of this representation, because it tells me nothing about what properties a thing must have in order to count as such a first subject. The categories without schemata are therefore merely functions of the understanding for producing concepts; they represent no object. They receive this meaning from sensibility, which realizes the understanding at the same time that it restricts it.

### Chapter II. System of All Principles of the Pure Understanding

In the preceding chapter we considered only the general conditions under which the transcendental faculty of judgment is entitled to use the pure concepts of the understanding in synthetic judgments. Our task now is to set out, in systematic connection, the judgments that the understanding actually produces a priori. Our table of the categories will give us natural and reliable guidance here. It is precisely the categories whose application to possible experience must make up all pure a priori knowledge of the understanding, and for that very reason their relation to sensibility will yield a complete and systematic catalogue of all the transcendental principles governing the use of the understanding.

A priori principles earn their name for two reasons. They contain within themselves the grounds of other judgments, and they are not themselves grounded in any higher or more general knowledge. Yet this distinction does not exempt them entirely from the need for proof. No higher knowledge can be found to supply an objective proof, and such a principle forms, if anything, the foundation of all knowledge of the object. None of this, however, prevents us from drawing a proof from the subjective sources that make knowledge of an object possible. Such a proof is in fact necessary, since without it the principle would be open to the charge of being a mere unfounded assertion.

Second, we shall confine our inquiry to those principles that relate to the categories. The principles of the transcendental aesthetic, according to which space and time are the conditions that make things possible as phenomena, fall outside the scope of the present investigation. So does the restriction placed on those principles, namely that they cannot be applied to objects as things in themselves. Likewise, the principles of mathematics form no part of this system, because they are all drawn from intuition and not from the pure concepts of the understanding. Their possibility, however, must still be considered here, since they are synthetic a priori judgments. The point will not be to prove their correctness and apodictic, or necessary, certainty, which would be unnecessary. It will be only to make conceivable, and to deduce, the possibility of such evident a priori knowledge.

We shall also have to discuss the principle of analytic judgments, in contrast with that of synthetic judgments, which are the proper subject of our inquiry. This very contrast will free the theory of synthetic judgments from all ambiguity and set its true nature clearly before us.

#### System of the Principles of the Pure Understanding

#### Section I. Of the Supreme Principle of All Analytic Judgments

Whatever the content of our knowledge, and however it may relate to its object, there is one universal condition of all our judgments, though a purely negative one: they must not contradict themselves. A self-contradictory judgment is nothing at all, even before any question of its object arises. But a judgment free of contradiction may still join concepts in a way that does not correspond to the object. It may also join them without any ground, either a priori or a posteriori, for doing so. A judgment can therefore be free of self-contradiction and still be false or groundless.

The proposition "No subject can have a predicate that contradicts it" is called the principle of contradiction. It is a universal but purely negative criterion of all truth. It belongs to logic alone, because it holds of cognitions merely as cognitions, regardless of their content, and declares that a contradiction annuls them entirely. We can, however, also put this principle to positive use. It can do more than banish falsehood and error, insofar as these rest on contradiction; it can also serve to recognize truth. If a judgment is analytic, whether affirmative or negative, its truth must always be recognizable through the principle of contradiction. The opposite of whatever already lies, as a concept, in our knowledge of the object will always be rightly denied of it, while the concept itself must necessarily be affirmed of it, since its opposite would contradict the object.

We must therefore regard the principle of contradiction as the universal and wholly sufficient principle of all analytic knowledge. Beyond that, however, it has no further use or authority as a sufficient criterion of truth. No knowledge can conflict with this principle without annulling itself, and this makes the principle the *sine qua non*, the indispensable condition, of the truth of our knowledge, but not its determining ground. Since our present concern is solely with the synthetic part of our knowledge, we shall always take care never to violate this inviolable principle. At the same time, we shall not expect it to give any direct help in establishing the truth of a synthetic proposition.

There is, however, a familiar formulation of this celebrated principle, which is merely formal and wholly without content. This formulation contains a synthesis that has been mixed into it carelessly and quite needlessly. It runs: "It is impossible for a thing to be and not to be at the same time." The word "impossible" is superfluous, since it is added to signal an apodictic certainty that ought to be evident from the proposition itself. More importantly, the formula is affected by the condition of time. In effect it says: "A thing A, which is something B, cannot at the same time be non-B." Yet B and non-B can perfectly well exist in succession. A man who is young cannot at the same time be old, but the same man can very well be young at one time and not young, that is, old, at another. Now the principle of contradiction, as a purely logical proposition, must in no way restrict its application to relations of time, and a formula like the one above is therefore quite foreign to its real purpose.

The confusion arises as follows. We first separate a predicate of a thing from the concept of the thing, and then connect the opposite of that predicate to it. The resulting contradiction is therefore not with the subject but only with its predicate, which was joined to the subject synthetically. Even then, the contradiction holds only when the first and second predicates are affirmed at the same time. If I say "A man who is ignorant is not learned," the condition "at the same time" must be added, for someone ignorant at one time may be learned at another. But if I say "No ignorant man is learned," the proposition is analytic, because the attribute of ignorance now forms part of the concept of the subject. In this case the negative proposition follows immediately from the principle of contradiction, with no need to add the condition "at the same time." This is why I have altered the formula of the principle, and the alteration shows very clearly the nature of an analytic proposition.

#### Section II. Of the Supreme Principle of All Synthetic Judgments

Explaining how synthetic judgments are possible is a task with which general logic has nothing to do; it need not even know the problem by name. In transcendental logic, however, it is the most important matter of all. Indeed, it is the only one, if the question concerns the possibility of synthetic a priori judgments, together with the conditions and extent of their validity. Once that question has been fully settled, transcendental logic can reach its goal with perfect ease: to determine the extent and limits of the pure understanding.

In an analytic judgment I do not go beyond the given concept in order to decide something about it. If the judgment is affirmative, I predicate of the concept only what was already thought in it; if it is negative, I merely exclude from it its opposite. In synthetic judgments, by contrast, I must go beyond the given concept in order to think, in relation to it, something entirely different from what was thought in it. This relation is therefore never one of identity or of contradiction, and the judgment alone can never reveal whether it is true or false.

Granted, then, that we must go beyond a given concept in order to compare it synthetically with another, a third thing is required, in which alone the synthesis of the two concepts can arise. What is this *tertium quid*, this third element that must mediate all synthetic judgments? It can only be the one totality that contains all our representations: inner sense, together with its a priori form, time.

The synthesis of our representations rests on the imagination. Their synthetic unity, which a judgment requires, rests on the unity of apperception. Here, then, is where we must look for the possibility of synthetic judgments. And since all three, inner sense, imagination, and apperception, contain sources of a priori representations, here too we must look for the possibility of pure synthetic judgments. Indeed, on these grounds such judgments are necessary if we are to have any knowledge of objects at all, since such knowledge rests entirely on the synthesis of representations.

If a piece of knowledge is to have objective reality, that is, to relate to an object and to have sense and meaning with respect to it, the object must be given in some way. Without this our concepts are empty. We may indeed have thought by means of them, but through such thinking we have not actually known anything; we have merely played with representations. To give an object, if the phrase is taken to mean presenting it not indirectly but immediately in intuition, means nothing other than to relate its representation to experience, whether actual or merely possible. Even space and time are subject to this condition. However pure these concepts are of everything empirical, and however certain it is that the mind represents them entirely a priori, they would be wholly without objective validity, sense, or significance if their necessary use in objects of experience were not demonstrated. Their representation is in fact a mere schema, always related to the reproductive imagination, which calls up the objects of experience. Without those objects, space and time would have no meaning. The same is true of all concepts without exception.

The possibility of experience, then, is what gives objective reality to all our a priori knowledge. Experience depends on the synthetic unity of phenomena, that is, on a synthesis carried out according to concepts of an object of phenomena in general. Without such a synthesis experience could never become knowledge. It would remain a mere rhapsody of perceptions, a loose string of fragments that never fit together into a connected text according to the rules of a thoroughly unified (possible) consciousness. Such fragments would therefore never be subject to the transcendental and necessary unity of apperception. Experience consequently rests on a priori principles of its form, which are general rules of unity in the synthesis of phenomena. The objective reality of these rules, as necessary conditions of the very possibility of experience, can always be shown in experience. Apart from this relation, however, synthetic a priori propositions are entirely impossible, because they would lack a third term, a pure object, in which the synthetic unity could display the objective reality of its concepts.

We know a great deal a priori, in synthetic judgments, about space and about the figures that the productive imagination traces within it, and we genuinely need no experience for this purpose. Yet such knowledge would amount to nothing but busy trifling with a mere figment of the brain, were space not regarded as the condition of the phenomena that make up the material of outer experience. Those pure synthetic judgments therefore do relate, though only indirectly, to possible experience, or rather to the possibility of experience, and on that alone rests the objective validity of their synthesis.

On the one hand, then, experience, as empirical synthesis, is the only possible kind of knowledge that gives reality to every other synthesis. On the other hand, that other synthesis, as a priori knowledge, possesses truth, or agreement with its object, only insofar as it contains nothing more than what is necessary for the synthetic unity of experience.

Accordingly, the supreme principle of all synthetic judgments is this: "Every object is subject to the necessary conditions of the synthetic unity of the manifold of intuition in a possible experience."

Synthetic a priori judgments are possible when we relate three things to a possible empirical knowledge: the formal conditions of a priori intuition, the synthesis of the imagination, and the necessary unity of that synthesis in a transcendental apperception. We can then say: "The conditions of the possibility of experience in general are at the same time conditions of the possibility of the objects of experience, and for that reason they have objective validity in a synthetic a priori judgment."

#### Section III. Systematic Representation of All Synthetic Principles of the Pure Understanding

That there are any principles at all is due solely to the pure understanding. The understanding is not only the faculty of rules for whatever happens. It is also the source of the principles according to which everything that can be presented to us as an object necessarily stands under rules, since without such rules we could never arrive at knowledge of an object. Even the laws of nature, considered as principles of the empirical use of the understanding, carry a mark of necessity. We may therefore at least suspect that they are determined on grounds valid a priori and prior to all experience. But all laws of nature without exception stand under higher principles of the understanding, since they are merely applications of those principles to particular cases of experience. These higher principles alone, therefore, supply the concept that contains the condition of a rule, what might be called the rule's exponent or governing expression. Experience, by contrast, supplies the case that falls under the rule.

There is no danger of confusing merely empirical principles with principles of the pure understanding, or the reverse. Principles of the pure understanding are marked by necessity according to concepts. Every empirical proposition lacks this necessity, however widely it may hold, and that difference is a complete safeguard against confusing the two. There are, however, pure a priori principles that I would still not attribute to the pure understanding, because they are derived not from pure concepts but from pure intuitions, even though the understanding mediates them. The understanding, after all, is the faculty of concepts. Mathematics possesses principles of this kind. But their application to experience, and hence their objective validity, rests entirely on the pure understanding. So too does the very possibility of such synthetic a priori knowledge, that is, its deduction.

For this reason I shall not count the principles of mathematics among my principles. I shall, however, include the principles on which the possibility and a priori objective validity of mathematical principles depend. These are to be regarded as the foundation of mathematical principles, and they proceed from concepts to intuition, not from intuition to concepts.

When the pure concepts of the understanding are applied to possible experience, their synthesis is used either mathematically or dynamically, since it is directed partly at intuition alone and partly at the existence of a phenomenon. Now the a priori conditions of intuition are absolutely necessary with respect to a possible experience. The conditions of the existence of the objects of a possible empirical intuition, however, are in themselves contingent. The principles of the mathematical use of the categories will therefore carry absolute necessity; they will be apodictic. The principles of the dynamical use will also carry a priori necessity, but only under the condition of empirical thought in an experience, and so only mediately and indirectly. They will consequently lack the immediate evidence peculiar to the mathematical principles, though their application to experience loses none of its truth and certainty on that account. We shall be in a better position to judge this point at the end of this system of principles.

The table of the categories is naturally our guide to the table of principles, since principles are nothing but rules for the objective use of the categories. All principles of the pure understanding are accordingly:

1. Axioms of Intuition
2. Anticipations of Perception
3. Analogies of Experience
4. Postulates of Empirical Thought in General

I have chosen these names deliberately, so that we do not lose sight of the differences in the evidence and use of these principles. It will soon become clear that the principles of the categories of quantity and quality differ from those of the other two classes, if we attend only to their form. This difference concerns both the evidence of these principles and the a priori determination of phenomena. The first two possess an intuitive certainty, the last two a merely discursive one, though in both cases the certainty is complete. I shall therefore call the former mathematical and the latter dynamical principles. It should be noted, however, that by these terms I mean neither the principles of mathematics in the one case nor those of general physical dynamics in the other. I have in view only the principles of the pure understanding in their application to inner sense, without regard to the particular representations given in it. It is through these principles that the sciences of mathematics and dynamics first become possible. I have named them, then, with reference to their application rather than their content, and I shall now consider them in the order in which they appear in the table.

All combination (*conjunctio*) is either composition (*compositio*) or connection (*nexus*). Composition is the synthesis of a manifold whose parts do not necessarily belong to one another. The two triangles into which a square is divided by its diagonal, for example, do not necessarily belong to each other. The synthesis of the homogeneous in everything that can be treated mathematically is of this kind. This synthesis can be further divided into aggregation and coalition, the first applying to extensive quantities and the second to intensive ones. The second kind of combination, connection, is the synthesis of a manifold insofar as its parts do necessarily belong to one another, as an accident belongs to a substance or an effect to its cause. It is therefore a synthesis of elements that, though heterogeneous, are represented as connected a priori. This combination is not arbitrary, and because it concerns the connection of the existence of the manifold, I call it dynamical. It too can be divided: into the physical synthesis of phenomena among themselves, and the metaphysical synthesis, which is the a priori connection of phenomena in the faculty of knowledge.

**1. Axioms of Intuition**

The principle of these axioms is: All intuitions are extensive quantities.

**Proof**

All phenomena contain, as regards their form, an intuition in space and time, which underlies every one of them a priori. Phenomena can therefore be apprehended, or taken up into empirical consciousness, only through the synthesis of a manifold. This synthesis generates the representations of a determinate space or time through the composition of the homogeneous and the consciousness of the synthetic unity of this homogeneous manifold. Now the consciousness of a homogeneous manifold in intuition, insofar as it makes possible the representation of an object, is the concept of a quantity (*quantum*). Even the perception of an object as a phenomenon, therefore, depends on a particular synthetic unity of the manifold of given sensible intuition. This is the same unity through which we think the unity of the composition of the homogeneous manifold in the concept of a quantity. All phenomena, then, are quantities, and specifically extensive quantities, because as intuitions in space or time they must be represented through the same synthesis by which space and time themselves are determined.

An extensive quantity is one in which the representation of the parts makes possible the representation of the whole, and therefore necessarily precedes it.
