I cannot represent to myself any line, however short, without drawing it in thought, generating all its parts one after another from a point, and only in this way do I produce this intuition. Exactly the same holds for every portion of time, even the smallest. In it I think only the successive advance from one moment to the next, and so a determinate quantity of time is produced through its various portions and their addition. Since the pure intuition in all phenomena is either space or time, every phenomenon, considered as intuition, is an extensive quantity, because it can be known in our apprehension only through successive synthesis, from part to part. All phenomena are accordingly to be regarded as aggregates, that is, as collections of previously given parts. This is not true of every kind of quantity, but only of those we represent and apprehend as extensive.

On this successive synthesis of the productive imagination, as it generates figures, is founded the mathematics of extension, or geometry, together with its axioms. These axioms express the conditions of a priori sensible intuition under which alone the schema of a pure concept of outer intuition can arise. Examples are "Between two points only one straight line is possible" and "Two straight lines cannot enclose a space." These are the axioms that properly concern only quantities as such (*quanta*). The magnitude of a thing (*quantitas*) is a different matter. On the question "How large is this or that object?" we possess various propositions that are synthetic and immediately certain (*indemonstrabilia*, incapable of demonstration), yet strictly speaking we have no axioms. The propositions "If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal" and "If equals are taken from equals, the remainders are equal," for example, are analytic, because I am immediately conscious of the identity of the production of the one quantity with the production of the other, whereas axioms must be synthetic propositions a priori. The self-evident propositions about the relations of numbers, on the other hand, are certainly synthetic, but they are not general in the way the propositions of geometry are, and for that reason they cannot be called axioms, only numerical formulas. That 7 + 5 = 12 is not an analytic proposition, for I do not think the number twelve in the representation of seven, or in that of five, or in the representation of combining the two. (Whether I think the number twelve when I actually add them is not the question here, because with an analytic proposition the only point at issue is whether I really think the predicate in the representation of the subject.) Yet although the proposition is synthetic, it is only a singular proposition. Since we attend here solely to the synthesis of homogeneous units, that synthesis can take place in only one way, even though our use of these numbers afterward is general. When I say, "A triangle can be constructed from three lines, any two of which together are longer than the third," I am exercising only the pure function of the productive imagination, which can draw the lines longer or shorter and set the angles however it pleases. The number seven, by contrast, is possible in only one way, and so is the number twelve, which results from the synthesis of seven and five. Such propositions must therefore be called not axioms, for then we would have infinitely many of them, but numerical formulas.

This transcendental principle of the mathematics of phenomena greatly extends our a priori knowledge. This principle alone makes pure mathematics applicable, in all its precision, to objects of experience. Without it, the validity of that application would be far from self-evident, and this very point has in fact often given rise to contradictions and confusion. Phenomena are not things in themselves. Empirical intuition is possible only through the pure intuition of space and time, so whatever geometry asserts of pure intuition holds indisputably of empirical intuition as well. Every evasion must therefore collapse, such as the claim that objects of the senses do not conform to the rules of construction in space (for instance, to the rule that lines or angles are infinitely divisible). For if such objections held, we would be denying objective validity to space, and with it to all mathematics, and we would no longer know why, or how far, mathematics can be applied to phenomena. The synthesis of spaces and times, as the essential form of all intuition, is what makes possible the apprehension of a phenomenon. It therefore makes possible every outer experience, and with it all knowledge of the objects of experience. Whatever mathematics proves in its pure use about space and time must necessarily hold of those objects. All objections to the contrary are merely the quibbles of a poorly instructed reason. Such a reason mistakenly supposes it can free the objects of the senses from the formal conditions of our sensibility, and it treats them, though they are mere phenomena, as things in themselves given as such to our understanding. But in that case no synthetic a priori knowledge of them would be possible at all, and therefore none through pure concepts of space. The science that determines those concepts, namely geometry, would itself be impossible.

**2. Anticipations of Perception**

The principle of the anticipations is this: In all phenomena the real, which is the object of sensation, has intensive quantity, that is, a degree.

**Proof**

Perception is empirical consciousness, meaning a consciousness that contains an element of sensation. Phenomena, as objects of perception, are not pure, merely formal intuitions as space and time are, for phenomena cannot be perceived in themselves. They can be perceived only as phenomena, and some part of them always belongs to what lies outside the self, whereas pure intuitions are wholly products of the mind and as such are known in themselves. Beyond the intuition, then, phenomena contain the material for an object, through which something existing in space or time is represented. They contain the real of sensation. This is a merely subjective representation that makes us conscious only that the subject has been affected, and we refer it to some external object. Now a gradual transition from empirical consciousness to pure consciousness is possible, in which the real in that consciousness vanishes entirely and nothing remains but a merely formal, a priori consciousness of the manifold in space and time. It follows that a synthesis is also possible in the production of the quantity of a sensation, from its beginning in pure intuition, = 0, up to some given quantity of that sensation. Since sensation is not in itself an objective representation, and contains neither the intuition of space nor that of time, it cannot possess any extensive quantity. Yet a quantity does belong to it, by way of its apprehension, in which empirical consciousness can rise within a certain time from nothing, = 0, to the given amount. That quantity is therefore intensive. Accordingly, we must ascribe to all objects of perception, insofar as the perception contains sensation, an intensive quantity, which is a degree of influence on the senses.

All knowledge by which I can know and determine a priori what belongs to empirical knowledge may be called an anticipation, and this is no doubt the sense in which Epicurus used his term *prolepsis*. But there is something in phenomena that is never known a priori, and for this reason it constitutes the real difference between pure and empirical knowledge. That something is sensation, the matter of perception. It follows that sensation is precisely the element in knowledge that cannot be anticipated at all. By contrast, we could quite properly call the pure determinations in space and time, with respect both to shape and to quantity, anticipations of phenomena, because they represent a priori what may at any time be given a posteriori in experience. But suppose that in every sensation, taken as sensation in general and without any particular sensation in mind, there were something that could be known a priori. This would deserve to be called anticipation in an exceptional sense. It would be exceptional because it seems strange to get ahead of experience in precisely what concerns the matter of experience, which we can draw only from experience itself. Yet that is exactly the case here.

Apprehension, here taken in the broadest sense to include both perception proper and sensation proper, fills only a single moment when it proceeds by means of sensation alone, provided I do not consider a succession of many sensations. Sensation is that element in a phenomenon whose apprehension is not a successive synthesis advancing from parts to a complete representation. Sensation therefore has no extensive quantity. The absence of sensation in a given moment would represent that moment as empty, and therefore as = 0. What corresponds to sensation in empirical intuition is reality (*realitas phaenomenon*, reality as phenomenon), and what corresponds to its absence is negation, = 0. Now every sensation can be diminished, so that it decreases and gradually vanishes. Between reality in a phenomenon and negation, therefore, there runs a continuous chain of many possible intermediate sensations, any two of which differ from each other by less than the given sensation differs from zero, or complete negation. The real in a phenomenon always has a quantity. That quantity, however, is not encountered in apprehension, because apprehension by means of mere sensation takes place in a single instant, not through the successive synthesis of many sensations, and so it does not advance from parts to the whole. The real therefore has a quantity, but not an extensive one.

A quantity that is apprehended only as a unity, and in which plurality can be represented only by approaching negation, = 0, I call intensive quantity. Reality in a phenomenon therefore has intensive quantity, that is, a degree. If we consider this reality as a cause, whether of sensation or of some other reality in the phenomenon such as a change, we call its degree, in its character as a cause, a momentum. The word is used here in the older sense of the strength with which a cause acts at a given instant, as when we speak of the momentum of weight. We use this term because a degree indicates only a quantity whose apprehension is not successive but instantaneous. I touch on this only in passing, however, since I am not concerned with causality at present.

Every sensation, then, and therefore every reality in phenomena, however small, has a degree, an intensive quantity that can always be diminished further. Between reality and negation there is a continuous connection of possible realities and of possible smaller perceptions. Every color, red for example, has a degree that, however small, is never the smallest possible. The same holds for heat, for the momentum of weight, and so on.

This property of quantities, by which no part of them is the smallest possible and no part is simple, is called their continuity. Space and time are continuous quantities (*quanta continua*), because no part of them can be given without being enclosed within boundaries, namely points and moments, so that the given part is itself a space or a time. Space thus consists only of spaces, and time only of times. Points and moments are merely boundaries, the bare positions at which space and time are limited. But positions always presuppose the intuitions they are meant to limit or determine, and we cannot compose either space or time out of constituent parts that would be given prior to space or time. Quantities of this kind may also be called flowing. The synthesis of the productive imagination that produces them is a progression in time, and we customarily express the continuity of time with the word "flowing."

All phenomena, then, are continuous quantities, both with respect to their intuition and with respect to mere perception, which is sensation, and with it reality. In the first respect they are extensive quantities, and in the second they are intensive. When the synthesis of the manifold of a phenomenon is interrupted, the result is merely an aggregate of several phenomena, not properly a phenomenon as a quantity. Such an aggregate is produced not by simply continuing a productive synthesis of a certain kind, but by repeating a synthesis that keeps coming to a stop. Suppose I call thirteen dollars a sum or quantity of money. I use the term quite correctly if by thirteen dollars I mean the value of one mark of standard silver, the mark being a fixed weight of silver of legal fineness. That value is indeed a continuous quantity. No part of it is the smallest, and every part could make up a coin that would itself contain material for still smaller coins. But if by thirteen dollars I mean thirteen coins, whatever their value in silver may be, it would be quite wrong to call them a quantity of dollars. I must call them an aggregate, that is, a number of coins. And just as every number must rest on unity as its foundation, a phenomenon taken as a unity is a quantity, and as such always a continuous quantity (*quantum continuum*).

Since all phenomena, whether considered as extensive or as intensive, are continuous quantities, the proposition that "all change (the passage of a thing from one state into another) is continuous" could easily be proved here, and with mathematical certainty. It could be proved if the causality of change did not lie wholly outside the bounds of transcendental philosophy and presuppose empirical principles. The understanding gives us no a priori knowledge of how a cause that alters the condition of things is possible, meaning a cause that determines them to the opposite of some given state. This is not merely because the understanding has no insight into that possibility, since such insight is lacking in a number of a priori cognitions. It is because the concept of change concerns only certain determinations of phenomena, which experience alone can make known to us, while their cause lies in what is unchangeable. Here we have nothing at our disposal except the pure fundamental concepts of all possible experience, among which nothing empirical may be admitted. We therefore cannot, without damaging the unity of our system, anticipate general natural science, which is built on certain fundamental experiences.

Nevertheless, there is no lack of evidence for the great influence that the principle developed above exerts in anticipating perceptions. It even makes up for their absence, to the extent of guarding us against false conclusions we might otherwise draw too hastily.

All reality in perception has a degree, and between that degree and negation there lies an endless series of ever smaller degrees. Every sense must nonetheless have a definite degree of receptivity for sensations. If both of these are true, then no perception, and therefore no experience, could prove, directly or indirectly, a complete absence of all reality in a phenomenon. That is, experience can never furnish a proof of empty space or empty time. In the first place, a complete absence of reality in sensible intuition obviously cannot itself be perceived. In the second place, such an absence cannot be inferred from any single phenomenon and the differences of degree in its reality, nor should it ever be assumed in order to explain any phenomenon. Suppose the whole intuition of a determinate space or time is real through and through, so that no part of it is empty. Every reality still has its degree, and while the extensive quantity of the phenomenon stays unchanged, that degree can diminish through endless gradations down to nothing, the void. There must therefore be infinitely graduated degrees with which space or time is filled. The intensive quantity in different phenomena can be smaller or greater while the extensive quantity of the intuition remains equal and unaltered.

I will give an example. Nearly all natural philosophers observe a great difference in the quantity of matter of different kinds in bodies of the same volume. This difference shows itself partly in the momentum of gravity, or weight, and partly in the momentum of resistance to other bodies in motion. From it they conclude unanimously that this volume, the extensive quantity of the phenomenon, must contain empty space in all bodies, though in differing proportions. But who would suspect that these investigators of nature, most of them mathematical and mechanical in their approach, base this conclusion solely on a metaphysical hypothesis, precisely the kind of hypothesis they claim to scorn and avoid? Yet they do so when they assume that the real in space is always the same in kind and can be distinguished only by its extensive quantity, that is, by amount. (I must not call this real "impenetrability" or "weight" here, since those are empirical concepts.) This presupposition has no basis in experience and is therefore purely metaphysical, and against it I set a transcendental demonstration. My demonstration will not, admittedly, explain the difference in the way spaces are filled. It does, however, entirely remove the supposed necessity of the presupposition that this difference can be explained only by assuming empty spaces. It has the further merit of leaving the understanding free to conceive the difference in some other way, should the explanation of the facts call for some such hypothesis. For we see that two equal spaces may be completely filled by entirely different kinds of matter, so that in neither is there a single point where matter is absent. Every reality nonetheless has its degree of resistance or of weight, and without any reduction in extensive quantity, that degree can grow smaller and smaller without limit before it passes into nothing and vanishes. Consider an expansion that fills a space, such as caloric, the subtle fluid then held to be the substance of heat, or any other reality in the world of phenomena. It can decrease in degree without end, yet without leaving the smallest part of that space empty. It fills the space with those lesser degrees just as completely as another phenomenon could with greater ones. I do not at all mean to assert that this is actually how matters differ in their specific gravity. I wish only to show, from a principle of the pure understanding, that the nature of our perceptions makes such an explanation possible. I also wish to show that it is a mistake to treat the real in a phenomenon as equal in degree and different only in aggregation and extensive quantity, and especially to do so while claiming the authority of an a priori principle of the understanding.

Even so, this principle of the anticipation of perception must somewhat startle an inquirer whom training in transcendental philosophy has made cautious. One will naturally doubt whether the understanding can assert any synthetic proposition of this kind. The proposition concerns the degree of all reality in phenomena, and therefore the possibility of an internal difference within sensation itself, once its empirical quality is set aside. The following question is therefore well worth answering: How can the understanding make synthetic a priori assertions about phenomena, and so anticipate them, even in what is distinctively and purely empirical, namely in what concerns sensation itself?

The quality of sensation, as with colors, tastes, and so forth, is always merely empirical and cannot be represented a priori. But the real, which is what corresponds to sensation, stands opposed to negation, = 0. It represents only something whose concept contains a being (*ein Sein*), and it signifies nothing but the synthesis in an empirical consciousness. Empirical consciousness in inner sense can be raised from 0 to any higher degree. As a result, one and the same extensive quantity of intuition, such as an illuminated surface, can excite as strong a sensation as an aggregate of many other, less brightly illuminated surfaces. We can therefore abstract entirely from the extensive quantity of a phenomenon. In the bare sensation at a given moment, we can represent a synthesis of uniform ascent from 0 up to the given empirical consciousness. All sensations, as such, are given only a posteriori, but the property that they have a degree can be known a priori. It is worth noting that with respect to quantities in general, we can know only a single quality a priori, namely continuity. With respect to all quality, meaning the real in phenomena, we can know nothing more a priori than its intensive quantity, namely that it has a degree. Everything else is left to experience.

**3. Analogies of Experience**

The principle of the analogies is this: Experience is possible only through the representation of a necessary connection of perceptions.

**Proof**

Experience is empirical knowledge, meaning knowledge that determines an object by means of perceptions. It is therefore a synthesis of perceptions. This synthesis is not itself contained in perception, but it contains the synthetic unity of the manifold of perception in one consciousness. That unity is the essential element in our knowledge of objects of the senses, which is to say in experience, as distinct from mere intuition or sensation. In experience, however, our perceptions come together only contingently, so that no necessity in their connection appears, or can appear, from the perceptions themselves. Apprehension merely places the manifold of empirical intuition side by side, and no representation of necessity in the connected existence of the phenomena it brings together can be found in it. But experience is knowledge of objects by means of perceptions. The relation in the existence of the manifold must therefore be represented in experience not as it happens to be put together in time, but as it objectively is in time. And because time itself cannot be perceived, the existence of objects in time can be determined only through their connection in time in general, and therefore only through a priori connecting concepts. These concepts always carry the character of necessity, and so experience is possible only through the representation of a necessary connection of perceptions.

The three modes of time are permanence, succession, and coexistence. There are accordingly three rules governing all relations of phenomena in time, and by these rules the existence of every phenomenon is determined with respect to the unity of all time. These rules precede all experience and make it possible.

The general principle of all three analogies rests on the necessary unity of apperception with respect to all possible empirical consciousness, or perception, at every time. And since this unity lies a priori at the foundation of all mental operations, the principle rests on the synthetic unity of all phenomena according to their relations in time. Original apperception relates to inner sense, the sum of all representations, and it relates a priori to the form of inner sense, which is the temporal relation of the manifold of empirical consciousness. This manifold must be combined in original apperception according to relations of time. That necessity is imposed by the a priori transcendental unity of apperception, to which everything is subject that can belong to my own knowledge, and therefore everything that can become an object for me. This synthetic unity, determined a priori, in the temporal relation of perceptions therefore yields the rule: "All empirical determinations of time must be subject to rules of the general determination of time." The analogies of experience, which we are now about to treat, must be rules of this kind.

These principles have a peculiar feature. They concern not phenomena and the synthesis of their empirical intuition, but only the existence of phenomena and their relations to one another with respect to that existence. The way in which we apprehend something in a phenomenon can be determined a priori, so that the rule of its synthesis can supply this a priori intuition, and in fact produce it, in every empirical instance. But the existence of phenomena cannot be known a priori. Even if we could infer by this route that something exists, we could not know that existence determinately. We could not anticipate how its empirical intuition would differ from that of other things.

The two principles discussed above, which I called mathematical because they justify the application of mathematics to phenomena, concern phenomena only with respect to their possibility, and show how phenomena, as regards both their intuition and the real in their perception, can be generated according to the rules of a mathematical synthesis. In both cases, therefore, we may use numerical quantities, and with them the determination of a phenomenon as a quantity. For example, I could compose and give a priori, that is, construct, the degree of our sensation of sunlight out of 200,000 times the illumination of the moon. I could compute the sun's light and declare it a definite number of times greater than the moon's, just as heat is measured by comparing its various effects on water, for instance, or on the mercury in a thermometer. These two principles, the Axioms of Intuition and the Anticipations of Perception, authorize us to apply size and number to phenomena in this way, and so we may call them constitutive.

The case is very different with the principles whose task is to subject the *existence* of phenomena to a priori rules. Since existence cannot be constructed, these principles can concern only the relations of existence, and they can be only regulative. Here there is no question of either axioms or anticipations. If a perception is given to us in a certain temporal relation to other perceptions, even though those others are undetermined, we cannot say a priori what the other perception necessarily connected with it is, or how great it is. We can say only how it is connected with the first, as regards its existence, in this given mode of time.

Analogies mean something very different in philosophy from what they mean in mathematics. In mathematics they are formulas that state the equality of two quantitative relations, and they are always constitutive: if two terms of the proportion are given, the third is also given, because it can be constructed by means of these formulas. In philosophy, however, an analogy is the equality not of two quantitative relations but of two qualitative ones. From three given terms I can know and state a priori the relation to a fourth term, but not the fourth term itself. I do, however, possess a rule for seeking that fourth term in experience, and a mark by which to recognize it there. An analogy of experience is therefore only a rule according to which unity of experience must arise out of perceptions with respect to objects (phenomena), and it is a regulative principle, not a constitutive one. The same is true of the postulates of empirical thought in general, which concern the synthesis of mere intuition (the form of phenomena), the synthesis of perception (their matter), and the synthesis of experience (the relation of these perceptions). They too are only regulative principles, and they are clearly distinguishable from the mathematical principles, which are constitutive. The difference does not lie in certainty, since both kinds possess certainty a priori. It lies in the kind of evidence each provides, and therefore also in the way each must be demonstrated.

Something holds for all synthetic propositions, however, and must be stressed particularly here. These analogies have meaning and validity not as principles of the transcendental use of the understanding but only of its empirical use, and their truth can therefore be proved only in that capacity. It follows that phenomena must be subsumed not directly under the categories but only under their schemata. If the objects to which these principles apply were things in themselves, it would be quite impossible to know anything about them synthetically a priori. But they are nothing but phenomena, and complete knowledge of them, the knowledge to which all a priori principles must ultimately relate, is simply possible experience. These principles can therefore aim at nothing except the conditions of empirical knowledge in the unity of the synthesis of phenomena. This synthesis, however, is thought only in the schema of the pure concept of the understanding, while the category contains the function of its unity, as the unity of a synthesis in general, unrestricted by any sensory condition. These principles will therefore entitle us to connect phenomena according to an analogy with the logical and universal unity of concepts, and so to use the categories in the principles themselves. When we apply the principles to experience, though, we shall use only the schemata, as the key to their proper application, in place of the categories. More precisely, we shall treat the categories as restricting conditions, under the name of "formulas" of the schemata.

**A. First Analogy**

**Principle of the Permanence of Substance**

In all changes of phenomena, substance persists, and its quantity in nature is neither increased nor diminished.

**Proof**

All phenomena exist in time. Only in time, as their substratum and as the permanent form of inner intuition, can coexistence and succession be represented. Time itself, in which all changes of phenomena must be thought, therefore remains and does not change, because it is that in which succession and coexistence can be represented only as its determinations. But time in itself cannot be perceived. It follows that in the objects of perception, that is, in phenomena, there must be a substratum that represents time in general, and in which all change or coexistence can be perceived through the relation of phenomena to it. Now the substratum of everything real, of everything that belongs to the existence of things, is substance; whatever belongs to existence can be thought only as a determination of substance. The permanent, then, in relation to which alone all temporal relations among phenomena can be determined, is substance in the world of phenomena. It is the real in phenomena, which, as the substratum of all change, always remains the same. And since substance cannot change in its existence, its quantity in nature can be neither increased nor diminished.

Our apprehension of the manifold in a phenomenon is always successive, and therefore always changing. By apprehension alone, then, we could never determine whether this manifold, as an object of experience, is coexistent or successive, unless it rested on something fixed and permanent, of whose existence all succession and coexistence are nothing but so many modes, or modes of time. Relations of time are possible only in the permanent, since simultaneity and succession are the only relations in time. The permanent is thus the substratum of our empirical representation of time itself, and only in it is any determination of time possible. Permanence is, in fact, simply another expression for time, as the abiding correlate of all existence of phenomena, of all change, and of all coexistence. Change does not affect time itself, only the phenomena in time, just as coexistence cannot be regarded as a mode of time itself, since in time no parts coexist; all are successive. If we were to ascribe succession to time itself, we would have to think of yet another time in which that succession could take place. Only through the permanent does existence in different parts of the temporal series acquire a quantity, which we call duration. In mere succession, existence is perpetually vanishing and beginning again, and so never has even the smallest quantity. Without the permanent, then, no temporal relation is possible. Now, time in itself cannot be perceived. The permanent in phenomena must therefore be regarded as the substratum of every determination of time, and so also as the condition of the possibility of all synthetic unity of perceptions, which is to say, of experience. All existence and all change in time can be regarded only as a mode of existence of what abides unchanged. In all phenomena, therefore, the permanent is the object itself, namely substance as phenomenon, while everything that changes or can change belongs only to the way this substance or these substances exist, and hence to their determinations.

I find that in every age not only philosophers but even ordinary common sense have presupposed this permanence as the substratum of all change in phenomena, and I can only believe they will always accept it as beyond doubt. The philosopher merely puts it more precisely: "In all changes in the world, substance remains, and only the accidents change." Yet I nowhere find even an attempt to prove this plainly synthetic proposition. Indeed, it rarely enjoys the place it deserves, at the head of the pure and wholly a priori laws of nature. The statement that substance is permanent is, in truth, tautological, because permanence is the very ground on which we apply the category of substance to a phenomenon. What needed proving was that in all phenomena there is something permanent, of whose existence the changeable is nothing but a determination. A proof of this kind cannot be dogmatic, however. It cannot be drawn from concepts, because the proposition is synthetic and a priori. And since philosophers never reflected that such propositions are valid only in relation to possible experience, and so can be proved only through a deduction of the possibility of experience, it is no wonder that this principle, though it has always been the foundation of experience (we feel the need of it in empirical knowledge), has never been proved.

A philosopher was once asked, "How much does smoke weigh?" He replied, "Subtract the weight of the remaining ashes from the weight of the wood you burned, and you will have the weight of the smoke." He took it as beyond dispute that even in fire, matter (substance) does not perish, and only its form undergoes a change. In the same way, the saying "Nothing comes from nothing" was simply another inference from the principle of permanence, or rather from the perpetual existence of the true subject in phenomena. If what we call substance in a phenomenon is to be the proper substratum of every determination of time, then all existence, in past time as well as future, must be determinable through it alone. We are entitled to call a phenomenon a substance, therefore, only because we suppose it to exist at all times. The word "permanence" does not fully capture this notion, since it seems to point chiefly to future time. Still, the inner necessity of always being is inseparable from the necessity of always having been, and so the term may stand. "Nothing is born from nothing; nothing can return to nothing": these two propositions, in the words of the Roman satirist Persius, the ancients never separated. People today sometimes mistakenly separate them, because they imagine that the propositions apply to objects as things in themselves, and they fear that the first might conflict with the world's dependence on a supreme cause, even with respect to its substance. That fear is entirely unnecessary. The question here concerns only phenomena within experience, and the unity of experience would be impossible if we admitted that new things, new in respect of their substance, could arise. We would then lose the one thing that can represent the unity of time: the identity of the substratum, through which alone all change has complete and thoroughgoing unity. This permanence, however, is nothing more than the way we represent to ourselves the existence of things in the world of phenomena.

The determinations of a substance, which are only particular modes of its existence, are called accidents. They are always real, because they concern the existence of substance; negations are merely determinations that express the nonexistence of something in substance. Now if we ascribe a particular existence to this real element in substance, to motion, for instance, as an accident of matter, that existence is called inherence, as opposed to the existence of substance itself, which is called subsistence. Many misunderstandings arise from this, however, and it would be more accurate to describe an accident simply as the way in which the existence of a substance is positively determined. Even so, the conditions under which our understanding operates logically make it impossible to avoid separating out, as it were, whatever in the existence of a substance is subject to change while the substance remains, and regarding it in relation to what is genuinely permanent and fundamental. For this reason the category of substance stands under the heading of relation, more because it is the condition of relations than because it contains any relation in itself.

On this notion of permanence rests the proper concept of change. Coming into being and passing away are not changes in what comes into being or passes away. Change is a mode of existence that follows another mode of existence of the same object. Everything that changes is therefore permanent, and only its state changes. Since this alteration affects only determinations, which can begin and end, we may say, in what sounds like a paradox: "Only the permanent (substance) changes; the changeable undergoes no change, but only alternation, in which certain determinations cease and others begin."

Change can therefore be perceived only in substances. Absolute coming into being or passing away, which does not concern merely a determination of the permanent, cannot be a possible perception at all, because it is precisely the concept of the permanent that makes it possible to represent a transition from one state to another, and from nonbeing to being. Such transitions can therefore be known empirically only as alternating determinations of what is permanent. Suppose that a thing absolutely begins to exist. There must then be a point in time at which it did not exist. But how, and by what, could we fix that point in time, except by something that already exists? An empty preceding time is not an object of perception. If instead we connect this beginning with things that existed beforehand and continue to exist until the new object begins, then the new object can only be a determination of what already existed, as the permanent. The same holds for passing away, which presupposes the empirical representation of a time in which a phenomenon no longer exists.

Substances, in the world of phenomena, are the substratum of all determinations of time. If some substances came into being and others ceased to be, the one condition of the empirical unity of time would be destroyed. Phenomena would then relate to two different times, in which existence would flow side by side, which is absurd. There is only one time, and all different times must be placed within it, not as coexistent but as successive. Permanence is therefore a necessary condition under which alone phenomena can be determined as things or objects in a possible experience. As for the empirical criterion of this necessary permanence, and with it of the substantiality of phenomena, we shall have ample occasion to discuss it later.

**B. Second Analogy**

**Principle of Temporal Succession According to the Law of Causality**

All changes take place according to the law of the connection of cause and effect.

**Proof**

(The treatment of the preceding principle fully established that all phenomena in the succession of time are only changes, that is, a successive being and nonbeing of the determinations of substance, which is permanent. It follows that substance itself cannot come to be after not having been, or cease to be after having been, and so the origin or extinction of substance itself is impossible. That principle could also have been expressed thus: "All alteration (succession) of phenomena is merely change." Changes of substance are not its origin or extinction, because the concept of change presupposes the same subject existing with two opposite determinations, and therefore as permanent. With this preliminary note, we proceed to the proof.)

I perceive that phenomena follow one another: a state of things exists at one time whose opposite existed in an earlier state. Here, then, I am really connecting two perceptions in time. Connection, however, is not the work of mere sense and intuition. It is the product of a synthetic faculty of imagination, which determines inner sense with respect to a relation of time. But imagination can connect these two states in two ways, placing either one first in time, because time in itself cannot be perceived, and what comes first and what follows in an object cannot be empirically determined by reference to it. I am conscious only that my imagination places one state before and the other after, not that one state precedes the other in the object. Mere perception, in short, leaves the objective relation of successive phenomena entirely undetermined. For this relation to be known as determined, the relation between the two states must be thought in such a way that it is thereby determined as necessary which state must come first and which after, and not the reverse. But a concept that carries with it a necessity of synthetic unity can only be a pure concept of the understanding, one not found in mere perception. In this case it is the concept of the relation of cause and effect, in which the cause determines the effect in time as its necessary consequence, not as something that might come first, or that might in some cases not be perceived to follow at all. It follows that experience itself, the empirical knowledge of phenomena, is possible only because we subject the sequence of phenomena, and therefore all change, to the law of causality. Phenomena themselves, as objects of experience, are possible only by virtue of this law.

Our apprehension of the manifold of phenomena is always successive. The representations of the parts follow one another. Whether they also follow one another in the object is a second question, not contained in the first. We may of course call anything an object, even any representation, so far as we are conscious of it. But what the word means in the case of phenomena, not insofar as they are themselves objects (as representations) but insofar as they designate an object, calls for deeper inquiry. Insofar as phenomena, taken merely as representations, are also objects of consciousness, they cannot be distinguished from apprehension, that is, from their reception into the synthesis of imagination. We must therefore say that the manifold of phenomena is always produced successively in the mind. If phenomena were things in themselves, no one could infer from the succession of our representations how this manifold is connected in the object, since we deal only with our representations. How things may be in themselves, apart from the representations through which they affect us, lies wholly beyond the range of our knowledge. Phenomena are not things in themselves, and yet they are the only thing given to us to know. I am therefore obliged to show what kind of temporal connection belongs to the manifold in phenomena themselves, even though the representation of that manifold in apprehension is always successive. Consider a house standing before me. My apprehension of its manifold is successive. Is the manifold of the house therefore successive in itself? No one will grant that. But as soon as I raise my concept of an object to its transcendental meaning, I find that the house is not a thing in itself but only a phenomenon, a representation whose transcendental object remains entirely unknown. What, then, am I to understand by the question of how the manifold can be connected in the phenomenon itself, considered not as a thing in itself but merely as a phenomenon? Here what lies in my successive apprehension is regarded as representation, while the phenomenon given to me, though it is nothing more than a combination of these representations, is regarded as their object, with which the concept I draw from the representations of apprehension must agree. It soon becomes clear that, since truth consists in the agreement of knowledge with its object, the present question can concern only the formal conditions of empirical truth. The phenomenon, as opposed to the representations of apprehension, can be distinguished from them as their object only if it stands under a rule that distinguishes it from every other apprehension and makes one particular way of connecting the manifold necessary. Whatever in the phenomenon contains the condition of this necessary rule of apprehension is the object.

Let us now turn to our task. That something happens, that something or some state exists which did not exist before, cannot be perceived empirically unless it is preceded by a phenomenon that does not contain this state. A reality that followed an empty time, a beginning preceded by no state of things, could no more be apprehended than empty time itself. Every apprehension of an event is therefore a perception that follows another perception. But since this is true of every synthesis of apprehension, as I showed above with the example of the house, it does not yet suffice to distinguish my apprehension of an event from other apprehensions. I notice, however, that if in a phenomenon containing an event I call the earlier state of my perception A and the later state B, then in apprehension B can only follow A, and A cannot follow B but can only precede it. Suppose I watch a ship drifting downstream. My perception of its position farther down follows my perception of its position farther up the river, and in apprehending this phenomenon it is impossible to perceive the vessel first downstream and afterward upstream. Here, then, the order in which perceptions follow one another in apprehension is fixed, and apprehension is bound by that order. In the earlier example, my perceptions of the house could begin at the roof and end at the foundation, or the reverse; or I could apprehend the manifold of this empirical intuition by moving from left to right or from right to left. Accordingly, in the series of these perceptions there was no fixed order that obliged me to begin at a particular point in order to connect the manifold empirically. But a rule of this kind is always present in the perception of something that happens, and it makes the order of the successive perceptions in the apprehension of such a phenomenon necessary.

In the present case, therefore, I must derive the subjective sequence of apprehension from the objective sequence of phenomena, because otherwise the subjective sequence is entirely undetermined, and one phenomenon cannot be distinguished from another. The subjective sequence, taken by itself, proves nothing about how the manifold is connected in an object, since it is completely arbitrary. The objective sequence, by contrast, must consist in the order of the manifold within the phenomenon, an order according to which the apprehension of one thing (what happens) follows the apprehension of another thing (what precedes it) in accordance with a rule. Only in this way am I entitled to say of the phenomenon itself, and not merely of my own apprehension, that a certain order or sequence is found in it. That is, I cannot arrange my apprehension in any order other than this one.

In accordance with this rule, then, whatever precedes an event must contain the condition for a rule according to which this event always and necessarily follows. But I cannot reverse the process, starting from the event and working backward to determine, through apprehension, what preceded it. No phenomenon runs back from a later point of time to an earlier one, although it certainly relates to some earlier point. From a given time, on the other hand, there is always a necessary progression to the determinate time that follows. Therefore, because there certainly is something that follows, I must of necessity connect it with something else that precedes it, upon which it follows according to a rule, that is, necessarily. The event, as something conditioned, thus gives a reliable indication of some condition, and that condition determines the event.

Suppose that nothing preceded an event upon which the event had to follow according to a rule. All sequence of perception would then exist only in apprehension. It would be merely subjective, and nothing could determine objectively which perception ought to come first and which ought to come after. We would have nothing but a play of representations with no bearing on any object. Perception would give us no means of distinguishing one phenomenon from another with respect to their relations in time, because the succession in the act of apprehension would always be of the same kind, and so there would be nothing in the phenomenon to determine the succession and make a particular sequence objectively necessary. In such a case I could not say that two states in a phenomenon follow one upon the other, but only that one apprehension follows upon another. And this is merely subjective. It determines no object, and so it cannot count as cognition of an object, not even of an object in the world of phenomena.

Accordingly, whenever we learn through experience that something happens, we always presuppose that something precedes it, upon which it follows according to a rule. Without this presupposition I could not say of the object that it follows, because the mere succession in my apprehension, unless it is determined by a rule in relation to something preceding it, gives me no right to assert a succession in the object. Only by reference to a rule, according to which phenomena are determined in their sequence (that is, in their happening) by the preceding state, can I make my subjective synthesis of apprehension objective. And only under this presupposition is even the experience of an event possible.

This may seem to contradict outright everything that has hitherto been believed about how the human understanding proceeds. On the received view, the understanding discovers a rule by perceiving and comparing similar consequences that follow upon certain antecedent phenomena, a rule according to which certain events always follow certain phenomena, and only by this process do we arrive at the concept of cause. On such a foundation, the concept would obviously be merely empirical, and the rule it supplies, "Everything that happens must have a cause," would be just as contingent as experience itself. The universality and necessity attributed to the rule or law would be entirely spurious. Indeed, the rule could not be universally valid at all, since it would not be a priori but grounded only on induction. Yet this law is in the same position as other pure a priori representations, such as space and time. We can draw these out of experience with perfect clarity and completeness only because we ourselves first put them there, and by doing so, and only by doing so, made experience possible. It is true that the logical clarity of this representation of a rule determining the series of events becomes possible only once we have made use of it in experience. Nevertheless, the recognition of this rule, as a condition of the synthetic unity of phenomena in time, was the ground of experience itself, and therefore preceded experience a priori.

We must now show by an example that, even in experience, we never attribute succession or effect to an object (that is, an event, the happening of something that did not exist before) and distinguish it from the subjective succession of apprehension, unless a rule lies at the foundation that compels us to observe this order of perception rather than any other. We must show, moreover, that it is precisely this necessity that first makes the representation of a succession in the object possible.

We have representations within us, and we can be conscious of them. But however extensive, however exact and thorough this consciousness may be, these representations remain nothing more than representations, that is, inner determinations of the mind in one relation of time or another. How, then, does it come about that we posit an object for these representations, or that, beyond their subjective reality as modifications of the mind, we attribute to them some further, unknown objective reality? Their objective significance clearly cannot consist in a relation to some other representation (of whatever it is we wish to call the object), for then the same question arises again: how does this other representation go beyond itself and acquire objective significance over and above the subjective significance that belongs to it as a determination of a state of mind? If we try to discover what new property the relation to an object confers on our subjective representations, and what new standing they gain from it, we find that its only effect is to make the connection of our representations necessary in a certain way and to subject them to a rule. Conversely, it is only because a certain order is necessary in the time relations of our representations that objective significance is ascribed to them.

In the synthesis of phenomena, the manifold of our representations is always successive. This alone does not represent an object, because such succession is common to all apprehension, and through it no one thing is distinguished from another. But as soon as I perceive or assume that in this succession there is a relation to a preceding state, from which the representation follows according to a rule, I represent something as an event, as a thing that happens. That is, I cognize an object to which I must assign a definite position in time, a position that cannot be altered because of the preceding state in the object. When I perceive that something happens, then, this representation contains, first of all, the fact that something precedes it, since only in relation to this does the phenomenon acquire its proper time relation, namely that of existing after a preceding time in which it did not exist. But it can receive its determinate place in time only on the presupposition that something existed in the foregoing state upon which it follows inevitably and always, that is, according to a rule. Two conclusions are evident from this. First, I cannot reverse the order of succession and make what happens precede that upon which it follows. Second, if the preceding state is posited, a determinate event inevitably and necessarily follows. Hence there is an order among our representations in which the present points with certainty to some previously existing state. This earlier state is a correlate of the given event, still undetermined in itself, which relates to the event as its consequence, conditions it, and connects it necessarily with itself in the series of time.

If, then, it is a necessary law of our sensibility, and therefore a formal condition of all perception, that the preceding time necessarily determines the succeeding time (since I cannot reach the succeeding time except by passing through the preceding one), then it must equally be an indispensable law of the empirical representation of the time series that phenomena of past time determine every phenomenon in the time that follows. Events in that later time cannot take place except insofar as the earlier phenomena determine their existence in time, that is, fix it according to a rule. For it is only in phenomena that we can cognize this continuity in the connection of times empirically.

Understanding is indispensable to all experience and to its very possibility, and its first act in this sphere is not to make the representation of objects clear but to make the representation of any object at all possible. It does this by carrying the order of time over into phenomena and their existence. It assigns to each phenomenon, as a consequence, a place relative to preceding phenomena, a place determined a priori in time, without which the phenomenon could not agree with time itself, since time determines a place a priori for all of its parts. This determination of place cannot be derived from the relation of phenomena to absolute time, because absolute time is not an object of perception. On the contrary, phenomena must determine one another's places in time and make those places necessary in the temporal order. Whatever follows or happens must follow, according to a universal rule, upon what was contained in the preceding state. The result is a series of phenomena that, by means of the understanding, produces and makes necessary in the series of our possible perceptions exactly the same order and continuous connection that is found a priori in the form of inner intuition, which is time, where all our perceptions must have their place.

That something happens, then, is a perception belonging to a possible experience. This experience becomes actual only because I regard the phenomenon as determined with respect to its place in time, and therefore as an object that can always be found, by means of a rule, within the connected series of my perceptions. And the rule for determining something according to succession in time is this: "In what precedes is to be found the condition under which an event always, that is, necessarily, follows." From all this it is plain that the principle of cause and effect is the principle of possible experience, that is, of the objective cognition of phenomena with respect to their relations in the succession of time.

The proof of this fundamental proposition rests entirely on the following steps. All empirical cognition involves the synthesis of the manifold by the imagination, a synthesis that is always successive, in which representations always follow one another. In imagination, however, the order of succession is not determined, and the series of successive representations can be run through backward as well as forward. But if this synthesis is a synthesis of apprehension, of the manifold of a given phenomenon, then the order is determined in the object. More precisely, there is in it an order of successive synthesis that determines an object, an order according to which something necessarily comes first, and when this is posited, something else necessarily follows. If my perception is to contain the cognition of an event, of something that actually happens, it must therefore be an empirical judgment in which we think of the succession as determined. It presupposes another phenomenon upon which this event follows necessarily, or according to a rule. If, on the contrary, the event did not necessarily follow when I posited the antecedent, I would have to regard it merely as a subjective play of my imagination, and if I nonetheless represented anything in it as objective, I would have to treat it as a mere dream. Thus the relation of phenomena (considered as possible perceptions) according to which what happens is necessarily determined in time, with respect to its existence, by something preceding it according to a rule, the relation, that is, of cause and effect, is the condition of the objective validity of our empirical judgments about the sequence of perceptions. It is therefore the condition of their empirical truth, and so of experience. The principle of the causal relation in the succession of phenomena is therefore valid for all objects of experience, because it is itself the ground of the possibility of experience.

Here, however, a difficulty arises that must be resolved. Our formula restricts the principle of causal connection among phenomena to their succession, yet in practice we find that the principle also applies when phenomena exist at the same time, and that cause and effect can be simultaneous. Suppose, for example, that there is heat in a room that is not present in the open air. I look for the cause and find it in the fire. Now the fire, as the cause, is simultaneous with its effect, the heat of the room. There is no succession in time between cause and effect here; they are simultaneous, and still the law holds. Most of the efficient causes in nature are simultaneous with their effects, and the effects unfold in temporal succession only because a cause cannot accomplish its entire effect in a single instant. But at the moment the effect first arises, it is always simultaneous with the causality of its cause, since if the cause had ceased to exist a moment earlier, the effect could never have arisen. It is essential to remember that what matters is the order of time, not the lapse of time. The relation remains even when no time has elapsed. The interval between the causality of the cause and its immediate effect may vanish entirely, so that cause and effect are simultaneous, yet the relation of one to the other remains determinable in time. Consider, for example, a lead ball lying on a cushion and pressing a hollow into it. Taken as a cause, the ball is simultaneous with its effect. Yet I distinguish the two by the time relation of their dynamical connection. If I place the ball on the cushion, the hollow follows upon the previously smooth surface. But if the cushion already has a hollow in it, from whatever cause, a lead ball does not follow from that.

The law of temporal succession is therefore, in every case, the only empirical criterion of an effect in relation to the causality of the cause that precedes it. A glass is the cause of water rising above its level surface, even though the two phenomena occur at the same time. For as soon as I draw some water from a larger vessel with the glass, an effect follows: the water changes from the level surface it had in the large vessel to the concave surface it takes on in the glass.

This concept of causality leads to the concept of action, the concept of action leads to the concept of force, and through force we arrive at the concept of substance. The sole purpose of this critical inquiry is to treat the sources of our synthetic a priori cognition, and I do not want to crowd it with analyses that merely clarify our concepts without extending them. I therefore reserve a detailed account of these concepts for a future system of pure reason. Such an analysis, carried out in great detail, can in any case already be found in well-known works on the subject. But I cannot pass over, at present, a few remarks on the empirical criterion of a substance, insofar as substance seems to reveal itself more clearly and more readily through the concept of action than through the permanence of a phenomenon.

Wherever there is action, and therefore activity and force, there must also be substance, and in substance alone must we look for the seat of this fertile source of phenomena. That much is easily said. But if we are asked to explain what we mean by substance, and we wish to avoid arguing in a circle, the answer is by no means easy. How are we to infer directly from action to the permanence of whatever acts, given that permanence is the essential and distinctive mark of substance as phenomenon? After what has been said above, the solution is easy enough, though by the usual method of merely analyzing our concepts it would be quite impossible. The concept of action signifies the relation of the subject of causality to the effect. Since every effect consists in something that happens, and therefore in what is changeable, the ultimate subject of this change is the permanent, the substratum of everything that changes, which is to say, substance. For according to the principle of causality, actions are always the first ground of all change in phenomena, and so they cannot belong to a subject that itself changes, since in that case further actions and a further subject would be needed to determine that change. It follows that action, as an empirical criterion, is by itself sufficient proof of substantiality, and I need not try to establish the permanence of the substance by comparing perceptions. Such a method of induction could not, in any case, achieve the completeness that the scope and strict universality of the concept demand. That the first subject of the causality of all arising and passing away, of all origination and extinction, cannot itself arise and pass away (within the sphere of phenomena) is a sound and safe conclusion. It leads to the concept of empirical necessity and permanence in existence, and therefore to the concept of a substance as phenomenon.

When something happens, the bare fact of its happening, regardless of what it is that happens, is already an object of inquiry. The transition from the non-being of a state to its existence, supposing that this state contains no quality previously present in the phenomenon, is in itself something that calls for explanation. Such an event, as was shown earlier in discussing the principle of the permanence of substance, does not concern substance, since substance does not come into being in this way, but only its condition or state. It is therefore merely change, and not origination out of nothing. If such origination is regarded as the effect of an external cause, it is called creation, and creation cannot be admitted as an event among phenomena, since its very possibility would destroy the unity of experience. If, however, I regard all things not as phenomena but as things in themselves, objects of the understanding alone, then they may be considered, although they are substances, as dependent for their existence on an external cause. But this would give the words an entirely different meaning, one that could not apply to phenomena as objects of possible experience.

How a thing can change at all, how it is possible that one state existing at one point of time should be followed at another point of time by an opposite state, is something of which we have not the slightest a priori concept. That requires knowledge of actual powers, which can only be given empirically, such as knowledge of moving forces, or, to put it differently, of certain successive phenomena, such as movements, that indicate the presence of those forces. But the form of every change, the condition under which alone change can occur as the coming into existence of another state (whatever the content of the change, that is, whatever the state that is changed), and therefore the succession of the states themselves, can very well be considered a priori in relation to the law of causality and the conditions of time. It should be noted that I am speaking here not of a change in certain relations but of a change of state. A body moving uniformly, for instance, does not change its state of motion at all; its state changes only when its motion increases or decreases.

When a substance passes from one state, a, into another state, b, the point of time at which the second state exists is different from, and later than, the point at which the first existed. In the same way, the second state, as reality in the phenomenon, differs from the first, in which this reality did not exist, as b differs from zero. That is, if state b differs from state a only in quantity, the change is the coming into existence of b minus a, which did not exist in the earlier state and in relation to which that earlier state equals zero.

The question now arises how a thing passes from one state, a, into another state, b. Between any two moments there is always some time, and between two states existing at those moments there is always a difference of some magnitude, since all parts of phenomena are themselves magnitudes. Every transition from one state into another therefore takes place in a time contained between two moments, the first of which determines the state the thing leaves and the second the state into which it passes. Both moments are thus boundaries of the time of a change, and therefore of the intermediate state between the two, and as such they belong to the change as a whole. Now every change has a cause, which exhibits its causality throughout the entire time in which the change takes place. The cause therefore does not produce the change all at once, in a single moment, but over a period of time. As the time increases gradually from its starting instant, a, to its completion at b, so too the quantity of reality, b minus a, is generated through all the smaller degrees contained between the first and the last. All change is therefore possible only through a continuous action of causality, which, insofar as it is uniform, we call a momentum. The change does not consist of these momenta; it is generated by them as their effect.

This is the law of the continuity of all change. Its ground is that neither time itself nor any phenomenon in time consists of parts that are the smallest possible, and yet a thing in the course of a change passes through all these parts, as elements, on its way to its second state. There is no smallest degree of reality in a phenomenon, just as there is no smallest quantity of time. The new state of reality therefore grows out of the earlier one through all of that state's infinitely many degrees, and the differences between these degrees, taken all together, are smaller than the difference between 0 and *a*.

We need not consider here how useful this principle is in the investigation of nature. But it is worth asking how such a proposition, which seems to extend our knowledge of nature so greatly, can be possible entirely a priori. At first glance the principle appears plainly true and real, and the question of how it is possible may seem superfluous. But reason makes so many groundless claims to enlarge our knowledge that we must adopt a general rule: distrust every such claim, and without a thorough and radical deduction, believe nothing of the kind even on the clearest dogmatic evidence.

Every addition to our empirical knowledge, and every advance in perception, is nothing more than an extension of the determination of inner sense. It is a progression in time, whatever the objects themselves may be, whether phenomena or pure intuitions. This progression in time determines everything and is itself determined by nothing else. Its parts exist only in time and through the synthesis of time; they are not given before that synthesis. For this reason every transition in perception to something that follows upon another in time is a determination of time, brought about by producing this perception. And since this determination of time is always, and in all its parts, a quantity, the perception it produces must be regarded as a quantity that passes through all its degrees, none of which is the smallest possible, from zero up to its determinate degree. Here we see how it is possible to know a law of change a priori, though only a law that concerns the form of change. We are simply anticipating our own apprehension. The formal condition of that apprehension is present in the mind before any phenomena are given, and so it must certainly be knowable a priori.

Time contains the sensory a priori condition that makes possible a continuous progression from what exists to what follows it. In the same way, the understanding, by virtue of the unity of apperception, contains the a priori condition that makes possible a continuous determination of the position in time of all phenomena. It does this through the series of causes and effects. Causes necessitate the sequence of their effects, and they thereby make our empirical knowledge of temporal relations valid universally, for all time, and therefore objectively.

**C. Third Analogy**

**The Principle of Coexistence, according to the Law of Reciprocity or Community**

All substances, insofar as they can be perceived as existing at the same time in space, stand in thoroughgoing reciprocal action.

**Proof**

Things are coexistent when, in empirical intuition, the perception of one can follow the perception of the other, and the reverse is also possible. This cannot happen in a succession of phenomena, as we showed in explaining the second principle. Thus I can perceive first the moon and then the earth, or first the earth and then the moon. Because my perceptions of these objects can follow each other in either order, I say that the objects exist at the same time. Now coexistence is the existence of the manifold in the same time. But time itself cannot be perceived. We therefore cannot infer, simply from the fact that things are placed in the same time, that our perceptions of them can follow each other in either order. The synthesis of imagination in apprehension would only present each of these perceptions as present in the subject when the other is absent, and the reverse. It would not show that the objects are coexistent. It would not show that if one exists, the other also exists in the same time, or that this must be so if the perceptions are to be able to follow each other in either order. It follows that we need a concept of the understanding, a category of the reciprocal sequence of the determinations of phenomena. These phenomena exist apart from one another and yet at the same time. Only such a category can justify us in saying that the reciprocal succession of our perceptions is grounded in the object, and only it allows us to represent coexistence as objective. But when one substance contains determinations whose ground lies in another substance, the relation between them is one of influence. When this influence is mutual, the relation is one of community, or reciprocity. Consequently the coexistence of substances in space cannot be known in experience except on the presupposition that they act on one another. Reciprocal action is therefore the condition that makes things themselves possible as objects of experience.

Things are coexistent insofar as they exist in one and the same time. But how can we know that they exist in one and the same time? Only by observing that the order in which apprehension synthesizes the manifold is arbitrary and indifferent. It can run from A through B, C, and D to E, or in reverse from E to A. If these things were successive in time, in an order that begins, let us suppose, with A, apprehension in perception could not possibly begin with E and work backward to A, since A would belong to past time and could no longer be an object of apprehension.

Suppose that among a number of substances, considered as phenomena, each is completely isolated, so that none acts on any other. I maintain that in this case their coexistence could not be an object of possible perception, and that the existence of one could not, by any kind of empirical synthesis, lead us to the existence of another. For we would be imagining them as separated by a completely empty space. Perception, moving from one to the other in time, would indeed determine the existence of the second through a later perception. But it would be entirely unable to tell whether that phenomenon objectively follows the first or coexists with it.

Beyond mere existence, then, there must be something by which A determines the position of B in time, and by which B in turn determines the position of A. Only under this condition can substances be represented empirically as existing at the same time. Now the only thing that determines the position of another thing in time is the cause of that thing or of its determinations. Succession can be predicated of a substance only with respect to its determinations. Every substance must therefore contain the causality of certain determinations in another substance, and must at the same time contain within itself the effects of the other's causality. Substances must stand, directly or indirectly, in dynamical community with one another if their coexistence is to be known in any possible experience. With regard to objects of experience, whatever is required for the experience of those objects to be possible at all is absolutely necessary. It is therefore absolutely necessary that all substances in the world of phenomena, insofar as they coexist, stand in a relation of thoroughgoing community of reciprocal action.

In our language, German, the word for community has two meanings and carries both of the notions expressed by the Latin *communio* and *commercium*. We use it here in the latter sense. It denotes a dynamical community, without which even the community of place (*communio spatii*) could never be known empirically. Our experience readily shows several things. Only continuous influences in every part of space can lead our senses from one object to another. The light that plays between our eyes and the heavenly bodies creates a mediating community between them and us, and so shows that they coexist with us. We cannot empirically change our position, which means we cannot perceive such a change, unless matter throughout the whole of space makes it possible to perceive where we are. And this perception can prove the simultaneous existence of these places only through their reciprocal influence. In the same way it can prove the coexistence even of the most remote objects, though in that case the proof is only indirect. Without community, every perception of a phenomenon in space is cut off and isolated from every other. The chain of empirical representations, which is experience itself, would then have to begin entirely afresh with each new object. It would have no connection with earlier representations and would not stand in any temporal relation to them. I do not mean by this to argue against the notion of empty space. Empty space may exist where our perceptions cannot reach, and where, therefore, no empirical perception of coexistence takes place. But in that case it is not an object of possible experience.

The following remarks may help to explain the point. In the mind, all phenomena, as contents of a possible experience, must stand in a community (*communio*) of apperception, or consciousness. Objects must be represented as coexistent and connected, and to that extent they must reciprocally determine one another's position in time and so form a whole. If this subjective community is to rest on an objective ground, or to apply to substances as phenomena, then the perception of one substance must make possible the perception of another, and the reverse must also hold. Otherwise succession, which is always present in perceptions considered as acts of apprehension, would be attributed to the external objects themselves, and it would become impossible to represent them as coexistent. But this mutual enabling is a reciprocal influence, a real community (*commercium*) of substances. Without it, the empirical relation of coexistence would lie beyond the reach of our minds. Through this *commercium*, phenomena that are apart from one another and yet connected form a real composite (*compositum reale*). Such composites are possible in many different ways. The three dynamical relations from which all others arise are therefore those of inherence, consequence, and composition.

These, then, are the three analogies of experience. They are nothing more than principles for determining the existence of phenomena in time, and they follow the three modes of such determination.
