The first is the relation to time itself as a quantity, which is the quantity of existence, or duration. The second is the relation in time as a series, or succession. The third is the relation in time as the sum of all existence, which is simultaneity. This unity of temporal determination is thoroughly dynamical. Time is not treated as something in which experience directly assigns each existing thing its position. That is impossible, because absolute time is not an object of perception through which phenomena could be connected with one another. Instead, a rule of the understanding determines the position of each phenomenon in time. Only through this rule can the existence of phenomena acquire synthetic unity with respect to temporal relations, and the rule determines that position a priori and validly for each and every time.

By nature, in the empirical sense of the word, we mean the totality of phenomena connected in their existence according to necessary rules, that is, according to laws. There are, therefore, certain laws, and a priori ones, that make nature possible in the first place. All empirical laws can exist only through experience, and only by virtue of those original laws through which experience itself becomes possible. The purpose of the analogies is thus to present the unity of nature in the connection of all phenomena under certain exponents. The sole function of these exponents is to express the relation of time, insofar as time contains all existence within it, to the unity of apperception, which can operate in synthesis only according to rules. Taken together, the analogies amount to this: "All phenomena exist in one nature, and must so exist, since without this a priori unity no unity of experience, and therefore no determination of objects in experience, would be possible."

One remark must be made about the method of proof we have used for these transcendental laws of nature and about its distinctive character. The remark will also be important as a guide in every other attempt to demonstrate propositions that are both intellectual and synthetic a priori. Suppose we had tried to prove these analogies dogmatically, that is, from concepts. Suppose we had tried by this method to show that everything that exists exists only in what is permanent, that every thing or event presupposes something in a preceding state upon which it follows according to a rule, and finally, that in a coexisting manifold the states coexist in connection with one another according to a rule. All our labor would have been entirely wasted. For mere concepts of things, however thoroughly we analyze them, can never allow us to infer from the existence of one object to the existence of another. What other course was open to us? Only this: to demonstrate the possibility of experience as a kind of knowledge in which all objects must ultimately be capable of being presented to us, if our representation of them is to have objective reality. Experience was the third, mediating term, and its essential form consists in the synthetic unity of the apperception of all phenomena. In it we found a priori conditions for the universal and necessary determination in time of everything that exists in the world of phenomena. Without these conditions even empirical determination in time would be impossible. We also discovered in it rules of a priori synthetic unity by which we could anticipate experience. Other thinkers lacked this method and imagined that a dogmatic proof could be found for the synthetic propositions required in the empirical use of the understanding. This explains why so many attempts have been made to prove the principle of sufficient reason, always in vain. No one has ever even considered the other two analogies, although the mind has always silently made use of them. The guiding thread supplied by the categories was missing, and only that guide can enable us to discover every gap, both in the system of concepts and in the system of principles.

The unity of the universe, in which all phenomena are to be connected, is evidently a mere consequence of the accepted principle that all coexisting substances stand in community. If substances were isolated, they could not form a whole as its parts. And if their connection, the reciprocal action of the manifold, were not already necessary because of their coexistence, we could not infer from coexistence, which is a merely ideal relation, to connection, which is a real one. We have shown in its proper place, however, that community is the true ground that makes an empirical knowledge of coexistence possible. We may therefore legitimately reason from coexistence to community as its condition.

**4. The Postulates of Empirical Thought**

1. Whatever agrees with the formal conditions of experience, in intuition and in concepts, is possible.

2. Whatever is connected with the material conditions of experience, that is, with sensation, is real.

3. Whatever is connected with the real in a way determined by the universal conditions of experience is necessary, or exists necessarily.

**Explanation**

The categories of modality have a peculiar feature. They do not determine the object in the least, nor do they enlarge the concept to which they are attached as predicates. They only express the concept's relation to the faculty of knowledge. Even when my concept of a thing is complete in itself, I can still ask whether its object is merely possible, or also real, and if real, whether it is also necessary. Yet in asking this I do not determine the object itself any further in thought. The only question is how the object, together with all its determinations, is related to the understanding and its use in experience, to the empirical power of judgment, and to reason in its application to experience.

For this very reason, the categories of modality are nothing more than explanations of the concepts of possibility, reality, and necessity as they are used in experience. At the same time they restrict all the categories to empirical use alone, and they do not authorize any transcendental use. These categories might be meant to have more than a merely logical significance, to be more than an analytic expression of the form of thought, and to relate to things and to their possibility, reality, or necessity. If so, they must concern possible experience and its synthetic unity, because objects of knowledge can be given only there.

The postulate of the possibility of things further requires that the concept of a thing agree with the formal conditions of experience in general. This objective form of experience contains every kind of synthesis required for the knowledge of objects. A concept that contains a synthesis must be regarded as empty, and as referring to no object, if its synthesis does not belong to experience. A synthesis can belong to experience in one of two ways. It may be borrowed from experience, in which case the concept is called empirical. Or it may be the ground and a priori condition of experience, its form, in which case the concept is pure, yet it still belongs to experience, since its object can be found only there. A concept that is synthetic a priori thinks an object, and we need a criterion, or mark, of that object's possibility. We can find it only in the synthesis that constitutes the form of the empirical knowledge of objects. That such a concept contains no contradiction is indeed a necessary logical condition. But it is far from sufficient to establish the concept's objective reality, which is the possibility of an object such as the concept thinks. Thus the concept of a figure enclosed by two straight lines contains no contradiction, for the concepts of two straight lines and of their meeting contain no negation of a figure. The impossibility here does not lie in the concept itself but in its construction in space, that is, in the conditions of space and its determinations. These conditions, however, have objective reality and apply to possible things, because they contain a priori the form of experience in general.

We shall now show how widely useful and influential this postulate of possibility is. Suppose I represent to myself a thing that is permanent, such that everything in it that changes belongs merely to its state. From that concept alone I can never know that such a thing is possible. Or suppose I represent to myself something so constituted that, when it is posited, something else always and infallibly follows. My thought contains no contradiction, but it gives me no means of judging whether such a property as causality can be found in any possible thing. Finally, I can represent to myself different things, or substances, so constituted that the state of one brings about a change in the state of the other, and the reverse. But I cannot discover from these concepts whether such a relation can belong to things, because the concepts contain a merely arbitrary synthesis. We know that these concepts have objective reality, or transcendental truth, only because they express a priori the relations of perceptions in every experience. We know this independently of experience. We do not know it independently of all relation to the form of an experience in general and to its synthetic unity, which is the only place where objects can be known empirically.

We may also fashion new concepts of substances, forces, and actions and reactions from the material that perception supplies, without taking the connections that experience shows us as our model. Then we produce mere fantasies, and we can find no criterion for their possibility. We have borrowed the concepts from experience but have not taken experience as our teacher. Such invented concepts do not acquire their possibility a priori, as the categories do, for the categories are concepts on which all experience depends. These concepts acquire it only a posteriori, as concepts given through experience itself. Their possibility must therefore either be known a posteriori and empirically, or not be known at all. Consider a substance permanently present in space yet without filling it. Some have tried to introduce such a *tertium quid*, a third kind of thing between matter and the thinking subject, into metaphysics. Consider also a special fundamental power of the mind to intuit the future in advance, rather than merely infer it from past and present events. Or consider a power of the mind to enter into a community of thought with other people, however distant they may be. These are concepts whose possibility has no ground to rest on. They are not based on experience and its known laws, and without experience they are merely an arbitrary combination of thoughts. Though free of internal contradiction, such a combination can make no claim to objective reality, and therefore no claim to the possibility of the object it describes. As for reality, it is self-evident that we cannot think it *in concreto* without the help of experience. Reality concerns only sensation, the matter of experience, and not the form of thought, with which we can certainly amuse ourselves by inventing fancies.

I set aside here everything whose possibility is derived from its reality in experience, and I intend to treat only the possibility of things through a priori concepts. My claim is that the possibility of things is never derived from such concepts taken by themselves. It is derived from them only when they are considered as formal and objective conditions of an experience in general.

It does seem as if the possibility of a triangle could be known from its concept alone, which is certainly independent of experience. We can give that concept a corresponding object entirely a priori, because we can construct it. But a triangle is only the form of an object, and so it would remain a mere product of the imagination. The possibility of an object corresponding to it would remain doubtful unless we could find some further ground, unless we knew that the figure can be thought under the conditions on which all objects of experience rest. Two facts alone connect the notion of the possibility of such a thing with the concept of it: that space is an a priori formal condition of outer experience, and that the formative synthesis by which we construct a triangle in imagination is exactly the same synthesis we use when we apprehend a phenomenon in order to form an empirical concept of it. In the same way, the possibility of continuous quantities, and indeed of quantities in general, is never evident from the concepts themselves, since those concepts are without exception synthetic. It becomes evident only when they are regarded as the formal conditions for determining objects in experience. And where else should we look for objects corresponding to our concepts, if not in experience, through which alone objects are given to us? It is true that, without any prior experience, we can know and characterize the possibility of things with respect to the formal conditions under which something is determined as an object in experience, and can therefore do so entirely a priori. Even so, this is possible only in relation to experience and within its limits.

The postulate governing our knowledge of the reality of things requires perception, and therefore sensation of which we are conscious. It does not require that this perception be immediate, a perception of the very object whose existence is to be known. But it does require that the object have some connection with an actual perception, in accordance with the analogies of experience, which set out every kind of real connection within experience.

From the mere concept of a thing it is impossible to infer its existence. However complete the concept may be, and however fully it states all the determinations of the thing, existence has nothing to do with any of this. Existence concerns only whether such a thing is given to us, so that the perception of it can in every case precede the concept. If the concept comes before the perception, this shows only that the thing is possible. Perception, which supplies the concept with its material, is the sole mark of reality. Even before we perceive a thing, however, and therefore comparatively a priori, we can know of its existence, provided it stands in connection with certain perceptions according to the principles by which perceptions are empirically linked, that is, according to the analogies of perception. In that case the existence of the supposed thing is bound up with our perceptions in a possible experience, and, guided by these analogies, we can reason along the series of possible perceptions from a thing we actually perceive to a thing we do not. Thus we know of the existence of a magnetic matter that permeates all bodies from our perception of steel filings drawn toward a magnet, even though the constitution of our sense organs makes it impossible for us to perceive this matter directly. According to the laws of sensibility and the interconnection of our perceptions, we would, in the course of experience, also arrive at an immediate empirical intuition of this matter if our senses were keener. Their dullness has no bearing on the form of possible experience in general and cannot alter it. Our knowledge of the existence of things therefore extends exactly as far as our perceptions reach, together with whatever can be inferred from them according to empirical laws. If we do not begin from experience, or do not proceed according to the laws governing the empirical connection of phenomena, our claims to discover the existence of something we do not directly perceive are empty. Idealism, however, raises powerful objections to these rules for proving existence indirectly, and so this is the proper place to refute it.

#### Refutation of Idealism

Idealism, by which I mean material idealism, is the theory that declares the existence of objects in space outside us to be either (1) doubtful and indemonstrable, or (2) false and impossible. The first is the problematic idealism of Descartes, who accepts as indubitably certain only one empirical assertion (*assertio*): "I am." The second is the dogmatic idealism of Berkeley, who holds that space, together with all the objects of which it is the inseparable condition, is something impossible in itself, and that objects in space are therefore mere products of the imagination. Dogmatic idealism is unavoidable if we regard space as a property belonging to things in themselves, for then space, along with everything it conditions, is a nonentity. But we have already destroyed the foundation of this kind of idealism in the Transcendental Aesthetic. Problematic idealism makes no such assertion. It alleges only that we are unable to prove, through immediate experience, the existence of anything other than ourselves. This is a reasonable theory, and it reflects a thorough and philosophical way of thinking, since it observes the rule of reaching no decisive judgment until sufficient proof has been produced. The proof it demands must therefore show that we have experience of external things, and not mere imaginings. To that end, we must prove that our inner experience, which Descartes held to be indubitable, is itself possible only on the prior assumption of outer experience.

**Theorem**

The mere, but empirically determined, consciousness of my own existence proves the existence of objects in space outside me.

**Proof**

I am conscious of my own existence as determined in time. All determination of time presupposes something permanent in perception. This permanent element, however, cannot be something within me, precisely because my existence in time is itself determined by it. It follows that the perception of this permanent element is possible only through a thing outside me, and not through the mere representation of a thing outside me. Consequently, the determination of my existence in time is possible only through the existence of actual things external to me. Now, consciousness in time is necessarily bound up with consciousness of the possibility of this determination in time. It follows that consciousness in time is also necessarily bound up with the existence of things outside me, since the existence of these things is the condition of determination in time. The consciousness of my own existence is therefore, at the same time, an immediate consciousness of the existence of other things outside me.

Remark I. The reader will notice that in this proof the game idealism plays is turned back against it, and with better right. Idealism assumed that the only immediate experience is inner experience, and that from it we can merely infer the existence of external things. But, as always happens when we reason from given effects to determinate causes, idealism reasoned too hastily and too uncertainly, for the cause of our representations may very well lie in ourselves, and we may be wrongly attributing it to external things. Our proof, by contrast, shows that outer experience is in fact immediate, and that only by virtue of it is inner experience possible. What it makes possible is not, indeed, the consciousness of our own existence, but certainly the determination of that existence in time. It is true that the representation "I am," which expresses the consciousness that can accompany all my thoughts, immediately includes the existence of a subject. But this representation contains no knowledge of that subject, and therefore no empirical knowledge, which is to say no experience. Experience requires, beyond the thought of something existing, an intuition. Here that intuition would have to be inner intuition, namely time, in relation to which the subject must be determined. The existence of external things is absolutely required for this, and so it follows that inner experience is itself possible only indirectly, by way of outer experience.

In the theorem above, the immediate consciousness of the existence of external things is not presupposed but proved, whether or not we understand how such consciousness is possible. The question of its possibility would run as follows: "Do we have an inner sense but no outer sense, so that our belief in outer perception is a mere delusion?" Yet it is plain that, merely to imagine something as external, that is, to present it to the senses in intuition, we must already possess an outer sense. Through that sense we must immediately distinguish the mere receptivity of an outer intuition from the spontaneity that marks every act of imagination. If we were merely to imagine an outer sense as well, we would destroy the very faculty of intuition that the imagination is supposed to determine.

Remark II. All empirical use of our cognitive faculty in determining time agrees fully with this view. Its truth is supported by the fact that we can perceive a determination of time only through a change in outer relations, that is, through motion relative to what is permanent in space. We become aware of the sun's motion, for example, by observing how its relation to objects on the earth changes. Nor is this all. We find that the only permanent thing we possess that can correspond to the concept of a substance, and be placed under it as an intuition, is matter. This idea of permanence is not itself drawn from outer experience. It is an a priori necessary condition of all determination of time, and therefore also of the determination of inner sense with respect to our own existence, a determination made through the existence of external things. In the representation "I," the consciousness of myself is not an intuition but a purely intellectual representation produced by the spontaneous activity of a thinking subject. Consequently this "I" has no predicate of intuition which, by virtue of being permanent, could serve as the correlate of the determination of time in inner sense, in the way that impenetrability serves as the correlate of matter considered as an empirical intuition.

Remark III. The existence of external things is a necessary condition for a determinate consciousness of ourselves. It does not follow from this that every intuitive representation of external things implies that those things exist. Such representations may very well be mere products of the imagination, as in dreams or in madness. Even these, however, are produced by reproducing earlier outer perceptions, which, as has been shown, are possible only through the reality of external objects. The sole aim of these remarks has been to prove that inner experience in general is possible only through outer experience in general. Whether this or that supposed experience is purely imaginary must be determined from its particular characteristics and by comparing them with the criteria of all real experience.

Finally, the third postulate concerns material necessity in existence, not merely formal and logical necessity in the connection of concepts. We cannot know the existence of any object of sense entirely a priori, though we can know it comparatively a priori, that is, relative to some other existence already given. Even then, what we know can only be an existence that must be contained within the whole of experience of which the previously given perception is a part. It follows that the necessity of an existence can never be known from concepts, but only from its connection with something that is an object of perception. Yet the only existence we know to be necessary under the condition of other given phenomena is the existence of effects arising from given causes in accordance with the laws of causality. What we know, therefore, is not the necessity of the existence of things as substances, but the necessity of the state of things. Even this we know not immediately but through the existence of other states given in perception, according to empirical laws of causality. Hence the criterion of necessity lies solely in the law of possible experience: that everything which happens is determined a priori in the phenomenon by its cause. We thus know only the necessity of those effects in nature whose causes are given to us. Moreover, the criterion of necessity in existence has no application beyond the field of possible experience. Even within that field it does not hold for the existence of things as substances, since substances can never be regarded as empirical effects, or as something that happens and has a beginning. Necessity, therefore, concerns only the relations of phenomena according to the dynamical law of causality, together with the possibility, grounded in that law, of reasoning a priori from one given existence (a cause) to another (an effect). "Everything that happens is hypothetically necessary" is a principle that subjects the changes taking place in the world to a law, that is, to a rule of necessary existence, without which nature itself could not exist at all. Hence the proposition "Nothing happens by blind chance" (*in mundo non datur casus*: in the world there is no chance) is an a priori law of nature. The same holds for the proposition "Necessity in nature is not blind." Such necessity is conditioned, and therefore intelligible (*non datur fatum*: there is no fate). Both laws subject the play of change to "a nature of things (as phenomena)," or, what amounts to the same thing, to the unity of the understanding. Only through the understanding can changes belong to an experience, understood as the synthetic unity of phenomena. Both laws belong to the class of dynamical principles. The first is strictly a consequence of the principle of causality, one of the analogies of experience. The second belongs to the principles of modality, which add to the determination of causality the concept of necessity, a concept that is itself subject to a rule of the understanding.

The principle of continuity forbids any leap in the series of phenomena considered as changes (*in mundo non datur saltus*: in the world there is no leap). It likewise forbids, within the whole of all empirical intuitions in space, any gap or hiatus between two phenomena (*non datur hiatus*: there is no gap). We may express the principle this way: experience can admit nothing that proves the existence of a vacuum, or that even admits one as part of an empirical synthesis. We might also think of a vacuum or void as lying outside and beyond the field of possible experience, that is, beyond the world. Such a question cannot come before the tribunal of the mere understanding, which rules only on questions concerning the use of given phenomena to build empirical knowledge. It is rather a problem for ideal reason, which goes beyond the sphere of possible experience and seeks to judge what surrounds and bounds that sphere, and its proper place is the Transcendental Dialectic. These four propositions, "*In mundo non datur hiatus, non datur saltus, non datur casus, non datur fatum*," could very easily be set out in their proper order, like all principles of transcendental origin. That is, they could be arranged according to the order of the categories, with each assigned its proper place. But the practiced reader will do this for himself, or will find the clue to such an arrangement. The combined upshot of them all is simply this: to admit into the empirical synthesis nothing that might break, or be foreign to, the understanding and the continuous connection of all phenomena, which is to say the unity of the concepts of the understanding. For only in the understanding is the unity of experience possible, in which all perceptions must have their assigned place.

Whether the field of possibility is larger than that of reality, and whether the field of reality is in turn larger than that of necessity, are interesting enough questions, and quite capable of a synthetic solution. But they fall under the jurisdiction of reason alone. They amount to asking whether all things, as phenomena, belong without exception to the connected whole of a single experience, of which every given perception is a part that therefore cannot be joined with any other phenomena, or whether my perceptions could belong to more than one possible experience. The understanding gives to experience the rules that alone make this experience possible, in accordance with the subjective and formal conditions of both sensibility and apperception. We can neither imagine nor make intelligible to ourselves any forms of intuition other than space and time, or any forms of understanding other than the discursive forms of thought, that is, knowledge through concepts. Even if we could, they would still not belong to experience, which is the only kind of knowledge through which objects are given to us. Whether there are other perceptions besides those belonging to the totality of our possible experience, and so whether some entirely different domain of matter exists, the understanding has no power to decide, since its proper business is the synthesis of what is given.

Moreover, the usual arguments for a vast realm of possibility, of which everything real (every object of experience) is only a small part, are remarkably poor. "Everything real is possible." From this follows naturally, by the logical laws of conversion, the particular proposition "Some possible things are real," which in turn seems equivalent to "Much is possible that is not real." It does indeed look as though we ought to regard the sum of the possible as greater than that of the real, since something must be added to the possible in order to make it real. But this notion of adding to the possible is absurd. Whatever is not contained in the sum of the possible, and must therefore be added to it, is plainly impossible. Beyond agreement with the formal conditions of experience, the understanding requires connection with some perception. But whatever is connected with that perception is real, even if it is not immediately perceived. Suppose we claim that another series of phenomena, fully coherent with what is given in perception, is possible, and with it more than one all-embracing experience. That claim cannot be inferred from the data experience gives us, and still less without any data at all. What is possible only under conditions that are themselves merely possible is not possible in any respect. And yet we have no firmer ground than this on which to discuss whether the sphere of possibility is wider than that of experience.

I have mentioned these questions only so that, in treating the concepts of the understanding, nothing commonly thought to belong to them would be omitted. In fact, however, the notion of absolute possibility, meaning possibility valid in every respect, is not a mere concept of the understanding that can be used empirically. It belongs to reason alone, which passes beyond the bounds of all empirical use of the understanding. We have therefore contented ourselves here with a merely critical remark, leaving the subject to be explained later.

Before concluding this fourth section, and with it the system of all principles of the pure understanding, I should explain why I have called the principles of modality postulates. I do not use the term in the sense that some recent philosophers have given it, contrary to its meaning for mathematicians, to whom the word properly belongs. In that sense a postulate is a proposition that is immediately certain and needs neither deduction nor proof. If we granted unqualified belief to synthetic propositions without deduction, simply on the strength of their own claims, all critique of the understanding would be lost entirely, however evident those propositions might be. And there is no shortage of bold claims that common belief does not reject, though for the philosopher such acceptance is no credential. The understanding would therefore lie open to every delusion and fancy, unable to withhold its assent from assertions that, however illegitimate, demand to be accepted as genuine axioms. Whenever an a priori determination is synthetically added to the concept of a thing, such a proposition must therefore be supplied, if not with a proof, then at least with a deduction of the legitimacy of its claim.

The principles of modality, however, are not objectively synthetic. The predicates of possibility, reality, and necessity do not in the least enlarge the concept of which they are asserted, since they add nothing to the representation of the object. Yet because they are nevertheless always synthetic, they are synthetic merely subjectively. That is, they are reflective. To the concept of a thing, about which they otherwise assert nothing, they add the cognitive faculty in which that concept arises and has its seat. Thus, if the concept merely agrees with the formal conditions of experience, its object is called possible. If it is connected with perception and determined by it, the object is real. And if it is determined according to concepts through the connection of perceptions, the object is called necessary. The principles of modality, then, predicate of a concept nothing more than the procedure of the cognitive faculty that produced it. A postulate in mathematics is a practical proposition containing nothing but the synthesis by which we present an object to ourselves and produce its concept. An example is "With a given line, from a given point, to describe a circle on a plane." Such a proposition cannot be proved, because the procedure it calls for is precisely the one through which alone we can generate the concept of such a figure. With the same right, then, we may postulate the principles of modality, since they do not enlarge the concept of a thing but merely indicate the way in which it is connected with the faculty of cognition.

When I think the reality of a thing, I do indeed think more than its possibility, but not in the thing itself, for the thing can never contain more in reality than was contained in its complete possibility. The notion of possibility is merely the notion of the thing's position in relation to the understanding and its empirical use, whereas reality is the thing's conjunction with perception.

#### General Remark on the System of Principles

It is very remarkable that we cannot see the possibility of a thing from the category alone, but must always have an intuition at hand in order to display the objective reality of the pure concept of the understanding. Take, for example, the categories of relation. How (1) a thing can exist only as a subject and never as a mere determination of other things, that is, how it can be a substance; how (2), because something exists, something else must exist, and so how a thing can be a cause; or how (3), when several things exist, from the fact that one of them exists, some consequence follows for the others, and reciprocally, so that a community of substances becomes possible—these are questions that cannot be answered from mere concepts. The same holds for the other categories: how, for instance, a thing can be of the same kind as many others, which is to say, how it can be a quantity, and so on. As long as intuition is lacking, we cannot know whether we are really thinking an object through the categories, or whether any object can be found anywhere that fits them. This establishes that the categories are not in themselves cognitions at all. They are merely forms of thought by which cognitions are constructed out of given intuitions. For the same reason, no synthetic proposition can be formed from the categories alone. Take the proposition "In everything that exists there is substance," meaning something that can exist only as a subject and never as a mere predicate, or the proposition "Everything is a quantity." To construct propositions like these, we need something that allows us to go beyond the given concept and connect another concept with it. This is also why every attempt to prove a synthetic proposition from mere concepts, such as "Everything that exists contingently has a cause," has failed. The most such an attempt could ever show is that without this relation we could not conceive the existence of the contingent, that is, could not grasp a priori through the understanding how such a thing exists. It does not follow that this relation is also the condition of the possibility of the contingent thing itself. If we look back at our proof of the principle of causality, we will find that we could prove it valid only for objects of possible experience, and only as the principle that makes experience possible in the first place, and therefore as the principle that makes possible the cognition of an object given in empirical intuition. We did not prove it from mere concepts. It cannot be denied, however, that the proposition "Everything contingent must have a cause" seems evident to everyone from concepts alone. But in that case the concept of the contingent is being thought under the category of relation, as something that can exist only as the consequence of something else, and not under the category of modality, as something whose non-existence can be conceived. The proposition then becomes an identical one: "Whatever can exist only as a consequence has a cause." Indeed, whenever we must give examples of contingent existence, we always point to changes, and not merely to the possibility of conceiving the opposite. A change, however, is an event, and an event is possible only through a cause; considered in itself, its non-existence is therefore possible. We recognize its contingency from the fact that it can exist only as the effect of a cause. So if a thing is assumed to be contingent, to say that it has a cause is an analytic proposition.

We can easily conceive that matter might not exist, yet the ancients did not infer from this that matter is contingent. Nor does the mere alternation between the existence and non-existence of a given state in a thing, which is all that change consists in, prove that the state is contingent on the grounds that its opposite is real. A body, for example, comes to rest after being in motion, but we cannot infer that the motion was contingent from the fact that rest is its opposite. This opposite is merely a logical opposite of the motion and not a real one. To demonstrate that the motion was contingent, we would have to prove that at the earlier moment, instead of moving, the body could have been at rest at that very time. Proving that it is at rest afterward is not enough, because in that case the two opposites are perfectly consistent with each other.

Still more remarkable is the fact that, to understand the possibility of things according to the categories, and so to demonstrate the objective reality of the categories, we need not merely intuitions but external intuitions. Consider the pure concepts of relation. First, to present something permanent in intuition that corresponds to the concept of substance, and so to demonstrate that concept's objective reality, we need an intuition in space, an intuition of matter. Space alone is permanent and determines things as permanent, whereas time, and with it everything in inner sense, is in continual flux. Second, to represent change as the intuition corresponding to the concept of causality, we need the representation of motion, which is change in space. Only through motion can changes be intuited at all, although no pure understanding can grasp how they are possible. Change is the combination of contradictorily opposed determinations in the existence of one and the same thing. How one state can follow from another, quite opposite state in the same thing is something reason cannot conceive without an example, and cannot even make intelligible without intuition. That intuition is the motion of a point in space, and the point's existence in different places, as a consequence of opposite determinations, is what makes the intuition of change possible. Even to make inner change knowable, we must represent time, the form of inner sense, figuratively as a line, and inner change as the drawing of that line, which is motion. We are thus obliged to rely on external intuition to represent our own successive existence in different states. The real reason for this is that any change, in order to be perceived as change, presupposes something permanent in intuition, and in inner sense no permanent intuition is to be found. Finally, the objective possibility of the category of community cannot be conceived by reason alone, and so its objective reality cannot be demonstrated without intuition, specifically external intuition in space. Community means that when several substances exist, some effect on the existence of one follows from the existence of another, and reciprocally. Because something exists in the second substance, something must therefore exist in the first that could not be understood from the first's own existence alone. How could we conceive the possibility of such a thing? This is the very essence of community, and it is inconceivable among things that are entirely isolated from one another. That is why Leibniz, in ascribing a community to the substances of the world as conceived by the understanding alone, needed a deity to mediate it; he rightly found that such a property could not be conceived as following from their existence. We can, however, quite easily conceive the possibility of community among substances considered as phenomena if we represent them to ourselves in space, and therefore in external intuition. External intuition contains within itself a priori formal external relations, and these are the conditions of the possibility of the real relations of action and reaction, and so of the possibility of community. It could be shown just as easily that the possibility of things as quantities, and hence the objective reality of the category of quantity, can be grounded only in external intuition, and that inner sense acquires the notion of quantity only by means of external intuition. But I must avoid going on at too great a length, and will leave the task of illustrating this with examples to the reader's own reflection.

These remarks are of the greatest importance. They confirm our earlier refutation of idealism, and they will matter even more when we come to discuss self-knowledge through mere inner consciousness, the attempt to determine our own nature without the help of external empirical intuitions, because they indicate the grounds on which any such knowledge is possible.

The result of this entire part of the analytic of principles, then, is this: "All principles of the pure understanding are nothing more than a priori principles of the possibility of experience, and all synthetic a priori propositions apply and relate to experience alone." Indeed, their very possibility rests entirely on this relation.

### Chapter III. Of the Ground of the Division of All Objects into Phenomena and Noumena

We have now not only traveled through the territory of the pure understanding and carefully surveyed each of its regions, but have also measured it and assigned everything in it its proper place. This land, however, is an island, and nature herself has enclosed it within unchangeable limits. It is the land of truth, an attractive name, and it is surrounded by a vast and stormy ocean, the region of illusion. There many a fog bank and many an iceberg looks to the mariner on his voyage of discovery like a new country. Again and again they deceive him with empty hopes and draw him into dangerous adventures that he can never abandon and yet never bring to an end. Before we venture out onto this sea to explore it in its full extent and to determine whether anything is to be found there, it will be worthwhile first to look over the map of the land we are about to leave. We should ask ourselves two questions. First, could we be perfectly satisfied with what this land contains, or must we be satisfied with it of necessity, if there is nowhere else a solid foundation on which to build? Second, by what title do we hold this land at all, and how can we secure it against all hostile claims? The course of our analytic has already answered these questions sufficiently, but a brief recapitulation of the answers may strengthen our conviction by bringing the various strands of the argument together at a single point.

We have seen that everything the understanding draws from itself, without borrowing from experience, it nonetheless possesses solely for the sake and use of experience. The principles of the pure understanding, whether they are constitutive a priori like the mathematical principles or merely regulative like the dynamical ones, contain nothing but what amounts to the pure schema of possible experience. Experience derives its unity from the synthetic unity that the understanding, originally and of its own accord, imparts to the synthesis of the imagination in relation to apperception. Phenomena, as data for a possible cognition, must stand a priori in relation to this unity and in agreement with it. These rules of the understanding are not only true a priori but are the very source of all truth, that is, of the agreement of our knowledge with objects, precisely because they contain the ground of the possibility of experience, understood as the sum total of all knowledge. Yet it does not seem enough to us to be told what is true; we also want to be told what we wish to know. If this critical examination teaches us nothing more than what we would have practiced anyway in the merely empirical use of the understanding, without any such subtle inquiry, then the benefit we gain from it would seem not to be worth the labor spent on it. One might certainly reply that no reckless curiosity does more harm to the growth of our knowledge than the kind that insists on knowing in advance the usefulness of this or that piece of information. Such curiosity demands an answer before the necessary investigations have even begun, and before one could form the slightest idea of that usefulness even if it were set before one's eyes. But there is one advantage of such transcendental inquiries that can be made clear even to the dullest and most reluctant learner. An understanding occupied only with empirical exercise, one that never reflects on the sources of its own knowledge, may perform its functions very well and very successfully. Yet there is one thing it cannot do, and it is a thing of great importance: it cannot determine the boundaries that limit its own use, or know what lies inside or outside its own sphere. Only investigations as deep as the ones we have undertaken can accomplish this. And if the understanding cannot tell whether certain questions lie within its horizon, it can never be sure of either its claims or its possessions. It must instead expect many humiliating corrections whenever it oversteps the limits of its own territory, as it inevitably will, and loses itself in fanciful opinions and blinding illusions.

The proposition that the understanding can make no use of its a priori principles, or even of its concepts, other than an empirical one therefore leads to the most important consequences. A concept is put to transcendental use in a principle when it is referred to things in general and considered as things in themselves. It is put to empirical use when it is referred merely to phenomena, that is, to objects of a possible experience. The following reasons make it evident that only the empirical use is admissible. Every concept requires, first, the logical form of a concept, or of thought, in general, and second, the possibility of presenting it with an object to which it can apply. Without the second, it has no sense and is completely empty of content, even though it may still contain the logical function for forming a concept out of whatever data might be given. Now an object cannot be given to a concept except through intuition. Even if a pure intuition is possible a priori, prior to the object, this pure intuition can acquire objective validity only through empirical intuition, of which it is merely the form. All concepts, therefore, and all principles along with them, however a priori they may be, relate to empirical intuitions, that is, to data for a possible experience. Without that relation they have no objective validity whatever and are a mere play of the imagination or of the understanding with images or notions. Take the concepts of mathematics, beginning with its pure intuitions: "Space has three dimensions," "Between two points there can be only one straight line," and so on. All these principles, together with the representation of the object this science is concerned with, are generated in the mind entirely a priori. Even so, they would have no significance if we could not always exhibit that significance in phenomena, which are empirical objects. An abstract concept must therefore be made sensible. An object corresponding to it must be produced in intuition, or else the concept remains, as we say, without sense, which is to say without meaning. Mathematics meets this requirement by constructing the figure, which is a phenomenon present to the senses. The same science finds support and significance in number, and number in turn finds it in the fingers, in counting tokens, or in lines and points. The concept itself is always produced a priori, together with the synthetic principles or formulas derived from such concepts. Their proper use, however, and their application to objects, can be found nowhere but in experience, whose possibility, as far as its form is concerned, they contain a priori.

The same is true of all the categories and of the principles based on them. This is evident from the fact that we cannot make intelligible the possibility of an object corresponding to them without recourse to the conditions of sensibility, and so to the form of phenomena. Their use must therefore be confined to phenomena as their only proper objects. If this condition is removed, all significance, which is to say all relation to an object, disappears, and no example can be found to make clear what sort of thing we ought to think under such concepts.

The concept of quantity cannot be explained except by saying that it is the determination of a thing through which we can think how many times one unit is contained in it. But this "how many times" rests on successive repetition, and therefore on time and on the synthesis of the homogeneous within time. Reality, as opposed to negation, can be explained only by thinking of a time that is either filled with it or empty. If I leave out the notion of permanence, which is existence at all times, nothing remains in the concept of substance but the logical notion of a subject, a notion I try to realize by representing to myself something that can exist only as a subject. But I am completely ignorant of the conditions under which this logical privilege could belong to any thing. Beyond that, I can make nothing of the notion and draw no inference from it, because no object to which the concept could apply is determined, and so we do not know whether it means anything at all. Likewise, if I leave out the notion of time, in which one thing follows another according to a rule, I find nothing in the pure category except that there is something of such a kind that from it we may infer the existence of something else. In that case, however, it would be impossible to distinguish cause from effect. Moreover, this power of inference requires conditions of which I know nothing, and so the concept is not determined as to how it ought to apply to an object. The so-called principle "Everything contingent has a cause" arrives with a gravity and a self-assumed authority that seem to need no outside support. But what, I ask, is meant by "contingent"? The answer is: that whose non-existence is possible. I would very much like to know how this possibility of non-existence is to be known if we do not represent to ourselves a succession in the series of phenomena, and in that succession an existence that follows a non-existence, or the reverse, which is to say a change. To say that the non-existence of a thing is not self-contradictory is a feeble appeal to a logical condition. That condition is certainly necessary for the concept, but it is far from sufficient for the real, objective possibility of non-existence. I can abolish every existing substance in thought without contradicting myself, but I cannot infer from this that substances are objectively contingent in their existence, that is, that their non-existence is possible in itself. As for the category of community, the pure categories of substance and causality cannot be defined or explained well enough to determine their object without the aid of intuition. It is therefore easy to infer that the category of reciprocal causality in the relation of substances to one another, called *commercium*, is just as incapable of such a definition. No one has ever managed to explain possibility, existence, and necessity without obvious tautology whenever the definition was drawn entirely from the pure understanding. The logical possibility of a concept requires only that the concept not contradict itself. The transcendental possibility of things requires that an object correspond to the concept. To substitute the first for the second is a trick that can deceive only the inexperienced.

In a word, no corresponding object belongs to any of these concepts, and their real possibility therefore cannot be demonstrated once we take away sensible intuition, the only intuition we possess. All that then remains is logical possibility, the fact that the concept or thought is possible. But that is not the question. What we want to know is whether the concept relates to an object and so has any meaning.

It follows beyond dispute that the pure concepts of the understanding can never have a transcendental use and must always have an empirical one alone. The principles of the pure understanding relate only to the general conditions of a possible experience, to objects of the senses, and never to things in general, apart from the way in which we intuit them.

Transcendental analytic therefore has this important result: the understanding can accomplish nothing a priori except to anticipate the form of a possible experience in general. Since what is not a phenomenon cannot be an object of experience, the understanding can never overstep the limits of sensibility, within which alone objects are given to us. Its principles are merely principles for the exposition of phenomena. The proud name of ontology, which claims to offer synthetic a priori knowledge of things in general in a systematic doctrine, must give way to the modest title of an analytic of the pure understanding.

Thought is the act of relating a given intuition to an object. If the mode of this intuition is unknown to us, the object is merely transcendental, and the concept of the understanding is used only transcendentally, that is, to produce unity in the thought of a manifold in general. Now a pure category, from which all conditions of sensible intuition (the only intuition we have) have been abstracted, does not determine an object. It merely expresses the thought of an object in general according to different modes. To use a concept, however, we need the function of judgment, by which an object is subsumed under the concept, and therefore at least the formal condition under which something can be given in intuition. Without this condition of judgment, which is the schema, subsumption is impossible, because nothing is given that could be subsumed under the concept. The merely transcendental use of the categories is therefore in fact no use at all, and it has no determinate object, nor even one whose form could be determined. It follows that the pure category cannot establish any synthetic a priori principle, and that the principles of the pure understanding are only ever of empirical and never of transcendental use. Beyond the sphere of possible experience, no synthetic a priori principles are possible.

It may therefore be advisable to put the matter this way. The pure categories, apart from the formal conditions of sensibility, have a merely transcendental meaning, yet they are not of transcendental use. Such use is impossible in itself, because all the conditions for any employment of the categories in judgments are absent, namely the formal conditions for subsuming an object under these concepts. As pure categories, then, they can be used only empirically and not transcendentally, and so they are of no use at all once separated from sensibility; they cannot be applied to any object. They are merely the pure form of the understanding's employment with respect to objects in general and to thought, and through them alone it is not possible to think or determine any object. But at the root of this subject lies an illusion that is very hard to avoid. The categories do not originate in sensibility, as the forms of intuition, space and time, do; they seem, therefore, to be capable of an application beyond the sphere of sensuous objects. But this is not so. The categories are nothing but forms of thought. They contain only the logical capacity to unite, a priori and within a single consciousness, the manifold given in intuition. Apart from the only kind of intuition possible for us, then, they have even less meaning than the pure forms of sensibility, space and time. Through space and time an object is at least given, but a mode of connecting the manifold means nothing at all when the intuition that alone supplies the manifold is missing. At the same time, when we call certain objects phenomena, or sensuous beings, we distinguish the way we intuit them from their own nature as things in themselves. By that very distinction we set something over against phenomena. It may be those same objects considered in their own nature, even though we do not intuit them that way. Or it may be other possible things that are not objects of our senses at all but are thought by the understanding alone, which we call intelligible beings, or noumena. The question then arises whether the pure concepts of our understanding have any meaning with respect to these noumena, and whether they might offer a way of knowing them.

At the very outset, however, we meet an ambiguity that can easily cause serious misunderstanding. When the understanding calls an object, in a certain relation, a phenomenon, it also forms, apart from that relation, a representation of an object in itself, and so believes that it can form concepts of such objects as well. Since the understanding has no fundamental concepts other than the categories, it assumes that an object considered as a thing in itself must be capable of being thought through these pure concepts. It is thereby misled into taking the wholly undetermined concept of an intelligible being, a something lying outside the sphere of our sensibility, for a determinate concept of a being that we could somehow know through the understanding.

If by "noumenon" we mean a thing insofar as it is *not an object of our sensuous intuition*, setting aside our particular way of intuiting it, then it is a noumenon in the *negative* sense of the word. But if we mean an *object of a non-sensuous intuition*, we are assuming a special kind of intuition, namely an intellectual intuition. That kind of intuition does not belong to us, and we cannot even conceive how it would be possible. This would be a noumenon in the *positive* sense.

The doctrine of sensibility is at the same time the doctrine of noumena in the negative sense. It concerns things that the understanding must think without any reference to our mode of intuition, and therefore not as mere phenomena but as things in themselves. Yet the understanding also recognizes that it cannot use its categories to consider things in themselves. The categories have meaning only in relation to the unity of intuitions in space and time, and they can determine this unity through general a priori connecting concepts only because space and time are purely ideal. Where this unity of time is absent, as it is with noumena, the entire use of the categories, indeed their entire meaning, disappears, since we cannot even comprehend how things corresponding to them would be possible. On this point I need only refer the reader to what I said at the beginning of the General Remark appended to the preceding chapter. The possibility of a thing can never be proved from the fact that its concept is free of contradiction. It can be proved only by an intuition corresponding to that concept. If we want to apply the categories to objects that cannot be regarded as phenomena, we must therefore possess an intuition other than the sensuous kind, and the objects in that case would be noumena in the positive sense. Since such an intuition, an intellectual intuition, forms no part of our faculty of knowledge, it is absolutely impossible for the categories to have any application beyond the limits of experience. There may well be intelligible beings to which our faculty of sensuous intuition bears no relation and cannot be applied. But our concepts of the understanding, being mere forms of thought for our sensuous intuition, do not reach that far. What we call a noumenon must therefore be understood by us only in the negative sense.

If I remove all thought, that is, all the work of the categories, from an empirical intuition, no knowledge of any object remains. Through mere intuition nothing is thought, and the fact that some affection of sensibility occurs in me does not mean that this affection or representation relates to any object outside me. But if I remove all intuition, the form of thought still remains: the way of determining an object for the manifold of a possible intuition. In this respect the categories do extend somewhat further than sensuous intuition, since they think objects in general without regard to the particular mode of sensibility through which those objects might be given. Yet they do not thereby apply to or determine a wider range of objects. We cannot assume that such objects could be given without presupposing that some mode of intuition other than the sensuous is possible, and that is a supposition we have no right to make.

I call a concept *problematic* when it contains no contradiction and is connected with other knowledge as a limitation of given concepts, but when its objective reality cannot be known in any way. The concept of a noumenon, a thing that must be thought not as an object of the senses but as a thing in itself, through the pure understanding alone, is not self-contradictory. We have no grounds for claiming that sensibility is the only possible kind of intuition. More than that, the concept is necessary in order to keep sensuous intuition from extending to things in themselves, and so to limit the objective validity of sensuous knowledge. The things in themselves that lie beyond the reach of sensuous knowledge are called noumena precisely to indicate that this knowledge does not extend to everything the understanding thinks. In the end, however, the possibility of such noumena cannot be comprehended at all. Beyond the sphere of phenomena, everything is for us an empty void. We possess an understanding whose domain extends problematically beyond that sphere, but we possess no intuition, not even the concept of a possible intuition, through which objects outside the region of sensibility could be given to us and to which the understanding could be applied assertorically, that is, with actual claims about what is so. The concept of a noumenon is therefore merely a *limiting concept*, and its use is only negative. It is not an arbitrary invention, however. It is bound up with the limitation of sensibility, even though it cannot supply anything positive beyond that limit.

It follows that the division of objects into phenomena and noumena, and of the world into a sensible world (*mundus sensibilis*) and an intelligible world (*mundus intelligibilis*), cannot be accepted in a positive sense, although concepts can certainly be divided this way. The class of noumena has no determinate object corresponding to it and therefore cannot have objective validity. Once we abandon the senses, how could we make it intelligible that the categories, which are the only concepts that could serve for noumena, have any sense or meaning at all? Applying them to an object requires something more than the mere unity of thought. It requires a possible intuition. The concept of a noumenon, taken as merely problematic, remains not only permissible but, as a concept that limits sensibility, absolutely necessary. In that case, however, a noumenon is not a special intelligible object for our understanding. On the contrary, the kind of understanding to which it could belong is itself a problem. We cannot form the faintest idea of how an understanding could be possible that knows its object not discursively, through categories, but intuitively, in a non-sensuous intuition. In this way our understanding gains a kind of negative extension. It is not limited by sensibility but instead limits sensibility, by applying the name noumena to things considered not as phenomena but as things in themselves. Yet in the same act it sets limits on itself. It admits that it cannot know these things through any of the categories, and so it must think of them only as an unknown something.

In the writings of modern authors, however, I find the expressions *mundus sensibilis* and *mundus intelligibilis* used in an entirely different way, one that departs completely from the meaning the ancients gave them. This usage presents no difficulty, but it rests on mere wordplay. Some writers have chosen to call the whole of phenomena the sensible world insofar as it is intuited, and the intelligible world insofar as its connections are thought according to general laws of the understanding. On this view, astronomy taken as the mere observation of the starry sky would represent the first, while a system of astronomy such as the Copernican or the Newtonian would represent the second. But twisting words in this way is a sophistical evasion. It sidesteps a difficult question by altering its meaning to suit our convenience. Of course understanding and reason are used in knowing phenomena. The real question is whether they can still be used when the object is *not* a phenomenon, which is how we regard it when it is thought as given to the understanding alone and not to the senses. The question, therefore, is whether a transcendental use of the understanding is possible over and above its empirical use, a use that would apply to the noumenon as an object. This question we have answered in the negative.

So when we say that the senses represent objects *as they appear* and the understanding represents them *as they are*, the second claim must be taken not in a transcendental but only in an empirical sense. It means that objects must be represented as objects of experience, within the complete connection of phenomena. It does not mean what they might be apart from their relation to possible experience, and therefore apart from the senses, as objects of the pure understanding. That must always remain unknown to us. Indeed, we do not even know whether such transcendental or extraordinary knowledge is possible under any circumstances, or at least whether it is possible through our categories. For us, understanding and sensibility can determine objects only when they work together. If we separate them, we have intuitions without concepts or concepts without intuitions, and in both cases representations that we cannot apply to any determinate object.

If anyone, after all these inquiries and explanations, still hesitates to give up the merely transcendental use of the categories, let him try to construct a synthetic proposition with them. There would be no point in constructing an analytic proposition for this purpose, because an analytic proposition does not extend the understanding. It concerns only what is already thought in the concept itself and leaves entirely open whether the concept relates to any object at all or merely expresses the unity of thought, setting aside every way in which an object might be given. In such a proposition the understanding needs only to know what lies within the concept; what the concept applies to is a matter of indifference. The attempt must therefore be made with a synthetic and supposedly transcendental principle, such as "Everything that exists, exists as substance," or "Everything contingent exists as the effect of some other thing, namely its cause." Now I ask: where could the understanding obtain such synthetic propositions, if the concepts they contain are meant to apply not to possible experience but to things in themselves, to noumena? Where is the third term, which every synthetic proposition requires, that would join in one proposition concepts having no logical, or analytic, connection with one another? Such a proposition can never be proved. More than that, the very possibility of any such pure assertion can never be shown without appealing to the empirical use of the understanding, and that appeal by its nature abandons pure, non-sensuous judgment altogether. The concept of pure and merely intelligible objects is therefore entirely lacking in any principles for its application, because we cannot conceive any way in which such objects might be given. The problematic thought that keeps a place open for them functions only like an empty space: it limits the use of empirical principles without containing any other object of knowledge beyond their range.

### Appendix: On the Amphiboly, or Equivocal Nature, of the Concepts of Reflection, Arising from the Confusion of the Empirical Use of the Understanding with the Transcendental

Reflection (*reflexio*) is not concerned with objects themselves, in order to obtain concepts of them directly. It is the state of mind in which we set out to discover the subjective conditions under which we can arrive at concepts. It is the awareness of how given representations relate to our different sources of knowledge, and only through that awareness can their relation to one another be correctly determined. The first question that arises about our representations is this: to which faculty of knowledge do they belong, the understanding or the senses? Many judgments are accepted as true out of habit or inclination, and because no reflection comes before or after them, they are taken to be judgments that originate in the understanding. Not every judgment requires *examination*, that is, an inquiry into the grounds of its truth. When a judgment is immediately certain, as with "Between two points there can be only one straight line," no better or more direct evidence of its truth can be found than what the judgment itself contains and expresses. But every judgment, indeed every comparison, requires *reflection*, that is, a determination of the faculty of knowledge to which the given concepts belong. The act by which I relate my representations to the faculty of knowledge that produces them, and by which I determine whether they are being compared with one another as belonging to the pure understanding or to sensuous intuition, I call *transcendental reflection*. The relations in which concepts can stand to one another are those of identity and difference, agreement and opposition, the internal and the external, and finally the determinable and the determining, that is, matter and form. Determining these relations correctly depends on answering a prior question: to which faculty of knowledge do they subjectively belong, sensibility or the understanding? How we answer that question decides how we must think the relations themselves.

Before forming any objective judgment, we compare the concepts that are to enter into it. We note whether there is identity, many representations under one concept, if a universal judgment is to be formed, or difference, if a particular one; whether there is agreement, for an affirmative judgment, or opposition, for a negative one; and so on. For this reason these concepts ought to be called concepts of comparison (*conceptus comparationis*). But the matter changes when the question concerns not the logical form of concepts but their content, that is, whether the things themselves are identical or different, in agreement or in opposition, and so forth. Things can stand in a twofold relation to our faculty of knowledge, either to sensibility or to the understanding, and their relation to one another depends on which of these it is. Only transcendental reflection, the relating of given representations to one faculty of knowledge or the other, can therefore settle their relation to one another. We cannot discover whether things are identical or different, in agreement or in opposition, merely by comparing our concepts of them (*comparatio*). We can discover it only by first distinguishing the kind of knowledge to which they belong, which is to say, through transcendental reflection. It is accurate, then, to say that *logical reflection* is mere comparison, because it takes no account of the faculty of knowledge to which the given representations belong and so treats them, as far as their origin is concerned, as all of one kind. *Transcendental reflection*, which concerns the objects themselves, contains the ground of the possibility of objectively comparing representations with one another. It is therefore very different from logical reflection, since the faculties of knowledge to which the representations belong are not even the same. Transcendental reflection is a duty that no one can neglect who wants to judge anything about things a priori. We shall now take up this duty, and in doing so shed considerable light on the question of what the proper task of the understanding is.

1. *Identity and Difference.* Suppose an object is presented to us several times, each time with the same internal determinations of quality and quantity. If it is an object of the pure understanding, it is always the same object, not several things but only one (*numerica identitas*, numerical identity). If it is a phenomenon, however, we are not concerned with comparing concepts at all. However completely the concepts may coincide, the mere difference of location at the same moment is sufficient ground for holding that these objects of the senses are numerically different. Take two drops of water. We may set aside every internal difference of quality and quantity between them, and the fact that they are intuited at the same time in different places is still enough to justify regarding them as numerically distinct. Leibniz took phenomena to be things in themselves, and therefore *intelligibilia*, objects of the pure understanding, although he called them phenomena because of the confused character of our representations of them. On that assumption his principle of the identity of indiscernibles (*principium identitatis indiscernibilium*) cannot be disputed. But phenomena are objects of sensibility, and with respect to them the understanding must be used empirically, not purely or transcendentally. For phenomena, then, plurality and numerical difference are already given by space itself, as the condition of outer appearances. One part of space, however perfectly similar and equal it may be to another part, still lies outside it, and for that reason alone it is distinct from the part that is joined to it to make up a larger space. The same must therefore hold for all things that occupy different parts of space at the same time, however similar and equal they may otherwise be.

2. *Agreement and Opposition.* When reality is represented only through the pure understanding (*realitas noumenon*), no opposition between realities can be conceived. By opposition I mean a relation in which realities, combined in one subject, cancel each other's effects, as expressed in the formula 3 − 3 = 0. The real in a phenomenon (*realitas phaenomenon*), on the other hand, can certainly stand in mutual opposition, and when realities of this kind are united in the same subject, one may wholly or partly cancel the effect of the other. Two moving forces acting along the same straight line, pulling or pushing a point in opposite directions, are an example; so is a pleasure that counterbalances a given amount of pain.

3. *The Internal and the External.* In an object of the pure understanding, only that is internal which has no relation, as far as its existence is concerned, to anything distinct from itself. The internal determinations of a phenomenal substance in space (*substantia phaenomenon*), by contrast, are nothing but relations, and the substance itself is entirely a sum of mere relations. We know substance in space only through the forces that act within it, either drawing other things toward it, which is attraction, or preventing other things from penetrating it, which is repulsion and impenetrability. We know of no other properties that make up the concept of the substance that appears in space and that we call matter. As an object of the pure understanding, on the other hand, every substance must have internal determinations and internal powers that bear on its inner reality. But what internal accidents can I conceive, other than those my inner sense presents to me? Only something that is itself thought, or something analogous to thought. This is why Leibniz, who regarded things as noumena, first denied them everything resembling external relation, and with it all composition, and then declared that all substances, even the constituent parts of matter, are simple substances endowed with powers of representation. In a word, he made them monads.

4. *Matter and Form.* These two concepts underlie all other reflection, so inseparably are they bound up with every use of the understanding. The first signifies the determinable in general; the second, its determination. Both are meant in a transcendental sense, setting aside every difference in what is given and every difference in the way it is determined. Logicians formerly called the universal the matter and the specific difference that marks off one part of the universal the form. In a judgment, the given concepts may be called its logical matter, and their relation to one another, by means of the copula, the form of the judgment. In any being, its constituent elements (*essentialia*) are the matter, and the way they are combined in that being is the essential form. With respect to things in general, unlimited reality was regarded as the matter of all possibility, and its limitation, or negation, as the form by which one thing is distinguished from another according to transcendental concepts. The understanding requires that something first be given, at least in concept, before it can determine that something in a particular way. In a concept of the pure understanding, therefore, matter comes before form. For this reason Leibniz first assumed things, the monads, together with an internal power of representation within them, and only then founded upon these their external relations and the community of their states, that is, of their representations. On his account, accordingly, space and time were possible: space through the relation of substances, and time through the connection of their determinations with one another as causes and effects.
