And so it would actually be, if the pure understanding could be applied directly to objects, and if space and time were determinations of things in themselves. But since they are merely sensuous intuitions, in which we determine all objects solely as phenomena, the form of intuition, as a subjective property of sensibility, must precede all matter, that is, all sensations. Consequently space and time must precede all phenomena and all data of experience; indeed, they are what make experience possible in the first place. The intellectual philosopher could not tolerate the idea that form should come before the things themselves and determine their possibility. His objection would be entirely correct if we assumed that we intuit things as they actually are, only in a confused representation. But sensuous intuition is a distinctive subjective condition that lies a priori at the basis of all perception, and its form is original. That form must therefore be given on its own. Matter, or the things themselves that appear, does not lie at the foundation of experience, as we would have to conclude if we judged by concepts alone. On the contrary, the very possibility of matter presupposes a given formal intuition, namely space and time.

#### Remark on the Amphiboly of the Concepts of Reflection

Allow me to call the position we assign to a concept, whether in sensibility or in the pure understanding, its *transcendental place*. On this basis, a *transcendental topic* would assign each concept the position it must occupy according to the different ways it is used, and would supply rules for determining this place for every concept. Such a doctrine would protect us thoroughly against the sleights of hand of the pure understanding and the illusions that arise from them, because it would always establish which faculty of knowledge each concept properly belongs to. Every concept, every heading under which many items of knowledge are grouped together, can be called a *logical place*. Aristotle's logical topic was built on this idea. Teachers and orators could draw on it, consulting certain headings of thought to find what best suited the subject at hand. It allowed them to split hairs and hold forth fluently, with an appearance of depth.

A transcendental topic, by contrast, contains nothing more than the four headings of all comparison and distinction mentioned above. These differ from the categories because they do not present the object according to what constitutes its concept, such as quantity or reality. They merely set out the comparison of representations that comes before our concepts of things. This comparison, however, first requires reflection. We must determine the place to which the representations of the things being compared belong: whether they are thought by the pure understanding or given by sensibility.

Concepts can be compared logically without troubling to ask which faculty their objects belong to, whether to the understanding as noumena or to sensibility as phenomena. But if we want to apply these concepts to objects, a prior transcendental reflection is necessary. Without it, I would make a very unreliable use of these concepts. I would construct supposed synthetic propositions that critical reason cannot accept, propositions that rest solely on a transcendental amphiboly. An amphiboly is a confusion arising from a double meaning, and here it consists in mistaking an object of pure understanding for a phenomenon.

The celebrated Leibniz lacked this doctrine of transcendental topic, and so he was deceived by the amphiboly of the concepts of reflection. He constructed an intellectual system of the world. Or rather, he believed himself able to know the inner nature of things by comparing all objects only with the understanding and with the abstract, formal concepts of thought. Our table of the concepts of reflection gives us an unexpected advantage. It lets us lay out the distinguishing features of his system in all its parts, and at the same time expose the fundamental principle of this peculiar way of thinking, which rested on nothing but a misunderstanding. He compared all things with one another purely by means of concepts. He therefore found, naturally enough, no differences other than those by which the understanding distinguishes its pure concepts from one another. The conditions of sensuous intuition carry their own means of distinction, but he did not regard them as original. For him, sensibility was only a confused mode of representation and not a distinct source of representations. He took a phenomenon to be the representation of the thing in itself, differing from knowledge through the understanding only in its logical form. In his view, a phenomenon is ordinarily unanalyzed and so contains in its concept of a thing a certain admixture of incidental representations, which it is the task of the understanding to separate and sort out. In a word, Leibniz intellectualized phenomena. Locke did the reverse. In his system of noogony, if I may use such a term for a theory of the origin of concepts, he sensualized the concepts of the understanding, declaring them to be nothing more than empirical or abstracted concepts of reflection. Understanding and sensibility are two different sources of representations, and they can yield objectively valid judgments about things only in combination. Yet instead of looking for these two sources, each of these great men recognized only one faculty. Each believed that this one faculty related directly to things in themselves, while the other did nothing but confuse or arrange its representations.

Accordingly, Leibniz compared the objects of the senses as things in general, and he did so solely within the understanding.

First, he compared them with respect to their identity or difference, as judged by the understanding. He considered only the concepts of objects and not their position in intuition, where alone objects can be given. He entirely ignored the transcendental location of these concepts, that is, whether their object should be classed among phenomena or among things in themselves. It was therefore to be expected that he would extend the principle of indiscernibles to objects of the senses, the *mundus phaenomenon* or world as appearance, even though that principle holds only for concepts of things in general. It was also to be expected that he would believe he had greatly extended our knowledge of nature by doing so. Certainly, if I know a drop of water as a thing in itself, in all its inner determinations, I cannot regard one drop as different from another when the concept of the one is completely identical with the concept of the other. But if the drop is a phenomenon in space, it has its place not only in the understanding, among concepts, but also in external sensuous intuition, in space. In that case its physical location has no bearing on the inner determinations of things. A place B can contain a thing perfectly similar and equal to a thing in place A, and the two will be distinct just as surely as if they differed in every respect. Difference of place, with no further conditions, makes the plurality and distinctness of objects as phenomena not only possible but necessary. The so-called law above is therefore not a law of nature. It is merely an analytic rule for comparing things by means of concepts alone.

Second, consider the principle that "realities, as simple affirmations, never logically contradict one another." It is perfectly true as regards the relation of concepts. As regards nature, however, or things in themselves, of which we have no concept whatever, it has no meaning at all. For real opposition, in which A − B = 0, exists everywhere. In such opposition, one reality combined with another in the same subject cancels the effects of the other. We see this constantly in the various opposing actions and operations of nature. Because these depend on real forces, they must be called *realitates phaenomena*, realities as phenomena. General mechanics can even state the empirical condition of this opposition in an a priori rule, because it attends to the opposition in the direction of forces, a condition about which the transcendental concept of reality can tell us nothing. Leibniz did not announce this proposition with quite the fanfare of a new principle. He did, however, use it to establish new propositions, and his followers incorporated it into their Leibnizian-Wolffian system of philosophy. According to this principle, for example, all evils are merely consequences of the limitations of created beings. They are negations, since negations are the only opposite of reality. (In the mere concept of a thing in general this is indeed so, but not in things as phenomena.) Likewise, the adherents of this system consider it not only possible but natural to unite all reality in a single being. They recognize no kind of opposition other than contradiction, in which the very concept of a thing is annulled. They cannot conceive an opposition of mutual cancellation, so to speak, in which one real cause destroys the effect of another. We encounter the conditions for representing such an opposition only in sensibility.

Third, Leibniz's monadology has no better foundation than this philosopher's mistaken way of representing the difference between inner and outer solely in relation to the understanding. Substances in general must have something inner, something free of all external relations and consequently free of composition as well. The simple, which can be represented as a unit, is therefore the foundation of what is inner in things in themselves. It follows that the inner state of substances cannot consist in place, shape, contact, or motion, since these are all external relations. We can attribute to substances no inner state other than the one by which we inwardly determine our own sense, namely the state of representation. This is how the monads were constructed. They were to be the elements of the universe, their active power was to consist in representation, and the effects of that power were to remain confined entirely within themselves.

For the same reason, Leibniz could represent the possible community of substances only as a preestablished harmony, and in no way as physical influence. Each thing is occupied only inwardly, with its own representations. The state of representations in one substance therefore could not stand in any active, living connection with the state of another. Some third cause, acting on all substances without exception, was needed to make their different states correspond. This correspondence did not come about through assistance applied in each particular case, the *systema assistentiae* or system of occasional intervention. It came about through the unity of the idea of a cause that is occupied with and connected to all substances. According to the Leibnizian school, all substances necessarily receive from this cause their existence and permanence, and therefore also their mutual correspondence according to universal laws.

Fourth, this philosopher's celebrated doctrine of space and time, in which he intellectualized these forms of sensibility, arose from the same illusion of transcendental reflection. If I try to represent the external relations of things through the understanding alone, I can do so only by means of the concept of their reciprocal action. If I want to connect one state of a thing with another state of the same thing, I must rely on the concept of the order of cause and effect. Accordingly, Leibniz regarded space as a certain order in the community of substances, and time as the dynamical sequence of their states. Space and time possess certain features in their own right, independently of things. He attributed these features to a necessary confusion in our concepts, a confusion that makes what is merely a form of dynamical relations appear to be a self-subsisting intuition that precedes even the things themselves. Space and time were thus the intelligible form of the connection of things, meaning substances and their states, in themselves. And the things were intelligible substances, *substantiae noumena*. At the same time, he treated these concepts as valid for phenomena. He granted sensibility no distinctive mode of intuition and sought everything in the understanding, even the empirical representation of objects. He left to the senses only the contemptible task of confusing and disordering the understanding's representations.

But suppose we could form some synthetic proposition about things in themselves through the pure understanding, which is impossible. Even then it could not apply to phenomena, because phenomena do not represent things in themselves. In transcendental reflection I would have to compare my concepts only under the conditions of sensibility, and so space and time would be determinations not of things in themselves but of phenomena. What things may be in themselves I do not know, nor do I need to know, because a thing is never presented to me except as a phenomenon.

I must proceed in the same way with the other concepts of reflection. Matter is *substantia phaenomenon*, substance as appearance. I look for what is inner in it in every part of the space it occupies and in all the functions and operations it performs. These are never anything but phenomena of outer sense. I can therefore find nothing absolutely inner in matter, only what is comparatively inner, and this in turn consists of external relations. The absolutely inner in matter, as the pure understanding would require it to be, is a mere chimera, since matter is not an object for the pure understanding at all. The transcendental object that underlies the phenomenon we call matter is a mere *nescio quid*, an "I know not what." We could not understand its nature even if someone were able to tell us, because we can understand nothing that does not bring with it something in intuition corresponding to the words used. People complain that we cannot perceive the inner nature of things. If they mean that we do not grasp through the pure understanding what the things that appear to us may be in themselves, the complaint is foolish and unreasonable. Those who make it really want us to be able to know, and therefore to intuit, things without senses. They wish we had a faculty of knowledge entirely different from the human one, different not merely in degree but in the very kind and manner of intuition. We would then not be human beings at all, but beings of a kind whose very possibility we have no means of knowing, let alone their nature and constitution. Through observation and the analysis of phenomena we penetrate into the interior of nature, and no one can say how far this knowledge may advance over time. But we could never answer those transcendental questions that go beyond nature, even if all of nature lay open before us, because we have no power to observe our own mind through any intuition other than that of inner sense. Here lies the mystery of the origin and source of our sensibility. Its relation to an object, and the transcendental ground of this unity of subjective and objective, lie too deeply hidden for us. We know ourselves only through inner sense, and therefore only as phenomena. We cannot discover in our existence anything but phenomena, even as we earnestly desire to penetrate to their non-sensuous cause.

The great value of this critique of conclusions drawn by mere reflection lies in its clear demonstration that all conclusions about objects compared with one another in the understanding alone are void. At the same time it confirms the point we have particularly insisted on. Phenomena are not included, as things in themselves, among the objects of the pure understanding. Nevertheless, they are the only things through which our knowledge can have objective reality, because they alone give us intuitions corresponding to our concepts.

When we reflect in a purely logical way, we do nothing more than compare concepts in our understanding. We ask whether both have the same content, whether or not they contradict each other, whether anything is contained in either concept, which of the two is given, and which is merely a way of thinking what is given. Suppose, however, that I apply these concepts to an object in general, in the transcendental sense, without first determining whether it is an object of sensuous or of intellectual intuition. Certain limitations then appear that forbid us to go beyond the concepts and that make any empirical use of them impossible. These limitations prove that the representation of an object as a thing in general is not merely insufficient. Without sensuous determination and apart from empirical conditions, it is self-contradictory. We must therefore either abstract from all objects, as logic does, or, if we admit objects, think them under the conditions of sensuous intuition. The intelligible would require a wholly distinctive intuition, which we do not possess, and without it the intelligible is nothing for us. On the other hand, phenomena cannot be objects in themselves. For when I merely think things in general, a difference in their external relations cannot constitute a difference in the things themselves. On the contrary, the external difference presupposes an internal one. If the concept of one of two things is not inwardly different from that of the other, I am simply thinking one and the same thing in different relations. Further, when one affirmation, or reality, is added to another, the positive is actually increased, and nothing is subtracted or taken away from it. Hence the real in things cannot contradict or oppose itself, and so on.

As we have shown, Leibniz misunderstood the true use of the concepts of reflection in the exercise of the understanding. He was one of the most acute philosophers of either ancient or modern times, yet this misunderstanding led him to construct a groundless system of intellectual knowledge that claims to determine its objects without the help of the senses. For this reason, exposing the cause of the amphiboly of these concepts, which is the origin of these false principles, is of great value in determining with certainty the proper limits of the understanding.

It is correct to say that whatever is affirmed or denied of a concept as a whole can be affirmed or denied of any part of it. This is the *dictum de omni et nullo*, the principle "of all and of none." But it would be absurd to alter this logical proposition so that it reads: whatever is not contained in a general concept is likewise not contained in the particular concepts that fall under it. The particular concepts are particular precisely because their content is greater than what is thought in the general concept. Yet Leibniz's entire intellectual system rests on this false principle. With that principle it must necessarily collapse, together with all the ambiguous principles about the use of the understanding that have sprung from it.

Leibniz's principle of the identity of indiscernibles, or indistinguishables, really rests on a presupposition: that if a certain distinction is not found in the concept of a thing, it is not to be found in the things themselves either. It follows, on this view, that all things are completely identical, *numero eadem* or numerically one and the same, if they cannot be distinguished from one another in quality or quantity in our concepts of them. But the mere concept of anything abstracts from many necessary conditions of intuition. What has been abstracted from is then rashly taken to be nonexistent, and nothing is attributed to the thing except what is contained in its concept.

The concept of a cubic foot of space, however I think it, is in itself completely identical. Yet two cubic feet in space are distinct from each other simply because they are in different places; they are *numero diversa*, numerically different. These places are conditions of the intuition in which the object of this concept is given, and they belong not to the concept but to the faculty of sensibility. Similarly, there is no contradiction in the concept of a thing so long as nothing negative is combined with something affirmative, and purely affirmative concepts cannot, in combination, produce any negation. But reality, motion for example, is given in sensuous intuition, and there we find conditions such as opposite directions. The concept of motion in general abstracted from these conditions, yet they make possible a contradiction or opposition, though not of a logical kind, that produces zero out of pure positives. We are therefore not entitled to say that all reality is in perfect agreement and harmony merely because no contradiction can be found among its concepts. According to mere concepts, what is inner is the substratum of all relations or external determinations. When, therefore, I abstract from all conditions of intuition and confine myself solely to the concept of a thing in general, I can abstract from all external relations. There must still remain a concept of something that signifies no relation, only inner determinations. From this it seems to follow that in every thing, every substance, there is something absolutely inner that precedes all external determinations, since it makes them possible. This substratum would then contain no external relations and would consequently be simple, for corporeal things are never anything but relations, at least of their parts external to one another. And since we know of no absolutely inner determinations other than those of inner sense, this substratum would be not only simple but also determined through representations, by analogy with our inner sense. In short, all things would properly be monads, simple beings endowed with the power of representation. All this would be perfectly correct if the concept of a thing were the only necessary condition for objects of outer intuition to be given. On the contrary, it is evident that a permanent phenomenon in space, impenetrable extension, can contain nothing but relations, with nothing absolutely inner, and yet be the primary substratum of all outer perception. Through mere concepts I cannot think anything external without at the same time thinking something internal, because concepts of relations presuppose things already given and are impossible without them. But in intuition there is something that is not found in the mere concept of a thing in general, namely space, which, with everything it contains, consists of purely formal or even real relations. Space presents us with the substratum that could not be known through concepts alone. I therefore cannot say: because a thing cannot be represented through mere concepts without something absolutely internal, there is also, in the things themselves that fall under these concepts, and in their intuition, nothing external to which something absolutely internal does not stand as a foundation. Once we have set aside all the conditions of intuition, what remains in the bare concept is indeed nothing but the internal in general, through which alone the external is possible. But this necessity rests on abstraction alone, and it does not hold for things themselves insofar as they are given in intuition with determinations that express mere relations and have nothing internal as their foundation. Such things are not things in themselves but only phenomena. What we know in matter is nothing but relations; what we call its internal determinations are internal only by comparison. Yet some of these relations are self-subsistent and permanent, and through them a determinate object is given to us. Suppose that, once I set these relations aside, I have nothing left to think. That does not destroy the concept of a thing as phenomenon, nor the concept of an object in the abstract. It does, however, eliminate the possibility of an object that can be determined by concepts alone, which is to say, of a noumenon. It is certainly startling to hear that a thing consists entirely of relations. But such a thing is simply a phenomenon, and it cannot be thought through the categories alone, because it consists in nothing more than the relation of something in general to the senses. In the same way, if we begin with concepts alone, we can think the relations of things in the abstract only by taking one thing to be the cause of determinations in another, because that is precisely the understanding's concept, or category, of relation. In doing so, however, we set aside all intuition, and we lose entirely the mode in which the manifold assigns each of its parts its place. That mode is the form of sensibility, namely space, and it comes before all empirical causality.

Someone may wish to fall back here on the usual evasion and claim that realities considered as noumena, *realitates noumena*, at least cannot be in opposition to one another. In that case he must produce an example of this pure, non-sensuous reality, so that we can tell whether the notion represents something or nothing. But an example can be found only in experience, and experience never presents us with anything but phenomena. The claim therefore means no more than this: a concept that contains only affirmations contains nothing negative. No one has ever doubted that proposition.

If by intelligible objects we mean things that can be thought through the pure categories alone, without the schemata of sensibility, then such objects are impossible. The condition for any objective use of the concepts of the understanding is the character of our sensuous intuition, through which objects are given to us. If we set that intuition aside, our concepts can have no relation to an object at all. And even if we were to suppose some kind of intuition different from our own, our functions of thought would still have no use or meaning with respect to it. But suppose we mean by the term objects of a non-sensuous intuition, to which our categories do not apply and of which we can therefore have no knowledge, neither intuition nor concept. In this merely negative sense, noumena must be admitted. To admit them is no more than to say that our mode of intuition does not apply to all things but only to objects of our senses. Its objective validity is therefore limited, and room is left for another kind of intuition, and so also for things that might be its objects. In this sense, however, the concept of a noumenon is problematic. It is the notion of a thing that we can call neither possible nor impossible, because we know of no mode of intuition except the sensuous and no kind of concept except the categories, and neither of these applies to a non-sensuous object. For this reason we cannot extend the sphere of our objects of thought beyond the conditions of our sensibility, nor assume that objects of pure thought, that is, noumena, exist, because such objects have no genuine positive meaning. It must be acknowledged that the categories are not by themselves sufficient for knowing things in themselves. Without the data of sensibility they are merely subjective forms of the unity of the understanding. Thought is certainly not a product of the senses, and to that extent it is not limited by them. It does not follow, however, that thought can be used purely, without the intervention of sensibility, because it would then have no reference to an object. Nor can we call a noumenon an object of pure thought. Our representation of it is only the problematic concept of an object for an intuition and an understanding entirely different from ours, and both of these are themselves problematic. The concept of a noumenon is therefore not the concept of an object. It is a problematic concept bound up inseparably with the limitation of our sensibility. It contains the answer to the question "Are there objects entirely unconnected with, and independent of, our intuition?" Only an indeterminate answer can be given, and the answer is this: "Since sensuous intuition does not extend to all things without distinction, room remains for other and different objects." The existence of these problematic objects is therefore not flatly denied, since we have no determinate concept of them. But since no category is valid for them, neither may they be admitted as objects for our understanding.

The understanding therefore limits sensibility without enlarging its own domain. It forbids sensibility to apply its forms and modes to things in themselves and confines it to the sphere of phenomena. In doing so it does think an object in itself, but only as a transcendental object, the cause of a phenomenon and therefore not itself a phenomenon. This object cannot be thought as a quantity, as a reality, or as a substance, because these concepts always require sensuous forms in which to determine an object. It is therefore an object of which we cannot say whether it is to be found within us or outside us, or whether it would be annihilated along with sensibility or would continue to exist if sensibility were taken away. If we wish to call this object a noumenon because our representation of it is non-sensuous, we are free to do so. But since none of the concepts of our understanding apply to it, the representation is entirely empty for us. Its only use is to mark the limits of our sensuous intuition, and it leaves an empty space that we can fill neither from possible experience nor from the pure understanding.

The critique of the pure understanding, then, does not permit us to create a new field of objects beyond those presented to us as phenomena, or to wander off into intelligible worlds. It does not even allow us to attempt so much as a concept of them. The plausible error that leads us there is an entirely forgivable one. It arises because the understanding is put to a transcendental use contrary to its proper purpose and function. Objects, which is to say possible intuitions, are made to conform to concepts, instead of concepts conforming to the intuitions on which alone their objective validity depends. The reason for this, in turn, is that apperception, and thought along with it, comes before every possible determinate arrangement of representations. We therefore think something in general. On the one hand we determine it sensuously; on the other, we distinguish the object represented generally and in the abstract from this particular way of intuiting it. What remains is a way of determining the object by thought alone. This is really nothing but a logical form without content, yet it appears to us as a mode in which the object exists in itself, as a noumenon, independent of the intuition that is confined to our senses.

Before concluding this transcendental analytic, we must add something that, though of no great importance in itself, seems necessary for the completeness of the system. The highest concept with which a transcendental philosophy usually begins is the division into the possible and the impossible. But every division presupposes a concept that is divided, so there must be a still higher one. That concept is the concept of an object in general, understood problematically, without any decision as to whether it is something or nothing. Since the categories are the only concepts that apply to objects in general, the work of distinguishing whether an object is something or nothing must follow the order and direction of the categories.

1. Opposed to the categories of quantity, which are the concepts of *all*, *many*, and *one*, is the concept that cancels all of them: the concept of *none*. Accordingly, the object of a concept to which no corresponding intuition can be found is equal to nothing. It is a concept without an object (*ens rationis*, a "being of reason"). Noumena are of this kind. They cannot be counted among the possibilities of the real world, yet they must not for that reason be declared impossible. Certain hypothetical new fundamental forces in matter are another example. We can think of their existence without contradiction, but since experience offers no instance of them, we must not regard them as possible.

2. Reality is something; negation is nothing. Negation is the concept of the absence of an object, as cold is the absence of heat and a shadow the absence of light (*nihil privativum*, a "nothing of privation").

3. The mere form of intuition, taken without any content, is not in itself an object. It is only the formal condition of an object as a phenomenon, as pure space and pure time are. As forms of intuition these are certainly something, but they are not themselves objects that are intuited (*ens imaginarium*, a "being of the imagination").

4. The object of a self-contradictory concept is nothing, because the concept itself is nothing. It is impossible, like a plane figure enclosed by only two straight lines (*nihil negativum*, a "negative nothing").

The table of this division of the concept of nothing must therefore be arranged as follows. The corresponding division of the concept of something needs no separate description.

**NOTHING, AS**

1. Empty concept without an object, *ens rationis*
2. Empty object of a concept, *nihil privativum*
3. Empty intuition without an object, *ens imaginarium*
4. Empty object without a concept, *nihil negativum*

The *ens rationis* differs from the *nihil negativum*, or pure nothing, in an important respect. The first must not be counted among possibilities because it is a mere fiction, though not a self-contradictory one. The second is wholly opposed to all possibility, because its concept cancels itself. Both, however, are empty concepts. The *nihil privativum* and the *ens imaginarium*, by contrast, are empty data for concepts. If light were not given to the senses, we could not represent darkness to ourselves, and if we did not perceive extended objects, we could not represent space. Without something real, neither a negation nor the mere form of intuition can be an object.

## Transcendental Dialectic: Introduction

### I. On Transcendental Illusion

We have called dialectic in general a logic of illusion. This does not mean a theory of probability. Probability is truth, though truth known on insufficient grounds. The knowledge it gives is incomplete but not therefore deceptive, and so it must not be separated from the analytic part of logic. Still less should appearance, in the sense of phenomenon, be confused with illusion. Truth and illusion do not reside in the object insofar as it is intuited. They reside in our judgment about the object insofar as it is thought. It is therefore quite correct to say that the senses do not err, not because they always judge correctly but because they do not judge at all. Truth and error, and with them illusion as the cause of error, are found only in judgment, that is, in the relation of an object to our understanding. In knowledge that fully agrees with the laws of the understanding, there can be no error. Nor is there error in a representation of the senses, since it contains no judgment. And no power of nature can of its own accord deviate from its own laws. Hence neither the understanding by itself, free of the influence of any other cause, nor the senses by themselves would fall into error. The understanding could not, because if it acts only according to its own laws, its effect, the judgment, must necessarily agree with those laws, and agreement with the laws of the understanding is what constitutes the formal element in all truth. The senses could not, because in them there is no judgment at all, neither true nor false. We have no source of knowledge besides these two, so it follows that error arises solely from the unnoticed influence of sensibility on the understanding. Through this influence the subjective grounds of a judgment merge with the objective ones, become confused with them, and turn the judgment from its proper course. A moving body would of itself continue in a straight line, but if another force pushes it in a different direction, it veers into a curved path. To separate the understanding's own activity from the force that mingles with it, we must therefore treat an erroneous judgment the way physics treats the combined effect of two forces: as the diagonal between two forces that pull the judgment in two different directions and enclose, as it were, an angle between them. We must then resolve this compound operation into the simple operations of the understanding and of sensibility. In pure *a priori* judgments this is done through transcendental reflection, which, as has already been shown, assigns each representation its place in the corresponding faculty of knowledge and so makes visible the influence of one faculty upon the other.

Sensibility is the source of genuine knowledge when it is subordinated to the understanding as the object on which the understanding exercises its functions. But insofar as sensibility influences the activity of the understanding itself and moves it to judge, sensibility is the cause of error.

We are not concerned here with empirical illusion, such as optical illusion. Empirical illusion arises when otherwise correct rules of the understanding are applied empirically and the judgment is led astray by the influence of the imagination. Our subject is transcendental illusion, which affects principles that are never even applied to experience. If they were, we would have a sure test of their correctness. Instead, transcendental illusion draws us, in defiance of every warning of criticism, entirely beyond the empirical use of the categories, and it deludes us with the fantasy of extending the domain of the pure understanding. We will call principles whose application is confined wholly within the limits of possible experience *immanent*. Those that cross these limits we will call *transcendent*. By transcendent principles, however, I do not mean the transcendental use, or misuse, of the categories. That is merely an error of judgment when judgment is not properly restrained by criticism and fails to attend to the limits of the territory in which the pure understanding may operate. I mean actual principles that urge us to tear down all these boundaries and to lay claim to an entirely new field of knowledge that recognizes no frontier. *Transcendental* and *transcendent* are therefore not the same thing. The principles of pure understanding that we set out earlier ought to have only an empirical use, not a transcendental one, which means they do not apply to any object beyond the realm of experience. A principle that removes these limits, and even entitles us to cross them, is called transcendent. If our critique succeeds in exposing the illusion in these supposed principles, then the principles whose use is confined to experience may be called, in contrast, the immanent principles of the pure understanding.

Logical illusion consists merely in imitating the form of reason, as in sophistical syllogisms, and it arises entirely from a lack of attention to logical rules. As soon as attention is directed to the case at hand, the illusion vanishes completely. Transcendental illusion, by contrast, persists even after it has been exposed and transcendental criticism has clearly revealed its emptiness. Consider the illusion in the proposition "The world must have a beginning in time." Its source is this. Our reason, considered subjectively as a faculty of human knowledge, contains fundamental rules and maxims for its own exercise, and these look in every respect like objective principles. As a result, the subjective necessity of connecting our concepts in a certain way is taken for an objective necessity in the determination of things in themselves. This illusion cannot be avoided. In the same way we cannot help seeing the sea as higher in the distance than near the shore, because the light from the distant water reaches the eye along a higher line of sight than the light from the near water. A still stronger case is the astronomer, who cannot keep himself from seeing the moon as larger when it rises than some time afterward, even though he is not deceived by the illusion.

Transcendental dialectic will therefore be content to expose the illusion in transcendental judgments and to guard us against it. It is entirely beyond its power to make the illusion disappear altogether and cease to be illusion, as can be done with logical illusion. Here we are dealing with a natural and unavoidable illusion, one that rests on subjective principles and passes them off on us as objective. Logical dialectic, in detecting sophisms, deals only with an error in the logical sequence of propositions, or with an illusion artificially constructed in imitation of the natural one. There is, then, a natural and unavoidable dialectic of pure reason. It is not the dialectic in which a bungler entangles himself through lack of knowledge, nor the one a sophist contrives in order to mislead. It is inseparable from human reason itself, and even after its illusions have been exposed, it never stops deceiving. It continually draws reason into momentary errors that must be continually corrected.

### II. On Pure Reason as the Seat of Transcendental Illusion

#### A. On Reason in General

All our knowledge begins with the senses, proceeds from there to the understanding, and ends with reason. Beyond reason the human mind has no higher faculty for working up the material of intuition and bringing it under the highest unity of thought. At this point in our inquiry I am obliged to explain this highest faculty of knowledge, and I confess that I find myself in some difficulty. Reason, like the understanding, has a merely formal or logical use, in which it abstracts from all the content of knowledge. But it also has a real use, because it contains within itself the source of certain concepts and principles that it borrows neither from the senses nor from the understanding. Logicians have long defined reason in its formal use as the faculty of mediate inference, as opposed to immediate inferences (*consequentiae immediatae*). This definition tells us nothing about reason in its real use, the reason that itself generates concepts. Since a division of reason into a logical and a transcendental faculty presents itself here, we must look for a higher concept of this source of knowledge, one that embraces both. Following the analogy with the concepts of the understanding, we may expect the logical concept to give us the key to the transcendental one, and the table of the functions of the former to give us the clue to the concepts of reason.

In the first part of our transcendental logic, we defined the understanding as the faculty of rules. Reason may be distinguished from it as the faculty of principles.

The term *principle* is ambiguous. Ordinarily it means merely a piece of knowledge that can be used as a principle, even though in itself, and with respect to its actual origin, it has no claim to the title. Every general proposition, even one drawn from experience by induction, can stand as the major premise in a syllogism, but that does not make it a principle. Mathematical axioms, such as the axiom that only one straight line can be drawn between two points, are general *a priori* knowledge, and so they are rightly called principles relative to the cases that can be subsumed under them. Yet I cannot say on that account that I know this property of straight lines from principles. I know it only in pure intuition.

Knowledge from principles, then, is knowledge in which I grasp the particular in the universal through concepts. Every syllogism is accordingly a form of deriving knowledge from a principle, because the major premise always supplies a concept through which everything subsumed under its condition is known according to a principle. Since any general knowledge can be used as the major premise of a syllogism, and since the understanding provides us with such general *a priori* propositions, these propositions may be called principles with respect to their possible use.

If we consider these principles of the pure understanding with respect to their origin, however, we find them to be anything but knowledge from concepts. They would not even be possible *a priori* unless we could rely on the help of pure intuition, as in mathematics, or on the conditions of a possible experience. That everything that happens has a cause cannot be inferred from the general concept of what happens. On the contrary, the principle of causality shows us how to obtain from what happens a determinate empirical concept.

The understanding cannot supply synthetic knowledge from concepts, and only such knowledge deserves to be called principles. All general propositions, however, may be called comparative principles.

There is a long-cherished wish, which may one day, who knows how far in the future, be happily fulfilled: that the principles underlying the endless variety of civil laws might be investigated and brought to light, since only in this way could we discover the secret of simplifying legislation. But in this case, laws are nothing more than limitations placed on our freedom under conditions in which it agrees completely with itself. Their object is therefore something entirely of our own making, something of which we ourselves can be the cause through these very concepts. How objects as things in themselves, how the nature of things, can be subject to principles and determined according to concepts is a question that seems almost impossible to answer. However that may be, and this is a matter still to be investigated, what we have said makes at least one thing clear. Knowledge from principles is something very different from knowledge through the understanding. Knowledge through the understanding may indeed precede other knowledge in the form of a principle, but in itself, insofar as it is synthetic, it neither rests on mere thought nor contains a general proposition drawn from concepts alone.

The understanding may be a faculty for producing the unity of appearances by means of rules. Reason is a faculty for producing the unity of the understanding's rules under principles. Reason therefore never applies directly to experience or to any object of the senses. Its object is the understanding, to whose manifold knowledge it gives an *a priori* unity through concepts. This unity may be called the unity of reason, and it is of a very different nature from the unity that the understanding produces.

This is the general concept of the faculty of reason, as far as it could be made intelligible without examples. Examples will be given later.

#### B. On the Logical Use of Reason

We commonly distinguish between what is known immediately and what is inferred. That a figure bounded by three straight lines has three angles is known immediately; that these angles together equal two right angles is an inference. We employ this kind of thinking constantly and have grown so accustomed to it that we no longer notice the distinction. As with the so-called deceptions of the senses, we take as immediately perceived what has in fact been inferred. Every piece of reasoning, or syllogism, contains a fundamental proposition, then a second proposition drawn from it, and finally the conclusion, which connects the truth of the first with the truth of the second, and does so infallibly. If the judgment inferred is so contained in the first proposition that it can be derived without the mediation of a third concept, the inference is called immediate (*consequentia immediata*). I prefer to call it an inference of the understanding. But if, in addition to the fundamental knowledge, a second judgment is required to produce the conclusion, it is called an inference of reason. The proposition "All men are mortal" contains the propositions "Some men are mortal" and "Nothing that is not mortal is a man," and these are therefore immediate inferences from the first. The proposition "All the learned are mortal," by contrast, is not contained in the original proposition, since the concept of a learned person does not appear in it. It can be derived from that proposition only by means of a mediating judgment.

In every syllogism I first think a rule, the major premise, through the understanding. Next, through the power of judgment, I subsume a cognition under the condition of the rule; this is the minor premise. Finally, I determine my cognition through the predicate of the rule; this is the conclusion, and in this step I determine it *a priori* through reason. The relations that the major premise, as the rule, represents between a cognition and its condition therefore constitute the different kinds of syllogism. There are exactly three, corresponding to the three ways in which all judgments differ in expressing the relation of a cognition in the understanding: categorical, hypothetical, and disjunctive.

Often the conclusion is a judgment that may follow from other given judgments, through which an entirely different object is thought. In that case I try to find out in the understanding whether the assertion in this conclusion stands under certain conditions according to a general rule. If I find such a condition, and if the object of the conclusion can be subsumed under it, then the conclusion follows from a rule that also holds for other objects of knowledge. We see from this that reason strives to bring the great variety of the understanding's cognitions under the smallest possible number of principles, or general conditions, and so to achieve the highest unity among them.

#### C. On the Pure Use of Reason

Can reason be isolated? If so, is it then a distinctive source of concepts and judgments that arise from it alone and through which it can be applied to objects? Or is it merely a subordinate faculty whose task is to give a certain form to cognitions already given? That form is called logical, and through it the understanding's cognitions are ordered under one another, and lower rules under higher ones, namely those whose condition includes within its scope the conditions of the others, so far as this can be done by comparison. This is the question we must now answer.

Reason demands unity of principles amid the manifold variety of rules, in order to bring the understanding into complete agreement with itself, just as the understanding brings the manifold content of intuition under concepts and so gives it connection. But this principle prescribes no law to objects. It contains no ground of the possibility of knowing or determining them as such, and is merely a subjective law for the orderly arrangement of what the understanding contains. Its purpose is to compare the concepts of the understanding and reduce them to the smallest possible number. It does not, however, entitle us to demand from objects themselves a uniformity that would suit the convenience of the understanding and enlarge its domain, nor to expect that the law itself will thereby acquire objective validity from those objects. In a word, the question is this: Does reason in itself, does pure reason, contain *a priori* synthetic principles and rules, and what are those principles?

The formal, logical procedure of reason in syllogisms tells us enough about the ground on which the transcendental principle of reason, in its pure synthetic knowledge, will rest.

1. Reason, as we observe it in syllogistic reasoning, does not apply to intuitions in order to bring them under rules, which is the business of the understanding with its categories. It applies to concepts and judgments. If pure reason does refer to objects and to the intuition of them, it does so not immediately but indirectly, through the understanding and its judgments, which relate directly to the senses and their intuition in order to determine their objects. The unity of reason is therefore not the unity of a possible experience. It is essentially different from that unity, which belongs to the understanding. That everything that happens has a cause is not a principle known and prescribed by reason. This principle makes the unity of experience possible and borrows nothing from reason, which, without reference to possible experience, could never have produced such a synthetic unity from mere concepts.

2. Reason in its logical use seeks the general condition of its judgment, the conclusion, and a syllogism is itself nothing but a judgment made by subsuming its condition under a general rule, the major premise. This rule can in turn be subjected to the same procedure of reason, so that the condition of the condition is sought through a prosyllogism, a prior syllogism whose conclusion supplies the premise of the next, for as long as the process can be continued. It is therefore plain that the distinctive principle of reason in its logical use is to find, for the conditioned knowledge of the understanding, the unconditioned that completes its unity.

But this logical maxim cannot become a principle of pure reason unless we assume something further: that if the conditioned is given, then the whole series of conditions subordinated one to another is also given, that is, contained in the object and its connections. This series is consequently itself unconditioned.

Such a principle of pure reason, however, is clearly synthetic. Analytically, the conditioned certainly refers to some condition, but not to the unconditioned. From this principle, moreover, there must arise various synthetic propositions of which the pure understanding knows nothing, since it deals only with objects of possible experience, whose cognition and synthesis are always conditioned. The unconditioned, if it really exists, must be considered specifically with regard to the determinations that distinguish it from everything conditioned, and it will thus supply material for many *a priori* synthetic propositions.

The principles that follow from this highest principle of pure reason will, however, be transcendent with respect to phenomena: no adequate empirical use can ever be made of them. This sets the principle entirely apart from all the principles of the understanding, whose use is wholly immanent, since their only object and purpose is the possibility of experience. Our task in the transcendental dialectic, then, is as follows. We must discover whether the principle that the series of conditions (in the synthesis of phenomena, or of thought in general) extends all the way to the unconditioned is objectively true or not, and what consequences follow from it for the empirical use of the understanding. More precisely, we must discover whether any such objectively valid proposition of reason exists at all, or whether we have instead a merely logical precept. Such a precept would direct us to keep ascending to ever higher conditions, to approach completeness in their series, and so to bring the highest possible unity of reason into our knowledge. We must determine, I say, whether this demand of reason has been mistaken for a transcendental principle of pure reason, one that postulates a thoroughgoing completeness in the series of conditions within objects themselves. We must also expose the misconceptions and illusions that creep into syllogisms that reason from experience upward to its conditions and whose major premise pure reason has supplied. That premise is perhaps closer to a *petitio*, a begging of the question, than to a legitimate postulate. Solving these problems is the business of transcendental dialectic, which we now propose to lay bare down to its source, buried deep in human reason. We will divide it into two parts: the first will treat the transcendent concepts of pure reason, the second, transcendent and dialectical syllogisms.

## Transcendental Dialectic, Book I: Of the Concepts of Pure Reason

The concepts of pure reason are obtained not by reflection but by inference. (We are not speaking here of whether such concepts are possible.) The concepts of the understanding are also thought a priori, prior to experience, and they make experience possible. But they contain nothing more than the unity of reflection upon phenomena, insofar as those phenomena must necessarily belong to a possible empirical consciousness. Through them alone are cognition and the determination of an object possible. They are therefore what first supplies us with material for reasoning, and prior to them we possess no a priori concepts of objects from which they could be deduced. At the same time, the sole basis of their objective reality is this: because they contain the intellectual form of all experience, they are necessarily confined in their application and influence to the sphere of experience.

The very term "concept of reason," or "rational concept," already signals that such a concept does not stay within the limits of experience. Its subject matter is a cognition of which every empirical cognition is only a part. Indeed, the whole of possible experience may itself be only a part of it. No actual experience ever fully reaches this cognition, even though every experience belongs to it. Rational concepts aim at comprehension, just as the concepts of the understanding aim at understanding perceptions. If they contain the unconditioned, they refer to that to which all experience is subordinate but which is never itself an object of experience. Reason strives toward it in all its inferences from experience and measures the degree of their empirical use against it, yet it never enters as an element into any empirical synthesis. If such concepts nonetheless possess objective validity, they may be called *conceptus ratiocinati*, concepts that have been legitimately inferred. Where they lack it, they have been admitted only because they appear to have been correctly inferred, and they may be called *conceptus ratiocinantes*, sophistical concepts. Since this can be adequately demonstrated only in the part of our treatise that deals with the dialectical inferences of reason, we will set it aside here. Just as we called the pure concepts of the understanding categories, we will now give the concepts of pure reason a new name and call them transcendental ideas. These terms, however, we must first explain and justify.

### Section I—Of Ideas in General

Despite the great wealth of words in the European languages, a thinker often finds himself at a loss for an expression that fits his concept exactly, and without one he can make himself understood neither to others nor to himself. Coining new words amounts to claiming the right to legislate for a language, and that claim rarely succeeds. Before resorting to so desperate a measure, it is wise to search the dead and learned languages, in the hope, and with some likelihood, of finding there an adequate expression for the notion we have in mind. The original meaning of such a word may have grown somewhat uncertain through the carelessness of those who used it, and it may even be doubtful whether the word was formerly used in exactly this sense. Even so, it is always better to hold fast to its proper meaning and confirm it than to waste our labor by failing to take the care needed to make ourselves understood.

Suppose, then, that only a single word exists to express a certain concept, that the word in its ordinary sense fits the concept perfectly, and that it matters greatly to distinguish this concept precisely from related ones. In that case we should not use the word carelessly, nor treat it as a synonym for kindred words for the sake of variety and elegance of style. Our duty, on the contrary, is to guard its distinctive meaning carefully. Otherwise, once the reader's attention is no longer drawn to the term in particular, and it disappears among a crowd of words of very different meaning, the thought it conveyed, which it alone conveyed, disappears with it.

Plato used the word *idea* in a way that plainly shows he meant something never derived from the senses. It went far beyond even the concepts of the understanding with which Aristotle concerned himself, since nothing in experience could ever be found that perfectly corresponds to it. For Plato, ideas are the archetypes of things themselves, and not merely keys to possible experiences, as the categories are. In his view they flow from the highest reason, which imparted them to human reason. But human reason no longer exists in its original state, and it must labor to recall the old ideas, now sadly obscured, through reminiscence, which is what we call philosophy. I will not undertake here any scholarly investigation into the sense this sublime philosopher attached to the term. I will only remark that it is nothing unusual, in ordinary conversation as well as in written works, to understand an author better than he understood himself by comparing the thoughts he has expressed on a subject. He may not have defined his concept sufficiently, and so at times have spoken, and even thought, against his own meaning.

Plato saw very clearly that our faculty of cognition feels itself called to something far higher than merely spelling out phenomena according to synthetic unity, deciphering them letter by letter so that they can be read as experience. He saw that our reason naturally rises to cognitions far too exalted for any object given in experience ever to correspond to them. These cognitions are nonetheless real, and not mere figments of the brain.

Plato found his ideas above all in the practical sphere, that is, in whatever rests on freedom, which in turn belongs among the cognitions that are the distinctive product of reason. He did, admittedly, extend his concept to speculative cognitions as well, provided they were given purely and completely a priori, and even to mathematics, although that science can have no object anywhere except in possible experience. In this I cannot follow him, any more than I can follow his mystical deduction of these ideas or his hypostatization of them, his treatment of them as self-subsisting realities. Still, the lofty and exaggerated language in which he described them is quite open to a more restrained interpretation, one more in keeping with fact and with the nature of things. Anyone who tried to derive the concept of virtue from experience would turn virtue into a nonentity, shifting with time and circumstance and utterly unfit to be used as a rule. Many have in fact tried, taking what can at best be an imperfect illustration and treating it as the model from which a perfectly adequate idea is to be formed. Everyone knows, on the contrary, that when someone is held up to him as a model of virtue, he compares this so-called model with the true original he carries in his own mind and judges the person by that standard. That standard is the idea of virtue. Every possible object of experience may indeed be useful as an example of it, as proof that what the concept of virtue demands can be achieved to some degree, but never as its archetype. That human actions will never fully accord with everything the pure ideas of reason require does not prove the thought chimerical. For only through this idea are any judgments of moral merit or demerit possible. It therefore lies at the foundation of every approach to moral perfection, however far we may be kept from that perfection by the obstacles in human nature, whose extent cannot be determined.

Plato's *Republic* has become proverbial as a striking example of imaginary perfection, the kind that can exist only in the head of an idle thinker. The historian of philosophy Brucker ridicules Plato for maintaining that a prince can never govern well unless he partakes of the ideas. But we would do better to pursue this thought further and, where this admirable thinker leaves us without help, make fresh efforts to bring it into clearer light. That is wiser than tossing it carelessly aside as useless on the wretched and harmful pretext that it is impracticable. Consider a constitution that secures the greatest possible human freedom according to laws, laws by which each person's freedom can coexist with the freedom of all others. (I say freedom, not the greatest possible happiness, for happiness follows of itself from freedom.) Such a constitution is, at the very least, a necessary idea. It must lie at the foundation not only of the first draft of a state's constitution but of all its laws. In framing it, we need not at the outset take account of the obstacles in our path. Those obstacles perhaps do not arise inevitably from human nature but rather from the neglect of true ideas in legislation up to now. Nothing is more harmful, or more unworthy of a philosopher, than the vulgar appeal to supposedly contrary experience. That experience would never have existed had those institutions been established at the right time and in accordance with ideas. Instead, crude concepts, crude precisely because they were drawn from experience, have spoiled and defeated all our better intentions. The more closely legislation and government accord with this idea, the rarer punishments become; so it is quite reasonable to maintain, as Plato did, that in a perfect state no punishments would be needed at all. A perfect state may never exist. Yet the idea is no less sound for that, since it holds up this maximum as the archetype of a constitution in order to bring legal government ever closer to the greatest possible perfection. No one can or should determine at what precise point human nature must halt in its progress, or how wide the gap between the idea and its realization must necessarily remain. The reason is that it is the very vocation of freedom to pass beyond every limit assigned to it.

But Plato saw ideas at work not only where human reason acts as a genuine cause and ideas are operative causes of actions and their objects, that is, in ethics. In nature itself he saw clear proof that things originate from ideas. A plant, an animal, the regular order of nature, and probably the arrangement of the entire universe plainly show that they are possible only through and in accordance with ideas. No single creature, under the particular conditions of its existence, perfectly matches the idea of the most perfect member of its kind. Neither does a human being match the idea of humanity, though he carries that idea in his soul as the archetypal standard for his actions. Yet these ideas are, in the highest sense, individually, unchangeably, and completely determined, and they are the original causes of things. Only the whole of connected objects in the universe is fully adequate to that idea. Setting aside the exaggerations in this philosopher's way of expressing himself, his ascent shows great intellectual power. He rose from the ectypal view of the physical world, which regards things as mere copies, to its architectonic connection according to ends, that is, according to ideas. That effort deserves imitation and commands respect. But in the principles of ethics, legislation, and religion, Plato earned a merit entirely his own. In these spheres ideas alone make experience possible, even though they never find complete expression in it. His merit goes unrecognized only because it is judged by the very empirical rules whose validity as principles the ideas themselves overturn. With regard to nature, experience supplies us with rules and is the source of truth. With regard to moral laws, however, experience is the mother of illusion, and it is in the highest degree reprehensible to limit the laws that dictate what I ought to do by what is actually done, or to derive them from it.

We must, however, set aside these important subjects, whose development is in truth the proper duty and dignity of philosophy. For now we will confine ourselves to a humbler but no less useful task: laying a firm foundation for those majestic structures of moral science. Until now that foundation has been unstable, undermined by the many tunnels that reason, in its confident but fruitless hunt for buried treasure, has dug in every direction. Our present task is to become thoroughly acquainted with the transcendental use of pure reason, with its principles and its ideas, so that we can properly determine and assess its influence and its true worth. Before closing these introductory remarks, I have a request for those who genuinely care about philosophy, and they are few. If they find themselves persuaded by what follows as well as by what has already been said, I ask them to work to preserve the original meaning of the word *idea*. It must not be lost among the other terms by which every kind of representation is loosely designated, lest science suffer for it. We have no shortage of words to name each mode of representation properly without trespassing on terms that belong to others. Here is a graded list of them. The genus is representation in general (*representatio*). Under it stands representation with consciousness (*perceptio*). A perception that refers solely to the subject, as a modification of its state, is a sensation (*sensatio*); an objective perception is a cognition (*cognitio*). A cognition is either an intuition or a concept (*intuitus vel conceptus*). An intuition relates immediately to its object and is singular and individual. A concept relates to its object only mediately, by means of a characteristic mark that several things may share. A concept is either empirical or pure. A pure concept that originates in the understanding alone, and not in a pure image of sensibility, is called a notion (*notio*). A concept formed from notions that goes beyond the possibility of experience is an idea, or concept of reason. To anyone accustomed to these distinctions, it must be intolerable to hear the representation of the color red called an idea. It should not even be called a notion, or concept of the understanding.

### Section II—Of Transcendental Ideas

Transcendental analytic showed us how the mere logical form of our cognition can contain the origin of pure a priori concepts. These concepts represent objects prior to all experience. More exactly, they indicate the synthetic unity that alone makes an empirical cognition of objects possible. The form of judgments, converted into a concept of the synthesis of intuitions, produced the categories, which direct the use of the understanding in experience. This entitles us to expect something parallel from the form of syllogisms. When applied to the synthetic unity of intuitions under the rule of the categories, it should likewise contain the origin of special a priori concepts. We may call these pure concepts of reason, or transcendental ideas, and they will determine, according to principles, the use of the understanding within the totality of experience.

The function of reason in inference consists in the universality of a cognition according to concepts. The syllogism itself is a judgment determined a priori across the whole extent of its condition. The proposition "Caius is mortal" could be drawn from experience by the understanding alone. But I want to find a concept that contains the condition under which the predicate of this judgment is given, in this case the concept of man. I subsume Caius under this condition, taken in its full extent ("all men are mortal"). Then I determine the cognition of my object accordingly and say: "Caius is mortal."

In the conclusion of a syllogism, then, we restrict a predicate to a particular object after first having thought it, in the major premise, in its whole extent under a certain condition. This complete quantity of extent in relation to such a condition is called universality (*universalitas*). To it corresponds totality (*universitas*) of conditions in the synthesis of intuitions. The transcendental concept of reason is therefore nothing other than the concept of the totality of conditions for a given conditioned. Only the unconditioned makes a totality of conditions possible, and conversely, the totality of conditions is itself always unconditioned. A pure concept of reason in general can therefore be defined through the concept of the unconditioned, insofar as that concept contains a ground for the synthesis of the conditioned.

The number of pure concepts of reason will correspond to the number of kinds of relation that the understanding thinks through the categories. We must therefore look for three things. First, we must find an unconditioned of the categorical synthesis in a subject. Second, we must find an unconditioned of the hypothetical synthesis of the members of a series. Third, we must find an unconditioned of the disjunctive synthesis of the parts in a system.

There are exactly as many kinds of syllogism. Each advances toward the unconditioned through prosyllogisms, chains of prior syllogisms in which each supplies a premise for the next. One advances toward the subject that can never itself be a predicate. Another advances toward the presupposition that presupposes nothing further. The third advances toward an aggregate of the members of the complete division of a concept. The pure concepts of reason, which aim at totality in the synthesis of conditions, therefore have a necessary foundation in the nature of human reason, at least as ways of raising the unity of the understanding to the unconditioned. They may have no valid application *in concreto* that corresponds to their transcendental use. In that case their only use would be to direct the understanding to extend its operations as far as possible while keeping them entirely consistent and harmonious.

In speaking here of the totality of conditions and of the unconditioned as the common heading for all concepts of reason, we again come upon a term we cannot do without. Yet long misuse has made it ambiguous, and so we cannot use it safely. The word *absolute* is one of the few words that, in its original meaning, was perfectly fitted to the concept it was meant to convey. No other word in the same language suits that concept exactly. To lose the word, or, what amounts to the same thing, to use it carelessly and loosely, must therefore mean losing the concept itself. And because this concept occupies reason a great deal, its loss would do serious harm to all of transcendental philosophy. The word *absolute* is now often used to indicate that something holds of a thing considered in itself, intrinsically. In this sense, "absolutely possible" would mean what is possible in itself (*interne*), which is in fact the least that can be said of an object. At other times the word is used to indicate that something holds in every respect, as in "absolute sovereignty." In this sense, "absolutely possible" would mean what is possible in all relations and in every respect, which is the most that can be said about a thing's possibility. These meanings do often coincide. What is intrinsically impossible, for instance, is also impossible in every relation, and so absolutely impossible. In most cases, however, they are worlds apart. I can by no means infer that because something is possible in itself it is also possible in every relation, and therefore absolutely. Indeed, I will show later that absolute necessity does not depend in any way on internal necessity, and so must not be treated as its synonym. If the opposite of something is intrinsically impossible, we may say that this opposite is impossible in every respect, and that the thing itself is therefore absolutely necessary. But I cannot reverse the inference and say that the opposite of what is absolutely necessary is intrinsically impossible, as if the absolute necessity of things were an internal necessity. In certain cases this internal necessity is an empty phrase to which not the slightest concept can be attached. The concept of a thing's necessity in all relations, by contrast, carries quite distinctive determinations. The loss of a concept so useful to speculative philosophy cannot be a matter of indifference to the philosopher. I trust, then, that the careful definition and preservation of the term on which that concept depends will not be a matter of indifference to him either.

It is in this broader sense, then, that I shall use the word *absolute*, in contrast to what is valid only in some particular respect. What is valid in a particular respect is restricted by conditions. What is absolute is valid without any restriction whatever.

Now the transcendental concept of reason has no object other than absolute totality in the synthesis of conditions, and it is not satisfied until it reaches what is unconditioned absolutely, that is, unconditioned in every respect and every relation. Pure reason leaves to the understanding everything that bears directly on objects of intuition, or more precisely on their synthesis in the imagination. Reason confines itself to the absolute totality in the use of the understanding's concepts, and seeks to carry the synthetic unity that is thought in the category all the way to the unconditioned. This unity may therefore be called the rational unity of phenomena, just as the unity expressed by the category may be called the unity of the understanding. Reason thus relates directly to the use of the understanding, though not insofar as the understanding contains the ground of possible experience, for the concept of the absolute totality of conditions cannot be applied in experience, since no experience is unconditioned. Reason relates to the understanding solely in order to direct it toward a certain unity of which the understanding itself has no concept, a unity whose aim is to gather all the acts of the understanding into an absolute whole. Hence the objective use of the pure concepts of reason is always transcendent, whereas the use of the pure concepts of the understanding must by its very nature always be immanent, since those concepts are confined to possible experience.

By an *idea* I mean a necessary concept of reason to which no corresponding object can be found in the world of the senses. The pure concepts of reason now under consideration are therefore transcendental ideas. They are concepts of pure reason, because they regard all empirical cognition as determined by an absolute totality of conditions. They are not arbitrary inventions but natural and necessary products of reason, and they consequently bear a necessary relation to the entire field in which the understanding is exercised. Finally, they are transcendent. They exceed the limits of all experience, so that no object perfectly adequate to a transcendental idea can ever appear within experience. When we call something an idea, we say a great deal about its object, which is an object of the pure understanding, but very little about its subject, that is, about its reality under the conditions of experience. An idea, being the concept of a maximum, can never be fully and adequately presented in concrete form. In the merely speculative use of reason, such full presentation is properly the only aim. And since, in that case, approaching a concept that is never actually reached amounts to the same thing as having no such concept at all, people commonly say of a concept of this kind, "It is only an idea." We might well say, then, "The absolute totality of all phenomena is only an idea," for since we can never form an adequate representation of it, it remains for us a problem without a solution.
