In the practical use of the understanding, by contrast, we are concerned only with action and conduct according to rules, and here an idea of pure reason can always be given actually and concretely, though only in part. Indeed, it is the indispensable condition of every practical use of reason. The carrying out of the idea is always limited and imperfect, yet its limits cannot be fixed in advance, and so it always remains under the influence of the concept of an absolute perfection. The practical idea is therefore always supremely fruitful, and with respect to actual conduct it is indispensably necessary. In the idea, pure reason even possesses causality, the power to bring into being what its concept contains. We cannot, then, say dismissively of wisdom, "It is only an idea." Precisely because wisdom is the idea of the necessary unity of all possible ends, it must stand as the original condition and rule for all practical effort, a rule that, if not constitutive, is at least limiting.

So although we must say of the transcendental concepts of reason that "they are only ideas," we should not therefore regard them as superfluous or empty. Even though no object can be determined by means of them, they can be of great use. Working unnoticed at the foundation of the structure of the understanding, they provide the canon, the governing standard, for its extended and internally consistent exercise. This canon does not allow the understanding to know more in an object than it could know through its own concepts, but it guides the understanding more securely in what it does come to know. Moreover, these ideas may make possible a transition from our concepts of nature and of the non-self to practical concepts, and in this way give even moral ideas a kind of footing and connection with the speculative knowledge of reason. The explanation of all this must be sought in what follows.

In keeping with our original plan, we set aside the practical ideas and turn to consider reason in its speculative use alone, and indeed within a narrower field still, its transcendental use. Here we must take the same path we followed in deducing the categories. We shall examine the logical form of reason's cognition in order to see whether reason may thereby become a source of concepts that allow us to regard objects in themselves as determined synthetically and a priori with respect to one or another of reason's functions.

Reason, considered as the faculty of a certain logical form of cognition, is the faculty of inference, that is, of mediate judgment. It works by subsuming the condition of a possible judgment under the condition of a given judgment. The given judgment is the general rule, the major premise. The subsumption of the condition of another possible judgment under the condition of the rule is the minor premise. The actual judgment, which asserts the rule as it applies to the subsumed case, is the conclusion. The rule states something universally under a certain condition. That condition is met in some particular case. It follows that whatever held universally under that condition must also be taken to hold in the particular case that satisfies it. Reason therefore reaches a cognition through acts of the understanding that form a series of conditions. Suppose I arrive at the proposition "All bodies are changeable." I begin with a more remote cognition, in which the concept of body does not appear but which nonetheless contains the condition of that concept: "Everything composite is changeable." I proceed from this to a less remote cognition that stands under the condition of the first: "Bodies are composite." From there I reach a third, which finally connects the remote cognition (changeable) with the one before me: "Therefore bodies are changeable." In doing so I have reached a cognition, the conclusion, through a series of conditions, the premises. Now any series whose exponent, the governing relation of its categorical or hypothetical judgment, is given can be continued. The same procedure of reason therefore leads us to the *ratiocinatio polysyllogistica*, a chain of syllogisms that can be extended indefinitely, either toward the conditions, by means of prosyllogisms (*per prosyllogismos*), or toward the conditioned, by means of episyllogisms (*per episyllogismos*).

We soon see, however, that the chain or series of prosyllogisms must stand in a very different relation to the faculty of reason than the opposite series does. The prosyllogisms are the cognitions deduced on the side of the grounds or conditions of a given cognition, forming the ascending series of syllogisms. The opposite, descending series is the one in which reason advances on the side of the conditioned by means of episyllogisms. In the ascending case, the cognition, the conclusion, is given only as conditioned. Reason can therefore arrive at it only on the assumption that all the members of the series on the side of the conditions are given, which is to say a totality in the series of premises, because only on that assumption is the judgment in question possible a priori. On the side of the conditioned, or of the inferences, by contrast, what is thought is only an incomplete series still in the process of becoming, not one presupposed or given as a whole. It is merely a potential progression. Hence when a cognition is regarded as conditioned, reason is compelled to treat the series of its conditions, in the ascending line, as complete and given in its totality. But if that same condition is also regarded as the condition of other cognitions, which together form a series of inferences or consequences in a descending line, reason can remain entirely indifferent as to how far this progression extends *a parte posteriori*, forward toward its consequences, and whether a totality of this series is even possible. Reason has no need of such a series in order to reach the conclusion before it, since that conclusion is already sufficiently secured and determined by its grounds *a parte priori*, from the side of what precedes it. On the side of the conditions, the series of premises may have a first or highest condition, or it may have none and so be unlimited *a parte priori*. In either case it must contain the totality of conditions, even granting that we might never succeed in grasping that totality completely. And the whole series must be unconditionally true if the conditioned, regarded as an inference drawn from it, is to be held true. This is a demand of reason, which proclaims its cognition to be determined a priori and necessary. That cognition is either necessary in itself, in which case it needs no grounds to rest on, or, if it is derived, necessary as a member of a series of grounds that is itself unconditionally true.

### Section III. System of Transcendental Ideas

We are not at present concerned with a logical dialectic, which abstracts entirely from the content of cognition and seeks only to expose the false appearance in the form of syllogisms. Our subject is transcendental dialectic. It must contain, entirely a priori, the origin of certain cognitions drawn from pure reason, and the origin of certain derived concepts whose object cannot be given empirically and which therefore lie beyond the reach of the faculty of understanding. In syllogisms as well as in judgments, the transcendental use of our cognition bears a natural relation to its logical use. From that relation we have seen that there are three kinds of dialectical argument, corresponding to the three forms of inference by which reason arrives at cognitions from principles. In all of them, reason's task is to ascend from the conditioned synthesis, beyond which the understanding never goes, to the unconditioned, which the understanding can never reach.

The most general relations our representations can have are, first, the relation to the subject, and second, the relation to objects, either as phenomena or as objects of thought in general. If we combine this subdivision with the main division, all the relations of our representations of which we can form either a concept or an idea are threefold: first, the relation to the subject; second, the relation to the manifold of the object as a phenomenon; and third, the relation to all things in general.

All pure concepts are concerned in general with the synthetic unity of representations. The concepts of pure reason, the transcendental ideas, are concerned instead with the unconditioned synthetic unity of all conditions. It follows that all transcendental ideas fall into three classes. The first contains the absolute, or unconditioned, unity of the thinking subject. The second contains the absolute unity of the series of conditions of a phenomenon. The third contains the absolute unity of the condition of all objects of thought in general.

The thinking subject is the subject matter of psychology. The sum of all phenomena, the world, is the subject matter of cosmology. And the thing that contains the highest condition of the possibility of everything that can be thought, the being of all beings, is the subject matter of all theology. Pure reason thus supplies the idea of a transcendental doctrine of the soul (*psychologia rationalis*), a transcendental science of the world (*cosmologia rationalis*), and finally a transcendental doctrine of God (*theologia transcendentalis*). The understanding cannot produce even the outline of any of these sciences. It cannot do so even when joined with the highest logical use of reason, that is, with every conceivable syllogism by which we might proceed from one object, or phenomenon, to all the others, out to the farthest limits of empirical synthesis. These sciences are, on the contrary, pure and genuine products, or problems, of pure reason.

Precisely which modes of the pure concepts of reason these transcendental ideas are will be set out fully in the next chapter. They follow the guiding thread of the categories, for pure reason never relates directly to objects, but only to the concepts of objects that the understanding contains. The detailed explanation of these ideas will also make clear three things. It will show how reason, simply through the synthetic use of the same function it employs in a categorical syllogism, necessarily arrives at the concept of the absolute unity of the thinking subject. It will show how the logical procedure of hypothetical syllogisms necessarily gives rise to the idea of the absolutely unconditioned in a series of given conditions. And it will show how the mere form of the disjunctive syllogism carries with it the highest concept of a being of all beings, a thought that at first sight seems extremely paradoxical.

An objective deduction of the kind we were able to give for the categories is impossible for these transcendental ideas. Being only ideas, they have in truth no relation to any object that could be given in experience. But a subjective deduction of them from the nature of our reason is possible, and that deduction has been given in the present chapter.

It is easy to see that pure reason aims solely at the absolute totality of synthesis on the side of the conditions, and is not concerned with absolute completeness on the side of the conditioned. Reason needs only the former, in order to presuppose the whole series of conditions and so present it to the understanding a priori. Once we have a condition that is given completely and unconditionally, no further concept of reason is needed to continue the series, for the understanding takes every step downward, from condition to conditioned, on its own. The transcendental ideas are therefore useful only for ascending through the series of conditions until we reach the unconditioned, that is, principles. In descending toward the conditioned, reason makes a wide-ranging logical use of the laws of the understanding, but a transcendental use of them is impossible. Suppose we form an idea of the absolute totality of such a descending synthesis, for example, of the entire series of all future changes in the world. That idea is a mere *ens rationis*, a creature of thought, an arbitrary invention, and not a necessary presupposition of reason. The possibility of the conditioned presupposes the totality of its conditions, but not the totality of its consequences. Such a concept, therefore, is not a transcendental idea, and transcendental ideas alone concern us here.

Finally, the transcendental ideas share a certain connection and unity, and through them pure reason gathers all its cognitions into a single system. The progression from knowledge of the self to knowledge of the world, and through these to the supreme being, is so natural that it seems to mirror reason's logical advance from premises to conclusion. Whether an analogy of the same kind as that between the logical and the transcendental procedure of reason lies hidden at the foundation of these ideas is another of those questions whose answer we must not expect until our inquiry is further advanced. In this brief, preliminary survey we have meanwhile achieved our aim. Philosophers have commonly mixed up the transcendental concepts of reason with other concepts in their systems and failed to distinguish them properly from the concepts of the understanding. We have cleared away the ambiguity that resulted. We have shown the origin of these concepts, and with it their definite number. We have presented them in systematic connection, and we have thereby marked out and enclosed a determinate domain for pure reason.

The science of metaphysics has, as the proper objects of its inquiry, only three great ideas: God, freedom, and immortality. It aims to show that the second of these concepts, joined with the first, must lead to the third as a necessary conclusion. Everything else with which metaphysics occupies itself is merely a means of reaching and realizing these ideas. It does not need them to construct a science of nature. It needs them, on the contrary, in order to pass beyond the sphere of nature. A complete insight into and understanding of these ideas would make theology, ethics, and, through the union of the two, religion dependent solely on the speculative faculty of reason. In a systematic presentation of these ideas, the order just described, which is synthetic, would be most fitting. In the investigation that must necessarily come first, however, the analytic order, which reverses it, is better suited to our purpose. That order lets us proceed from what experience presents to us directly, psychology, to cosmology, and from there to theology.

## Transcendental Dialectic, Book II: Of the Dialectical Procedure of Pure Reason

It may be said that the object of a merely transcendental idea is something of which we have no concept, even though the idea is a necessary product of reason according to its original laws. And in fact a concept of an object adequate to the idea that reason gives is impossible, because such an object would have to be capable of being presented and intuited in a possible experience. We would express ourselves better, and with less risk of being misunderstood, if we said that we can have no knowledge of an object that perfectly corresponds to an idea, although we may have a problematic concept of it, one that can be thought without contradiction even though we cannot establish that anything answers to it.

The transcendental, that is, subjective, reality of the pure concepts of reason rests at least on the fact that a necessary procedure of reason leads us to such ideas. There must therefore be syllogisms that contain no empirical premises. By means of them we infer, from something we do know, something else of which we have not even a concept, yet to which an unavoidable illusion leads us to ascribe objective reality. With respect to their result, such arguments deserve to be called sophisms rather than syllogisms. With respect to their origin, however, they are fully entitled to the name of syllogism, since they are neither fictions nor accidental products of reason but are necessitated by its very nature. They are sophisms not of human beings but of pure reason itself, and even the wisest person cannot free himself from them. After long effort he may learn to guard against the error, but he can never wholly rid himself of the illusion that continually mocks and misleads him.

There are three kinds of these dialectical arguments, corresponding to the number of ideas their conclusions present. In an argument of the first class, I infer from the transcendental concept of the subject, which contains nothing manifold, the absolute unity of this subject itself, a unity of which I cannot, by this route, obtain any concept at all. This dialectical argument I shall call the *transcendental paralogism*. The second class of sophistical argument concerns the transcendental concept of the absolute totality of the series of conditions for a given phenomenon. Here, because my concept of the unconditioned synthetic unity of the series on one side always turns out to be self-contradictory, I infer the truth of the opposite unity, of which I nevertheless have no concept. The condition of reason in these dialectical arguments I shall call the *antinomy of pure reason*. Finally, in the third kind of sophistical argument, I infer from the totality of conditions for thinking objects in general, insofar as they can be given, the absolute synthetic unity of all conditions of the possibility of things in general. That is, from things that I do not know through their merely transcendental concept, I infer a being of all beings. I know this being even less through a transcendental concept, and of its unconditioned necessity I can form no concept whatever. This dialectical argument I shall call the *ideal of pure reason*.

## Transcendental Dialectic, Book II, Chapter I: Of the Paralogisms of Pure Reason

A logical paralogism consists in the formal falsity of an argument, whatever its content may be. A transcendental paralogism, however, has a transcendental ground, and draws a false conclusion even though its form is correct and beyond reproach. In this way the paralogism is rooted in the nature of human reason itself, and gives rise to an illusion of the mind that is unavoidable, though not insoluble.

We come now to a concept that was not included in the general list of transcendental concepts, yet must be counted among them, without altering that table in the least or revealing any gap in it. This is the concept, or if one prefers, the judgment, "I think." This thought is, as it were, the vehicle of all concepts whatever, and therefore of transcendental concepts as well. For that reason it is regarded as a transcendental concept, although it has no special claim to that rank, since its only function is to indicate that all thought is accompanied by consciousness. Yet pure as this concept is of empirical content, of impressions of the senses, it allows us to distinguish two different kinds of objects. "I," as thinking, am an object of inner sense, and am called soul. What is an object of the outer senses is called body. The expression "I," as a thinking being, therefore designates the subject matter of psychology, which may be called "the rational doctrine of the soul." In this science I seek to know nothing about the soul except what can be inferred from the concept "I," insofar as it occurs in all thought, independently of all experience, since experience determines me only in concrete particulars.

The rational doctrine of the soul really is an undertaking of this kind. For if even the smallest empirical element of thought, if any particular perception of my inner state were admitted among the grounds of knowledge in this science, it would no longer be a rational doctrine of the soul but an empirical one. What lies before us, then, is a would-be science built on the single proposition "I think," and it is entirely proper, and in keeping with the nature of a transcendental philosophy, to examine here whether that foundation holds or gives way. It should not be objected that this proposition, which expresses a perception of oneself, asserts an inner experience, so that the rational doctrine of the soul founded on it is not pure but rests partly on an empirical principle. This inner perception is nothing more than bare apperception, the "I think" that makes all transcendental concepts possible in the first place, as when we say, "I think substance, cause," and so on. Inner experience in general and its possibility, or perception in general and its relation to other perceptions, cannot be counted as empirical knowledge unless some particular distinction or determination of it is given empirically. It is knowledge *of* the empirical, not empirical knowledge, and it belongs to the inquiry into the possibility of all experience, an inquiry that is unquestionably transcendental. Were even the slightest object of experience, such as a mere feeling of pleasure or pain, included in the general representation of self-consciousness, rational psychology would at once turn into empirical psychology.

"I think" is therefore the sole text of rational psychology, and from it the science must unfold its entire system. Plainly, when this thought is applied to an object, namely myself, it can contain nothing but transcendental predicates of that object, since even the smallest empirical predicate would destroy the purity of the science and its independence from all experience.

Here, however, we shall have to take the categories as our guide. But because what is first given in this case is a thing, the "I" as a thinking being, we shall not alter the order of the categories as it stands in the table. Instead we shall begin with the category of substance, through which a thing in itself is represented, and from there work backward through the series. The topic, or scheme of headings, of the rational doctrine of the soul, from which everything else it may contain must be derived, is accordingly as follows:

1. The soul is *substance*.
2. As regards its quality, it is *simple*.
3. As regards the different times in which it exists, it is numerically identical: that is, it is a *unity*, not a plurality.
4. It stands in relation to possible objects in space.

The reader who does not readily grasp the psychological sense of these expressions, taken here in their transcendental abstraction, and who cannot guess why the last of these attributes of the soul belongs to the category of existence, will find the terms adequately explained and justified in what follows. I must also apologize for having used Latin terms in place of their German equivalents, against the rules of good writing; I judged it better to sacrifice elegance to clarity.

All the concepts of pure psychology arise from these elements by combination alone, without the help of any other principle. This substance, taken merely as an object of inner sense, yields the concept of immateriality; as a simple substance, it yields the concept of incorruptibility; its identity, as an intellectual substance, yields the concept of personality; and all three together yield spirituality. Its relation to objects in space yields the concept of interaction (*commercium*) with bodies. In this way rational psychology represents thinking substance as the principle of life in matter, that is, as a soul (*anima*), and as the ground of animality; and animality, limited and determined by the concept of spirituality, yields the concept of immortality.

To these concepts correspond four paralogisms, or fallacious syllogisms, of a transcendental psychology that is falsely taken for a science of pure reason concerning the nature of our thinking being. Yet the only thing we can lay at the foundation of this science is the simple representation "I," which in itself is wholly empty of content. It cannot even be called a concept; it is merely a consciousness that accompanies all concepts. Through this "I," or "he," or "it" that thinks, nothing more is represented than a transcendental subject of thoughts, an x, which is known only through the thoughts that are its predicates, and of which, apart from them, we cannot form the slightest concept. We therefore turn in a perpetual circle, since we must always already make use of this "I" in order to judge anything about it. And we cannot rid ourselves of this inconvenience, because consciousness in itself is not so much a representation that singles out a particular object as a form of representation in general, insofar as such representation is to count as knowledge; for only in and through knowledge do I think anything at all.

At first sight it must seem strange that the condition under which I think, which is therefore a property of my own subject, should be held valid for everything else that thinks as well. It seems equally strange that we should presume to base on a seemingly empirical proposition a judgment that is apodictic, or necessarily certain, and universal: namely, that everything that thinks is constituted as the voice of my own consciousness declares it to be, that is, as a self-conscious being. The reason for this belief is that we necessarily ascribe to things a priori all the properties that make up the conditions under which alone we can think them. Now I cannot obtain the least representation of a thinking being through outer experience, but only through self-consciousness. Such objects, then, are nothing more than the transference of this consciousness of mine onto other things, which can be represented as thinking beings only in this way. In the present inquiry, the proposition "I think" is taken in a problematic sense. It is not taken insofar as it contains the perception of an existence, as in Descartes's "*Cogito, ergo sum*" ("I think, therefore I am"), but only with regard to its mere possibility, in order to discover what properties can be inferred from so simple a proposition and predicated of its subject.

If our pure rational knowledge of thinking beings rested on anything more than the bare *Cogito*, and if we could also draw on observations of the play of our thoughts and on the natural laws of the thinking self derived from them, the result would be an empirical psychology. This would be a kind of physiology of inner sense, and it might perhaps be able to explain the phenomena of that sense. But it could never reveal properties that lie beyond all possible experience, such as simplicity, nor could it make any apodictic pronouncement about the nature of thinking beings. It would not, therefore, be a rational psychology.

Now, since the proposition "I think," taken problematically, contains the form of every judgment whatever and accompanies all the categories, it is evident that conclusions drawn from it can rest only on a transcendental use of the understanding. Such a use excludes every empirical element, and, as has already been shown, we cannot form any favorable expectation of its procedure in advance. We shall therefore follow this proposition with a critical eye through all the predicaments, or basic categories, of pure psychology, though for the sake of brevity we shall let the examination run on in one unbroken sequence.

Before taking up this task, however, a general remark may sharpen our attention to this way of arguing. I do not know an object merely by thinking; I know it only by determining a given intuition with respect to the unity of consciousness in which all thinking consists. It follows that I know myself not by being conscious of myself as thinking, but only when I am conscious of the intuition of myself as determined with respect to the function of thought. All the modes of self-consciousness in thinking are therefore not concepts of objects, not concepts of the understanding or categories, but mere logical functions. They present no object to thought for it to know, and so they cannot present my self as an object either. The object is not the consciousness of the determining self, but only that of the determinable self: the consciousness of my inner intuition, insofar as the manifold it contains can be connected in accordance with the universal condition of the unity of apperception in thought.

1. In all judgments I am the determining subject of the relation that makes up the judgment. That the "I" which thinks must always count in thinking as a subject, as something that cannot be attached to thought as a mere predicate, is an apodictic proposition, and indeed an identical one that merely restates its own terms. But it does not mean that I, as an object, am for myself a self-subsistent being, or substance. That further claim is an ambitious one. It would need the support of data that are not to be found in thought, and perhaps, so long as I consider the thinking self purely as such, not to be found in the thinking self at all.

2. That the "I" of apperception, and hence the "I" in all thought, is singular, cannot be broken up into a plurality of subjects, and therefore designates a logically simple subject: all this follows directly from the very concept of an "I," and so is an analytic proposition. But this is not the same as declaring that the thinking "I" is a simple substance, which would be a synthetic proposition. The concept of substance always refers to intuitions, and in my case these can only be sensible; they therefore lie entirely outside the sphere of the understanding and its thinking. Yet the statement that the "I" is simple in thought belongs to that sphere alone. It would be remarkable indeed if the concept of substance were handed to me directly, as if by revelation, in the poorest of all representations, when in other cases it demands so much labor to separate it from the other elements offered by intuition, and still more trouble to determine whether it can be simple, as with the parts of matter.

3. The proposition that my self remains identical throughout all the manifold representations of which I am conscious is likewise contained in the concepts themselves, and is therefore analytic. But this identity of the subject, of which I am conscious in all its representations, does not concern the intuition of the subject through which it is given as an object. The proposition cannot, therefore, assert the identity of the person, by which is meant the consciousness that one's own substance, as a thinking being, remains identical through every change of circumstance. Proving that would require not a mere analysis of the proposition but synthetic judgments based on a given intuition.

4. I distinguish my own existence, as that of a thinking being, from that of other things outside me, among which I also count my body. This, too, is an analytic proposition, since other things are precisely those I think of as distinct from myself. But whether this consciousness of myself is possible at all without things outside me, and so whether I could exist merely as a thinking being without being a human being, cannot be known or inferred from this proposition.

Analyzing the consciousness of my self in thought has therefore gained us nothing toward knowledge of myself as an object. The logical exposition of thinking in general has been mistaken for a metaphysical determination of the object.

Our whole critique would be a needless undertaking if it were possible to prove a priori that all thinking beings are in themselves simple substances, that as such they possess personality as an inseparable attribute, and that they are conscious of their existence as separate from and unconnected with matter. In that case we would have stepped beyond the world of the senses and entered the realm of noumena, things as they are in themselves apart from how they appear to us. No one could then deny us the right to extend our knowledge in that realm, to settle there, and, under a favorable star, to claim possessions in it for ourselves. For the proposition "Every thinking being, as such, is a simple substance" is a synthetic a priori proposition. First, it goes beyond the concept that is its subject, adding to the mere notion of a thinking being the mode of that being's existence. Second, it attaches to that concept a predicate, simplicity, that could never have been discovered within experience. It would follow that synthetic a priori propositions are possible and legitimate not only, as we have maintained, in relation to objects of possible experience and as principles of the possibility of that experience, but also in application to things in themselves. That conclusion would put an end to this entire critique and force us back onto the old way of doing metaphysics. But on closer inspection the danger is not so great.

The procedure of rational psychology conceals a paralogism, which can be set out in the following syllogism:

That which cannot be thought otherwise than as subject does not exist otherwise than as subject, and is therefore substance.

A thinking being, considered merely as such, cannot be thought otherwise than as subject.

Therefore it also exists as such, that is, as substance.

The major premise speaks of a being that can be thought in general and in every respect, and hence as it might be given in intuition. The minor premise speaks of the same being only insofar as it regards itself as subject in relation to thought and the unity of consciousness, not in relation to the intuition through which it would be presented to thought as an object. The conclusion is therefore reached by a *sophisma figurae dictionis*, a fallacy of equivocation, in which a single term silently shifts its meaning between the premises.

"Thought" is taken in two entirely different senses in the two premises. In the major premise it is understood as relating and applying to objects in general, and therefore to objects of intuition as well. In the minor premise it is understood as relating only to self-consciousness. In this second sense we think no object at all, but merely the relation to the subject's self-consciousness, as the form of thought. The first premise speaks of things that cannot be thought otherwise than as subjects; the second speaks not of things but of thought, with all objects abstracted away, in which the "I" is always the subject of consciousness. Hence the conclusion cannot be "I cannot exist otherwise than as subject," but only "In thinking my existence, I can use my 'I' only as the subject of the judgment." That, however, is an identical proposition, and it sheds no light on the manner of my existence.

That this famous argument is a mere paralogism will be clear to anyone who considers the general remark preceding our account of the principles of pure understanding, together with the section on noumena. It was proved there that the concept of a thing that can exist by itself (*per se*), only as a subject and never as a predicate, has no objective reality. We can never know whether any object corresponds to it, so the concept remains merely a concept and yields no genuine knowledge. If this concept, under the name of substance, is to indicate an object that can be given, and so become knowledge, then a permanent intuition must lie at the basis of that knowledge as the indispensable condition of its objective reality, for only through intuition can an object be given. But in inner intuition there is nothing permanent, since the "I" is only the consciousness of my thinking. If, then, we appeal to thought alone, we cannot find the necessary condition for applying the concept of substance, that is, of a subject existing by itself, to the subject as a thinking being. With that, the concept of the simplicity of substance, which is bound up with the objective reality of this concept, is also shown to be invalid. It is in fact nothing more than the logical, qualitative unity of self-consciousness in thought, while we remain entirely ignorant whether the subject is composite or not.

### Refutation of Mendelssohn's Argument for the Substantiality or Permanence of the Soul

This acute philosopher readily saw the weakness of the usual argument, which tries to prove that the soul, granted that it is a simple being, cannot perish by dissolution, that is, by falling apart into components. He recognized that it might still cease to be through extinction, by simply vanishing. In his *Phaedo* he therefore set out to prove that the soul cannot be annihilated, by showing that a simple being cannot cease to exist. A simple being, he argued, cannot diminish. It cannot gradually lose portions of its being and so be reduced by degrees to nothing, for it has no parts and hence no multiplicity within it. There could therefore be no interval of time between the moment in which it exists and the moment in which it does not, and such an abrupt leap is impossible. But this philosopher failed to consider that even if we grant the soul this simple nature, containing no parts outside one another and therefore no extensive magnitude, we cannot deny it, any more than we can deny any other being, an intensive magnitude: a degree of reality with respect to all its faculties, and indeed to everything that makes up its existence. And this degree of reality can grow smaller and smaller through an infinite series of lesser degrees. It follows that this supposed substance, this thing whose permanence is not secured in any other way, might be turned into nothing, if not by decomposition, then by a gradual slackening (*remissio*) of its powers: by a kind of languishing away, or "elanguescence," if I may use the word. For consciousness itself always has a degree, and that degree can be lessened. Consequently the capacity for consciousness can diminish, and so can every other faculty. The permanence of the soul as an object of inner sense therefore remains unproven, and indeed cannot be proven. Its permanence during life is evident in itself, since the thinking being, as a human being, is at the same time an object of the outer senses to itself. But this does not entitle the rational psychologist to assert, from mere concepts, that it persists beyond life.

Clarity is not, as logicians maintain, simply consciousness of a representation. A certain degree of consciousness, though perhaps not enough for recollection, is found even in many obscure representations. Without any consciousness at all, we could not recognize any difference among the obscure representations we combine, as in fact we can with many concepts, such as those of right and justice, and as the musician does who strikes several notes at once while improvising. A representation is clear when our consciousness of it suffices for consciousness of how it differs from others. If we are conscious only that there is a difference, without being conscious of the difference itself, of what it actually is, the representation must be called obscure. There is, therefore, an infinite series of degrees of consciousness, reaching down to its complete disappearance.

Some people believe they have done enough to establish a new possibility for the way souls exist once they have shown that their hypotheses on the subject involve no contradiction. Such are those who assert that thought is possible after this life has ended, although their only knowledge of thought comes from its use in connecting empirical intuitions within our present human life. But they are easily embarrassed by counter-possibilities that rest on quite as good a foundation. One such is the possibility that a simple substance might divide into several substances, and, conversely, that several might merge into one simple substance. Although divisibility presupposes composition, it does not necessarily require a composition of substances; it requires only a composition of degrees, that is, of the various faculties of one and the same substance. Now we can conceive all the powers and faculties of the soul, even that of consciousness, as diminished by half while the substance still remains. In the same way we can imagine without contradiction that this lost half is preserved, not within the soul but outside it. Since in this case everything real in the soul that has a degree, and hence its entire existence, has been halved, we can suppose that a separate substance would arise out of the soul. For the multiplicity that has been divided existed before, though not as a multiplicity of substances but as a multiplicity of every reality making up the quantum of existence within the soul; and the unity of substance was only a mode of existence, which this division alone has turned into a plurality of subsistence. In the same way several simple substances might fuse into one, with nothing lost except their plurality of subsistence, since the one substance would contain the degree of reality of all the former ones. Perhaps, indeed, the simple substances that appear to us in the form of matter might produce other souls through such a dynamic division of the parent souls, regarded as intensive magnitudes, while the parent souls made good their loss with new matter of the same kind. This would happen not by any mechanical or chemical influence on one another, but by an unknown influence of which those processes would be only the outward appearance. I am far from attaching any value to such fantasies, and the principles of our Analytic have clearly established that no use of the categories other than an empirical one, of substance for example, is possible. But suppose the rationalist is bold enough to construct a self-subsistent being on the sole authority of the faculty of thought, without any intuition through which an object is given, merely because the unity of apperception in thought will not let him regard it as composite, when he ought instead to admit that he cannot explain how a thinking nature is possible. What, then, is to stop the materialist, with just as complete an independence from experience, from using the rationalist's own principle in exactly the opposite direction, while still preserving the formal unity his opponent demands?

If we now take the above propositions, which in the system of rational psychology must be accepted as valid for all thinking beings, in their synthetic connection, and proceed from the category of relation, with the proposition "All thinking beings are, as such, substances," backward through the series until the circle closes, we arrive at last at their existence. In this system of rational psychology, such substances are held to be conscious of this existence independently of external things; indeed, it is claimed that, with respect to the permanence that is a necessary characteristic of substance, they can determine external things by themselves. It follows that idealism, or at least problematic idealism, is entirely unavoidable in this rationalist system. And if the existence of external things is not held to be necessary for determining the existence of a substance in time, then the existence of those external things at all becomes a gratuitous assumption that can never be proved.

Suppose, however, that we proceed analytically. We would take the "I think" as a proposition that already contains an existence as given, so that modality becomes the guiding principle, and we would dissect this proposition to establish its content and to discover whether, and how, this I determines its existence in space and time without help from anything external. In that case the propositions of rational psychology would begin not with the concept of a thinking being but with a reality, and the properties of a thinking being in general would be deduced from the way this reality is thought once everything empirical had been stripped away. The following table shows the sequence:

1. I think,
2. as subject,
3. as simple subject,
4. as identical subject, in every state of my thought.

The second proposition does not settle whether I can exist and be thought only as a subject, and never also as the predicate of some other being. The concept of a subject is therefore taken here in a merely logical sense, and it remains undetermined whether it should be understood as substance or not. The third proposition is different. The absolute unity of apperception, the simple I in the representation to which all the connecting and separating that make up thought refers, is significant in its own right, even though it tells us nothing about the constitution or the subsistence of the subject. Apperception is something real, and its simplicity is already given in the very fact that it is possible. But nothing real in space is at the same time simple. Points, the only simple things in space, are merely limits of space, not parts out of which it is composed. It follows that materialism cannot account for the constitution of my I as a merely thinking subject. Yet in the first proposition my existence is treated as given. That proposition does not say, "Every thinking being exists," which would attribute absolute necessity to thinking beings. It says only, "I exist thinking." It is therefore entirely empirical, and it contains the determinability of my existence only in relation to my representations in time. To determine my existence in time, however, I need something permanent, and nothing permanent is given in inner intuition. So the mode of my existence, whether as a substance or as an accident, cannot be determined through this simple self-consciousness. If materialism fails to explain how I exist, spiritualism fails just as badly, and the conclusion is that we can gain no knowledge whatever of the soul's constitution so far as the possibility of its existing apart from external objects is concerned.

And how could it be possible to pass beyond the bounds of experience, beyond our existence in this life, with nothing but the unity of consciousness, which we know only because it is indispensable to the possibility of experience? How could we extend our knowledge to the nature of all thinking beings by means of the proposition "I think," a proposition that is empirical, yet wholly undetermined with respect to every kind of intuition?

There is, then, no rational psychology in the sense of a doctrine that adds anything to our knowledge of ourselves. It is only a discipline that sets impassable limits to speculative reason in this domain, preventing it on one side from throwing itself into the arms of a soulless materialism and on the other from losing itself in the maze of a groundless spiritualism. It teaches us to read reason's refusal to answer questions that reach beyond the limits of our human life as a signal to abandon fruitless speculation, and to turn our self-knowledge toward practical use. That knowledge, though it applies only to objects of experience, takes its principles from a higher source and governs its conduct as if our destiny reached far beyond the boundaries of experience and of life.

All this makes plain that rational psychology springs from a mere misunderstanding. The unity of consciousness that underlies the categories is mistaken for an intuition of the subject as an object, and the category of substance is then applied to it. But this unity is only the unity of thought, through which no object is given, and so the category of substance, which always presupposes a given intuition, cannot be applied to it. Consequently the subject cannot be known. The subject of the categories cannot form a concept of itself as an object of the categories precisely because it is what thinks them. To think them at all, it must presuppose its own pure self-consciousness, which is the very thing it hoped to explain and describe. In the same way, the subject in which the representation of time is grounded cannot, for that very reason, determine its own existence in time. And if the latter is impossible, then the former, the attempt to determine itself through the categories as a thinking being in general, is impossible as well.

The "I think" is, as already stated, an empirical proposition, and it contains within it the proposition "I exist." But I cannot say, "Everything that thinks exists," for then the mere property of thinking would make every being that possesses it a necessary being. My existence therefore cannot be regarded as an inference from the proposition "I think," as Descartes held, because such an inference would require the major premise "Everything that thinks exists" to come first. The two propositions are instead identical. "I think" expresses an undetermined empirical intuition, that is, a perception, and it thus shows that sensation, which belongs to sensibility, lies at its foundation. Yet it precedes experience, whose task is to determine an object of perception through the categories in relation to time. Existence in this proposition is not a category. The category of existence does not apply to an undetermined object that is simply given, but only to an object of which we already have a concept and about which we want to know whether it exists outside and apart from that concept. An undetermined perception here means only something real that has been given, and given only to thought in general. It is given neither as an appearance nor as a thing in itself (a noumenon), but simply as something that actually exists and is designated as such in the proposition "I think." It should be noted that when I call "I think" an empirical proposition, I do not mean that the I in it is an empirical representation. On the contrary, it is purely intellectual, because it belongs to thought in general. But without some empirical representation to supply the mind with material for thought, the act "I think" would never take place. The empirical is only the condition under which the pure intellectual faculty is applied or employed.

Thus the hope of establishing a knowledge that extends beyond the limits of experience, a knowledge bound up with humanity's highest interests, proves vain, and the effort of speculative philosophy in this domain proves futile. Yet in this very matter the rigor of criticism has done reason no small service, by demonstrating that no dogmatic claim can be made about an object of experience beyond the boundaries of experience. Criticism has thereby secured reason against every assertion of the opposite view. This can be achieved in only two ways. Either our own proposition must be proved with apodictic certainty, or, if that fails, we must seek out the sources of the failure. If those sources turn out to lie in the natural and necessary limits of our reason, our opponents must submit to the same law of renunciation and refrain from any claim to dogmatic assertion.

Yet the right, indeed the necessity, of assuming a future life on principles of the practical use of reason, joined with its speculative use, has lost nothing through this renunciation. The merely speculative proof never had any influence on the common reason of humankind. It is balanced on the point of a hair, so precariously that even the schools have kept it from falling only by discussing it without pause, keeping it spinning like a top that stays upright only while it whirls. Even in their eyes it never offered a secure foundation on which to build a theory. The proofs that have long circulated among ordinary people keep their value undiminished. Once the dogmatic pretensions of speculative reason are set aside, they even gain in clarity and in plain, unsophisticated force. For reason is thereby confined to its own proper province: the order of ends, which is at the same time the order of nature. As a practical faculty, and without restricting itself to the order of nature, reason is justified in extending the order of ends, and with it our own existence, beyond the boundaries of experience and of life. Consider the analogy offered by living beings in this world. In studying them, reason must accept as a principle that no organ, no faculty, no appetite is useless; that nothing is superfluous, nothing out of proportion to its use, nothing unsuited to its end; and that everything is perfectly fitted to its purpose in life. Measured against this principle, human beings, who alone are the final end and aim of this whole order, turn out to be the only animals that seem exempt from it. Their natural endowments, not only their talents and the motives that might lead them to use those talents, but above all the moral law within them, extend so far beyond any earthly utility or advantage that they feel bound to value the bare consciousness of integrity above everything else. They value it apart from any beneficial consequences, and apart even from the shadowy reward of posthumous fame. They are conscious of an inner calling to make themselves, through their conduct in this world and without regard to merely earthly interests, citizens of a better one. This powerful and irresistible proof remains to humanity even after theoretical self-knowledge has failed to establish the necessity of a life after death. It is accompanied by an ever-growing recognition of purposiveness in everything around us, by the conviction that creation is boundless and immense, by the awareness of a certain limitlessness in the possible extension of our knowledge, and by a longing in proportion to it.

### Conclusion of the Solution of the Psychological Paralogism

The dialectical illusion of rational psychology arises from confusing an idea of reason, the idea of a pure intelligence, with the concept, undetermined in every respect, of a thinking being in general. I think myself for the sake of a possible experience while abstracting from all actual experience, and I infer from this that I can be conscious of myself apart from experience and its empirical conditions. I thus confuse the possibility of abstracting from my empirically determined existence with a supposed consciousness that my thinking self could exist separately. And I believe I know what is substantial in me as a transcendental subject, when all I have in thought is the unity of consciousness that underlies every determination of knowledge.

The task of explaining the communion of the soul with the body does not properly belong to the psychology under discussion here. That psychology aims to prove the personality of the soul apart from this communion, that is, after death. It is therefore transcendent in the strict sense of the word: it does concern an object of experience, but only insofar as that object ceases to be an object of experience. Our system nonetheless supplies a sufficient answer to the question. The well-known difficulty lies in the presumed heterogeneity between the object of inner sense, the soul, and the objects of the outer senses, since the formal condition of intuition for the former is time alone, while for the latter it is space as well. But consider that the two kinds of objects differ not inwardly but only insofar as one appears outwardly to the other, so that what underlies appearances as a thing in itself may not be heterogeneous at all. Then the difficulty vanishes. The only difficulty that remains is the question of how any community of substances is possible. That question lies outside psychology, and the reader, recalling what was said in the Analytic about fundamental forces and faculties, will readily judge that it lies beyond human knowledge as well.

### General Remark on the Transition from Rational Psychology to Cosmology

The proposition "I think," or "I exist thinking," is empirical. But such a proposition must rest on empirical intuition, and its object must be thought as an appearance. Our theory therefore seems to maintain that the soul, even in thinking, is only an appearance, so that our consciousness itself would ultimately amount to nothing.

Thought in itself is merely the purely spontaneous logical function of connecting the manifold of a possible intuition. It does not represent the subject of consciousness as an appearance, for the simple reason that it pays no attention to whether the mode of intuition is sensible or intellectual. In thought, then, I represent myself neither as I am nor as I appear to myself. I think myself only as an object in general, abstracting from the way in which it is intuited. When I represent myself as the subject of thoughts or as the ground of thinking, these ways of representing myself are not the categories of substance or cause, for those categories are functions of thought that apply only to our sensible intuition. I would need to apply them to the I if I wanted to make myself an object of knowledge. But I want only to be conscious of myself as thinking. How my self is given in intuition I leave aside. It may be that I who think am an appearance, though not insofar as I am a thinking being. In the consciousness of myself in mere thought I am a being, yet this consciousness offers me no property of that being as material for thought.

But the proposition "I think," insofar as it asserts "I exist thinking," is more than the representation of a logical function. It determines the subject, which here is also an object, with respect to existence, and it cannot be given without inner sense, whose intuition presents its object never as a thing in itself but always as an appearance. This proposition therefore contains more than the bare spontaneity of thought. It also contains the receptivity of intuition, which is my thought of myself applied to the empirical intuition of myself. In this intuition the thinking self would have to look for the conditions under which its logical functions could be used as categories of substance, cause, and the rest. It would need them not only to distinguish itself, through the representation "I," as an object in itself, but also to determine the mode of its existence, that is, to know itself as a noumenon. This is impossible. Inner empirical intuition is sensible and supplies nothing but data of appearance. Such data do nothing to help the object of pure consciousness know itself as a separate existence; they are useful only as contributions to experience.

But suppose we were to find grounds for regarding ourselves as legislating a priori with respect to our own existence, and as determining that existence. Suppose we found these grounds not in experience, but in certain firmly established a priori laws governing the use of pure reason, laws concerning our existence. On this supposition we would discover in ourselves a spontaneity through which our actual existence could be determined without the conditions of empirical intuition. We would also become aware that the consciousness of our existence contains an a priori element capable of determining that existence, an existence otherwise determinable only through the senses. It would do so, however, only with reference to a certain inner faculty related to an intelligible world, a world accessible to the intellect rather than to the senses.

This would not give the least help to rational psychology. This remarkable faculty, which my consciousness of the moral law first reveals to me, would indeed supply me with a purely intellectual principle for determining my existence. But through what predicates? Through none other than those given in sensible intuition. I would therefore find myself back in the position I occupied in rational psychology, still needing sensible intuitions to give meaning to my concepts of substance and cause, which are the only means by which I can know myself. And those intuitions can never lift me above the sphere of experience. I would, however, be justified in applying these concepts to freedom and its subject for practical purposes, a use always directed to objects of experience, in keeping with the analogical meaning they have in their theoretical use. In doing so I would understand by them only the logical functions of subject and predicate, of ground and consequence. These are the functions according to which actions are determined in such a way that they can be explained together with the laws of nature, in accordance with the categories of substance and cause, even though they arise from an entirely different principle.

We have offered these observations to guard against the misunderstanding to which our doctrine of self-intuition as appearance is exposed. Their usefulness will become apparent later.

## Transcendental Dialectic, Book II, Chapter II: The Antinomy of Pure Reason

We showed in the introduction to this part of our work that every transcendental illusion of pure reason arises from dialectical inferences. Logic supplies the pattern for these inferences in the three formal kinds of syllogism, just as the categories find their logical pattern in the four functions of all judgments. The first kind of these sophistical inferences concerned the unconditioned unity of the subjective conditions of all representations in general, that is, the unity of the subject or soul. It corresponded to the categorical syllogism, whose major premise, as the principle, states the relation of a predicate to a subject. The second kind of dialectical argument will therefore follow the analogy of the hypothetical syllogism and concern the unconditioned unity of the objective conditions in appearance. And the theme of the third kind, to be treated in the following chapter, will be the unconditioned unity of the objective conditions of the possibility of objects in general.

It is worth noting, however, that the transcendental paralogism produced a merely one-sided illusion concerning the idea of the subject of our thinking, and that the concepts of reason offered no grounds for maintaining the opposite proposition. The advantage lies entirely with Pneumatism, the doctrine that the soul is a spiritual substance, even though this doctrine itself dissolves into nothing in the crucible of pure reason.

The case is very different when reason is applied to the objective synthesis of appearances. Here reason does establish its principle of unconditioned unity with considerable plausibility, but it soon becomes entangled in such contradictions that it is forced to give up its claims in the field of cosmology.

For here we encounter a new phenomenon of human reason: a wholly natural antithetic, a conflict between opposing propositions that does not need to be sought out through subtle sophistry, because reason falls into it of its own accord and unavoidably. This does protect reason from the slumber of an imagined conviction, the kind a merely one-sided illusion produces. But it also forces reason into a choice. It must either abandon itself to despairing skepticism, or adopt a dogmatic confidence and cling stubbornly to certain assertions without giving a fair hearing to the opposing case. Either course is the death of sound philosophy, although the first might perhaps be called the euthanasia of pure reason.

Before entering this region of discord and confusion produced by the conflict of the laws of pure reason, its antinomy, we will offer the reader some remarks that explain and justify the method we intend to follow. I call all transcendental ideas cosmological concepts insofar as they concern absolute totality in the synthesis of appearances. I do so partly because of this unconditioned totality, on which the concept of the world as a whole rests, a concept that is itself only an idea. I do so also because these ideas concern only the synthesis of appearances, that is, empirical synthesis. By contrast, absolute totality in the synthesis of the conditions of all possible things gives rise to an ideal of pure reason, which is entirely distinct from the cosmological concept, although related to it. Accordingly, just as the paralogisms of pure reason laid the groundwork for a dialectical psychology, the antinomy of pure reason will present the transcendental principles of a supposed pure, or rational, cosmology. It will do so not in order to declare that cosmology valid and adopt it, but, as the very phrase "conflict of reason" makes clear, to exhibit it as an idea that cannot be reconciled with appearances and experience.

### Section I. System of Cosmological Ideas

To enumerate these ideas with systematic precision according to a principle, we must first note that pure and transcendental concepts originate in the understanding alone. Reason does not, strictly speaking, generate any concept. It only frees a concept of the understanding from the unavoidable limitations of possible experience, and so tries to extend it beyond the empirical, though always in connection with it. This happens because, for any given conditioned thing, reason demands absolute totality on the side of the conditions to which the understanding subjects all appearances, and in doing so it turns the category into a transcendental idea. Reason does this in order to give absolute completeness to empirical synthesis by carrying it all the way to the unconditioned, which is never found in experience but only in the idea. Reason demands this according to the principle: if the conditioned is given, then the whole sum of its conditions, and therefore the absolutely unconditioned through which alone the conditioned was possible, is also given. First, then, the transcendental ideas are, properly speaking, nothing but categories extended to the unconditioned, and they can be arranged in a table under the headings of the categories. Second, not every category is suited to this purpose, but only those in which the synthesis forms a series, and specifically a series of conditions that are subordinated to one another rather than coordinated with one another. Reason demands absolute totality only for the ascending series of conditions that lead up to a given conditioned thing. It does not demand it for the descending series of consequences, nor for the aggregate of coordinated conditions belonging to those consequences. The reason is that, with respect to a given conditioned, its conditions are presupposed and are considered to be given along with it. Consequences, by contrast, do not make their conditions possible but presuppose them. So when we follow the procession of consequences, descending from a given condition to what it conditions, it does not matter to us whether the series comes to an end, and reason does not necessarily demand its totality.

We therefore necessarily think of the time that has elapsed up to a given moment as complete, even though we cannot determine it. Future time, however, is not a condition of our arriving at the present, and so, for the purpose of conceiving the present, it makes no difference whether we think of future time as ending at some point or as stretching on to infinity. Take, for example, the series m, n, o, in which n is given as conditioned with respect to m but also as the condition of o. Let the series run upward from the conditioned n to m, and beyond to l, k, i, and so on, and also downward from the condition n to the conditioned o, and beyond to p, q, r, and so on. I must presuppose the upward series in order to regard n as given, since according to reason, which demands the totality of conditions, n is possible only through that series. But the possibility of n does not rest on the downward series o, p, q, r. For this reason that series cannot be regarded as given, but only as capable of being given (*dabilis*).

I shall call the synthesis that runs along the side of the conditions, from the condition nearest to the given appearance toward the more remote ones, *regressive*. The synthesis that runs along the side of the conditioned, from the immediate consequence toward the more remote ones, I shall call *progressive*. The first proceeds *in antecedentia*, toward what comes before; the second proceeds *in consequentia*, toward what comes after. The cosmological ideas are therefore concerned with the totality of the regressive synthesis, and they proceed toward antecedents, not toward consequences. When reason does pursue the progressive synthesis, it is taking up an optional problem, not a necessary one. To understand completely what is given in an appearance, we need not the consequences that follow from it but the grounds that precede it.

To construct the table of ideas in correspondence with the table of categories, we begin with the two original magnitudes of all our intuition, time and space. Time is in itself a series, and indeed the formal condition of every series. With respect to a given present, therefore, we must distinguish a priori within time between the antecedents, which are conditions (past time), and the consequents (future time). The transcendental idea of the absolute totality of the series of conditions for a given conditioned thus concerns only past time. According to the idea of reason, the whole of past time, as the condition of the given moment, is necessarily thought of as given. In space, however, there is no distinction between progression and regression, because space is an aggregate and not a series: its parts exist together, all at once.

I can regard a given moment only as conditioned with respect to past time, because this moment comes into existence only through the passing of the time before it. But the parts of space are coordinated with one another, not subordinated to one another, so no part can be the condition of the possibility of another. Space, unlike time, is not in itself a series. Yet the synthesis of the many parts of space, the synthesis through which we apprehend space, is nevertheless successive. It therefore takes place in time and does contain a series. Consider a series of aggregated spaces, such as the feet that together make up a rood, an old unit of measure several yards in length. We begin with a given portion of space, and the portions successively added to it form the condition of its limits. The measurement of a space must therefore also be regarded as a synthesis of the series of conditions of a given conditioned. It differs from the synthesis of time in one respect: in space, the side of the conditioned cannot in itself be distinguished from the side of the condition, so that regression and progression in space appear to be identical. But since one part of space is not given by another part, only limited by it, we must also regard every limited space as conditioned, insofar as it presupposes some other space as the condition of its limitation, and so on. With respect to limitation, then, our procedure in space is also a regression, and the transcendental idea of the absolute totality of the synthesis in a series of conditions applies to space as well. I am therefore entitled to demand the absolute totality of the synthesis of appearances in space as well as in time. Whether that demand can be satisfied is a question to be answered later.

Second, the real in space, which is matter, is conditioned. Its internal conditions are its parts, and the parts of those parts are its remote conditions. Here too, then, we find a regressive synthesis, and reason demands its absolute totality. That totality can be reached only by a complete division of parts, in which the real in matter turns either into nothing or into something that is no longer matter, namely the simple. So here too we find a series of conditions and an advance toward the unconditioned.

Third, among the categories of real relation between appearances, the category of substance and accident is not suited to forming a transcendental idea, because it gives reason no ground for proceeding regressively through conditions. Accidents, insofar as they inhere in a substance, are coordinated with one another and do not form a series. Nor are they, strictly speaking, subordinated to the substance; they are simply the way in which the substance itself exists. The concept of the substantial might still seem to be an idea of transcendental reason. But this concept means nothing more than the concept of an object in general, which subsists insofar as we think in it merely a transcendental subject without any predicates. Since the question here concerns an unconditioned within the series of appearances, the substantial plainly cannot be a member of that series. The same holds for substances in community, which are mere aggregates and do not form a series. They are not subordinated to one another as conditions of one another's possibility. That relation can be affirmed of spaces, whose limits are never determined by themselves but always by some other space; it cannot be affirmed of substances. Only in the category of causality, therefore, do we find a series of causes for a given effect, in which we ascend from the effect, as the conditioned, to the causes, as its conditions, and so answer the question that reason poses.

Fourth, the concepts of the possible, the actual, and the necessary do not lead to any series, with one exception. What is contingent in existence must always be regarded as conditioned, and according to a law of the understanding it points to a condition under which we must rise to a higher condition, until reason arrives, in the totality of the series, at unconditioned necessity.

There are accordingly only four cosmological ideas, corresponding to the four headings of the categories, since we can select only those categories that necessarily give us a series in the synthesis of the manifold.

1. The absolute completeness of the *composition* of the given whole of all appearances.
2. The absolute completeness of the *division* of a given whole in appearance.
3. The absolute completeness of the *origination* of an appearance.
4. The absolute completeness of the *dependence of the existence* of what is changeable in appearance.

The first thing to note here is that the idea of absolute totality concerns only the exposition of appearances, and not the pure concept of a totality of things. Appearances are therefore regarded here as given, and reason demands the absolute completeness of the conditions of their possibility, insofar as those conditions form a series. It demands, consequently, a synthesis complete in every respect, through which an appearance could be explained according to the laws of the understanding.

Second, what reason is really seeking in this serial, regressive synthesis of conditions is the unconditioned alone. It wants to reach completeness in the series of premises, so that no further premises need be presupposed. This unconditioned is always contained in the absolute totality of the series, whenever we try to represent that totality in thought. But this absolutely complete synthesis is itself only an idea, for we cannot know, at least in advance, whether any such synthesis is possible in the case of appearances. If we represent everything that exists solely through pure concepts of the understanding, without any conditions of sensible intuition, we may rightly say that for a given conditioned the whole series of conditions subordinated to one another is also given, since the conditioned is given only through that series. With appearances, however, we meet a particular restriction on the way conditions are given: they are given through the successive synthesis of the manifold of intuition, and this synthesis would have to be completed in the regress. Whether such completeness is possible in sensible terms is an open problem. The idea of it nevertheless lies in reason, whether or not it is possible to connect adequate empirical concepts with that idea. The absolute totality of the regressive synthesis of the manifold in an appearance, which follows the guidance of the categories that represent it as a series of conditions for a given conditioned, necessarily contains the unconditioned, even while it remains undecided whether and how this totality exists. Reason therefore sets out from the idea of totality, although its real and final aim is the unconditioned, whether of the whole series or of some part of it.

This unconditioned can be thought in one of two ways. It may be thought as existing only in the series as a whole, so that every member without exception is conditioned and only the totality is absolutely unconditioned; in this case the regress is called infinite. Or the absolutely unconditioned may be thought as only one part of the series, a part to which the other members are subordinated but which is not itself subject to any further condition. In the first case the series is unlimited *a parte priori*, on the side of what comes before. It has no beginning and is therefore infinite, and yet it is given as complete. The regress through it, however, is never completed, and can be called infinite only potentially. In the second case there is a first member of the series. With respect to past time, this first is called the beginning of the world; with respect to space, the limit of the world; with respect to the parts of a given limited whole, the simple; with respect to causes, absolute spontaneity, or freedom; and with respect to the existence of changeable things, absolute natural necessity.

The absolute totality of the series of conditions for a given conditioned is always unconditioned, because beyond it there are no further conditions on which it could depend. But the absolute totality of such a series is only an idea, or more precisely a problematic concept, and its possibility must be investigated, especially with regard to how the unconditioned, the transcendental idea that is the real object of this inquiry, could be contained within it.

We have two expressions, *world* and *nature*, which are commonly used interchangeably. The first signifies the mathematical whole of all appearances and the totality of their synthesis, whether that synthesis advances by composition or by division. The world is called nature when it is regarded as a dynamic whole, that is, when our attention is directed not to its aggregation in space and time, so as to think of it as a magnitude, but to the unity in the existence of appearances. In this case the condition of what happens is called a cause. The unconditioned causality of a cause in appearance is called freedom, and the conditioned cause is called, in a narrower sense, a natural cause. What is conditioned in existence is called contingent, and what is unconditioned is called necessary. The unconditioned necessity of appearances may be called natural necessity.

The word *nature* has two senses. Taken adjectivally, or formally, it signifies the whole set of a thing's determinations, connected according to an internal principle of causality. Taken as a noun, or materially, it signifies the sum of all appearances, insofar as they are connected with one another throughout by virtue of an internal principle of causality. In the first sense we speak of the nature of liquid matter, of fire, and so on, using the word only adjectivally; when we speak of the objects of nature, by contrast, we have in mind the idea of a whole that subsists.

I have called the ideas now under discussion *cosmological* ideas for two reasons. First, the word *world* means the entire content of all appearances, and our ideas are directed solely at the unconditioned among appearances. Second, *world* in the transcendental sense means the absolute totality of the content of existing things, and we are attending only to the completeness of the synthesis, though strictly speaking only in the regressive direction. These ideas are all transcendent. They do not exceed appearances in kind, since they are concerned solely with the world of the senses and not with noumena, yet they carry their synthesis to a degree far beyond any possible experience.
