Even so, it seems to me entirely proper to call them cosmic concepts. With regard to the distinction between the mathematically unconditioned and the dynamically unconditioned, either of which may be the aim of the regressive synthesis, I would call the first two, in a narrower sense, cosmic concepts, and the remaining two transcendent physical concepts. This distinction does not seem especially important at present, but we shall later find it to be of some value.

### Section II. The Antithetic of Pure Reason

*Thetic* is the name for any body of dogmatic propositions. By *antithetic* I do not mean dogmatic assertions of the opposite, but the conflict between cognitions that appear dogmatic (*thesis cum antithesi*, a thesis together with its antithesis), where neither side can claim any decisive advantage over the other. Antithetic, then, does not concern itself with one-sided assertions. It examines the conflicting character of reason's general cognitions and the causes of that conflict. Transcendental antithetic is an investigation into the antinomy of pure reason, its causes, and its outcome. If we use our reason not merely to apply the principles of the understanding to objects of experience, but venture with it beyond those boundaries, certain sophistical propositions, or theorems, arise. These assertions have the following peculiarities. Experience can neither confirm nor refute them. Each is consistent with itself, and each finds the conditions of its necessity in the very nature of reason. The misfortune is that there are equally valid and necessary grounds for asserting the opposite.

The questions that naturally arise in considering this dialectic of pure reason are therefore three. First, in which propositions is pure reason unavoidably caught in an antinomy? Second, what are the causes of this antinomy? Third, can reason free itself from this contradiction, and if so, how?

According to what has been said, a dialectical proposition of pure reason must differ from all merely sophistical propositions in two ways. First, it is not an answer to an arbitrary question that anyone might raise at whim, but to a question that human reason must necessarily encounter as it advances. Second, such a proposition, together with its opposite, does not carry the appearance of a merely artificial illusion that vanishes as soon as it is examined. It carries a natural and unavoidable illusion, one that goes on mocking us even after it no longer deceives us, and that can be rendered harmless but never entirely removed.

This dialectical doctrine will concern not the unity of the understanding in empirical concepts, but the unity of reason in pure ideas. As a synthesis according to rules, it must conform to the understanding; as the absolute unity of that synthesis, it must also conform to reason. The result is that if it is adequate to the unity of reason, it is too large for the understanding, and if it fits the understanding, it is too small for reason. From this arises a mutual opposition that cannot be avoided, whatever we do.

These sophistical assertions open up something like a battlefield, where victory goes to the side permitted to attack, and the side forced to stand on the defensive must give way. Skilled champions, whether their cause is good or bad, are therefore sure to carry off the victor's crown, provided they secure the right to make the last attack and are not required to withstand another charge from their opponent. We may well believe that this arena has often been trampled by combatants, that many victories have been won on both sides, and that whenever the final, decisive victory went to the one who fought for the right cause, it was only because his adversary had been forbidden to continue the tournament. As impartial umpires, we must set aside entirely the question of whether the combatants are fighting for the right or the wrong side, for the true or the false, and let the contest first be decided. Perhaps, once they have tired each other out more than they have wounded each other, they will discover that their quarrel was about nothing, and part as good friends.

This method of observing a conflict of assertions, or rather of provoking one, not in order to decide finally in favor of either side but to find out whether the object of the struggle is a mere illusion that each side grasps at in vain and that would be worth nothing even if it were reached, may be called the *skeptical method*. It is altogether different from *skepticism*, which is a doctrine of deliberate, systematic ignorance that undermines the foundations of all knowledge in order, if it can, to destroy our trust and confidence in it. The skeptical method aims at certainty. It seeks to locate the point of misunderstanding in a dispute that both sides conduct honestly and intelligently, much as wise legislators learn, from the difficulties judges encounter in lawsuits, which parts of their statutes are defective or poorly defined. The antinomy that comes to light when laws are applied is, for our limited wisdom, the best test of legislation. Reason, which in abstract speculation does not easily become aware of its own errors, is thereby roused to attend to the decisive factors in determining its principles.

This skeptical method, however, belongs essentially to transcendental philosophy alone, and can perhaps be dispensed with in every other field of inquiry. In mathematics its use would be absurd, because no false assertion can remain hidden there for long: mathematical demonstrations must always proceed under the guidance of pure intuition and through a synthesis that is always evident. In experimental philosophy, doubt and suspended judgment may be very useful, but no misunderstanding can arise there that cannot easily be cleared up, and experience must eventually supply the means of resolving the difficulty and ending the dispute, whether sooner or later. Moral philosophy can always present its principles, together with their practical consequences, in concrete form, at least in possible experiences, and so avoid the errors and ambiguities of abstraction. But transcendental propositions, which claim insight beyond the domain of all possible experience, can neither present their abstract synthesis in any a priori intuition nor expose a hidden error with the help of experience. Transcendental reason therefore offers us no other test than the attempt to reconcile such assertions with one another, and for that purpose to let them contend freely and without restraint. This contest we shall now arrange, presenting the antinomies in the order of the four transcendental ideas set out above.

**First Conflict of the Transcendental Ideas**

**Thesis**

The world has a beginning in time, and it is also limited with respect to space.

**Proof**

Suppose that the world has no beginning in time. Then up to any given moment an eternity has elapsed, and with it an infinite series of successive states of things in the world has passed away. But the infinity of a series consists precisely in the fact that it can never be completed through successive synthesis. It follows that an infinite series that has already elapsed is impossible, and that a beginning of the world is therefore a necessary condition of its existence. This was the first point to be proved.

As for the second point, let us again assume the opposite. In that case the world must be an infinite given whole of things existing at the same time. Now we can think the magnitude of a quantity that is not given within definite limits of intuition only through the synthesis of its parts, and we can think the whole of such a quantity only through a completed synthesis, that is, through the repeated addition of one unit to another. (A quantity of undetermined size can indeed be thought of as a whole when it is enclosed within limits, even if we cannot construct or ascertain its totality by measurement, through the successive synthesis of its parts, because its limits by themselves determine its completeness as a whole.) Accordingly, to think of the world that fills all spaces as a whole, we would have to regard the successive synthesis of the parts of an infinite world as completed. That is, we would have to regard an infinite time as having elapsed in the enumeration of all coexisting things, which is impossible. An infinite aggregate of actual things therefore cannot be regarded as a given whole, and so cannot be regarded as a whole given all at once. Consequently the world, with respect to its extension in space, is not infinite but enclosed within limits. This was the second point to be proved.

**Antithesis**

The world has no beginning and no limits in space, but is infinite with respect to both time and space.

**Proof**

Suppose that the world has a beginning. A beginning is an existence which is preceded by a time in which the thing does not exist. On this supposition, there must have been a time in which the world did not exist: an empty time. But nothing can come into being in an empty time, because no part of such a time contains any distinguishing condition of existence rather than nonexistence, whether we suppose the thing to arise of itself or through some other cause. Many series of things within the world may therefore have a beginning, but the world itself cannot have one, and it is consequently infinite with respect to past time.

As for the second claim, let us first assume the opposite: that the world is finite and bounded in space. It would then have to exist within an empty space that is itself unbounded. We would encounter not only a relation of things *in* space but also a relation of things *to* space. Yet the world is an absolute whole, beyond which no object of intuition can be found, and therefore no correlate with which the world could stand in relation. Its relation to empty space would thus be a relation to no object at all. Such a relation, and with it the bounding of the world by empty space, is nothing. The world, therefore, is not bounded in space; it is infinite in extension.

Space, it should be understood, is merely the form of outer intuition (a formal intuition), and not a real object that can be perceived from without. Considered prior to all the things that determine it, whether by filling or by bounding it, or more precisely prior to the things that supply an empirical intuition conforming to it, space, under the name of absolute space, is nothing but the bare possibility of outer phenomena, insofar as these either exist in themselves or can be added to intuitions already given. Empirical intuition, then, is not a compound of phenomena and space, of perception joined to empty intuition. Neither one is the correlate of the other within a synthesis. Instead they are bound together within one and the same empirical intuition as its matter and its form. If we try to separate the two, setting space apart from phenomena, we generate all kinds of empty determinations of outer intuition that could never be actual perceptions. The motion or rest of the world within an infinite empty space, for instance, or any determination of the relation between the world and that space, can never be perceived, and is therefore merely the predicate of a thing of thought.

**Observations on the First Antinomy: On the Thesis**

In presenting these opposing arguments, I have not gone hunting for sophisms in order to engage in what lawyers call special pleading, the tactic that exploits the carelessness of the opposing party, appeals to a misunderstood statute, and builds unjust claims on an unfair interpretation. Both proofs arise fairly from the nature of the case, and I have set aside entirely any advantage that might be gained from the mistakes of the dogmatists on either side.

The thesis could also have been proved unfairly, by introducing a mistaken concept of the infinity of a given magnitude. On that concept, a magnitude is infinite if no greater magnitude can possibly exist. A magnitude is measured by the number of given units, taken as a standard, that it contains. But no number can be the greatest, since one or more units can always be added. It would follow that an infinite given magnitude, and therefore a world infinite in both time and extension, is impossible, and that the world is limited in both respects. I could have conducted my proof this way, but the concept it relies on does not agree with the true concept of an infinite whole. The true concept does not represent the magnitude of that whole; it does not say how large the whole is, and so it is not the concept of a maximum. It thinks only the whole's relation to an arbitrarily chosen unit, relative to which the whole is greater than any number. As the chosen unit is larger or smaller, the infinite will be correspondingly larger or smaller. But the infinity itself, which consists solely in this relation to the given unit, always remains the same, even though the absolute magnitude of the whole is not thereby known.

The true, transcendental concept of infinity is this: that the successive synthesis of units in the measurement of a given quantum can never be completed. (A quantum in this sense contains a collection of given units that is greater than any number, and this is the mathematical concept of the infinite.) From this it follows, with no possibility of error, that an eternity of actual successive states cannot have elapsed up to a given moment, namely the present one, and that the world must therefore have a beginning.

With regard to the second part of the thesis, the difficulty of a series that is infinite and yet has elapsed disappears, since the manifold of a world infinite in extension is given all at once. But in order to think the totality of this manifold, we cannot rely on limits that would by themselves constitute this totality in intuition, and so we are obliged to give some other account of our concept. Here the concept cannot proceed from the whole to the determinate magnitude of its parts; it must demonstrate the possibility of a whole through a successive synthesis of the parts. Yet since this synthesis must form a series that can never be completed, we cannot think a totality prior to it, and therefore cannot think one by means of it either. For the concept of totality is in this case itself the representation of a completed synthesis of the parts, and that completion, and therefore its concept, is impossible.

**On the Antithesis**

The proof that the world is infinite in its succession through time and in its contents through space rests on the consideration that, if it were otherwise, an empty time and an empty space would have to form the world's limits. I am aware that there are ways of escaping this conclusion. It may be argued, for example, that the world can perfectly well be limited in space and time without our having to accept either an absolute time before the world's beginning or an absolute space stretching beyond the actual world, both of which are impossible. With the latter part of this view, held by philosophers of the Leibnizian school, I fully agree. Space is merely the form of outer intuition, not a real object that can itself be intuited from without. It is not a correlate of phenomena; it is the form of phenomena themselves. Space cannot, therefore, be regarded as something that absolutely and in itself determines the existence of things, since it is not itself an object but only the form of possible objects. It is things, as phenomena, that determine space: they make it possible that, of all the possible predicates of space, namely size and relation, certain ones belong to reality. The converse does not hold. Space, taken as something self-subsistent, cannot determine real things in size or shape, because in itself it is not a real thing. Space, whether filled or empty, may therefore be bounded by phenomena, but phenomena cannot be bounded by an empty space lying outside them. (By empty space I mean here only such space as is bounded by phenomena, that is, space within the world. This at least does not contradict transcendental principles and may, so far as they are concerned, be admitted, although its possibility cannot on that account be affirmed.) The same holds for time. Yet granting all this, it remains indisputable that if we assume the world has limits in space or in time, we must also assume these two nonentities: an empty space outside the world and an empty time before it.

Consider the evasion adopted by those who try to avoid the consequence that, if the world is limited in space and time, the infinite void must determine the existence of actual things with respect to their dimensions. It arises entirely from substituting one thing for another. In place of a sensible world, these thinkers conceive an intelligible world, of which nothing is known. In place of a real beginning, which is an existence preceded by a period in which nothing exists, they conceive an existence that presupposes no condition other than time. And in place of limits of extension, they conceive boundaries of the universe. But the question concerns the *mundus phaenomenon*, the world as it appears, and its magnitude; and in this case we cannot abstract from the conditions of sensibility without destroying the essential reality of this world itself. If the world of sense is limited, it must necessarily lie within the infinite void. If we leave that void out of view, and with it space as the a priori condition of the possibility of phenomena, the entire world of sense vanishes. Yet in our problem this world alone is considered as given. The *mundus intelligibilis*, the intelligible world, is nothing but the general concept of a world from which every condition of intuition has been abstracted, and about which no synthetic proposition, whether affirmative or negative, is possible.

**Second Conflict of the Transcendental Ideas: Thesis**

Every composite substance in the world consists of simple parts, and nothing exists that is not either itself simple or composed of simple parts.

**Proof**

Suppose that composite substances did not consist of simple parts. If all composition were then removed in thought, no composite part would remain, and, since by hypothesis there are no simple parts, no simple part either. No substance would remain, and consequently nothing at all would exist. Either, then, it is impossible to remove composition in thought, or else something must remain after its removal that subsists without composition, which is to say something simple. In the first case, however, the composite would not itself consist of substances, because for substances composition is only a contingent relation, apart from which they must still exist as self-subsistent beings. Since this case contradicts the original supposition, only the second can be true: the substantial composite in the world consists of simple parts.

It follows directly that the things of the world are all, without exception, simple beings; that composition is merely an external state belonging to them; and that, although we can never separate the elementary substances from their state of composition and isolate them, reason must think of them as the primary subjects of all composition, and therefore as prior to it, and as simple substances.

**Antithesis**

No composite thing in the world consists of simple parts, and nowhere in the world does any simple substance exist.

**Proof**

Suppose that a composite thing, considered as substance, consists of simple parts. Since every external relation, and therefore every composition of substances, is possible only in space, the space occupied by the composite must consist of as many parts as the composite itself contains. But space does not consist of simple parts; it consists of spaces. Every part of the composite must therefore occupy a space. But the absolutely primary parts of the composite are simple. It follows that the simple occupies a space. Now everything real that occupies a space contains a manifold of parts lying outside one another, and is therefore composite. It is, moreover, a real composite made not of accidents, which cannot exist outside one another apart from substance, but of substances. The simple would thus have to be a composite of substances, which contradicts itself.

The second proposition of the antithesis, that nothing simple exists in the world, amounts here to the following. The existence of the absolutely simple cannot be demonstrated from any experience or perception, whether outer or inner. The absolutely simple is a mere idea, whose objective reality can never be shown in any possible experience, and which therefore has no application and no object in the explanation of phenomena. For suppose an object could be found in experience corresponding to this transcendental idea. The empirical intuition of that object would then have to be recognized as containing no manifold whatsoever, no parts lying outside one another and joined into a unity. But we cannot infer from our being unaware of such a manifold that it is impossible for one to exist in the intuition of an object, and proof of precisely this impossibility is required to establish absolute simplicity. It follows that such simplicity cannot be inferred from any perception whatever. Since, then, an absolutely simple object can never be given in any experience, and since the world of sense must be regarded as the sum of all possible experiences, nothing simple exists in the world.

This second proposition of the antithesis reaches further than the first. The first merely banishes the simple from the intuition of the composite, whereas the second drives it out of nature altogether. For this reason we could not demonstrate it from the concept of a given object of outer intuition, the composite, but had to prove it from the relation of a given object to possible experience in general.

**Observations on the Second Antinomy: Thesis**

When I speak of a whole that necessarily consists of simple parts, I mean only a substantial whole, a composite in the proper sense. That is, I mean the contingent unity of a manifold whose elements are given as separate, at least in thought, and are then placed in reciprocal connection and so made into a unity. Space ought not to be called a *compositum*, a composite, but a *totum*, a whole, because its parts are possible only within the whole, rather than the whole being possible through its parts. It might perhaps be called a *compositum ideale*, an ideal composite, but not a *compositum reale*, a real one. This, however, is of no importance. Since space is not a composite of substances, nor even of real accidents, nothing at all remains if I abstract all composition from it, not even a point, since a point is possible only as the limit of a space, and therefore of a composite. Space and time, therefore, do not consist of simple parts. Likewise, whatever belongs only to the condition or state of a substance, even if it has magnitude, as motion or change does, does not consist of simple parts: a given degree of change does not arise from adding together many simple changes. Our inference from the composite to the simple is valid only for self-subsistent things, and the accidents of a state are not self-subsistent. The proof that the simple is necessary as the component of everything substantial and composite can therefore fail, and the whole case for the thesis be lost, if we stretch the proposition too far and try to make it hold for everything composite without distinction, as has in fact happened now and then. Moreover, I am speaking here only of the simple insofar as it is necessarily given in the composite, the composite being resolvable into it as into its component parts. The proper meaning of the word *monas*, as Leibniz used it, should refer to the simple that is given immediately as simple substance, in consciousness for instance, and not to the simple as an element of the composite. For the simple considered as an element, the term *atomus* would be more fitting. And since I wish to prove the existence of simple substances only in relation to the composite, as its elements, I might call the thesis of the second antinomy transcendental atomism. But because that word has long been used to designate a particular theory of bodily phenomena, the theory of *moleculae*, or molecules, and so presupposes empirical concepts, I prefer to call it the dialectical principle of monadology.

**Antithesis**

Against the claim that matter is infinitely divisible, a claim whose proof is purely mathematical, the Monadists have raised objections. These objections invite suspicion at first sight, because they refuse to accept the clearest mathematical proofs as propositions about the constitution of space, insofar as space really is the formal condition of the possibility of all matter. Instead, they treat these proofs as mere inferences from abstract and arbitrary concepts that cannot be applied to real things. They argue as if it were possible to imagine some mode of intuition other than the one given in the original intuition of space, and as if the a priori determinations of space did not apply to everything whose existence is possible only through its filling space. If we listen to them, we find ourselves required to think not only of the mathematical point, which is simple but is not a part of space, only its limit, but also of physical points. These are likewise simple, yet they have the peculiar property of filling space, as parts of it, merely by being aggregated together. I will not repeat here the familiar and clear refutations of this absurdity, which can be found everywhere in great number; everyone knows that the evidence of mathematics cannot be undermined by merely discursive concepts. I will only remark that if philosophy here tries to gain an advantage over mathematics through sophistical tricks, it is because it forgets that the discussion concerns only phenomena and their conditions. It is not enough to find, for the pure concept of the composite, the concept of the simple; we must find, for the intuition of the composite, which is matter, the intuition of the simple. And according to the laws of sensibility, and therefore in the case of objects of sense, this is utterly impossible. In the case of a whole made of substances and thought solely by the pure understanding, it may well be necessary to possess the simple before composition is possible. But this does not hold for the *totum substantiale phaenomenon*, the substantial whole as it appears, which, being an empirical intuition in space, necessarily contains no simple part, for the very reason that no part of space is simple. The Monadists, however, have been subtle enough to escape this difficulty. Rather than regarding space as the condition of the possibility of the objects of outer intuition, that is, of bodies, they presuppose intuition and the dynamic relation of substances as the condition of the possibility of space. But we have a concept of bodies only as phenomena, and as phenomena they necessarily presuppose space as the condition of all outer appearance. The evasion is therefore futile, as we have sufficiently shown in the Transcendental Aesthetic. If bodies were things in themselves, the Monadists' proof would be beyond objection.

The second dialectical assertion has a peculiarity: it is opposed by a dogmatic proposition which, of all such sophistical claims, is the only one that undertakes to prove, in an object of experience, what is properly a transcendental idea, namely the absolute simplicity of substance. This proposition holds that the object of inner sense, the thinking I, is an absolutely simple substance. Without entering into the subject now, since it was examined at length in an earlier chapter, I will remark only this. If something is thought merely as an object, without the addition of any synthetic determination of its intuition, as happens in the bare representation "I," then it is certain that no manifold and no composition can be perceived in that representation. Moreover, since the predicates through which I think this object are merely intuitions of inner sense, nothing can be found in them that would prove the existence of a manifold of parts lying outside one another, and so nothing that would prove real composition. Consciousness is so constituted that, because the thinking subject is at the same time its own object, it cannot divide itself, although it can divide the determinations that inhere in it; for every object, in relation to itself, is absolute unity. Nevertheless, if the subject is regarded from without, as an object of intuition, it must, in its character as a phenomenon, possess the property of composition. And it must always be regarded in this way if we wish to know whether or not it contains a manifold of parts lying outside one another.

**Third Conflict of the Transcendental Ideas: Thesis**

Causality according to the laws of nature is not the only causality from which the phenomena of the world arise. To account for these phenomena fully, a causality through freedom must also be assumed.

**Proof**

Suppose there were no causality other than that according to the laws of nature. Then everything that happens presupposes a prior state, which it follows with absolute certainty according to a rule. But this prior state must itself be something that has happened, something that arose in time, having not existed before. If it had always existed, its consequence would not now be arising for the first time but would likewise have always existed. The causality of a cause through which something happens is therefore itself an event. This event, in turn, presupposes according to the law of nature a prior state and its causality, and that state presupposes one still earlier, and so on. If everything happens solely according to the laws of nature, there can never be a true first beginning, only a subordinate or relative one. There can therefore be no completeness of the series on the side of the causes that arise one from another. But the law of nature is precisely that nothing happens without a cause sufficiently determined a priori. The proposition that all causality is possible only according to the laws of nature thus contradicts itself when stated in this unlimited and universal form, and natural causality cannot be the only kind.

It follows that we must admit a causality through which something happens without its cause being determined, according to necessary laws, by some other cause preceding it. There must exist, then, an absolute spontaneity of causes, capable of beginning of itself a series of phenomena that then proceeds according to natural laws. This is transcendental freedom, without which, even in the course of nature, the series of phenomena on the side of causes is never complete.

**Antithesis**

There is no freedom; everything in the world happens solely according to the laws of nature.

**Proof**

Suppose that freedom in the transcendental sense does exist, as a special kind of causality by which events in the world could be produced: a power, that is, of beginning a state, and with it a series of consequences of that state. In that case, not only the series begun by this spontaneity, but also the determination of the spontaneity itself to produce the series, which is to say the causality itself, must have an absolute beginning, such that nothing precedes it to determine this action according to fixed laws. But every beginning of action presupposes a state in which the acting cause is not yet acting; and a dynamically first beginning of action presupposes a state that has no connection—as regards causality—with the preceding state of the cause, and which therefore does not in any way follow from it. Transcendental freedom thus stands opposed to the natural law of cause and effect. A connection of successive states in active causes of this kind would destroy the possibility of unity in experience; for that reason it can never be found in experience, and it is consequently a mere fiction of thought.

It is to nature alone, then, that we must look for connection and order in the events of the world. Freedom, meaning independence from the laws of nature, certainly releases us from constraint, but it also abandons the guidance of law and rule. Nor can it be claimed that laws of freedom might take the place of the laws of nature in the causality of the world's course. If freedom were determined according to laws, it would no longer be freedom; it would simply be nature. Nature and transcendental freedom therefore differ as lawfulness differs from lawlessness. Nature burdens the understanding with the task of tracing the origin of events ever higher in the series of causes, since causality within that series is always conditioned, but it repays this labor with the guarantee of a unity that is complete and governed by law. Transcendental freedom, by contrast, promises the understanding a resting point in the chain of causes, leading it to an unconditioned causality that claims the power to originate events spontaneously. Yet because this causality is utterly blind, it strips the understanding of the guidance of rules, and only that guidance makes a fully connected experience possible.

**Observations on the Third Antinomy: On the Thesis**

The transcendental idea of freedom does not make up the whole content of the psychological concept that goes by that name, which is largely empirical. It supplies only the concept of spontaneity of action, as the proper ground for attributing freedom to the cause of a certain class of objects. It is nonetheless the true stumbling block for philosophy, which meets insurmountable difficulties when it tries to admit this kind of unconditioned causality. What has for so long thrown speculative reason into perplexity over the freedom of the will is, strictly speaking, only the transcendental element of that question: whether we must assume the existence of a faculty capable of spontaneously originating a series of successive things or states. How such a faculty is possible is not a question we are required to answer. Even with natural causality, we must content ourselves with knowing a priori that such causality must be presupposed. We cannot in the least comprehend how the existence of one thing is made possible by the existence of another, and for that information we must look entirely to experience.

We have demonstrated the necessity of a free first beginning of a series of appearances only insofar as it is needed to make an origin of the world comprehensible, with all later states regarded as a succession governed solely by the laws of nature. But since this proof has established that there exists a faculty able to originate a series in time by itself, even though we cannot explain how such a faculty exists, we now feel entitled to admit causal beginnings of various successions of appearances even in the midst of the natural course of events, and to attribute to all substances a capacity for free action. Here, however, we must not fall into a common misunderstanding. It might be supposed that because a successive series in the world can have only a comparatively first beginning, since some other state of things always precedes it, an absolutely first beginning of a series within the course of nature is impossible. But we are speaking here of an absolutely first beginning in causality, not in time. Suppose, for example, that I rise from my chair entirely of my own free will, without the necessarily determining influence of natural causes. With this event, together with all its consequences in the physical world stretching on to infinity, an absolutely new series begins, even though in time this event is merely the continuation of a preceding series. This decision and this act of mine are not part of the succession of natural effects, nor are they mere continuations of it. On the contrary, the determining causes of nature cease to operate with respect to this event: it certainly follows upon the workings of nature, but it does not proceed from them. For these reasons, the action of a free agent must be called an absolutely first beginning of a series of appearances, if not with respect to time, then with respect to causality.

Reason needs to rest on a free act as the first beginning of the series of natural causes, and the justice of that need is confirmed by the fact that all the philosophers of antiquity, except the Epicureans, felt compelled to accept a prime mover when they constructed a theory of the motions of the universe. This prime mover was a freely acting cause that, spontaneously and before all other causes, set this series of states in motion. These philosophers always felt the need to go beyond mere nature in order to make a first beginning comprehensible.

**On the Antithesis**

The defender of nature's all-sufficiency in matters of causality, a position that might be called transcendental physiocracy, would argue against the doctrine of freedom in roughly the following way. In reply to the sophistical arguments of the other side, he would say: If you do not accept a mathematical first in time, you have no need to look for a dynamical first in causality. Who compelled you to imagine an absolutely first state of the world, and with it an absolute beginning of the gradually unfolding successions of appearances? Who compelled you, in order to give this fancy some footing, to set limits to boundless nature? The substances in the world have always existed, or at least the unity of experience makes that assumption necessary. There is therefore no difficulty in supposing that the changes in the states of those substances have also always existed, and consequently that no first beginning, whether mathematical or dynamical, is required. Admittedly, the possibility of such an infinite derivation, with no first member from which all the others follow, is wholly incomprehensible. But if you are rash enough to reject the riddles of nature on that ground, you will be obliged to reject many fundamental properties of natural objects as well, such as fundamental forces, which you can comprehend just as little. Even so simple a concept as change would then present you with insurmountable difficulties. If experience did not teach you that change is real, you could never conceive a priori how this ceaseless succession of being and not-being is possible.

And even if a transcendental faculty of freedom were granted, a faculty of originating changes in the world, it would at least have to exist outside the world. That is itself a bold assumption: that beyond the entire content of all possible intuitions there exists some further object that can never be given in any possible perception. But to attribute such a faculty to substances within the world itself is entirely inadmissible. We call nature the connection of appearances that determine one another according to universal laws. If we granted this faculty to substances in the world, nature would almost entirely vanish, and with it the criteria of empirical truth that allow us to distinguish experience from mere dreaming. Alongside such a lawless faculty of freedom, a system of nature could scarcely be conceived. Its laws would be constantly disturbed by the intrusions of freedom, and the course of appearances, which would otherwise proceed with regularity and uniformity, would be thrown into confusion and disconnection.

**The Fourth Conflict of the Transcendental Ideas: Thesis**

There exists, belonging to the world either as a part of it or as its cause, an absolutely necessary being.

**Proof**

The world of sense, as the sum total of all appearances, contains a series of changes. Without such a series, even the representation of the time-series itself, which is the condition of the possibility of the sensible world, could not be given to us. Objectively, time, as the formal condition of the possibility of change, comes before all change; but subjectively, in actual consciousness, the representation of time, like every other representation, arises only on the occasion of perception. Every change stands under a condition that precedes it in time and makes it necessary. The existence of any given condition, in turn, presupposes a complete series of conditions reaching up to the absolutely unconditioned, which alone is absolutely necessary. It follows that if change exists as its consequence, something absolutely necessary must exist.

This necessary thing must itself belong to the sensible world. Suppose instead that it existed outside that world. The series of changes in the world would then derive its beginning from it, yet this necessary cause would not itself belong to the world of sense, and that is impossible. The beginning of a series in time can be determined only by what precedes it in time. The highest condition of the beginning of a series of changes must therefore have existed at a time when the series itself did not yet exist, since a beginning presupposes a preceding time in which the thing that begins did not yet exist. The causality of the necessary cause of change, and therefore the cause itself, must belong to time, and so to appearances, since time is possible only as the form of appearances. It cannot, then, be thought of as separate from the world of sense, the sum total of all appearances. There is therefore something absolutely necessary contained within the world, whether it is the entire world-series itself or only a part of it.

**Antithesis**

There exists no absolutely necessary being, either in the world or outside it as its cause.

**Proof**

Suppose either that the world itself is necessary or that it contains a necessary being. Two cases are possible. In the first, there is a beginning in the series of changes in the world that is unconditionally necessary and therefore uncaused, which conflicts with the dynamical law that determines all appearances in time. In the second, the series itself has no beginning and, though contingent and conditioned in all its parts, is nevertheless absolutely necessary and unconditioned as a whole. That contradicts itself, since the existence of an aggregate cannot be necessary if none of its parts exists necessarily.

Suppose, on the other hand, that an absolutely necessary cause of the world exists outside it. As the highest member in the series of causes of changes in the world, this cause would have to begin the existence of those changes and of their series. The word "begin" carries two senses here. In the active sense, the cause begins a series of conditions as its effect, which in Latin is *infit*. In the passive sense, the causality within the cause itself begins to operate, which is *fit*. The argument moves from the first sense to the second. If the cause begins the series, it must also begin to act, and its causality would therefore belong to time, and so to the sum total of appearances, which is the world. It follows that the cause cannot be outside the world, which contradicts the hypothesis. Therefore no absolutely necessary being exists, either in the world or outside it in causal connection with it.

**Observations on the Fourth Antinomy: On the Thesis**

To demonstrate the existence of a necessary being, I may use no argument here other than the cosmological one. That argument ascends from the conditioned in appearance to the unconditioned in concept, regarding the unconditioned as the necessary condition of the absolute totality of the series. The proof from the mere idea of a supreme being belongs to a different principle of reason and must be discussed separately.

The pure cosmological proof establishes that a necessary being exists, but leaves entirely undecided whether that being is the world itself or something quite distinct from it. To establish the latter, we would need principles that are not cosmological and that do not proceed along the series of appearances. We would have to bring into the proof concepts of contingent beings considered merely as objects of the understanding, along with a principle that connects them, by means of mere concepts, with a necessary being. The proper home for all such arguments, however, is a transcendent philosophy, which unfortunately has not yet been established.

But if we begin the proof cosmologically, grounding it on the series of appearances and on the regress through that series according to empirical laws of causality, we are not free to abandon this mode of demonstration midway and jump to something that is not a member of the series. The condition must be understood in exactly the same sense as the relation of conditioned to condition within the series, since the series is supposed to lead us by an unbroken regress to this highest condition. If that relation is sensible and belongs to the possible empirical use of the understanding, then the highest condition or cause can close the regress only according to the laws of sensibility, and must therefore belong to the time-series. It follows that this necessary being must be regarded as the highest member of the world-series.

Certain philosophers have nevertheless permitted themselves such a leap, a *saltus*, or what the Greeks called *metabasis eis allo genos*, a shift into another kind altogether. From the changes in the world they inferred the world's empirical contingency, its dependence on empirically determined causes, and so they admitted an ascending series of empirical conditions. In this they were quite right. But because they could find no first beginning or highest member in this series, they passed abruptly from the empirical concept of contingency to the pure category. The category presents a series that is intellectual rather than sensible, and whose completeness does indeed rest on the existence of an absolutely necessary cause. This intellectual series, moreover, is bound to no sensible conditions, and is therefore free from the condition of time, which would require the cause itself to begin its causality in time. But this procedure is entirely illegitimate, as what follows will make clear.

In the pure meaning of the categories, something is contingent if its contradictory opposite is possible. We cannot, however, infer intellectual contingency from empirical contingency. When something changes, the opposite of its state is actual at another time, and is therefore possible; but that opposite is not the contradictory opposite of the earlier state. For it to be the contradictory opposite, its opposite would have to have been able to exist in its place at the very time the earlier state existed, and no such knowledge is given to us in the mere appearance of change. A body that was in motion, call it A, comes to rest, which is non-A. From the fact that a state opposed to A follows A, we cannot conclude that the contradictory opposite of A is possible, and therefore that A is contingent. To prove that, we would need to know that rest could have existed at the very same time the motion took place. All we know is that rest was actual in the time following the motion, and was therefore also possible. But motion at one time and rest at another are not contradictory opposites. It follows that the succession of opposite determinations, which is what change is, does not demonstrate contingency in the sense represented by the concepts of pure understanding, and so it cannot lead us to the existence of a necessary being. Change proves only empirical contingency: that the new state could not have come into existence without a cause belonging to the preceding time. And that cause, even if it is regarded as absolutely necessary, must be given to us in time and must belong to the series of appearances.

**On the Antithesis**

We meet difficulties when we try to ascend through the series of appearances to the existence of an absolutely necessary supreme cause. These difficulties must not stem from our inability to establish the truth of our mere concepts of the necessary existence of a thing. Our objections, that is, must not be ontological. They must be directed against the causal connection of an unconditioned condition with a series of appearances. In a word, they must be cosmological and concern empirical laws. We must show two things. First, the regress in the series of causes within the sensible world can never end in an empirically unconditioned condition. Second, the cosmological argument from the contingency of the world's states, a contingency supposedly established by change, gives us no warrant to assume a first cause, an absolute originator of the world-series.

The reader will notice a remarkable contrast in this antinomy. The very same grounds of proof that established the existence of a supreme being in the thesis demonstrated its nonexistence in the antithesis, and with equal rigor. We found, first, that a necessary being exists, because the whole of past time contains the series of all conditions, and therefore also contains the unconditioned, the necessary. We found, second, that no necessary being exists, for precisely the same reason: the whole of past time contains the series of all conditions, and these, taken together, are therefore all conditioned. The cause of this apparent inconsistency is as follows. In the first argument, we attend only to the absolute totality of the series of conditions, each determining the next in time, and so we arrive at something unconditioned and necessary. In the second, we consider instead the contingency of everything determined in the time-series. Every event is preceded by a time in which its condition must itself be determined as conditioned, and so everything unconditioned or absolutely necessary disappears. In both cases, the mode of proof is entirely in keeping with the ordinary procedure of human reason, which often falls into conflict with itself by considering an object from two different standpoints. Herr von Mairan considered a dispute between two celebrated astronomers, which arose from a similar difficulty over choosing the right standpoint, important enough to deserve a separate treatise. One astronomer concluded that the moon rotates on its own axis because it always turns the same side toward the earth. The other declared, for exactly the same reason, that the moon does not rotate on its axis. Measured against the fixed stars, the moon does turn once on its axis with each orbit; measured against the earth, it never turns at all. Both conclusions were perfectly correct, depending on the point of view from which the moon's motion was considered.

### Section III: Of the Interest of Reason in These Self-Contradictions

We now have before us the entire dialectical procedure of the cosmological ideas. No possible experience can present an object that matches them in scope, and reason itself cannot even think them in a way consistent with the universal laws of experience. Yet they are not arbitrary inventions. In its uninterrupted advance through empirical synthesis, reason is necessarily led to them whenever it tries to free from all conditions, and to grasp in its unconditioned totality, what can only ever be determined conditionally under the laws of experience. These dialectical propositions are so many attempts to solve four natural and unavoidable problems of reason. There are neither more nor fewer than four, because there are no other series of synthetic presuppositions that limit empirical synthesis a priori.

As reason strives to extend its dominion beyond the limits of experience, it makes dazzling claims, and so far these have been presented only in dry formulas that contain nothing but the grounds of those claims. In keeping with the character of a transcendental philosophy, they have also been stripped of every empirical element, although the full splendor of the promises they hold out and the hopes they awaken appears only when they are joined to empirical knowledge. Philosophy applies these ideas and steadily widens the use of reason, struggling upward from the realm of experience toward these exalted ideas. In doing so, it reveals a value and dignity that would raise it far above every other branch of human knowledge, if only it could make good its claims, since it promises a secure foundation for our highest hopes and for the ultimate ends toward which all the efforts of reason are directed. Does the world have a beginning, and a limit to its extension in space? Is there anywhere, perhaps in my own thinking self, an indivisible and indestructible unity, or does nothing exist but what is divisible and transitory? Am I free, or am I, like other beings, bound in the chains of nature and fate? And finally, is there a supreme cause of the world, or must all our thought and speculation come to an end in nature and the order of external things? To solve these questions, the mathematician would gladly give up his entire science, for it offers no satisfaction to the highest aspirations and most ardent desires of humanity. It might even be said that the true worth of mathematics, that pride of human reason, lies in what it does for reason. It guides reason to knowledge of nature in its large and small manifestations alike, in all its beautiful order and regularity. It leads reason to insight into the remarkable unity of the moving forces at work in nature, far beyond anything a philosophy built solely on experience could expect. And it thereby encourages philosophy to extend the domain of reason beyond all experience, while supplying it with the finest materials for supporting its inquiries with fitting and harmonious intuitions, so far as the nature of those inquiries allows.

Unfortunately for speculation, though perhaps fortunately for the practical concerns of humanity, reason finds itself beset by opposing and contradictory arguments in the midst of its highest expectations, and neither its honor nor its security will allow it to retreat. Nor can it look on these conflicting lines of argument with indifference, as if they were mere fencing matches, and still less can it simply order a truce, for it has a deep interest in the matter under dispute. No course remains open to it but to reflect on the origin of this disunion in reason itself, asking whether it may not spring from a simple misunderstanding. Such an inquiry would require both sides to surrender their arrogant claims, but it would also establish the sovereignty of reason over understanding and sense on a secure foundation.

For now we will postpone this fundamental inquiry. Instead, we will consider for a moment which side of the controversy we would most willingly join if we were forced to take sides at all. We are setting aside the logical criterion of truth entirely and consulting only our own interest in the question, so these considerations cannot decide which party is in the right. They will, however, help us understand why those who have joined the struggle adopt one view rather than the other, even though no special insight into the subject has guided their choice. Along the way they will explain several other things as well: the fiery zeal of one side and the cool persistence of the other, and why one party has been greeted with the warmest approval while the other has always met with irreconcilable prejudice.

One thing, however, fixes the proper standpoint from which alone this preliminary inquiry can be undertaken and carried through with due completeness. That standpoint is a comparison of the principles from which each side, thesis and antithesis, proceeds. The reader will have noticed that the propositions of the antithesis display a complete uniformity of thought and a perfect unity of principle. That principle was pure empiricism, applied not only to explaining the phenomena within the world but also to resolving the transcendental ideas, including the idea of the universe itself. The assertions of the thesis, by contrast, rested on intellectual propositions in addition to the empirical mode of explanation used within the series of phenomena, and to that extent its principles were not simple. In view of its essential character, I shall call the thesis the dogmatism of pure reason.

On the side of dogmatism, then, which is the side of the thesis, we find the following in the determination of the cosmological ideas.

1. First, there is a practical interest, which every right-thinking person must hold dear. That the world had a beginning; that my thinking self is simple in nature and therefore indestructible; that I am free in my actions and raised above the compulsion of nature and its laws; and finally, that the entire order of things making up the world depends on a Supreme Being, from whom the whole derives its unity and connection: these are so many foundation stones of morality and religion. The antithesis strips us of all these supports, or at least appears to.

2. Second, a speculative interest of reason shows itself on this side. If we take the transcendental ideas and use them as the thesis directs, we can lay out the whole chain of conditions entirely a priori and grasp how the conditioned is derived, beginning from the unconditioned. The antithesis cannot do this, and for that reason it is less warmly received. To our question about the conditions of its synthesis, it can give no answer that does not raise a further question, and so on without end. On its account, we must always climb from a given beginning to one still earlier; every part leads us to a still smaller part; every event is preceded by another event that is its cause; and the conditions of existence always rest on further and higher conditions, never reaching an end or a footing in some self-subsistent thing as the primal being.

3. Third, this side has the advantage of popularity, which forms no small part of its appeal. Ordinary understanding finds not the slightest difficulty in the idea of an unconditioned beginning of all synthesis, since it is accustomed to follow consequences forward rather than to search for a proper ground of knowledge. In the concept of an absolute first, whose possibility it never examines, it is pleased to find a firm point of departure for its attempts at theory. In the restless, unending ascent from the conditioned to its condition, always with one foot in the air, it can find no satisfaction.

On the side of the antithesis, or empiricism, we find the following in the determination of the cosmological ideas.

1. First, we can discover here no practical interest arising from pure principles of reason, of the kind that morality and religion carry with them. On the contrary, pure empiricism seems to drain morality and religion of all their power and influence. Suppose there is no Supreme Being distinct from the world; suppose the world has no beginning and therefore no Creator; suppose our wills are not free, and the soul is as divisible and perishable as matter. Then the ideas and principles of morality lose all validity and collapse together with the transcendental ideas that formed their theoretical support.

2. In compensation, however, empiricism offers reason important advantages in its speculative interest, far exceeding anything the dogmatist can promise. When the empiricist employs the understanding, it always stands on its own proper ground of investigation, which is the field of possible experience. There it can explore the laws of experience and so extend its knowledge securely and with clear comprehension, without meeting a limit in any direction. Here it can and should find its proper object and present it to intuition, not only in itself but in all its relations; or, if it uses concepts, it can always furnish the corresponding images in clear and unmistakable intuitions. It has no need to give up the guidance of nature and attach itself to ideas whose objects it cannot know, since these ideas, as mere products of the intellect, can never be presented in any intuition. Indeed, it is not even permitted to abandon its proper work on the pretext that the work is finished, for it never can be finished, and to cross into the region of idealizing reason and transcendent concepts. In that region it is no longer required to observe and investigate the laws of nature, but only to think and imagine. There it is safe from contradiction by the facts, because the facts have not been called as witnesses. They have been passed over, or perhaps made subordinate to the so-called higher interests and considerations of pure reason.

The empiricist, therefore, will never allow himself to treat any epoch of nature as the first, the absolutely original state. He will not believe there can be limits to his view across nature's wide domains. He will not pass from the objects of nature, which he can explain satisfactorily through observation and mathematical reasoning and can determine synthetically in intuition, to objects that neither sense nor imagination can ever present in concrete form. He will not grant the existence of any power in nature that operates independently of nature's laws, since such a concession would introduce uncertainty into the procedure of the understanding, which is guided by necessary laws in its observation of phenomena. Nor, finally, will he allow himself to look for a cause beyond nature, because nature is all we know, and from nature alone we receive an objective basis for all our concepts and our instruction in the unchanging laws of things.

Suppose the empirical philosopher had no other aim in setting up his antithesis than to check the presumption of a reason that mistakes its true vocation. Such a reason boasts of insight and knowledge precisely where insight and knowledge end, and it treats what is valid only in relation to a practical interest as though it advanced the speculative interests of the mind. It does this so that, whenever it suits it, it can break off the thread of our physical investigations and, under the pretense of extending our knowledge, tie them to transcendental ideas through which we really know only that we know nothing. If the empiricist were content with this benefit, his principle would be a maxim urging moderation in the claims of reason and modesty in its assertions. At the same time, it would show us the right way to extend the province of the understanding, with the help of its only true teacher, experience. Following this advice, we would not call on intellectual hypotheses and faith to support our practical interests, nor would we parade them under the grand titles of science and insight. Speculative knowledge can find an objective basis nowhere but in experience. Once we pass beyond the limits of experience, our synthesis, which demands ever new knowledge independent of experience, has no foundation in intuition on which to build.

But empiricism often becomes dogmatic itself with respect to ideas, and boldly denies whatever lies beyond the sphere of its knowledge of appearances. When it does, it falls into the error of intemperance. That error is all the more blameworthy here, because it does irreparable harm to the practical interest of reason.

This is the opposition between Epicureanism and Platonism.

It remains doubtful, however, whether Epicurus ever put forward these principles as rules for the objective use of the understanding. If they were nothing more than maxims for the speculative exercise of reason, then he showed in them a more genuinely philosophical spirit than any other philosopher of antiquity. The principles are these: that in explaining phenomena we must proceed as though the field of inquiry had no limits in space and no beginning in time; that we must be content with what experience teaches about the material of which the world is composed; that we must seek no way in which events originate other than the one determined by the unalterable laws of nature; and, finally, that we must not invoke the hypothesis of a cause distinct from the world to account for any phenomenon or for the world itself. These are principles for extending speculative philosophy and for discovering the true sources of the principles of morality, and however little they are followed today, they are undoubtedly correct. At the same time, anyone who wishes to set aside these dogmatic propositions in pure speculation need not, for that reason, be accused of denying them.

Both Epicurus and Plato assert more in their systems than they know. The first encourages and advances science, though to the detriment of the practical. The second offers excellent principles for investigating the practical. In every matter where we can attain speculative knowledge, however, he allows reason to attach idealistic explanations to natural phenomena, to the great harm of physical inquiry.

3. As for the third motive behind a preliminary choice of sides in this war of assertions, it seems remarkable that empiricism should be so thoroughly unpopular. One would expect ordinary understanding to welcome it gladly, since it promises to satisfy that understanding without stepping beyond the bounds of experience and its connected order. Transcendental dogmatism, by contrast, compels ordinary understanding to rise to concepts that far exceed the intelligence and ability of the most practiced thinkers. Yet this is precisely the real motive. Here ordinary understanding finds itself in a position where even the most learned have no advantage over it. If it understands little or nothing of these transcendental concepts, no one else can boast of understanding them any better. It may not express itself in such scholastically correct terms as others, but it can busy itself endlessly with reasoning and argument, wandering among mere ideas. About such ideas one can always be highly eloquent, precisely because we know nothing about them. In the observation and investigation of nature, by contrast, it would be forced to fall silent and confess its utter ignorance. Laziness and vanity, then, are in themselves strong recommendations for these principles. Moreover, a philosopher finds it hard to adopt a principle he cannot justify to himself, and harder still to use concepts whose objective reality cannot be established, yet nothing is more common for ordinary understanding. It wants something that lets it set to work with confidence. The difficulty of even comprehending a supposition does not trouble it, because, not knowing what comprehending means, it never even reflects on the supposition it may be adopting as a principle, and it regards as known whatever has become familiar through constant use. In the end, all speculative interests vanish before the practical interests it holds dear, and it imagines that it understands and knows whatever its needs and hopes prompt it to assume or believe. In this way the empiricism of transcendentally idealizing reason is deprived of all popularity. However damaging it may be to the highest practical principles, there is no danger that it will ever pass beyond the walls of the schools or gain any favor or influence in society or among the general public.

Human reason is by nature architectonic. It regards all knowledge as belonging to a possible system, and so it accepts only those principles that at least do not prevent any knowledge we have gained from taking its place alongside other knowledge in a general system. But the propositions of the antithesis are of such a kind that they make it impossible ever to complete an edifice of knowledge. According to them, beyond any given state or epoch of the world there is always an earlier one; within every part there are always further parts, themselves divisible; before every event there is another, whose origin must in turn be sought still further back; and everything in existence is conditioned, yet never dependent on an unconditioned and primal existence. Since the antithesis will not grant any first beginning that could be used as a foundation, a complete edifice of knowledge is utterly impossible under such a hypothesis. The architectonic interest of reason, which demands a unity that is not empirical but a priori and rational, therefore forms a natural recommendation for the assertions of the thesis in our antinomy.

But suppose someone could free himself entirely from every consideration of interest and weigh the assertions of reason impartially, attending only to their content and disregarding the consequences that follow from them. If such a person knew no way out of the confusion except to settle which of the conflicting doctrines was true, he would live in a state of continual wavering. Today he would be convinced that the human will is free. Tomorrow, reflecting on the unbroken chain of nature, he would regard freedom as a mere illusion and declare nature to be everything. Yet if he were called upon to act, this play of merely speculative reason would vanish like the shapes of a dream, and practical interest would dictate his choice of principles. Still, it is fitting for a reflective and inquiring being to devote certain periods of time to examining its own reason, to strip itself of all partiality, and to submit its observations openly to the judgment of others. For that reason no one can be blamed for, much less prevented from, putting both parties on trial and allowing them to defend themselves, free from intimidation, before a sworn jury who share their own condition, the condition of weak and fallible human beings.

### Section IV. Of the Necessity Imposed upon Pure Reason of Presenting a Solution of Its Transcendental Problems

To claim the ability to solve every problem and answer every question would be a boast certain to convict any philosopher of extravagance and self-conceit, and it would instantly destroy whatever confidence might otherwise have been placed in him. Yet some sciences are so constituted that every question arising within their domain must be answerable from the knowledge we already possess, because the answer must come from the same source as the question itself. In such sciences we may not excuse ourselves by pleading necessary and unavoidable ignorance; a solution is absolutely required. The rule of right and wrong must enable us to know what is right or wrong in every possible case. Otherwise the very idea of obligation or duty would be empty, for we cannot be obligated to do what we cannot know. In our investigations of natural phenomena, by contrast, much must remain uncertain and many questions must stay unsolved, because what we know of nature falls far short of explaining all the phenomena presented to our observation.

The question, then, is whether transcendental philosophy contains any question about an object presented to pure reason that this same reason cannot answer. Must we regard the subject of such a question as entirely uncertain, as far as our knowledge reaches? Must we assign it a place among those subjects of which we have just enough of a concept to raise a question, while the faculty or the materials fail us when we try to answer it?

I maintain that, of all speculative knowledge, transcendental philosophy has this peculiarity: no question about an object presented to pure reason is insoluble by that reason. No profession of unavoidable ignorance, and no claim that the problem lies beyond the reach of our faculties, can release us from the obligation to give a complete and satisfactory answer. The very concept that allows us to raise the question must also give us the power to answer it, since here, as in the case of right and wrong, the object is not to be found anywhere outside the concept.

In transcendental philosophy, however, the cosmological questions are the only ones to which we can demand a satisfactory answer about the constitution of their object, and here the philosopher may not take refuge in the pretext of necessary ignorance and impenetrable obscurity. These questions concern the cosmological ideas alone. In their case the object must be given in experience, and the question concerns only whether that object is adequate to an idea. Matters are different if the object is transcendental, and therefore itself unknown. We might ask, for instance, whether the something whose appearance we think inwardly, within ourselves (that is, the soul), is in itself a simple being, or whether there exists an absolutely necessary cause of all things. In such cases we are seeking an object for our idea, and we may admit that this object is unknown to us, though we must not conclude on that account that it is impossible.

The question "What is the constitution of a transcendental object?" admits of no answer, because we cannot say what such an object is. But we can see that the question itself is empty, because it does not concern any object that could be presented to us. For this reason all the questions raised in transcendental psychology must be regarded as answerable, and indeed as actually answered. They concern the transcendental subject of all inner phenomena, which is not itself a phenomenon and so is not given as an object. Nor do any of the categories find in it any conditions for their application, and it is to the categories that these questions are really addressed. Here, then, is a case where giving no answer is the only proper answer. A question about the constitution of something that cannot be thought through any determinate predicate, because it lies wholly beyond the sphere of objects and experience, is completely null and void.

The cosmological ideas alone have this peculiarity: we can presuppose that their object is given, together with the empirical synthesis required for the concept of that object. The question these ideas raise concerns only the progress of this synthesis, insofar as it must contain absolute totality. That totality is not empirical, since no experience can ever give it. Because the question here concerns a thing only as the object of a possible experience, and not as a thing in itself, the answer to the transcendental cosmological question need not be sought outside the idea, for the question does not concern an object in itself. With regard to possible experience, the question is not "What can be given concretely in an experience?" but "What is contained in the idea to which the empirical synthesis must approximate?" The question must therefore be answerable from the idea alone. The idea is a creation of reason itself, and reason therefore cannot disown the obligation to answer it, or refer us to some unknown object.

It is not as strange as it may first appear that a science should demand and expect satisfactory answers to all the questions that arise within its own domain, its *quaestiones domesticae*, even if those answers have not yet been found at a given time. Besides transcendental philosophy, there are only two pure sciences of reason, one with a speculative content and the other with a practical content: pure mathematics and pure ethics. Has anyone ever heard it claimed that, because of our complete and necessary ignorance of the conditions, it remains uncertain what exact relation the diameter of a circle bears to the circle, whether in rational or in irrational numbers? In rational numbers the value cannot be given exactly at all, and in irrational numbers it can be given only approximately. We therefore conclude that the impossibility of a solution is evident, and Lambert has supplied a demonstration of this. In the general principles of morals nothing can be uncertain, because their propositions either mean nothing at all or must arise solely from our rational concepts. In physical science, on the other hand, there must be countless conjectures that can never become certainties, because the phenomena of nature are not given as objects dependent on our concepts. The key to such questions therefore cannot be found in our concepts or in pure thought. It must lie outside us, and for that reason it often cannot be discovered, so that a satisfactory explanation cannot be expected. The questions of the transcendental analytic, which concern the deduction of our pure knowledge, are not of the same kind as those just mentioned. Our present concern is not with the certainty of judgments in relation to the origin of our concepts, but only with their certainty in relation to objects.

We cannot, therefore, evade the responsibility of giving at least a critical solution to the questions of reason. We cannot escape it by complaining about the limits of our faculties, or by the seemingly humble confession that reason lacks the power to decide whether the world has existed from all eternity or had a beginning; whether it is infinitely extended or enclosed within definite limits; whether anything in the world is simple or whether everything must be infinitely divisible; whether freedom can give rise to phenomena or whether everything depends absolutely on the laws and order of nature; and, finally, whether there exists a being that is wholly unconditioned and necessary, or whether the existence of everything is conditioned, and therefore dependent on something outside itself and contingent in its own nature. All these questions concern an object that can be given nowhere but in thought: the absolutely unconditioned totality of the synthesis of phenomena. If the concepts in our minds do not lead us to a definite result on these problems, we must not defend ourselves by claiming that the object itself remains hidden and unknown to us. No such thing or object can be given, for it is not to be found anywhere outside the idea in our minds. We must look for the cause of our failure in the idea itself. That idea poses an insoluble problem, and we stubbornly assume that a real object exists that corresponds and is adequate to it. A clear account of the dialectic contained in our concept will soon enable us to reach a satisfactory decision on any such question.

To those who plead that certainty on these problems is beyond our reach, we may put a question that demands at least a plain answer: "Where do these ideas come from, whose solution entangles you in such difficulties? Are you trying to explain certain phenomena, and do you expect these ideas to supply the principles or the rules of that explanation?" Suppose that all of nature lay open before you, and that nothing was hidden from your senses or your consciousness. Even then you could not know the object of your ideas concretely in any experience. What is demanded is not only this full and complete intuition, but also a complete synthesis together with the consciousness of its absolute totality, and no empirical knowledge can provide that. It follows that your question, your idea, is in no way necessary for explaining any phenomenon, and that the idea cannot in any sense have been given by the object itself. Such an object can never be presented to us, because no possible experience can give it. Whatever perceptions you may reach, you remain surrounded by conditions, whether in space or in time. You can discover nothing unconditioned, nor can you decide whether this unconditioned is to be located in an absolute beginning of the synthesis or in an absolute totality of a series that has no beginning. A whole, in the empirical sense of the term, is always merely relative. No possible experience can teach us anything about the absolute whole of magnitude (the universe), of division, of derivation, or of the condition of existence, or about whether this whole is to be produced by a finite or an infinite synthesis.
