You will not, for example, be able to explain the phenomena of a body any better by believing that it consists of simple parts than by believing that it consists of composite ones, since neither a simple phenomenon nor an infinite series of composition can ever be presented to your perception. Phenomena require and admit of explanation only insofar as the conditions of that explanation are given in perception. But the sum total of what is given in phenomena, considered as an absolute whole, is itself a perception, and so we cannot seek explanations of this whole beyond it, in other perceptions. The explanation of this whole is the proper object of the transcendental problems of pure reason.

Although the solution of these problems can never be reached through experience, we must not allow ourselves to say that it is uncertain how the object of our inquiry is constituted. That object exists in our own minds and cannot be discovered in experience. We need only ensure that our thoughts are consistent with one another, and avoid the amphiboly, or equivocation, of treating our idea as the representation of an object given empirically, and therefore to be known according to the laws of experience. A dogmatic solution is therefore not merely unsatisfactory but impossible. The critical solution, which can be perfectly certain, does not consider the question objectively. It proceeds instead by examining the foundation of the knowledge on which the question rests.

### Section V. Sceptical Exposition of the Cosmological Problems Presented in the Four Transcendental Ideas

We would gladly give up demanding a dogmatic answer to our questions if we understood in advance that, whatever the answer might be, it would only increase our ignorance. It would throw us from one incomprehensibility into another and from one obscurity into a still greater one, and might lead us into irreconcilable contradictions. If a dogmatic answer, affirmative or negative, is demanded, is it not prudent to set aside for a moment the apparent grounds for a solution that lie before us, and to consider first what we would gain if the answer favoured one side or the other? If in both cases the answer proves to be mere nonsense, we have an irresistible summons to investigate the question critically. Such an investigation would discover whether the question rests on a groundless presupposition and concerns an idea whose falsity would be exposed more easily in its application and consequences than in the bare representation of its content. This is the great usefulness of the sceptical method of treating the questions that pure reason puts to itself. By this method we can readily free ourselves from the confusions of dogmatism and put in their place a sober criticism. Like a genuine purgative, that criticism will successfully clear away the presumptuous notions of philosophy together with their consequence, the vain pretension to universal knowledge.

Suppose, then, that I could grasp the nature of a cosmological idea and see, before entering into any discussion of the subject, that whichever side of the question about the unconditioned in the regressive synthesis of phenomena it favoured, it must be either too large or too small for every concept of the understanding. I would then understand how the idea must be entirely empty and meaningless, since its object fails to fit, however we consider it. The idea relates to an object of experience, and therefore to an experience that must be adequate to and in agreement with a possible concept of the understanding. This is in fact the case with all cosmological concepts, which, for the reason just given, entangle reason in an unavoidable antinomy for as long as it remains attached to them. For suppose:

First, that the world has no beginning. In that case it is too large for our concept, because this concept, which consists in a successive regress, can never catch up with the whole of the eternity that has elapsed. Suppose instead that it has a beginning. Then it is too small for the concept of the understanding. A beginning presupposes a preceding time and so cannot be unconditioned, and the law governing the empirical use of the understanding obliges us to look for a still higher condition in time. The world is therefore plainly too small for this law.

The same holds for the double answer to the question of the world's extent in space. If the world is infinite and unbounded, it must be too large for every possible empirical concept. If it is finite and bounded, we are entitled to ask what determines these bounds. Empty space is not a self-subsistent correlate of things and cannot be a final condition, still less an empirical condition forming part of a possible experience, for how could we have any experience or perception of an absolute void? Yet the absolute totality of the empirical synthesis requires that the unconditioned be an empirical concept. A finite world is therefore too small for our concept.

Second, if every phenomenon in space (matter) consists of infinitely many parts, the regress of division is always too large for our concept. If the division of space must stop at some member of the division (the simple), the regress is too small for the idea of the unconditioned, since the member at which we have stopped still allows a regress to many further parts contained in the object.

Third, suppose that every event in the world happens according to the laws of nature. Then the causality of a cause must itself be an event, which requires a regress to a still higher cause, and so an unending extension of the series of conditions *a parte priori*, backward toward ever earlier conditions. Nature in its operation is therefore too large for any concept we can form in the synthesis of cosmic events.

If instead we admit spontaneously produced events, that is, free agency, then in our search for sufficient reasons we are driven by an unavoidable law of nature and compelled to appeal to the empirical law of causality. We then find that any such totality of connection in our synthesis is too small for our necessary empirical concept.

Fourth, if we assume the existence of an absolutely necessary being, whether it is the world itself, something in the world, or the cause of the world, we must place it in a time infinitely remote from any given moment, since otherwise it would depend on some other, higher existence. Such an existence is then too large for our empirical concept and can never be reached by any continued regress of synthesis. But if we believe that everything in the world, whether condition or conditioned, is contingent, then every given existence is too small for our concept, because we are compelled to look for some further existence on which it depends.

We have said that in all these cases the cosmological idea is either too large or too small for the empirical regress in a synthesis, and therefore for every possible concept of the understanding. Why did we not put it the other way around? Instead of accusing the cosmological idea of overshooting or falling short of its true aim, possible experience, why not say that in the first case the empirical concept is always too small for the idea, and in the second too large, and so lay the blame for these contradictions on the empirical regress? The reason is this. Possible experience alone can give reality to our concepts; without it a concept is a mere idea, lacking truth or any relation to an object. A possible empirical concept must therefore be the standard by which we judge whether an idea is anything more than an idea and a fiction of thought, or whether it relates to an object in the world. When we say that one thing is too large or too small in relation to another, we regard the first as existing for the sake of the second and as needing to be adapted to it. Among the idle questions debated in the old schools of dialectic was this one: "If a ball cannot pass through a hole, should we say that the ball is too large or that the hole is too small?" Here it makes no difference which expression we use, because we do not know which exists for the sake of the other. But we cannot say, "The man is too tall for his coat." We must say, "The coat is too short for the man."

We are thus led to the well-founded suspicion that the cosmological ideas, and all the conflicting sophistical assertions bound up with them, rest on a false and fictitious notion of the way in which the object of these ideas is presented to us. This suspicion may well show us how to expose the illusion that has so long led us away from the truth.

### Section VI. Transcendental Idealism as the Key to the Solution of Pure Cosmological Dialectic

In the transcendental aesthetic we proved that everything intuited in space and time, all objects of a possible experience, are nothing but phenomena, that is, mere representations. We also proved that these phenomena, as they are presented to us, whether as extended bodies or as series of changes, have no self-subsistent existence apart from human thought. This doctrine I call transcendental idealism. The realist, in the transcendental sense, treats these modifications of our sensibility, these mere representations, as things subsisting in themselves.

Elsewhere I have called this theory formal idealism, to distinguish it from material idealism, which doubts or denies the existence of external things. To avoid ambiguity, it seems advisable in many cases to use that term instead of the one given here.

It would be unjust to accuse us of holding the long-discredited theory of empirical idealism. That theory admits the reality of space but denies, or at least doubts, the existence of the bodies extended in it, and so leaves us without any adequate criterion for distinguishing reality from illusion. Its supporters have no difficulty admitting the reality of the phenomena of inner sense in time. Indeed, they go so far as to maintain that this inner experience is by itself sufficient proof of the real existence of its object as a thing in itself.

Transcendental idealism grants that the objects of outer intuition, as intuited in space, are real, and that all changes in time, as represented by inner sense, are real as well. Space is the form of the intuition we call outer, and no empirical representation could be given to us without objects in space, so we can and should regard the extended bodies in it as real. The same is true of representations in time. But time and space, together with all the phenomena in them, are not things in themselves. They are nothing but representations and cannot exist outside and apart from the mind. Even the mind's sensuous inner intuition of itself, as the object of consciousness, is not the real, proper self as it exists in itself. The determination of that intuition is represented by the succession of the mind's different states in time, and it is not the transcendental subject but only a phenomenon presented to the sensibility of this being, which remains unknown to us. This inner phenomenon cannot be accepted as a self-subsisting thing, for its condition is time, and time cannot be the condition of a thing in itself. Yet the empirical truth of phenomena in space and time is secured beyond any possible doubt and is sufficiently distinguished from the illusions of dreams or fancy, since phenomena of both kinds have a proper and thorough connection within one experience according to empirical laws.

The objects of experience, then, are not things in themselves. They are given only in experience and have no existence apart from and independent of it. We must certainly admit that there may be inhabitants on the moon, although no one has ever observed them. But this assertion means only that we might encounter them someday in the possible progress of experience, for whatever stands in connection with a perception according to the laws governing the progress of experience is real. Such beings therefore really exist if they stand in empirical connection with my actual consciousness, although they are not real in themselves, that is, apart from the progress of experience.

Nothing is actually given to us, and we can be conscious of nothing as real, except a perception and the empirical progression from it to other possible perceptions. Phenomena, as mere representations, are real only in perception, and perception is in fact nothing but the reality of an empirical representation, that is, of a phenomenon. To call a phenomenon a real thing before it is perceived means either that we must meet with it in the progress of experience, or it means nothing at all. Only of a thing in itself can I say that it exists without relation to the senses and to experience.

But here we are speaking only of phenomena in space and time, both of which are determinations of sensibility, and not of things in themselves. It follows that phenomena are not things in themselves but mere representations, which do not exist at all unless they are given in us, in perception.

The faculty of sensuous intuition is, properly speaking, a receptivity: a capacity to be affected in a certain way by representations whose relation to one another is a pure intuition of space and time, the pure forms of sensibility. These representations are called objects insofar as they are connected and determinable in this relation (in space and time) according to the laws of the unity of experience. The non-sensuous cause of these representations is entirely unknown to us and therefore cannot be intuited as an object. Such an object could be represented neither in space nor in time, and without these conditions no intuition or representation is possible. We may nonetheless call the non-sensuous cause of phenomena the transcendental object, but only as a correlate that the mind posits for sensibility understood as a receptivity. To this transcendental object we may ascribe the entire connection and extent of our possible perceptions, and we may say that it is given and exists in itself prior to all experience. The phenomena that correspond to it, however, are not given as things in themselves. They are given in experience alone. They are mere representations, and they acquire significance and a relation to a real object only from perceptions. This holds only on the condition that this or that perception, indicating an object, stands in complete connection with all the others according to the rules of the unity of experience. So we can say: "The things that really existed in past time are given in the transcendental object of experience." Yet they are real objects for me only insofar as I can represent to myself a regressive series of possible perceptions that leads me back through elapsed time as the condition of the present. That series follows the indications of history or the footsteps of cause and effect, according to empirical laws; in a word, it follows the course of the world. This series in past time is represented as real not in itself but only in connection with a possible experience. When I say that certain events occurred in the past, then, I am asserting nothing more than the possibility of extending the chain of experience from the present perception back to the conditions that determine it in time.

If I represent to myself all objects existing throughout all space and all time, I do not thereby place them in space and time prior to all experience. On the contrary, such a representation is nothing more than the idea of a possible experience taken in its absolute completeness. Only in experience are those objects, which are nothing but representations, given. When I say that they existed before my experience, I mean only that I must begin with the perception now present to me and follow the track it indicates until I find them in some part or region of experience. The cause of the empirical conditions of this progression is transcendental, and so necessarily beyond our knowledge. The same holds for the question of which member I must stop at, and at what point in the regress I am to find it. But that is not our concern. We are concerned only with the law of progression in experience, in which objects, that is, phenomena, are given. It makes no difference whether I say, "In the progress of experience I may discover stars a hundred times farther away than the most distant now visible," or, "Stars at that distance may be found in space, even though no one has discovered them or ever will." If they were given as things in themselves, without any relation to possible experience, they would be nothing to me and therefore no objects at all, since they would not be contained in the regressive series of experience. But sometimes these phenomena must be used to build or support the cosmological idea of an absolute whole, and we find ourselves dealing with a question that oversteps the limits of possible experience. In that case it becomes very important to distinguish properly between the different theories of the reality of sensuous objects. Only then can we avoid the illusion that inevitably arises from misinterpreting our empirical concepts.

### Section VII. Critical Solution of the Cosmological Problem

The antinomy of pure reason rests on the following dialectical argument: "If the conditioned is given, the whole series of its conditions is also given; but objects of the senses are given as conditioned; therefore..." The major premise of this syllogism seems natural and evident. Yet the syllogism introduces as many cosmological ideas as there are different kinds of conditions in the synthesis of phenomena, insofar as those conditions form a series. These ideas demand absolute totality in the series, and so they entangle reason in difficulties from which it cannot free itself. Before exposing the fallacy in this dialectical argument, we need a correct understanding of certain concepts that appear in it.

First, the following proposition is evident and beyond doubt: "If the conditioned is given, a regress through the series of all its conditions is thereby imposed upon us as a task." The very concept of something conditioned is the concept of something related to a condition. If that condition is itself conditioned, it is related to a further condition, and so on through every member of the series. The proposition is therefore analytic and has nothing to fear from transcendental criticism. It is a logical postulate of reason: to follow, as far as possible, the connection of a concept with its conditions.

Second, suppose that both the conditioned and its condition are things in themselves, and that the conditioned is given. Then the regress to the condition is not merely required; the condition is actually given along with the conditioned. This holds for every member of the series. The conditioned can exist only in and through that series, and so the entire series of conditions, and with it the unconditioned, is given at once in the very fact that the conditioned is given. In this case the synthesis of the conditioned with its condition is a synthesis of the understanding alone. It represents things as they are, without asking whether or how we can come to know them. Phenomena are a different matter. As mere representations, they are not given at all unless I attain knowledge of them, which is to say unless I attain them, for they are nothing more than empirical cognitions. So when I am dealing with phenomena, I am not entitled to say: "If the conditioned is given, all its conditions (as phenomena) are also given." I therefore cannot infer, from the fact that something conditioned is given, the absolute totality of the series of its conditions. Phenomena are nothing but an empirical synthesis in apprehension or perception, and so they are given only in that synthesis. When we speak of phenomena, then, it does not follow that the synthesis making up the empirical condition of a given conditioned is given and presupposed along with it. That synthesis can be established only by actually carrying out the regress through the series of conditions. What we are entitled to say in this case is that a regress to the conditions of the conditioned is enjoined upon us. This regress is a continuous empirical synthesis. If the conditions are not given, they are at least demanded, and we are sure to find them in the course of this regress.

We can now see that the two premises of the cosmological syllogism use the word "conditioned" in different senses. The major premise takes it in the transcendental sense it has in the pure category. The minor premise takes it in the empirical sense it has in the category as applied to phenomena. The syllogism therefore contains a dialectical fallacy, what logicians call a *sophisma figurae dictionis*, a fallacy that arises when a term shifts its meaning between premises. Yet this fallacy is not deliberately contrived. It is an entirely natural illusion of ordinary human reason. When something is given as conditioned, we presuppose in the major premise its conditions and their series, unperceived and unseen, as it were. We do so because this is nothing more than the logical demand for complete premises sufficient to a given conclusion. Here time is left out entirely from the connection between conditioned and condition, and both are assumed to be given in themselves and at the same time. In the major premise we abstracted completely from all conditions of intuition. It is just as natural, in the minor premise, to treat phenomena in the same way, as things in themselves and as objects presented to the pure understanding. Yet it is only under those conditions of intuition that objects can be given at all. In doing so, we overlooked a significant distinction between the concepts. In the major premise, the synthesis of the conditioned with its condition, and the complete series of conditions, are not limited by time and contain no notion of succession. In the minor premise, by contrast, the empirical synthesis and the series of conditions in the world of phenomena are necessarily successive and given only in time. It follows that I cannot presuppose in the minor premise, as I did in the major, the absolute totality of the synthesis and of the series it represents. In the major premise all the members of the series are given as things in themselves, free of any limitation or condition of time. In the minor they are possible only in and through a successive regress, which exists only insofar as it is actually carried out in the world of phenomena.

The argument commonly used to support cosmological assertions has now been shown to be defective, and so both parties may rightly be dismissed as advancing claims without ground or title. But the case is not closed merely by convincing them that one or both were in the wrong and had defended an assertion without valid proof. Nothing seems clearer than this: if one person maintains, "The world has a beginning," and another, "The world has no beginning," one of the two must be right. But it is equally clear that if the evidence on both sides is equal, it is impossible to discover where the truth lies. The dispute goes on, even though the parties have been urged to make peace before the tribunal of reason. Only one way of settling the question remains. We must convince the two parties, who refute each other so conclusively and so ably, that they are disputing about nothing. A transcendental illusion has been mocking them with visions of reality where there is none. We shall now set before the reader this method of resolving a dispute that cannot be decided on its own merits.

Zeno of Elea was a subtle dialectician, and Plato sharply rebuked him as a sophist. The charge was that, from the low motive of displaying his skill in argument, Zeno would defend a proposition and then overturn it with arguments as strong and convincing on one side as on the other. He maintained, for example, that God is neither finite nor infinite, neither in motion nor at rest, neither similar nor dissimilar to any other thing. In his view, God was probably nothing more than the world. To the philosophers who criticized his method, it seemed that he meant to deny both of two mutually contradictory propositions outright, which is absurd. I cannot believe the charge is just. The first of these propositions I shall examine in more detail shortly. As for the others, suppose that by the word God he meant simply the universe. Then he must have meant that it can neither remain permanently in one place, that is, be at rest, nor change its place, that is, move. All places are within the universe, and the universe itself is therefore in no place. Again, if the universe contains within itself everything that exists, it can be neither similar nor dissimilar to any other thing, since there is in fact no other thing with which it could be compared. Sometimes two opposed judgments both presuppose a condition that is contingent, impossible, or arbitrary. Their opposition is not a genuine contradiction. When that condition vanishes, both judgments fall away together, because each depended on it for its validity.

Consider the statement "Every body has either a good smell or a bad smell." Here "body" means any physical body. The statement leaves out a third possible judgment, namely that a body has no smell at all, and so both of the conflicting statements may be false. Now consider instead "Every body is either good-smelling or not good-smelling (*vel suaveolens vel non-suaveolens*)." These two judgments are contradictory opposites. The contradictory of the first, "Some bodies are not good-smelling," also takes in those bodies that have no smell at all. The earlier pair of judgments was opposed *per disparata*, as disparate alternatives rather than as contradictories. In that pair, a contingent condition was attached to the concept of body, namely that it has a smell. That condition remained attached to both conflicting statements instead of being dropped from the second. The second is therefore not the contradictory of the first.

Accordingly, suppose we say, "The world is either infinite in extension or it is not infinite (*non est infinitus*)." If the first proposition is false, then its contradictory, "The world is not infinite," must be true. In that case I would be denying the existence of an infinite world without thereby affirming the existence of a finite one. But suppose we frame the proposition as "The world is either infinite or finite (non-infinite)." Then both statements may be false. Here we regard the world as determined in itself with respect to quantity. In one judgment we deny its infinitude, and with it, perhaps, its independent existence. In the other we attach to the world, regarded as a thing in itself, a further determination, finitude. The second judgment may be false just as well as the first, if the world is not given as a thing in itself at all. In that case it is neither finite nor infinite in quantity. I may be permitted to call this kind of opposition dialectical, and the opposition of contradictories analytic. Of two dialectically opposed judgments, then, both may be false. The one is not merely the contradictory of the other; it asserts more than a full and complete contradiction requires.

Take the two propositions "The world is infinite in quantity" and "The world is finite in quantity." When we treat them as contradictory opposites, we are assuming that the world, the complete series of phenomena, is a thing in itself. On that assumption it would remain a fixed quantity whether I deny the infinite or the finite regress in the series of its phenomena. But suppose we abandon this assumption, this transcendental illusion, and deny that the world is a thing in itself. Then the contradictory opposition is transformed into a merely dialectical one. The world does not exist in itself, independently of the regressive series of my representations. It therefore exists neither as a whole that is infinite in itself nor as a whole that is finite in itself. The universe exists for me only in the empirical regress of the series of phenomena, not in itself. If, then, it is always conditioned, it is never given completely, as a whole. It is therefore not an unconditioned whole, and it does not exist as such with either an infinite or a finite quantity.

What has been said here of the first cosmological idea, the absolute totality of quantity in phenomena, applies to the others as well. The series of conditions can be found only in the regressive synthesis itself. It cannot be found in the phenomenon considered as a thing in itself, given prior to any regress. I am therefore obliged to say: "The aggregate of parts in a given phenomenon is in itself neither finite nor infinite. These parts are given only in the regressive synthesis of division, a synthesis that is never given in absolute completeness, either as finite or as infinite." The same holds for the series of subordinated causes, and for the series that runs from the conditioned up to unconditioned and necessary existence. Neither series can ever be regarded as finite or infinite in itself and in its totality. Each is a series of subordinated representations, and as such it exists only in the dynamical regress. It cannot be regarded as existing before that regress, or as a self-subsistent series of things.

In this way the antinomy of pure reason in its cosmological ideas disappears. The demonstration above has shown that it is merely the product of a dialectical and illusory opposition. That opposition arises from applying the idea of absolute totality, which is admissible only as a condition of things in themselves, to phenomena. Phenomena exist only in our representations and, when they form a series, only in a successive regress. This antinomy of reason may nonetheless be of real benefit to our speculative interests. It contributes no dogmatic addition to knowledge, but it gives us further material support in our critical inquiries. It furnishes an indirect proof of the transcendental ideality of phenomena, should anyone remain unsatisfied with the direct proof set out in the Transcendental Aesthetic. The proof takes the form of a dilemma. If the world is a whole existing in itself, it must be either finite or infinite. But it is neither finite nor infinite, as the thesis has shown on the one side and the antithesis on the other. Therefore the world, the sum of all phenomena, is not a whole existing in itself. It follows that phenomena are nothing apart from our representations, and this is precisely what we mean by transcendental ideality.

This observation is of some importance. It shows that the proofs offered in the fourfold antinomy are not mere sophistries. They are not fallacious; they are grounded in the nature of reason and are valid, on the supposition that phenomena are things in themselves. The conflict between the judgments that follow from them makes it evident that the error lay in that initial supposition, and so helps us discover the true constitution of the objects of sense. This transcendental dialectic gives no support to skepticism. It does, however, offer a decisive demonstration of the advantages of the skeptical method. The great usefulness of that method is evident in the antinomy, where the arguments of reason were allowed to confront one another at full strength. The outcome of these conflicts of reason is not what we expected, and we have gained no positive, dogmatic addition to metaphysics. Still, we have reaped a great advantage in correcting our judgments on these subjects.

### Section VIII. Regulative Principle of Pure Reason in relation to the Cosmological Ideas

The cosmological principle of totality could give us no certain knowledge of the maximum in the series of conditions in the world of sense, considered as a thing in itself. The only means of approaching that maximum is the actual regress through the series. This principle of pure reason may therefore still be considered valid, though not as an axiom that lets us think totality as actually present in the object. It is valid instead as a problem set for the understanding. It requires the understanding to begin and to continue the regress through the series of conditions of a given conditioned, in conformity with the idea of totality in the mind. In the world of sense, that is, in space and time, every condition we discover in investigating phenomena is itself conditioned. Objects of the senses are not things in themselves. If they were, an absolutely unconditioned might be reached in the progress of knowledge. They are merely empirical representations, whose conditions must always be found in intuition. Properly speaking, then, the principle of reason is a mere rule. It prescribes a regress through the series of conditions for given phenomena and forbids us to halt or rest at anything absolutely unconditioned. It is therefore not a principle of the possibility of experience or of empirical knowledge of objects of sense. Consequently it is not a principle of the understanding, since every experience is confined within limits set by the given intuition. Still less is it a constitutive principle of reason authorizing us to extend our concept of the world of sense beyond all possible experience. It is merely a principle for enlarging and extending experience as far as human faculties allow. It forbids us to treat any empirical limit as absolute. It is thus a principle of reason that prescribes, as a rule, how we ought to proceed in our empirical regress. But it cannot anticipate or indicate, before that regress is carried out, what is given in the object itself. For this reason I have called it a regulative principle of reason. The principle of the absolute totality of the series of conditions, as existing in itself and given in the object, is by contrast a constitutive cosmological principle. This distinction immediately exposes the falsehood of the constitutive principle. It also keeps us from ascribing objective reality to an idea that is valid only as a rule, through what may be called a transcendental subreption: a covert substitution of one kind of claim for another.

To understand the proper meaning of this rule of pure reason, we must first note what it can and cannot tell us. It cannot tell us what the object is. It can tell us only how the empirical regress is to be carried on in order to arrive at the complete concept of the object. If it told us anything about what the object is, it would be a constitutive principle, and such a principle is impossible given the nature of pure reason. It will not, therefore, allow us to establish conclusions such as "The series of conditions for a given conditioned is in itself finite," or "It is infinite." In that case we would be thinking, in the mere idea of absolute totality, an object that is not and cannot be given in experience. We would be ascribing to a series of phenomena a reality that is objective and independent of the empirical synthesis. This idea of reason, then, can be regarded as valid only as a rule for the regressive synthesis in the series of conditions. According to this rule, we must proceed from the conditioned, through all intermediate and subordinate conditions, toward the unconditioned, even though this goal is never reached and can never be reached. The absolutely unconditioned cannot be found within the sphere of experience.

We now turn to defining clearly our concept of a synthesis that can never be complete. Two terms are commonly used for this purpose. They are taken to express different and distinguishable notions, although the basis of the distinction has never been clearly set out. Mathematicians speak of a *progressus in infinitum*, a progression to infinity. Philosophers prefer *progressus in indefinitum*, a progression to an indefinite extent. I will not detain the reader with an examination of the reasons for this distinction, or with remarks on the right or wrong use of the terms. Instead I shall try to define these concepts precisely, so far as this Critique requires.

We may properly say of a straight line that it can be produced, that is, extended, to infinity. Here the distinction between a *progressus in infinitum* and a *progressus in indefinitum* is a mere subtlety. For although, when we say "Produce a straight line," it is more correct to say *in*

*indefinitum* than *in infinitum*, since the former means "Produce it as far as you please" and the latter "You must never stop producing it," the expression *in infinitum* is perfectly correct when we are speaking only of our power to do so, because we can always make the line longer if we choose, on to infinity. This remark holds in every case where we speak of a *progressus*, an advance from the condition to the conditioned: such a possible advance always proceeds to infinity. We may start from a given pair in the descending line of generation, from father to son, and conceive of a never-ending line of descendants issuing from it. In such a case reason does not demand absolute totality in the series, because it does not presuppose that totality as a condition already given (*datum*), but only as something conditioned that is capable of being given (*dabile*).

The case is entirely different with the problem of how far the regress, the movement that ascends from a given conditioned to its conditions, must extend. Can I say that it is a regress *in infinitum*, or only *in indefinitum*? Setting out, for example, from the human beings now alive in the world, may I ascend through the series of their ancestors *in infinitum*? Or can I say only that, as far as I have gone, I have found no empirical ground for considering the series limited, so that I am justified, and indeed compelled, to search for still earlier ancestors, although the idea of reason does not oblige me to presuppose them?

My answer is this: if the series is given as a whole in empirical intuition, the regress through its internal conditions proceeds *in infinitum*; but if only one member of the series is given, and the regress must proceed from it toward absolute totality, then the regress is possible only *in indefinitum*. Take, for example, the division of a portion of matter given within certain limits, which is to say a body. This division proceeds *in infinitum*. The condition of the whole is its part, the condition of that part is a part of the part, and so on; and since no unconditioned, indivisible member of the series of conditions is ever found in this regress of decomposition, experience offers no reason for stopping the division. On the contrary, the more remote members of the division are actually and empirically given before the division is carried out, and so the division proceeds to infinity. The series of ancestors of any given human being, by contrast, is not given in its absolute totality in any experience. The regress still advances from every member of the genealogy to one still higher, and it never meets an empirical limit that would present an absolutely unconditioned member. But because the members of such a series are not contained in an empirical intuition of the whole before the regress begins, the regress does not proceed to infinity but only *in indefinitum*: we are called upon to discover further and higher members, which are themselves always conditioned.

In neither case, whether in the *regressus in infinitum* or in the *regressus in indefinitum*, is the series of conditions to be regarded as actually infinite in the object itself. That might be true of things in themselves, but it cannot be said of phenomena, which, as conditions of one another, are given only in the empirical regress itself. The question, then, is no longer "What is the magnitude of this series of conditions in itself? Is it finite or infinite?" for the series is nothing in itself. The question is rather "How is the empirical regress to be begun, and how far ought we to carry it?" And here a significant distinction in the application of this rule becomes clear. If the whole is given empirically, it is possible to go back through the series of its internal conditions to infinity. But if the whole is not given, and can be given only by and through the empirical regress, I can say only: "It is possible to go on to infinity, proceeding to still higher conditions in the series." In the first case, I am justified in asserting that more members are empirically given in the object than I reach in the regress of decomposition. In the second, I am justified only in saying that I can always go further in the regress, because no member of the series is given as absolutely unconditioned; a higher member is therefore always possible, and inquiry into it is necessary. In the one case it is necessary to find further members of the series; in the other it is necessary to inquire after them, since experience presents no absolute limit to the regress. For either you have no perception that absolutely limits your empirical regress, in which case the regress cannot be regarded as complete; or you do have such a limiting perception, in which case that perception is no part of your series, since what limits must be distinct from what it limits, and you are obliged to continue your regress up to this condition as well, and so on.

The application of these remarks in the following section will place them in their proper light.

### Section IX. Of the Empirical Use of the Regulative Principle of Reason with Regard to the Cosmological Ideas

We have shown that neither the concepts of reason nor those of the understanding admit of any transcendental use. We have shown, likewise, that the demand for absolute totality in the series of conditions in the world of sense arises from a transcendental use of reason, which rests on the belief that phenomena are to be regarded as things in themselves. It follows that we are not required to answer the question of the absolute magnitude of a series, whether it is in itself limited or unlimited. We are called upon only to determine how far we must carry the empirical regress from condition to condition in order to arrive, in conformity with the rule of reason, at a full and correct answer to the questions that reason itself proposes.

This principle of reason is therefore valid only as a rule for extending possible experience, since its invalidity as a principle constitutive of phenomena in themselves has been sufficiently demonstrated. And with that, the antinomial conflict of reason with itself is brought to a complete end. We have not only offered a critical solution of the fallacy concealed in reason's opposing claims, but have also shown the true meaning of the ideas that gave rise to them. The dialectical principle of reason has thus been converted into a doctrinal one. Indeed, if this principle, in the subjective sense we have shown to be its only true meaning, can be secured as a principle for the unceasing extension of the use of our understanding, its influence and value are just as great as if it were an axiom for determining objects a priori. Such an axiom could exert no stronger influence on the extension and correction of our knowledge than by securing for the principles of the understanding the widest possible use in the field of experience.

#### I. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Composition of Phenomena in the Universe

Here, as with the other cosmological problems, the regulative principle of reason rests on the proposition that in our empirical regress no experience of an absolute limit can be found, and therefore no experience of a condition that is itself absolutely unconditioned. The truth of this proposition rests in turn on the consideration that such an experience would have to represent phenomena as bounded by nothing, by mere emptiness, against which our continued regress through perception would have to come to a stop. And that is impossible.

This proposition, which declares that every condition reached in the empirical regress must itself be regarded as empirically conditioned, contains in explicit terms the rule that, however far I may have advanced in the ascending series, I must always look for some higher member of it, whether or not that member is to become known to me through experience.

Nothing more is needed, then, to solve the first cosmological problem than to decide whether, in the regress toward the unconditioned magnitude of the universe in space and time, this never-limited ascent should be called a *regressus in infinitum* or *in indefinitum*.

The general representation we form of the series of all past states of the world, or of all the things that now exist in it, is itself nothing more than a possible empirical regress, which the mind conceives, though in an indeterminate way, and which gives rise to the concept of a series of conditions for a given object. Now, I have a concept of the universe, but not an intuition of it as a whole. I therefore cannot infer the magnitude of the regress from the magnitude of the world and determine the one by the other. On the contrary, I must first form a concept of the magnitude of the world from the magnitude of the empirical regress. Yet of this regress I know nothing more than that I ought to proceed from every given member of the series of conditions to one still higher. This does not determine the magnitude of the universe, and we cannot affirm that the regress proceeds *in infinitum*. Such an affirmation would anticipate the members of the series not yet reached and represent their number as beyond the grasp of any empirical synthesis. It would thus determine the magnitude of the cosmos before the regress, even if only negatively, which is impossible. The world is not given in its totality in any intuition, and so its magnitude cannot be given before the regress. It follows that we can make no declaration about the magnitude of the cosmos in itself, not even that the regress within it is a regress *in infinitum*. We must only try to reach a concept of the magnitude of the universe in conformity with the rule that governs the empirical regress within it. This rule requires only that we never admit an absolute limit to our series, however far we have advanced in it, but always subordinate every phenomenon to another as its condition, and therefore advance to that higher phenomenon. Such a regress is the *regressus in indefinitum*, which, because it determines no magnitude in the object, is clearly distinguishable from the *regressus in infinitum*.

The cosmic series can be neither greater nor smaller than the possible empirical regress on which its concept rests. And since this regress can be neither a determinate infinite regress nor, still less, a determinate finite one, absolutely limited, it is evident that we cannot regard the world as either finite or infinite, because the regress that gives us our representation of the world is itself neither finite nor infinite.

It follows from what we have said that we are not justified in declaring the world infinite in space or in past time. The concept of an infinite given magnitude is empirical, but we cannot apply the concept of an infinite magnitude to the world as an object of the senses. I cannot say, "The regress from a given perception to everything limited in space or time proceeds *in infinitum*," for this presupposes an infinite cosmic magnitude. Nor can I say, "It is finite," for an absolute limit is equally impossible in experience. I am therefore not entitled to make any assertion at all about the whole object of experience, the world of sense; I must confine my claims to the rule by which experience, or empirical knowledge, is to be obtained.

To the question of the magnitude of the cosmos, therefore, the first and negative answer is: "The world has no beginning in time and no absolute limit in space."

If it had, it would be bounded by empty time on the one side and by empty space on the other. Now, the world as a phenomenon cannot be bounded in itself in this way, since a phenomenon is not a thing in itself. It would therefore have to be possible for us to perceive this boundary of empty time and empty space. But such a perception, such an experience, is impossible, because it has no content. An absolute cosmic limit is therefore empirically, and hence absolutely, impossible.

The reader will note that this proof differs sharply from the dogmatic demonstration offered in the antithesis of the first antinomy. That demonstration took for granted that the world is a thing in itself, given in its totality prior to any regress, and it denied the world any determinate position in space and time unless the world was taken to occupy all time and all space. Our conclusion there was accordingly different from the one reached here, for in the antithesis we inferred the actual infinity of the world.

From this follows the affirmative answer: "The regress in the series of phenomena, as a determination of the magnitude of the cosmos, proceeds *in indefinitum*." This is equivalent to saying: "The world of sense has no absolute magnitude, but the empirical regress, through which alone the world of sense is presented to us on the side of its conditions, rests on a rule. That rule requires the regress to proceed from every member of the series, as conditioned, to one still more remote, whether through our own experience, through history, or through the chain of cause and effect, and never to stop at any point in this extension of the possible empirical use of the understanding." And this is the proper and only use that reason can make of its principles.

This rule does not prescribe an unending regress within a single kind of phenomenon. It does not forbid us, for example, as we ascend from an individual human being through the line of his ancestors, to expect that at some point we shall arrive at a first, original pair; nor does it forbid us to admit, in the series of heavenly bodies, a sun at the farthest possible distance from some center. All it demands is a perpetual advance from phenomenon to phenomenon, even where these yield no actual perception, as when our perceptions are too faint for us to become conscious of them, since such phenomena nonetheless belong to possible experience.

Every beginning is in time, and every limit of extension is in space. But space and time exist only in the world of sense. Phenomena in the world are therefore limited conditionally, but the world itself is limited neither conditionally nor unconditionally.

For this reason, and because neither the world nor the cosmic series of conditions for a given conditioned can ever be completely given, our concept of the magnitude of the cosmos is given only in and through the regress, and not before it in a collective intuition. But the regress itself is nothing more than the process of determining that magnitude, and so it cannot give us any determinate concept of it, still less the concept of a magnitude that is infinite relative to some standard of measure. The regress therefore does not proceed to infinity, as though an infinity were given, but only to an indefinite extent, in order to present to us a magnitude that is realized only in and through the regress itself.

#### II. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Division of a Whole Given in Intuition

When I divide a whole given in intuition, I proceed from a conditioned to its conditions. The division of the whole into parts (*subdivisio* or *decompositio*) is a regress through the series of these conditions. The absolute totality of this series would be actually reached and given to the mind if the regress could arrive at simple parts. But if every part in a continuing decomposition is itself divisible, then the division, which is the regress, proceeds from the conditioned to its conditions *in infinitum*. The conditions, the parts, are themselves contained in the conditioned, and since the conditioned is given in a bounded intuition, its conditions are all given along with it. This regress, therefore, cannot be called a *regressus in indefinitum*, as was the case with the preceding cosmological idea, where the regress moved from the conditioned to conditions that were not given at the same time and along with it but could be discovered only through the empirical regress. Even so, we are not entitled to say of a whole of this kind, divisible *in infinitum*, that it consists of an infinite number of parts. Although all the parts are contained in the intuition of the whole, the whole division is not. The division exists only in the progressive decomposition, in the regress itself, which is what first makes the series possible and actual. Since this regress is infinite, all the members, or parts, that it reaches must be contained in the given whole as an aggregate. But the complete series of the division is not contained there. Being infinite in succession and never complete, this series cannot represent an infinite number of members, still less a combination of those members into a whole.

Apply this remark first to space. Every bounded portion of space presented in intuition is a whole whose parts are always themselves spaces, however far it is subdivided. Every bounded space is therefore divisible to infinity.

Apply it next to an external phenomenon enclosed within limits, which is to say a body. The divisibility of a body rests on the divisibility of space, which is the condition that makes the body possible as an extended whole. A body is therefore divisible to infinity, though it does not, for that reason, consist of an infinite number of parts.

It might certainly seem that, since a body must be conceived as substance in space, the law of divisibility would not apply to it insofar as it is substance. In the case of space, we may and must grant that division, however far carried, can never wholly abolish composition: the smallest part of space must still consist of spaces, since otherwise space would cease to exist altogether, which is impossible. By contrast, the claim that nothing would remain once all composition in matter had been abolished in thought does not seem consistent with the concept of substance. Substance, properly speaking, should be the subject of all composition, and it should remain even after the combination of its attributes in space, which made up the body, has been abolished in thought. But this does not hold for substance in the world of phenomena, which is not a thing in itself conceived through the pure category. Phenomenal substance is not an absolute subject. It is merely an enduring sensory image, nothing more than an intuition, and the unconditioned is nowhere to be found in it.

But although this rule of advance to infinity is legitimate and applies to the subdivision of a phenomenon considered simply as something that fills space, it does not apply to a whole made up of a number of distinct parts and constituting a *quantum discretum*, a discrete magnitude, which is to say an organized body. We cannot grant that every part of an organized whole is itself organized, so that in analyzing it to infinity we must always meet with organized parts, although we may allow that the parts of the matter we decompose *in infinitum* might be organized. The infinity of the division of a phenomenon in space rests entirely on the fact that its divisibility is given only in and through this infinity: an indeterminate number of parts is given, while the parts themselves are given and determined only in and through the subdivision. In short, the infinity of the division necessarily presupposes that the whole is not already divided in itself. Our division therefore determines a number of parts in the whole that extends exactly as far as the actual regress of the division. The very notion of a body organized to infinity, on the other hand, represents the whole as already divided in itself. We would then expect to find in it a number of parts that is determinate and yet infinite, which is self-contradictory. We should have a whole containing a series of members that could never be completed in any regress, a series infinite and yet at the same time complete in an organized composite. Infinite divisibility applies only to a *quantum continuum*, a continuous magnitude, and rests entirely on the infinite divisibility of space. In a *quantum discretum*, however, the multitude of parts or units is always determinate, and therefore always equal to some number. How far a body may be organized, only experience can tell us; and even if, as far as our experience of this or that body has reached, we have found no inorganic part, such parts must exist within possible experience. But how far the transcendental division of a phenomenon must extend is a question experience cannot answer. It is answered only by the principle of reason that forbids us ever to regard the empirical regress, in the analysis of an extended body, as absolutely complete.

#### Concluding Remark on the Solution of the Transcendental Mathematical Ideas, and Introduction to the Solution of the Dynamical Ideas

We presented the antinomy of pure reason in the form of a table, and we tried to show the ground of this self-contradiction in reason and the only means of bringing it to an end: declaring both contradictory statements false. In these antinomies we represented the conditions of phenomena as belonging to the conditioned according to relations of space and time, which is the usual assumption of the common understanding. In this respect, all the dialectical representations of totality in the series of conditions for a given conditioned were entirely homogeneous. The condition was always a member of the same series as the conditioned, and so the homogeneity of the whole series was assured. In that case the regress could never be conceived as complete; or, if it was, a member that was in fact conditioned was falsely taken to be a first member, and therefore unconditioned. In such an antinomy, then, we considered not the object itself, the conditioned, but the series of conditions belonging to the object and the magnitude of that series. Hence the difficulty arose, and it could not be settled by ruling on the claims of either party. It could be resolved only by cutting the knot, by declaring that the series proposed by reason was either too long or too short for the understanding, which in neither case could make its concepts adequate to the ideas.

But we have so far overlooked an essential difference among the concepts of the understanding that reason tries to raise to the rank of ideas: two of them concern a mathematical synthesis of phenomena, and two a dynamical one. Until now there was no need to call attention to this distinction. Just as, in our general representation of all the transcendental ideas, we considered them under the conditions of phenomena, so in the two mathematical ideas our discussion was concerned solely with an object in the world of phenomena. But as we now proceed to consider the dynamical concepts of the understanding, and their adequacy to ideas, we must keep this distinction firmly in view. It will open an entirely new perspective on the conflict in which reason finds itself entangled. In the first two antinomies, both parties were dismissed from court, because each had built its case on a false presupposition. In the present case, there is hope of finding a presupposition consistent with the demands of reason. Reason, acting as judge, can supply the grounds of claim that both parties had left incomplete, and the dispute can then be settled on its merits: not by throwing both claimants out of court, but by weighing the arguments on each side.

If we consider these series only in their extension, asking whether they are adequate to the ideas, the conditions within them may all be regarded as homogeneous, that is, of one and the same kind. But the concept of the understanding that underlies these ideas contains a synthesis either of the homogeneous or of the heterogeneous. The first is presupposed in every quantity, whether we are composing it or dividing it. The second occurs in the dynamical synthesis of cause and effect, and also of the necessary and the contingent. It follows that in the mathematical series of phenomena only a sensuous condition is admissible, a condition that is itself a member of the series. The dynamical series of sensuous conditions, by contrast, admits a heterogeneous condition: one that is not a member of the series but, being purely intelligible, lies outside and beyond it. In this way reason is satisfied, and an unconditioned can be placed at the head of the series of phenomena without throwing the series into confusion or breaking it off in violation of the principles of the understanding.

Because the dynamical ideas admit a condition of phenomena that is not itself part of the series of phenomena, a result follows that we would not have expected from an antinomy. In the earlier cases, both contradictory dialectical assertions were declared false. Here, by contrast, we find the conditioned in the dynamical series connected with a condition that is empirically unconditioned yet non-sensuous, and so justice is done both to the understanding on one side and to reason on the other. The understanding cannot admit among phenomena any condition that is itself empirically unconditioned. But if we can think of an intelligible condition for a conditioned phenomenon, one that is not a member of the series of phenomena, without breaking the series of empirical conditions, then such a condition may be admitted as empirically unconditioned, while the empirical regress continues regular, unceasing, and intact. Moreover, while the dialectical arguments for an unconditioned totality within mere phenomena collapse, both propositions of reason may be shown to be true, each taken in its proper sense. This could not happen with the cosmological ideas that demanded a mathematically unconditioned unity, since no condition could be placed at the head of the series of phenomena except one that was itself a phenomenon, and therefore itself a member of the series.

#### III. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Derivation of Cosmic Events from Their Causes

Only two kinds of causality can be conceived: the causality of nature and the causality of freedom. The first is the connection of one state in the world of sense with a preceding state, which the later one follows according to a law. The causality of phenomena is subject to conditions of time, and a preceding state that had always existed could not have produced an effect that first appears at a particular moment. The causality of the cause must therefore itself be an effect. It must itself have come into being, and so, according to the principle of the understanding, it in turn requires a cause.

By freedom, on the other hand, taken in its cosmological sense, we must understand a power of beginning a state spontaneously, a power whose causality is therefore not subordinated to some other cause that determines it in time. Freedom in this sense is a pure transcendental idea. In the first place, it contains nothing borrowed from experience. In the second place, its object cannot be given or determined in any experience, because it is a universal law of the very possibility of experience that everything that happens must have a cause, and consequently that the causality of a cause, being itself something that has happened, must also have a cause. On this view, the entire field of experience, however far it may extend, contains nothing that is not subject to the laws of nature. But since in this way we can never reach an absolute totality of conditions in the series of causes and effects, reason creates the idea of a spontaneity that can begin to act of itself, without any prior cause determining it to action according to the natural law of causality.

It is especially noteworthy that the practical concept of freedom rests on this transcendental idea, and that the question of whether practical freedom is possible is difficult only because it involves the question of whether the transcendental idea is true. Freedom in the practical sense is the will's independence from coercion by sensuous impulses. A will is sensuous insofar as it is affected "pathologically," that is, by sensuous impulses. It is called animal (*arbitrium brutum*) when it is pathologically necessitated. The human will is indeed an *arbitrium sensitivum*, a sensuous will, but it is not *brutum*; it is *liberum*, free. Sensuous impulses do not necessitate its action, for there exists in human beings a power of determining themselves independently of all sensuous coercion.

If all causality in the world of sense were natural, and natural only, then every event would be determined by another according to necessary laws. Phenomena, insofar as they determine the will, would then necessitate every action as their own natural effect, and all practical freedom would collapse along with the transcendental idea. Practical freedom presupposes that although something did not happen, it ought to have happened. It therefore presupposes that the cause of that event in the world of phenomena was not so powerful and decisive as to rule out the causality of our will, a causality capable of producing effects independently of, and even in opposition to, the power of natural causes, and therefore capable of beginning a series of events spontaneously.

Here, as with the self-contradictions and perplexities of a reason that tries to pass beyond the limits of possible experience generally, the problem is not, properly speaking, physiological, a question for the science of nature, but transcendental. The question of whether freedom is possible does concern psychology. But since it rests on dialectical arguments of pure reason, its solution falls to transcendental philosophy. Before attempting that solution, a task transcendental philosophy cannot refuse, it is advisable to say something about the method by which it will settle the question.

If phenomena were things in themselves, and if space and time were forms of the existence of things themselves, then condition and conditioned would always belong to the same series. Here too would arise the antinomy common to all transcendental ideas: their series would be either too large or too small for the understanding. But the dynamical ideas, which we are about to discuss in this section and the next, have the peculiarity that they relate to an object considered not as a quantity but as an existence. In discussing the present question, therefore, we can set aside the magnitude of the series of conditions and consider only the dynamical relation of condition to conditioned. The question then arises whether freedom is possible at all, and if it is, whether it can coexist with the universality of the natural law of causality. We must accordingly ask whether we state a genuine disjunction when we say, "Every effect must arise either from nature or from freedom," or whether both may operate together in the same event, in different respects. The principle that all events in the world of phenomena are linked in an unbroken connection according to the unchangeable laws of nature is a well-established principle of the transcendental analytic, and it admits no exception. The question, therefore, is this: "Can an effect that is determined according to the laws of nature also be produced by a free agent, or do freedom and nature exclude each other?"

Here the common but mistaken assumption that phenomena are absolutely real shows its harmful influence, throwing reason's procedure into confusion. If phenomena are things in themselves, freedom is impossible. Nature is then the complete and self-sufficient cause of every event, and condition and conditioned, cause and effect, all belong to the same series and are necessitated by the same law. If, on the other hand, phenomena are taken to be what they in fact are, nothing more than representations connected with one another according to empirical laws, then they must have a ground that is not itself a phenomenon. The causality of such an intelligible cause is not determined, and cannot be determined, by phenomena, even though its effects, as phenomena, must be determined by other phenomena. This cause and its causality therefore exist outside and apart from the series of phenomena, while its effects exist within the series of empirical conditions and can be found there. Such an effect may therefore be regarded as free with respect to its intelligible cause and, at the same time, as necessary with respect to the phenomena from which it necessarily follows. Stated in this entirely general and abstract form, the distinction is bound to seem extremely subtle and obscure, and what follows will make it clear. For now it is enough to note that, since the complete and unbroken connection of phenomena is an unalterable law of nature, freedom is impossible if phenomena are assumed to be absolutely real. For this reason, philosophers who hold the common view on this subject can never succeed in reconciling nature and freedom.

#### Possibility of Freedom in Harmony with the Universal Law of Natural Necessity

Whatever in an object of the senses is not itself sensuous I may be permitted to call intelligible. Suppose, then, that an object which must be regarded as a sensuous phenomenon possesses a power that is not itself an object of sensuous intuition, yet through which it can be the cause of phenomena. The causality of such a being can then be regarded from two different standpoints. With respect to its action, it may be regarded as intelligible, the action of a thing in itself. With respect to its effects, it may be regarded as sensuous, the effects of a phenomenon in the world of sense. We would therefore have to form both an empirical and an intellectual concept of the causality of such a power, though both would refer to the same effect.

This twofold way of thinking about a power residing in a sensuous object conflicts with none of the concepts we ought to form of the world of phenomena or of possible experience. Since phenomena are not things in themselves, they must rest on a transcendental object that determines them as mere representations. There seems to be no reason why we should not ascribe to this transcendental object, besides the property of appearing to us as phenomena, a causality whose effects are found in the world of phenomena, even though the transcendental object is not itself a phenomenon. Every efficient cause, however, must have a character, that is, a law of its causality, without which it would not be a cause at all. In the case before us, then, every sensuous object would first have an empirical character. This character ensures that its actions, as phenomena, stand in complete and harmonious connection with all other phenomena according to constant natural laws, that they can be derived from those phenomena as their conditions, and that together with them they form a series in the order of nature. Second, this sensuous object would have to possess an intelligible character, which ensures that it is the cause of those actions as phenomena, although it is not itself a phenomenon and is not subject to the conditions of the world of sense. The first may be called the character of the thing as phenomenon, the second its character as a thing in itself.

This acting subject, in its intelligible character, would not be subject to any conditions of time, for time is a condition only of phenomena and not of things in themselves. No action would begin or cease in this subject. It would therefore be exempt from the law that governs every determination in time, the law of change, which holds that everything that happens must have a cause in the phenomena of a preceding state. In short, the subject's causality, insofar as it is intelligible, would not belong to the series of empirical conditions that determine and necessitate an event in the world of sense. This intelligible character cannot be known directly, since we can perceive nothing but phenomena. But it must be capable of being thought in harmony with the empirical character, since we are always compelled to place in thought a transcendental object at the foundation of phenomena, even though we can never know what that object is in itself.

In its empirical character, this same subject would be subject to all the empirical laws of causality. As a phenomenon and a member of the world of sense, its effects would have to be explained by reference to preceding phenomena. External phenomena must be able to influence it, and its actions, as governed by natural laws, must show us how its empirical character, that is, the law of its causality, can be known in and through experience. In short, everything required for a complete and necessary determination of these actions must be given to us in experience.

In its intelligible character, on the other hand, though of this we have only a general concept, the same subject must be regarded as free from all sensuous influences and from every determination by phenomena. Since it is a noumenon, nothing happens in it. There is no change in it requiring dynamical determination in time, and for the same reason it has no connection with phenomena as its causes. This active being must therefore be free in its actions from natural necessity and independent of it, for such necessity exists only in the world of phenomena. It would be entirely correct to say that it begins its effects in the world of sense from itself, even though the action that produces these effects does not begin within it. We would not thereby be claiming that these sensuous effects began to exist of themselves. They are always determined by prior empirical conditions, by virtue of the empirical character, which is the phenomenal appearance of the intelligible character, and they are possible only as a continuation of the series of natural causes. In this way nature and freedom, each taken in the full and absolute sense of the term, can both be found in the same action without contradiction or conflict.

#### Exposition of the Cosmological Idea of Freedom in Harmony with the Universal Law of Natural Necessity

I have thought it best to set before the reader, at first, only an outline of the solution to this transcendental problem, so that he might more easily form a clear idea of the course reason must take in solving it. I shall now set out the several steps of that solution and consider them in order.

The natural law holds that everything that happens must have a cause. It holds that the causality of this cause, that is, its action, must itself have a cause among phenomena by which it is determined, since that action cannot have existed always but must itself be an event that precedes in time the effect it has brought about. And it holds that consequently all events are empirically determined in an order of nature. This law underlies the possibility of experience and of a connected system of phenomena, which is to say of nature. It is a law of the understanding from which no departure is permitted and to which no exception can be allowed. To exempt even a single phenomenon from its operation would be to place that phenomenon outside the sphere of possible experience, and so to concede that it is a mere fiction of thought, a phantom of the brain.

We are therefore obliged to acknowledge a chain of causes in which absolute totality can never be found. But we need not linger over this point, for it has already been sufficiently answered in our discussion of the antinomies into which reason falls when it tries to reach the unconditioned in the series of phenomena. If we allow ourselves to be deceived by the illusion of transcendental realism, the assumption that phenomena are things in themselves, we shall find that neither nature nor freedom remains. The question now is this: "Granting natural necessity in the world of phenomena, is it possible to regard one and the same effect as at once an effect of nature and an effect of freedom, or are these two kinds of causality contradictory and incompatible?"

No phenomenal cause can absolutely and of itself begin a series. Every action that produces an event is itself an event and presupposes a preceding state in which its cause was present. Everything that happens is thus merely the continuation of a series, and an absolute beginning is impossible in the world of sense. The actions of natural causes are therefore themselves effects, and they presuppose causes that precede them in time. An original action, one that forms an absolute beginning, lies beyond the causal power of phenomena.

But granted that all effects are phenomena, must the causality of their cause also be a phenomenon and belong to the empirical world? Is it not possible instead that every effect in the world of phenomena is connected with an empirical cause according to the universal law of nature, while this empirical causality is itself the effect of a non-empirical, intelligible causality, and its connection with natural causes nonetheless remains intact? With respect to phenomena, such a causality would be regarded as the original action of a cause that is, to that extent, not phenomenal but, by virtue of this power, intelligible. Yet as a link in the chain of nature it must at the same time be regarded as belonging to the world of sense.

If we are to seek out and present the natural conditions of natural events, that is, their causes, we must hold that phenomena act causally on one another. Once this is granted as valid without exception, the demands of the understanding, which recognizes nothing but nature in the realm of phenomena, are satisfied, and our physical explanations of physical phenomena may proceed on their regular course, unhindered and unopposed. Admitting the following creates no obstacle, even if the idea should be a pure fiction: some natural causes may possess a power that is not empirical but intelligible, in that it is determined to act not by empirical conditions but purely and solely by grounds supplied by the understanding, while this action, once the cause appears as a phenomenon, remains in perfect accordance with the laws of empirical causality. The acting subject, as a cause among phenomena, would thus keep its complete connection with nature and natural conditions. Only the phenomenal appearance of the subject, with all its phenomenal causality, would contain certain conditions that, if we ascend from the empirical to the transcendental object, must necessarily be regarded as intelligible.

If, in investigating causes in the world of phenomena, we follow the guidance of nature alone, we need not concern ourselves with how the transcendental subject, which is wholly unknown to us, is related to these phenomena and their connection in nature. The intelligible ground of phenomena in this subject has nothing to do with empirical questions. It concerns pure thought alone. And although the effects of this thought and of this action of the pure understanding can be found among phenomena, those phenomena must nevertheless admit of a full and complete explanation on purely physical grounds and according to natural laws. In that case we attend only to their empirical character.
