We set aside their intelligible character, which is the transcendental cause of the empirical one, as entirely unknown, except insofar as the empirical character displays it as its sensible sign.

Now let us apply this to experience. Man is a phenomenon of the world of sense and therefore also a natural cause, whose causality must be governed by empirical laws. As such, he must have an empirical character, like every other natural phenomenon. We observe this empirical character in his actions, which reveal the presence of certain powers and faculties. When we consider inanimate or merely animal nature, we find no reason to conceive of any faculty there as other than one determined in a purely sensuous way. But man, who otherwise knows the whole of nature only through the senses, knows himself also through pure apperception, and he does so in actions and inner determinations that he cannot count as impressions of sense. To himself, then, he is on the one hand a phenomenon. On the other hand, with respect to certain faculties, he is a purely intelligible object, intelligible because the action of these faculties cannot be attributed to the receptivity of sense. These faculties are understanding and reason. Reason in particular differs in a quite special way from all empirically conditioned powers, for it considers its objects solely through ideas, and by means of these it determines the understanding. The understanding then puts its own concepts, which, like the ideas of reason, are pure and non-empirical, to empirical use.

That reason has causality, or at least that we are compelled to represent it as having causality, is evident from the imperatives that, in practical matters, we set as rules for many of our active powers. The word *ought* expresses a kind of necessity and implies a connection with grounds that nature does not and cannot present to the human mind. The understanding can know of nature only what is, what has been, or what will be. It would be absurd to say that anything in nature ought to be other than it actually is in its relations of time. Indeed, when we consider only the course of nature, the *ought* has neither application nor meaning. To ask, "What ought to happen in nature?" is as absurd as to ask, "What properties ought a circle to have?" All we are entitled to ask is, "What happens in nature?" or, in the latter case, "What are the properties of a circle?"

The idea of an *ought*, or of duty, points instead to a possible action whose ground is a pure concept, whereas the ground of a merely natural action is always a phenomenon. If the moral imperative prescribes an action, that action must of course be possible under physical conditions. But those physical or natural conditions have no bearing on the determination of the will itself. They concern only its effects, and the consequences of those effects in the world of appearances. However many motives nature may present to my will, and however many sensuous impulses, they are powerless to produce the moral ought. They can produce a volition, but such a volition is never necessary; it is always conditioned, and the ought pronounced by reason sets it an aim and a standard, permitting or forbidding it. Whatever the object may be, whether purely sensuous, like pleasure, or presented by pure reason, like the good, reason will not yield to grounds of empirical origin. It refuses to follow the order of things as experience presents them. With complete spontaneity it arranges things anew according to ideas, and compels empirical conditions to conform to those ideas. In their name it declares certain actions necessary that have not in fact taken place and perhaps never will. Yet it presupposes that it has the power of causality in relation to those actions, since without this presupposition it could not expect its ideas to produce any effects in the world of experience.

Let us pause here and grant that it is at least possible that reason genuinely stands in a causal relation to phenomena. If so, reason, pure as it is, must exhibit an empirical character. Every cause presupposes a rule according to which certain phenomena follow from it as effects, and every rule requires uniformity in those effects. This uniformity is what properly grounds the concept of a cause as a faculty or power. This concept may be called the empirical character of reason. That character is permanent, while the effects it produces appear in various forms, according to the various conditions that accompany and partly limit them.

Every person's will, accordingly, has an empirical character. This is nothing more than the causality of his reason, insofar as its effects in the world of appearances reveal a rule. That rule allows us to examine the operations of this causality in their various kinds and degrees, along with the rational grounds behind them, and so to judge the subjective principles of the will. We learn what this empirical character is only from its effects in appearance and from the rule that experience discloses in them. For this reason, all of a person's actions in the world of appearances are determined by his empirical character together with the other causes in nature that act alongside it. If we could trace every phenomenon of human volition to its deepest foundation in the mind, there would be no action we could not predict with certainty and recognize as absolutely necessary given its preceding conditions. With respect to this empirical character, then, there is no freedom. And it is only in light of this character that we can consider the human will when we confine ourselves to observation and, as anthropology does, conduct a physiological investigation into the motives that drive human action.

But when we consider the same actions in relation to reason, we find a rule and an order quite different from those of nature and experience. Here we mean not speculative reason, which seeks to explain how the actions arose, but practical reason, regarded as the cause that produces them. Reason may well declare that what has happened in the course of nature, and could not have failed to happen, ought not to have happened. Sometimes, too, we discover, or believe we discover, that the ideas of reason really did stand in a causal relation to certain human actions, and that these actions occurred because they were determined not by empirical causes but by an act of will grounded in reason.

Granting, then, that reason stands in a causal relation to phenomena, can an action of reason be called free when we know that on its sensuous side, in its empirical character, it is completely determined and absolutely necessary? This empirical character, however, is itself determined by the intelligible character. The intelligible character we cannot know. We can only indicate it by means of phenomena, and phenomena give us immediate knowledge of the empirical character alone. An action, insofar as it is ascribed to an intelligible cause, therefore does not follow from that cause according to empirical laws. What precedes the act is not the conditions of pure reason themselves but only their effects in inner sense. Pure reason, as a purely intelligible faculty, is not subject to the conditions of time. The causality of reason in its intelligible character does not come into being; it does not appear at a particular moment in order to produce an effect. If it did, it would be subordinate to the natural law of phenomena, which orders them in time as a series of causes and effects, and it would cease to be freedom and become part of nature. We are therefore entitled to say: "If reason stands in a causal relation to phenomena, it is a faculty that originates the sensuous condition of an empirical series of effects." The condition that lies in reason is not sensuous, and therefore cannot itself be originated or come into being. Here, then, we find what no empirical series could ever supply: a condition of a successive series of events that is itself empirically unconditioned. In this case the condition stands outside and beyond the series of phenomena. It is intelligible, and so it cannot be subject to any sensuous condition or to any determination in time by a preceding cause.

The true morality of actions, their merit or their guilt, even in the case of our own conduct, remains entirely hidden from us. Our judgments can reach only their empirical character. How much of an action springs from free will, and how much must be credited to nature, to innocent error, or to a fortunate temperament (what the Latin calls *merito fortunae*, merit owed to luck), no one can discover, and so no one can judge with perfect justice.

In another respect, however, the same cause also belongs to the series of phenomena. A human being is himself a phenomenon. His will has an empirical character, which is the empirical cause of all his actions. Every condition that determines a person and his volition in accordance with this character is itself part of the series of natural effects and subject to their law: the law that no empirically undetermined cause of an event in time can exist. For this reason no given action can have an absolute and spontaneous origin, since all actions are phenomena and belong to the world of experience. But it cannot be said of reason that the state in which it determines the will is always preceded by some other state that determines it. Reason is not a phenomenon and is not subject to sensuous conditions. Consequently, even with respect to its causality, temporal sequence and the conditions of time have no influence on it, and the dynamical law of nature, which governs succession in time according to fixed rules, cannot be applied to it.

Reason is therefore the permanent condition of all the actions of the human will. Each of these actions is determined in the person's empirical character even before it occurs. The intelligible character, of which the empirical character is merely the sensuous schema, the pattern in which it appears to the senses, knows no before or after. Every action, regardless of its temporal relation to other phenomena, is the immediate effect of the intelligible character of pure reason. Reason accordingly acts freely, and is not dynamically determined by any preceding conditions, whether internal or external. This freedom must not be described merely negatively, as independence from empirical conditions, for then reason would cease to be a cause of phenomena at all. It must be understood positively, as a faculty that can spontaneously originate a series of events. At the same time, we must not suppose that anything begins within reason itself. On the contrary, reason, as the unconditioned condition of every act of will, admits no conditions of time, even though its effect really does begin within a series of phenomena. That beginning, however, is not absolutely first.

I shall illustrate this regulative principle of reason with an example drawn from its use in the world of experience. It can only be illustrated, not proved, for no amount of experience and no number of facts could prove it; arguments of that kind can never establish the truth of transcendental propositions. Consider a voluntary action, such as a lie, by which a person has introduced a certain amount of disorder into society. We judge the lie by the motives from which it arose, and we impute to the liar the blame for it and for its harmful consequences. Our first step is to examine the empirical character of the offense, and to that end we try to trace that character to its sources: a defective education, bad company, a shameless and malicious disposition, frivolity, thoughtlessness, not forgetting the immediate circumstances that prevailed at the moment of the offense. In this our procedure is exactly the same as when we investigate the series of causes that determine a given physical effect. Yet although we believe the act to have been determined by all these circumstances, we blame the offender no less. We do not blame him for his unfortunate disposition, nor for the circumstances that influenced him, nor even for the life he has led up to that point. We presuppose that all these considerations can be set aside, that the whole series of preceding conditions can be treated as though it had never existed, and that the act can be regarded as wholly unconditioned by any prior state, as if with it the agent had begun an entirely new series of effects. Our blame rests on a law of reason, which requires us to regard reason as a cause that could have, and ought to have, determined the person's conduct differently, independently of all empirical conditions. We do not regard this causality of reason as one contributing factor among others, but as complete in itself. Whether the sensuous impulses favored or opposed it makes no difference. The offense is judged according to its intelligible character, and the offender is unequivocally to blame the moment he tells the lie. It follows that, despite all the empirical conditions of the act, we regard reason as entirely free, and therefore, in this case, as culpable.

This judgment shows conclusively that we habitually think of reason as unaffected by sensuous conditions. We think that no change takes place within it, although its appearances, the ways it manifests itself in its effects, do change. We think that within it no earlier state determines a later one, and therefore that it is not a member of the series of sensuous conditions that necessitate phenomena according to natural laws. Reason is present, and the same, in all human actions and at all times. But it does not itself exist in time, and so it never enters a state in which it did not previously exist. With respect to new states or conditions, it determines but is not determined. We therefore cannot ask, "Why did reason not determine itself differently?" The question should instead be: "Why did reason not use its causal power to determine certain phenomena differently?" And this question has no answer. A different intelligible character would have produced a different empirical character. When we say that the offender, whatever the course of his previous life, could have refrained from lying, we mean only that the act fell under the power and authority of reason, which can permit or forbid. Reason is not subject, in its causality, to any conditions of phenomena or of time. A difference in time can make a difference in how phenomena relate to one another, since phenomena are not things in themselves and therefore not causes in themselves. But it can make no difference to the relation in which an action stands to the faculty of reason.

In our inquiry into free actions and the causal power that produced them, we thus arrive at an intelligible cause beyond which we cannot go. We can recognize that it is free, meaning independent of all sensuous conditions, and that in this way it may be the sensuously unconditioned condition of phenomena. But why the intelligible character produces precisely these phenomena, and displays precisely this empirical character under particular circumstances, our reason cannot determine. That question lies as far beyond the power and province of reason as this one: "Why does the transcendental object of our outer sensuous intuition admit of no form other than intuition in space?" The problem before us, however, does not require us to take up any such questions. It was simply whether freedom and natural necessity can coexist without conflict in the same action. To this we have given a sufficient answer. We have shown that because freedom relates to a different kind of condition from natural necessity, the law of the one does not affect the law of the other, and that both can therefore exist together, independently and without interfering with each other.

The reader should take care to note that my aim in these remarks has not been to prove the actual existence of freedom as a faculty containing the cause of certain sensuous phenomena. Such an argument would not have been transcendental in character, nor confined to the discussion of pure concepts. Moreover, every attempt to infer from experience something that cannot be thought in accordance with the laws of experience is bound to fail. I have not even tried to demonstrate that freedom is possible, for this too would have been futile: the mind cannot know the possibility of any reality or causal power through a priori concepts alone. Freedom has been treated here only as a transcendental idea. Through it, reason seeks to originate a series of conditions in the world of phenomena by means of something sensuously unconditioned, and in doing so falls into an antinomy with the very laws it prescribes for the operation of the understanding. That this antinomy rests on mere illusion, and that nature and freedom are at least not opposed to each other, was all it lay in our power to prove and all the question required us to solve.

#### IV. Solution of the Cosmological Idea of the Totality of the Dependence of Phenomenal Existences

In the preceding remarks we considered the changes in the world of sense as forming a dynamical series, in which each member is subordinated to another as its cause. Our purpose now is to use this series of states as a guide toward an existence that might be the highest condition of all changeable phenomena, which is to say, toward a necessary being. We are seeking not unconditioned causality but the unconditioned existence of substance itself. The series before us is therefore a series of concepts, and not a series of intuitions in which one intuition is the condition of another.

It is evident, however, that since all phenomena are subject to change and conditioned in their existence, the series of dependent existences cannot contain an unconditioned member whose existence would be absolutely necessary. Suppose, then, that phenomena were things in themselves, and that, as a direct consequence of this assumption, condition and conditioned belonged to the same series of phenomena. In that case a necessary being, as the condition of the existence of sensuous phenomena, would be utterly impossible.

There is, however, an important distinction between the dynamical and the mathematical regress. The mathematical regress concerns only the combination of parts into a whole, or the division of a whole into parts. The conditions in its series are therefore themselves parts of the series. They must be regarded as homogeneous with it, and hence as consisting, without exception, of phenomena. The dynamical regress has a different aim. It does not seek to establish the possibility of an unconditioned whole made up of given parts, or of an unconditioned part of a given whole. It seeks to show how a given state can be derived from its cause, or how the contingent existence of substance can be derived from what exists necessarily. In this regress it is not required that the condition form part of the same empirical series as the conditioned.

In the apparent antinomy now before us, there is a way out of the difficulty, for it is not impossible that both contradictory statements may be true in different respects. All sensuous phenomena may be contingent, possessing only an empirically conditioned existence, and yet there may also be a non-empirical condition of the whole series, namely a necessary being. Such a being, as an intelligible condition, would not be a member of the series, not even its highest member, and the entire world of sense would be left untouched in its empirically determined existence. This also marks a difference between the solutions to the third and fourth antinomies. In treating freedom in the third antinomy, the thing itself, the cause considered as *substantia phaenomenon* or substance as it appears, was regarded as belonging to the series of conditions, and only its causality was assigned to the intelligible world. In the present case, by contrast, we must think of this necessary being as purely intelligible and as existing wholly apart from the world of sense, as an *ens extramundanum*, a being outside the world. Otherwise it would fall under the phenomenal law of contingency and dependence.

With respect to the present problem, then, the regulative principle of reason is as follows. Everything in the sensuous world has an empirically conditioned existence. No property of the sensuous world possesses unconditioned necessity. We must expect, and as far as possible seek, the empirical condition of every member in the series of conditions. And we have no sufficient grounds for deriving any existence from a condition lying outside and beyond the empirical series, or for regarding any existence within it as independent and self-sufficient. None of this, however, should prevent us from recognizing that the whole series may possibly rest on a being that is intelligible and therefore free of all empirical conditions.

It has been far from my intention in these remarks to prove the existence of this unconditioned and necessary being, or even to establish the possibility of a purely intelligible condition for the existence of all sensuous phenomena. Limits were set to reason to keep it from abandoning the guiding thread of empirical conditions and losing itself in transcendent theories that can never be given concrete form. In the same way, my purpose was to set limits, from the other side, to the law of the purely empirical understanding. I wished to protest against any attempt on its part to rule on the possibility of things, or to declare the existence of the intelligible impossible merely because it cannot be used to explain and account for phenomena. At the same time, it has been shown that the contingency of all natural phenomena and their empirical conditions is entirely consistent with the arbitrary hypothesis of a necessary, though purely intelligible, condition; that there is no real contradiction between the two; and that both may therefore be true. The existence of such an absolutely necessary being may be impossible. But this can never be demonstrated from the universal contingency and dependence of sensuous phenomena, nor from the principle that forbids us to halt the series at any member or to seek its cause in some realm beyond nature. Reason goes its own way in the empirical world, and follows its own distinct path in the sphere of the transcendental.

The sensuous world contains nothing but phenomena, which are mere representations and always sensuously conditioned; things in themselves are not, and cannot be, objects for us. It is no surprise, then, that we have no right to leap from some member of an empirical series beyond the world of sense. To do so would be to treat empirical representations as though they were things in themselves, existing apart from their transcendental ground in the human mind, whose cause might be sought outside the empirical series. Such a procedure might be legitimate with contingent things in themselves. It cannot be legitimate with mere representations of things, whose contingency is itself only a phenomenon and can relate to no regress other than the one that determines phenomena, namely the empirical regress. To think of an intelligible ground of phenomena, however, and one free from their contingency, conflicts neither with the unlimited character of the empirical regress nor with the thoroughgoing contingency of phenomena. Demonstrating this was all that was needed to resolve the apparent antinomy. For if the condition of every conditioned thing, with respect to its existence, is sensuous, and therefore belongs to the same series, it must itself be conditioned, as was shown in the antithesis of the fourth antinomy. Either the difficulties into which reason inevitably falls when it demands the unconditioned must remain, or the unconditioned must be placed in the sphere of the intelligible. There its necessity neither requires nor even permits an empirical condition, and it is therefore unconditionally necessary.

The empirical use of reason is unaffected by the assumption of a purely intelligible being. It continues to operate on the principle that all phenomena are contingent, advancing from empirical conditions to higher and higher conditions that are themselves empirical. Nor, conversely, does this regulative principle exclude the assumption of an intelligible cause when the question concerns only the pure use of reason, in relation to ends or purposes. In that case an intelligible cause means nothing more than the transcendental ground of the possibility of sensory appearances, a ground that remains unknown to us. Its existence, necessary and independent of every sensory condition, does not conflict with the contingency of appearances, nor with the unlimited regress that remains open in the series of empirical conditions.

### Concluding Remarks on the Antinomy of Pure Reason

As long as our rational concepts take as their object the totality of conditions within the world of appearances, and look to that world to satisfy the demands of reason, our ideas remain transcendental and cosmological. But once we place the unconditioned, which is the goal of all our inquiries, in a domain lying outside the world of sense and of possible experience, our ideas become transcendent. They then no longer merely help to complete the exercise of reason, a completion that remains an idea, never achieved but always to be pursued. Instead they break away from experience entirely and construct objects for themselves. Experience has never supplied the material of these objects, and their objective reality rests not on the completion of the empirical series but on pure a priori concepts. We may grant that these transcendent ideas have an intelligible object, considered as a transcendental object. But we cannot think of it as a thing that definite predicates describing its inner nature could determine, since it has no connection with empirical concepts. Nor are we entitled to assert that any such object exists. It is therefore a mere product of the mind alone. Among all the cosmological ideas, however, it is the one that gives rise to the fourth antinomy that forces us to take this step. The existence of appearances, which is always conditioned and never self-sufficient, requires us to look for an object distinct from appearances: an intelligible object, at which all contingency must come to an end. Yet once we have allowed ourselves to assume a self-subsistent reality outside the field of experience, we are obliged to regard appearances as merely a contingent way in which beings who are themselves intelligences represent intelligible objects. No course then remains but to proceed by analogy, forming some concept of intelligible things, of which we have not the slightest knowledge, by the same method that nature taught us to use in forming empirical concepts. Experience acquainted us with the contingent. But we are now dealing with things that are not objects of experience, and so we must derive our knowledge of them from what is necessary absolutely and in itself, which is to say, from pure concepts. Consequently, the very first step we take beyond the world of sense compels us to begin our system of new knowledge by investigating a necessary being, and to derive from our concept of that being all our concepts of intelligible things. This is what we propose to attempt in the following chapter.

## Transcendental Dialectic, Book II, Chapter III: The Ideal of Pure Reason

### Section I. Of the Ideal in General

We have seen that pure concepts cannot present objects to the mind except under sensory conditions. The conditions of objective reality are not contained in these concepts, which in fact contain nothing but the bare form of thought. When applied to appearances, however, they can be presented *in concreto*, in an actual concrete instance. Appearances supply them with the material for forming empirical concepts, and empirical concepts are nothing more than concrete forms of the concepts of the understanding. Ideas, however, stand even further from objective reality than the categories do, for no appearance can ever present them to the human mind *in concreto*. They contain a kind of completeness that no possible empirical knowledge can reach, and they give reason a systematic unity that the unity of experience tries to approach but can never fully attain.

Still further from objective reality than the idea is what I call the Ideal. By this term I mean the idea taken not merely *in concreto* but *in individuo*: as a single, individual thing that the idea alone can determine, or has determined. The idea of humanity in its complete perfection presupposes that all the powers and faculties making up our concept of human nature have been developed to the full attainment of their final ends. It also presupposes everything else required for the complete determination of the idea, for of every pair of contradictory predicates, only one can fit the idea of the perfect human being. What I have called an ideal was, in Plato's philosophy, an idea of the divine mind. It was an individual object present to that mind's pure intuition, the most perfect of every kind of possible being, and the archetype of everything that exists as appearance.

Without climbing to such speculative heights, we must admit that human reason contains not only ideas but ideals. These do not possess creative power, as Plato's did, but they do possess practical power. They work as regulative principles and form the basis on which certain actions can be perfected. Moral concepts are not entirely pure concepts of reason, because an empirical element, pleasure or pain, lies at their foundation. Yet we may still count them as pure concepts of reason when we consider only their form, that is, with regard to the principle by which reason sets limits to a freedom that is in itself lawless. Virtue and wisdom in their perfect purity are ideas. The wise man of the Stoics, by contrast, is an ideal: a human being who exists only in thought but who corresponds completely to the idea of wisdom. Just as the idea provides a rule, the ideal provides the archetype for the complete and thorough determination of its copy. The conduct of this wise and godlike man thus gives us a standard for our own actions. Against it we can compare and judge ourselves, and by it we can reform ourselves, even though we can never reach the perfection it demands. We cannot grant these ideals objective reality, but we should not dismiss them as fantasies. On the contrary, they supply reason with a standard by which it can measure, through comparison, how far the objects presented to it fall short of completeness. To try to realize the ideal in an example drawn from experience, however, cannot be done, as when an author portrays the character of the perfectly wise man in a novel. There is something absurd in the attempt, and the result is bound to be of little benefit. The natural limitations of any real person keep breaking in upon the perfection and completeness of the idea. They destroy the illusion of the story and cast suspicion even on what is good in the idea itself, which then looks fictitious and unreal.

Such is the nature of the ideal of reason. It always rests on determinate concepts and acts as a rule and a model, whether for imitation or for criticism. The ideals of the imagination are of a very different kind. No intelligible concept of them can be given. They are a kind of monogram, a loose outline sketch drawn according to no definite rule, forming a vague composite picture produced from many different experiences rather than a determinate image. Such are the ideals that painters and physiognomists, who claim to read character from the features of the face, profess to carry in their minds. These ideals can provide neither a model for production nor a standard for judgment. They may be called sensuous ideals, though the term is improper, since people claim they are models of certain possible empirical intuitions. They cannot, however, furnish rules or standards for explanation or examination.

In its ideals, reason aims at complete and thorough determination according to a priori rules. It therefore thinks of an object that principles must be able to determine completely, even though all empirical conditions are absent, and for this reason the concept of the object is transcendent.

### Section II. Of the Transcendental Ideal (Prototypon Transcendentale)

Every concept is undetermined with respect to whatever it does not contain, and is subject to the principle of determinability. This principle states that of every two contradictory predicates, only one can belong to a concept. It is a purely logical principle, resting on the principle of contradiction, since it abstracts completely from the content of knowledge and attends only to its logical form.

Every thing, however, is also subject, with regard to its possibility, to the principle of complete determination. According to this principle, of all the possible predicates of things, each taken together with its contradictory, one from each pair must belong to it. This principle does not rest merely on the principle of contradiction. Beyond the relation between two contradictory predicates, it regards every thing as standing in relation to the whole of possibility, understood as the sum total of all predicates of things. It presupposes this sum as an a priori condition. It then represents each thing as deriving its own particular possibility from the relation it bears to that sum and from the share it has in it. The principle of complete determination therefore concerns content, not merely logical form. It is the principle of the synthesis of all the predicates required to make up the complete concept of a thing. It is not merely a principle of analytic representation, stating that one of two contradictory predicates must belong to a concept. It also contains a transcendental presupposition, namely that there exists a material for all possibility, which must contain a priori the data for each particular possibility.

This principle declares that every thing stands in relation to a common correlate, the sum total of possibility. If that sum were found to reside in the idea of a single individual thing, it would establish an affinity among all possible things, because the ground of their complete determination would be identical. The determinability of every concept falls under the universality (*Allgemeinheit*, *universalitas*) of the principle of excluded middle. The determination of a thing, by contrast, falls under the totality (*Allheit*, *universitas*) of all possible predicates.

The proposition "everything that exists is completely determined" means more than that one of every pair of given contradictory attributes can always be predicated of the thing. It means that one attribute out of every pair of all possible attributes can always be predicated of it. Here the predicates are not merely compared logically with one another. The thing itself is compared transcendentally with the sum total of all possible predicates. The proposition amounts to saying: "To know a thing completely, one must know everything that is possible, and determine the thing thereby, either positively or negatively." Complete determination is therefore a concept that can never be presented in its totality *in concreto*. It rests on an idea that has its seat in reason, the faculty that prescribes to the understanding the laws of its harmonious and complete exercise.

Insofar as this idea of the sum total of all possibility is the condition for the complete determination of every thing, it is itself undetermined with respect to the predicates that may make up that sum, and we think in it nothing more than the sum total of all possible predicates. On closer examination, however, we find that this idea, as an original concept of the mind, excludes a great many predicates: those derived from others, and those that cannot coexist with others. It thereby refines itself into a concept completely determined a priori. It becomes the concept of an individual object that the mere idea determines completely, and so it must be called an ideal of pure reason.

Suppose we consider all possible predicates not merely logically but transcendentally, that is, with respect to the content that can be thought in them a priori. We then find that some express a being, while others express a mere non-being. Logical negation, signified by the word *not*, does not properly attach to a concept itself. It attaches only to the relation of one concept to another in a judgment, and it is therefore wholly incapable of representing the content of a concept. The expression *not mortal* does not indicate that some non-being is thought in the object; it does not concern the content at all. A transcendental negation, by contrast, signifies non-being in itself. It stands opposed to transcendental affirmation, whose very concept expresses a being. This affirmation is therefore called a reality, because through it alone objects are thought of as something, as things. The opposite negation signifies a mere lack, a privation, an absence. Where such negations alone are attached to a representation, they signify that nothing whatever corresponds to it.

No negation can be thought determinately unless the opposite affirmation is thought at the same time. A man born blind has not the faintest notion of darkness, because he has none of light. The vagabond knows nothing of poverty, because he has never known comfort. The ignorant man has no concept of his ignorance, because he has none of knowledge. All concepts of negations are therefore derivative. It is realities that contain the data, the material, so to speak, or the transcendental content, for the possibility and complete determination of all things.

The investigations and calculations of astronomers have taught us much that is wonderful. The most important lesson they have taught us, however, is the depth of our ignorance about the universe. Without the knowledge gained in this way, reason could never have conceived the magnitude of that ignorance. Discovering our deficiencies in this manner must greatly change how we define the aims of human reason.

Suppose, then, that a transcendental substratum underlies the complete determination of things, a substratum meant to supply the store from which all possible predicates of things are drawn. This substratum can be nothing other than the idea of a sum total of reality (*omnitudo realitatis*). On this view, negations are nothing but limitations, and that term could not properly apply to them unless the unlimited, the All, formed the true basis of our concept.

This concept of a sum total of reality is the concept of a thing in itself regarded as completely determined. The concept of an *ens realissimum*, a most real being, is the concept of an individual being, because one predicate determines it out of every possible pair of contradictory predicates: the predicate that expresses and belongs to being. A transcendental ideal therefore underlies the complete determination of everything that exists. It is the highest material condition of that thing's possibility, the condition on which all thought of objects, with respect to their content, must rest. Indeed, this is the only true ideal of which the human mind is capable, because only in this one case is a general concept of a thing completely determined by and through itself and known as the representation of an individual.

The logical determination of a concept rests on a disjunctive syllogism. Its major premise contains the logical division of the extent of a general concept. Its minor premise restricts this extent to one part, and its conclusion determines the concept by means of that part. The general concept of a reality cannot be divided a priori, because without the aid of experience we know no determinate kinds of reality that fall under it as their genus. The transcendental principle of the complete determination of all things is therefore merely the representation of the sum total of all reality. It is not a concept that holds all predicates beneath itself, as a genus holds its species, but one that comprehends them all within itself. The complete determination of a thing therefore rests on the limitation of this totality of reality. A certain portion of it is ascribed to the thing, and everything that remains is excluded. This procedure agrees exactly with that of the disjunctive syllogism, in which one of the members of the division determines the object in the conclusion. It follows that reason, in laying the transcendental ideal at the foundation of its determination of all possible things, proceeds in exact analogy with its procedure in disjunctive syllogisms. This was the very proposition on which the systematic division of all transcendental ideas was based, according to which they arise in complete parallel with the three kinds of syllogistic reasoning the human mind employs.

Reason, in thinking the necessary complete determination of things, plainly does not presuppose the existence of a being that corresponds to its ideal. It presupposes only the idea of the ideal, in order to derive from the unconditioned totality of complete determination the conditioned totality, the totality of what is limited. The ideal is therefore the prototype of all things. As imperfect copies (*ectypa*), they all receive from it the material of their possibility, and they approach it to a greater or lesser degree, though they can never attain its perfection.

The possibility of things must therefore be regarded as derived, with the single exception of the thing that contains all reality within itself, whose possibility must be regarded as primary and original. All negations are mere limitations of a greater and higher reality, indeed of the highest reality, and they are the only predicates by which all other things can be distinguished from the *ens realissimum*. They therefore presuppose this reality, and their content derives from it. The whole variety of things is nothing but an infinitely varied way of limiting the concept of the highest reality, which is their common substratum, just as all geometrical figures are possible only as different ways of limiting infinite space. The object of the ideal of reason exists only in reason itself. It is also called the primal being (*ens originarium*). Because nothing exists above it, it is called the supreme being (*ens summum*). And because it is the condition of all other beings, which rank beneath it, it is called the being of all beings (*ens entium*). None of these terms, however, signifies the objective relation of an actually existing object to other things. They signify only the relation of an idea to concepts, and all our investigations into this subject still leave us in complete uncertainty as to whether such a being exists.

A primal being cannot be said to consist of many other beings whose existence is derivative. Those beings presuppose the primal being and therefore cannot be its constituent parts. It follows that the ideal of the primal being must be thought of as simple.

Strictly speaking, then, the derivation of the possibility of all other things from this primal being cannot be regarded as a limitation of its reality, or as a kind of division of it. That would be to treat the primal being as a mere aggregate, which has been shown to be impossible, although our first rough sketch represented it that way. The highest reality must be regarded as the ground of the possibility of all things rather than as their sum total. The variety of things must rest not on the limitation of the primal being itself, but on the complete series of effects that flow from it. On this view, all our powers of sense, together with all reality in the world of appearances, may properly be counted among this series of effects, whereas they could not have formed parts of the idea if it were considered an aggregate. Suppose we pursue this line of thought and hypostatize the idea, treating it as an actually existing thing. We shall then find ourselves entitled to determine our notion of the Supreme Being, through the mere concept of a highest reality, as one, simple, all-sufficient, eternal, and so on. In short, we shall determine it in its unconditioned completeness by means of every possible predicate. The concept of such a being is the concept of God in the transcendental sense, and the ideal of pure reason thus becomes the subject matter of a transcendental theology.

Using the transcendental idea in this way, however, would overstep the limits of its validity and purpose. Reason placed it at the foundation of the complete determination of things as the concept of all reality, without requiring that this concept be regarded as the concept of an objectively existing thing. Such an existence would be pure fiction, and nothing entitles us to hypostatize the content of the idea into an ideal, as an individual being. Indeed, we are not even required to assume that such a hypothesis is possible. None of the consequences drawn from such an ideal would bear on the complete determination of things in general, and that determination is the only purpose for which the idea is needed.

It is not enough to describe the procedure of reason and its dialectic. We must also try to discover the sources of this dialectic, so that we can give a rational explanation of this illusion as a phenomenon of the human mind. The ideal we are discussing rests not on an arbitrary idea but on a natural one. So the question arises: how does reason come to regard the possibility of all things as derived from a single possibility, that of the highest reality, and then to presuppose that this possibility exists in an individual and primal being?

The answer lies ready at hand in the procedure of the Transcendental Analytic. The possibility of objects of the senses is a relation of these objects to thought, in which something, the empirical form, can be thought a priori. What constitutes the matter, however, must be given from outside. This matter is the reality of the appearance, the element corresponding to sensation, and if it were not given from outside, it could not even be thought, nor could its possibility be represented to the mind. An object of the senses is completely determined when it has been compared with all the predicates of appearance and represented through them, either positively or negatively. But what constitutes the thing itself, the real in an appearance, must be given. The medium in which the real of all appearances is given is experience, single and all-embracing. The material for the possibility of all objects of the senses must therefore be presupposed as given in one whole. The possibility of all empirical objects, their distinction from one another, and their complete determination all rest on the limitation of this whole. No objects other than objects of the senses are presented to us, and these can be given only in connection with a possible experience. It follows that nothing is an object for us unless it presupposes the whole, the sum total of empirical reality, as the condition of its possibility. A natural illusion, however, leads us to treat this principle, which holds only for objects of the senses, as valid for things in general. And so, by leaving out this limiting condition, we come to take the empirical principle that governs our concepts of the possibility of things as appearances for a transcendental principle of the possibility of things in general.

We then go on to hypostatize this idea of the sum total of all reality, treating it as a real, independently existing thing. We do this, first, by converting the distributive unity that belongs to the understanding's empirical use into the collective unity of an empirical whole, which is a dialectical illusion. We do it, second, by thinking of this whole, this sum of experience, as an individual thing that contains within itself all empirical reality. Then, through the transcendental subreption described above, the illicit swapping of one concept for another, this individual thing or being is substituted for our notion of a thing that stands at the head of the possibility of all things and supplies the real conditions for their complete determination.

This ideal of the *ens realissimum*, the most real being, is in truth only a representation in the mind. Yet it is first objectified, which is to say that objective existence is attributed to it. It is then hypostatized. Finally, as reason naturally presses toward the completion of unity, it is personified, as will be shown shortly. This happens because the regulative unity of experience does not rest on phenomena themselves. It rests on the understanding's act of connecting the manifold of phenomena within a single consciousness. Consequently, the unity of the supreme reality and the complete determinability of all things appear to reside in a supreme understanding, and therefore in a conscious intelligence.

### Section III. Of the Arguments employed by Speculative Reason in Proof of the Existence of a Supreme Being

Reason feels a pressing need to form some presupposition that will give the understanding an adequate basis for completely determining its concepts. Even so, the idealistic and fabricated character of such a presupposition is too obvious for reason to persuade itself, even for a moment, that a mere creation of its own thought actually exists. But other considerations compel reason to look for some resting place in the regress from the conditioned to the unconditioned. This unconditioned is not given as actually existing through its concept alone, yet it alone can bring the series of conditions to completion. This is the natural course of every human reason, even the most untutored, although reason does not always keep to the path it first takes. It begins not from concepts but from ordinary experience, and so it requires a footing in actual existence. That footing is insecure, however, unless it rests on the immovable rock of the absolutely necessary. And that foundation is itself untrustworthy if it leaves empty space beneath and above it, if it fails to fill everything and to leave no room for any further why or wherefore. In a word, it is untrustworthy unless it is infinite in its reality.

If we admit that some one thing exists, whatever it may be, we must also admit that something exists necessarily. For what is contingent exists only on condition of something else, which is its cause. From this we must go on to infer a cause that is not contingent and that therefore exists necessarily and unconditionally. This is the argument by which reason justifies its advance toward a primal being.

Reason then looks about for the concept of a being that can, without inconsistency, be judged worthy of the attribute of absolute necessity. Its purpose is not to infer *a priori*, from the concept of such a being, that the being objectively exists. If reason permitted itself that course, it would need no basis in given, actual existence at all, only the support of pure concepts. Its purpose is rather to find, among all our concepts of possible things, the one concept that contains nothing inconsistent with absolute necessity. Reason regards it as already established that some absolutely necessary being exists. If, then, it can eliminate every existence incapable of bearing the attribute of absolute necessity except one, that one must be the absolutely necessary being. This holds whether or not we can comprehend its necessity, that is, whether or not its necessity can be deduced from its concept alone.

Now consider the being whose concept contains a "therefore" for every "wherefore," which is deficient in no respect whatever, and which is all-sufficient as a condition. This seems to be the being to which we may rightly ascribe absolute necessity. Since it possesses the conditions of everything possible, it does not and cannot itself require any condition. In at least one respect, therefore, it meets the requirements of the concept of absolute necessity. In this it surpasses all other concepts, which are deficient and incomplete and so lack the mark of independence from every higher condition. It is true that we cannot infer from this that whatever does not contain within itself the supreme and complete condition, the condition of all other things, must therefore have only a conditioned existence. But neither can we assert the opposite. Such a being lacks the one characteristic that would allow reason to know, through an *a priori* concept, that its existence is unconditioned and necessary.

The concept of an *ens realissimum* is the one that best agrees with the concept of an unconditioned and necessary being. It does not satisfy every requirement of the latter concept, but we have no choice and are obliged to hold to it. We find that we cannot do without the existence of a necessary being. Yet once we admit it, we cannot discover anywhere in the whole sphere of possibility any being with better-founded claims to that distinction.

The natural course of human reason is therefore as follows. It first persuades itself that some necessary being exists. In this being it recognizes the marks of unconditioned existence. It then looks for the concept of whatever is independent of all conditions, and it finds this in what is itself the sufficient condition of everything else, namely in what contains all reality. But this unlimited all is an absolute unity, and the mind conceives it as a single, supreme being. Reason thus concludes that the Supreme Being, as the primal ground of all things, exists with absolute necessity.

This concept must be considered satisfactory to some degree, provided we admit the existence of a necessary being and recognize that these questions demand a definite and final answer. In that case we cannot make a better choice. Indeed, we have no choice at all, and we feel compelled to declare for the absolute unity of complete reality as the highest source of the possibility of things. But suppose nothing compels us to reach a definite conclusion, and we may leave the question open until we have fully weighed both sides. Suppose, that is, that we are asked only to judge how much we actually know about the question and how much we merely flatter ourselves that we know. Then the conclusion above no longer looks so advantageous. On the contrary, the grounds on which it rests appear defective.

For let us grant everything that has been said. First, the inference from some given existence, my own for example, to the existence of an unconditioned and necessary being is valid and unassailable. Second, a being that contains all reality, and therefore all the conditions of other things, must be regarded as absolutely unconditioned. Third, we have thereby found the concept of a thing to which absolute necessity may be ascribed without inconsistency. Even granting all this, it does not follow that the concept of a limited being, one in which the supreme reality does not reside, is incompatible with absolute necessity. I may not find in the concept of such a being the element of the unconditioned, which is plainly present in the sum total of all conditions. But I am not thereby entitled to conclude that its existence is conditioned. In the same way, in a hypothetical syllogism I am not entitled to argue that where a certain condition is absent, the conditioned is absent too. In the present case, the absent condition is completeness, so far as pure concepts are concerned. On the contrary, we remain free to regard all limited beings as equally unconditionally necessary, even though we cannot infer this from the general concept we have of them. Conducted in this way, the argument cannot give us the slightest notion of the properties of a necessary being, and it must prove fruitless in every respect.

Yet the argument retains a weight and an authority that it has never lost, despite its objective insufficiency. Suppose that certain obligations lie upon us that are grounded in the ideas of reason and deserve respect and obedience. Suppose further that these obligations could have no real or practical application to our nature unless we presupposed a Supreme Being to give effect and influence to the practical laws, so that without that presupposition they would be obligations without motives. In that case we would be bound to follow our concepts. Though objectively insufficient, those concepts would outweigh, by the standard of reason, any claims advanced from another quarter. The balance of doubt would be tipped by a practical addition. Indeed, Reason would have to condemn herself if she refused to comply with the demands of a judgment than which we know none higher, however imperfectly she might understand the grounds of those demands.

This argument is in fact transcendental, since it rests on the inherent insufficiency of the contingent. Yet it is so simple and natural that the most ordinary understanding can appreciate its force. We see things around us change, come into being, and pass away, so they, or their states, must have a cause. The same demand must then be made of that cause, insofar as it too is given in experience. It is natural, then, that we should locate the highest causality where we locate supreme causality. We place it in the being that contains the conditions of all possible effects, whose concept, that of an all-embracing reality, is so simple. We regard this highest cause as absolutely necessary because we find it absolutely necessary to ascend to it, and we see no reason to go beyond it. This is why, among all peoples and even through the darkest polytheism, a few faint sparks of monotheism glimmer. These idolaters were led to them not by reflection and deep thought but by the natural workings and progress of the common understanding.

There are only three ways of proving the existence of a Deity on the grounds of speculative reason.

Every path toward this goal begins in one of three ways. It may start from determinate experience and the particular constitution of the world of sense, and climb from there, by the laws of causality, to a highest cause existing outside the world. It may start from a purely indeterminate experience, that is, from some empirical existence or other. Or it may abstract from all experience and infer the existence of a supreme cause from *a priori* concepts alone. The first is the physico-theological argument, the second the cosmological, and the third the ontological. There are no others, and there can be no others.

I shall show that reason fares no better on the one path, the empirical, than on the other, the transcendental. It spreads its wings in vain when it tries to soar beyond the world of sense by the sheer power of speculative thought. The order in which these arguments must be examined will be exactly the reverse of the order in which reason arrives at them as it develops, which is the order in which they are listed above. For the reader will see that experience provides the occasion and the starting point, but it is the transcendental idea of reason that guides reason on its pilgrimage and is the goal of all its efforts. I shall therefore begin by examining the transcendental argument. Afterward I shall ask how much additional strength this mode of proof gains from the addition of the empirical element.

### Section IV. Of the Impossibility of an Ontological Proof of the Existence of God

It is evident from the foregoing that the concept of an absolutely necessary being is a mere idea. The fact that reason needs this idea falls far short of establishing its objective reality. The idea merely points toward a certain unattainable perfection. Rather than extending the understanding's domain by presenting it with new objects, it limits the understanding's operations. But a strange anomaly confronts us at the very threshold. The inference from any given existence to an absolutely necessary existence seems correct and unavoidable, yet the conditions of the understanding refuse to help us form any concept of such a being.

Philosophers have always spoken of an absolutely necessary being without troubling to ask whether such a being can even be thought, and how, let alone whether its existence can actually be demonstrated. A verbal definition of the concept is easy enough: it is something whose non-existence is impossible. But does this definition shed any light on the conditions that make it impossible to think of a thing as not existing? Those are precisely the conditions we need to identify, so that we can discover whether in the concept of such a being we are thinking anything at all. By means of the word "unconditioned," I discard all the conditions the understanding ordinarily requires in order to regard something as necessary. But doing so leaves it very far from clear whether, with the concept of the unconditionally necessary, I am thinking of something or of nothing whatsoever.

Worse still, many have tried to explain this concept, which was picked up by chance and is now so widely current, through examples that seemed to make any inquiry into its intelligibility entirely unnecessary. Every proposition of geometry, it was said, is absolutely necessary, such as the proposition that a triangle has three angles. And so people spoke of an object lying wholly outside the sphere of our understanding as though the meaning of its concept were perfectly plain.

Every example offered has been drawn, without exception, from judgments and not from things. But the unconditioned necessity of a judgment does not amount to the absolute necessity of a thing. On the contrary, the absolute necessity of a judgment is only the conditioned necessity of a thing, or of the predicate in the judgment. The proposition just cited does not say that three angles necessarily exist. It says that if a triangle exists, three angles necessarily exist in it. This logical necessity has been the source of the greatest delusions. People formed an *a priori* concept of a thing and made its content include existence. They then believed they could safely conclude that, because existence belongs necessarily to the object of the concept, the thing's existence is itself necessarily posited. Existence belongs to that object only on condition that I posit the thing as given. Yet they concluded that the thing is absolutely necessary, simply because its existence has been thought in its concept.

If, in an identical judgment, I cancel the predicate in thought while keeping the subject, a contradiction results, and I therefore say that the predicate belongs necessarily to the subject. But if I cancel both subject and predicate together, no contradiction arises, because nothing remains that could contradict anything. To posit a triangle while denying its three angles is self-contradictory. To deny both the triangle and its angles is perfectly permissible. The same holds for the concept of an absolutely necessary being. Cancel its existence in thought, and you cancel the thing itself together with all its predicates. Where, then, could a contradiction arise? It cannot arise externally, because nothing is necessary externally. Nor can it arise internally, because in cancelling the thing itself you have cancelled all its internal properties as well. "God is omnipotent" is a necessary judgment. Omnipotence cannot be denied once you posit the existence of a Deity, that is, of an infinite being, since the two concepts are identical. But if you say "God does not exist," you affirm neither omnipotence nor any other predicate. They all vanish together with the subject, and this judgment contains not the slightest self-contradiction.

You have now seen that when the predicate of a judgment is cancelled in thought together with its subject, no internal contradiction can arise, whatever the predicate may be. Your only way to escape this conclusion is to declare that there are certain subjects that cannot be cancelled in thought. But that amounts to saying that there exist subjects that are absolutely necessary, which is the very hypothesis you set out to prove. For I cannot form the slightest concept of a thing that, when cancelled in thought together with all its predicates, leaves a contradiction behind. And in the domain of pure *a priori* concepts, contradiction is the sole criterion of impossibility.

Against these general considerations, whose soundness no one can dispute, one argument is put forward that is supposed to settle the matter by an actual case. It is claimed that there is one and only one concept in which the non-being or cancellation of its object is self-contradictory, and that this is the concept of an *ens realissimum*. This being, you say, possesses all reality, and you consider yourselves entitled to assume that such a being is possible. I am willing to grant this for the moment, though a concept's freedom from self-contradiction is far from sufficient to prove that its object is possible. A concept is always possible if it does not contradict itself. That is the logical criterion of possibility, and it distinguishes the object of such a concept from the *nihil negativum*, the sheer nothing of a self-contradictory notion. Yet a concept may still be empty unless the objective reality of the synthesis that generates it has been demonstrated. Any such proof must rest on principles of possible experience, not on the principle of analysis or contradiction. This is a warning against inferring the possibility of a thing, which is real, from the possibility of a concept, which is merely logical. The argument then proceeds as follows. The notion of all reality includes that of existence, so existence lies within the concept of this possible thing. If the thing is cancelled in thought, its internal possibility is cancelled as well, and that is self-contradictory.

My reply is this. It is absurd to smuggle the concept of a thing's existence, under whatever name, into the concept of a thing that is to be thought solely with regard to its possibility. If this is allowed, you will appear to have won, but in reality you will have stated nothing but a tautology. I ask whether the proposition "this or that thing (which I grant to be possible) exists" is analytic or synthetic. Suppose it is analytic. Then the assertion of existence adds nothing to your thought of the subject. But in that case either the concept in your mind is the thing itself, or you have presupposed an existence as belonging to the possible and then inferred that existence from the thing's internal possibility. That is nothing but a wretched tautology. Using the word "reality" in the concept of the thing and the word "existence" in the concept of the predicate will not rescue you. If you call every positing of a thing "reality," you have already posited the thing, with all its predicates, in the concept of the subject and assumed it to be actual, and you merely repeat this in the predicate. Suppose instead you admit, as every reasonable person must, that every existential proposition is synthetic. How, then, can you maintain that the predicate of existence cannot be denied without contradiction? That property belongs to analytic propositions alone.

I might reasonably hope to put an end once and for all to this sophistical line of argument by giving a strict definition of the concept of existence. But my own experience has taught me how stubbornly a certain illusion resists nearly every effort at explanation and illustration. It is the illusion that comes from confusing a logical predicate with a real one, that is, with a predicate that helps to determine a thing. Anything at all may be used as a logical predicate, and the subject may even be predicated of itself, because logic disregards the content of a judgment. But a determination is a predicate that is added to the concept of the subject and enlarges it. It must therefore not already be contained in that concept.

Being is plainly not a real predicate. It is not a concept of something that could be added to the concept of a thing. It is merely the positing of a thing, or of certain determinations in it. In logic it is merely the copula of a judgment. The proposition "God is omnipotent" contains two concepts, and each has its object or content. The word "is" adds no further predicate. It only indicates the relation of the predicate to the subject. Now suppose I take the subject, God, together with all its predicates, omnipotence among them, and say "God is," or "There is a God." I attach no new predicate to the concept of God. I merely posit or affirm the existence of the subject with all its predicates, positing the object in relation to my concept. The content of both is the same. My concept expresses only the possibility of the object, and nothing is added to it when, through the expression "it is," I think of its object as absolutely given or existing. Thus the actual contains no more than the possible. A hundred real dollars contain no more than a hundred possible dollars. The possible dollars signify the concept, and the real dollars signify the object. If the object contained more than the concept, my concept would not express the whole object and would therefore be an inadequate concept of it. In reckoning my wealth, however, there may be said to be more in a hundred real dollars than in a hundred possible dollars, that is, than in the mere concept of them. The real object, the dollars themselves, is not contained analytically in my concept. It is a synthetic addition to my concept, which is merely a determination of my state of mind. Yet this objective reality, this existence apart from my concepts, does not in the least increase the hundred dollars themselves.

However many predicates I use to think a thing, and whatever they may be, even to the point of determining it completely, I add nothing whatever to the object of my concept by further declaring that this thing exists. Otherwise what existed would not be exactly what I had thought in my concept but something more, and I could not say that the exact object of my concept actually existed. If I think of a thing as containing every mode of reality but one, the missing mode is not supplied to the concept when I affirm that the thing exists. On the contrary, the thing exists, if it exists at all, with exactly the defect I thought into its concept; otherwise what exists would not be what I thought, but something different. Now suppose I think of a being as the highest reality, without defect or imperfection. The question still remains whether this being exists or not. Although nothing is lacking from the possible real content of my concept, something is lacking in its relation to my state of mind: I do not know whether knowledge of the object the concept indicates is possible a posteriori. Here the source of the present difficulty becomes clear. If the question concerned only an object of the senses, I could never confuse the concept of a thing with its existence. The concept merely allows me to think the object as agreeing with the general conditions of experience, whereas the object's existence allows me to think it as contained within the realm of actual experience. Yet this connection with the world of experience adds nothing whatever to the concept, even though a possible perception has been added to the mind's experience. If, however, we think existence through the pure category alone, it is no wonder that we cannot produce any criterion sufficient to distinguish it from mere possibility.

Whatever our concept of an object may contain, we must go beyond it if we wish to attribute existence to the object. With objects of the senses, we do this by connecting them, according to empirical laws, with one or another of my perceptions. But there is no means of knowing the existence of objects of pure thought, because such existence would have to be known entirely a priori. All our knowledge of existence, whether it comes directly through perception or through inferences that link some object to a perception, belongs wholly to the realm of experience, which forms a perfect unity with itself. An existence outside this realm cannot be declared absolutely impossible, but it is a hypothesis whose truth we have no means of establishing.

The notion of a Supreme Being is in many respects a highly useful idea. But precisely because it is an idea, it cannot extend our knowledge of what exists. It is not even enough to inform us about the possibility of a being we do not know to exist. It cannot be denied the analytic criterion of possibility, which consists in the absence of contradiction among propositions. But the combination of real properties in a thing is a synthesis, and we cannot judge a priori whether such a synthesis is possible, because these realities are not given to us specifically. Even if they were, a judgment would still be impossible, because the criterion for the possibility of synthetic knowledge must be sought in the world of experience, and the object of an idea cannot belong to that world. The celebrated Leibniz therefore failed entirely in his attempt to establish on a priori grounds the possibility of this sublime ideal being.

The celebrated ontological, or Cartesian, argument for the existence of a Supreme Being is therefore insufficient. We might as well hope to enlarge our knowledge through mere ideas as a merchant might hope to increase his wealth by adding zeros to the balance in his account book.

### Section V. Of the Impossibility of a Cosmological Proof of the Existence of God

The attempt to extract from a mere idea a proof that some corresponding object exists was not a natural procedure at all. It was entirely an invention of scholastic subtlety. No one would ever have attempted it but for a certain need of reason. Reason must assume the existence of a necessary being as the foundation of the empirical regress, the backward chain of conditions within experience. Because this necessity must be unconditioned and a priori, reason is compelled to look for a concept that will, if possible, meet this demand and allow us to know such a being a priori. Philosophers believed they had found this concept in the idea of an *ens realissimum*, a "most real being." They used this idea to gain a more precise knowledge of a necessary being whose existence they were already convinced of, or persuaded of, on other grounds. Reason was thus lured away from its natural course. Instead of ending with the concept of an *ens realissimum*, it tried to begin with it, so as to infer from it the very idea of necessary existence that the concept had in fact been called in to complete. This is how that unfortunate ontological argument arose, an argument that satisfies neither the sound common sense of humanity nor the scientific scrutiny of the philosopher.

The cosmological proof, which we are now about to examine, keeps the link between absolute necessity and the highest reality. But rather than reasoning from the highest reality to necessary existence, as the previous argument did, it reasons from the given unconditioned necessity of some being to that being's unlimited reality. The path it follows, whether rational or sophistical, is at least a natural one. It goes a long way toward persuading the ordinary understanding, and it shows itself worthy of respect even from the speculative intellect. At the same time, it contains the outline of every argument used in natural theology, arguments that have always been in use and in authority and always will be. However they are adorned, and whatever embellishments of rhetoric and sentiment conceal them, they are at bottom identical with the argument we are about to discuss. Leibniz called this proof the *argumentum a contingentia mundi*, the argument from the contingency of the world. I shall now set it before the reader and subject it to strict examination.

It runs as follows. If anything exists, an absolutely necessary being must also exist. Now I, at least, exist. Therefore an absolutely necessary being exists. The minor premise contains an experience; the major premise reasons from experience in general to the existence of a necessary being. That inference is too familiar to need detailed discussion. It rests on the spurious transcendental law of causality, which holds that everything contingent has a cause, and that this cause, if itself contingent, must in turn have a cause, and so on, until the series of subordinate causes ends in an absolutely necessary cause, without which the series would be incomplete. The argument thus really begins from experience and is not wholly a priori, or ontological. Because the object of all possible experience is the world, it is called the cosmological proof. It makes no reference to any particular property of the objects of the senses by which this world of sense might be distinguished from other possible worlds. In this respect it differs from the physico-theological proof, which rests on a consideration of the specific constitution of our sensible world.

The proof then proceeds. A necessary being can be determined in only one way: of every pair of possible opposed predicates, it can be determined by only one. Consequently it must be completely determined in and through its concept. But only one concept of a thing is possible that determines it completely a priori, namely the concept of the *ens realissimum*. It follows that the concept of the *ens realissimum* is the only concept through which, and in which, a necessary being can be thought. Therefore a Supreme Being necessarily exists.

So many sophistical propositions are gathered together in this cosmological argument that speculative reason seems to have spent all its dialectical skill on it to produce a transcendental illusion of the most extreme kind. We shall postpone a full investigation of it and confine ourselves for now to exposing its stratagem. It passes off an old argument in new clothing and appeals to the agreement of two witnesses, one bearing the credentials of pure reason and the other those of empiricism, when in fact only the first witness has changed his clothes and his voice in order to pass himself off as a second. To give itself a secure foundation, the argument rests its conclusions on experience and so appears entirely distinct from the ontological argument, which puts its whole trust in pure a priori concepts. But experience helps reason take only a single step: to the existence of a necessary being. Experience cannot teach what the properties of that being are. Reason therefore abandons experience altogether and pursues its inquiry in the realm of pure concepts, seeking to discover what properties an absolutely necessary being ought to have, that is, which among all possible things contains the requisite conditions (*requisita*) of absolute necessity. Reason believes it has found these requisites in the concept of an *ens realissimum*, and in that concept alone, and therefore concludes that the *ens realissimum* is an absolutely necessary being. Yet reason has plainly presupposed here that the concept of an *ens realissimum* fully corresponds to the concept of a being of absolute necessity, so that we may infer the existence of the second from the first.
