This is the very proposition on which the ontological argument was founded, and it is now pressed into service to support the cosmological argument, against the wishes and declared intentions of its inventors. For the existence of an absolutely necessary being is here given in concepts alone. If I say, "The concept of the *ens realissimum* is a concept of this kind, and indeed the only concept adequate to our idea of a necessary being," then I am obliged to admit that the necessary being can be inferred from the most real being. So it is really the ontological argument that appears within the cosmological one and supplies its entire force. The supposed basis in experience has been of no further use than to lead us to the concept of absolute necessity, and it is wholly incapable of demonstrating that this attribute belongs to any determinate existing thing. Once we set ourselves such a goal, we must leave the realm of experience and rise to that of pure concepts, examining them to discover whether any one of them contains the conditions for the possibility of an absolutely necessary being. But if the possibility of such a being is demonstrated in this way, its existence is proved as well. We may then assert that among all possible beings there is one that possesses the attribute of necessity, which is to say that this being exists with absolute necessity.

Every illusion in an argument is easier to detect when the argument is set out in the formal manner of the schools, and we shall now do exactly that.

If the proposition "Every absolutely necessary being is also an *ens realissimum*" is correct (and this proposition is the *nervus probandi*, the sinew on which the whole proof depends), then, like every affirmative judgment, it must be capable of conversion, at least in the limited form logicians call *conversio per accidens*, by which "Every A is B" yields "Some B is A." It follows that some *entia realissima* are absolutely necessary beings. But one *ens realissimum* does not differ in any respect from another, and what holds of some holds of all. In this case, therefore, I may use simple conversion and say: "Every *ens realissimum* is a necessary being." Since this proposition is determined a priori by the concepts it contains, the mere concept of an *ens realissimum* must carry with it the further attribute of absolute necessity. Yet this is exactly what the ontological argument maintained and what the cosmological argument refused to acknowledge, even though it formed the real ground of its disguised and illusory reasoning.

The second method by which speculative reason tries to demonstrate the existence of a Supreme Being is therefore not only illusory and inadequate, like the first, but suffers from the further flaw of an *ignoratio elenchi*, a proof that misses the point at issue. It claims to lead us by a new road to the desired destination, but after a short detour it brings us back to the old path we had abandoned at its invitation.

I said earlier that this cosmological argument harbors a whole nest of dialectical assumptions, which transcendental criticism can expose and dispel without difficulty. I shall merely list them here, leaving it to the reader, who must by now be well practiced in such matters, to investigate the fallacies they contain.

The following fallacies, among others, can be found in this mode of proof:

1. The transcendental principle "Everything contingent must have a cause," a principle that has no meaning except in the world of the senses. The purely intellectual concept of the contingent cannot generate any synthetic proposition such as that of causality, which itself has no meaning or distinguishing mark except in the world of appearances. Yet here it is used to carry us beyond the limits of its own domain.
2. The inference of a first cause from the impossibility of an infinite ascending series of causes in the world of sense. The principles governing the use of reason do not justify this conclusion even within experience, still less when we try to pass beyond its limits.
3. Reason's willingness to rest satisfied, on insufficient grounds, regarding the completion of this series. It removes all conditions, although without conditions no concept of necessity can be formed at all. Then, since it is no longer able to form any further concepts, it accepts this as the completion of the concept it wishes to form of the series.
4. The confusion of the logical possibility of a concept of the sum of all reality, whose criterion is merely the absence of contradiction, with its transcendental possibility, which requires a principle showing that such a synthesis can actually be carried out. That principle, once again, refers us back to the world of experience. And so on.

The cosmological argument aims to avoid the need to prove the existence of a necessary being a priori from mere concepts, a proof that would have to be ontological and that we feel wholly unable to supply. To this end, we reason from an actual existence, from experience in general, to an absolutely necessary condition of that existence. In this case there is no need to demonstrate the condition's possibility, since once we have proved that something exists, the question of whether it is possible becomes superfluous. Now, when we want to define the nature of this necessary being more precisely, we do not look for a being whose concept would let us understand the necessity of its existence, because if we could do that, we would need no empirical starting point at all. We try instead to discover only the negative condition, the *conditio sine qua non*, without which a being would not be absolutely necessary. This would be entirely legitimate in any other reasoning from a consequence back to its ground. In the present case, however, the condition of absolute necessity can unfortunately be found in only a single being. The concept of that being must therefore contain everything needed to demonstrate absolute necessity, and so entitle me to infer that necessity a priori. It must be possible, then, to reason in reverse and say: the thing to which the concept of the highest reality belongs is absolutely necessary. But if I cannot reason in this way, and I cannot unless I accept the sufficiency of the ontological argument, I meet insurmountable obstacles on my new path and find myself no farther along than where I began. The concept of a Supreme Being answers every a priori question about the internal determinations of a thing, and for that reason it is an ideal without equal or parallel; its general concept marks it out at the same time as an *ens individuum*, a single individual being among all possible things. But the concept does not answer the question of its existence, which was the whole purpose of our inquiry. And even if the existence of a necessary being were granted, we would be unable to answer the question: which of all the things in the world must be regarded as that being?

It is certainly permissible to assume the existence of an all-sufficient being, a cause of all possible effects, so that reason can bring unity into its methods and grounds of explanation with respect to appearances. But to assert that such a being necessarily exists is no longer the modest statement of an admissible hypothesis. It is the boldest claim to apodictic certainty, for knowledge of what is absolutely necessary must itself be absolutely certain.

The transcendental ideal that the mind forms aims either to find a concept that agrees with the idea of absolute necessity or a concept that contains that idea. If one is possible, so is the other, for reason recognizes as absolutely necessary only what is necessary from its concept. But both attempts are equally beyond our power. We find it impossible to satisfy the understanding on this point, and just as impossible to persuade it to rest content with this incapacity.

Unconditioned necessity, which the mind indispensably requires as the ultimate support and foundation of all existing things, is an abyss at whose edge human reason trembles in dismay. Even the idea of eternity, terrible and sublime as the poet Haller portrays it, does not strike the mind's eye with such awe and dread. Eternity measures the duration of things, but it does not support them. We cannot endure the thought, nor can we rid ourselves of it, that a being we regard as the greatest of all possible beings might say to itself: "I am from eternity to eternity; apart from me there is nothing, except what exists through my will. But where, then, do I come from?" Here everything gives way beneath us. The greatest perfection, like the smallest, floats without support or footing before speculative reason, which finds it as easy to let go of the one as of the other.

Many natural forces reveal their existence through their effects while remaining wholly inscrutable in their nature; they elude all our powers of observation. The transcendental object that underlies appearances, and with it the reason why our sensibility is subject to these conditions rather than others, are and must always remain hidden from the mind's eye. The fact is there; the reason for the fact we cannot see. An ideal of pure reason, however, cannot be called mysterious or inscrutable, because its reality has no other credential than reason's own need for it in order to complete the world of synthetic unity. An ideal is not even given as an object that can be thought, so it cannot be inscrutable. On the contrary, as a mere idea it must have its seat in the very constitution of reason, and for that reason it must admit of explanation and solution. The very essence of reason lies in its ability to account for all our concepts, opinions, and assertions, on objective grounds or, when they happen to be illusory and fallacious, on subjective ones.

#### Detection and Explanation of the Dialectical Illusion in All Transcendental Arguments for the Existence of a Necessary Being

Both of the preceding arguments are transcendental: they do not proceed from empirical principles. The cosmological argument claimed to lay a foundation of experience for its structure of reasoning, but it did not base its procedure on the specific character of experience. It relied instead on pure principles of reason, applied to an existence given in empirical consciousness, and then abandoned this guidance altogether in order to rest its claims entirely on pure concepts. What, then, in these transcendental arguments, produces the dialectical yet natural illusion that links the concepts of necessity and supreme reality, and turns into a real thing what can only ever be an idea? What causes reason to take the unavoidable step of admitting that some one among all existing things must be necessary, while it recoils from asserting the existence of such a being as if from an abyss? And how is reason to explain this anomaly to itself, and pass from the wavering state of a timid and reluctant assent, always taken back again, to a calm and settled understanding of its cause?

It is a remarkable fact that, once I suppose something exists, I cannot avoid inferring that something exists necessarily. The cosmological argument rests on this inference, which is entirely natural but not, for that reason, reliable. Yet whatever concept of a thing I form, I find that I cannot think its existence as absolutely necessary, and that nothing prevents me, whatever the thing or being may be, from thinking of it as not existing. I may therefore be obliged to admit that all existing things have a necessary basis, while being unable to think any single individual thing as necessary. I can never complete the regress through the conditions of existence without admitting a necessary being, and yet I can never begin from that being.

If I must think of something as existing necessarily as the foundation of existing things, and yet am not permitted to think of any individual thing as necessary in itself, the inevitable conclusion is that necessity and contingency are not properties of things themselves, since otherwise an internal contradiction would result. Neither of these two principles, then, is objective. Both are merely subjective principles of reason. The first requires us to seek a necessary ground for everything that exists, and to be satisfied with no explanation short of one that is complete a priori. The second forbids us ever to hope for that completeness, and requires us to regard no member of the empirical world as unconditioned. Viewed in this way, as purely heuristic and regulative principles that concern only the formal interest of reason, the two are entirely consistent with each other. The first says: philosophize about nature as if there were a necessary first foundation of all existing things, solely in order to bring systematic unity into your knowledge by pursuing such an idea, a foundation you arbitrarily accept as ultimate. The second warns you never to treat any individual determination concerning the existence of things as such an ultimate foundation, that is, as absolutely necessary, but always to keep the way open for further progress in the derivation and to treat every determination as determined by something else. But if everything we perceive must be regarded as only conditionally necessary, then nothing given empirically can possibly be absolutely necessary.

It follows that you must place the absolutely necessary outside and beyond the world. It is useful only as a principle of the highest possible unity in experience, and you cannot find any such necessary existence within the world, because the second rule requires you to regard every empirical cause of unity as itself derived.

The philosophers of antiquity regarded all the forms of nature as contingent, while they treated matter, in keeping with the judgment of ordinary human reason, as primal and necessary. But had they considered matter not relatively, as the underlying substratum of appearances, but absolutely and in itself, as an independent existence, the idea of its absolute necessity would have vanished at once. Nothing binds reason absolutely to such an existence. On the contrary, reason can always abolish it in thought without contradicting itself, and it was in thought alone that the idea of absolute necessity resided. Their opinion must therefore have rested on a regulative principle. And in fact, extension and impenetrability, which together make up our concept of matter, form the supreme empirical principle of the unity of appearances, and insofar as this principle is empirically unconditioned, it has the character of a regulative principle. But every determination of matter that constitutes what is real in it, impenetrability included, is an effect that must have a cause, and so is always derived. For this reason the concept of matter cannot be reconciled with the idea of a necessary being understood as the principle of all derived unity. Each of matter's real properties, being derived, can be only conditionally necessary and can therefore be abolished in thought, and with them the entire existence of matter can be abolished or suppressed. If this were not so, we would have found within the world of appearances the highest ground or condition of unity, which the second regulative principle declares impossible. It follows that matter, and everything else belonging to the world of the senses, can be neither a necessary primal being nor even a principle of empirical unity. That being or principle must be assigned a place outside the world. In this way we can proceed with complete confidence to derive the appearances of the world, and their existence, from other appearances, as if no necessary being existed at all. At the same time we can strive without ceasing toward completeness in that derivation, as if such a being, the supreme condition of all existence, were presupposed by the mind.

These remarks will have made it clear to the reader that the ideal of the Supreme Being, far from asserting the existence of a being necessary in itself, is nothing more than a regulative principle of reason. It directs us to regard every connection among appearances as if it arose from an all-sufficient necessary cause, and on that basis it lays down the rule of a systematic and necessary unity in our explanation of appearances. Yet we cannot help committing what may be called a transcendental subreption, a covert substitution by which we treat this merely formal principle as constitutive and turn the unity it prescribes into an actual thing. Our notion of space follows precisely the same pattern. Space is the primal condition of all shapes, which are really just so many different limitations of it. And so, although space is merely a principle of sensibility, we cannot help regarding it as an absolutely necessary and self-subsistent thing, an object given in itself prior to all experience. In the same way, since the systematic unity of nature cannot be established as a principle for the empirical use of reason unless it rests on the idea of an *ens realissimum*, a most real being, as the supreme cause, it is entirely natural that we should regard this idea as a real object, and regard that object, in its role as supreme condition, as absolutely necessary. In this way a regulative principle is transformed into a constitutive one. The substitution becomes evident when I take this supreme being, which was absolutely or unconditionally necessary only in relation to the world, and consider it as a thing in itself. I then find it impossible to represent its necessity through any concept whatever. That necessity exists only in my own mind, as a formal condition of thought, and not as a material and substantial condition of existence.

### Section VI. Of the Impossibility of a Physico-Theological Proof

If, then, neither a pure concept nor the general experience of some existing thing can provide a sufficient basis for proving the existence of God, only one other approach remains. We can ground our argument on a determinate experience of the things of the present world, their constitution and arrangement, and see whether this leads us to a sound conviction that a Supreme Being exists. We shall call this the physico-theological argument. If it proves insufficient, speculative reason has no satisfactory proof to offer of the existence of a being corresponding to our transcendental idea.

The observations of the preceding sections make it plain that the answer to this question will be neither difficult nor doubtful. How could any experience ever be adequate to an idea? The very essence of an idea is that no experience can ever be found that matches it. The transcendental idea of a necessary and all-sufficient being is so immeasurably great, so far above everything empirical, which is always conditioned, that we hope in vain to find materials in experience ample enough to fill out the concept. We search in vain for the unconditioned among things that are conditioned, and the laws of empirical synthesis give us no examples, nor even any guidance. If the Supreme Being forms a link in the chain of empirical conditions, it must be a member of the empirical series and, like the lower members that follow from it, must have its own origin in some still higher member. If, on the other hand, we detach it from the chain and conceive it as a purely intelligible being, standing apart from the series of natural causes, how is reason to bridge the abyss that separates the one from the other? All laws governing the regress from effects to causes, and every synthetic addition to our knowledge, apply solely to possible experience and to the objects of the sensible world. Apart from these, they have no meaning.

The world around us opens before our eyes so magnificent a spectacle of order, variety, beauty, and fitness to purpose that, whether we follow our observations outward into the infinity of space or inward into its endless divisions, whether we consider the world in its greatest or its smallest manifestations, we find, even after reaching the highest summit of knowledge our feeble minds can attain, that language loses its force before such inconceivable wonders, and number its power to reckon. Thought itself fails to grasp them adequately, and our conception of the whole dissolves into an astonishment beyond expression, all the more eloquent for being mute. Everywhere we see a chain of causes and effects, of means and ends, of death and birth. Since nothing has entered by itself into the condition in which we find it, we are constantly referred onward to something else, which in turn raises the same question about its own cause. The whole universe would thus sink into the abyss of nothingness unless we admitted that, beyond this infinite chain of contingent things, there exists something primal and self-subsistent, something that, as the cause of this world of appearances, secures its continuance and preservation.

What magnitude, then, shall we ascribe to this highest cause? We do not know the full content of the world, still less can we measure its magnitude against the whole range of what is possible. But since this supreme cause is a necessity of the human mind, what prevents us from attributing to it a degree of perfection that places it above everything possible? This we can easily do, though only through the faint outline of an abstract concept, by representing this being to ourselves as a single individual substance containing within itself all possible perfection. Such a concept satisfies reason's demand for economy in its principles. It is free of self-contradiction. It even extends the use of reason within experience, by the guidance it gives toward order and system, and it conflicts in no respect with any law of experience.

This argument always deserves to be treated with respect. It is the oldest, the clearest, and the one most in harmony with the common reason of mankind. It enlivens the study of nature, just as it owes its own existence to that study and constantly draws fresh strength from it. It introduces purposes and ends into a domain where our observation alone could never have discovered them, and it extends our knowledge of nature by directing our attention to a unity whose principle lies beyond nature. This knowledge of nature, in turn, reacts upon the idea that gave rise to it, and so our belief in a divine author of the universe grows into an irresistible conviction.

For these reasons it would be utterly hopeless to try to strip this argument of the authority it has always enjoyed. The mind, continually lifted by these considerations, which, though empirical, are remarkably powerful and constantly gaining in force, will not let itself be cast down by the doubts that subtle speculation raises. It tears itself free from such uncertainty the moment it turns its gaze toward the wondrous forms of nature and the majesty of the universe, and it rises from height to height, from condition to condition, until it has lifted itself to the supreme and unconditioned author of all things.

We have nothing to object to in the reasonableness and usefulness of this procedure; on the contrary, we would commend and encourage it. What we cannot approve is the argument's claim to demonstrative certainty, and its claim to be accepted on its own merits without the support or favor of any other argument. Nor can it harm the cause of morality to bring down the tone of the arrogant sophist and teach him the modesty and moderation proper to a belief that brings calm and contentment to the mind without demanding of it an unworthy submission. I maintain, then, that the physico-theological argument cannot by itself prove the existence of a Supreme Being. It must hand this task over to the ontological argument, for which it is merely a preface, and consequently the ontological argument contains the only possible ground of proof, so far as speculative reason has one, for the existence of such a being.

The main steps of the physico-theological argument are as follows. First, we observe in the world clear signs of a purposeful arrangement, carried out with great wisdom, within a whole of indescribably varied content and of unlimited extent. Second, this arrangement of means and ends is entirely foreign to the things that exist in the world and belongs to them only as a contingent attribute. The natures of different things could not of themselves, by whatever means, work together harmoniously toward definite purposes unless they had been chosen and directed toward those purposes by a rational, ordering principle acting according to certain fundamental ideas. Third, there therefore exists a sublime and wise cause, or perhaps several, which is not merely a blind, all-powerful nature producing the beings and events that fill the world through an unconscious fertility, but a free and intelligent cause of the world. Fourth, the unity of this cause may be inferred from the unity of the reciprocal relations among the parts of the world, which fit together like the parts of a work of craftsmanship, an inference that all our observation favors and all principles of analogy support.

In this argument, we infer from the analogy between certain products of nature and the products of human art, where human skill compels nature to bend to its purposes, as in a house, a ship, or a watch, that the same kind of causality, namely understanding and will, is at work in nature. It is further asserted that the inner possibility of this freely acting nature, which is the source of all art and perhaps of human reason as well, derives from yet another art, a superhuman one. This conclusion might well fail to survive the scrutiny of a rigorous transcendental critique. But for the present we shall raise no objection to either of these claims. We shall only observe that, if we are to speak of a cause at all, we have no surer guide than the analogy between nature and such products of design, since these are the only products whose causes and manner of construction are completely known to us. Reason could not satisfy her own demands if she abandoned a causality she does know for obscure and unprovable principles of explanation she does not know.

According to the physico-theological argument, the connection and harmony in the world prove the contingency only of its form, not of its matter, that is, of the world's substance. To establish the contingency of the substance as well, one would have to prove that the things of the world would in themselves be incapable of such harmony and order unless they were, even in their very substance, the product of a supreme wisdom. That would require grounds of proof altogether different from the analogy with human art. At most, therefore, this proof can show the existence of an architect of the world, whose work is always limited by the capacities of the material he works with, but not of a creator of the world, to whom all things are subject. The argument is thus wholly inadequate to the task before us, which is to demonstrate the existence of an all-sufficient being. If we want to prove the contingency of matter itself, we must turn to a transcendental argument, and avoiding such an argument was the very purpose for which the physico-theological proof was devised.

From the order and design visible in the universe, which we take to be an arrangement of a thoroughly contingent kind, we infer the existence of a cause proportionate to it. The concept of this cause must contain certain determinate qualities, and so it must be the concept of a being that possesses all power, all wisdom, and so on, in a word, all perfection: the concept of an all-sufficient being. For predicates such as very great, astonishing, or immeasurable power and excellence give us no determinate concept of the thing and tell us nothing about what it is in itself. They merely express the relation between the magnitude of the object and the observer, who compares it with himself and with his own capacity to comprehend. They are simply expressions of praise and reverence, which either magnify the object or diminish the observer in relation to it. Where we are dealing with the magnitude of a thing's perfection, the only determinate concept available is the one that includes all possible perfection or completeness, and only the totality of reality, the *omnitudo realitatis*, is completely determined in and through its concept alone.

No one, surely, will be bold enough to claim a perfect insight into how the magnitude of the world he observes, both in its extent and in its content, relates to omnipotence; how the order and design in the world relate to the highest wisdom; or how the unity of the world relates to the absolute unity of a Supreme Being. Physico-theology is therefore incapable of supplying a determinate concept of a supreme cause of the world, and so it is insufficient as the principle of a theology that is itself meant to be the foundation of religion.

Absolute totality cannot possibly be reached by the path of empiricism. Yet this is exactly the path the physico-theological argument follows. By what means, then, shall we bridge the abyss?

Having risen to admiration of the greatness of the power, wisdom, and other attributes of the world's author, and finding that we can go no further, we abandon the empirical grounds of the argument and proceed instead to infer the contingency of the world from the order and purposiveness we observe in it. From this contingency we infer, with the help of transcendental concepts alone, the existence of something absolutely necessary. And continuing onward, we move from the concept of the absolute necessity of the first cause to the concept that completely determines it, the concept of an all-embracing reality. Thus the physico-theological argument, failing in its undertaking, falls back in its embarrassment on the cosmological argument. And since the cosmological argument is merely the ontological argument in disguise, the physico-theological argument accomplishes its purpose solely by means of pure reason, even though it began by disclaiming any connection with that faculty and professing to rest its entire procedure on experience alone.

The physico-theologians therefore have no grounds for treating the transcendental mode of argument with such contempt, or for looking down on it, with the self-satisfaction of clear-sighted observers of nature, as the cobweb spun in the brains of obscure speculators. If they reflect on and examine their own arguments, they will find that after following the path of nature and experience for some time, and finding themselves no closer to their goal, they abruptly leave that path and pass into the realm of pure possibility, where they hope to reach on the wings of ideas what had escaped all their empirical inquiries. Having gained what they believe is firm footing after this enormous leap, they extend their determinate concept, which has come into their possession they know not how, across the whole of creation. They then illustrate their ideal, which is entirely a product of pure reason, with examples drawn from experience, examples wretchedly unworthy of the grandeur of the object, while refusing to admit that they arrived at this knowledge, or this hypothesis, by a road quite different from that of experience.

So the physico-theological proof of the existence of a Supreme Being rests on the cosmological proof, and the cosmological rests on the ontological. And since speculative reason has no path open to it apart from these three, the ontological proof, grounded on pure concepts of reason, is the only one possible, if any proof at all can be given of a proposition that so far transcends the empirical use of the understanding.

### Section VII. Critique of All Theology Based upon Speculative Principles of Reason

If by "theology" I mean knowledge of a primal being, that knowledge rests either on reason alone (*theologia rationalis*) or on revelation (*theologia revelata*). Rational theology conceives its object in one of two ways. It may conceive it purely through transcendental concepts, as the original being (*ens originarium*), the most real being (*ens realissimum*), or the being of all beings (*ens entium*), and it is then called transcendental theology. Or it may conceive it through a concept borrowed from the nature of our own minds, as a supreme intelligence, and it must then be called natural theology. Someone who accepts transcendental theology alone is called a deist. Someone who also accepts the possibility of a natural theology is called a theist. The deist grants that pure reason alone can know that a Supreme Being exists, but he holds that our concept of this being is purely transcendental. All we can say of it is that it possesses all reality, and we cannot define it any more closely. The theist maintains that reason, by analogy with nature, can give us a more definite concept of this being, and that its activity as the cause of all things proceeds from intelligence and free will. The deist therefore regards the Supreme Being as the cause of the world, and leaves open whether it acts from the necessity of its nature or as a free agent. The theist regards it as the author of the world.

Transcendental theology takes one of two forms. It may try to infer the existence of a Supreme Being from experience in general, without referring more closely to the particular world to which that experience belongs, and it is then called cosmotheology. Or it may try to know the existence of such a being through concepts alone, without any help from experience, and it is then called ontotheology.

Natural theology infers the attributes and the existence of an author of the world from the world's constitution, and from the order and unity we observe in it. In this world we must admit two kinds of causality, the causality of nature and the causality of freedom. Natural theology therefore rises from the world to a supreme intelligence, which it treats either as the source of all natural order and perfection or as the source of all moral order and perfection. In the first case it is called physico-theology. In the second it is called ethical or moral theology. Moral theology in this sense should not be confused with theological ethics. Theological ethics contains moral laws that already presuppose the existence of a Supreme Governor of the world. Moral theology works the other way around: it is a conviction that a Supreme Being exists, and that conviction is founded on moral laws.

By "God" we usually mean more than an eternal nature whose operations are blind and without sense. We mean a Supreme Being who is the free and intelligent author of all things, and only this second conception can matter to human beings. Strictly speaking, then, we could deny that the deist believes in God at all, and describe him as someone who merely affirms the existence of a primal being or thing, the supreme cause of everything else. Yet no one should be blamed simply because he does not feel entitled to assert a certain opinion, as though he denied it outright and asserted its opposite. It is more accurate, as well as less harsh, to say that the deist believes in a God and the theist in a living God (*summa intelligentia*). We will now examine where all these attempts of reason to prove the existence of a Supreme Being come from.

For present purposes, theoretical knowledge can be defined as knowledge of what is, and practical knowledge as knowledge of what ought to be. On this definition, the theoretical use of reason is the one by which I know a priori, as necessary, that something is, and the practical use is the one by which I know a priori what ought to happen. Suppose it is certain beyond doubt, though only conditionally true, that something is or that something ought to happen. Then either some definite condition of this truth is absolutely necessary, or such a condition may be assumed at our discretion. In the first case the condition is postulated (*per thesin*). In the second it is merely supposed (*per hypothesin*). Certain practical laws, namely the laws of morality, are absolutely necessary. If these laws necessarily presuppose the existence of some being as the condition that makes their binding force possible, then that being must be postulated, because the conditioned thing from which we reason back to this condition is itself known a priori to be absolutely necessary. We will show later that the moral laws do not merely presuppose the existence of a Supreme Being. Because they are themselves absolutely necessary in another respect, they also demand or postulate it, though only from a practical point of view. We set that argument aside for now.

When the question concerns only what is, and not what ought to be, the conditioned thing that experience presents to us is always thought of as contingent. Its condition therefore cannot be regarded as absolutely necessary. It can only be regarded as relatively necessary, or more precisely as needed. In itself, and a priori, the condition is an assumption we are free to make in order to help reason understand the conditioned thing. If we are to have theoretical knowledge that something exists with absolute necessity, we can reach it only a priori, through concepts. But by that route it is impossible to know that there exists a cause standing in any relation to an existence given in experience.

Theoretical knowledge is speculative when it concerns an object, or certain concepts of an object, that is not given in experience and cannot be reached through it. Speculative knowledge stands opposed to knowledge of nature, which deals only with objects or predicates that could appear in some possible experience. The principle that everything that happens, everything empirically contingent, must have a cause is a principle of the knowledge of nature, and not of speculative knowledge. If we turn it into an abstract principle and strip away its reference to experience and to the empirical, we find that it can no longer rightly count as a synthetic proposition, and that there is no way at all to pass from what exists to something entirely different from it, which we call its cause. Indeed, when the concept of cause is used speculatively in this way, it loses all meaning, and so does the concept of the contingent, because the objective reality and sense of both can be understood from experience alone.

When we infer from the existence of the universe and the things in it that there exists a cause of the universe, reason is proceeding by the speculative method and not by the method of natural knowledge. The principle of natural knowledge states only that what happens, the changing states of things, has a cause because it is empirically contingent. It says nothing of the kind about things themselves, about substances. The claim that the very existence of substance is contingent finds no support in experience; it is the claim of a reason using its principles speculatively. Suppose instead that I infer, from the form of the universe, from the way all things are connected and act on one another, that there exists a cause wholly distinct from the universe. This too would be a judgment of purely speculative reason, because the object in question, the cause, can never be an object of possible experience. In both cases the principle of causality, which holds only within the field of experience and is useless and even meaningless outside it, would be turned away from its proper purpose.

I maintain, therefore, that every attempt of reason to establish a theology through speculation alone is fruitless. The principles of reason, as applied to nature, lead us to no theological truths, and consequently a rational theology cannot exist unless it is founded on the laws of morality. All the synthetic principles of the understanding are valid only within experience, as immanent principles. Knowledge of a Supreme Being would require us to use them transcendentally, beyond experience, and the understanding is entirely incapable of this. If the empirical law of causality were to lead us to a Supreme Being, that being would have to belong to the chain of empirical objects, and it would then be conditioned, like every other appearance. And suppose we allowed that the dynamical law relating an effect to its cause could carry us beyond the limits of experience. What sort of concept would this procedure yield? It certainly would not yield the concept of a Supreme Being, because experience never presents us with the greatest of all possible effects, and only an effect of that kind could bear witness to a corresponding cause. If, in order to satisfy fully the demands of Reason, we grant her the right to assert that a perfect and absolutely necessary being exists, we grant it as a favor, and not as the outcome of irresistible proof. The physico-theological proof may add weight to other proofs, if there are any others, by connecting speculation with experience. In itself, though, it does more to prepare the mind for theological knowledge, and to point it in a right and natural direction, than to lay a secure foundation for theology.

It is now quite clear that transcendental questions admit only transcendental answers, answers given a priori through pure concepts with no empirical element whatever. But the question here is plainly synthetic. It aims to extend our knowledge beyond the bounds of experience, and it asks for assurance that there exists a being corresponding to an idea in our minds, an idea that no experience can ever match. We have already shown at length that all a priori synthetic knowledge is possible only as an expression of the formal conditions of a possible experience, and that every principle is valid only so far as it remains within the field of experience, in relation to objects of empirical knowledge, to appearances. Every transcendental procedure in speculative theology therefore comes to nothing.

Someone may prefer to doubt the force of the proofs given in our Analytic rather than give up his confidence in these old and long-honored arguments. Even so, he cannot refuse to answer one question: how can he pass beyond the limits of all possible experience with the help of mere ideas? If he speaks of new arguments, or of improved versions of the old ones, I ask him to spare me. There is not much choice in this field, since every speculative argument must finally lean on the ontological one, and I have little to fear from the argumentative inventiveness of the dogmatic champions of a reason that operates apart from the senses. Without thinking of myself as especially combative, I will not refuse the challenge to expose the fallacy and overturn the claims of every attempt at speculative theology. Yet those who are used to the dogmatic method never lose hope that their fortunes will improve. I will therefore confine myself to one simple and fair demand. Let these reasoners show, from the nature of the human mind and from the nature of our other sources of knowledge, how we are to extend our knowledge entirely a priori and carry it to the point where experience abandons us and nothing remains to guarantee the objective reality of our concepts. However the understanding may have arrived at a concept, analysis of that concept can never reveal that its object exists. Knowing that the object exists depends on the object being posited and given in itself, independently of the concept. And without the help of experience, which presents the mind with nothing but appearances, it is utterly impossible to get beyond our concept, or to reach, through concepts alone, a conviction that new kinds of objects or supernatural beings exist.

Pure speculative reason falls far short of proving that a Supreme Being exists. It is nevertheless of the highest value in correcting our concept of this being, assuming we can come to know it by some other means. It can make that concept consistent with itself and with all our other concepts of intelligible objects, clear it of everything incompatible with the concept of a highest being (*ens summum*), and remove from it every limitation and every admixture of empirical elements.

For all its objective insufficiency, then, transcendental theology still has a negative importance. It is useful as a test of how reason proceeds when it deals with pure ideas, a domain in which no standard other than a transcendental one is admissible. If, from a practical point of view, the hypothesis of a supreme and all-sufficient being is to hold its ground unchallenged, it is of the greatest importance to define this concept correctly and rigorously, as the transcendental concept of a necessary being. That means removing everything drawn from appearances, which is anthropomorphism in the widest sense of the word, and at the same time overturning every contrary assertion, whether atheist, deist, or anthropomorphic. This is easy enough to do. The same arguments that showed human reason unable to affirm the existence of a Supreme Being must be equally sufficient to show that it cannot validly deny it. Pure speculative reason can never prove that no Supreme Being exists as the ground of everything that exists. Nor can it prove that this being has none of the properties we conceive by analogy with the active powers of a thinking being, or that, as the anthropomorphists would have us believe, it is subject to all the limitations that sensibility imposes on the intelligences we meet in experience.

For speculative reason, therefore, the Supreme Being remains a mere ideal, though a flawless one: a concept that completes and crowns the whole system of human knowledge, but whose objective reality pure reason can neither prove nor disprove. If a moral theology should ever make good this deficiency, the problematic transcendental theology that came before it will at least have proved useful. By the complete determination of the concept it provides, it will have shown that the mind needs this concept, and it will have kept up a constant check on the conclusions of a reason that is often deceived by the senses and not always in agreement with its own ideas. Necessity, infinity, unity, existence apart from the world (and not as a world-soul), eternity (free from the conditions of time), omnipresence (free from the conditions of space), omnipotence, and other such attributes are pure transcendental predicates. The precise concept of a Supreme Being that every theology needs is therefore supplied by transcendental theology alone.

## Appendix to the Transcendental Dialectic: Of the Regulative Employment of the Ideas of Pure Reason

The outcome of all the dialectical attempts of pure reason confirms what we already proved in the Transcendental Analytic: every inference that would carry us beyond the limits of experience is fallacious and groundless. At the same time it teaches an important lesson. Human reason has a natural tendency to overstep these limits, and transcendental ideas belong to reason as naturally as the categories belong to the understanding. There is one difference. The categories never lead us astray, because outer objects always agree with them perfectly. Ideas, on the other hand, give rise to illusions we cannot resist, and only the most rigorous and subtle criticism can protect us from the errors they produce.

Whatever is rooted in the nature of our powers will prove to agree with the final purpose and proper use of those powers, once we have found out their true direction and aim. We may therefore suppose that there is a proper and immanent way of using transcendental ideas, even though, when we misunderstand them and take them for concepts of actual things, we apply them in a transcendent and deceptive way. It is not the idea itself that is transcendent or immanent, but only the way it is used in relation to possible experience. An idea is used transcendently when it is applied to an object that we wrongly believe corresponds to it and matches it. It is used immanently when it is applied only to the work of the understanding within experience. All errors of subreption, in which one thing is surreptitiously passed off for another, are therefore to be blamed on faults of judgment, and not on understanding or reason.

Reason never relates directly to an object. It relates directly only to the understanding, and only through the understanding can it be used in the field of experience. It does not form concepts of objects. It merely arranges these concepts and gives them the unity they are capable of once their range of application has been extended as far as possible. Reason makes use of the understanding's concepts solely to produce totality in the various series of conditions. The understanding does not concern itself with this totality. Its only business is to connect experiences, and in doing so to establish series of conditions according to concepts. The object of reason, therefore, is the understanding and the proper fulfillment of its task. Just as the understanding unifies the manifold of objects by means of concepts, reason unifies the manifold of concepts by means of ideas. It sets a collective unity as the final goal of the understanding's operations, which, left to themselves, are concerned only with distributive unity, the unity that belongs to each case taken one at a time.

I therefore maintain that transcendental ideas can never be used constitutively. They cannot be concepts of objects, and when they are treated as such they take on a deceptive, dialectical character. On the other hand, they have an excellent and indispensable use as regulative ideas. They direct the understanding toward a certain goal, like guiding lines along which all its rules run and at which they all converge in a single point. This point is only an idea, a *focus imaginarius*, an imaginary focus. The understanding's concepts do not actually start from it, since it lies beyond the sphere of possible experience. Even so, it gives those concepts the greatest possible unity together with the greatest possible extension. From this arises the natural illusion that these lines start from an object lying outside the sphere of empirical knowledge, in the same way that objects reflected in a mirror appear to be behind the glass. We can prevent this illusion from deceiving us, but it is necessary and unavoidable if we wish to see not only the objects in front of us but also those far behind our backs. In the present case, that means directing the understanding beyond every given experience, toward the greatest extension it can possibly reach.

If we survey the full extent of our knowledge, we find that reason's distinctive task is to arrange it into a system, to connect it according to a principle. This unity presupposes an idea, the idea of the form of a whole of knowledge. The idea comes before any definite knowledge of the parts, and it contains the conditions that determine a priori the place of each part and its relation to the other parts of the whole system. The idea therefore demands complete unity in the knowledge supplied by the understanding: not the unity of a random aggregate, but the unity of a system connected by necessary laws. Strictly speaking, this idea is not a concept of an object. It is a concept of the complete unity of our concepts of objects, insofar as that unity can serve the understanding as a rule. Concepts of reason of this kind are not drawn from nature. On the contrary, we use them to question and investigate nature, and we regard our knowledge as deficient so long as it falls short of them. We admit that pure earth, pure water, or pure air cannot be found anywhere. Yet we need these concepts, whose absolute purity and completeness have their origin in reason, in order to determine how much each of these natural causes contributes to any given phenomenon. Natural philosophers accordingly trace every kind of matter back to a few basic types. Earths stand for mere weight. Salts and combustible bodies stand for pure force. Water and air stand for the carriers, the *vehicula*, of these other substances, the instruments by which they do their work. All of this is meant to explain how bodies act and react chemically on one another according to the idea of a mechanism. Even when it is not expressed in so many words, the influence of such ideas of reason on the procedure of natural philosophers is plain to see.

If reason is the faculty of deriving the particular from the universal, and if the universal is already certain in itself and given, then judgment need only place the particular under the universal, and the particular is thereby necessarily determined. I will call this the demonstrative or apodictic use of reason. Suppose, however, that the universal is accepted only as problematic, as a mere idea. Then the particular case is certain, but whether the rule covering it holds universally remains an open question. In that case we take several particular cases whose certainty is beyond doubt and examine them to find out whether the rule applies to them. If every particular case we can gather turns out to follow from the rule, we infer that the rule is universal, and we conclude that all the cases we have not observed, or cannot observe, are of the same kind as those we have. I will call this the hypothetical use of reason.

The hypothetical use of reason, which relies on ideas employed as problematic concepts, is not, properly speaking, constitutive. Considered strictly, the fact that reason makes use of a rule as a hypothesis does not establish that the rule is true.

For how can we know every case that might arise, when some of them may prove to be exceptions to the universality of the rule? This use of reason is merely regulative. Its sole aim is to bring unity into the aggregate of our particular cognitions, and so to bring the rule ever closer to universality.

The object of the hypothetical use of reason, then, is the systematic unity of our cognitions, and this unity is the criterion of a rule's truth. Yet this systematic unity, being a mere idea, is only a projected unity. It must not be regarded as given, but only as a problem. That problem nonetheless functions as a principle for the understanding in its many particular operations within experience. It guides the understanding in cases not presented to our observation, and it brings harmony and consistency to all its activity.

All we can conclude with certainty from these considerations is that systematic unity is a logical principle. Wherever the understanding cannot arrive at rules on its own, this principle helps it, by means of ideas, to bring all its various rules under a single principle, and so to secure the most complete consistency and connection attainable. Suppose, however, that someone made a much stronger claim: that objects, and the understanding that knows them, are so constituted as to be destined for systematic unity; that this can be postulated a priori, without any reference to the interest of reason; and that we are entitled to declare that all possible cognitions, empirical and otherwise, possess systematic unity and fall under general principles from which, however varied they may be, they can all be derived. Such an assertion could rest only on a transcendental principle of reason, one that would make systematic unity necessary not merely subjectively and logically, as a method, but objectively.

Let me illustrate this with an example. Among the many kinds of unity that the concepts of the understanding make known to us is the causality of a substance, which we call a power. The various ways in which a single substance manifests itself seem at first glance so unlike one another that we are inclined to assume there are as many distinct powers as there are distinct effects. In the human mind, for instance, we find feeling, consciousness, imagination, memory, wit, analysis, pleasure, desire, and so on. A logical maxim, however, requires us to reduce these differences to as few as possible by comparing them and uncovering the hidden identity among them. We must ask, for example, whether imagination (joined with consciousness), memory, wit, and analysis are not simply different forms of understanding and reason. The idea of a fundamental power, whose existence no effort of logic can guarantee, is the problem we must solve if we are to represent this variety of powers systematically. The logical principle of reason demands that we achieve as much unity as possible in the system of our knowledge. The more the phenomena of one power and another turn out to be identical, the more probable it becomes that they are merely different expressions of one and the same power, which may be called, in a relative sense, a fundamental power. The same holds in other cases.

These relatively fundamental powers must in turn be compared with one another, in order to discover, if possible, the single radical and absolutely fundamental power of which they are all manifestations. But this unity is purely hypothetical. No one claims that it actually exists. The claim is only that, in the interest of reason, we must try to discover it and bring it into our knowledge as far as we can. Reason's interest here is to establish principles for the many rules that experience presents to us.

The transcendental use of the understanding, however, would lead us to believe that this idea of a fundamental power is not problematic but has objective reality. On this view the understanding demands the systematic unity of the various powers in a substance and raises it to an apodictic, or necessary, principle. For without ever having tried to find the unity among the various powers in nature, and even after all our attempts have failed, we still presuppose that such a unity exists and may sooner or later be discovered. Reason does this not only in the case just described, which concerns the unity of a single substance. It does the same wherever we find many substances that are to some degree homogeneous, as with matter in general. Here too reason presupposes a systematic unity of various powers, on the grounds that particular laws of nature are subordinate to general ones, and that economy in principles is not merely a thrifty rule of reason but an essential law of nature.

Indeed, we cannot see how a logical principle of unity could legitimately exist unless we presuppose a transcendental principle by which such systematic unity is regarded as necessary a priori, as a property of objects themselves. Suppose reason were free to admit that all forces might just as well differ in kind, and that systematic unity might not accord with the design of nature. By what right, then, could reason in its logical use require us to treat the variety of forces nature displays as a unity in disguise, and to derive them all from a single fundamental force? On that view, reason would be working directly against its own purpose, since it would be setting itself a goal wholly at odds with the way nature operates and is arranged. Nor can we say that reason first inferred this unity from the contingent character of phenomena. The law of reason that compels us to seek this unity is a necessary law. Without it we would have no faculty of reason. Without reason we would have no coherent, self-consistent use of the understanding, and without that we would have no adequate criterion of empirical truth. With respect to this criterion, then, we must assume that the idea of the systematic unity of nature possesses objective validity and necessity.

This transcendental presupposition lies hidden, in various forms, in the principles of philosophers, though they have neither recognized it nor admitted its presence to themselves. One such principle holds that the diversity of individual things does not exclude identity of species. It holds further that the various species must be regarded as merely different specifications of a few genera, and these in turn as divisions of still higher classes, and so on. It concludes that we must therefore seek a certain systematic unity among all possible empirical concepts, insofar as they can be derived from higher and more general ones. This is a scholastic maxim, a logical principle without which we could make no use of reason at all. For we can infer the particular from the general only insofar as the general properties of things form the foundation on which the particular rests.

That nature itself contains this same unity is presupposed by philosophers in the familiar scholastic maxim forbidding us to multiply entities or principles beyond necessity: *entia praeter necessitatem non esse multiplicanda*. This maxim asserts that nature herself cooperates in establishing this unity of reason. It holds that the seemingly infinite diversity of phenomena should not discourage us from expecting to find beneath it a unity of fundamental properties, of which that variety is only a more or less specified form. Mere idea though it is, this unity has always been sought so eagerly that thinkers have found more reason to restrain the desire for it than to encourage it. Chemists considered it a great advance when they succeeded in reducing all salts to two main genera, acids and alkalis, and they are inclined to regard even this difference as merely a variety, or a different manifestation, of one and the same fundamental material. They have likewise tried to reduce the different kinds of earths, the materials of stones and even of metals, first to three and then to two. Yet they are not content with this progress. They cannot help thinking that behind these differences lies a single genus, and even that salts and earths share a common principle.

One might suppose that this is merely an economizing device by which reason spares itself effort. On that reading it would be a purely hypothetical attempt that, when it succeeds, lends an air of probability to the explanatory principle reason has used. But a self-interested purpose of this kind is easily distinguished from the idea itself. According to that idea, everyone presupposes that this unity accords with the laws of nature. Here reason does not merely request this unity but requires it, even though we are quite unable to fix its proper limits.

Consider the diversity among phenomena, a diversity not of form, in which they might be alike, but of content. If that diversity were so great that even the most acute human reason could never, by comparing them, find the slightest similarity among them, then the logical law of genera would have no foundation. Nor is this impossible. The concept of a genus, and indeed every general concept, would then be impossible, and the understanding, whose activity is confined to the realm of concepts, could not exist. The logical principle of genera, therefore, presupposes a transcendental principle if it is to be applied to nature, by which I mean the objects presented to our senses. According to this transcendental principle, homogeneity is necessarily presupposed in the manifold of phenomena, though we cannot determine a priori how great this homogeneity is. Without it no empirical concepts, and therefore no experience, would be possible.

The logical principle of genera, which demands identity among phenomena, is counterbalanced by another principle, that of species. This principle requires variety and diversity in things, despite their agreement within the same genus, and it directs the understanding to attend to the one no less than to the other. Because it belongs to the faculty of discrimination, it acts as a check on reason. In this respect reason reveals a double and conflicting interest. On one side lies an interest in extension, or generality, with regard to genera. On the other lies an interest in content, or determinateness, with regard to the variety of species. In the first case the understanding thinks more things *under* its concepts, and in the second it thinks more *in* them. The same distinction shows itself in the characteristic habits of thought among natural philosophers. Some of them, those of a markedly speculative cast of mind, are almost hostile to heterogeneity in phenomena and keep their eyes always fixed on the unity of genera. Others, of a strongly empirical bent, are constantly breaking phenomena down into their differences. They do this so thoroughly that they nearly destroy our hope of ever judging phenomena according to general principles.

The latter way of thinking is plainly grounded in a logical principle whose aim is the systematic completeness of all knowledge. This principle entitles me to begin with the genus and descend to the diverse things contained under it. In this way the system gains extension, just as in the former case it gained unity. By examining only the sphere of the concept that designates a genus, we cannot tell how far its division may be carried. In the same way, we cannot determine how far matter can be divided merely by considering the space it occupies. Hence every genus must contain different species, and these in turn different subspecies. Each subspecies must itself have a sphere: it must possess a certain extent as a *conceptus communis*, a concept common to many things. For this reason, reason demands that no species or subspecies be regarded as the lowest possible. A species or subspecies is always a concept containing only what is common to a number of different things. It therefore never completely determines an individual thing or relates to it directly, and so it must contain still other concepts, further subspecies, beneath it. This law of specification may be stated as follows: *entium varietates non temere sunt minuendae*, the varieties of things are not to be rashly diminished.

It is easy to see, however, that this logical law would also be empty and inapplicable if it did not rest on a transcendental law of specification. Such a law certainly does not require that the differences among phenomena be actually infinite in number. The logical principle asserts only that the logical sphere of a concept is indeterminate with respect to its possible division, and that gives no warrant for such a claim. What the transcendental law does is impose on the understanding the duty of seeking subspecies for every species and lesser differences within every difference. If there were no lower concepts, there could be no higher ones either. The understanding knows only through concepts. However far it carries its division, then, it proceeds never by mere intuition but always by lower and lower concepts. To know phenomena in their complete determination is possible only through the understanding. It requires an endlessly continued specification of concepts and an advance toward ever finer differences. These are the differences that abstraction set aside in forming the concept of the species, and still more in forming that of the genus.

This law of specification cannot be derived from experience, which can never furnish a principle of such universal scope. Empirical specification soon comes to a halt in distinguishing differences. It needs the guidance of the transcendental law as a principle of reason, a law that obliges us never to stop searching for differences, even when they do not present themselves to the senses. Chemists grouped certain substances together as absorbent earths because of their capacity to take up acids. That these earths are in fact of different kinds could be discovered only by obeying this anticipatory law of reason. The law sets the understanding the task of finding the differences among these earths, and it assumes that nature is richer in substances than our senses would suggest. The faculty of understanding is ours just as much on the presupposition that the objects of nature differ as on the condition that they are homogeneous. We could have no concepts, and make no use of our understanding, unless the phenomena falling under those concepts were in some respects unlike, as well as alike, in character.

Reason thus prepares the field of the understanding for its operations in three ways. First, it supplies the principle of the homogeneity of the manifold under higher genera. Second, it supplies the principle of the variety of the homogeneous within lower species. Third, to complete systematic unity, it adds a law of the affinity of all concepts, which prescribes a continuous transition from every species to every other by a gradual increase of diversity. We may call these the principles of the homogeneity, the specification, and the continuity of forms. The last arises from the union of the first two, since we regard the systematic connection as complete in thought both in the ascent to higher genera and in the descent to lower species. All diversities are then related to one another, because they all spring from a single highest genus and descend through the various gradations of an ever more extended determination.

The systematic unity produced by these three logical principles may be illustrated as follows. Every concept can be regarded as a point which, like the standpoint of an observer, has its own horizon. That horizon encloses a number of things that can be represented and surveyed, as it were, from that center. Within this horizon there must be an infinite number of other points, each with its own narrower and more restricted horizon. By the principle of specification, every species contains subspecies, and so the logical horizon is made up of smaller horizons (subspecies), not of points (individuals), which have no extent. But different horizons, or genera, each comprising so many concepts, may share a common horizon from which, as from a central point, all of them can be surveyed. We may proceed in this way until we reach the highest genus, the universal and true horizon. It is determined by the highest concept and contains beneath it all differences and varieties as genera, species, and subspecies. The law of homogeneity leads me up to this highest standpoint, just as the law of specification leads me down to all the lower and more variously determined concepts.

In this way there is no empty space anywhere in the whole range of possible concepts, and the mind can find nothing outside that range. The presupposition of this universal horizon and its complete division therefore gives rise to the principle *Non datur vacuum formarum*: there is no void among forms. This principle asserts that there are not several distinct, primitive, highest genera standing isolated, as it were, from one another. All the various genera are merely divisions and limitations of one highest and universal genus. From it follows directly the principle *Datur continuum formarum*: there is a continuum of forms. This principle states that all differences of species border on one another. They allow no transition from one species to another by a leap, a *saltus*, but only through smaller degrees of difference. In short, there are no species or subspecies that are, in the eyes of reason, the closest possible to one another. Intermediate species or subspecies are always possible, and their difference from each of the first two is always smaller than the difference between those two themselves.

The first law, then, keeps us from supposing that there are different primal genera, and it declares perfect homogeneity. The second checks this tendency toward unity and requires us to distinguish subspecies before applying our general concepts to individuals. The third unites the other two by declaring that homogeneity persists even amid the greatest diversity, through the gradual transition from one species to another. It thereby points to a kinship among the different branches or species, insofar as they all grow from the same stem.

This logical law of the *continuum specierum (formarum logicarum)*, the continuum of species or of logical forms, presupposes a transcendental principle, the *lex continui in natura*, the law of continuity in nature. Without that principle, the understanding might follow the logical law alone and be led astray onto a path contrary to the one nature prescribes. This law must therefore rest on purely transcendental grounds, not empirical ones. Were it empirical, it would come after the system, whereas in truth it is the source of everything systematic in our knowledge of nature. These principles are not mere hypotheses adopted for the purpose of experimenting on nature. Even so, they are not without use in that respect. Whenever such a connection is actually discovered, it gives solid grounds for regarding the hypothetical unity as valid within nature. But we go further, and we maintain that these principles of economy in fundamental causes, variety in effects, and affinity among phenomena plainly accord with both reason and nature. They are not mere methods or devices invented to help us observe the external world.

Yet it is evident that this continuity of forms is a mere idea, for which no corresponding object can be found in experience. There are two reasons for this. First, species in nature are actually divided and therefore constitute *quanta discreta*, discrete quantities. If the gradual progression through their affinity were continuous, the intermediate members between any two given species would have to be infinite in number, which is impossible. Second, we can make no determinate empirical use of this law. It gives us no criterion of affinity that could tell us how far we ought to pursue the gradation of differences. It contains only a general instruction that we are to seek such gradations and, if possible, find them.

If we arrange these principles of systematic unity in the order suited to their use in experience, they stand as follows: variety, affinity, unity. Each of them, as an idea, is taken in the highest degree of its completeness. Reason presupposes the cognitions of the understanding, which relate directly to experience, and it seeks the ideal unity of these cognitions, a unity that far exceeds all experience and all empirical concepts. The affinity of the manifold, despite the differences among its parts, bears on things, but still more closely on their mere properties and powers.

Imperfect experience, for example, may represent the orbits of the planets as circular. But we then discover deviations from this path, and we go on to suppose that the planets move along a course which, if not a circle, closely resembles one. The orbits of those planets that do not form a circle will approximate more or less to the properties of a circle, and probably form an ellipse. The paths of comets show still greater deviations, since, as far as our observation reaches, they do not return upon themselves in a circle or an ellipse. Still, we go on to conjecture that comets follow a parabola, a figure closely related to the ellipse. A parabola is in fact simply an ellipse whose major axis has been extended indefinitely. In this way these principles lead us to a unity among the kinds of shapes these orbits take. Going further, they lead us to a unity in the cause of the motions of the heavenly bodies, which is gravitation. And we continue to extend our conquests over nature, trying to explain every apparent deviation from these rules. We even add to our system things that no experience can ever confirm. One example is the theory, related to that of ellipses, that comets may travel hyperbolic paths. Along such paths they would leave our solar system altogether and, passing from sun to sun, link together the most distant parts of an infinite universe held together by one and the same moving force.

The most remarkable thing about these principles is that they seem to be transcendental. And although they contain nothing but ideas to guide the empirical use of reason, and although that empirical use stands to these ideas only in an asymptotic relation (to borrow a term from mathematics), approaching them ever more closely without ever reaching them, they nevertheless possess, as a priori synthetic propositions, an objective though indeterminate validity, and they can function as rules for possible experience. In working out our experience, they can also be used to great advantage as heuristic principles, that is, as principles of discovery, from the Greek word meaning "to find." A transcendental deduction of them cannot be given, since, as has already been shown, such a deduction is always impossible in the case of ideas.

In the Transcendental Analytic we distinguished the dynamical principles of the understanding, which are merely regulative with respect to intuition, from the mathematical principles, which are constitutive of intuition. Yet these dynamical laws are constitutive with respect to experience, since they make possible a priori the concepts without which experience could not exist. The principles of pure reason, by contrast, cannot be constitutive even with respect to empirical concepts, because no sensory schema corresponding to them can be found, and so they can have no object in concrete form. Now, if I concede that they cannot be used within experience as constitutive principles, how am I to secure for them a use and an objective validity as regulative principles, and in what way can they be used as such?

Reason takes the understanding as its object, just as the understanding takes sensibility as its object. The proper task of reason is to produce systematic unity across all the empirical operations of the understanding, just as the task of the understanding is to connect the varied content of appearances through concepts and bring it under empirical laws. But without the schemata of sensibility, the operations of the understanding remain undetermined; in the same way, the unity of reason is wholly undetermined as to the conditions under which, and the extent to which, the understanding should carry the systematic connection of its concepts. Yet although no schema can be found in intuition for the complete systematic unity of all the concepts of the understanding, there must be some analogue of such a schema. This analogue is the idea of the maximum of division and connection in our knowledge under a single principle. For we can form a determinate notion of a maximum, of something absolutely complete, once we have set aside all the limiting conditions bound up with an indeterminate and varied content. The idea of reason is thus analogous to a sensory schema, with one difference: applying the categories to the schema of reason does not yield knowledge of any object, as applying them to sensory schemata does, but supplies only a rule or principle for the systematic unity of the understanding's activity. Now, since every principle that requires the understanding, a priori, to conform to the rule of systematic unity also relates, if only indirectly, to an object of experience, the principles of pure reason will likewise have objective reality and validity with respect to experience. They will not, however, aim to determine our knowledge of any empirical object. They will only indicate the procedure by which the empirical and determinate use of the understanding can be brought into complete agreement and connection with itself. This result is achieved by bringing that use, as far as possible, into harmony with the principle of systematic unity and deriving it from that principle.
