I call maxims of reason all those subjective principles that are drawn not from observing the constitution of an object but from reason's interest in achieving a certain completeness in its knowledge of that object. There are, accordingly, maxims of speculative reason that rest solely on its speculative interest, even though they appear to be objective principles.

When principles that are really regulative are treated as constitutive and used as objective principles, contradictions inevitably arise. But if they are regarded simply as maxims, there is no room for contradiction of any kind, since they then express only the different interests of reason, which give rise to different ways of thinking. Reason, in fact, has only a single interest, and the apparent conflict between its maxims reflects nothing more than a difference in, and a mutual limitation of, the methods by which that interest is satisfied.

One thinker is especially devoted to the interest of diversity, following the principle of specification; another is devoted to the interest of unity, following the principle of aggregation. Each believes that his judgment rests on a thorough insight into the subject at hand, when in fact it has been shaped entirely by a stronger or weaker attachment to one of the two principles. Neither principle is objective. Both arise solely from the interest of reason, and for that reason they are better called maxims than principles. Consider intelligent people disputing the distinguishing traits of human beings, animals, plants, and even minerals. One side assumes certain national characteristics and certain well-defined, hereditary distinctions of family, race, and so on, while the other insists that nature has given all races of humankind the same faculties and dispositions and that every difference is merely the product of external and accidental circumstances. When I watch such a dispute, I need only consider for a moment the real nature of the question to conclude that it is far too deep for us to judge, and that neither party is likely to be speaking from a complete insight into the nature of the subject itself. Both are in reality contending for the twofold interest of reason, each defending one side of it. This difference between the maxims of diversity and unity can easily be reconciled and adjusted. Yet so long as the two are taken for objective principles, they will produce contradiction and polemic and will also obstruct the progress of truth, until some way is found to reconcile these competing interests and bring reason into agreement with itself.

The same holds for the so-called law discovered by Leibniz and defended with remarkable skill by Bonnet: the law of the continuous gradation of created beings, according to which all living things form an unbroken ladder. This law is nothing more than an inference from the principle of affinity, since observation and study of the order of nature could never present it to the mind as an objective truth. The rungs of this ladder, as they appear in experience, stand too far apart, and what are called the slight differences between kinds of animals are in nature usually such wide gaps that no confidence can be placed in such views (especially when we consider the great variety of things and how easily we can find resemblances among them), and no faith can be placed in the laws said to express nature's aims and purposes. On the other hand, the method of investigating the order of nature in light of this principle, together with the maxim that directs us to treat this order as really existing in nature, though how far it extends remains undetermined, is beyond doubt a legitimate and excellent principle of reason. It reaches farther than any experience or observation of ours can follow, and, without giving us positive knowledge of anything within experience, it guides us toward the goal of systematic unity.

### Of the Ultimate End of the Natural Dialectic of Human Reason

The ideas of pure reason cannot be dialectical in and of themselves; fallacies and illusions arise only from their misuse. They spring from the very nature of reason, and it is impossible that this supreme tribunal for all the rights and claims of speculation should itself be untrustworthy and a source of error. We may therefore expect these ideas to have a genuine and legitimate purpose. The crowd of sophists, it is true, raise against reason the charge of inconsistency and contradiction and affect to despise its authority, because they cannot understand its constitution. Yet it is to reason's beneficial influence alone that they owe the standing and the intelligence that allow them to criticize and censure its procedure.

We cannot use an a priori concept with confidence until we have provided a transcendental deduction of it. The ideas of pure reason do not admit of the same kind of deduction as the categories. But if they are to have even the slightest objective validity, and to represent something other than mere products of thought (*entia rationis ratiocinantis*, beings produced by reason in the act of reasoning), a deduction of them must be possible. This deduction will complete the critical task assigned to pure reason, and it is to this part of our work that we now turn.

There is a great difference between something's being given to the mind as an object in the absolute sense and its being given merely as an object in idea. In the first case I use my concepts to determine the object. In the second, nothing is present to the mind but a schema, which relates directly to no object, not even hypothetically, and which is useful only for representing other objects to the mind indirectly, through their relation to this idea. Thus I say that the concept of a supreme intelligence is a mere idea. Its objective reality does not consist in its relating directly to an object, since in that sense we have no means of establishing its objective validity. It is only a schema constructed according to the necessary conditions of the unity of reason, the schema of a thing in general. That schema helps produce the highest degree of systematic unity in the empirical use of reason, as we derive this or that object of experience from the imagined object of the idea as its ground or cause. In this way the idea is properly a heuristic concept rather than an ostensive one: it does not point to an object and display its constitution, but only shows how, under its guidance, we ought to investigate the constitution and relations of objects in the world of experience. Now suppose it can be shown that the three kinds of transcendental ideas (psychological, cosmological, and theological), though they neither relate directly to any object nor determine one, nevertheless, on the assumption of an ideal object, produce systematic unity in the laws of the empirical use of reason and extend our empirical knowledge without ever conflicting with it. In that case it must be a necessary maxim of reason to regulate its procedure by these ideas. This constitutes the transcendental deduction of all the speculative ideas, though not as constitutive principles for extending our knowledge beyond the bounds of experience. They figure in it as regulative principles of the systematic unity of empirical knowledge, which, with their help, is ordered and corrected within its own proper limits to a degree that the principles of the understanding alone could never achieve.

I will make this clearer. Guided by the principles these ideas contain, we must, first, connect all the appearances, actions, and feelings of the mind as if the mind were a simple substance that, endowed with personal identity, persists (in this life at least), while its states, among which those of the body belong only as external conditions, are in constant change. Second, in cosmology, we must investigate the conditions of all natural appearances, inner as well as outer, as if they belonged to a chain that is infinite and has no first or highest member. We do not thereby deny that these appearances have intelligible grounds. We simply never use such grounds to explain appearances, because they are not objects of our knowledge. Third, in theology, we must regard the whole system of possible experience as forming an absolute unity, though a dependent and sensibly conditioned one, and at the same time as resting on a single, supreme, and all-sufficient ground existing apart from the world itself. This ground is a self-subsistent, original, and creative reason, and in relation to it we use our reason within experience as if all objects had their origin in that archetype of all reason. That is to say, we should not derive the inner appearances of the mind from a simple thinking substance, but derive them from one another under the guidance of the regulative idea of a simple being; and we should not derive the appearances, order, and unity of the universe from a supreme intelligence, but merely draw from the idea of a supremely wise cause the rules by which reason ought to connect causes and effects.

Now nothing prevents us from granting these ideas an objective and hyperbolic existence, an existence that overshoots the bounds of experience, except in the case of the cosmological ideas, which lead reason into an antinomy. The psychological and theological ideas involve no antinomy. They contain no contradiction, so how could anyone dispute their objective reality, when whoever denies it knows as little about their possibility as we who affirm it? And yet, when we wish to assume that something exists, it is not enough to satisfy ourselves that nothing positively stands in the way. We are not entitled to treat mere products of thought, which exceed all our concepts without contradicting them, as real and determinate objects merely on the authority of a speculative reason bent on fulfilling its own purposes. They cannot, therefore, be accepted as real in themselves. They can have only a comparative reality, the reality of a schema for the regulative principle of the systematic unity of all knowledge. They are to be regarded not as actual things but as in some measure analogous to them. We remove from the object of the idea all the conditions that limit the use of our understanding, even though those same conditions are the only ones under which we can have a determinate concept of any given thing. And so we think of a something whose real nature we cannot conceive in the least, but which we represent to ourselves as standing in a relation to the whole system of appearances analogous to the relation in which appearances stand to one another.

In assuming such ideal beings, we do not actually extend our knowledge beyond the objects of possible experience. We extend only the empirical unity of experience, by means of a systematic unity whose schema the idea supplies; the idea is therefore valid not as a constitutive but as a regulative principle. For although we posit a thing corresponding to the idea, a something, an actual existence, we do not thereby aim to extend our knowledge through transcendent concepts. This existence is purely ideal, not objective. It is merely the expression of the systematic unity that is to guide reason within experience. No attempt is made to decide what the ground of this unity may be, or what the real nature of this imagined being is.

Thus the transcendental concept of God, the only determinate one that speculative reason offers us, is deistic in the strictest sense. Reason does not assure us of the objective validity of this concept; it gives us only the idea of something on which the supreme and necessary unity of all experience rests. If we regard this something as an individual object, we cannot, following the analogy of a real substance, think of it except as the cause of all things, acting according to rational laws. Yet we ought to be content with the idea alone as a regulative principle of reason, and make no attempt to complete the sum of conditions that thought imposes. Such an attempt is, indeed, at odds with the great aim of complete systematic unity in knowledge, a unity to which reason sets no limits.

Hence, if I assume a divine being, I can form no concept of the inner possibility of its perfection or of the necessity of its existence. The only benefit of this assumption is that it lets me answer every other question concerning the contingent, and gives reason the fullest satisfaction with respect to the unity it seeks in the world of experience. But I cannot satisfy reason concerning the hypothesis itself. This shows that what leads reason to start from a point lying far beyond the sphere of our knowledge is not its insight into the subject but its speculative interest alone, its wish to be able to regard all objects as parts of a systematic whole.

At this point a distinction arises concerning the ways in which we may think a presupposition. It is a rather subtle distinction, but one of great importance in transcendental philosophy. I may have sufficient grounds to assume something, or the existence of something, in a relative sense (*suppositio relativa*), without being entitled to assume it in an absolute sense (*suppositio absoluta*). This distinction is certainly required in the case of a regulative principle whose necessity we recognize while remaining ignorant of the source and cause of that necessity, and which we assume to rest on some ultimate ground so that we can think the universality of the principle more determinately. Suppose, for example, that I think of the existence of a being corresponding to a pure transcendental idea. I cannot assume that this being exists absolutely and in itself, because none of the concepts by which I can think an object determinately is sufficient to assure me of its existence. Indeed, the conditions under which my concepts have objective validity are excluded by the idea, simply because it is an idea. The concepts of reality, substance, causality, and even necessity in existence have no meaning outside the sphere of empirical knowledge and cannot determine any object beyond it. They can therefore be used to explain the possibility of things in the world of sense, but they are wholly inadequate to explain the possibility of the universe itself taken as a whole, because in that case the ground of explanation must lie outside and beyond the world and so cannot be an object of possible experience. Now, I may assume the existence of such an incomprehensible being, the object of a mere idea, relative to the world of sense, even though I have no ground to assume its existence absolutely and in itself. Suppose an idea (the idea of a systematic and complete unity, of which I shall soon speak more fully) underlies the widest possible empirical use of reason. Suppose further that this idea cannot be adequately represented in concrete form, even though it is indispensable for bringing empirical unity as close as possible to its highest degree. Then I am not only entitled but compelled to realize this idea, that is, to posit a real object corresponding to it. But I cannot claim to know this object. It is for me merely a something to which, as the ground of systematic unity in knowledge, I ascribe properties analogous to the concepts the understanding uses in experience. Following the analogy of the concepts of reality, substance, causality, and necessity, I think of a being that possesses all these attributes in the highest degree. And since this idea is the product of my reason alone, I think of this being as self-subsistent reason, the cause of the universe, acting through ideas of the greatest possible harmony and unity. I thus set aside every condition that would limit my idea, solely in order to make systematic unity possible amid the diversity of experience and so to secure the widest possible scope for the use of reason within it. I can do this by regarding all connections and relations in the world of sense as if they were the arrangements of a supreme reason, of which our own reason is only a faint image. I then go on to think of this Supreme Being through concepts that properly have meaning and application only in the world of sense. But since I am entitled to use the transcendental hypothesis of such a being only in a relative respect, as the substratum of the greatest possible unity in experience, I may ascribe to a being I regard as distinct from the world properties that belong solely to the sphere of sense and experience. For I do not wish, and have no right to wish, to know this object of my idea as it is in itself. I have no concepts adequate to that task: reality, substance, causality, and even necessity in existence all lose their meaning when I try to carry them beyond the limits of the world of sense, and become mere signs for concepts, empty of content and incapable of application. I think only of the relation of an entirely unknown being to the greatest possible systematic unity of experience, solely in order to use it as the schema of the regulative principle that directs reason in its empirical use.

It is evident at first glance that we cannot presuppose the reality of this transcendental object by means of the concepts of reality, substance, causality, and so on, because these concepts cannot be applied to anything distinct from the world of sense. The assumption of a Supreme Being or cause is therefore purely relative. It is thought only for the sake of the systematic unity of experience, and such a being is merely a something of whose existence in itself we have not the slightest concept. This also makes sufficiently clear why we needed the idea of a necessary being in relation to objects given by the senses, even though we can never have the least concept of this being or of its absolute necessity.

We can now see clearly what our transcendental dialectic has produced, and what the ideas of pure reason are properly meant to accomplish. These ideas become dialectical only through misunderstanding and carelessness. Pure reason is, in fact, occupied with itself and not with any object. Objects are not presented to it so that it may gather them into the unity of an empirical concept. What is presented to it are only the cognitions of the understanding, so that these may receive the unity of a rational concept, which means being connected according to a principle. The unity of reason is the unity of a system, and this systematic unity is not an objective principle that extends its rule over objects. It is a subjective maxim that extends its authority over our empirical knowledge of objects. Yet the systematic connection that reason gives to the empirical use of the understanding does more than widen the scope of that use; it also secures its correctness. To that extent the principle of such systematic unity is objective as well, though only in an indefinite respect, as a *principium vagum*, an indeterminate principle. It is not, however, a constitutive principle that determines some object to which it directly refers. It is merely a regulative principle, a maxim that advances and strengthens the empirical exercise of reason by opening up new paths of which the understanding knows nothing, while never conflicting with the laws that govern that exercise within experience.

But reason cannot think this systematic unity without at the same time thinking an object for the idea. This object can never be presented in any experience, because experience contains no concrete example of complete systematic unity. This being (*ens rationis ratiocinatae*, an entity produced by reason's own reasoning) is therefore a mere idea, and it is not assumed to be something real absolutely and in itself. It is only the problematic foundation of the connection that the mind introduces among the phenomena of the sensible world. In the light of this idea, we regard that connection as if it originated from the supposed being that corresponds to the idea. Yet all we are after is to possess this idea as a secure foundation for the systematic unity of experience. That unity is indispensable to reason, beneficial to the understanding, and favorable to the interests of empirical knowledge.

We misread this idea entirely if we take it as an assertion, or even as a hypothetical claim, that a real thing exists which we are to regard as the origin or ground of the systematic constitution of the universe. The nature and properties of this so-called ground are left wholly undetermined. The idea is to be adopted only as a standpoint from which this unity, so essential to reason and so useful to the understanding, may be viewed as radiating outward. In a word, this transcendental thing is merely the schema of a regulative principle, by means of which reason, as far as lies within her power, extends the rule of systematic unity over the entire domain of experience.

The first object of an idea of this kind is the self, considered simply as a thinking nature, or soul. If I want to investigate the properties of a thinking being, I must question experience. But I find that I cannot apply any of the categories to this object, because the schema of the categories, which is the condition under which alone they can be applied, is given only in sensible intuition. And in this way I cannot arrive at knowledge of a systematic unity among all the phenomena of inner sense. Instead of an empirical concept of what the soul actually is, therefore, reason takes the concept of the empirical unity of all thought. By thinking of this unity as unconditioned and original, it constructs the rational concept, or idea, of a simple substance: one that is unchangeable in itself, possesses personal identity, and stands in connection with other real things outside it. In a word, it constructs the idea of a simple, self-subsistent intelligence. But what reason really aims at in this procedure is to obtain principles of systematic unity for explaining the phenomena of the soul. It wants to be able to represent all the determinations of inner sense as existing in one subject, all powers as derived from one fundamental power, all changes as mere variations in the state of a being that is permanent and always the same, and all phenomena in space as entirely different in kind from the activity of thought. Essential simplicity, together with the other attributes predicated of the self, is regarded only as the schema of this regulative principle. It is not assumed to be the actual ground of the soul's properties. Those properties may rest on entirely different grounds of which we know nothing. Likewise, the predicates listed above could give us no knowledge of the soul as it is in itself even if we treated them as valid for it, since they make up a mere idea that cannot be represented *in concreto*, in any concrete instance. A psychological idea of this kind can produce nothing but good, provided only that we take care not to treat it as anything more than an idea. We must regard it as valid solely in relation to the use of reason within the sphere of the soul's phenomena. Under the guidance of this idea, or principle, no empirical laws of bodily phenomena are brought in to explain what is purely a phenomenon of inner sense. No airy hypotheses about the generation, annihilation, and palingenesis, or rebirth, of souls are admitted. In this way our consideration of this object of inner sense is kept pure and free of foreign elements, while reason's investigation aims at reducing all the explanatory grounds used in this field of knowledge to a single principle. All of this is best accomplished, and indeed can only be accomplished, by means of such a schema, which requires us to regard this ideal thing as an actual existence. The psychological idea, therefore, has no meaning or application except as the schema of a regulative concept. For if I ask whether the soul is not, in reality, of a spiritual nature, the question has no meaning. From such a concept we have abstracted not merely all bodily nature but all nature whatsoever, which is to say all the predicates of any possible experience. With them have vanished all the conditions that allow us to think of an object corresponding to the concept. And when those conditions are absent, the concept is plainly meaningless.

The second regulative idea of speculative reason is the concept of the universe. For nature, properly speaking, is the only object given to us with respect to which reason needs regulative principles. Nature is twofold: thinking nature and corporeal nature. To think corporeal nature with respect to its inner possibility, that is, to determine how the categories apply to it, we need no idea, no representation that goes beyond experience. In this domain, therefore, an idea is impossible, since sensible intuition is our only guide. In psychology, by contrast, we require the fundamental idea of the "I," which contains a priori a certain form of thought, namely the unity of the self. What remains for pure reason, then, is nothing but nature in general, together with the completeness of the conditions within nature according to some principle. The absolute totality of the series of these conditions is an idea that can never be fully realized in the empirical use of reason, though it is useful as a rule for how reason should proceed with respect to that totality. When we explain given phenomena, moving backward or upward through the series, it requires us to proceed as if the series were infinite in itself, that is, extended *in indefinitum*, without assignable limit. On the other hand, where reason itself is regarded as the determining cause, in the domain of freedom, we are required to proceed as if what lay before us were not an object of the senses but an object of the pure understanding. In this latter case the conditions do not lie within the series of phenomena. They may be placed entirely outside and beyond it, and the series of conditions may be regarded as if it had an absolute beginning in an intelligible cause. All this shows that the cosmological ideas are nothing but regulative principles, not constitutive ones, and that their aim is not to realize an actual totality in such series. This subject is discussed in full in its proper place, the chapter on the antinomy of pure reason.

The third idea of pure reason, which contains the hypothesis of a being valid only as a relative hypothesis, is the idea of the one and all-sufficient cause of every cosmological series. In other words, it is the idea of God. We have not the slightest ground for absolutely admitting the existence of an object corresponding to this idea. What could possibly entitle or authorize us to affirm the existence of a being of the highest perfection, a being whose existence is absolutely necessary, merely because we possess the concept of such a being? The reply comes: it is the existence of the world that makes this hypothesis necessary. But that reply makes it entirely clear that the idea of this being, like every other speculative idea, is at bottom nothing more than a demand upon reason. Reason is required to regulate, by principles of systematic unity, the connection that it and its subordinate faculties introduce among the phenomena of the world, and therefore to regard all phenomena as arising from a single, all-embracing being as their supreme and all-sufficient cause. It follows plainly that reason's only aim in this procedure is to establish its own formal rule for extending its dominion over the world of experience. It does not aim to extend its knowledge beyond the limits of experience, and consequently this idea contains no constitutive principle.

The highest formal unity, which rests on ideas alone, is the unity of all things according to an aim or purpose. The speculative interest of reason makes it necessary to regard all order in the world as if it had sprung from the intention and design of a supreme reason. This principle opens up to reason, within experience, new and wider prospects. It invites reason to connect the phenomena of the world according to teleological laws, and in this way to reach the highest possible degree of systematic unity. The hypothesis of a supreme intelligence as the sole cause of the universe, an intelligence that has for us no more than an ideal existence, is therefore always of the greatest use to reason. Thus, if we presuppose wise designs on the part of an author of the universe with respect to the shape of the earth, or of mountains or seas, we cannot fail to make many interesting discoveries by the light of this assumption. The earth's figure is a case in point: it is round, but somewhat flattened at the poles. The advantages of a round form over every other are well known. But few people realize that this slight polar flattening, which gives the earth the shape of a spheroid, is the sole reason why the elevation of continents, or even of mountains perhaps thrust up by some internal upheaval, does not continually shift the position of the earth's axis, and to a considerable degree within a short time. The great bulge of the earth at the equator outweighs the momentum of all other masses of land and so keeps the axis, as far as we can observe, in its present position. Yet this wise arrangement has been thoughtlessly explained as merely the result of the equilibrium of a mass that was once fluid. If we keep to this hypothesis as a purely regulative principle, even error can do little harm. For in that case the worst consequence of an error is that where we expected to find a teleological connection (*nexus finalis*, a connection of ends), only a mechanical or physical one appears. We simply fail to find the additional kind of unity we were looking for, but we do not lose the rational unity that the mind requires in its dealings with experience. And even a failure of this sort cannot affect the law itself in its general and teleological bearing. We may convict an anatomist of error when he links some animal's limb to a particular purpose, but it is quite impossible to prove in any single case that an arrangement of nature, whatever it may be, is entirely without aim or design. Thus medical physiology, aided by a principle supplied to it by pure reason, extends its very limited empirical knowledge of the purposes of the various parts of an organic body so far that it can assert with the greatest confidence, and with the assent of every thoughtful person, that every organ or part of an animal's body has its use and fulfills a certain design. Now this assumption, if taken as constitutive, goes far beyond anything our experience or observation could justify. It is therefore clearly nothing more than a regulative principle of reason. Reason aims at the highest degree of systematic unity by means of the idea of a causality according to design in a supreme cause, a cause that it regards as the highest intelligence.

If, however, we disregard this restriction of the idea to a purely regulative role, reason falls into numerous errors. For it has then abandoned the ground of experience, where alone the criteria of truth are to be found, and has ventured into the realm of the incomprehensible and unsearchable. On those heights it loses its strength and composure, because it has cut its ties to experience entirely.

The first error arises when we use the idea of a Supreme Being as a constitutive principle rather than a regulative one, which runs contrary to the very nature of an idea. This is the error of lazy reason (*ignava ratio*). The old dialecticians gave this name to a sophistical argument that ran: "If it is your fate to die of this disease, you will die whether you call a physician or not." Cicero says the argument earned the name because, if followed, it would put an end to the use of reason in the affairs of life. For a similar reason, I apply the same term to the sophistical argument of pure reason. We may give this name to every principle that requires us to regard our investigation of nature as absolutely complete and allows reason to stop inquiring, as if its task had been fully carried out. Thus the psychological idea of the self may be used as a constitutive principle to explain the phenomena of the soul and to extend our knowledge of it beyond the bounds of experience, even to the state of the soul after death. Used in this way, it is convenient enough for pure reason, but harmful and even ruinous to reason's interests in the domain of nature and experience. The dogmatizing spiritualist explains the unchanging unity of our personality through every change of condition by appealing to the unity of a thinking substance. He explains the interest we take in things and events that can happen only after our death by appealing to our consciousness of the immaterial nature of the thinking subject, and so on. In this way he excuses himself from any empirical investigation into the causes of these inner phenomena and from any possible explanation of them on purely natural grounds. At the bidding of a transcendent reason, he passes over the immanent sources of knowledge in experience. This is very much to his own ease and convenience, but it comes at the cost of all genuine insight and understanding. These damaging consequences are even more evident in the dogmatic treatment of our idea of a Supreme Intelligence, and in the theological system of nature, or physico-theology, that is falsely built upon it. Here the purposes we observe in nature, and often those we merely imagine to be there, make the search for causes a very easy business. They direct us to refer this or that phenomenon straight to the unsearchable will and counsel of the Supreme Wisdom, when we ought to be seeking its causes in the general laws of the mechanism of matter. We are thus invited to consider reason's labor finished when we have merely dispensed with its use. Yet that use is guided surely and safely only by the order of nature and by the series of changes in the world, which are arranged according to immanent and general laws. This error can be avoided if we stop considering only certain parts of nature from the standpoint of final purposes, such as the division and structure of a continent, the composition and direction of particular mountain chains, or even the organization of the plant and animal kingdoms. Instead, we should regard this systematic unity of nature in an entirely general way, in relation to the idea of a Supreme Intelligence. If we follow this advice, we lay down as the foundation of all inquiry the purposiveness of all the phenomena of nature according to universal laws. No particular arrangement of nature is exempt from these laws, though we recognize their operation with greater or lesser difficulty. We then possess a regulative principle of the systematic unity of a teleological connection, one that we make no attempt to anticipate or determine in advance. All we do, and all we ought to do, is to trace the physico-mechanical connections in nature according to general laws, in the hope of discovering sooner or later the teleological connection as well. In this way, and only in this way, can the principle of purposive unity help extend the use of reason within experience without ever damaging its interests.

The second error that arises from misunderstanding the principle of systematic unity is that of perverted reason (*perversa ratio*, or *hysteron proteron rationis*, a reversal of reason's proper order). The idea of systematic unity is useful as a regulative principle for connecting phenomena according to general laws of nature. However far we must travel along the path of experience to discover some fact or event, this idea requires us to believe that we have come all the closer to completing its use in the sphere of nature, although that completion can never be reached. This error, however, reverses reason's procedure. We begin by hypostatizing the principle of systematic unity, treating it as a real thing, and by giving an anthropomorphic character to the concept of a Supreme Intelligence. Then we proceed to impose purposes on nature by force. As a result, teleology, which ought to help complete the unity of nature according to general laws, works to destroy that influence. It also prevents reason from reaching its proper goal, which is the proof, on natural grounds, of the existence of a supreme intelligent cause. For if we cannot presuppose supreme purposiveness in nature a priori, as belonging to nature's very essence, how can we be directed to seek out this unity? How can we, rising gradually through its various degrees, approach the supreme perfection of an author of all things, a perfection that is absolutely necessary and therefore knowable a priori? The regulative principle directs us to presuppose systematic unity absolutely, and so as following from the essential nature of things. But it presupposes this only as a unity of nature, one not merely known empirically but presupposed a priori, though only in an indeterminate way. If, however, I insist on grounding nature in a supreme ordaining Being, the unity of nature is in effect lost. That unity then becomes entirely foreign and inessential to the nature of things, and it cannot be known from nature's general laws. The result is a vicious circle, since what ought to have been proved has been presupposed.

To take the regulative principle of systematic unity in nature for a constitutive principle entangles reason in hopeless difficulties. The same holds when we hypostatize and turn into a cause what is properly only the ideal ground of reason's consistent and harmonious exercise. The investigation of nature follows its own path, guided by the chain of natural causes in accordance with the general laws of nature. It always follows the light of the idea of an author of the universe, but not in order to deduce from this Supreme Being the purposiveness it constantly pursues. Its aim is to arrive at knowledge of his existence from the purposiveness it seeks in the existence of the phenomena of nature, and if possible in the existence of all things, and so to know this being as absolutely necessary. Whether or not this latter aim succeeds, the idea is, and must always remain, a true one. Its use, when merely regulative, must always bring truthful and beneficial results.

Complete unity in conformity with purposes constitutes absolute perfection. But suppose we do not find this unity in the nature of the things that make up the world of experience, which is the world of objective knowledge, and therefore do not find it in the universal and necessary laws of nature. How, then, can we infer from this unity the idea of the supreme and absolutely necessary perfection of a primal being, the origin of all causality? The greatest systematic unity, and consequently teleological unity, is the very foundation that makes possible the widest use of human reason. The idea of unity is therefore essentially and inseparably bound up with the nature of our reason. This idea is a legislative one, and it is entirely natural that we should assume the existence of a legislative reason corresponding to it. From that reason the systematic unity of nature, the object of reason's operations, must be derived.

In discussing the antinomies, we stated that it is always possible to answer every question pure reason may raise. We also stated that the plea of our limited knowledge cannot be admitted here, although it is unavoidable and proper in many questions about natural phenomena. The questions in this case do not concern the nature of things; they arise necessarily from the nature of reason itself and concern its own internal constitution. We can now establish this claim, which at first sight seemed so rash, with respect to the two questions in which reason takes the greatest interest, and so complete our discussion of the dialectic of pure reason.

If, then, it is asked with regard to transcendental theology, first, whether there is anything distinct from the world that contains the ground of cosmic order and connection according to universal laws, the answer is: certainly. The world is a sum of appearances, and there must therefore be some transcendental ground of these appearances, a ground that can be conceived by the pure understanding alone. If the second question is whether this being is a substance, whether it possesses the highest reality, whether it is necessary, and so forth, I answer that the question has no meaning at all. All the categories that help me form a concept of an object can be used only within the world of the senses, and they lose their meaning when they are not applied to objects of actual or possible experience. Outside that sphere they are not really concepts, only the bare marks or indicators of concepts. We may admit them, but without the help of experience they cannot help us understand any subject or thing. If the third question is whether we may not think of this being, distinct from the world, by analogy with the objects of experience, the answer is: undoubtedly, but only as an ideal and not as a real object. We must think of it only as an unknown substratum underlying the systematic unity, order, and purposiveness of the world, a unity that reason must adopt as the regulative principle of its investigation of nature. We may go further and admit into this idea certain anthropomorphic, or humanlike, features that advance the purposes of this regulative principle. For it is nothing more than an idea. It does not refer directly to a being distinct from the world but to the regulative principle of the world's systematic unity, and it does so by means of a schema, or working image, of that unity: the schema of a Supreme Intelligence who is the wise and purposeful author of the universe. What this ground of the world's unity may be in itself, we do not know and cannot learn from the idea. We know only how we ought to use the idea of this unity in the systematic work of reason within the field of experience.

Having already discussed the psychological idea of the self and its proper use as a regulative principle of reason's operations, I need not go into detail about the transcendental illusion by which the systematic unity of all the various appearances of inner sense is turned into a real thing. The procedure in that case closely resembles the one just discussed in connection with the theological ideal.

But, it will be asked again, can we on these grounds admit the existence of a wise and all-powerful author of the world? Without doubt; and not only may we, we must assume the existence of such a being. Do we thereby extend the limits of our knowledge beyond the field of possible experience? By no means. We have merely presupposed a something of which we have no concept and which we do not know as it is in itself. In relation to the systematic arrangement of the universe, which we must presuppose in all our observation of nature, we have thought of this unknown being by analogy with an intelligent existence, which is an empirical concept. We have, that is, endowed it with those attributes which, judging from the nature of our own reason, might contain the ground of such systematic unity. This idea is therefore valid only in relation to the use of our reason in experience. If we ascribe absolute and objective validity to it, we forget that what we are thinking of is merely an ideal being. And by starting from a ground that cannot be determined by anything drawn from experience, we put ourselves in a position where we can no longer apply this principle to the empirical use of reason.

It will be asked further whether I can make any use of this concept and hypothesis in my investigations of the world and of nature. Yes; reason laid down the idea as a foundation for precisely this purpose. May I then regard certain arrangements that seem to have been made with some fixed aim in view as arrangements of design, and look upon them as proceeding from the divine will, though by way of certain other particular arrangements disposed to that end? Yes, you may. But you must at the same time treat it as a matter of indifference whether one asserts that divine wisdom has ordered all things in conformity with its highest aims, or that the idea of supreme wisdom is a regulative principle for investigating nature and also a principle of nature's systematic unity under universal laws, even in cases where we cannot discover that unity. When you have discovered such unity, it must be entirely indifferent to you whether you say "God has wisely willed it so" or "Nature has wisely arranged this." What justified you in accepting the idea of a supreme intelligence as a schema for a regulative principle was nothing other than the systematic unity that reason requires as a basis for investigating nature, and the further you advance in discovering design and purposiveness, the more fully your idea is confirmed. Since the whole aim of this regulative principle was to discover a necessary and systematic unity in nature, we must, to the extent that we achieve it, credit our success to the idea of a Supreme Being. Yet we cannot, without falling into contradiction, lose sight of the universal laws of nature, since it was solely with reference to them that this idea was used. We cannot, I repeat, ignore the universal laws of nature and treat the purposiveness we observe in nature as accidental or as supernatural in origin, because nothing entitles us to admit a being with such properties existing apart from and above nature. All we are entitled to assert is that this idea may be used as a principle, and that the properties of the being assumed to correspond to it may be regarded as systematically connected in a way analogous to the causal determination of appearances.

For the same reasons we are justified in introducing other anthropomorphic features into the idea of the supreme cause, since without them we could say nothing about it at all. We may legitimately think of this cause as a being with understanding, with feelings of pleasure and displeasure, and with corresponding faculties of desire and will. At the same time, we may ascribe infinite perfection to this being, a perfection that necessarily exceeds anything our knowledge of the world's order and design would entitle us to claim for it. The regulative law of systematic unity requires us to study nature on the assumption that systematic and purposive unity, extending without limit, can be found everywhere, even amid the greatest diversity. However little of this cosmic perfection we may actually discover, it belongs to the lawgiving authority of reason to demand that we always seek and expect it, and it can only be beneficial to conduct every inquiry into nature according to this principle. It is evident, however, that by this idea of a supreme author of all things, which I place at the foundation of every inquiry into nature, I do not mean to assert that such a being exists, or that I have any knowledge of its existence. Consequently, I do not really derive anything from the existence of this being, but only from its idea, that is, from the nature of the things in this world considered in accordance with this idea. Some dim awareness of the true use of this idea seems to have prompted the restrained language that philosophers of every age have used about the cause of the world. We find them using the expressions "the wisdom and providence of nature" and "divine wisdom" as equivalent, and in purely speculative discussions even preferring the former, because it does not appear to claim more than we are entitled to claim, and because it directs reason toward its proper field of activity: nature and its appearances.

Pure reason, then, which at first seemed to promise nothing less than the extension of our knowledge beyond the limits of experience, turns out on thorough examination to contain nothing but regulative principles. Their power and function is to bring into our knowledge a higher degree of unity than the understanding could achieve on its own. By placing the goal of all our efforts at so great a distance, these principles bring about the most thorough connection among the different parts of our knowledge and the highest degree of systematic unity. If, on the other hand, they are misunderstood and used as constitutive principles of knowledge reaching beyond experience, they give birth to illusions and contradictions, all while pretending to lead us into new regions of knowledge.

All human knowledge thus begins with intuitions, proceeds from there to concepts, and ends with ideas. In relation to all three of these elements it possesses a priori sources of knowledge, which seemed to reach beyond the limits of all experience. Yet a thoroughgoing critique shows that speculative reason can never, with the help of these elements, cross the bounds of possible experience. The proper vocation of this highest faculty of knowledge is to use every method, and every principle of those methods, to penetrate into the innermost secrets of nature by means of the principles of unity, of which purposive, or teleological, unity is the highest. It ought not, however, to attempt to soar above the sphere of experience, beyond which there lies nothing for us but empty void. The critical examination in our Transcendental Analytic of every proposition that claimed to extend knowledge beyond experience demonstrated conclusively that such propositions can lead us only to a possible experience. If we were not suspicious even of the clearest abstract theorems, and if we were not tempted by attractive and plausible prospects to escape the binding force of their evidence, we could have spared ourselves the laborious examination of all the dialectical arguments that a transcendent reason puts forward in support of its claims. We would have known with complete certainty that such claims, however sincerely made, are empty and worthless, because they concern a kind of knowledge that no human being can possibly attain. But discussion never comes to an end unless we uncover the true cause of the illusions that deceive even the wisest. Moreover, analyzing all our transcendent knowledge into its elements has considerable value in its own right as a psychological study, and it is a duty incumbent on every philosopher. For these reasons it was necessary to trace the dialectical procedure of reason back to its original sources. And since the inferences this dialectic produces are not only deceptive but also naturally of profound interest to humanity, it seemed advisable at the same time to give a full account of each step in this dialectical procedure, and to deposit that account in the archives of human reason as a warning to all future metaphysicians to avoid these causes of speculative error.

## The Transcendental Doctrine of Method

If we think of the whole body of knowledge that pure speculative reason can attain as a building, one whose idea at least exists in the human mind, then in the Transcendental Doctrine of Elements we have taken stock of the building materials and determined what kind of structure they are fit for, and how tall and how stable it can be. We found that although we had meant to build a tower reaching to heaven, the materials on hand were enough only for a dwelling. That dwelling was roomy enough for every earthly purpose and tall enough to let us look out over the level plain of experience, but the bolder project was bound to fail for lack of materials. And that is to say nothing of the confusion of tongues, which, as at Babel, set the workers quarreling endlessly over the plan of the building and finally scattered them across the world, each to put up a separate structure according to his own designs and inclinations. Our present task concerns not the materials but the plan of the building. We have been warned clearly enough not to rush blindly into a design that may prove to exceed our natural powers, yet we cannot abandon our intention of building a secure home for the mind. We must therefore scale our design to the materials we actually have, materials that are, at the same time, sufficient for all our needs.

By the transcendental doctrine of method, then, I mean the determination of the formal conditions of a complete system of pure reason. Accordingly, we will treat the discipline, the canon, the architectonic, and finally the history of pure reason. This part of the Critique will accomplish, from the transcendental standpoint, what has usually been attempted, and miserably carried out, under the name of practical logic. I say it has been badly carried out because general logic is not restricted to any particular kind of knowledge (not even to the pure knowledge of the understanding) or to any particular objects. Without borrowing from other sciences, therefore, it can do no more than lay out the bare titles or labels of possible methods, along with the technical terms used in the systematic parts of every science. The student thus becomes acquainted with names whose meaning and application he will learn only at some later date.

## Doctrine of Method, Chapter I: The Discipline of Pure Reason

Negative judgments, meaning those that are negative not merely in their logical form but in their content, are not usually held in any special esteem. On the contrary, they are regarded as jealous enemies of our insatiable appetite for knowledge, and it takes something close to an apology to persuade us even to tolerate them, let alone to value and respect them.

Any proposition can, of course, be expressed logically in negative form. But with respect to the content of our knowledge, the proper function of negative judgments is solely to prevent error. For the same reason, negative propositions designed to correct false knowledge where error is entirely impossible are no doubt true, but they are empty and senseless. They accomplish nothing, and for that reason they are often quite ridiculous. An example is the schoolman's proposition that Alexander could not have conquered any countries without an army.

But in certain conditions the negative element in knowledge, useful only for guarding us against error, matters far more than much of the positive instruction that adds to the sum of what we know. Those conditions are these: the limits of our possible knowledge are very narrow, the lure of new fields of inquiry is strong, the illusions to which the mind is prone are of the most deceptive kind, and the harmful consequences of error are considerable.

The restraint used to curb, and eventually to root out, a persistent tendency to stray from certain rules is called discipline. It differs from culture, which aims at developing a certain degree of skill without trying to curb or eliminate any other mental power that already exists. In cultivating a talent that has shown an impulse toward self-development, discipline plays a negative role, while culture and doctrine play a positive one. I am well aware that in the language of the schools the word "discipline" is commonly used as a synonym for instruction. But in many cases we must distinguish discipline, understood as a course of corrective training, from instruction, understood as the communication of knowledge, and the nature of things itself demands that we assign the most fitting words to this distinction. I therefore wish the term "discipline" never to be used in anything but this negative sense.

Everyone will readily grant that natural gifts and talents such as imagination and wit, which call for free and unlimited development, need the corrective influence of discipline in many respects. It may well seem strange, however, that reason, whose proper office is to prescribe rules of discipline to all the other powers of the mind, should itself need such correction. In fact, reason has escaped this humiliation until now only because, given its grand pretensions and exalted position, no one could easily suspect it of substituting fancies for concepts and words for things.

Reason does not need critique when it is employed in the field of experience, because there its principles are continually tested against empirical observation. Nor is critique needed in mathematics, where reason's concepts must always be presented concretely in pure intuition, so that baseless or arbitrary assertions are exposed without difficulty. But where neither empirical nor pure intuition holds reason to a clear track, as when it is employed in the transcendental sphere of pure concepts, it greatly needs discipline. Only discipline can restrain its tendency to overstep the limits of possible experience and keep it from wandering into error. Indeed, the usefulness of the philosophy of pure reason is entirely of this negative kind.

Particular errors can be corrected by particular criticisms, and their causes can be uprooted by critique. But in the case of pure reason we find a complete system of illusions and fallacies, closely bound up with one another and resting on grand general principles. Here something more seems to be required: a special, negative code of mental legislation. Under the name of a discipline, and grounded in the nature of reason and of the objects on which it is exercised, such a code would constitute a system of thorough examination and testing that no fallacy could withstand or evade, whatever disguise or hiding place it might adopt.

The reader should note, however, that in this second division of our transcendental Critique, the discipline of pure reason is directed not at the content of pure reason's knowledge but at its method. The first of these tasks was completed in the Doctrine of Elements. But reason works in much the same way whatever object it is applied to, while its use in the transcendental sphere differs fundamentally in kind from every other use. Without the cautionary, negative influence of a discipline aimed specifically at this sphere, therefore, errors become unavoidable. These errors arise from the unskillful use of methods that reason itself originates but that are out of place in this sphere.

### Section I. The Discipline of Pure Reason in the Sphere of Dogmatism

Mathematics offers the most brilliant example of pure reason extending its domain without the help of experience. Examples are always contagious, and they exert a particular influence on the very faculty that produced them, which naturally flatters itself that it will enjoy in other cases the same good fortune it met with in one happy instance. Pure reason therefore hopes to extend its empire into the transcendental sphere with equal success and security, especially when it applies the same method that yielded such brilliant results in mathematics. It is therefore of the utmost importance for us to know whether the method of reaching demonstrative certainty that we call mathematical is the same as the method by which we try to reach the same degree of certainty in philosophy, the method that philosophy calls dogmatic.

Philosophical knowledge is knowledge gained by reason through concepts. Mathematical knowledge is knowledge gained through the construction of concepts. To construct a concept is to present a priori the intuition that corresponds to it. This requires a non-empirical intuition. As an intuition, it is an individual object, but as the construction of a concept, which is a general representation, it must be seen to hold universally for all possible intuitions that fall under that concept. Thus I construct a triangle by presenting the object that corresponds to this concept. I may do so through imagination alone, in pure intuition, or on paper, in empirical intuition, and in both cases entirely a priori, without borrowing the pattern of the figure from any experience. The individual figure drawn on paper is empirical, yet it still represents the concept in its universality. In this empirical intuition we attend only to the act of constructing the concept and ignore the various ways it might be specified, such as the size of the figure, the length of its sides, or the magnitude of its angles, since none of these affect the essential character of the concept.

Philosophical knowledge, then, considers the particular only in the universal, while mathematical knowledge considers the universal in the particular, and indeed in the individual case. Yet mathematics does this entirely a priori and through pure reason. Because this individual figure is determined under certain universal conditions of construction, the object of the concept, to which the individual figure corresponds as its schema, must be thought of as universally determined.

The essential difference between these two kinds of knowledge therefore lies in this formal feature. It has nothing to do with any difference in their subject matter or objects. Those who try to distinguish philosophy from mathematics by saying that philosophy deals only with quality and mathematics with quantity have mistaken the effect for the cause. The reason mathematical knowledge can relate only to quantity lies in its form alone. Only the concept of quantity can be constructed, that is, presented a priori in intuition, whereas qualities can be given only in empirical intuition. Rational knowledge of qualities is therefore possible only through concepts. No one can find an intuition corresponding to the concept of reality except in experience. Such an intuition cannot be presented to the mind a priori, prior to our empirical consciousness of some reality. From the mere concept of a cone we can form an intuition of it without the help of experience, but the color of the cone we can know only from experience. I cannot present an intuition of a cause except in some instance that experience supplies.

Moreover, philosophy, like mathematics, deals with quantities, such as totality and infinity. Mathematics, for its part, deals with the difference between lines and surfaces, which are spaces of different quality, and with the continuity of extension, which is one of extension's qualities. But although in such cases the two disciplines share an object, reason considers that object very differently in philosophy than in mathematics. Philosophy confines itself to general concepts. Mathematics can do nothing with a bare concept and hurries on to intuition. There it considers the concept concretely. It does so not empirically but in an a priori intuition that it has itself constructed, and in this intuition, everything that follows from the general conditions of constructing the concept holds in every case for the object of the constructed concept.

Suppose a philosopher is given the concept of a triangle and asked to discover, by the philosophical method, how the sum of its angles relates to a right angle. He has before him nothing but the concept of a figure enclosed by three straight lines and therefore having the same number of angles. He may analyze the concept of a straight line, of an angle, or of the number three for as long as he likes, but he will discover no properties beyond those already contained in these concepts. Put the same question to a geometer, however, and he immediately begins by constructing a triangle. He knows that all the adjacent angles formed at a single point on a straight line together equal two right angles. So he extends one side of his triangle, creating two adjacent angles that together equal two right angles. He then divides the exterior angle by drawing a line parallel to the opposite side of the triangle, and he sees at once that he has produced an exterior adjacent angle equal to an interior one. Proceeding in this way through a chain of inferences, always guided by intuition, he arrives at a clear and universally valid answer to the question.

Mathematics, however, does not confine itself to constructing quantities as determinate magnitudes (quanta), as geometry does. It also concerns itself with pure quantity as such (quantitas), as in algebra, which abstracts entirely from the properties of the object that the concept of quantity indicates. Algebra adopts a particular system of notation by signs, and these signs indicate the various possible constructions of quantities, the extraction of roots, and so on. Once the general concept of quantities has been denoted in this way according to their different relations, the various operations by which quantity or number is increased or decreased are presented in intuition according to general rules. When one quantity is to be divided by another, for instance, the signs denoting both are arranged in the form proper to division. Algebra thus uses a symbolic construction of quantity, just as geometry uses an ostensive, or geometrical, construction, which constructs the objects themselves. Through it, algebra arrives at results that discursive knowledge, working with concepts alone, could never hope to reach.

What, then, accounts for the different fortunes of the philosopher and the mathematician? The philosopher follows the path of concepts. The mathematician follows the path of intuitions, which he represents a priori in correspondence with his concepts. The cause is evident from what was already demonstrated in the Introduction to this Critique. We are not seeking here to discover analytic propositions, which can be produced simply by analyzing our concepts, for in that task the philosopher would have the advantage over his rival. We aim instead at discovering synthetic propositions, and specifically synthetic propositions that can be known a priori. I must not confine myself to what I actually think in my concept of a triangle, for that is nothing more than its definition. I must try to go beyond it and arrive at properties that are not contained in the concept, although they belong to it. This is impossible unless I determine the object before my mind according to the conditions of either empirical or pure intuition. In the first case, I would have an empirical proposition, obtained by actually measuring the triangle's angles, which would possess neither universality nor necessity and would therefore be worthless. In the second, I proceed by geometrical construction. Through it I gather together in a pure intuition, just as I would in an empirical one, all the various properties that belong to the schema of a triangle in general, and therefore to its concept. In this way I construct synthetic propositions that are universal.

It would be futile to philosophize about the triangle, that is, to reflect on it discursively. I would get no further than the definition I was obliged to start from. There are certainly transcendental synthetic propositions formed through pure concepts, and these are the distinctive mark of philosophy. But they do not concern any particular thing. They concern a thing in general, and they state the conditions under which the perception of it can become part of possible experience. Mathematics has nothing to do with such questions, nor with the question of existence in any form. It is concerned only with the properties of objects in themselves, and only insofar as these properties are connected with the concept of the objects.

The example above was meant only to show the great difference between the discursive use of reason in the sphere of concepts and its intuitive use through the construction of concepts. A question naturally arises. What makes this twofold use of reason necessary, and how can we tell whether reason, in a given argument, is following the philosophical method or the mathematical one?

All our knowledge relates ultimately to possible intuitions, since these alone present objects to the mind. An a priori, or non-empirical, concept either contains a pure intuition, in which case it can be constructed, or it contains nothing but the synthesis of possible intuitions that are not given a priori. In the latter case, it can help us form synthetic a priori judgments, but only discursively, through concepts, and not intuitively, through the construction of concepts.

The only a priori intuition is that of the pure form of phenomena, namely space and time. A concept of space and time as quanta can be presented a priori in intuition, that is, constructed. It can be constructed together with its quality, which is figure, or as pure quantity, which is the mere synthesis of the homogeneous, by means of number. But the matter of phenomena, through which things are given in space and time, can be presented only in perception, a posteriori. The only concept that represents this empirical content of phenomena a priori is the concept of a thing in general. Synthetic a priori knowledge of this concept can give us nothing more than the rule for synthesizing whatever the corresponding a posteriori perception may contain. It is wholly incapable of presenting an a priori intuition of the real object, which must necessarily be empirical.

Synthetic propositions that concern things in general, of which no a priori intuition is possible, are transcendental. For this reason, transcendental propositions can never be formed through the construction of concepts. They are a priori and rest entirely on concepts themselves. They contain only the rule by which we are to seek, in the world of perception or experience, the synthetic unity of what cannot be intuited a priori. But they cannot present any of the concepts that appear in them in an a priori intuition. Those concepts can be given only a posteriori, in experience, and experience itself is possible only through these very synthetic principles.

If we are to form a synthetic judgment about a concept, we must go beyond it to the intuition in which it is given. If we stay within what the concept contains, the judgment is merely analytic, a mere explanation of what we have already thought in the concept. But I can pass from the concept to the pure or empirical intuition that corresponds to it. I can examine my concept concretely and come to know, either a priori or a posteriori, what I find in its object. The first, a priori knowledge, is rational-mathematical knowledge through the construction of the concept. The second, a posteriori knowledge, is purely empirical knowledge, which lacks necessity and universality. Thus I may analyze my concept of gold, but I gain no new information from doing so. I merely list the various properties I had already associated with the notion the word designates. My knowledge has gained in logical clarity and order, but nothing has been added to it. If, however, I take the substance that this name designates and submit it to the examination of my senses, I can form several synthetic propositions, though they remain empirical. The mathematical concept of a triangle I would construct, that is, present a priori in intuition, and in this way I would attain rational synthetic knowledge. But when the transcendental concept of reality, or substance, or force is presented to my mind, I find that it neither relates to nor indicates any intuition, whether empirical or pure. It indicates only the synthesis of empirical intuitions, which of course cannot be given a priori. The synthesis contained in such a concept cannot proceed a priori, without the help of experience, to the intuition that corresponds to the concept. For this reason none of these concepts can yield a determinative synthetic proposition. They can never provide more than a principle for the synthesis of possible empirical intuitions. Take the concept of cause. Here I do genuinely go beyond the empirical concept of an event. I go not to an intuition that presents this concept concretely, however, but only to the conditions of time that may be found in experience to correspond to it. My procedure in such a case is therefore strictly conceptual. I cannot use the construction of concepts here, because the concept is merely a rule for synthesizing perceptions, which are not pure intuitions and therefore cannot be given a priori. A transcendental proposition, then, is synthetic knowledge gained by reason through pure concepts and by the discursive method. It makes possible all synthetic unity in empirical knowledge, yet it cannot give us any intuition a priori.

There is thus a twofold use of reason. The two kinds share universality and an a priori origin, but their procedures differ widely. In the world of phenomena, the only world in which objects are presented to us, there are two main elements. The first is the form of intuition, space and time, which can be known and determined completely a priori. The second is the matter, or content, which is what is presented in space and time and which therefore contains a something, an existence corresponding to our powers of sensation. As regards this second element, which can never be given in any determinate way except through experience, there are no a priori notions relating to it except the undetermined concepts of the synthesis of possible sensations, insofar as these belong, within a possible experience, to the unity of consciousness. As for the form, we can determine our concepts a priori in intuition, because we ourselves create the objects of those concepts in space and time, regarding them simply as quanta, or magnitudes. In the one case, reason proceeds according to concepts and can do no more than bring phenomena under them. Those phenomena can be determined only empirically, that is, a posteriori, though always in conformity with these concepts as the rules of all empirical synthesis. In the other case, reason proceeds by constructing its concepts, and because these concepts relate to an a priori intuition, they can be given and determined a priori in pure intuition, without the help of any empirical data. Consider everything that exists in space or time: whether it is a quantum or not; to what extent the particular something that fills space or time is a primary substratum or merely a determination of some other existence; whether it relates to anything else as cause or effect; whether its existence is isolated or stands in reciprocal connection with and dependence upon other things; and its possibility, reality, and necessity, or their opposites. The examination of all this belongs to rational knowledge drawn from concepts, and such knowledge is called philosophical. But to determine an intuition in space a priori (that is, its shape), to divide time into periods, or simply to know the quantity of an intuition in space and time and fix it by number, is an operation of reason through the construction of concepts, and it is called mathematical.

The success that reason enjoys in mathematics naturally encourages the hope that the same good fortune will follow if it applies the mathematical method to other fields of inquiry besides that of quantity. Its success there is great because it can support all its concepts with a priori intuitions and in this way make itself, so to speak, master over nature, whereas pure philosophy, working with discursive a priori concepts, fumbles about in the natural world and can neither vouch for the reality of those concepts nor display any a priori evidence of it. The masters of mathematics are confident that their method will succeed. Indeed, it is a common conviction that the method can be applied to any subject of human thought. Yet they have rarely reflected or philosophized on their favorite science, which is a task of great difficulty, and the specific difference between these two ways of using reason has never occurred to them. They treat as axioms the rules that circulate in ordinary experience and that common sense everywhere stamps with its approval. Where the concepts of space and time come from (the only original quanta they deal with) is a question they do not trouble to answer, and they think it just as unnecessary to investigate the origin of the pure concepts of the understanding and the extent of their validity. Their only concern is to use them. In all this they are perfectly right, so long as they do not overstep the boundaries of nature. But without realizing it, they pass from the world of sense onto the treacherous ground of pure transcendental concepts. This is the "unstable earth and unswimmable water" that Ovid describes in primeval chaos, where they can neither stand nor swim, and where time erases the tracks of their footsteps. Mathematics, meanwhile, advances along a broad and magnificent highway that the most distant generations will travel without fear of danger or obstruction.

We have undertaken to determine, clearly and with certainty, the limits of pure reason in its transcendental use. Reason nevertheless persists in its efforts in this direction, even after the plainest and most emphatic warnings, because hope still beckons it beyond the limits of experience into the splendors of the intelligible world. It therefore becomes necessary to cut away the last anchor of this deceptive and fantastic hope. We shall show that the mathematical method brings philosophy not the slightest advantage, except perhaps that it exposes its own inadequacy more plainly. We shall also show that geometry and philosophy are two entirely different things, even though they go hand in hand in natural science, and that the procedure of the one can therefore never be imitated by the other.

The evidence of mathematics rests on definitions, axioms, and demonstrations. I shall be content to show that none of these can be employed or imitated in philosophy in the sense mathematicians give them. A geometer who applies his method in philosophy will build nothing but houses of cards, and applying the philosophical method in mathematics can produce nothing but empty talk. Indeed, the essential business of philosophy is to mark out the limits of science, and even the mathematician, unless his talent is naturally confined to his own field, cannot turn a deaf ear to philosophy's warnings or place himself above its guidance.

I. Of Definitions. A definition, as the term itself indicates, presents the complete concept of a thing, originally and within its own limits. It must present the concept completely, omitting none of the marks or characteristics of which the concept is composed. It must stay within the concept's own limits, which means it must be precise and list no more characteristics than actually belong to the concept. And it must be original, meaning that the boundaries of the concept must not be derived from other concepts. If they were, a proof would be required, and the so-called definition could not take its place at the head of all the judgments we form about an object.

Accordingly, an empirical concept cannot be defined; it can only be explained. Such a concept contains only a certain number of marks, which denote a certain class of sensible objects, and we can never be sure that under the word designating the same object we do not think a larger number of marks at one time and a smaller number at another. One person, for instance, may include in his concept of gold not only its weight, color, and malleability but also its resistance to rust, while another may know nothing of this property. We use particular marks only as long as we need them to make distinctions. New observations remove some and add others, so that an empirical concept never stays within fixed limits. Defining a concept of this kind is, in fact, pointless.
