When we speak of water and its properties, for example, we do not stop at what we actually think by the word "water" but go on to observation and experiment, and the word, with the few marks attached to it, is more properly a label for the thing than a concept of it. A definition here would plainly do nothing more than fix the meaning of the word. Second, no a priori concept, such as substance, cause, right, or fitness, can be defined. I can never be sure that the clear representation of a given concept, which was first given in a confused state, has been fully developed unless I know that the representation is adequate to its object. But the concept, as it presents itself to the mind, may contain many obscure representations that we overlook in our analysis even though we rely on them when we apply the concept. So I can never be sure that my analysis is complete. Examples may make its completeness probable, but they can never prove it. Instead of the word "definition," I would rather use the term "exposition." It is a more modest expression, which a critic can accept while still keeping his doubts about whether the analysis of such a concept is complete.

Since neither empirical nor a priori concepts can be defined, we must ask whether the only remaining kind, arbitrary concepts, can undergo this operation. A concept of this kind can always be defined, because I must know exactly what I meant to think in it. I created it myself, and it was given to me neither by the nature of my understanding nor by experience. Yet I cannot claim that such a definition defines a real object. Suppose the concept rests on empirical conditions, as when I form the concept of a ship's clock, meaning a timepiece built to keep accurate time at sea. This arbitrary concept assures me neither of the object's existence nor even of its possibility, and my definition of it would more properly be called the declaration of a project than the definition of an object. The only concepts that admit of definition, then, are those containing an arbitrary synthesis that can be constructed a priori. Consequently, mathematics alone possesses definitions. The object it thinks is presented a priori in intuition, and so the object can never contain more or less than the concept, because the concept of the object was given by the definition, and given originally, without the definition being drawn from any other source. Philosophical definitions are therefore merely expositions of given concepts, whereas mathematical definitions are constructions of concepts the mind itself formed in the first place. The former arise through analysis, whose completeness is never certain by demonstration; the latter arise through synthesis. A mathematical definition forms its concept, while a philosophical definition only explains one. From this it follows:

(a) That in philosophy we must not imitate the mathematical practice of beginning with definitions, except by way of hypothesis or experiment. All so-called philosophical definitions are merely analyses of given concepts, so those concepts, however confused, must come before the analysis. The incomplete exposition must come before the complete one, so that we can draw certain inferences from the characteristics an incomplete analysis has revealed before we arrive at the complete exposition, or definition, of the concept. In short, in philosophy a full and clear definition should mark the end of our labors rather than the beginning. In mathematics, by contrast, we have no concept before the definition. The definition itself gives us the concept, and for that reason it must stand at the beginning of every chain of mathematical reasoning.

Philosophy abounds in faulty definitions, especially ones that contain some, but not all, of the elements a complete definition requires. If a concept could not be used in reasoning until it had been defined, all philosophical thought would fare badly. But incompletely defined concepts can always be used without harm to truth, as far as our analysis of their elements has gone. Imperfect definitions, meaning propositions that are not strictly definitions but only approximations to them, can therefore be used to great advantage. In mathematics, definition belongs to the very being of the science; in philosophy, it belongs only to its improvement. Constructing a proper definition is difficult. Jurists still lack a complete definition of the concept of right.

(b) That mathematical definitions can never be mistaken. The concept is given only in and through the definition, and so it contains exactly what the definition thought into it. But although a definition cannot be wrong in its content, an error may occasionally, though rarely, creep into its form, and this error consists in a lack of precision. The common definition of a circle is faulty in this way. It calls a circle a curved line every point of which is equally distant from another point called the center, but the word "curved" adds a superfluous determination. There ought instead to be a separate theorem, easily proved from the definition, stating that every line all of whose points are equidistant from a single point must be curved, so that not even the smallest part of it can be straight. Analytic definitions, on the other hand, can go wrong in many ways. They may introduce marks that do not actually belong to the concept, or they may lack the completeness that is the essence of a definition. In the latter case the defect is unavoidable, because we can never be fully certain that our analysis is complete. For these reasons, the mathematical method of definition cannot be imitated in philosophy.

2. Of Axioms. Axioms, insofar as they are immediately certain, are synthetic a priori principles. Now, one concept cannot be connected with another both synthetically and immediately, because if we want to go beyond a concept, a third, mediating piece of knowledge is needed. And since philosophy is rational knowledge derived from concepts alone, it contains no principle that deserves the name of axiom. Mathematics, on the other hand, can have axioms, because by constructing its concepts in intuition it can always connect the predicates of an object a priori and without any middle term. The proposition that three points always lie in a plane is an example. By contrast, no synthetic principle based on concepts can ever be immediately certain. Take the proposition that everything that happens has a cause. To connect the two concepts of event and cause, I need a mediating term, namely the condition of time-determination within an experience, and I cannot know any such principle immediately and from concepts alone. Discursive principles are therefore very different from intuitive principles, or axioms. The former always require a deduction, while the latter can dispense with one entirely. For this reason axioms are always self-evident, while philosophical principles, however certain they may be, can make no such claim. Despite what is often rashly declared, no synthetic proposition of pure transcendental reason can be as evident as the statement that two times two is four. It is true that in the Analytic I included certain axioms of intuition in the table of principles of the pure understanding. But the principle discussed there was not itself an axiom. It merely presented the principle of the possibility of axioms in general, and it was in fact nothing more than a principle based on concepts, for it is part of the task of transcendental philosophy to establish the possibility of mathematics itself. Philosophy, then, has no axioms, and it has no right to impose its a priori principles on thought until it has established their authority and validity through a thorough deduction.

3. Of Demonstrations. Only an apodeictic proof, one that is necessarily certain and based on intuition, can be called a demonstration. Experience teaches us what is, but it cannot convince us that it could not have been otherwise, and so a proof on empirical grounds can never be apodeictic. In discursive knowledge, a priori concepts can never produce intuitive certainty, or self-evidence, however certain the judgment they yield may otherwise be. Mathematics alone, therefore, contains demonstrations, because it derives its knowledge not from concepts but from the construction of concepts. It derives it, that is, from intuition, which can be given a priori in accordance with concepts. Even the algebraic method of solving equations, in which the correct answer is reached by reduction, is a kind of construction, symbolic rather than geometric. In it, all concepts, especially those of the relations between quantities, are represented in intuition by signs, and the conclusions of that science are protected against error because every proof is laid before the eye. Philosophical knowledge lacks this advantage. It must always consider the universal in the abstract, by means of concepts, while mathematics can consider it in the concrete, in a single intuition, and yet through a priori representation, so that every error becomes visible to the senses. Discursive proofs should therefore be called acroamatic proofs, from the Greek for what is meant to be heard, rather than demonstrations, since they use words alone. Demonstrations proper, as the term itself indicates, always involve a showing, a reference to the intuition of the object.

It follows from all these considerations that the dogmatic method does not suit the nature of philosophy, especially in the domain of pure reason, and that philosophy should not adorn itself with the titles and insignia of mathematics. It does not belong to that order, though it may hope for a fraternal bond with that science. Its attempts at mathematical evidence are empty pretensions that can only hold it back from its true aim. That aim is to expose the illusory procedures of reason when it oversteps its proper limits, and, by fully explaining and analyzing our concepts, to lead us out of the dim regions of speculation into the clear region of modest self-knowledge. In its transcendental efforts, therefore, reason must not look ahead with such confidence, as though its path led straight to its goal. Nor should it rely so securely on its premises that it thinks it unnecessary to step back, or to keep strict watch for errors. Errors overlooked in the principles may come to light in the arguments themselves, and then it may be necessary either to define those principles more strictly or to replace them altogether.

I divide all apodeictic propositions, whether demonstrable or immediately certain, into dogmata and mathemata. A direct synthetic proposition based on concepts is a dogma; a proposition of the same kind based on the construction of concepts is a mathema. Analytic judgments teach us nothing more about an object than what was already contained in our concept of it. Because they do not extend our knowledge beyond that concept but merely clarify it, they cannot properly be called dogmas. Of the two kinds of synthetic a priori propositions just mentioned, only those used in philosophy can bear this name in ordinary usage. Those of arithmetic or geometry would not rightly be called dogmas. Common usage thus confirms the explanation given above and the conclusion drawn from it: only judgments based on concepts, not on the construction of concepts, can be called dogmatic.

Pure reason in its speculative use, then, does not contain a single direct synthetic judgment based on concepts. Through ideas, as we have shown, it cannot produce any objectively valid synthetic judgments at all. Through the concepts of the understanding, it does establish certain indubitable principles. It does so, however, not directly from concepts but only indirectly, through the relation of these concepts to something wholly contingent, namely possible experience. When experience is presupposed, these principles are apodeictically certain. But in themselves, considered directly, they cannot even be known a priori. Thus the given concepts of cause and event are not enough to demonstrate the proposition that every event has a cause. For this reason it is not a dogma, although from another standpoint, that of experience, it can be strictly proved. The proper name for such a proposition is a principle rather than a theorem, even though it does require proof. It has the remarkable peculiarity of being the condition that makes possible its own ground of proof, namely experience, and of being a necessary presupposition of all empirical observation.

If, then, no dogmata are to be found in the speculative domain of pure reason, all dogmatic methods, whether borrowed from mathematics or invented by philosophers, are equally unsuited and ineffective. They only hide errors and fallacies and mislead philosophy, whose task is to see that reason keeps to a safe and straight path. A philosophical method may, however, be systematic. Our reason, considered subjectively, is itself a system, and in the domain of mere concepts it is a system of inquiry governed by principles of unity, for which experience alone supplies the material. This is not the place, however, to discuss the method proper to transcendental philosophy. Our present task is simply to assess whether our faculties are capable of raising a building on the foundation of pure reason, and how far they can proceed with the materials at their disposal.

### Section II. The Discipline of Pure Reason in Polemics

Reason must submit to criticism in all its undertakings, and criticism must always be free to do its work without restraint. Otherwise reason's interests are endangered and its influence falls under suspicion. Nothing, however useful or however sacred, can claim exemption from the searching examination of this supreme tribunal, which shows no favor to anyone. Reason's very existence depends on this freedom. The voice of reason is not that of a dictatorial and despotic power. It is more like the vote of the citizens of a free state, each of whom must be free to voice his doubts and must even possess the right of veto.

But although reason can never refuse to submit to the tribunal of criticism, it does not always have cause to fear that court's judgment. Pure reason in its dogmatic use, however, is not so fully conscious of having strictly observed its own highest laws that it can appear with complete confidence before a higher, judging reason. On the contrary, it must give up its grand dogmatic pretensions in philosophy.

The situation is quite different when reason must defend itself not before a judge but against an equal. Suppose dogmatic assertions are advanced on the negative side against those reason makes on the positive side. Then its justification *kat' anthrōpon*, that is, as measured against its opponent, is complete, even though its proof *kat' alētheian*, according to the truth itself, remains unsatisfactory.

By the polemic of pure reason I mean reason's defense of its own propositions against the dogmatic counter-propositions advanced by others. The question here is not whether its own assertions might also be false. The point is only that reason proves that the opposite can neither be established with demonstrative certainty nor even asserted with a higher degree of probability. Reason does not hold her possessions merely by someone else's leave. Although she cannot show a perfectly satisfactory title to them, no one can prove that she is not their rightful owner.

It is a melancholy reflection that reason, in its highest exercise, falls into an antithetic, a conflict with itself, and that the supreme tribunal for settling disputes should be divided against itself. We did, it is true, have to discuss what appeared to be such an antithetic, but we found that it rested on a misunderstanding. Following the common prejudice, phenomena had been treated as things in themselves, and so an absolute completeness in their synthesis was demanded in one form or the other (and was shown to be impossible in both). That demand is wholly out of place where phenomena are concerned. There was, therefore, no real self-contradiction of reason in the two propositions "The series of phenomena given in themselves has an absolutely first beginning" and "This series is absolutely and in itself without beginning." The two are perfectly consistent with each other, because phenomena, as phenomena, are nothing in themselves. The assumption that they are things in themselves must therefore lead to self-contradictory conclusions.

But there are cases in which no similar misunderstanding can be pointed out to dissolve the conflict, and the dispute must remain unsettled. Take the theistic proposition "There is a Supreme Being," and its atheistic counterpart, "There exists no Supreme Being." Or, in psychology, take the proposition "Everything that thinks possesses the attribute of absolute and permanent unity, utterly different from the transitory unity of material phenomena," and the counter-proposition "The soul is not an immaterial unity, and its nature is transitory, like that of phenomena." The objects of these questions contain no heterogeneous or contradictory elements, for they concern things in themselves, not phenomena. A genuine contradiction would indeed arise if reason were to speak only on the negative side of these questions. As for the criticism to which the arguments on the affirmative side must be subjected, that can be freely conceded without requiring us to give up the affirmative propositions themselves. These have at least the interest of reason in their favor, an advantage the opposing party cannot claim.

I cannot share the opinion of several admirable thinkers, Sulzer among them, that despite the weakness of the arguments used so far, we may hope one day to see adequate demonstrations of the two cardinal propositions of pure reason: the existence of a Supreme Being and the immortality of the soul. I am certain, on the contrary, that this will never happen. For on what ground could reason base such synthetic propositions, which do not concern objects of experience and their internal possibility? Yet it is equally certain, with demonstrative force, that no one will ever be able to maintain the contrary with the slightest appearance of probability. Since he can attempt such a proof only on the basis of pure reason, he is obliged to prove that a Supreme Being, and a thinking subject in the character of a pure intelligence, are impossible. But where will he find the knowledge that would entitle him to make synthetic judgments about things that lie beyond the region of experience? We may therefore rest assured that the opposite will never be demonstrated. We need not resort to scholastic arguments. We may always accept the truth of those propositions that are consistent with the speculative interests of reason in the sphere of experience, and that are, moreover, the only means of uniting the speculative interest with the practical one. Our opponent, who must not be regarded here merely as a critic, we can always meet with a *non liquet*, the old judicial verdict of "not proven," and this cannot fail to disconcert him. We cannot deny him the right to answer us in the same way. But we have on our side the support of the subjective maxim of reason, and so we can regard all his sophistical arguments with calm indifference.

From this point of view, there is properly no antithetic of pure reason. The only arena for such a struggle would be the field of pure theology and psychology, and on that ground no combatant can appear whom we need fear. Ridicule and boasting are his only weapons, and these can be laughed off as mere child's play. This consideration gives Reason back her courage. For what source of confidence could remain if she, whose vocation is to destroy error, were at odds with herself and had no reasonable hope of ever reaching a state of lasting peace?

Everything in nature is good for some purpose. Even poisons have their use: they counteract the harmful effects of other poisons generated in our bodies, and they must always have a place in any complete pharmacopoeia, the authoritative catalogue of medicines. The objections raised against the fallacies and sophistries of speculative reason arise from the very nature of that reason, and must therefore have a purpose and destination that can only be for the good of humanity. Why has Providence placed many objects in which we take the deepest interest so far above us that we try in vain to know them with certainty, and that the glimpses we happen to catch stimulate our mental vision more than they satisfy it? It is very doubtful whether it benefits us to make bold affirmations about subjects shrouded in such obscurity; it might even harm our best interests. But it is undoubtedly always beneficial to leave reason perfectly free, in its investigative as well as its critical capacity, and to let it look after its own interests. Those interests are advanced as much by the limitation of its views as by their extension, and they always suffer when outside powers interfere, forcing reason against its natural tendencies to bend to certain preconceived designs.

Let your opponent say what he thinks reasonable, and fight him only with the weapons of reason. Have no fear for the practical interests of humanity; they are never endangered by a purely speculative dispute. Such a dispute merely exposes the antinomy of reason, which ought to be thoroughly investigated, since it springs from the nature of reason itself. Reason profits from examining a subject from both sides, and its judgments are corrected by being limited. What may give rise to dispute is not the substance but the manner. For it is perfectly permissible, in the presence of reason, to speak the language of firmly rooted faith, even after we have been forced to give up every claim to knowledge.

Suppose we were to ask David Hume, that dispassionate philosopher, endowed as few are with a well-balanced judgment: "What led you to spend so much labor and thought undermining the comforting and beneficial conviction that reason can assure us of the existence of a Supreme Being and give us a determinate concept of it?" His answer would be: "Nothing but the wish to teach reason to understand its own powers better, together with a dislike of the procedure by which that faculty was forced to support conclusions decided in advance, and prevented from admitting the internal weaknesses it cannot help but feel when it undertakes a rigorous self-examination." Suppose, on the other hand, we were to ask Priestley, a philosopher with no taste for transcendental speculation who was wholly devoted to the principles of empiricism, what moved him to overturn those two main pillars of religion, the freedom of the will and the immortality of the soul. (In his view, the hope of a future life is nothing but the expectation of the miracle of resurrection.) This philosopher, himself a zealous and devout teacher of religion, could give no other answer than this: "I acted in the interest of reason, which always suffers when certain objects are explained and judged by reference to supposed laws other than those of material nature, the only laws we know in a determinate way." It would be unfair to disparage Priestley, who tried to reconcile his paradoxical opinions with the interests of religion, or to belittle an honest and thoughtful man because he finds himself at a loss the moment he leaves the field of natural science. The same courtesy must be extended to Hume, a man no less well-intentioned and just as blameless in his moral character. He pushed his abstract speculations to an extreme length because, as he rightly believed, their object lies entirely beyond the bounds of natural science, within the sphere of pure ideas.

What, then, is to be done about the danger that seems in this case to threaten the best interests of humanity? The course to follow is perfectly plain and natural. Let each thinker go his own way. If he shows talent, if he gives evidence of profound thought, if, in a word, he shows that he has the power of reasoning, then reason always gains. If you resort to other means, if you try to coerce reason, if you raise the cry of treason against humanity, if you stir up the feelings of the crowd, which can neither understand nor sympathize with such subtle speculations, you will only make yourselves ridiculous. For the question is not what advantage or disadvantage we may expect to reap from such inquiries. The question is simply how far reason can advance in the field of speculation, independently of every kind of interest, and whether we can rely on the efforts of speculative reason or must give up all reliance on it. Rather than joining the combatants, your part is to be a calm spectator of the struggle. It is a laborious struggle for those engaged in it, but one that brings, both in its course and in its outcome, the greatest benefits to the interests of thought and knowledge. It is absurd to expect enlightenment from Reason while dictating in advance which side of the question she must take. Moreover, reason is sufficiently held in check by its own power; the limits its own nature imposes on it are enough. There is no need for you to post additional guards over it, as though its power were a danger to the constitution of the intellectual state. In the dialectic of reason no victory is won that need disturb your peace of mind in the least.

The conflict of dialectic is a necessity of reason, and we can only wish that it had long ago been conducted with the perfect freedom that ought to be its essential condition. Had that been so, we would have arrived earlier at a mature and searching critique, one that must have put an end to all dialectical disputes by exposing the illusions and prejudices from which they arose.

There is in human nature an unworthy propensity to conceal our real sentiments and to express only certain received opinions, which are considered both safe and conducive to the common good. Like everything that springs from nature, this propensity must in its final purpose contribute to the good of humanity. It is true that this tendency, not only to hide our real sentiments but to profess those that may win us favor in society, has civilized us and, to a certain degree, moralized us. Since no one can see through the outward covering of respectability, honor, and morality, the seemingly good examples we see around us form an excellent school for moral improvement, so long as our belief in their genuineness remains unshaken. But this disposition to present ourselves as better than we are, and to voice opinions that are not our own, can be nothing more than a kind of provisional arrangement of nature. Its purpose is to lead us out of the crudeness of an uncivilized state and to teach us to adopt at least the appearance and manner of the good we see. Once true principles have been developed and have gained a secure foundation in our habits of thought, this conventionalism must be attacked with earnest vigor. Otherwise it corrupts the heart and chokes the growth of good dispositions with the noxious weed of fair appearances.

I regret to observe the same tendency toward misrepresentation and hypocrisy in the sphere of speculative discussion, where there is less temptation to restrain the free expression of thought. For what could be more damaging to the interests of understanding than to falsify our real sentiments, to hide the doubts we feel about our own statements, or to insist on the validity of proofs we know perfectly well to be insufficient? As long as mere personal vanity lies behind these unworthy tactics, the vanity of the opposing party exaggerates just as much in the other direction. This is generally the case in speculative discussions, which mostly lack practical interest and cannot be completely demonstrated. The result is therefore the same, though it is reached more slowly than if the dispute had been conducted in a sincere and upright spirit. But where the public believes that certain subtle speculators aim at nothing less than shaking the very foundations of public welfare and morality, it seems not only prudent but even praiseworthy to defend the good cause with illusory arguments. Doing so appears better than giving our supposed opponents the advantage of forcing us to lower our declarations to the moderate tone of a merely practical conviction, and of compelling us to admit that we cannot attain apodictic certainty, the certainty of strict demonstration, in speculative matters. But we ought to reflect that nothing in the world is more fatal to the defense of a good cause than deceit, misrepresentation, and falsehood. That the strictest rules of honesty be observed in discussing a purely speculative subject is the least that can be asked. If we could count with confidence on even this much, the conflict of speculative reason over the great questions of God, immortality, and freedom would either have been decided long ago or would very soon be brought to a close. But in general, the integrity of the defense stands in inverse proportion to the goodness of the cause, and perhaps more honesty and fairness are shown by those who deny these doctrines than by those who uphold them.

I shall assume, then, that I have readers who do not wish to see a righteous cause defended by unfair arguments. Such readers will now recognize that, according to the principles of this Critique, if we consider not what is the case but what ought to be, there can really be no polemic of pure reason. For how can two people argue about a thing whose reality neither of them can present in actual or even in possible experience? Each one meditates on his idea in order to extract from it, if he can, something more than the idea, namely the reality of the object it signifies. How are they to settle the dispute, when neither can make his own assertions directly intelligible and certain, and each must confine himself to attacking and refuting the other's? All statements put forward by pure reason go beyond the conditions of possible experience, outside of which we can find no criterion of truth. Yet they are framed according to the laws of the understanding, which apply only to experience. It is therefore the fate of all such speculative discussions that while one party attacks his opponent's weaker side, he unfailingly exposes his own weaknesses.

The critique of pure reason may be regarded as the highest tribunal for all speculative disputes. It is not itself caught up in these disputes, which concern certain objects directly rather than the laws of the mind; it is established for the purpose of determining the rights and limits of reason. Without the oversight of criticism, reason is in a kind of state of nature, and can establish its claims and assertions only by war. Criticism, by contrast, decides every question according to the fundamental laws of its own constitution. It thereby secures for us the peace of law and order and allows us to settle all differences in the calmer manner of a legal proceeding. In the first case, disputes end in a victory that both sides may claim, followed by a hollow armistice. In the second, they end in a verdict which, because it strikes at the root of all speculative differences, guarantees a lasting peace for everyone concerned. The endless disputes of a dogmatizing reason compel us to seek some way of reaching a settled decision through a critical investigation of reason itself. Hobbes maintains in the same way that the state of nature is a state of injustice and violence, and that we must leave it and submit to the constraint of law, which does limit individual freedom, but only so that each person's freedom can coexist with the freedom of others and with the common good of all.

This freedom will, among other things, allow us to state openly the difficulties and doubts we ourselves cannot resolve, without being denounced on that account as turbulent and dangerous citizens. This privilege belongs to the native rights of human reason, which recognizes no judge other than the universal reason of humanity. Since that reason is the source of all progress and improvement, the privilege must be held sacred and inviolable. It is unwise, moreover, to denounce as dangerous any bold assertions against, or reckless attacks on, an opinion held by the largest and most moral part of the community, for that would grant them an importance they do not deserve. When I hear that the freedom of the will, the hope of a future life, and the existence of God have been overthrown by the arguments of some able writer, I feel a strong desire to read his book. I expect that the argumentative power shown in his writing will add to my knowledge and give my views greater clarity and distinctness. But I am perfectly certain, even before I open the book, that he has not succeeded on a single point. This is not because I believe myself in possession of irrefutable demonstrations of these important propositions. It is because this transcendental critique, which has revealed to me the power and the limits of pure reason, has fully convinced me that reason is just as powerless to assure us of the truth of the negative answer to these questions as it is to establish the affirmative, and indeed even more so. Where does this free-thinker get his knowledge that there is, for example, no Supreme Being? That proposition lies outside the field of possible experience, and therefore beyond the limits of human knowledge. On the other hand, I would not bother to read at all the reply that the dogmatic defender of the good cause makes to his opponent, because I know in advance that he will merely attack his adversary's faulty grounds without being able to establish his own assertions. Besides, a new illusory argument, built with talent and acuteness, suggests new ideas and new lines of reasoning, whereas the old, everyday sophistries are quite useless in this respect. Further, the dogmatic opponent of religion gives criticism work to do and lets us test and correct its principles, while there is no cause for anxiety about the influence and results of his reasoning.

But, it will be said, must we not warn the young people entrusted to academic care against such writings? Must we not shield them from knowledge of these dangerous assertions until their judgment has matured, or rather until the doctrines we wish to instill are so firmly rooted in their minds that they can withstand every attempt to implant the opposite dogmas, from whatever quarter these may come?

Suppose we confine ourselves to the dogmatic procedure in the sphere of pure reason, and find ourselves unable to settle such disputes except by taking a side in them and setting counter-assertions against our opponents' claims. In that case there is certainly no plan more advisable for the moment, and also none more absurd and ineffective in the long run, than to keep the youthful mind under guardianship for a time and so protect it, for that long at least, from being led into error. But when, later on, curiosity or the prevailing fashion of thought puts such writings into their hands, will the so-called convictions of their youth hold firm? The young thinker has nothing in his armory but dogmatic weapons with which to resist his opponent's attacks, and he cannot detect the hidden dialectic that lies in his own opinions as much as in those of the other side. He sees illusory arguments and proofs that have the advantage of novelty advancing against equally illusory proofs that lack it, and these older proofs may even arouse his suspicion that his teachers took advantage of his youthful credulity. He thinks he can find no better way of showing that he has outgrown the discipline of his minority than by scorning those well-meant warnings. And knowing no system of thought but dogmatism, he drinks deep of the poison that will erode the principles in which he was raised.

Academic instruction ought to follow exactly the opposite of the course just proposed. This can be done, however, only through a thorough training in the critical investigation of pure reason. In order to put the principles of this critique into practice as early as possible, and to demonstrate their perfect adequacy even in the face of the strongest dialectical illusion, the student ought to examine the assertions made on both sides of speculative questions step by step, testing them against these principles. It should not be hard for him to expose the fallacies inherent in these propositions, and so he begins early to feel his own power to protect himself against the influence of such sophistical arguments, which must in the end lose all their illusory force for him. The same blows that bring down his opponent's edifice are just as fatal to any speculative structures he himself may have wished to build. Yet he need feel no sorrow over this apparent misfortune, for he now has before him a clear view into the practical domain, where he may reasonably hope to find a more secure foundation for a rational system.

There is, accordingly, no genuine polemic in the sphere of pure reason. Both parties beat the air and fight their own shadows, for they have passed beyond the limits of nature and can find no tangible point of attack, no firm footing for their dogmatic conflict. However vigorously they fight, the shadows they cut down spring up again at once, like the slain heroes of Valhalla in Norse legend who rise to do battle anew each day, and they renew the bloodless and unending contest.

But neither can we admit any proper skeptical use of pure reason, one that might be founded on the principle of neutrality in all speculative disputes. To set reason against itself, to hand weapons to both sides alike, and then to look on, undisturbed and sarcastic, at the fierce struggle that follows, appears from the dogmatic point of view to be a role fit only for a malicious disposition. But when the sophist displays an invincible obstinacy and blindness, and a pride that no criticism can moderate, there is no other practical course than to meet this pride and obstinacy with equal feelings and pretensions on the other side, just as well or as poorly founded. Reason, shaken by the reflections thus forced upon it, then finds it necessary to moderate its confidence in such claims and to listen to the counsel of criticism. Yet we cannot stop at these doubts. Still less can we treat the conviction of our own ignorance as more than a cure for the conceit that comes naturally to dogmatism; it does not settle the disputes in which reason is entangled with itself. Skepticism is only a means of waking reason from its dogmatic dreams and spurring it to a more careful examination of its own powers and claims. But skepticism seems to be the shortest road to lasting peace in philosophy, and it is the path taken by the many who wish to give a philosophical veneer to their contemptuous dislike of all inquiries of this kind. For these reasons I think it necessary to show my readers this way of thinking in its true light.

#### Skepticism Is Not a Permanent State for Human Reason

The awareness of our ignorance, unless that ignorance is recognized as absolutely necessary, ought not to be the conclusion of my inquiries but the strongest motive for pursuing them. All ignorance is either ignorance of things or ignorance of the limits of knowledge. If my ignorance is accidental rather than necessary, then in the first case it must prompt me to a dogmatic inquiry into the objects of which I am ignorant, and in the second, to a critical investigation into the bounds of all possible knowledge. Observation cannot establish that my ignorance is absolutely necessary and unavoidable, and that it therefore releases me from the duty of any further investigation. Only critical grounds can establish this, through a thorough investigation into the primary sources of knowledge. It follows that the bounds of reason can be determined only a priori. The empirical limitation of reason, by contrast, can be recognized only a posteriori, because it is merely an indefinite awareness of an ignorance that can never be entirely removed. Our empirical knowledge, that is, is limited by whatever still remains for us to learn. The first kind of awareness of our ignorance, possible only on a rational basis, is a science. The second is merely a perception, and we cannot say how far the inferences drawn from it may reach. If I regard the earth as it actually appears to my senses, as a flat surface, I do not know how far that surface extends. Experience teaches me, however, that no matter how far I travel, I always see before me a space into which I can go farther. I therefore know the limits of my actual knowledge of the earth, though these are purely visual limits, and I do not know the limits of the earth itself. But once I have come to know that the earth is a sphere and its surface spherical, I can work out its diameter and circumference a priori and from principles, using my knowledge of a small part of that surface, say the length of a single degree. And although I remain ignorant of the objects this surface contains, I have complete knowledge of its limits and extent.

The sum of all possible objects of our knowledge appears to us as a level surface with an apparent horizon. That horizon is the line marking the limit of its extent, and we have called it the idea of unconditioned totality. To reach this limit by empirical means is impossible, and every attempt to determine it a priori according to a principle is equally futile. Yet all the questions raised by pure reason concern what lies beyond this horizon, or at least on its boundary line.

The celebrated David Hume was one of those geographers of human reason who believe they have adequately answered all such questions by declaring that they lie beyond the horizon of our knowledge. Hume himself, however, was unable to fix that horizon. His attention was directed above all to the principle of causality. He observed, quite rightly, that the truth of this principle, and even the objective validity of the concept of a cause, is not ordinarily grounded in clear insight, that is, in a priori knowledge. From this he concluded that the law does not draw its authority from its universality and necessity. It draws its authority, he held, merely from its general applicability in the course of experience, and from a kind of subjective necessity arising from that applicability, which he called habit. Reason, he found, cannot establish this principle as a necessary law for the acquisition of all experience. From this inability he inferred that every attempt by reason to pass beyond the region of the empirical was null and void.

This procedure of submitting the facta of reason, the things it has actually done, to examination and, where necessary, to disapproval may be called the censura, or censorship, of reason. Such censorship must inevitably lead us to doubt every transcendent use of principles. But this is only the second step in our inquiry. The first step with respect to the matters of pure reason, the one that marks the infancy of that faculty, is dogmatism. The second, just described, is skepticism, and it shows that experience has improved our judgment. A third step is still needed, one that marks the maturity and adulthood of judgment, which now builds on a firm foundation of universal and necessary principles. This is the stage of criticism. Here we examine not the facta of reason but reason itself, in the whole extent of its powers and with respect to its capacity for a priori knowledge. In this way we determine the necessary and eternal limits of our knowledge, and not merely its empirical and ever-shifting bounds. We demonstrate from indubitable principles our ignorance regarding all possible questions of a certain class, and not merely our ignorance regarding this or that subject. Skepticism, then, is a resting place for reason. There it can reflect on its dogmatic wanderings and survey the region in which it finds itself, so that it may continue on its way with greater certainty. But skepticism cannot be reason's permanent dwelling. Reason can settle only in the region of complete certainty, whether that certainty concerns knowledge of objects themselves or the limits that bound all our knowledge.

Reason is not to be thought of as an indefinitely extended plane whose bounds we know only in a general way. It should rather be compared to a sphere. The radius of such a sphere can be found from the curvature of its surface, which here means the nature of a priori synthetic propositions, and from the radius we can determine its circumference and extent. Beyond the sphere of experience there are no objects that reason can know. Even questions about such supposed objects concern only the subjective principles for completely determining the relations among the concepts of the understanding that lie within this sphere.

We do in fact possess a priori synthetic knowledge, as the principles of the understanding, which anticipate experience, prove. Someone who cannot comprehend how such principles are possible may have some reason to doubt whether they are really a priori. But he cannot on that account declare them impossible and pronounce void the steps reason may have taken under their guidance. He can say only this: if we understood their origin and their authenticity, we would be able to determine the extent and limits of reason, and until we can do so, every proposition about those limits is mere random assertion. On this view, doubt about all dogmatic philosophy that proceeds without the guidance of criticism is well founded. But we cannot therefore deny reason the ability to build a sound philosophy once the way has been prepared by a thorough critical investigation. All the concepts produced and all the questions raised by pure reason lie not in the sphere of experience but in that of reason itself. They must therefore be resolved by that faculty and shown to be either valid or inadmissible. We have no right to decline to solve such problems on the grounds that the solution can be found only in the nature of things, or on the pretext that human faculties are limited. Reason alone is the creator of all these ideas, and it is therefore bound either to establish their validity or to expose them as illusions.

The polemic of skepticism is properly aimed at the dogmatist who erects a philosophical system without having examined the fundamental objective principles on which it rests. Its purpose is to expose the futility of his designs and so to bring him to a knowledge of his own powers. In itself, however, skepticism gives us no certain information about the bounds of our knowledge. Every unsuccessful dogmatic attempt of reason is a factum, a matter of record, and it is always useful to submit such facta to the skeptic's censure. But this cannot help us decide anything about the hopes reason cherishes of greater success in future efforts. The investigations of skepticism therefore cannot settle the dispute over the rights and powers of human reason.

Hume is perhaps the ablest and most ingenious of all skeptical philosophers. His writings have undoubtedly done more than any others to awaken reason to a thorough investigation of its own powers. It will therefore repay our effort to consider for a moment the course of reasoning he followed and the errors into which he strayed, even though he set out on the path of truth and certainty.

Hume was probably aware, though he never clearly developed the idea, that in judgments of a certain class we go beyond our concept of the object. I have called judgments of this kind synthetic. As to how I go beyond my concept with the help of experience, there can be no doubt. Experience is itself a synthesis of perceptions, and it uses perceptions to enlarge the concept I have obtained through another perception. But we are persuaded that we can also go beyond a concept and extend our knowledge a priori. We attempt this in two ways. Through the pure understanding, we attempt it with respect to what can become an object of experience. Through pure reason, we attempt it with respect to properties of things, or the existence of things, that can never be presented in any experience. Hume did not distinguish these two kinds of judgment, as he should have done. Instead he regarded this enlargement of concepts as altogether impossible. He rejected what might be called the spontaneous generation of understanding and reason, without any impregnation by experience. He therefore held the so-called a priori principles of these faculties to be invalid and imaginary. In his view they were nothing but subjective habits of thought originating in experience, and thus purely empirical and contingent rules to which we ascribe a spurious necessity and universality.

In support of this strange claim he pointed to the universally acknowledged principle of the relation between cause and effect. No faculty of the mind can lead us from the concept of one thing to the existence of something else. From this he believed he could infer that, without experience, we have no source from which to enlarge a concept, and no ground sufficient to justify a judgment that would extend our knowledge a priori. The light of the sun shining on a piece of wax melts it, while it hardens clay. No power of the understanding could infer this from the concepts we previously had of these substances. Still less is there any a priori law that could lead us to such a conclusion, which only experience can confirm.

We saw, however, in our discussion of transcendental logic, that we can never go directly beyond the content of a given concept. Yet we can always know completely a priori the law of its connection with other things, though only in relation to a third term, namely possible experience. If I observe, for example, that a piece of wax melts, I can know a priori that something must have preceded it (the sun's heat) upon which the melting followed according to a fixed law. Without the help of experience, however, I could not know a priori, in any determinate way, either the cause from the effect or the effect from the cause. Hume was therefore wrong to infer the contingency of the law itself from the contingency of our determination according to that law. Going beyond the concept of a thing to possible experience is an a priori procedure, and it constitutes the objective reality of the concept. Hume confused this procedure with our synthesis of objects in actual experience, which is of course always empirical. In the same way he treated the principle of affinity as a mere rule of association lying in the imitative faculty of the imagination. That principle in fact has its seat in the understanding and signifies a necessary connection. The imagination, by contrast, can present only contingent connections, not objective ones.

The skeptical errors of this remarkably acute thinker arose chiefly from a defect he shared with the dogmatists. He had never made a systematic survey of all the different kinds of a priori synthesis performed by the understanding. Had he done so, he would have found, to take just one example among many, that the principle of permanence is of this kind, and that it anticipates experience no less than the principle of causality does. He might then have been able to mark out the determinate limits of the a priori operations of understanding and reason. Instead, he merely declared the understanding to be limited, without showing what its limits were. He bred a general mistrust of our faculties without giving us any determinate knowledge of the bounds of our necessary and unavoidable ignorance. He examined and condemned some of the principles of the understanding without investigating all its powers with the completeness that criticism requires. He rightly denies certain powers to the understanding. But he goes further and declares it utterly inadequate to the a priori extension of knowledge, even though he has not fully examined all the powers that reside in that faculty. And so the fate that always overtakes skepticism overtakes him too, and his own declarations are doubted. His objections rested on facta, which are contingent, and not on principles, which alone can demonstrate the necessary invalidity of all dogmatic assertions.

Hume draws no distinction between the well-grounded claims of the understanding and the dialectical pretensions of reason, against which his attacks are mainly directed. As a result, reason does not feel itself excluded from every attempt to extend a priori knowledge, and despite a few setbacks here and there, it refuses to give up such efforts. One naturally arms oneself against an attack and grows more stubborn in the resolve to make good the claims one has advanced. A complete review of the powers of reason, however, ends all doubt and dispute. It brings the conviction that we possess a limited field of action and must admit the emptiness of any higher claims. Reason is then content to rest in the undisturbed possession of its limited domain.

The uncritical dogmatist has neither surveyed the sphere of his understanding nor determined by principles the limits of possible knowledge. He is therefore ignorant of his own powers, and he believes he will discover them through the attempts he makes in the field of knowledge. To such a thinker these attacks of skepticism are not merely dangerous but ruinous. Suppose there is a single proposition in his chain of reasoning that he cannot prove, or whose fallacy he cannot explain by reference to a principle. Suspicion then falls on all his statements, however plausible they may seem.

And so skepticism, the bane of dogmatic philosophy, leads us to a sound investigation of the understanding and of reason. Once we have advanced this far, we need fear no further attacks. The limits of our domain are clearly marked, and we can make no claims, and become entangled in no disputes, about the region beyond them. The skeptical procedure in philosophy does not itself solve the problems of reason. But it is an excellent exercise of reason's powers. It awakens reason's caution and shows it the means by which it can most securely establish its claim to its legitimate possessions.

### Section III. The Discipline of Pure Reason in Hypothesis

This critique of reason has now taught us that all its efforts to extend the bounds of knowledge through pure speculation are utterly fruitless. It might seem, then, that an all the wider field lies open to hypothesis, since where we cannot know with certainty we are free to guess and to form suppositions.

Imagination may be permitted, under the strict supervision of reason, to invent suppositions. But these must rest on something perfectly certain, namely the possibility of the object. If we are well assured on that point, we may resort to supposition regarding the object's reality. Unless the supposition is to be utterly groundless, however, it must be connected, as an explanation, with what is actually given and absolutely certain. A supposition of this kind is called a hypothesis.

We cannot form the slightest concept a priori of the possibility of dynamical connection among phenomena. The categories of the pure understanding will not enable us to think up any such connection; they only help us understand it when we encounter it in experience. For this reason we cannot, in accordance with the categories, imagine or invent any object or property of an object that is not given, or cannot be given, in experience, and then use it in a hypothesis. Otherwise we would be resting our chain of reasoning on mere chimerical fancies rather than on concepts of things. We have no right, therefore, to assume new powers that do not exist in nature. We may not assume, for example, an understanding with a non-sensuous intuition, a force of attraction acting without contact, or some new kind of substance occupying space yet lacking the property of impenetrability. Nor, consequently, can we assume any kind of community among substances other than that observable in experience, any kind of presence other than presence in space, or any kind of duration other than duration in time. In a word, the conditions of possible experience are, for reason, the only conditions of the possibility of things. Reason cannot venture to form concepts of things independently of these conditions. Such concepts, although not self-contradictory, have no object and no application.

The concepts of reason are, as we have already shown, mere ideas, and they do not relate to any object in any kind of experience. Yet they do not designate imaginary or possible objects either. They are purely problematic in nature. As aids to the heuristic, or exploratory, use of our faculties, they form the basis of the regulative principles for the systematic use of the understanding in the field of experience. If we leave the ground of experience, they become mere fictions of thought whose possibility cannot be demonstrated at all. They therefore cannot be used as hypotheses to explain real phenomena. It is entirely permissible to think of the soul as simple for a particular purpose. Doing so lets us use the idea of a perfect and necessary unity of all the mind's faculties as the principle of all our inquiries into its inner phenomena, even though we cannot know this unity in concreto, as it actually exists. But to assume that the soul is a simple substance (a transcendental concept) would be to assert a proposition that is not merely indemonstrable, as many physical hypotheses are. It would be purely arbitrary and rash in the highest degree. The simple is never presented in experience. And if by substance we mean here the permanent object of sensuous intuition, then the possibility of a simple phenomenon is utterly inconceivable. Reason offers no good grounds for admitting the existence of intelligible beings, or of intelligible properties of sensuous things. Yet since we have no concept of either their possibility or their impossibility, we will never be in a position to assert dogmatically that they do not exist.

In explaining given phenomena, we may use no other things and no other grounds of explanation than those connected with the given phenomena according to the known laws of experience. A transcendental hypothesis uses a mere idea of reason to explain the phenomena of nature. It would give us no better insight into a phenomenon, because we would be explaining something we do not sufficiently understand on known empirical principles by means of something we do not understand at all. The principles of such a hypothesis might help to satisfy reason, but they would not assist the understanding in its application to objects. Order and purposiveness in nature must themselves be explained on natural grounds and according to natural laws. Here even the wildest hypotheses, so long as they are physical, are more admissible than a hyperphysical one, such as that of a divine author. Such a hypothesis would introduce the principle of ignava ratio, or "lazy reason," which bids us abandon the search for causes that might be discovered in the course of experience and rest content with a mere idea. The absolute totality of the grounds of explanation in the series of these causes presents no obstacle to the understanding where phenomena are concerned. Phenomena are for us nothing more than phenomena, and so we have no right to expect anything like completeness in the synthesis of the series of their conditions.

Transcendental hypotheses are therefore inadmissible, and we cannot take the liberty of resorting to hyperphysical grounds of explanation where physical ones are lacking. There are two reasons for this. First, such hypotheses do not advance reason but rather halt its progress. Second, this license would make all of reason's efforts fruitless in its own proper sphere, which is that of experience. Whenever the explanation of natural phenomena proves difficult, we would always have a transcendental ground of explanation at hand to relieve us of the need to investigate nature. Our inquiries would then come to a close not because we had obtained all the necessary knowledge. They would close because we had run up against an incomprehensible principle, one so far back along the track of thought that it contains the concept of the absolutely primal being.

The next requirement for the admissibility of a hypothesis is its sufficiency. It must determine a priori the consequences that are given in experience and that are supposed to follow from the hypothesis itself. If we need to call in auxiliary hypotheses, we naturally begin to suspect that they are mere fictions, since each of them demands the same justification as the original hypothesis, and their testimony is therefore worthless. If we suppose the existence of an infinitely perfect cause, we have sufficient grounds to explain the purposiveness, the order, and the grandeur we observe in the universe. But when we observe the evil in the world and the exceptions to these laws, we are forced to bring in new hypotheses to prop up the original one. Similarly, we take the simple nature of the human soul as the foundation for every theory we form about its phenomena. Yet when difficulties arise, when we observe in the soul phenomena resembling the changes that take place in matter, we must summon further auxiliary hypotheses. These may not, in fact, be false, but we do not know them to be true, because the only witness to their certainty is the very hypothesis they were called in to explain.

We are not treating the claims just mentioned, the immaterial unity of the soul and the existence of a Supreme Being, as dogmas, which certain philosophers claim to demonstrate a priori. We are treating them purely as hypotheses. If they were offered as dogmas, the dogmatist would have to ensure that his arguments carried the apodictic certainty, the strict and necessary certainty, of a demonstration. To argue that the reality of such ideas is merely probable is as absurd as offering a proof that a proposition in geometry is probably true. Pure reason, operating in abstraction from all experience, either knows with necessity or knows nothing at all. Its judgments are therefore never mere opinions: they are either apodictic certainties or declarations that nothing can be known on the subject. Opinions and probable judgments about the nature of things can be used only to explain phenomena that are actually given, or else they may concern the effect, under empirical laws, of a cause that actually exists. The proper domain of opinion, then, is confined to the world of experience and nature. Beyond that domain, opinion is pure invention, unless we are groping for the truth along a path not yet fully explored and hope to stumble upon it by chance.

Although hypotheses are inadmissible as answers to the questions of pure speculative reason, they may still be used to defend those answers. Hypotheses, that is, have a place in polemic but not in dogmatic assertion. By defending such claims I do not mean searching for new grounds to support them, but simply refuting the arguments of opponents. Every a priori synthetic proposition has a peculiar feature: although the philosopher who affirms the reality of the ideas it contains lacks sufficient knowledge to establish his claim with certainty, his opponent is equally unable to prove the opposite. This equality of fortune prevents either party from gaining the upper hand in the field of speculative knowledge, which is precisely why that field is the arena of these endless speculative conflicts. We shall show later, however, that in its practical exercise reason has the right to accept what, in pure speculation, it could not assume without perfectly sufficient grounds. All such assumptions would destroy the completeness that speculation requires, but practical reason does not consider that completeness necessary. In the practical sphere, therefore, reason holds a possession whose title she need not prove, and in fact could not prove. The burden of proof falls on the opponent. Yet he knows just as little about the subject under dispute, and is just as unable to prove that the object of an idea does not exist as the philosopher on the other side is to demonstrate that it does. Clearly, then, the advantage lies with the philosopher who maintains his proposition as a practically necessary assumption, according to the legal maxim *melior est conditio possidentis*: the one in possession holds the stronger position. He is free to defend himself with the same weapons his opponent uses to attack him. He has the right to employ hypotheses, not to strengthen the case for his own propositions, but to show that his opponent knows no more about the subject than he does and can claim no speculative advantage.

Within the sphere of pure reason, then, hypotheses are admissible only as weapons of self-defense, never as supports for dogmatic assertions. But the opposing party must always be sought within ourselves. In the transcendental sphere, speculative reason is dialectical by its very nature, and the difficulties and objections we have to fear lie within us. They are like old claims that never lapse, and if we hope for a lasting peace we must seek them out and settle them once and for all. An outward calm is hollow and unreal. The root of these contradictions, which lies in the nature of human reason itself, must be destroyed, and this can be done only by first allowing it the freedom to grow, and even by nourishing it, so that it sends out shoots and thereby reveals its existence. It is our duty, therefore, to search for new objections, to place weapons in our opponent's hands, and to grant him the most favorable position in the arena he could wish for. We have nothing to fear from these concessions. On the contrary, we may hope by this means to secure a possession that no one will ever dare to dispute.

To be fully equipped, the thinker needs the hypotheses of pure reason. They are only leaden weapons, since they have not been tempered into steel in the armory of experience, yet they are as serviceable as any his opponents can wield. Suppose, then, that from a non-speculative standpoint we have assumed the immaterial nature of the soul, and we meet the objection that experience seems to show that the growth and decline of our mental faculties are merely modifications of the bodily organism. We can weaken the force of this objection by assuming that the body is nothing more than the fundamental phenomenon to which, as a necessary condition, all sensibility, and therefore all thought, is related in our present state of existence; and that the separation of soul and body marks the end of the sensory exercise of our cognitive power and the beginning of its intellectual exercise. On this view the body would be regarded not as the cause of thought but merely as its limiting condition, something that furthers our sensory and animal life but hinders our pure and spiritual life. The dependence of animal life on the constitution of the body would then prove nothing about whether the whole of human life depends on the state of the organism. We might go further still, discovering new objections or pressing those already raised to their extreme consequences.

Reproduction, in the human race as among the animals that lack reason, depends on so many accidents (of opportunity, of adequate sustenance, of the laws a government enacts, even of vice) that it is hard to believe in the eternal existence of a being whose life began under circumstances so mean and trivial, and so entirely subject to our own control. As for the continued existence of the species as a whole, there is no difficulty, since accident in individual cases is governed by general laws. But in the case of each individual, it seems we could hardly expect so remarkable an effect from such insignificant causes. In answer to these objections, we may put forward the transcendental hypothesis that all life is, properly speaking, intelligible rather than sensible, not subject to the changes of time, and that it neither began at birth nor will end at death. We may assume that this present life is nothing more than a sensory representation of a purely spiritual life; that the whole world of the senses is merely an image hovering before the faculty of cognition we exercise in this sphere, possessing no more objective reality than a dream; and that if we could intuit ourselves and other things as they really are, we would see ourselves in a world of spiritual beings, our connection with which did not begin at our birth and will not cease when the body is destroyed. And so on.

We cannot claim to know any of what has just been asserted, nor do we seriously maintain that it is true. The notions involved are not even ideas of reason; they are purely fictitious concepts. Yet this hypothetical procedure conforms perfectly to the laws of reason. Our opponent mistakes the absence of empirical conditions for proof that everything we have asserted is utterly impossible, and we must show him that he has not exhausted the whole range of possibility. He can no more encompass that range by the laws of experience and nature than we can lay a secure foundation for the operations of reason beyond the bounds of experience. Hypothetical defenses of this kind, raised against an opponent's pretensions, must not be taken as declarations of opinion. The philosopher abandons them as soon as the other side renounces its dogmatic conceit. To take a purely negative stance toward propositions that rest on insecure foundations suits the moderation of a true philosopher. But to treat the objections one raises against an opponent as proofs of the opposite thesis is just as unwarranted and arrogant as attacking the position of a philosopher who advances affirmative propositions on such a subject.

Hypotheses in the speculative sphere are therefore valid not as independent propositions, but only in relation to opposing transcendent assumptions. To make the principles of possible experience into conditions for the possibility of things in general is just as transcendent a procedure as asserting the objective reality of ideas that can apply only to objects lying beyond the limits of possible experience. The judgments of pure reason must be necessary, or they must not be made at all. Reason cannot concern herself with opinions. The hypotheses we have been discussing, however, are merely problematic judgments, which can be neither refuted nor proved. They are not personal opinions, but they are indispensable as answers to objections that are bound to arise. We must take care to confine them to this function and to prevent them from claiming any absolute validity, for that would entangle reason in inextricable difficulties and contradictions.

### Section IV. The Discipline of Pure Reason in Relation to Proofs

The proofs of transcendental synthetic propositions differ from those of all other a priori synthetic knowledge in one distinctive respect. In the transcendental case, reason does not apply its concepts directly to an object. It must first prove, a priori, the objective validity of those concepts and the possibility of their synthesis. This is not merely a rule of prudence; it is essential to the very possibility of proving a transcendental proposition. If I am required to pass a priori beyond the concept of an object, I find it utterly impossible to do so without the guidance of something not contained in that concept. In mathematics, a priori intuition guides my synthesis, and all our conclusions can be drawn directly from pure intuition. In transcendental knowledge, so long as we are dealing only with concepts of the understanding, our guide is possible experience. A proof in this domain does not show that a given concept, that of an event, for example, leads directly to another concept, that of a cause, for this would be a *saltus*, a leap that nothing could justify. Instead, it shows that experience itself, and therefore the object of experience, would be impossible without the connection these concepts express. Such a proof must therefore demonstrate that it is possible to arrive, synthetically and a priori, at a certain knowledge of things that was not contained in our concepts of them. Unless we attend closely to this requirement, our proofs will abandon the straight path that reason marks out and wander down the winding road of merely subjective association. A conviction that rests on subjective causes of association, but is mistaken for the perception of a real and objective natural affinity, is illusory and always open to doubt and suspicion. This is why every attempt to prove the principle of sufficient reason has, by the general admission of philosophers, failed. Before transcendental criticism appeared, since the principle could not be abandoned, it was thought better to appeal boldly to the common sense of mankind than to search for new dogmatic proofs. Such an appeal always reveals that the problem reason ought to solve is one that philosophers find deeply troublesome.

But if the proposition to be proved belongs to pure reason, and I intend to pass beyond my empirical concepts by means of mere ideas, the proof must first show that such a step in synthesis is possible, which it is not, before it can go on to establish the truth of the proposition itself. The so-called proof that the soul is simple, drawn from the unity of apperception, is highly plausible. Yet it offers no answer to the following objection. Absolute simplicity is not a concept that can be applied directly to a perception; it is an idea that must be inferred from observation, if it can be inferred at all. It is therefore by no means evident how the mere fact of consciousness, which is contained in all thought and is to that extent a simple representation, can lead me to the consciousness and knowledge of a thing that is purely a thinking substance. When I picture the moving force of my body, my body is, in that thought, an absolute unity, and my representation of it is simple. I can therefore represent it by the motion of a point, because I have abstracted from the body's size or volume. But I cannot infer from this that, given only the moving force of a body, the body may be conceived as a simple substance merely because my representation disregards its extension in space and is therefore simple. What is simple in abstraction is very different from what is objectively simple. The Ego, which is simple in the first sense, may in the second sense, as designating the soul itself, be a highly complex concept with a widely varied content. Clearly, then, a paralogism, a fallacious inference, lurks in all arguments of this kind. We suspect its presence (and without some such suspicion we would never question a proof of this sort) by keeping constantly in view a criterion for the possibility of synthetic propositions that claim to prove more than experience can teach. We obtain this criterion by observing that such proofs do not lead directly from the subject of the proposition to the required predicate, but must presuppose that our knowledge can be extended a priori by means of ideas. We must therefore always proceed with the greatest caution. Before attempting any proof, we must consider how the sphere of knowledge could possibly be extended by the operations of pure reason, and from what source we are to obtain knowledge that is neither derived from the analysis of concepts nor an anticipation of possible experience. In this way we will spare ourselves much hard and fruitless labor, by not expecting from reason what lies beyond its power, or rather by subjecting it to discipline and teaching it to restrain its vehement desire to extend the sphere of knowledge.

The first rule, therefore, is this: attempt no transcendental proof until you have considered from what source you are to draw the principles on which it will rest, and by what right you can expect conclusions drawn from those principles to be true. If they are principles of the understanding, it is futile to hope to reach the ideas of pure reason through them, since such principles are valid only for objects of possible experience. If they are principles of pure reason, the effort is equally futile. For the principles of reason, when used as objective principles, are without exception dialectical; they have no validity or truth except as regulative principles guiding the systematic use of reason within experience. When deceptive proofs of this kind are presented to us, our duty is to answer them with the *non liquet*, the verdict of "not proven," that a mature judgment delivers. Even if we cannot expose the particular sophism on which a given proof rests, we have the right to demand a deduction, a justification, of the principles it employs; and if those principles originate in pure reason alone, such a deduction is absolutely impossible. We need not, then, trouble ourselves with exposing and refuting every sophistical illusion. We can bring all dialectic, which is inexhaustible in producing fallacies, at once before the tribunal of critical reason, which tests the principles on which every dialectical procedure rests.

The second peculiarity of transcendental proof is that a transcendental proposition can rest on only a single proof. When I draw conclusions not from concepts but from the intuition corresponding to a concept, whether pure intuition, as in mathematics, or empirical intuition, as in natural science, the intuition that grounds my inferences supplies material for many synthetic propositions. I can connect these in various ways, and since I am free to begin from different points in the intuition, I can reach the same proposition by different paths.

Every transcendental proposition, however, starts from a concept and sets out the synthetic condition under which an object corresponding to that concept is possible. There can therefore be only one ground of proof, because the concept alone determines the object, and the proof can contain nothing beyond the determination of the object according to that concept. In our Transcendental Analytic, for example, we derived the principle "Every event has a cause" from the sole condition under which our concept of an event is objectively possible: an event cannot be determined in time, and so cannot form part of experience, unless it falls under this dynamic law. This is the only possible ground of proof, for our concept of an event has objective validity, that is, it is a true concept, only because the law of causality determines an object to which it can refer. Other arguments for this principle have been attempted, such as the argument from the contingent nature of a phenomenon. But when we examine that argument, we find no criterion of contingency other than the fact of an event, of something happening, that is, of an existence preceded by the non-existence of an object. And so we fall back on the very thing that was to be proved. If the proposition "Every thinking being is simple" is to be proved, we confine ourselves to the concept of the Ego, which is simple and to which all thought is related.
