The same holds for the transcendental proof of the existence of God, which rests solely on the harmony and mutual fit between the concepts of an *ens realissimum*, a most real being, and a necessary being, and cannot be attempted in any other way.

This caution greatly simplifies the criticism of all propositions of reason. When reason works with concepts alone, only one proof of its thesis is possible, if any is possible at all. So when the dogmatist comes forward with ten arguments for a proposition, we can be sure that not one of them is conclusive. If he had a single argument that actually proved the proposition, as must always be the case with propositions of pure reason, what need would he have for more? His purpose can only resemble that of the advocate who kept different arguments for different judges, exploiting the weakness of those who examine his case: judges who, without investigating deeply, adopt whichever view seems most probable at first glance and decide accordingly.

The third rule governing pure reason in the conduct of proof is that transcendental proofs must never be apagogic, or indirect, but always ostensive, or direct. A direct proof not only establishes the truth of the proposition in question but also reveals the grounds of that truth. An apagogic proof, by contrast, may assure us that the proposition is true, but it cannot help us understand the grounds of its possibility. It is therefore more an auxiliary device in argument than a strictly philosophical and rational procedure. In one respect, however, indirect proofs do have an advantage over direct ones: their method of arguing by contradiction makes our grasp of the question clearer and brings the proof closer to the certainty of a demonstration grounded in intuition.

The real reason indirect proofs are used in the various sciences is this. When the grounds on which we try to base a piece of knowledge are too numerous or lie too deep, we test whether we can establish its truth from its consequences instead. The *modus ponens*, reasoning from the truth of a proposition's consequences to the truth of the proposition itself, would be legitimate only if every consequence that could be drawn from it were known to be true, for in that case there could be only one possible ground for those consequences, namely the true one. But this procedure is wholly impracticable, since discovering every possible consequence of a proposition lies far beyond our powers. We do employ this mode of reasoning, by a kind of indulgence, when we try to prove a hypothesis. In that case we grant, on the strength of analogy, that if all the consequences we have drawn and examined agree with the assumed proposition, all other possible consequences will agree with it as well. By this route, however, a hypothesis can never be established as a demonstrated truth. The *modus tollens*, reasoning from known consequences back to the unknown proposition, is not only a rigorous but also a very easy mode of proof. For if even one consequence of a proposition can be shown to be false, the proposition itself must be false. So instead of tracing, as a direct argument would, the entire series of grounds on which the truth of a proposition rests, we need only take the opposite of that proposition, and if a single consequence drawn from it is false, then must the opposite itself must be false; and consequently the proposition we set out to prove must be true.

The apagogic, or indirect, method of proof is admissible only in those sciences where it is impossible to mistake a subjective representation for objective knowledge. Where such a mistake is possible, the opposite of a given proposition may contradict only the subjective conditions of thought, not objective knowledge itself. Or the two propositions may contradict each other only under a subjective condition that has been wrongly taken to be objective. In that case, since the condition is itself false, both propositions may be false, and it becomes impossible to infer the truth of one from the falsity of the other.

In mathematics such subreptions, or covert substitutions of the subjective for the objective, cannot occur, and so it is in mathematics that indirect proof has its proper place. In natural science, where every assertion rests on empirical intuition, such substitutions can be guarded against by repeatedly comparing observations; yet even there this form of proof is of little value. The transcendental endeavors of pure reason, by contrast, all take place within the sphere of the subjective, which is the true medium of every dialectical illusion. Here reason tries, in its premises, to pass off subjective representations on us as objective knowledge. In the transcendental sphere of pure reason, then, and wherever synthetic propositions are concerned, it is inadmissible to support a claim by refuting its counterclaim. For only two cases are possible. In the first, the counterclaim does nothing more than declare that the opposing view is inconsistent with the subjective conditions of reason, which leaves the real question untouched. For example, we cannot comprehend the unconditioned necessity of any being's existence, and so every speculative proof that such a being exists must be resisted on subjective grounds; yet the possibility of this being in itself cannot justly be denied. In the second case, both propositions are dialectical by nature and rest on an impossible concept. Here the rule applies: *non entis nulla sunt praedicata*, "of what does not exist, nothing can be predicated." Whatever we affirm and whatever we deny about such an object are equally untrue, and the apagogic route to truth is closed. Suppose, for example, we presuppose that the world of sense is given in itself as a complete totality. Then it is false that the world is infinite, and equally false that it is finite and bounded in space. Both are false because the hypothesis is false. The notion that phenomena, which are mere representations, are given in themselves as objects is self-contradictory. The infinity of this imaginary whole would indeed be unconditioned. But since everything in the world of phenomena is conditioned, that infinity would be inconsistent with the unconditioned determination and finitude of magnitude that our concept presupposes.

The apagogic method of proof is the true source of those illusions that have always held so strong an attraction for the admirers of dogmatic philosophy. It resembles a champion in the old chivalric sense: a knight who upholds the honor and claims of the party he has chosen to serve by challenging to single combat anyone who doubts the validity of those claims or the purity of that honor. Such combat proves nothing except the relative strength of the fighters, and in this respect the advantage always lies with the side that attacks. Spectators, seeing each party win and lose by turns, are led to conclude that the matter in dispute lies beyond human power to decide. But that conclusion is unjustified, and it is enough to apply to these disputants the line:

*Non defensoribus istis*
*Tempus eget.*

"The hour has no need of defenders such as these."

Each party must instead try to establish its assertions through a transcendental deduction of the grounds of proof it employs, so that we can see how the claims of reason may legitimately be supported. If an opponent rests his assertions on subjective grounds, he is easily refuted. This gives no advantage to the dogmatist, however, who likewise depends on subjective sources of knowledge and is driven into a corner by his opponent in exactly the same way. If both parties adopt the direct method of proof, they will soon discover how difficult, indeed how impossible, it is to prove their assertions. They will then be forced either to fall back on prescription and precedence, the mere claim of long possession and prior standing, or else, with the help of criticism, to detect the dogmatic illusions that had been deceiving them. In that second case they will compel reason to give up its inflated pretensions to speculative insight and to confine itself within the limits of its proper sphere, which is that of practical principles.

## Doctrine of Method, Chapter II: The Canon of Pure Reason

It is humbling for human reason to recognize that it cannot discover truth through pure speculation, and that it instead needs a discipline to curb its departures from the straight path and to expose the illusions it generates. Yet this same recognition ought also to raise its spirits and give it confidence, for the discipline is one that reason exercises upon itself alone, and it answers to the judgment of no other power. The limits that reason is compelled to set on its speculative activity also check the false pretensions of its opponents. Whatever remains of its possessions, once these exaggerated claims have been disallowed, is therefore secure from attack or usurpation. The greatest, and perhaps the only, use of the whole philosophy of pure reason is accordingly purely negative. It is not an organon, an instrument for extending knowledge, but a discipline for determining the limits within which reason may be exercised. It lays no claim to discovering new truths, but it has the modest merit of guarding against error.

At the same time, there must be some source of positive knowledge that belongs to the domain of pure reason. Such knowledge leads to error only when we mistake its true character, and it forms the goal toward which reason constantly strives. How else could we account for the inextinguishable desire of the human mind to find firm footing somewhere beyond the limits of experience? Reason hopes to gain possession of a knowledge in which it has the deepest interest. It sets out on the path of pure speculation, but in vain. We have some grounds, however, to expect that along the only other path open to it, the path of practical reason, it may meet with better success.

By a canon I mean the complete set of a priori principles governing the proper use of certain faculties of knowledge. General logic, in its analytic part, is thus a formal canon for the faculties of understanding and reason. In the same way, the Transcendental Analytic proved to be a canon of the pure understanding, since the understanding alone is capable of genuine a priori synthetic knowledge. But where no proper use of a faculty of knowledge is possible, there can be no canon for it. And the synthetic knowledge of pure speculative reason, as has been shown, is entirely impossible. There can therefore be no canon for the speculative use of this faculty, since that use is wholly dialectical, and transcendental logic in this respect is merely a discipline, not a canon. If there is any proper use of pure reason at all, there must be a canon for it, and that canon will concern not the speculative but the practical use of reason. It is this canon that we now investigate.

### Section I. Of the Ultimate End of the Pure Use of Reason

There is in the faculty of reason a natural desire to venture beyond the field of experience, to reach for the outermost bounds of all knowledge by means of ideas alone, and not to rest until it has completed its course and gathered the sum of its knowledge into a self-sufficient systematic whole. Is the motive for this effort to be found in reason's speculative interests, or in its practical interests alone?

Setting aside for now what pure reason has achieved in its speculative use, I shall ask only about the problems whose solution constitutes its ultimate aim, whether or not that aim is ever reached. All of reason's other aims are merely partial and intermediate in relation to these problems. These highest aims must, by the very nature of reason, form a complete unity; otherwise the highest interest of humanity could not be successfully advanced.

The transcendental speculation of reason concerns three things: the freedom of the will, the immortality of the soul, and the existence of God. Reason's speculative interest in these questions is very slight. For its sake alone, we would never take on the labor of transcendental inquiry, a labor full of toil and unending struggle. We would be reluctant to undertake it because whatever we discovered would be of not the slightest use in concrete or physical investigation. We might find that the will is free, but this knowledge concerns only the intelligible cause of our volition. The phenomena of the will, its outward expressions, are our actions. These we are bound to explain exactly as we explain every other natural phenomenon, according to nature's unchanging laws. This obligation follows from an inviolable maxim without which reason cannot be used in the realm of experience at all. We might have discovered that the soul is spiritual and immortal, but we could not use this knowledge to explain the phenomena of the present life, or the particular character of a future one. Our concept of an incorporeal nature is purely negative; it adds nothing to our knowledge, and any inferences drawn from it are pure fiction. Again, if we proved the existence of a supreme intelligence, we could use it to make intelligible the purposiveness evident in the arrangement of the world. But we would not be justified in deducing from it any particular arrangement or disposition, or in inferring one where it is not actually perceived. For it is a necessary rule of the speculative use of reason that we must not pass over natural causes, or refuse to heed what experience teaches, in order to derive what we know and perceive from something that transcends all our knowledge. In a word, for speculative reason these three propositions always remain transcendent. They cannot serve as immanent principles applied to objects of experience, and so they are of no use to us in that sphere. They are merely the worthless results of reason's strenuous but unprofitable efforts.

If actual knowledge of these three cardinal propositions is entirely useless, and yet reason urges us with all her might to accept them, it is plain that their real value and importance lie in our practical interest, not our speculative one.

I call practical everything that is possible through freedom of the will. But where the conditions under which free choice is exercised are empirical, reason can have only a regulative influence on it, not a constitutive one, and serves merely to bring unity into its empirical laws. In the moral philosophy of prudence, for instance, reason's sole task is to unite all the ends pursued by our inclinations into a single ultimate end, which is happiness, and to show how the means of attaining that end ought to agree with one another. In this sphere, then, reason can offer only pragmatic laws of free action, guiding us toward aims set by the senses; it cannot give us laws that are pure and determined entirely a priori. Pure practical laws would be a different matter. Their ends would be given by reason wholly a priori; they would not be empirically conditioned but absolutely imperative; and they would be products of pure reason. The moral laws are of this kind, and they alone belong to the practical use of reason and admit of a canon.

In what may be called pure philosophy, all the powers of reason are in fact directed to the three problems named above, and to these alone. Those problems in turn serve a still higher end: the answer to the question of what we ought to do if the will is free, if there is a God, and if there is a future world. Since this question concerns our conduct in relation to the highest aim of humanity, it is evident that nature's ultimate intention in constituting our reason as it did was directed to the moral alone.

In turning our attention to a subject foreign to transcendental philosophy, however, we must take care not to damage the unity of our system through digression. We must equally avoid sacrificing clarity by saying too little about the new topic. I hope to avoid both extremes by keeping as close as possible to the transcendental and excluding everything psychological, that is, empirical. The subject is foreign because all practical concepts relate to objects of pleasure and pain, and thus, at least indirectly, to objects of feeling. Feeling, however, is not a faculty of representation; it lies outside the sphere of our cognitive powers. The elements of our judgments that relate to pleasure or pain, which are the elements of our practical judgments, therefore do not belong to transcendental philosophy, which deals with pure a priori knowledge alone.

I must note, first, that I am treating the concept of freedom here only in its practical sense. I set aside the corresponding transcendental concept, which cannot serve as a ground of explanation in the world of phenomena but is itself a problem for pure reason. A will is purely animal (*arbitrium brutum*) when it is determined by sensuous impulses or instincts alone, that is, when it is determined pathologically, by what the senses undergo. A will that can be determined independently of sensuous impulses, and therefore by motives presented by reason alone, is called a free will (*arbitrium liberum*). Everything connected with this free will, whether as its ground or as its consequence, is called practical. Practical freedom can be proved from experience alone. The human will is not determined solely by what immediately affects the senses. We have the power to overcome the immediate impressions on our sensuous faculty of desire by calling to mind what is useful or harmful in a more remote way. These considerations of what is desirable for our condition as a whole, of what is in the end good and useful, rest entirely on reason. Reason therefore lays down laws that are imperative, objective laws of freedom, telling us what ought to happen. In this they differ from the laws of nature, which concern what does happen. The laws of freedom, or of free will, are accordingly called practical laws.

Reason itself, in actually laying down these laws, may in turn be determined by other influences. An action we call free in relation to sensuous impulses might, in relation to higher and more remote efficient causes, really belong to nature after all. These questions do not concern us here. They are purely speculative, and in the practical sphere our only task is to inquire into the rule of conduct that reason prescribes. Experience shows us that practical freedom is one of the causes operating in nature; it shows us the causal power of reason in determining the will. The idea of transcendental freedom, on the other hand, requires that reason, in its causal power to begin a series of phenomena, be independent of all sensuous determining causes. It therefore appears to conflict with the law of nature and with all possible experience, and so it remains a problem for the human mind. But this problem does not concern reason in its practical use. In a canon of pure reason, then, we are concerned with only two questions bearing on the practical interest of pure reason: Is there a God? and Is there a future life? The question of transcendental freedom is purely speculative, and we may set it aside entirely when we come to treat of practical reason. Besides, we have already discussed this subject in the antinomy of pure reason.

### Section II. Of the Ideal of the Summum Bonum as a Determining Ground of the Ultimate End of Pure Reason

In its speculative use, reason led us through the field of experience. Since it could never find complete satisfaction there, it led us onward to speculative ideas, and these in the end brought us back to experience once more. In this way reason fulfilled its purpose in a manner that was useful but did not at all match our expectations. It remains to consider whether pure reason can be used in a practical sphere, and whether there it will lead us to those ideas that attain the highest ends of pure reason as we have just stated them. We shall thereby learn whether reason, from the standpoint of its practical interest, may be able to supply what it wholly denies us on the speculative side.

The entire interest of reason, speculative as well as practical, is concentrated in the following three questions:

1. WHAT CAN I KNOW?
2. WHAT OUGHT I TO DO?
3. WHAT MAY I HOPE?

The first question is purely speculative. I flatter myself that we have exhausted every answer it admits of. We have at last arrived at the answer with which reason must content itself, and with which it ought to be content so long as it takes no account of the practical. Yet we remain as far from the two great ends toward which all these efforts of pure reason were really directed as if we had consulted our own ease and declined the task from the start. As far as knowledge is concerned, this much at least is settled: with respect to those two problems, knowledge lies beyond our reach.

The second question is purely practical. As such it may indeed fall within the province of pure reason, but it is moral rather than transcendental, and so it cannot in itself be the subject of our critique.

The third question, "If I do what I ought, what may I then hope?", is at once practical and theoretical. The practical serves as a guide to answering the theoretical question, and to answering the speculative question that is its highest form. For all hope aims at happiness. Hope stands in exactly the same relation to the practical and to the moral law as knowledge stands to the theoretical cognition of things and to the law of nature. Hope arrives in the end at the conclusion that something is, namely something that determines the ultimate end, because something ought to happen. Knowledge arrives at the conclusion that something is, namely something that acts as the highest cause, because something does happen.

Happiness is the satisfaction of all our desires: extensively, with respect to their number; intensively, with respect to their degree; and protensively, with respect to their duration. A practical law based on the motive of happiness I call a pragmatic law, or rule of prudence. A law whose only motive is worthiness to be happy, supposing such a law exists, I call a moral or ethical law. The first tells us what we must do if we wish to attain happiness; the second prescribes how we ought to act in order to deserve it. The first rests on empirical principles, since only through experience can I learn which inclinations exist that seek satisfaction, or what natural means are available for satisfying them. The second disregards our desires and the means of satisfying them. It considers only the freedom of a rational being and the necessary conditions under which alone this freedom can harmonize with a distribution of happiness made according to principles. This second law can therefore rest on mere ideas of pure reason and can be known a priori.

I assume that there really are pure moral laws. These laws determine the conduct of a rational being, that is, the use it makes of its freedom, entirely a priori and without regard to empirical motives such as happiness. They command absolutely, not merely hypothetically on the supposition of some further empirical end, and they are therefore necessary in every respect. I am entitled to assume this not only on the strength of the arguments of the most enlightened moralists, but on the moral judgment of every person who makes the effort to form a distinct conception of such a law.

Pure reason, then, contains principles of the possibility of experience. It contains them not in its speculative use, but in its practical, or more precisely its moral, use. They are principles of the possibility of those actions which accord with ethical precepts and which might be found in the history of mankind. Since reason commands that such actions take place, it must be possible for them to take place; and hence a particular kind of systematic unity, the moral, must also be possible. We found, it is true, that the systematic unity of nature could not be established according to speculative principles of reason. Reason has causal power with respect to freedom but none with respect to nature as a whole, and moral principles of reason can produce free actions but cannot produce natural laws. It is therefore in its practical use, and especially its moral use, that the principles of pure reason possess objective reality.

I call the world a moral world insofar as it accords with all ethical laws. Through the freedom of rational beings it can so accord, and according to the necessary laws of morality it ought to. But this world must be conceived only as an intelligible world, since in conceiving it we abstract from all conditions, meaning ends, and even from every obstacle to morality, such as the weakness or depravity of human nature. To that extent it is a mere idea. Yet it is a practical idea, which can and ought to influence the world of sense so as to bring it as far as possible into conformity with itself. The idea of a moral world therefore has objective reality. It does not refer to an object of intelligible intuition, for of such an object we can form no conception whatever. It refers instead to the world of sense, conceived as an object of pure reason in its practical use. It also refers to a *corpus mysticum*, a mystical body made up of the rational beings within that world. This body exists insofar as the free choice (*liberum arbitrium*) of each individual stands, under and by virtue of moral laws, in complete systematic unity both with itself and with the freedom of every other.

That is the answer to the first of the two questions of pure reason that bear on its practical interest: Do that which will make you worthy of happiness. The second question is this: If I conduct myself so as not to be unworthy of happiness, may I hope thereby to obtain it? To answer this, we must ask whether the principles of pure reason that prescribe the law a priori also necessarily connect this hope with it.

I say, then, that just as the moral principles are necessary according to reason in its practical use, so it is equally necessary, according to reason in its theoretical use, to assume that everyone has grounds to hope for happiness in the measure to which he has made himself worthy of it by his conduct. The system of morality is therefore inseparably connected with the system of happiness, though only in the idea of pure reason.

Consider an intelligible world, that is, a moral world, in whose concept we set aside every obstacle to morality, such as the desires of the senses. In such a world, a system of happiness bound up with and proportioned to morality can be conceived as necessary. Freedom of the will, partly prompted and partly restrained by moral laws, would itself be the cause of general happiness, and rational beings guided by such principles would be the authors of their own lasting welfare and of the welfare of others. But such a system of self-rewarding morality is only an idea. Its realization depends on the condition that everyone acts as he ought: all the actions of rational beings would have to be such as they would be if they sprang from a Supreme Will that embraced all particular wills within or beneath itself. Yet the moral law binds each individual in the use of his freedom even if others fail to act in accordance with it. Consequently, neither the nature of things, nor the causality of actions and their relation to morality, determines how the consequences of those actions will relate to happiness. If we take nature alone as our guide, reason cannot recognize any necessary connection between the hope of happiness and the unceasing effort to become worthy of it. That connection can be hoped for only on the assumption that the cause of nature is a supreme reason that governs according to moral laws.

I give a name to the idea of an intelligence in which the morally most perfect will, united with supreme blessedness, is the cause of all happiness in the world, insofar as that happiness stands in exact relation to morality, understood as the worthiness to be happy. I call this idea the ideal of the supreme good. Only in the ideal of the supreme original good, then, can pure reason find the ground of the practically necessary connection between the two elements of the highest derived good, and therefore the ground of an intelligible, or moral, world. Reason compels us to think of ourselves as belonging to such a world, while the senses present us with nothing but a world of appearances. We must therefore assume the moral world as a consequence of our conduct in the world of sense, since the world of sense offers no hint of it, and hence as lying in our future. God and a future life are thus two hypotheses which, according to the principles of pure reason, cannot be separated from the obligation that this same reason imposes on us.

Morality in itself forms a system. Happiness does not, except insofar as it is distributed in exact proportion to morality, and that is possible only in the intelligible world, under a wise author and ruler. Reason finds itself compelled to assume such a ruler, together with life in such a world, which we must regard as future. Otherwise it would have to treat the moral laws as idle fantasies, since without this hypothesis the necessary consequence that reason itself attaches to them would collapse. This is also why moral laws are universally regarded as commands. They could not be commands unless they linked appropriate consequences to their precepts a priori, and so carried promises and threats with them. And they could not do that unless they resided in a necessary being, the supreme good, which alone makes such a teleological unity possible.

Leibniz gave the name "kingdom of grace" to the world viewed with regard to the rational beings it contains and the moral relations among them under the government of the supreme good. He distinguished it from the kingdom of nature, in which these same rational beings live under moral laws but expect no consequences from their actions beyond those that follow from the ordinary course of nature in the world of sense. To regard ourselves as belonging to the kingdom of grace, where every happiness awaits us unless we ourselves restrict our share in it by acts that make us unworthy of happiness, is therefore a practically necessary idea of reason.

Practical laws, insofar as they are also the subjective grounds of action, that is, subjective principles, are called maxims. We judge morality, in its purity and its consequences, according to ideas; we obey its laws according to maxims.

The whole course of our life must be governed by moral maxims. Yet this is impossible unless reason joins to the moral law, which is a mere idea, an efficient cause that assigns to all conduct conforming to that law an outcome corresponding exactly to our highest aims, whether in this life or in another. Without a God, and without a world invisible to us now but hoped for, the noble ideas of morality may well be objects of approval and admiration, but they cannot be the springs of purpose and action. For they do not fulfill the whole of the aims that are natural to every rational being, aims determined a priori by pure reason itself, and necessary.

Happiness alone is, in the eyes of reason, far from the complete good. However much inclination may desire it, reason does not approve of happiness unless it is united with desert. Morality alone, and with it mere desert, is likewise far from the complete good. To make the good complete, whoever has conducted himself so as not to be unworthy of happiness must be able to hope to possess it. Even reason free of private ends and of every consideration of self-interest could not judge otherwise if it put itself in the place of a being whose task was to distribute all happiness to others. For in the practical idea the two elements are essentially combined, but in a particular order: the moral disposition, as the condition, makes participation in happiness possible, and the prospect of happiness does not make the moral disposition possible. A disposition that required the prospect of happiness as its necessary condition would not be moral. It would therefore not be worthy of complete happiness, a happiness that, in the view of reason, admits no limit except one arising from our own immoral conduct.

Happiness in exact proportion to the morality of rational beings, through which they are made worthy of it, therefore constitutes by itself the supreme good of a world into which, by the commands of pure but practical reason, we absolutely must transport ourselves. This world is, admittedly, only an intelligible one, since the world of sense gives us no hint of the systematic unity of ends that it requires. Its reality can rest on nothing but the hypothesis of a supreme original good. In that world, independent reason, equipped with all the sufficiency of a supreme cause, founds, sustains, and completes the universal order of things in the most perfect teleological harmony, however hidden this order may remain from us in the world of sense.

This moral theology has a distinctive advantage over speculative theology: it leads inevitably to the concept of a single, perfect, and rational first cause. Speculative theology offers no indication of such a cause on objective grounds, much less convincing evidence for it. However far reason may carry us in transcendental or in natural theology, we find in neither any ground for assuming the existence of one single being that stands at the head of all natural causes and on which they wholly depend. But suppose we take our stand on moral unity as a necessary law of the universe, and consider from that standpoint what is needed to give this law adequate effect and, for us, binding force. We must then conclude that there is a single supreme will that comprehends all these laws within itself. For how could we find a complete unity of ends among different wills? This will must be omnipotent, so that all of nature and its relation to morality in the world may be subject to it; omniscient, so that it may know our most secret feelings and their moral worth; omnipresent, so that it may be at hand to meet every need that the highest welfare of the world may produce; eternal, so that this harmony between nature and freedom may never fail; and so on.

Considered as mere nature, the world of intelligences is only a world of sense. Considered as a system of freedom, it may be called an intelligible or moral world: the *regnum gratiae*, or kingdom of grace. The systematic unity of ends in this world leads inevitably to the teleological unity of all the things that make up this great whole, according to universal laws of nature, just as the unity of the moral world follows universal and necessary moral laws. In this way it unites practical reason with speculative reason. The world must be represented as having arisen from an idea if it is to agree with that use of reason without which we could not even regard ourselves as worthy of reason, namely its moral use, which rests entirely on the idea of the supreme good. Our investigation of nature therefore acquires a teleological direction, and in its widest extension becomes physico-theology, the inference from the order of nature to its divine author. This physico-theology originates in the moral order, a unity grounded in the very essence of freedom and not instituted arbitrarily by external commands. It therefore bases the teleological view of nature on grounds that must be inseparably bound up with the inner possibility of things. This gives rise to a transcendental theology, which takes the ideal of the highest ontological perfection as its principle of systematic unity. That principle connects all things according to universal and necessary laws of nature, because all things have their origin in the absolute necessity of a single primal being.

What use could we make of our understanding, even with respect to experience, if we did not set ends for ourselves? The highest ends are those of morality, and only pure reason can give us knowledge of them. Yet even when we possess these ends and place ourselves under their guidance, we can make no teleological use of our knowledge of nature, as far as cognition is concerned, unless nature itself has established a teleological unity. Without such unity we would not even possess reason, for we would have no school for it, and no cultivation through objects that supply the material for its concepts. But this teleological unity is necessary, and grounded in the essence of the individual will itself. The will that is the condition for applying this unity in concrete cases must therefore be necessary as well. In this way the transcendental enlargement of our rational knowledge would be not the cause but merely the effect of the practical teleology that pure reason imposes on us.

This is why we find a certain pattern in the history of human reason. Before moral concepts had been sufficiently purified and defined, and before people had grasped the systematic unity of ends according to those concepts and from necessary principles, the knowledge of nature could produce only crude and vague notions of the Deity. So could a considerable degree of intellectual culture in many other sciences. Sometimes this knowledge even allowed an astonishing indifference to the question altogether. But the fuller development of moral ideas, made necessary by the exceedingly pure moral law of our religion, awakened reason's interest in this object and thereby sharpened its perceptions. In this way people arrived at a concept of the Divine Being that we now hold to be correct. They did so without the help of any broad acquaintance with nature or any reliable transcendental insight, for these have been lacking in every age. We hold this concept to be correct not because speculative reason convinces us of it, but because it accords with the moral principles of reason. It is therefore to pure reason, though only in its practical use, that we must credit an achievement. It connected with our highest interest a piece of knowledge that mere speculation could only guess at but could not validate. It thereby made that knowledge not a demonstrated dogma but a hypothesis absolutely necessary to the essential ends of reason.

Yet once practical reason has reached this height and arrived at the concept of a single primal being as the supreme good, it must not suppose that it has transcended the empirical conditions of its application and risen to an immediate knowledge of new objects. It must not presume to start from the concept it has gained and derive the moral laws themselves from it. For it was precisely these laws, through their inner practical necessity, that led us to presuppose an independent cause, a wise ruler of the universe, who would give them effect. We are therefore not entitled to regard them in turn as contingent and derived from the mere will of that ruler, especially since we have no concept of such a will except one formed in accordance with these very laws. As far as practical reason has the right to lead us, then, we shall not regard actions as obligatory because they are God's commands; we shall regard them as divine commands because we are inwardly bound by them. We shall study freedom under the teleological unity that accords with the principles of reason. We shall consider ourselves to be acting in conformity with the divine will only insofar as we hold sacred the moral law that reason teaches us from the nature of actions themselves. And we shall believe that we can serve that will only by promoting the good of the world in ourselves and in others. Moral theology is therefore only of immanent use. It teaches us to fulfill our vocation here in the world by bringing ourselves into harmony with the whole system of ends. It also warns us against the fanaticism, and indeed the outright crime, of stripping reason of its legislative authority over the moral conduct of life in order to attach that authority directly to the idea of the Supreme Being. That would be a transcendent rather than an immanent use of moral theology, and like the transcendent use of mere speculation, it would inevitably pervert and frustrate the ultimate ends of reason.

### Section III. Of Opinion, Knowledge, and Belief

Holding something to be true is an occurrence in our understanding. It may rest on objective grounds, but it also requires subjective causes in the mind of the one who judges. If a judgment is valid for every rational being, its ground is objectively sufficient, and the holding-true is called conviction. If, on the other hand, the judgment has its ground only in the particular character of the subject, it is called persuasion.

Persuasion is a mere illusion, because a ground of judgment that lies solely in the subject is taken to be objective. Such a judgment therefore has only private validity: it holds only for the individual who makes it, and this kind of holding-true cannot be communicated. Truth, however, consists in agreement with the object. The judgments of all understandings, if they are true, must therefore agree with one another, according to the principle that things which agree with a third thing agree with each other (*consentientia uni tertio consentiunt inter se*). From the outside, then, conviction can be distinguished from persuasion by whether it can be communicated and shown to be valid for the reason of every human being. When it can, there is at least a presumption that the agreement of all these judgments, despite the differences among individuals, rests on a common ground: each one's agreement with the object. The correctness of the judgment is thereby established.

Subjectively, therefore, persuasion cannot be distinguished from conviction, so long as the subject regards its judgment merely as an occurrence in its own mind. But we can test whether the grounds of our judgment that are valid for us have the same effect on the reason of others as on our own. This gives us a means, though only a subjective one, not of producing conviction, but of detecting the merely private validity of the judgment, and so of discovering the element of mere persuasion within it. We can go further and lay bare the subjective causes of the judgment that we had mistaken for its objective grounds. We can then explain the deceptive judgment as an occurrence in our own mind, wholly apart from the character of the object. If we succeed, we can expose the illusion and need no longer be deceived by it. If its subjective cause lies in our nature, however, we cannot hope to escape its influence entirely.

I can assert, that is, declare as necessarily valid for everyone, only what produces conviction. Persuasion I may keep to myself if it pleases me, but I cannot and ought not try to impose it on others as binding.

Holding-true, or the subjective validity of a judgment in relation to conviction (which is at the same time objectively valid), has three degrees: opinion, belief, and knowledge. Opinion is a judgment consciously recognized as insufficient both subjectively and objectively. Belief is subjectively sufficient but recognized as objectively insufficient. Knowledge is sufficient both subjectively and objectively. Subjective sufficiency is called conviction (for myself); objective sufficiency is called certainty (for everyone). I need not dwell any longer on explaining such simple concepts.

I must never presume to hold an opinion without knowing at least something that connects my judgment, in itself merely problematic, with the truth. That connection, though incomplete, is still more than an arbitrary fiction. The law governing such a connection must, moreover, be certain. If I have nothing more than an opinion about that law as well, my judgment is a mere play of the imagination, without the slightest relation to truth. In judgments of pure reason, opinion has no place at all. Such judgments do not rest on empirical grounds, and the domain of pure reason is that of necessary truth and a priori knowledge. The principle of connection within it therefore requires universality and necessity, and so complete certainty; otherwise we would have no guide to truth whatever. It is therefore absurd to hold opinions in pure mathematics: there we must either know or refrain from judging altogether. The same holds for the maxims of morality, for we must not risk an action on the mere opinion that it is permitted; we must know it to be so. In the transcendental sphere of reason, by contrast, opinion is too weak a word, while knowledge is too strong. From a merely speculative standpoint, therefore, we cannot form a judgment here at all. The subjective grounds of a judgment, the kind that can produce belief, have no standing in speculative inquiries. They cannot hold up without empirical support, and they cannot be communicated to others in equal measure.

Only from the practical point of view can a theoretically insufficient judgment be called belief. This practical reference is either to skill or to morality: to skill when the end in view is arbitrary and contingent, to morality when it is absolutely necessary.

Once we have set ourselves any end at all, the conditions for attaining it are hypothetically necessary. This necessity is subjectively sufficient, but only comparatively so, if I know of no other conditions under which the end could be reached. It is sufficient absolutely, and for everyone, if I know with certainty that no one can know of any other conditions under which the proposed end could be attained. In the first case, my supposition, my judgment about certain conditions, is a merely contingent belief; in the second, it is a necessary belief. A physician must do something for a patient in danger, yet he does not know the nature of the illness. He observes the symptoms and concludes, to the best of his judgment, that the disease is phthisis, the wasting disease of the lungs also known as consumption. Even in his own estimation his belief is only contingent; someone else might come closer to the truth. A belief of this kind, contingent yet still the basis for actually employing means toward certain ends, I call pragmatic belief.

The usual test of whether what someone asserts is mere persuasion, or at least subjective conviction, meaning firm belief, is a bet. People often deliver their opinions with such boldness and assurance that they seem to have no fear whatever of being wrong. The offer of a bet startles such a person and gives him pause. Sometimes it turns out that his persuasion is worth one ducat, a gold coin, but not ten. He may not hesitate to risk the one, but if he is asked to stake ten, he immediately becomes aware that he might be mistaken, a possibility that had escaped him until then. If we imagine having to stake the happiness of our entire life on the truth of some proposition, our judgment loses its air of triumph, we grow alarmed, and we discover how strong our belief actually is. Pragmatic belief, therefore, has degrees, which vary with the interests at stake.

In some cases we cannot undertake any action with respect to an object, so our judgment is purely theoretical. Even then we can imagine in thought a course of action for which we suppose we would have sufficient grounds, if there were some way of settling the truth of the matter. Purely theoretical judgments thus contain an analogue of practical judgments, to which the word belief can properly be applied, and which we may call doctrinal belief. If it were possible to test the question by experience, I would not hesitate to stake everything I have on the proposition that at least one of the planets we can see is inhabited. Hence I say that it is not merely my opinion but my strong belief that there are inhabitants on other worlds, and I would wager many of life's advantages on its correctness.

We must admit that the doctrine of the existence of God belongs to doctrinal belief. In my theoretical knowledge of the universe I do not need to form any theory that necessarily involves this idea as the condition for explaining the phenomena the universe presents. On the contrary, I am obliged to use my reason as if everything were mere nature. Still, teleological unity is so important a condition for applying my reason to nature that I cannot ignore it, especially since experience also supplies abundant examples of it. But the sole condition, so far as my knowledge extends, under which this unity can guide me in the investigation of nature is the assumption that a supreme intelligence has ordered all things according to the wisest ends. The hypothesis of a wise author of the universe is therefore necessary to guide my investigation of nature. It is the only condition under which I can fulfill an end that is admittedly contingent, but by no means unimportant. Moreover, since the results of my efforts so often confirm the usefulness of this assumption, and since nothing decisive can be brought against it, it would be saying far too little to call my judgment in this case a mere opinion. Even in this theoretical context, I may assert that I firmly believe in God. Strictly speaking, however, this belief must be called doctrinal rather than practical, and it is the kind of belief that the theology of nature, or physico-theology, must also produce in my mind. In the wisdom of a Supreme Being, and in the brevity of human life, which is so inadequate to the full development of the glorious powers of human nature, we may find equally sufficient grounds for a doctrinal belief in the future life of the human soul.

In such cases, the language of belief expresses modesty from the objective standpoint and, at the same time, firm confidence from the subjective one. If I were to call this purely theoretical judgment even so much as a hypothesis that I am entitled to assume, I could then justly be asked for a fuller conception of another world and of the cause of the world than I am actually able to give. For if I assume anything, even as a mere hypothesis, I must at least know enough about the properties of such a being to be able, not to frame its concept, but to imagine its existence. The word *belief*, by contrast, refers only to the guidance an idea gives me, and to its subjective influence on the conduct of my reason. That influence compels me to hold fast to the idea, even though I may be in no position to give a speculative account of it.

Mere doctrinal belief, however, lacks a certain stability. We often lose our grip on it because of the difficulties that arise in speculation, although in the end we inevitably return to it.

Moral belief is entirely different. In this sphere, action is absolutely necessary: I must obey the moral law in every respect. Here the end is established beyond dispute, and as far as I can see, there is only one condition under which this end can harmonize with all other ends and so have practical validity, namely the existence of a God and of a future world. I also know with certainty that no one can know of any other conditions that lead to the same unity of ends under the moral law. Since the moral precept is at the same time my own maxim, as reason requires it to be, I am irresistibly constrained to believe in the existence of God and in a future life. I am sure that nothing can make this belief waver, because to abandon it would be to overthrow my moral maxims, and renouncing them would make me hateful in my own eyes.

Thus, although all of reason's ambitious attempts to reach beyond the limits of experience end in disappointment, enough remains to satisfy us from a practical point of view. No one, it is true, will be able to boast that he *knows* there is a God and a future life. If anyone does know this, he is exactly the man I have long wished to find. All knowledge concerning an object of pure reason can be communicated, and so I could hope that my own knowledge would be extended in this wonderful way through his instruction. No, my conviction is not logical certainty but moral certainty. Because it rests on subjective grounds, on moral sentiment, I must not even say, "It is morally certain that there is a God," and so on, but rather, "*I* am morally certain." My belief in God and in another world is so interwoven with my moral nature that I am in as little danger of having the belief torn from me as of losing that nature itself.

The only point in this argument that may seem open to suspicion is that this rational belief presupposes the existence of moral sentiments. If we give up that assumption and take a man who is entirely indifferent to moral laws, the question that reason poses becomes merely a problem for speculation. It may then be supported by strong arguments from analogy, but not by arguments that will force even the most stubborn skepticism to give way. Yet in these questions no one is free of all interest. Even if a lack of good sentiments places a man beyond the reach of moral interests, enough may still remain to make him *fear* the existence of God and a future life. He cannot claim to be certain that there is no God and no future life, because such a claim could only be proved by pure reason, and therefore with apodictic, or strictly necessary, certainty. He would have to establish that both are impossible, and no reasonable person would undertake that. What remains is a negative belief. It could not produce morality and good sentiments, but it could produce something analogous to them by acting as a powerful restraint on the outbreak of evil dispositions.

The human mind, as I believe every rational being must necessarily do, takes a natural interest in morality, although this interest is not undivided and may not prevail in practice. If you strengthen and increase it, you will find reason growing more receptive and more enlightened, and better able to unite the speculative interest with the practical. But if you do not take care at the outset, or at least partway along, to make people good, you will never compel them into an honest belief.

It will be objected, however: Is this all that pure reason can accomplish in opening up prospects beyond the limits of experience? Nothing more than two articles of belief? Common sense could have done as much without consulting the philosophers!

I will not praise philosophy here for the benefits that its laborious work of criticism has conferred on human reason, even granting that its merit should finally prove to be only negative, since more will be said on that point in the next section. But I ask: Do you really require that knowledge concerning all people should surpass ordinary understanding and be revealed to you only by philosophers? The very thing you criticize is the best confirmation that our earlier assertions are correct. It reveals something that could not have been foreseen. In matters that concern all people without distinction, Nature cannot be accused of distributing her gifts unequally, and with respect to the essential ends of human nature, the highest philosophy can take us no further than the guidance nature has granted to the humblest understanding.

## Doctrine of Method, Chapter III: The Architectonic of Pure Reason

By *architectonic* I mean the art of constructing systems. Without systematic unity, our knowledge cannot become science. It remains an aggregate rather than a system. Architectonic is therefore the doctrine of what makes our knowledge scientific, and so it necessarily forms part of our theory of method.

Reason cannot allow our knowledge to remain disconnected and haphazard, like a rhapsody stitched together from separate pieces. It requires that the sum of our knowledge form a system, because only then can that knowledge advance the ends of reason. By a *system* I mean the unity of various pieces of knowledge under a single idea. This idea is reason's concept of the form of a whole, insofar as that concept determines a priori both the limits of its content and the place each part is to occupy. The scientific idea therefore contains the end and the form of the whole that corresponds to that end. The unity of the end, to which all the parts relate and through which they are all related to one another, gives unity to the whole system. As a result, the absence of any part can be detected immediately from our knowledge of the rest. This unity also determines the system's limits a priori, excluding all contingent or arbitrary additions. The whole is thus articulated, like an organism (*articulatio*), rather than heaped together (*coacervatio*). It can grow from within, by taking nourishment into itself (*per intussusceptionem*), but not by having things attached to it from outside (*per appositionem*). In this it resembles an animal body, whose growth adds no new limb but makes each existing limb stronger and more capable in its own function, without altering their proportions.

To carry out the idea of a system, we need a *schema*: a content and an arrangement of parts determined a priori by the principle that the system's aim prescribes. A schema that is not drawn up according to an idea, that is, from the standpoint of reason's highest aim, but merely empirically, according to accidental aims and purposes whose number cannot be fixed in advance, can give us no more than *technical* unity. A schema that originates from an idea, in which reason supplies its aims a priori rather than looking for them in experience, is the basis of *architectonic* unity. A science in the proper sense cannot be formed technically, from observing the similarities among different objects and from the purely contingent use we make of our knowledge in concrete cases for all kinds of arbitrary external purposes. It must be constituted on architectonic principles. Its parts must be shown to have an essential affinity and to be derivable from a single supreme and internal end, which is the condition that makes the scientific whole possible. The schema of a science must provide its outline a priori (its *monogramma*, or preliminary sketch), together with the division of the whole into parts in conformity with the idea of the science. It must also distinguish this whole from all others according to definite principles.

No one sets out to construct a science without some idea to serve as its foundation. But as he works it out, he finds that the schema, and even the definition he first gave of the science, rarely corresponds to his idea. That idea lies in our reason like a seed, its parts undeveloped and hidden even from microscopic observation. For this reason, we ought to explain and define the sciences not according to the description their founders give of them, but according to the idea we find grounded in reason itself, which is suggested by the natural unity of the parts already accumulated. It will often be found that the founder of a science, and even his most recent successors, remain attached to a mistaken idea that they cannot make clear to themselves, and so fail to determine the true content of their science, its articulation or systematic unity, and its limits.

Unfortunately, it is only after we have spent a long time collecting materials, guided by an idea that lies undeveloped in the mind rather than by any definite plan of arrangement, and only after we have spent much time and labor arranging those materials technically, that we can see the idea of a science clearly and project a plan of the whole according to architectonic principles, in keeping with the aims of reason. Systems seem to arise in the way certain worms were once thought to arise, by a kind of spontaneous generation (*generatio aequivoca*), as if out of nothing, from the mere confluence of concepts, and to reach completeness only with the passage of time. Yet the schema, or seed, of every system lies in reason. Consequently, each system is organized according to its own idea, and all of them are united as members of one great system of human knowledge. This makes it possible to construct an architectonic of all human knowledge, and given the immense materials already collected or still to be found in the ruins of old systems, the task would not be very difficult at present. Our purpose here is only to sketch the plan of the architectonic of all knowledge arising from pure reason. We begin at the point where the main root of human knowledge divides into two branches, one of which is reason. By reason I mean here the whole higher faculty of knowledge, so that the rational is set in contrast to the empirical.

If I disregard entirely the content of knowledge considered objectively, all knowledge, considered subjectively, is either historical or rational. Historical knowledge is knowledge derived from what is given (*cognitio ex datis*); rational knowledge is knowledge derived from principles (*cognitio ex principiis*). Whatever the original source of a piece of knowledge, it is merely historical for the person who possesses it if he knows only what has been given to him from elsewhere, whether through direct experience or through instruction. Consider someone who has learned a system of philosophy, say the Wolffian system of Christian Wolff. Even if he knows perfectly all its principles, definitions, and arguments, as well as the divisions of the system, his knowledge of it is really no more than historical. He knows only what he has been told, and his judgments are only those he has received from his teachers. Challenge one of his definitions, and he is completely at a loss to supply another. He has formed his mind on someone else's, but the faculty of imitation is not the faculty of production. His knowledge has not been drawn from reason, and although it is rational knowledge considered objectively, subjectively it is merely historical. He has learned this or that philosophy and is no more than a plaster cast of a living man. Knowledge that is rational objectively, that is, knowledge whose source is reason, can be called rational subjectively only when the individual has drawn it himself from the sources of reason, from principles. Only in this way can criticism, or even the rejection of what one has already learned, arise in the mind.

All rational knowledge, in turn, rests either on concepts or on the construction of concepts. The first is called philosophical, the second mathematical. I have already shown the essential difference between these two methods of knowledge in the first chapter. Knowledge may be objectively philosophical and yet subjectively historical, as it is for most scholars and for those who cannot see beyond the limits of their system and remain pupils all their lives. It is remarkable, however, that mathematical knowledge, even when merely committed to memory, also counts subjectively as rational knowledge, so that the distinction drawn in the case of philosophical knowledge does not apply. The reason is that the only way to arrive at mathematical knowledge is through the essential principles of reason, so that it is always certain and beyond dispute. Here reason is employed concretely and yet a priori, in pure and therefore infallible intuition, which excludes every source of illusion and error. Of all the a priori sciences of reason, then, mathematics alone can be learned. Philosophy cannot be learned, except in a historical manner; at most we can learn to philosophize.

Philosophy is the system of all philosophical knowledge. We must take this term in an objective sense if we mean by it the archetype of every attempt at philosophizing and the standard by which every subjective philosophy is to be judged. In this sense, philosophy is merely the idea of a possible science that nowhere exists in concrete form. We try in various ways to approach it, until we have found the right path, a path overgrown by the errors and illusions of the senses, and until the image we have so far tried in vain to shape becomes a perfect copy of the great prototype. Until then, philosophy cannot be learned, for it does not exist. If it does exist, where is it, who possesses it, and how are we to recognize it? We can only learn to philosophize, which means exercising our powers of reasoning in accordance with general principles while keeping the right to investigate the sources of those principles, to test them, and even to reject them.

Until that time, our concept of philosophy is only a *scholastic* concept: the concept of a system of knowledge that we are trying to develop into a science, in which all we currently aim at is the systematic unity of this knowledge, and so its logical completeness for the desired end. But there is also a *cosmic* concept of philosophy (*conceptus cosmicus*), which has always formed the true basis of the term, especially when philosophy was personified and held up to us in the ideal of the philosopher. On this view, philosophy is the science of the relation of all knowledge to the ultimate and essential aims of human reason (*teleologia rationis humanae*, the doctrine of the ends of human reason), and the philosopher is not merely an artist who works with concepts but a lawgiver who legislates for human reason. In this sense of the word, it would be supremely arrogant to claim the title of philosopher and to pretend that we had attained the perfection of a prototype that exists in the idea alone. The mathematician, the natural philosopher, and the logician, however far the first may have advanced in rational knowledge and the other two in philosophical knowledge, are merely artists engaged in arranging and shaping concepts; they cannot be called philosophers. Above them all stands the ideal teacher, who uses them as instruments to advance the essential aims of human reason. Him alone can we call a philosopher, but he exists nowhere. The idea of his legislative authority, however, is present in every human mind, and it alone teaches us what kind of systematic unity philosophy requires in view of the ultimate aims of reason. This idea is therefore a cosmic concept.

By a cosmic concept I mean one in which all people necessarily take an interest. Accordingly, if a science is regarded merely as a means to certain arbitrarily chosen ends, its aim must be determined according to scholastic concepts.

Given the complete systematic unity of reason, there can be only one ultimate end of all the mind's operations. Every other aim is subordinate to it and is nothing more than a means of reaching it. This ultimate end is the destiny of humanity, and the philosophy concerned with it is called moral philosophy. The superior rank of moral philosophy over every other field in which reason operates explains why the ancients always included the idea of the moralist, and gave it special prominence, in their idea of the philosopher. Even today, we call a man a philosopher if he seems to have mastery over himself, however limited his knowledge may be.

The legislation of human reason, which is philosophy, has two objects, nature and freedom. It therefore contains both the laws of nature and the laws of morality, at first in two separate systems, which ultimately merge into a single philosophical system of knowledge. The philosophy of nature concerns what *is*; the philosophy of morals concerns what *ought to be*.

All philosophy, however, is either knowledge from pure reason or rational knowledge from empirical principles. The first is called pure philosophy, the second empirical philosophy.

The philosophy of pure reason is, first, either a propaedeutic, a preparatory inquiry into the powers of reason with respect to all pure a priori knowledge, and is then called critical philosophy; or it is, second, the system of pure reason, a science presenting systematically the whole body of philosophical knowledge, both true and illusory, that arises from pure reason, and is then called metaphysics. The name metaphysics may also be given to the whole system of pure philosophy, critical philosophy included. In that case it covers both the investigation into the sources and possibility of a priori knowledge and the presentation of the a priori knowledge that makes up a system of pure philosophy, while excluding all empirical and mathematical elements.

Metaphysics is divided according to the speculative and the practical use of pure reason, and is accordingly either the metaphysics of nature or the metaphysics of morals. The first contains all the pure rational principles of theoretical knowledge that are based on concepts alone, and therefore excludes mathematics. The second contains the principles that determine all action a priori and make it necessary. Now moral philosophy alone contains a body of laws for governing our actions that are derived entirely from a priori principles. The metaphysics of morals is therefore the only pure moral philosophy, since it rests on no anthropological or other empirical considerations. The metaphysics of speculative reason is what is usually called metaphysics in the narrower sense. But since pure moral philosophy properly belongs to this system of knowledge, we must let it keep the name of metaphysics, although we need not insist on calling it so in the present discussion.

It is of the greatest importance to isolate kinds of knowledge that differ from others in both nature and origin, and to take great care that they are not confused with the knowledge with which they are usually found combined. What the chemist does in analyzing substances, and what the mathematician does in pure mathematics, the philosopher is bound to do to an even greater degree, so that the value of each kind of knowledge, and the part it plays in the mind's operations, can be clearly defined. Ever since human reason acquired the power of thought, or rather of reflection, it has never lacked some kind of metaphysics, yet it has never managed to keep this sphere of thought and knowledge free from the admixture of foreign elements. The idea of such a science is as old as speculation itself, and what mind does not speculate, whether in the manner of the schools or in the popular manner? It must nevertheless be admitted that even professional thinkers have been unable to explain clearly the distinction between the two elements of our knowledge, the one entirely a priori, the other a posteriori. As a result, the proper definition of a distinctive kind of knowledge has never been established, and with it the true idea of a science that has occupied the human mind so long and so deeply. When it was said that "metaphysics is the science of the first principles of human knowledge," this definition marked a difference not in kind but only in degree. These first principles were declared to be more general than others, but no criterion was given for distinguishing them from empirical principles. Some empirical principles are themselves more general, and therefore higher, than others; and since we cannot distinguish what is entirely a priori from what is known to be a posteriori, where are we to draw the line that separates the higher and so-called first principles from the lower, subordinate principles of knowledge? What would we say if someone asked us to be satisfied with dividing the ages of the world into "the earlier centuries" and "those that followed"? We would immediately ask whether the fifth century, or the tenth, belongs to the earlier ones. In the same way, I ask: Does the concept of extension belong to metaphysics? You answer, "Yes." Then what about the concept of body? "Yes." And the concept of a fluid body? Here you stop short, unprepared to concede the point, because if you do, everything will belong to metaphysics. It is evident, then, that the mere degree of subordination, of the particular to the general, cannot fix the boundaries of a science. In the present case, we must expect the concepts of metaphysics to differ from all others both in kind and in origin.

The fundamental idea of metaphysics was obscured from another direction as well, by the resemblance this kind of a priori knowledge bears to mathematics. The two have an a priori origin in common. But in philosophy our knowledge rests on concepts, whereas in mathematics it rests on the construction of concepts, that is, on exhibiting them directly in intuition, as the geometer does when he draws a figure. Here a decided difference between philosophical and mathematical knowledge emerges. People always sensed this difference, but they could never state it clearly, because they lacked insight into the criteria that distinguish the two. And so, because philosophers themselves failed to develop the idea of their own science properly, the work of building that science could proceed neither toward a definite aim nor under trustworthy guidance. For the same reason, philosophers, ignorant of the path they ought to follow and forever disputing one another's claimed discoveries, brought their science into disrepute with the rest of the world, and finally even among themselves.

All pure a priori knowledge, then, forms a distinct unity of its own, by virtue of the particular faculty from which it springs, and "metaphysics" is the name we give to the philosophy that tries to present this knowledge in its systematic unity. The speculative part of metaphysics has claimed that name for itself in particular. We have called it the metaphysics of nature, and it considers everything as it is (not as it ought to be) by means of a priori concepts. It is divided in the following way.

Metaphysics in the narrower sense consists of two parts: transcendental philosophy and the physiology of pure reason. The first presents the system of all the concepts and principles of the understanding and of reason that relate to objects in general, without reference to any particular objects that are actually given; this is ontology. The second takes nature as its subject matter, meaning the sum of given objects, whether they are given to the senses or, if we like, to some other kind of intuition. It is therefore a physiology, in the old sense of a science of nature, although a purely rational one. In this rational treatment of nature, however, reason is used in one of two ways, either physically or hyperphysically, or more precisely, either immanently or transcendently. The immanent use concerns nature insofar as our knowledge of it can be applied in experience, to concrete cases. The transcendent use concerns a connection among the objects of experience that goes beyond all experience. Transcendent physiology, in turn, has either an internal or an external connection with its object, though both go beyond any possible experience. The internal kind is the physiology of nature as a whole, or the transcendental knowledge of the world. The external kind concerns the connection between the whole of nature and a being above nature, and is the transcendental knowledge of God.

Immanent physiology, by contrast, considers nature as the sum of all objects of the senses, and therefore as it is presented to us, though still according to a priori conditions, since only under those conditions can nature be presented to our minds at all. Its objects are of two kinds. The first are the objects of the outer senses, or corporeal nature. The second is the object of the inner sense, the soul, or, according to our fundamental concept of it, thinking nature. The metaphysics of corporeal nature is called physics, but because it may contain only the principles of an a priori knowledge of nature, we must call it rational physics. The metaphysics of thinking nature is called psychology, and for the same reason it must be understood as nothing more than the rational knowledge of the soul.

The whole system of metaphysics therefore consists of four principal parts: first, ontology; second, rational physiology; third, rational cosmology; and fourth, rational theology. The second part, the rational doctrine of nature, can be further divided into rational physics, *physica rationalis*, and rational psychology, *psychologia rationalis*.

By rational physics I do not mean what is usually called general physics, *physica generalis*, which is more mathematics than a philosophy of nature. The metaphysics of nature is entirely different from mathematics. It is not nearly as rich in results, but it is of great importance as a critical test of how the knowledge of the pure understanding is applied to nature. Without its guidance, even mathematicians have adopted certain common notions that are in fact metaphysical, and have unknowingly crowded their theories of nature with hypotheses. The fallacy of these hypotheses becomes evident as soon as the principles of this metaphysics are applied, though without any harm to the use of mathematics in this field of knowledge.

This division is dictated by necessity, by the fundamental idea of a philosophy of pure reason. It is therefore architectonic: it follows from the plan of the whole and accords with the highest aims of reason. It is not merely technical, assembled from similarities that happened to be noticed among the various parts of the science. For this reason the division is also unalterable and has the authority of law. The reader may nonetheless notice a few points in it to which he is inclined to object, and which might weaken his confidence in its truth and legitimacy.

The first objection runs as follows. How can I hope for an a priori knowledge, a metaphysics, of objects insofar as they are given a posteriori, through experience? And how is it possible to know the nature of things according to a priori principles, and so arrive at a rational physiology? The answer is this. We take from experience nothing more than what is needed to present us with an object, in general, of either the outer or the inner sense. For the outer sense, this is done through the bare concept of matter, understood as impenetrable, lifeless extension. For the inner sense, it is done through the concept of a thinking being, given in the inner empirical representation *I think*. Beyond this, we must not use any empirical principles in our metaphysics of these objects, that is, any principles that add to the content of our concepts by drawing on experience, in order to form judgments about those objects.

The second objection concerns empirical psychology. Where shall we place it? It has always been counted as part of metaphysics, and in our own time, after the hope of building an a priori system of knowledge was given up, people have expected important philosophical results from it. My answer is that it belongs beside empirical physics, or physics proper. It must be regarded as part of applied philosophy, whose a priori principles are contained in pure philosophy; pure philosophy is therefore connected with psychology, but must not be confused with it. Empirical psychology must accordingly be banished from the domain of metaphysics, and the very idea of that science already excludes it. Out of deference to the usage of the schools, however, we must allow it a place in metaphysics, but only as an appendix. We do this for practical reasons. Psychology is not yet substantial enough to stand as an independent study, yet it is too important to be excluded altogether or placed somewhere it would have even less affinity than it has with metaphysics. It is a stranger who has long been a guest among us, and we gladly let it stay until it can take up a more fitting residence in a complete system of anthropology, the counterpart to empirical physics.
