Such, then, is the general idea of metaphysics. Because more was expected of it than could fairly be hoped for, and because those pleasant expectations were unfortunately never fulfilled, it fell into general disrepute. Yet our Critique must have fully convinced the reader that, although metaphysics cannot be the foundation of religion, it must always remain one of religion's most important defenses. Human reason naturally follows a dialectical course, drawn toward illusory arguments, and it cannot do without this science. Metaphysics restrains that tendency, and by raising reason to a clear and scientific knowledge of itself, it prevents the devastation that a lawless speculative reason would inevitably cause in morals as well as in religion. Some people judge a science not by its own nature but by the accidental effects it has happened to produce, and they may heap contempt on metaphysics. We may nonetheless be sure that it can never be abandoned entirely, and that we will always return to it, as to a beloved from whom we have been estranged for a time. The questions it deals with concern the highest aims of humanity, and reason must always labor either to reach settled views about them or to tear down the views that others have already established.

Metaphysics, therefore, is philosophy in the truest sense of the word. This holds for the metaphysics of nature and the metaphysics of morals alike, but above all for the critique that serves as the preparatory discipline for every operation of reason. The path metaphysics follows is the path of science, which, once discovered, is never lost and never leads astray. Mathematics, natural science, and the ordinary experience of humankind are highly valuable as means, mostly to incidental ends, but ultimately also to ends that are necessary and essential to human existence. To guide them toward that high goal, however, they need the help of rational knowledge drawn from pure concepts, and this knowledge, whatever we choose to call it, is in truth nothing other than metaphysics.

For the same reason, metaphysics also completes the cultivation of human reason. In this respect it is indispensable, quite apart from whatever influence it exerts as a science. Its subject matter is the elements and highest maxims of reason, which make some sciences possible and underlie the use of all of them. As a purely speculative science, it does more to prevent errors than to extend knowledge, but this does not lessen its value. On the contrary, its supreme office as censor secures for it the highest authority and importance. It exercises this office in order to bring order, harmony, and well-being to the sciences, and to direct their noble and fruitful labors toward the highest possible end, which is the happiness of all humankind.

## Doctrine of Method, Chapter IV: The History of Pure Reason

This title stands here only to mark a division of the system of pure reason that I do not intend to treat at present. I will content myself with a brief glance, from a purely transcendental point of view, that is, from the standpoint of the nature of pure reason, at what philosophers have achieved up to now. They have aimed to erect an edifice of philosophy, but to my eye that edifice lies largely in ruins.

It is remarkable, though naturally it could not have been otherwise, that in the infancy of philosophy the human mind began its speculative efforts with the study of the nature of God and the constitution of a future world, where we would rather have it end. However crude the religious ideas that lingered on from the customs of a less cultivated age, the educated classes were not prevented from devoting themselves to free inquiry into the existence and nature of God. They readily saw that there could be no surer way to please the invisible ruler of the world, and so to attain happiness at least in another world, than to lead a good and honest life in this one. Theology and morals thus became the two chief motives, or rather the two points of attraction, for all abstract inquiry. But it was theology above all that occupied speculative reason, and that later became famous under the name of metaphysics.

I will not at present mark the periods in which the greatest changes in metaphysics took place. I will only sketch, in haste, the different ideas that brought about the most important revolutions in this field of thought. These revolutions took place with respect to three different questions.

The first concerns the object of rational knowledge. Here philosophers can be divided into sensualists and intellectualists, with Epicurus at the head of the first group and Plato at the head of the second. Subtle as this distinction is, it dates from the earliest times and was maintained for a long while. The sensualists held that reality resides in objects of the senses alone and that everything else is mere imagination. The intellectualists held that the senses are the source of illusion and that truth is found in the understanding alone. The sensualists did not deny the concepts of the understanding a certain kind of reality, but for them that reality was merely logical, whereas for the intellectualists it was mystical. The sensualists admitted intellectual concepts but declared that only objects of the senses really exist. The intellectualists maintained that all real objects are intelligible, and they believed that the pure understanding possesses a power of intuition independent of the senses, which in their view served only to confuse the ideas of the understanding.

The second question concerns the origin of the pure knowledge of reason. One school maintains that such knowledge is derived entirely from experience; another, that it originates in reason alone. Aristotle may be regarded as the head of the empiricists and Plato as the head of the noologists, those who trace knowledge to the intellect. In modern times, Locke has followed Aristotle and Leibniz has followed Plato, though Leibniz cannot be said to have copied Plato's mysticism, and neither of them has been able to bring the question to a settled conclusion. Epicurus, for his part, was far more consistent in his sensualist system than Aristotle and Locke, for he always confined his conclusions to the sphere of experience. Locke in particular, after deriving all the concepts and principles of the mind from experience, goes so far in using them as to claim that we can prove the existence of God and the immortality of the soul, both of which lie beyond the limits of possible experience, with the same demonstrative force as any proposition in mathematics.

The third question concerns method, and method is procedure according to principles. The methods now in use in this field of inquiry can be divided into the naturalistic and the scientific. The naturalist of pure reason adopts as his principle that ordinary reason, without the help of science, which he calls sound reason or common sense, can answer the most important questions of metaphysics more satisfactorily than speculation can. He must therefore maintain that we can determine the size and distance of the moon more reliably with the naked eye than by mathematical reasoning. But this system is nothing but misology, a hatred of reason, raised to the level of a principle. And the most absurd part of the doctrine is that the neglect of every scientific means is paraded as a special method for extending our knowledge. Those who are naturalists simply because they know no better are certainly not to blame. They follow common sense without parading their ignorance as a method that will teach us the wonderful secret of finding the truth that, as Democritus said, lies at the bottom of a well. Their motto is the line from the satirist Persius: *Quod sapio satis est mihi, non ego curo / Esse quod Arcesilas aerumnosique Solones*, "What I know is enough for me; I have no wish to be what Arcesilaus was, or those careworn Solons." Under this motto they may lead a pleasant and praiseworthy life, without troubling themselves about science or troubling science with themselves.

Those who wish to follow a scientific method now have a choice between the dogmatic method and the skeptical, though in either case they are bound never to abandon systematic procedure. If I name the celebrated Wolff as the representative of the first, and David Hume as the representative of the second, I may, in keeping with my present purpose, leave all others unnamed. The critical path alone remains open. If my reader has been kind and patient enough to accompany me along this hitherto untraveled route, he can now judge for himself whether, if he and others will lend their efforts to turning this narrow footpath into a highway of thought, what many centuries have failed to accomplish might be achieved before the close of the present one: namely, to bring Reason to complete satisfaction concerning the questions that have always occupied her powers and engaged her ardent desire for knowledge, though never with lasting results.
